15828-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, sold at five cents in New York. The copy held here offers books as premiums to any subscriber who secures one new name, including On Honour's Roll, tales of heroes in the nineteenth century. News, science, and serial stories fill the rest in plain words for young readers. The paper kept children abreast of the world week by week.

Hero tales, news notes, and nature items share the pages in the paper's usual brisk mix. Editors explain distant events and new inventions without talking down. A serial thread keeps readers coming back. Seen now, the issue shows an 1897 childhood of books, premiums, and a weekly window on a wide world.
5940-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-2:
Barcelona alone fills this Don Quixote installment, chapter sixty-one, on what happened to Quixote entering the city, with matters more true than ingenious. Quixote passed three days and three nights with Roque, and had he passed three hundred years he would have found enough to observe and wonder at in his host's world. From Roque's company, the knight proceeds into Barcelona itself.

Readers enter the great city with a famous knight, where bandits, hosts, and citizens treat him as a living legend. The single chapter favors observation over battle, letting Barcelona's streets and people become the adventure. It suits readers following volume two toward its climax, since the city prepares the enchanted head, the galleys, and the final defeat.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: Grover Cleveland opens this eighth volume part in his own inaugural voice. He pledges unreserved devotion to the welfare of the people who called him to service. The volume prints his messages and papers, including his thoughts on foreign relations and public questions. Cleveland's formal words stand here as the record of his presidency.
andersen-little-mermaid-1837:
Hans Christian Andersen published 'The Little Mermaid' in 1837, in his early set of tales told for children. The story, in a classic English rendering from his collected Fairy Tales, is the source of the modern mermaid tale. It is far sadder than the films that borrowed it.

The youngest daughter of the Sea King longs for the world above the waves and for a human soul. She trades her voice to a sea witch for legs, and wins the prince's love but not his hand. Refusing to kill him to save herself, she dissolves into foam, and is lifted toward a new hope. Andersen's tale turns on love, pain, and the hunger for an immortal soul.
arxiv-2412-01737:
Gertian Roose and Erez Zohar work on a physics problem in their twenty twenty-four paper. The problem is how to write down states of a lattice gauge theory, a grid-based model of forces and matter. Their tool is a class of states built from networks, known as PEPS.

Past work used a single such state with a neat math form, which made sums easy to compute. Roose and Zohar ask what happens with a mix of a few such states. They show the sums stay within reach when the mix is small. That case fits bound states above a strong-force ground state well. They also give an exact form for the ground state itself in this frame.
arxiv-2412-03237:
Priyanka Mishra and Carmine Autieri compute, from first principles, the electronic and magnetic character of the beta phase of iron oxide. The common alpha phase is an altermagnet and the gamma phase a ferrimagnet. The cubic beta phase, with all iron-iron couplings expected antiferromagnetic, risks magnetic frustration. That makes its true ground state hard to guess. Writing in twenty twenty-four, they screen candidate phases, including ferrimagnets, altermagnets, and Kramers antiferromagnets, and track the energy gap as electron correlations strengthen.

The ground state comes out a Kramers antiferromagnet, with a d-wave altermagnetic phase close behind. At realistic correlation strength the material is a charge-transfer insulator with an indirect gap. Same-kind neighbors align antiferromagnetically while the two iron sublattices vary, and first-neighbor effects cancel in the estimated ordering temperature, leaving it lower than in sibling phases. Nanoparticle and alloy studies can build on the result.
arxiv-2412-10537:
Jinnan Guo, Kapil Vaswani, Andrew Paverd, and Peter Pietzuch build a federated learning system whose training claims can actually be verified. In federated learning, data providers train a shared model without pooling their data. A cheating provider could skip steps or skip data cleaning, and nobody would know.

Earlier systems leaned on trusted execution environments, whose secrecy has repeatedly fallen to side-channel attacks. VerifiableFL instead uses exclaves, integrity-only environments with no software-managed secrets to leak. These attest each data transformation during training with fine-grained runtime proofs. Claims about the data, its sanitization, and the algorithm can then be checked without trusting the providers.
arxiv-2412-12337:
Emil Albrychiewicz, Andrés Franco Valiente, and Vi Hong wrote this physics paper in two thousand twenty-four. It studies open string solutions in a recent model called the tropological sigma model, which comes from a tropical limit of a known class of topological models.

With set boundary conditions, the quantized solutions give rise to a new kind of object the authors name tropical branes. These are a non-relativistic counterpart of the branes known in string theory. The paper gives a first worldsheet account of these objects. The authors say the work lays the base for a later paper on how tropical branes fit into brane quantization.
arxiv-2412-13337:
Aldo Pareja and Nikhil Shivakumar Nayak lead a large team on this guide from two thousand twenty-four. It lays out how to fine-tune small language models well, so lone builders and small shops can match what big labs do.

The study runs many set-ups across four open models in the small size range, on instruction data from many fields. Some stock tips fail: phased training from a known recipe adds cost with no gain, while stacked training is plainer and cheaper. Big batches with low learning rates win. Early training marks, such as gradient size and loss, foretell the end score well, so bad runs can be cut early.
arxiv-2412-17137:
Michael Hansen, Michael Mandl, Erhard Seiler, and Dénes Sexty study a flaw in a method that fakes systems whose weight is a complex count. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four.

The method, complex Langevin, is a bid to beat the sign ill that blocks many such fakes. It moves the system's parts into the complex plane and adds a fake time. Its worst flaw is wrong convergence: the run settles, yet on a wrong answer. A well-set kernel can fix the known tests for rightness. But the team shows a next flaw can still spoil the result: loops in the path of the run, called integration cycles. Tests with no edge terms bear this out.
arxiv-2501-00937:
Anna Zamojska-Dzienio brought algebra to a classic shapes problem in a 2025 note. Any point inside a convex shape can be written as a weighted average of the shape's corners, and barycentric coordinates give those weights. Such partitions of unity, groups of weight functions that sum to one. Are workhorses in interpolation, numerics, and computer graphics, where they are usually studied geometrically.

Zamojska-Dzienio instead uses barycentric algebras, symbol-based forms built to capture averaging itself. She matches subclasses of partitions of unity, including one family arising from a tautological map introduced by Guessab in the coordinate setting. The symbol-based view clarifies how the classes relate and where they differ. It may unify tricks that graphics and analysis developed separately.
arxiv-2501-01037:
Hao and co-authors launch MSC-Bench, a test bank for foul sense in self-drive cars. Twin-sense tools join cam and LiDAR feeds for road sight. They drive 3D finds and high-grade map builds for the cars. Those tools lean on full feeds from both sense types. Foul or lost feeds can break them and risk lives. No bank yet graded how such tools bear foul feeds in full.

MSC-Bench fills that gap as the first full bank of its kind. It holds 16 mixes of foul types for cam and LiDAR feeds. Mixes hit one feed or both feeds at one time. Six find tools and four map tools took the test runs. Scores fell hard in bad sky states and feed loss runs. Those falls flag grave safe gaps in live road use.
arxiv-2501-04537:
Antonio Beltrán and Changguo Shao wrote this math note in two thousand twenty-five. It describes the shape of non-solvable finite groups whose maximal subgroups are all either supersolvable or of prime or prime-squared index.

Two classic results frame the note. Doerk showed that groups whose maximal subgroups are all supersolvable must be solvable. Hall showed the same when all maximal subgroups have prime or squared prime index. The mixed case leaves room for non-solvable groups, and this note pins down how those groups are built. The paper is a short piece of finite group theory that closes a gap between the two classics.
arxiv-2501-05937:
Kevissen Sellapillay, Laurent Raymond, and Alberto Verga watched entanglement shift phases in a 2025 quantum study. Their setup is a ladder of spins: one rail is a cluster chain with a protected entangled pattern, and the other rail is a set of free spins acting as surroundings. A swap gate links the rails step by step, and a three-spin rule drives the chain in discrete time.

With weak linking, the chain clings to its starting cluster pattern. Stronger linking pushes it toward random states, which range from nearly pure to fully mixed depending on how many surrounding spins join in. Entanglement can thus be tuned across clear regimes by coupling strength alone.
arxiv-2501-06537:
Antonio Avilés and three co-authors settle a question in pure math in twenty twenty-five. They work with Banach spaces, a central class of spaces in analysis. The question concerns sequences and elements that are orthogonal in a special sense marked by the letter L. A prior paper had asked whether one can exist without the other.

The authors prove the answer cannot be settled from ZFC alone. ZFC is the standard foundation of mathematics. So the existence of such a space is independent of those axioms. Along the way, they introduce Q-measures, a broader form of a known ultrafilter idea. They also extend older theorems by Miller and Bartoszynski to this new setting.
arxiv-2501-10337:
Yi-Ping Chen, Ying-Kuan Tsai, Vispi Karkaria, and Wei Chen design a controller, in a 2025 preprint, for digital twins that must act fast under uncertainty. A digital twin mirrors a real system and updates as data arrives. Controllers for twins need forecasts of what the system will do next. They also need honest error ranges on those forecasts. Doing both in real time is a known pain point.

Their setup forecasts many steps ahead in one shot, using a model called TiDE. That lets the controller plan over a full horizon at once. Quantile learning gives the forecast a spread of likely outcomes, not just one line. The controller then plans against that spread, keeping a safety buffer for shocks. In a case study on metal 3D printing, the method beat older robust controllers. It kept parts inside limits more often while staying less cautious.
arxiv-2501-16337:
Ivan Knunyants and five co-authors save energy in language models in twenty twenty-five. Deploying large models on edge devices is limited by energy and latency. Recurrent language models avoid the quadratic cost of self-attention. That makes them a candidate for neuromorphic processors, which compute with sparse, brain-like activity.

The team proposes a low-cost, training-free algorithm to sparsify activations. It exploits structure already present in recurrent models. Sparser activations mean less energy burned on neuromorphic hardware. The method also generalizes to other architectures. Tests on the OPT transformer model reached comparable sparsity and efficiency gains. Readers get a practical trick for running language models where power is scarce.
arxiv-2502-06637:
The DUNE Collaboration reports a deep learning method to find where a neutrino interacts inside a detector. Their twenty twenty-five paper serves the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, a vast project to study neutrinos, ghost-like particles that barely interact. Pinpointing the interaction vertex is a first step to reading each event.

The team uses Pandora, a reconstruction toolkit, boosted with deep learning. The learned method locates the vertex in the detector's data, which records the trails of particles born in the collision. Better vertex finding sharpens all later steps, from energy estimates to the search for rare event types. The paper lays out the method and its performance for the collaboration.
arxiv-2502-13837:
Lefeuvre and nine co-authors probe how charge flows in crystals of Bi4Br4, a candidate second-order topological insulator. Such materials host safe one-dimensional states along their hinges, not across whole faces. The team hunted for those states in single crystals a few micrometers in size.

Fields from magnets and gate voltage shifts shaped the quantum interference in the samples. Aharonov-Bohm oscillations showed ballistic one-dimensional channels a few micrometers long, which kept phase coherence across that span. Cuts through samples, seen under a microscope, confirmed a disordered contact zone that makes the interference possible. Weak antilocalization and conductance fluctuations added more support, with a strong sense of direction. Put as one, the results pin down the hinge modes of this material in detail.
arxiv-2502-17737:
Arne Bang Huseby, writing solo, extends a classic reliability tool from on-off systems to many-level ones. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Domination theory grades system structures through a signed counting function. Binary monotone systems, where parts are simply up or down, are well understood. Matroid theory supplies many of their properties. Real systems often run at several levels, though.

Huseby defines a signed domination function for multistate systems. Möbius inversion ties it to the multistate structure function. Computing the new function reduces to a binary companion problem. That reduction imports binary results wholesale. Reliability engineers gain theory for graded systems like power or flow networks. Old theorems earn a second life.
arxiv-2502-17937:
Nashed rebuilds the changed pull view known as f(Q) pull with traits based on red shift. In place of a guess at the view's form straight off, the way starts from traits of how fast the world slows. It also starts from traits of the state rule for strength in work from past texts. How the trait for thick stuff acts at far range cuts the space of picks that can work more.

Two slow down models and one state rule model are worked through. One test model shows that small shifts make world pasts that can live. In those worlds the dark strength part turns live and comes in full from changed pull. It does not come from a fixed term for the world. The worlds that come out are not the same in kind as the base model. Yet they match it in counts.
arxiv-2502-20237:
Gianluca Bencomo and four co-authors ask what gives a neural network its built-in leanings, called inductive bias. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that bias shapes what a network can learn, beyond the data itself. Most talk centers on the network's architecture, its shape and wiring.

The team tests a second source: the starting weights. Using meta-learning, they train starting weights fit for set tasks, across four common architectures and three tasks. They trained hundreds of models in all. Good starting weights shrank or erased the gaps between architectures. Yet all models still failed on tasks far from their training, a sign that stronger biases are needed for broad skill.
arxiv-2503-02037:
Lucas Happ and Pascal Naidon wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It shows how a short-lived three-body state can be tuned into one that never decays, a bound state in the continuum.

Three-body resonances are common in few-body physics, yet they always leak away in finite time. In a two-channel frame the authors trace how the leak works. A smooth turn of the system knobs then stretches the life without end. Two cases back the claim: a mass-skewed trio in one dimension, and three like bosons in three, the Efimov case. For the bosons one knob is a magnetic field, a dial cold-atom labs turn at will. The trick may suit many shaky few-body systems.
arxiv-2503-03337:
Louis Gaillard unifies the size estimates behind a family of computer algebra algorithms in a 2025 math study. Many algorithms on differential equations with polynomial coefficients boil down to finding a linear relation among iterates of one simple operator, the pseudo-linear map. Examples include least common multiples and symmetric products of operators, each with its own historical degree bound derived through matrix determinant estimates.

Gaillard identifies the common scheme and derives precise degree bounds from that shared structure. Tighter, unified bounds tell implementers in advance how large outputs can grow, which decides whether a computation is feasible at all.
arxiv-2503-06237:
Yifan Chang leads a team fixing a blind spot in camera-only lane detection for self-driving cars. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Sparse-point methods mark lanes with few points to save compute. The authors show this shorthand can misplace a lane badly. Errors can reach twenty meters, a clear safety hazard. The flaw sits in the representation itself, not the networks.

Their patching strategy covers the full lane structure. An added EndPoint head predicts a patching distance at each lane end. Existing models can adopt the strategy through that head. Complex scenes with tricky geometry are the target. Accuracy rises where older sparse methods clipped lanes short. The work rethinks both how lanes are written and how models read them.
arxiv-2503-07937:
Siyuan Wang, James Foulds, Md Osman Gani, and Shimei Pan wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on checking scientific claims with language models. A claim should be judged by evidence for and against it, not by how confident a model sounds.

Their system, CIBER, grows out of retrieval-augmented generation, where a model first fetches documents, then answers. CIBER probes the model with varied questions and watches how steady its answers stay. Steady answers point to documents that truly back or refute the claim. The method never peeks inside the model, so it works on closed systems too, and it needs no labeled training data. Tests across models of unlike skill showed CIBER beating standard retrieval setups. The authors offer it as a tool for science fact-checking at scale.
arxiv-2503-08737:
In Cho and three co-authors compress 3D shapes for diffusion models in twenty twenty-five. Efficient 3D diffusion needs a compact latent space, usually built by a variational autoencoder. Their encoder, COD-VAE, squeezes a shape into just sixty-four latent vectors. Quality is meant to survive that squeeze.

A two-stage autoencoder scheme drives the compression. The encoder progressively condenses point clouds through intermediate patches. The decoder rebuilds dense triplanes from the latent vectors rather than decoding neural fields directly. That swap cuts heavy computation. Uncertainty-guided token pruning skips work in simple regions, saving more. Experiments showed sixteenfold compression against the baseline while maintaining quality. Readers get 3D generation that fits in a far smaller latent space.
arxiv-2503-10337:
Vivek Chari, Guanghui Qin, and Benjamin Van Durme wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It presents KV-Distill, a way to squeeze the long memory cache of a language model into a far shorter form with near no loss.

Long contexts help many tasks, but self-attention cost grows with the square of length, and the cache eats GPU memory. KV-Distill trains a light adapter that distills a span of cache into a short stand-in, with no tie to the query. A teacher and student pairing, matched by a divergence loss, keeps the outputs true. It beats rival squeezers on hard extraction tasks and can shrink domain text almost to a hundredth at fine-tune time.
arxiv-2503-12237:
Luis Arenas-Carmona and Marco Godoy study quotient graphs tied to arithmetic orders in a twenty twenty-five paper. Their objects are Eichler orders, a class of orders in quaternion algebras, and the Bruhat-Tits tree, a vast graph that codes the local structure at one prime place.

The question is how much of the quotient graph at one place can be computed from the same quotient at a distinct place. They show the computation works, apart from a small set of vertices that depends on the known place but not the unknown one. They also give geometric conditions that clear the exception. The work extends earlier formulas for maximal orders over the projective line.
arxiv-2503-13837:
Pin-Jie Lin, Ernie Chang, Yangyang Shi, and Vikas Chandra examine how machine translation models choose their working vocabulary during training. Standard byte-pair vocabularies are fixed before training begins, using statistics alone. The authors noticed that trained models naturally drift toward a smaller, distinct subset of tokens.

Their method, self-vocabularizing training, repeats that drift on purpose. Each round, the model labels training pairs with its own predictions, and a new vocabulary is drawn from what it actually uses. Retraining on the leaner set improved translation scores by up to about one and a half BLEU points. Deeper models used more distinct tokens yet needed smaller vocabularies overall.
arxiv-2503-16337:
Qiankun Shi, Jie Peng, Kun Yuan, Xiao Wang, and Qing Ling wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sets hard limits for training across many machines when some of them may be rogue, a setting called Byzantine-robust distributed optimization.

When the machines hold unlike data, the total error splits into a part from the rogue nodes that never fades and a part that shrinks with work. The authors bound both parts from below, and bound the least number of gradient calls needed to shrink the second part. Past methods sat well above these bounds. By joining acceleration with variance reduction tricks, the team builds methods that meet the bounds, up to small log factors. So the bounds are tight.
arxiv-2503-17337:
Darius Erös, Michael Kunzinger, Argam Ohanyan, and Alessio Vardabasso wrote this math paper in two thousand twenty-five. It sets out a new way to bound sectional curvature for surfaces whose metric is rough, not smooth.

Sectional curvature bounds sit at the heart of the study of curved spaces, both smooth and in the broader Alexandrov sense. The authors base their bound on a spread-out form of the classic curvature formula, fit for metrics of Geroch-Traschen class. Their main result shows that for once-smooth metrics the new bound matches the old triangle-based one. A weaker match holds for metrics that are merely Lipschitz. The work bridges smooth and rough geometry.
arxiv-2503-20437:
Nick Dewaele wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It asks which variables of a numeric problem carry the blame when the problem is ill-conditioned, so small input shifts cause big output swings.

Many problems can be cast as solving a set of equations for part of the variables, while the rest stay free. Dewaele defines a condition number for solving for one chosen part alone, and gives firm formulas for it. That gauge shows which parts are the worst conditioned. It also explains the condition of the whole solve, even when the answer is not unique. A tensor breakdown case shows the ideas at work.
arxiv-2503-20737:
Jeffery Painter, Francois Haguinet, Gregory Powell, and Andrew Bate test ways to group medical terms for drug safety work. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses MedDRA terms, the standard labels for side effects and conditions in drug reports. Grouping like terms helps analysts spot safety signals early.

The team trials six measures of semantic similarity drawn from a medical ontology, the UMLS. Some measures walk the paths of the ontology, while others weigh how much information each term carries. In tests against expert review, the information-based measures grouped terms best. A fast software framework, with Java, Python, and R links, lets the checks run at large scale.
arxiv-2503-23037:
Aske Plaat and five co-authors map the fast growth of work on agentic large language models. They set such tools by three skills: to think, to act, and to meet with more tools. The map sorts past work through those three lines. It draws a plan for new work from the trends it finds.

Work on thought deals with self checks and fetch for more good picks. Work on acts deals with tool use, bots, and help for users. Work on meets deals with more than one bot at joint tasks and with mock meets to study how group acts start. The team stresses gains that cross lines. Fetch lets tool use work, and self checks lift joint work. Uses are care calls, move of goods, and read of funds. They flag safe use, blame, and guard as open tasks when bots act in the real world.
arxiv-2504-03437:
Alfio Bonanno, Friederike Ihssen, and Jan Pawlowski compute the tunneling behavior of the anharmonic oscillator with a physics-informed renormalization group method. Tunneling lets a quantum particle slip through a barrier, and in the weakly coupled case the effect comes from instantons, brief imaginary-time events that ordinary perturbation theory cannot see. The energy gap between the two lowest states decays exponentially because of them. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team shows this physics is already captured at the first order of their flow approximation, provided the expansion is organized around the ground state. The numerics use a precise Galerkin scheme.

Their computed decay constant lands within about one percent of the known analytic value. The authors present this as strong evidence that physics-informed flows can capture fully non-perturbative effects even in simple truncations, a promising sign for harder quantum field problems.
arxiv-2504-03537:
Bernini-Peron and ten co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on the winds of B hypergiant stars. These bright, heavy stars sit near blue supergiants in their traits. Some flare as luminous blue variables. Their spectra mix dark and bright lines in ways that hint at odd winds. What drives those winds was not clear.

The team ran the first models that tie the air flow and the light flow in one loop for this class. A bright star of the class served as the test case, and the model matched its main lines. Mass loss ran higher than for like supergiants, yet the wind stayed thin. Iron in a set charge state drove the flow. Low clumping with an early onset fit best.
arxiv-2504-04637:
Stanislav Semenov rethinks the continuum through layers of definability, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The continuum hypothesis asks whether any set of reals sits strictly between the countable and the full continuum. Semenov proposes that the question rests on a mistaken picture of real numbers.

In his framework, a real number is an object expressible at some level of a formal hierarchy. These layered entities he calls fractal numbers. Irrationality becomes relative, depending on how deep the definition must go. Between countable and continuum lies not one jump but a stratified sequence of stages. Each stage is countable yet irreducibly approximates the continuum. The real line appears as an evolving architecture rather than a finished totality.
arxiv-2504-05837:
Manuel Friedrich, Leonard Kreutz, and Konstantinos Zemas rigorously derive a plate theory for thin elastic plates containing voids, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Their starting point is a three-dimensional model. It combines elastic bulk energy with interfacial energy that penalizes curvature in a Willmore-type way. The goal is an effective two-dimensional description.

The limiting model pairs classical elastic bending energy with surface terms. Those terms record that voids can survive the thin limit. They also allow the limiting plate to break into several pieces or to fold. The derivation builds on the authors' earlier work on brittle rods with voids. It generalizes earlier results by allowing general void geometries. Recovery sequences are constructed for every admissible limiting configuration.
arxiv-2504-06737:
Teo Gil Moreno de Mora Sardà proves a result in geometry that links large positive curvature to thin sheets found inside a space. The space is a complete Riemannian manifold whose homology in codimension one is not trivial. The curvature at play is macroscopic scalar curvature, a coarse form fit for shape at a large scale.

When that curvature is positive and large enough, the space must hold a sheet that is not nullhomologous and has small Urysohn width in codimension two. The result is much like a known theorem on spheres in three-manifolds with positive scalar curvature. The proof takes Guth's macroscopic form of the Schoen-Yau descent argument and adapts it. Such descent steps pass control of curvature down to slices with fewer dimensions.
arxiv-2504-08837:
Wang and co-authors train vision-language models to slow down and rethink, using reinforcement learning alone. Text models that reflect openly have leapt ahead on math and science tests. Their multimodal cousins, though, still match fast models on visual math benchmarks. The team adapts the GRPO training method for vision models. A trick called Selective Sample Replay fixes a fading-signal problem in training. Early runs gained strong scores with the fix.

Yet the trained models showed little true self-checking. They rarely paused to verify or revise an answer. That gap between score and habit is the paper's focus. The authors push training rewards toward genuine reflection, not just right answers.
arxiv-2504-18137:
Yimeng Sun, Jiacheng Xing, Li-Hua Shao, and Jianxiang Wang analyze topological vibrations in grid-like frames, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Such frames, built from rigidly jointed beams, are classics of structural mechanics. Their topological behavior, where vibrations localize at edges and corners, was recognized only recently.

In two-dimensional frames the topological states can overlap in frequency with ordinary bulk modes. That overlap makes the interesting modes hard to identify. The authors derive exact formulas for the frequencies of corner, edge, and bulk states. Kagome and square frames are both treated. They also give criteria for when each state exists and where it sits in the spectrum. The corner states proved robust under perturbations, which matters for practical vibration control.
arxiv-2504-19537:
Ruben Becker and six co-authors set out a new class tied to the Burrows-Wheeler transform, a key tool in compression and indexing. A Wheeler language is a regular language that a type of machine can accept. But the old class rests on one fixed order of the letters. The new class must hold for all orders.

The team place this class next to known groups. It holds all of the strictly locally testable group, and more. Yet it is not closed when you swap in the strings left out. If the left-out set is in the class too, the language is a definite or reverse definite kind. A test for a machine runs in time that grows with the square of the size. The team show this bound is the best one can do, short of a break with a claim experts take as true.
arxiv-2504-20437:
DiJia Su, Andrew Gu, and colleagues scale a memory-saving training method for large language models in a 2025 study. Training giants strains memory, and projecting gradients into a low-rank space slashes that cost because gradients naturally carry such structure. Follow-up work added quantization and tensor tricks, but costs remain, notably the repeated decompositions needed to find the projection.

The second-generation system tackles those overheads for pre-training at large scale. Keeping quality while cutting memory decides whether smaller labs can train serious models at all. The study reports progress on the practical bottlenecks that appear when the method meets industrial batch sizes and hardware.
arxiv-2504-20737:
Philippe Anjolras proves a result about the Euler equations of fluid flow in a solo twenty twenty-five paper. These equations govern an ideal fluid that cannot be compressed. Their weak solutions, rough flows that solve the equations in a loose sense, can be wild and many for the same start.

Anjolras shows the set of all such weak solutions is path-connected. Any two can be joined by a steady path of solutions, with a stated degree of smoothness along the way. The proof uses convex integration, a method from De Lellis and Szekelyhidi, widened from balls to any convex compact set. The result maps the shape of the solution set itself.
arxiv-2504-20837:
Julien Khlaut and six co-authors present RadSAM, in a 2025 preprint, a way to outline organs in 3D scans while prompting only once. Outlining anatomy in CT and MR images is slow, skilled work where mask accuracy matters. The Segment Anything Model made outlining interactive, but it was trained on ordinary photos and works slice by slice. A 3D organ could need dozens of prompts, and editing tools were thin. RadSAM trains a 2D model that also accepts a rough prior mask as a prompt, alongside boxes and points.

At run time, one prompt starts an iterative pass that rebuilds the 3D mask slice by slice. The authors add a benchmark for single-prompt 3D outlining in CT. On an abdominal organ dataset, RadSAM beat leading rivals. It also carried to new scan types and supports editing afterward.
arxiv-2504-21637:
Paolo Piersanti wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It puts Koiter's model for thin elastic shells on firm ground when the shell meets a soft contact rule inside its span.

Such shells are widely used, yet the simple model needs proof that it truly fits the full three-dimensional laws. The first gain here is a new density result for closed convex sets in Lebesgue spaces, covering cases past work missed. With that in hand, the model's use is shown to be sound. The paper also proves the shell's bend gains higher smoothness across the whole domain. A side trick gives a sound trace for the cross-wise part of the shift, whose trace was not even defined before.
arxiv-2504-21837:
Zhixin Lu and colleagues describe a simulation code for the turbulent plasma inside tokamak fusion reactors, built around several unusual design choices. The code advances charged particles under the gyrokinetic equations, including electromagnetic effects, several particle species, and the shear Alfven waves that energetic particles excite. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the authors highlight its object-oriented structure, a filter-free treatment, and a high-order finite element method whose pieces follow the magnetic field. A mixed-variable pullback scheme enables the electromagnetic physics, and parallel work is shared by particle splitting and whole-domain cloning across machines.

Demonstrations cover three instability types: an energetic-particle-driven Alfven mode, the ion temperature gradient mode, and the kinetic ballooning mode. Both simplified and experimentally reconstructed equilibria from three European tokamaks ran well. A successor code for edge physics is planned on the same numerical base.
arxiv-2505-01037:
Zihan Zhou, Muhammad Qasim Elahi, and Murat Kocaoglu study how to learn causal graphs from experiments. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with hard interventions, where a variable is forced to a set value. Data from many such experiments, plus plain observation, can reveal which arrows in a graph are real.

The team derives graph rules tied to Pearl's do-calculus, the formal logic of interventions. Each graph is matched to the set of experimental distributions it can produce. They then define when two graphs with hidden variables are equivalent under interventions, and give a picture that tells them apart. A learning algorithm with new orientation rules is proved sound.
arxiv-2505-02237:
Houri and Rochus compare two ways to drive tiny piezoelectric actuators used in micro devices. One drives the device directly; the other excites it through a parameter change. Such devices often behave as nonlinear Duffing systems. The team models the parametric regime with a single-mode view. They search for zones where parametric drive wins, which they call parametric advantage. Math, bench tests, and simulations all check the claim.

Once pump and signal voltages both count toward the budget, the advantage vanishes. No setting kept a true edge under full accounting. The team distills scaling rules from the result. Those rules help designers pick the right drive regime from the start.
arxiv-2505-05637:
Mtiri Foued proves nonexistence results for stable solutions of a weighted system of partial differential equations involving the Grushin operator. The system couples two positive functions through negative power terms with a spatial weight. Liouville-type theorems of this kind rule out well-behaved solutions under stated conditions.

The proof gives an explicit dimension bound, expressed through the largest root of a certain quartic equation in the exponents. Below that bound, no stable solution exists. The author notes the result improves earlier work on the same system. It also covers the single weighted equation with a negative exponent as a special case.
arxiv-2505-09237:
Paul Jolissaint describes the Haagerup property, a weak amenability-like condition, in terms of states on operator algebras. The paper gives two such descriptions. One covers locally compact, second countable groups. The other covers finite von Neumann algebras. Both are stated through approximation. Set non-ergodic invariant states are approached by mixing ones.

For groups, the steps concern actions on unital C-star algebras. For tracial von Neumann algebras, they concern pairs of algebras and mixing binormal states. To restate the Haagerup property this way links it to ergodic language of invariance and mixing. Such forms matter since the property sits where group theory, operator algebras, and ergodic theory meet. A states-based test can be easier to check, or to move between group and algebra settings.
arxiv-2505-11437:
Plüss and Gleiser study how connection density shapes an adaptive network of chaotic units. The units rewire their links based on their own states and local coherence. By sweeping density, the authors map distinct dynamic regimes and structural shifts.

Sparse networks tend to break into desynchronized clusters with weak global order. Dense networks settle into synchronized states that still keep modular splits. High density brings both local clustering and global synchrony at once. Inspired by neural systems, the model shows how simple local rules yield complex collective behavior. Spontaneous modularity and segregation emerge without any central control.
arxiv-2505-13337:
Babak Badnava, Jacob Chakareski, and Morteza Hashemi tackle 360-degree video for virtual reality in a twenty twenty-five paper. Many users watch at once over fast millimeter-wave links, and an edge server must split both bandwidth and computing among them. The aim is high quality with few stalls or jumps.

The team frames the task as a quality problem with linked choices across users and tasks. They solve it with deep reinforcement learning that learns from live stats, like speed and decode time, with no prior map of the network. Two added variants use cascades of neural networks to catch how tasks depend on each other. On real network traces, the best variant cut stalls a lot and raised image quality.
arxiv-2505-14337:
Seung Hun Lee, Wonse Jo, Lionel Robert, and Dawn Tilbury wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It teaches ground robots to foresee the dead ends, called local minima, that trap them in rough outdoor ground.

A robot with only a local view can roll into a pocket with no way onward. The method uses dynamic Bayesian filtering on the blocks it sees and the far goal, to gauge the odds of a trap ahead. With that warning, the robot can call for human help or plot a new path before it wedges. The work aims to make field robots less prone to stalls that waste a run.
arxiv-2505-14637:
Ze-Fang Jiang and four co-authors use computer models to study how flow splits left and right when heavy atomic nuclei crash at near light speed. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

The crash makes a hot blob of matter that flows as a fluid. The team joins a start-state model with a fluid model in three spatial dims plus time. They find the left-right split of oval flow rests most on odd flow parts and on the oval flow itself. A scale for the push of the parts sets the blob's tilt and shapes how the split shifts with speed along the beam. Their results add new bounds on what goes on at the small scale.
arxiv-2505-14937:
Mateo Neira, Valentina Marin, and Elsa Arcaute set out a frame to gauge split of folk by place at more than one scale at once. Such split looks not the same at town, zone, and land tiers. Work at one scale can miss how the tiers play on each. Their way joins facts from chance rules with flow through nets. It stresses how links in a zone meet how folk spread out.

A broad split gauge flags tracts that join grave split with low links. It marks them for acts aimed at them. Ecuador is the case work. It shows trends that shift through scales. The team says plans that heed scale need proof at more than one scale. The frame is set out as a step in ways to work on town gaps for all.
arxiv-2505-17537:
Shiyu Ni, Keping Bi, Jiafeng Guo, and Xueqi Cheng investigate why large language models answer wrongly with high confidence in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their lens is knowledge popularity, measured on factual questions built from Wikidata triplets. They track the popularity of the question entity, the popularity of the answer, and how often the two co-occur. Two consistent patterns emerged from the analysis.

First, hallucinated answers are not random: they tend to be more popular, or more strongly associated with the question, than the correct answers. Second, confidence tracks answer popularity even among wrong predictions. Adding popularity signals to confidence estimation sharply cut average confidence on wrong answers and improved calibration across six models and three datasets.
arxiv-2505-20837:
Liam Watson and a large team of co-authors report evidence for an excitonic charge density wave in monolayer tungsten ditelluride, in a two thousand twenty-five condensed matter paper. The material is a topological insulator long thought to host a condensate of excitons.

Using Fourier-transform scanning tunnelling spectroscopy, the team mapped quasiparticle interference and local density of states patterns. Back-gating through graphene bore out the interacting bandgap in neutral material and half-metal conduct when heavily doped. On metal bases they saw non-spreading patterns stamped on the topological edge mode. The authors read these as the edge mode coupling to the charge density wave order parameter of the excitonic condensate.
arxiv-2505-23337:
Chetan Verma and nine co-authors train families of models in twenty twenty-five. Industry models must meet serving limits that change fast, and rebuilding for each limit is costly. Their framework, MatTA, trains several accurate student models in one run. It uses a Teacher-TA-Student recipe, where TA models sit between teacher and student in size.

The TA models have more capacity, so students can relate better to the teacher. They also bring more domain expertise into the chain. Multiple students can then be drawn from one TA model. That gives servable options that trade accuracy against cost. Tests on proprietary data and live A/B tests in a production system backed the method. Readers get one training run yielding many deployable sizes.
arxiv-2506-01437: Andrew Mummery and Joseph Silk describe a natural particle collider in twenty twenty-five. Near a rapidly spinning black hole, some material plunges from the innermost stable orbit going backward against the spin. Other particles fall in freely from far away. When the two streams collide, the center-of-mass energy is enormous. The authors argue this is the only astronomically natural way to reach tens to hundreds of teraelectronvolts. In effect, near-extremal Kerr black holes act as supercolliders built by nature.
arxiv-2506-04737:
Mikhail Kennerley, Angelica Aviles-Rivero, Carola-Bibiane Schönlieb, and Robby Tan merge object detection datasets, in a 2025 preprint, whose labels do not line up. More data should mean better detectors, but datasets name classes differently and draw boxes by different rules. Relabeling by hand is slow, and forcing one shared label set may clash with a fixed target format. Their Label-Aligned Transfer framework projects each source dataset's labels into the target's label space. Dataset-specific detectors first draft extra labels on their own images.

A privileged proposal step then blends those drafts with the true annotations. A fusion module adds class-aware context from overlapping proposals, weighted by confidence. Both class mismatch and box sloppiness are handled together. Across benchmarks, detectors trained on the merged data gained up to about five points over semi-supervised rivals.
arxiv-2506-04837:
Kunshen Zhang takes three-dimensional segmentation beyond fixed labels in a 2025 computer vision study. Two-dimensional systems can already cut out objects described by hints about intent, not just category names. Comparable reasoning in three dimensions, where a query might describe a part by its use or relation, has lacked a framework.

The proposed system couples a detection transformer design with a large language model that interprets the query. Masks in point cloud scenes then follow from indirect descriptions. Open reasoning segmentation would let robots and design tools respond to requests like the part you sit on, without a preset label list.
arxiv-2506-05737:
Vyaas Ramakrishnan and Shantanu Desai published a physics paper in 2025 testing a basic law of nature. Lorentz invariance says physics works the same in every direction and speed. Some quantum gravity ideas allow tiny violations. Gamma-ray bursts offer a way to hunt for them, since their light travels so far.

The authors reanalyzed timing data from one bright burst seen by the Fermi satellite. Different energies arriving at slightly different times would signal a violation. They used a frequentist method that handles unknown burst properties cleanly. Their best-fit energy scales came out far below the Planck scale. The results matched earlier Bayesian estimates for the same burst. Agreement between methods strengthens confidence in the numbers.
arxiv-2506-05837:
Alexander Leitsch, Anela Lolić, and Stella Mahler measured in 2025 how much number work power a certain proof format can express. In proof theory, case-based proofs are often shown as proof schemata, set-valued sequences of proofs defined in loops. Schemata are useful because they allow schematic cut-removal and the building of Herbrand systems, tools for looking at what a proof really uses. The open question is their expressivity: which case-based claims can they catch at all?

The authors show that proof schemata can mimic primitive looping number work, a bedrock system of finitary thinking. Turning number work proofs into schemata is a key step in looking at case-based proofs. The result draws a firm lower bound around the schemata's strength. For logicians building proof-study software, knowing the format can carry full primitive looping number work means many real case-based proofs fall within reach.
arxiv-2506-10437:
Daniya Utepova and six co-authors study how a non-spherical mass bends the paths of nearby particles and light. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses the Zipoy-Voorhees spacetime, a solution of Einstein's equations that adds a quadrupole moment to the round Schwarzschild case. The quadrupole measures how far the source is from a perfect sphere.

Two effects are tracked. The Shirokov effect is a wobble in a test particle's orbit, read from the geodesic deviation equations. The Shapiro effect is a delay in radio waves that pass near the mass. At first order, the quadrupole shifts the time delay a lot, more than some recent work found. The results bear on neutron stars and black hole mimics.
arxiv-2506-13837:
Daniele Proverbio, Riccardo Tessarin, and Giulia Giordano review fresh work on models that join the spread of disease with the acts of people. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

What people do shapes how a disease spreads, and what they know of it shapes what they do. Models that track both can help us grasp, foretell, and curb outbreaks. The authors sort the field from broad group models to one-by-one agent models. They split work by a key line: some model acts themselves, while some model the roots of acts, such as trust or belief. They then test, with early data, the common guess that acts and their roots move in a straight line.
arxiv-2506-18137:
Premjith Thekkeppatt and colleagues describe a high-power radio frequency amplifier built for ultracold atom laboratories. Such experiments steer atoms with acousto-optic and electro-optic modulators, which need strong, clean radio signals across a wide band. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reports a rack-mounted unit covering the band from fifty megahertz to one gigahertz with forty decibels of gain. Output power reaches a level suited to driving several modulators, efficiency clears a third of the drawn power. The output stays steady to within a hundredth of a decibel over the long term.

Full schematics and design files are released under an open hardware license, so other labs can copy or adapt the build. The paper is a practical instrument note rather than a theory work, aimed at experimental physicists who need reliable radio power.
arxiv-2506-22937:
Tianrun Qiu, Changxin Chen, and colleagues built a support system that helps blind and low-vision players enjoy video games in a 2025 study. Visual scenes, menus, and timing cues lock many games away from such players. Adding access features game by game takes heavy programming work, so most titles ship without them.

Their framework, GamerAstra, splits help among several cooperating artificial intelligence agents. Vision-language models and computer vision read the screen and guide interaction for the player. The focus is two-dimensional games without fast twitch demands. A general system like this could open many existing games without rewriting each one.
arxiv-2506-23237:
Thomas Selig and Haoyue Zhu linked two classic chip-firing puzzles in a 2025 combinatorics paper. Parking functions describe cars that all find spots on a one-way street, and the sandpile model describes grains that topple when a pile grows too tall. On a general graph the two ideas mirror each other exactly, a fact known for two decades.

Selig and Zhu define prime parking functions, the ones that cannot be split into smaller blocks. On the sandpile side those match a new class they call strongly recurrent piles. They work out the match on wheels, complete graphs, and several other families. The link gives both puzzles a shared building-block view.
arxiv-2507-02537:
Paulo Ricardo Knob and co-authors wrote this study, presented in two thousand twenty-five, on teaching chatbots to listen with empathy. Chatbots now serve in health care, schools, and customer support, where a cold reply can do real harm.

The team began with a small set of dialogues written by an expert to show caring listening. They then stretched the set by having two large language models, ChatGPT and Gemini, write more of each talk. Automated sentiment checks showed the new talks kept the planned emotional shape. Human judges were less sure, finding gaps in felt empathy and flow. The authors say a good emotional outline is not enough for true empathy. They argue that builders must pair machine checks with human judgment when they train caring agents.
arxiv-2507-06437:
Benjamin Biaggi, Jan Draisma, and Magdaléna Mišinová settled an algebra-based question about models in 2025. Colored Gaussian graphical models describe multivariate normal spreads whose covariance form is painted by a graph's colors. Each such model is cut out by a vanishing ideal, and the model is tractable when that ideal is binomial, generated by two-term polynomials. Work had characterized some cases and conjectured that binomiality forces the color classes to be the orbits of the graph's symmetry group.

The authors give a complete needed and sufficient condition for binomiality, phrased through Jordan schemes, a variant of the link schemes used in algebra-based combinatorics. Armed with link schemes that arise without any transitive group action, they then refute the symmetry guess. A colored Gaussian model can have a binomial ideal even when its colors are not group orbits. So the rule is combinatorial rather than group-theoretic.
arxiv-2507-14037: Cacciapaglia, Deandrea, and Sannino comment on a recent paper that proposed a classification of gauge theories that stay asymptotically free down to very short scales. They argue that several statements in that paper may mislead readers. Their note works through the points that need correction or added care. It also places the proposal beside earlier literature and existing classifications of such theories. The goal is to keep the record straight on what is new and what was already known.
arxiv-2507-14837:
Yunxue Huang and colleagues reported direct evidence in 2025 of a solar wave crossing every layer of the Sun's atmosphere. Moreton waves sweep the visible surface, and matching waves race through the hot corona above, but seeing one wave pass through all layers at once had eluded observers. The team tracked a fast-mode wave from the corona down through the thin transition region into the chromosphere, slowing as it went.

On its way the wave shook three dark filaments suspended in the atmosphere. Two swung both sideways and up-down with large motions, each with its own period pattern, while the third only bobbed gently up and down. The event confirms a long-assumed link between the waves.
arxiv-2507-16337:
Xinyu Mao and colleagues proposed a medical image method in 2025 for finding polyps during colon checks. Spotting and outlining polyps early helps prevent colorectal cancer. Standard computer methods need many labeled images and often fail when polyps change shape or the images come from new settings. Their system, called OP-SAM, builds on a general image model nicknamed SAM.

OP-SAM needs only one labeled example image. From that single example it creates its own guiding prompts for new images, using a step that transfers meaning from the example and a step that adjusts for polyps of different sizes. The authors argue this removes the heavy labeling burden while keeping outlines accurate across varied cases, which could make automated polyp checks easier to adopt.
arxiv-2507-19037:
Yiwen Guan, Viet Anh Trinh, Vivek Voleti, and Jacob Whitehill wrote this speech research paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on when extra senses help a machine hear. Multi-modal language models can take in sound, text, and images at once, and noisy rooms are where speech recognition needs help most.

Experiments on synthetic and real data draw a nuanced map. More senses usually help, but the size of the gain depends on how loud the noise is. Lip motion, which moves in sync with speech, helps most at high noise. Scene images help most at middling noise. Sharper visual features always help. The order in which the senses are fed, and how the training loss weighs them, matter too. A Mamba model showed the same trends as transformer models. The paper gives builders rules of thumb for noisy settings.
arxiv-2507-19837:
Jiacheng Wang, Changyuan Zhao, Zehui Xiong, Tao Xiang, and Dusit Niyato are among the authors of this survey from two thousand twenty-five. It gives a full account of feature engineering, the step that turns raw wireless data into clean inputs that AI models can use.

The paper first lays out the core ideas and methods of the craft. It then shows how they are used in wireless networks, with a focus on systems that join sensing and communication at low altitude. A case study uses generative AI to rebuild a signal spectrum that an attack has harmed, lifting a key quality score by a small but real margin. The work maps a step that AI-driven wireless design often leans on but rarely spells out.
arxiv-2508-01337:
Wei Liu and colleagues described a testing tool in 2025 that judges phone app speed the way users feel it. Even short delays after a tap can annoy users and draw bad reviews. Factories test thousands of apps daily, and lab measures on system counters often miss the delay a person actually sees on screen.

Their tool watches screen recordings from automated tests, spots each tap, and tracks frame changes to time the wait. It reports when feedback first appears and when the screen settles. On a hand-labeled set of thousands of taps from popular Android apps, the tool timed delays accurately. Because it needs only video, it fits large testing pipelines without app changes.
arxiv-2508-05837:
B. McCluskey and colleagues present a way to turn a bending-of-light measurement into a two-dimensional map of electron density in a laser-made plasma. The diagnostic, angular filter refractometry, photographs contours of equal bending angle, but the density map behind them must be computed. Earlier analyses were stuck at one dimension or needed slow trial fitting. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team inverts the data directly with a fast marching solver for the eikonal equation, which governs ray paths. The method was first checked on synthetic data with known answers.

Applied to single and double plume shots at a major laser facility, the recovered densities matched one-dimensional results and, when pushed forward through a model of the diagnostic, reproduced the original images. The authors discuss extra measurements that could sharpen the maps further.
arxiv-2508-08537:
Anh Le and Asanobu Kitamoto wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It trains optical character recognition for Kindai texts, Japanese print from the late nineteenth to early twentieth century, where marked training data is scarce.

The team pairs lines of old print with the same lines set in new fonts, to grow the training stock. A loss term pulls the self-attention traits of each pair close, by one of two distance gauges. Both gauges cut the character error rate past a transformer baseline, the second by more. The traits also grow cleaner for telling glyphs apart. Such gains open old records on daily life and society to search.
arxiv-2508-11637:
Arash Azizi generalizes a quantum effect in a twenty twenty-five paper. An Unruh-DeWitt detector moving with uniform acceleration interacts with a massless scalar field. Such a detector is a standard probe for the Unruh effect, where acceleration acts like a thermal bath. Azizi treats processes where any number of photons are emitted at once.

He uses the Dyson series at each order to derive the final quantum state. Even-order processes return the detector to its starting state, while odd orders change it. A full time-ordered integration yields exact formulas for the multi-photon states. The results show resonance structures tied to multi-particle processes. Odd-order shifts carry an exponential factor that marks the Unruh thermal bath.
arxiv-2508-12837:
Aditya Varre, Gizem Yüce, and Nicolas Flammarion explain why transformer training on language-like tasks proceeds in sudden stages, in a two thousand twenty-five machine learning paper. Long plateaus followed by abrupt progress are a familiar sight in training curves.

The authors study in-context learning of n-gram models under cross-entropy loss. They give a condition for parameter settings to be stationary points, then construct configurations implementing every smaller k-gram estimator. In the limit of long sequences and large parameter norm, the gradient vanishes at those configurations. Sub-n-grams are thus near-stationary points that training lingers near before jumping onward. Numerical experiments display the predicted stage-wise transitions.
arxiv-2508-17837:
Matej Steinbacher, Mitja Steinbacher, and Matjaž Steinbacher simulate an man-made stock exchange where autonomous traders interact through a limit order book, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The market's price dynamics turn out to be intrinsically bistable.

Even from identical starting settings, prices settle into one of two long-run equilibria: a deterministic collapse to zero, or a persistent positive price. The bistability is not randomness but an emergent effect of the micro-level trading rules of myopic agents. Between the basins lies a metastable region of elevated volatility, and trajectories toward each equilibrium show distinct transient conduct. The system is neither fully regular nor fully chaotic, illustrating path dependence in man-made markets.
arxiv-2508-17937:
S. Lambie and colleagues hunted the source of a disagreement between two top quantum chemistry methods in 2025. Coupled cluster theory and diffusion Monte Carlo both aim at exact answers for how strongly molecules bind, yet for hydrogen-bonded pairs their interaction energies kept differing by worrying amounts. Since both frameworks are exact in principle, some practical approximation had to be at fault, and the team audited each one on the acetic acid dimer and a water-peptide system.

With carefully optimized backflow wave functions, they found the Monte Carlo side's fixed-node approximation dominated the gap. Coupled cluster errors, by contrast, barely moved its result. The verdict likely extends to other hydrogen-bonded systems and tells method developers where to spend effort.
arxiv-2508-19037: Aleksandar Miladinović looks at spaces that have an act of a compact Lie group G. The spaces sit in the class of weak Hausdorff spaces made in a compact way. He homes in on colimits and on colimits up to homotopy in that group act case. The work asks how those colimits link with maps from one space to the next. From those links he draws facts for groups up to homotopy.
arxiv-2509-00137:
Yi Ling and Zhangping Yu propose a gravity model in 2025 where both the cosmos and black holes bounce instead of hitting a singularity. A singularity is a point where standard gravity breaks down. Their frame is quasi-topological gravity, a class of theories that add higher terms while keeping equations tractable.

In a cosmic setting, the model yields the modified Friedmann equation known from loop quantum cosmology, a quantum account of the early universe. In a black hole setting, it yields a black bounce metric that matches a quantum Oppenheimer-Snyder model. The model also fixes a flaw in that prior black hole account. One covariant frame thus spans both cases and links two research lines.
arxiv-2509-00237:
Leo Stodolsky and J. Silk consider observable signals from explosive bursts in the very early universe in 2025. Such bursts might accompany massive black hole birth or the pinching off of baby universes. Major disruptions of spacetime would likely emit pulses of neutrinos and perhaps other particles.

Direct detection of those pulses seems out of reach. The authors instead trace how a pulse could escape to the last scattering epoch, when the cosmic microwave background was released, or be absorbed earlier. Escaped energy could mark small CMB patches, yield soft X-rays from positron creation, or add a nonthermal share to the relic neutrino background. Indirect traces may be the only way to glimpse the universe's first explosions.
arxiv-2509-00437:
Hamideh Haghiri, Rajesh Baidya, Stefan Dvoretskii, Klaus H. Maier-Hein, and Marco Nolden present a hybrid framework in 2025 for de-identifying medical imaging files. DICOM is the standard format for medical images and their metadata. Safe sharing requires stripping personal identifiers from both structured fields and text burned into images.

A rule-based component follows the DICOM standard and archive best practices for structured data. PaddleOCR extracts text from image pixels, and a fine-tuned RoBERTa model finds and removes personal and health identifiers in free text. The hybrid was built for the MIDI-B challenge on medical image de-identification. Combining rules with learned models covers both tidy fields and messy embedded text.
arxiv-2509-00937:
Paul Ruiz Alliata, with three co-authors, explores computing pipelines for Alzheimer's drug discovery. High-performance computing can reshape discovery through fast simulations. The work focuses on virtual screening, docking, and dynamics runs. Targets include amyloid-beta and tau proteins. Both proteins are tied to the disease in the record.

The team implements a parallel workflow using GROMACS. It uses hybrid MPI-OpenMP strategies to split the work. Scaling is benchmarked across minimisation, equilibration, and production stages. A docking prototype shows large runtime gains from process-based parallelism. Python's multiprocessing library drives that speedup in their tests. Case studies cover prolinamide derivatives and baicalein. Limits remain in data management, costs, and scaling. Still, the potential to speed up drug discovery is clear.
arxiv-2509-01437:
Drawing samples from a probability distribution can be costly when each check of the target density takes heavy computation. Takuo Matsubara, Andrew Duncan, Simon Cotter, and Konstantinos Zygalakis propose bandit importance sampling, a framework that cuts the number of such checks. Instead of tuning a proposal distribution, it builds the sample set directly, step by step.

The selection process is driven by multi-armed bandits, a classic method for balancing exploration with reward. The authors prove the weighted samples converge correctly, and the Monte Carlo estimates stay consistent, whatever bandit strategy the user picks. Their practical version uses Gaussian process surrogates to guide choices, borrowing ideas from Bayesian optimization. Tests on multimodal and heavy-tailed targets, plus real Bayesian tasks, showed stronger performance than rival samplers for the same evaluation budget.
arxiv-2509-01737:
Florian Stijven and Peter B Gilbert extend a gold standard method for judging stand-in endpoints in medical trials. A surrogate endpoint is an early measure, like a lab value, used to predict a true health outcome. The meta-analytic frame pools many trials to judge such measures, but it handles complex measures poorly. The authors replace a complex measure with a single score called the surrogate index.

They first spell out the hidden assumptions that any such judgment needs. Under set conditions, their index gives the strongest trial level link among all single scores. Judging an estimated index also stays valid with their method. A case study uses antibody marks from COVID-19 vaccine trials as candidate stand-ins.
arxiv-2509-01937:
Jonathan P Williams, Myriam Benisty, Christian Ginski, Giuseppe Lodato, and Maria Vincent model a young star disk that casts a huge shadow across its southern half. Millimeter data show a ring of large dust grains around a central cavity still filled with gas. Infrared views catch starlight scattered off the disk surface. The team fits the outer disk shape and the central star mass from the radio data.

A tilted inner disk, skewed in both lean and orientation, reproduces the shadow pattern in transfer models. A neural network trained on clean model images speeds the fit to the real data. The inner and outer rotation axes miss each other by a wide angle. The fit also narrows the mass and spot of a likely companion causing the tilt.
arxiv-2509-02037:
Seung-Yeon Cho, Byung-Hoon Hwang, Myeong-Su Lee, and Seok-Bae Yun propose a kinetic model for relativistic gas mixtures that react chemically. Kinetic models track particle distributions rather than bulk flow alone. The full Boltzmann equation is accurate but heavy to compute, so a BGK style relaxation model offers a lighter stand-in. Their version handles several species moving near light speed.

The relaxation step is built to respect conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy. Equilibrium takes the Juttner form, the relativistic cousin of the classic bell distribution, with one shared temperature and flow speed. Chemical potentials at equilibrium obey the law of mass action. An entropy theorem mirrors the Boltzmann case, and simulations confirm conserved quantities plus entropy decay toward equilibrium.
arxiv-2509-02137:
Salmane Naoumi, Ahmad Bazzi, Roberto Bomfin, and Marwa Chafii give two ways to sense targets with high detail in joint sense and talk systems. Such systems share one rig for data links and target scans at the same time. When the sender and reader sit apart, to pin down targets is more hard. Their ways reuse channel reads from talk marks that were meant for data.

One way uses a complex valued neural net to read target traits at far less cost than old ways. The next way is a strict math route that uses known array shapes and the system build. Both hold up well across a range of noise levels in the tests. The pair give a learn based and a model based choice to designers. Real joint rigs can use either path as needs change.
arxiv-2509-02437:
Yanwen Zou and six co-authors present a 2025 robotics paper on U-ARM, a cheap leader-follower teleoperation setup for teaching robot arms. A person moves a small leader arm, and a commercial follower arm copies the motion to collect training data.

Three structurally different printed leader arms share one control logic, so the kit fits many commercial robots. Mechanical design and servo choices were tuned to cut cost sharply. The six-axis leader costs about fifty dollars in parts, and the seven-axis version only slightly more. Extra design work eases control of redundant joints, a common annoyance. In tests, data collection ran much faster than with a game-controller rival, at similar task success. All designs and collected data are open-sourced.
arxiv-2509-02837:
Payel Santra, Madhusudan Ghosh, Debasis Ganguly, Partha Basuchowdhuri, and Sudip Kumar Naskar present a 2025 information retrieval paper on retrieval-augmented generation that draws evidence from both labelled and unlabelled sources. Labelled pairs give direct associations; unlabelled text gives wider context, but their scores cannot be compared directly.

Their HF-RAG method first fuses rankings from several retrieval models inside each source separately. Scores are then standardised with a z-score transformation within each source before the two source lists merge. That order keeps incommensurable scores from corrupting the blend. Evaluation on fact verification shows steady gains over the best single ranker or source. Generalisation to unseen domains also improved, a useful trait for verification systems facing new topics.
arxiv-2509-03037:
Shuzheng Wang and 4 co-authors built a 2025 tool called TraceLLM for diagnosing attacks on Ethereum smart contracts. Smart contracts are self-running programs that hold large sums in decentralized finance and digital collectibles. Many are unverified or hide behind proxy designs, so checking them by hand is slow.

Older tools either flag odd transactions without explaining the attack, or scan code that may not even be public. TraceLLM joins execution traces, the step-by-step record of what a transaction did, with decompiled code rebuilt from deployed programs. A language model then receives likely weak functions and explicit attack paths. On cases with expert reports, it named attacker and victim addresses with high precision. Reports on real incidents also scored well with experts.
arxiv-2509-03237: Miloš D. Davidović, Ljubica D. Davidović, and Milena D. Davidović reviewed in 2025 how quantum theory looks from phase space. Phase space is the joint map of positions and momenta. In classical statistical theory, both can be measured, with chance spread over their values. Quantum theory instead uses operators for them that do not commute, and outcomes still arrive with set chances. The review asks which classical-style object best stands for a quantum state in that space. It also covers how physical observables appear as operators in the theory.
arxiv-2509-03537:
Cheng-Kai Yeh and three co-authors introduce a 2025 framework for teaching large language models abstract reasoning in programming tasks. Abstraction means spotting the core computational pattern hidden inside a wordy problem statement. Most reinforcement learning training for code rewards surface pattern matching instead, they argue.

Their system, called AR2, works adversarially between two models. A teacher model rewrites a basic kernel problem as a rich, harder story without changing its underlying logic. A student coding model must then strip the story back down and solve the kernel. Training this way improves the student's accuracy on unseen, challenging programming tasks. The result supports abstraction as a trainable skill that helps models generalise beyond familiar wording.
arxiv-2509-03737:
Casper van Engelenburg and two co-authors examine LayoutGKN, a faster way to judge how similar two floor plans are, in a 2025 research paper. Floor plans are often turned into graphs, where rooms become nodes and connections become edges, capturing spatial layout. Comparing those graphs supports search, clustering, and visualisation tools for building data.

The most successful comparison methods, graph matching networks, let nodes from the two plans interact throughout the computation, which is costly and slow at inference time. LayoutGKN delays any cross-graph interaction until the very end of its joint embedding architecture. Each plan is first embedded on its own, node by node. A differentiable graph kernel then measures distance between the two finished embeddings. Similarity scores match or beat graph matching networks in their tests, while computation runs significantly faster. Code and data are released openly by the authors.
arxiv-2509-03937:
Yuhao Zhang and four co-authors survey SPFT-SQL, a self-play fine-tuning method teaching language models to translate questions into SQL database queries, in a 2025 research paper. Text-to-SQL parsing is valuable but hard to train for. An earlier self-play method, SPIN, strengthens a weak model through competition. Applied naively to SQL it has a flaw, though. The opponent produces so many correct queries that the main model learns little discrimination.

Their fix works in two phases. Before self-play, a verification-based loop synthesises fine-tuning data from schema and validation feedback, building models at varied capability levels. During self-play, an error-driven loss deliberately rewards the opponent for incorrect outputs. The main model then learns to separate correct SQL from plausible errors explicitly. Experiments span six open-source language models and five benchmarks. The approach beats leading methods at generating accurate queries.
arxiv-2509-04037:
Georgy Lukyanov, writing alone, asks in a 2025 theory paper when a strong reputation makes experts cautious, and what could undo that effect. His answer centers on one factor: how visible outcomes are. The short model uses simple either-or signals and results, plus a safe option that reveals little on its own.

Career worries alone do not produce caution when good and bad outcomes are seen equally, he shows. Making failures more visible, as registered reports do in research publishing, weakens caution among top experts. Lukyanov also gives a local test for the direction of the effect. He closes with guidance for studying staggered adoption of registered reports.
arxiv-2509-04237:
Pravin Kumar Natwariya and two co-authors test whether hypothetical axion particles could explain an odd radio signal from the early universe in a 2025 physics paper. The EDGES experiment reported an unusually deep absorption in the global 21-centimeter signal, a radio fingerprint of early hydrogen gas. Axion-like particles turning into photons inside ancient magnetic fields might account for the anomaly. Those same fields would also heat the gas between galaxies as they decay, changing the signal.

Both effects are modeled together here, which tightens the allowed combinations of particle coupling and field strength. Recovering the standard signal depth needs small values; matching the deeper reported dip allows somewhat larger ones. Future radio measurements can test these bounds.
arxiv-2509-04337:
Jie Liu and fourteen co-authors describe how Pinterest builds reusable user and item profiles for ranking advertisements in a 2025 research paper. Each user and each Pin, the platform's image posts, gets an embedding, a numeric summary of its traits. Upstream models learn those summaries from many data sources with complex designs, then refresh them on a schedule instead of computing them live. Downstream ranking and retrieval systems consume the ready-made features.

The split design lets heavy upstream training stay separate from fast ad decisions. Offline tests and live production metrics both improved across tasks, including click and conversion prediction. The framework now runs inside Pinterest's production ad ranking. Other platforms with huge catalogs could copy the decoupled pattern.
arxiv-2509-04537:
Ryosuke Takata and two co-authors let language-model agents loose in a classic crowded-bar dilemma in a 2025 research paper. The El Farol Bar problem asks each person to decide whether to visit a bar that is fun only when not overcrowded, with a sixty percent comfort threshold. Agents in a spatially extended version decided autonomously across repeated rounds. Spontaneous motivation to attend emerged, and decision making turned collective as agents responded to one another.

The agents never solved the problem cleanly, behaving more like humans instead. Prompt-specified incentives battled culturally encoded social preferences absorbed during pre-training. Group decision theory gains a new laboratory where formal rationality and social instinct visibly trade off inside artificial players.
arxiv-2509-04737:
Robots need to adjust their motions when a person adds a condition mid-task, such as asking for a gentler wipe. Ryoga Oishi, lead author with two co-authors, propose an imitation learning method for that problem in a 2025 robotics paper. Human instructions are often qualitative, so the robot must vary its behaviour while still completing the task.

Their model learns a mapping from modifier directives to actions. Demonstrations are cut into short sequences and given weak labels for modifier types. In wiping and pick-and-place tests, the system adjusts motion online during execution. Earlier batch methods cannot adapt in that way.
arxiv-2509-05137:
An adversary who sees each training sample before deciding how to corrupt it is stronger than one who only shifts the source.
