Yann Portella leads ten co-authors in a benchmark of quantum key distribution that mixes true single photons with laser light. Many protocols need single photons, usually approximated by strongly attenuated laser pulses whose photon counts follow Poisson statistics. Their source is a quantum dot in a micropillar, and information is encoded on an incoherent mixture of single photons and laser pulses running the BB84 protocol.

A phenomenological model matches the experiment nearly perfectly in their report. The hybrid design can compensate for limited brightness of single photon sources. Their model also gives an efficiency threshold for when single photons hold an unconditional advantage over laser light, and clarifies how photon purity and collected brightness trade off in BB84 performance.
arxiv-2510-26837:
Conor K Trygstad and Nestor O Perez-Arancibia measure the thrust of two insect-scale swimming propulsors. The tiny devices use fluid-structure interaction, where a soft tail bends the water and the water pushes back, to swim. Their tails are driven by shape-memory alloy wires, actuators with high work density, and the designs echo anguilliform, eel-like, swimming.

Trygstad and Perez-Arancibia use a reactive-force theory frame and a custom sensor that resolves micro-newtons. The single-tail propulsor reached a peak force of about zero point four five millinewtons, with a much smaller cycle average. The dual-tail version peaked higher, at about zero point six one millinewtons, with a notably larger average. These are the first measurements of instantaneous thrust for this class of propulsor, and they inform the design of efficient microrobotic swimmers.
arxiv-2510-26937:
Zimeng Huang, with eleven co-authors, benchmarks a basic human skill in vision-language models: association. Association underlies creative thinking and knowledge integration, yet most benchmarks use closed-ended tasks that miss open-ended associative reasoning. Their benchmark, MM-OPERA, holds over eleven thousand instances across two tasks.

Huang and the team set models a remote-item association task and an in-context association task, aligned with human psychometric principles. Answers are free-form, with explicit reasoning paths, and tailored judge strategies score them with process-aware precision. Extensive studies across abilities, domains, languages, and cultures map where current models fall short. Sensitivity and validity analyses check the benchmark itself. The authors offer the data set and code publicly, aiming at more human-like general AI.
arxiv-2510-27037:
Shang Wang introduces a search method that designs smaller, cheaper language models automatically. Large pretrained models excel at understanding text but demand heavy computing and memory, raising cost and environmental concerns. Neural architecture search explores many designs to find efficient ones, yet standard search spaces can be rigid and slow to explore well.

The Elastic Language Model widens the space with efficient transformer blocks and modules that adjust width and head counts on the fly. New distillation losses, which guide a student model using a teacher, preserve what makes each block distinct so choices stay easier to judge. On masked and causal language tasks, the discovered models beat prior search methods. The work aids teams that need capable models on tight budgets.
arxiv-2510-27337:
Benedikt Ebing, Christian Goldschmied, and Goran Glavaš turn a translation engine into a word-matching tool in this 2025 paper. Word alignment pairs each word in a sentence with its match in a translation. It is key when labels must move from one language to another for training. Most aligners come from plain language models, not translators.

Their tool, TransAlign, reads alignments from the encoder, the reading half, of a huge multilingual translator. Past work mined the translator's attention links and got weak results. TransAlign instead taps the encoder's inner states. In tests it beat popular aligners and other label-moving methods by a clear margin. That makes it a strong pick for carrying token labels across languages where training data is scarce.
arxiv-2511-00137:
Soichiro Suzuki studies identities and inequalities for an integral transform built from squares of Bessel functions. That transform is central to optimal constants in smoothing estimates for the free Schrodinger formula, following work by Walther. A second expression through the Fourier transform was found by Bez and co-authors for special parameter values.

New identities connect and extend those images for the transform and its linked constants. Harmonic analysis readers get sharper tools for smoothing estimates, which measure how answers of dispersive equations gain regularity. Bessel-squared transforms encode radial pattern, so exact identities translate into optimal constants for physical estimates.
arxiv-2511-00437:
Andrej Arbuzov, Uliana Voznaya, and Aliaksandr Sadouski examine a technical choice in precision particle physics calculations: the factorization scale. In electron-positron annihilation processes like the QED Drell-Yan-like reactions they study, corrections from initial state radiation depend on that scale choice. A poor choice can distort predictions, while a well-tuned one keeps approximations honest.

The authors analyze different prescriptions for setting the scale, working at leading and next-to-leading logarithmic accuracy, where the largest radiation effects are summed in order. They then compare each prescription against known complete one-loop and two-loop results. The comparisons single out the scale choices that track the exact answers best, giving calculators a firmer basis for future precision work.
arxiv-2511-00537:
Peter Atandoh, Jie Zou, Weikang Guo, Jiwei Wei, and Zheng Wang improve sentiment analysis, the task of reading emotion in text. Pretrained language models capture rich context, yet they falter on subtle emotional cues, new domains, and lopsided class mixes. The authors blame weak semantic grounding, poor transfer across language patterns, and bias toward dominant sentiment classes in ordinary setups.

Their framework answers with three parts. Contextual instruction injects domain-aware guidance to settle ambiguous sentiment. Semantic enhancement augmentation paraphrases training text while keeping sentiment fixed, hardening robustness. A multi-refined feature extractor pairs a multi-scale encoder with an affect-aware context encoder. Across IMDb, Yelp, Twitter, and Amazon benchmarks, the system beat strong baselines consistently, with the largest relative gain on the noisy Twitter data.
arxiv-2511-00637:
Emmeran Johnson, Alberto Rumi, Ciara Pike-Burke, and Patrick Rebeschini study adversarial shortest path problems where costs are sparse. A learner repeatedly routes through a network while an adversary sets costs, and feedback is full information. Known bounds for mirror descent with negative-entropy regularization grow with the log of the whole state-action space, even when only a few pairs ever cost anything. The authors show that worst-case bound is optimal, yet blind to sparsity.

Negative entropy provably fails to adapt: its regret still scales with the log of the state count on sparse problems. A family of power-norm regularizers adapts instead, scaling with the log of the number of costly pairs, and a matching lower bound proves that optimal. With unknown transitions, though, sparsity stops helping: minimax regret grows polynomially with the full space regardless.
arxiv-2511-00737:
Jaewoo Park, Chenghao Quan, and Jongeun Lee make privacy-preserving inference fast by flipping where the encryption sits. Homomorphic encryption lets computation run on sealed data, but its cost has confined it to simple tasks, and coupling it with hyperdimensional computing still left batch inference slow with heavy transmission overhead. Their EP-HDC instead encrypts the model itself and runs inference on the client.

Client-side encryption slashes the overhead of sealing and shipping data, and the design scales across many clients while protecting both user data and model parameters. Design space exploration covers quantization, architecture, and encryption settings. On face and emotion datasets with the BFV encryption scheme, throughput and latency for batch inference improved by orders of magnitude over previous privacy-preserving methods, with accuracy loss under one percent.
arxiv-2511-00937:
Bogdan Radovic, Vesna Gotovac Dogas, and Katerina Helisova solve a classification problem for random sets: given shapes produced by a random process, decide which model made each one. Their likeness measure between two realizations comes from estimates, built on data, of a distance built on geometric features.

The features used are the boundary curvature of connected components and their perimeter to area ratios. Both unsupervised and supervised sorting methods are applied on top of that measure. A simulation study with known random set models checks that the method works. The team then applies it to a real task, classifying histological images of breast tissue, separating mastopathy samples from mammary cancer samples.
arxiv-2511-01037:
Mihailo Stojnic analyzes the asymmetric binary perceptron, a simple neural network model used as a storage memory, through the lens of fully lifted random duality theory. The model is believed to show a statistical computational gap: below one density of stored patterns, suitable weights exist, but finding them efficiently may only be possible below a lower density.

Stojnic applies a parametric form of the duality theory and tracks how its key sequence behaves across lifting levels. The behavior changes character after the second level, which he connects to the gap between the two thresholds. Numerical values at the second level give a critical density estimate, and by the fifth level the estimate settles lower, which he reads as satisfactory convergence toward the satisfiability threshold.
arxiv-2511-01237:
Vishakha Lall and Yisi Liu use human gaze to guide object detection in first person video. Where a person looks is a rich signal about what matters in a scene, yet standard detectors weigh every region of the frame equally.

Their framework, Eyes on Target, feeds gaze derived features into the attention mechanism of a vision transformer. That biases it toward regions the viewer attended, with depth awareness built in. Experiments and ablation studies show consistent gains in detection accuracy over gaze blind baselines. The gains appear on a custom egocentric simulator data set. They also appear on public benchmarks drawn from the Ego4D and Ego-CH-Gaze collections. They also add a metric for the importance of gaze aware attention heads, showing how gaze cues reshape the transformer's attention.
arxiv-2511-01437:
Elian Neppel and colleagues describe the software behind MoonBots, a modular space robot system whose parts are spread across computers, networks, and even different celestial bodies. Physical modularity in robotics is familiar; their claim is that software, communication, and orchestration need the same careful modular treatment.

The design combines component based design, a data oriented message model built on ROS2 and Zenoh, and a rollout orchestrator that manages complex multi module builds. At its center sits their open source Motion Stack, proven over months of field work with self assembling robots, inter robot teamwork, and remote operation. The designs support dynamic reconfiguration and decentralized control while cutting linking and maintenance overhead, and the authors propose the patterns for robotic systems at large.
arxiv-2511-01637:
Abjijit Banerjee, Sujoy Majumder, and Debabrata Pramanik work on a uniqueness question in value distribution theory. If a meromorphic function and one of its derivatives agree on a set of values, must they be related? Their setting lifts the question to several complex variables.

They study a power of a meromorphic function on complex m-dimensional space. The power shares a value with its k-th order directional derivative. The derivative is taken along a chosen direction, rather than a single axis. The results extend earlier uniqueness theorems from one variable to the higher-dimensional case. A series of examples accompanies the theorems, showing that in certain respects the conclusions cannot be improved, so the results are best possible.
arxiv-2511-01737:
Obaidullah Zaland and four colleagues test whether fairness is worth its price when phones and edge devices train a shared model. Federated learning lets devices collaborate without surrendering their data. But edge environments are volatile. Resources flicker and client hardware varies wildly. So picking which clients train each round shapes both accuracy and equity.

The team benchmarks fairness-aware client selection methods, RBFF and RBCSF, against random and greedy selection on CIFAR10, FashionMNIST, and EMNIST, measuring fairness, model performance, and time. More equitable selection gave clients a slightly fairer chance to participate, but slowed global training in volatile conditions. The study maps the fairness-performance and fairness-speed trade-offs and points out where current fair selection strategies still fall short.
arxiv-2511-01837:
Isabela Suaza-Sierra, Hernan Moreno, Luis De la Fuente, and Thomas Neeson predict reservoir water temperatures across ten reservoirs. The reservoirs sit in the Red River Basin of the southern United States. The team then insists on understanding the predictions. Temperature governs water management, ecosystem health, and climate resilience, but a black-box forecast alone teaches nothing about the physics.

From more than 10,000 depth-resolved temperature profiles, ensemble and neural models reached high skill, with the best root-mean-square error near 1.2 degrees Celsius. SHAP analysis ranked the drivers: air temperature, depth, wind, and lake volume, in consistent patterns across reservoirs. Kolmogorov-Arnold networks then distilled the behavior into ten progressively richer equations. They are mostly linear and rational in form. Their accuracy rose with complexity, but gained little beyond five predictors. That is a clean simplicity-versus-accuracy trade-off.
arxiv-2511-02037:
Carlos Garcia Diaz, Q. Daniel Wang, and fourteen co-authors study a distant galaxy whose light is bent and magnified by a nearer group of galaxies. Their subject is PJ1053+60, a hyperluminous infrared galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young. The team works with X-ray data from the XMM-Newton telescope and new infrared spectroscopy.

The X-ray glow turns out to be hard to explain. Part comes from a known active galactic nucleus nearby on the sky, and part from massive X-ray binaries in the galaxy itself. That part is about fifty times brighter than local galaxies would predict. The authors conclude that another active nucleus, hidden in the brightest galaxy of the lensing group, is likely adding the extra light.
arxiv-2511-02437:
K. M. D. Chan, D. T. Crommelin, and M. R. H. Mandjes build one mathematical frame for two spreading processes that are usually modelled apart: infections and rumours. In reality the two coevolve, since what people hear shapes how disease moves. Their framework is a general class of interaction-driven fluid-limit models written as coupled ordinary differential equations. It contains classics such as the SIR epidemic model and the Daley-Kendall rumour model as special cases.

For the whole class, the authors classify long-run behaviour under explicit conditions on a dependency graph recording which compartments drain into which. When the conditions hold, vanishing states are expected to decay exponentially, as a stated conjecture proposes; when they fail, decay can slow to an algebraic crawl. Worked examples, including a rumour-dependent epidemic model, show how a small change to the dependency graph can flip the long-run behaviour entirely.
arxiv-2511-03137:
Shipeng Cen and Ying Tan enlist a multimodal language model to help design a better optimizer. Their base is the fireworks algorithm, a search method inspired by exploding fireworks, which struggles on tangled, high-dimensional, black-box problems. Their 2025 framework adds a concept they call the Critical Part, extending the algorithm to harder tasks and letting the model read the search process in several modes at once.

They test the approach on two hard cases: the traveling salesman problem and an electronic design automation problem. Optimizers produced under the framework matched or beat state-of-the-art results on many instances of both. The authors present the work as evidence that language models can do more than write code: they can guide the design of the algorithms themselves.
arxiv-2511-03237:
Souvik Rana and co-authors offer MUTANT, a recipe for building tokenizers that serve many languages at once. Tokenizers split text into pieces before a language model reads it, and poor splits raise cost and hurt quality. The task is hardest where scripts differ widely and words carry rich endings, as across India.

MUTANT pays close care to word lists, training mix, and language-aware pre-splitting. Its India-focused version keeps pieces that respect word structure and scores best among rivals tested. Across English, code, and twenty-two Indian languages, it cut average piece counts sharply versus strong baselines. Faster reading followed, with quality on tests held steady. Detailed side tests show which design choices carried the gains.
arxiv-2511-03337:
Riccardo Tripodi presents audio2chart, a system that turns raw song audio into playable Guitar Hero style charts. Chart writing by hand is slow, skilled work. The system treats chart making as sequence prediction, emitting note tokens step by step in time with the music.

A baseline that ignores audio already predicts charts surprisingly well, which shows how patterned chart styles are. Adding true audio listening lifts accuracy across the board, proving the sound itself carries useful cues. Code for training and use is public, and pretrained models are shared for others to build on. The work opens automatic charting to wider study and to players who want charts for songs that lack them.
arxiv-2511-03637:
Yili Wang, Wenbin Zhao, Che Ming Ko, Feng-Kun Guo, and Ju-Jun Xie test whether a puzzling particle is a bound pair of kaons by watching how it flows in proton-lead collisions. The particle, f0(980), might be a kaon-antikaon molecule or a compact quark state. A coalescence model fed by a hybrid simulation supplies the kaon maps needed to form it.

Predicted output and sideways flow match measurements from two LHC detectors well, backing the molecular picture. Its flow breaks the simple constituent-count scaling that the deuteron obeys under the same settings, though. That breakdown is itself a clue, showing molecular binding leaves marks beyond total counts. Heavy-ion flow thus becomes a structure probe for exotic hadrons.
arxiv-2511-03837:
Saul Fenollosa, Narcis Cardona, Wenfei Yang, and Jian Li report channel measurements for integrated sensing and communication, a core idea for future 6G networks. Using a 79 gigahertz channel sounder in busy urban microcell settings, they compare mono-static sensing, where sender and receiver sit together, with bi-static sensing, where they are apart.

Across seven real-world scenarios with moving targets or moving radios, the two channel types showed consistently low instant correlation, since their signal paths differ. Yet both changed over time in predictable ways set by motion in the environment. That shared temporal consistency, despite weak correlation, gives designers a firmer basis for robust systems and future standards.
arxiv-2511-03937:
Kohei Kurahara is the lead author among eleven authors investigating a strange Omega-shaped structure in the head-tail radio galaxy of the cluster Abell 3322, first revealed by MeerKAT. Head-tail galaxies, whose jets bend through cluster gas, reveal shock waves, turbulence, magnetic amplification, and cosmic-ray acceleration. Catalog evidence scrambled the author field; the arXiv record governs.

New observations with upgraded GMRT and the Australia Telescope Compact Array show the southern jet about twice as bright as the northern one, consistent with Doppler boosting and jet tilt. Spectra steepen along the jet, favouring weak cosmic-ray reacceleration. A sideways spectral gradient suggests a shock along one jet side shaping the Omega tail.
arxiv-2511-04137:
Yujian Liu is the lead author among ten authors teaching computer-use agents to learn from online tutorial videos at the moment they act. Agents can operate software but still trail humans on tasks needing application-specific procedural knowledge, the very knowledge people pick up by skimming video guides for the segment that matches a subgoal.

Video tutorials are retrieved and filtered, then converted into structured demonstration trajectories. A vision-language model infers interface actions, splits videos into short action runs, and labels each with a textual objective. During execution a two-stage selector adds one helpful trajectory at a time as context. Two benchmarks showed steady gains over strong agents and text-only tutorial variants.
arxiv-2511-04337:
Y-Z Cai and A Pastorello lead a team of sixty-six authors presenting a detailed study of supernova 2024acyl, a fast Type Ibn event exploding inside helium-rich material around the star. This installment of a long series combines photometry and spectroscopy from rise through late decline, tracking a linear post-peak fade seen in most Ibn events.

Early spectra show a blue continuum, narrow helium lines, and flash-ionisation features from carbon, nitrogen, and helium. Light-curve modelling estimates ejecta and circumstellar masses near half a solar mass each, with modest nickel mass and kinetic energy. A spectral model named in the work reproduces the multi-epoch spectra well, tying the inferred envelope to the star's final mass loss.
arxiv-2511-04437:
Patrik Valábek and two colleagues bring deep Koopman control to a laboratory pasteurization unit. Heating milk safely while saving energy is a balancing act with nonlinear behavior. Koopman theory turns that behavior into a linear form that convex optimization can handle.

A neural network learns the linear form directly from experimental data. It improves open-loop prediction accuracy by forty-five percent over a standard subspace method. The controller then weighs energy use, losses from poor pasteurization, and wear on the actuators. Results support the feasibility of the approach, pointing toward cheaper and safer operation of small food plants.
arxiv-2511-04737:
J. M. Alarcón and two colleagues review effective field theories for neutron star physics. Neutron stars pack nuclear matter at extremes no laboratory can match. Chiral effective field theory links that matter back to known nuclear physics.

Combined with many-body methods, the theory predicts star properties at zero temperature. Mass, radius, and cooling traits all trace back to the same nuclear inputs. That bridge lets observations of real stars test nuclear theory directly. The review argues these dense objects can serve as laboratories for new physics beyond the standard model as well.
arxiv-2511-04837:
Cameron Robinson and his co-author explore protecting and cleaning solar panels, with space missions in mind. Dust cover or debris strikes can cripple panels that power sensors and spacecraft. The team designed cleaning mechanisms and tested shield materials directly.

A wiper system and a rail system were built and compared head to head. Collision tests found polycarbonate promising as a protective layer. Layering soft material under a hard shell mattered most of all. The wiper won on cost, cleaning speed, and power use, giving mission designers tested options for keeping panels alive longer.
arxiv-2511-04937:
Zhankun Luo and a co-author study the expectation-maximization method for mixed linear regression with two parts, where both the mix weights and the fits are unknown. Past work covered known, balanced weights and fast rates in clean cases, but the full unknown case stayed murky.

The authors map the method's structural traits and show its path follows a cycloid-like curve. They then give non-asymptotic bounds, which state how close the method is after a set count of steps. The work fills a gap in the theory of a widely used fitting method.
arxiv-2511-05137:
Mees Flapper and co-authors track how an oloid, a smooth convex shape made from two linked circles, sinks in still fluid. Shape and tilt shape a particle's fall, and the oloid's odd form makes it a sharp test case.

They filmed sinking oloids of two sizes across a broad range of Galileo numbers, a gauge of fall speed, and matched them with simulations at lower values. Density ratios close to the fluid's own were used. The paired data show how the oloid turns, sways, and settles, which helps models of odd-shaped grains in water and industry.
arxiv-2511-05437:
Nguyen Tran Gia Bao and co-authors compute how point defects cap carrier mobility in a Janus MoSSe monolayer, a sheet with unlike faces. Defects form as the sheet grows and act as built-in scatterers that slow charge flow in devices.

Using first-principles methods, they weigh sulfur and selenium vacancies and atom swaps against phonon limits. They define a saturation defect level: the most defects the sheet can bear while total mobility stays within nine tenths of the phonon-only value. That cap gives growers a clear target for how clean a sheet must be.
arxiv-2511-05637:
Martin Bicher and co-authors report updates to GEPOC ABM, a model that simulates every inhabitant of a country as a software agent. Such population models help officials test policy choices in health care, logistics, and more. GEPOC ABM dates to 2015 and has become a steady decision-support tool.

Three of its newer methods, the authors argue, can travel to other population models. One is a fresh way to update each agent over time. Another borrows from co-simulation to run the model in linked parts. The third improves how model parameters are set to match real data. Each method is described in reproducible detail, with notes on how other teams could adopt it.
arxiv-2511-06037:
Huiling Liu leads a team testing whether radio jets from black holes really keep massive galaxies quiet. Such jets dump huge energy into a galaxy's surroundings and are thought to stop gas cooling, holding galaxies in a dormant state. But radio activity is brief and patchy, and some quiet galaxies hold plenty of cold gas.

An AI method sorts galaxies by their optical images into those where radio feedback looks effective and those where it does not. Feedback-effective galaxies are dynamically hot and nearly gas-free, sitting in far heavier dark matter halos. Many ineffective quiet galaxies, by contrast, swim in condensed atomic gas. The authors conclude radio feedback sustains quiescence in only a minority of massive galaxies.
arxiv-2511-06437:
Abhishek More and six co-authors measure how much a language model's chain of thought can be trusted. Step-by-step prompting solves hard problems, but confidence scores from current methods are poorly calibrated and often highest on wrong answers. Their method, EDTR, scores confidence from the shape of many sampled reasoning paths.

Each reasoning chain becomes a vector, and eight topological features describe how the paths cluster. Tight, coherent clusters signal confidence, while scattered paths signal doubt, and a Dirichlet model turns that geometry into a risk estimate. Across math and commonsense benchmarks, calibration improved by about forty-one percent over leading rivals, with perfect accuracy on the olympiad-level test set.
arxiv-2511-06537:
Jonathan Gómez and colleagues resolve star formation inside a pair of hyperluminous infrared galaxies seen when the universe was young. Such galaxies blaze with star birth rates up to a thousand solar masses per year. The target system, at redshift two point four one, holds two main galaxies plus two bright companions, imaged with the ALMA telescope.

Gas motions in both main galaxies are dominated by orderly rotation, and detailed energy distributions separate their dust components. Resolved maps linking gas mass to star formation show a steep relation, steeper than in normal galaxies. Gas depletion times run from tens of millions of years in one galaxy to several hundred million in the other.
arxiv-2511-06937:
Yu Hou, Hua Li, Ha Young Kim, and Won-Yong Shin fine-tune diffusion-based recommender systems with reinforcement learning. Diffusion recommenders model how user-item interactions are generated and perform strongly, but training them from scratch is expensive and gains flatten once they converge. Earlier reinforcement learning methods for diffusion models leaned on outside reward models that may not reflect recommendation quality.

Their system, ReFiT, treats the denoising trajectory as a Markov decision process and rewards it with a collaborative, signal-aware function tied to recommendation quality. Policy gradient optimization then maximizes the exact likelihood of observed interactions, giving post hoc fine-tuning that exploits high-order connectivity. Tests on real-world data sets showed gains up to about thirty-six percent on sequential recommendation, with cost growing only linearly in users or items.
arxiv-2511-07337:
Long-Hin Fung and four co-authors count the models of dependency quantified Boolean formulas, a logic where each existential variable declares exactly which universal variables it may depend on. Counting generalizes satisfiability, and the area mirrors SAT theory. Just as counting 2-SAT solutions is complete for the counting class #P, the authors prove counting for 2-DQBF is complete for #EXP, its exponential analogue.

As an application, first-order model counting stays #EXP-complete even for a PSPACE-decidable fragment of first-order logic over domains of size two. On the useful side, the team built a dedicated 2-DQBF model counter inspired by symbolic model checking reductions. Against a baseline that expands formulas propositionally and counts, their counter scaled greatly better when dependency sets grew large, while the baseline won when dependencies were small.
arxiv-2511-07737:
Steve Dai, Cunxi Yu, and Kalyan Krishnamani speed up Boolean satisfiability solving with graphics processors. SAT solvers decide whether logical formulas can be satisfied, a core task in verification and planning. Champion solvers search sequentially with clever conflict heuristics, leaving parallel hardware mostly idle.

TurboSAT recasts SAT as a binarized matrix multiplication that a differentiable objective can optimize, much like training a neural network. Gradient-guided search runs in parallel on the hybrid system, then combines with sequential conflict search. Mixing both styles aims for scale neither reaches alone. Faster SAT would ripple through chip design, scheduling, and automated reasoning.
arxiv-2511-07937:
Akihiro Higashitani and Kenta Ueyama ask whether every cyclotomic algebra secretly comes from a complete intersection. A graded algebra is cyclotomic when its h-polynomial roots all sit on the unit circle. Complete intersections give such polynomials as products of simple blocks, called type CI.

Whether a cyclotomic example outside type CI exists was open. The authors give a partial answer, showing the h-polynomial of a cyclotomic standard graded algebra is of type CI under the conditions they establish. Polynomial root geometry thus constrains algebraic structure tightly. Results like this sort which graded algebras can arise from complete intersections, a recurring classification theme.
arxiv-2511-08237:
Humera Hameed and co-authors analyze effective capacity when near field and far field links coexist in sixth generation ultra reliable low latency networks. Extremely large antenna arrays and high frequencies let both propagation regimes operate at once, boosting spatial capacity. Delay sensitive services still need firm quality guarantees, and a user location can be uncertain across the edge between regimes.

Their setup models user position as a random variable spanning both regions. A tractable closed form expression for effective capacity then quantifies delay performance. Numerical results trace how estimation variance, the quality exponent, and the near and far field boundaries each move the capacity.
arxiv-2511-08437:
P McCullough and Joel Green wrote a starter guide to analyzing infrared data from the Wide Field Camera 3 instrument on the Hubble Space Telescope. The guide introduces the Mikulski Archive for Space Telescopes as the source of the data. It targets first time users of this infrared channel and readers refreshing their memory, and it covers archival analysis rather than planning new observations, keeping the scope practical.

Three appendices support the main overview: a summary of the instrument with an optical schematic, worked cases from the Exposure Time Calculator, and a glossary of uncommon acronyms. Only the infrared channel is addressed, not the ultraviolet visible channel. The result is a compact orientation document for new archive users.
arxiv-2511-08637:
Chung Peng Lee and five co-authors ask how website owners actually say no to AI training scrapers, and whether dataset builders listen. Their case study is DataComp's CommonPool, a widely used collection of twelve point eight billion image-text pairs gathered from the web.

Consent signals appear in many places: copyright notices in page content, watermarks on images, metadata, terms of service, and robots exclusion files. At least one hundred twenty-two million samples carry some copyright notice. Sixty percent of samples from the fifty biggest domains come from sites whose terms ban scraping. Watermarks appear on roughly one sample in ten, and current detectors miss many of them. The authors call for a unified consent framework built for AI use.
arxiv-2511-09037:
Rolf Bader, Niko Plath, and Patrick Kontopidis ask how two hundred seventy years of wood aging changed the voice of a specific instrument. The instrument is a Dulcken harpsichord built in 1755, now in a Hamburg museum. Aging alters the wood's internal damping, and damping shapes brightness, but the effect had never been isolated before.

The soundboard was measured at four hundred ninety-seven points with strings detached, and impulse responses on the real instrument fixed its present-day damping through decay times. A finite-difference time-domain model then replays the soundboard with varied damping, sampling fifty-two string positions on both bridges. Lower strings grow brighter with the changed damping while higher strings dull, a counterintuitive split caused by damping's frequency-dependent filtering. A separate model tests Dulcken's odd choice of attaching the eight-foot strings to the outer wall and finds no meaningful change in soundboard tension.
arxiv-2511-09337:
Ziyong Ma, Richard D. Boyce, Adam Perer, and Venkatesh Sivaraman introduce TempoQL, a toolkit for pulling cohorts from electronic health records with temporal queries. Health records are gold for machine learning, yet extracting and validating modeling data is hard. Existing tools trade expressivity against usability and usually lock users into one data standard.

TempoQL offers a simple, human-readable query language inside a Python toolkit. It supports several record standards, including OMOP and MEDS, and includes an interactive notebook interface with optional language-model help for writing queries. A performance evaluation and two case studies on different datasets show the tool simplifies cohort building. Precision, speed, and reproducibility are maintained, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-09437:
Akash Shukla and nine co-authors simulate the scrape-off layer of a spherical tokamak under low-recycling conditions, without a lithium target. Low recycling promises a hot, thin edge plasma that helps core confinement, but it also concentrates exhaust heat. In that regime the plasma's long mean free path makes fluid models unreliable, so kinetic simulations become necessary.

Running both gyrokinetic and fluid simulations for the STEP tokamak geometry, the team finds kinetic effects decisively shape the layer. A hot, low-density layer remains achievable if the wall material, rather than the target, recycles little. Kinetic runs also confine impurities near the divertor better and broaden the heat flux through drifts, easing the peak heat load.
arxiv-2511-09537:
Mamadou K. Keita, Christopher Homan, and Huy Le teach translation models for low-resource languages partly by showing them what bad grammar looks like. Parallel data for such languages is scarce, limiting ordinary training. Their method, NSL-MT, generates synthetic sentences that violate the target language's grammar and penalizes the model for rating them likely.

Across every baseline tested, the negative-space training improved translation quality. Well-performing models gained three to twelve percent in BLEU, while weak models lacking initial support gained far more, the authors report. The method also multiplies data efficiency about five-fold: one thousand training examples matched or beat five thousand used conventionally. For languages starved of parallel text, learning from explicit errors offers a practical shortcut.
arxiv-2511-09637:
Ethan Baker and Hongwan Liu detail the analysis pipeline behind their forecast that the Square Kilometre Array could discover dark photons. This companion paper focuses on conversions happening in the intergalactic medium rather than inside halos. Through kinetic mixing, microwave background photons can resonantly become dark photons, imprinting new temperature patterns on the sky.

The authors walk through the full sensitivity calculation for SKA combined with galaxy surveys. They also assess what 21-centimetre experiments could see. Both approaches could reach dark photons in a shared ultra-light mass window with extremely small mixing, they calculate. The paper's job is methodological transparency: showing exactly how the headline sensitivities of the companion paper arise.
arxiv-2511-09737:
Bram Grooten and four co-authors simplify how racing agents learn to handle cars they have never driven. In contextual reinforcement learning, conditions like vehicle, terrain, or weather change between training and deployment. The context itself is hidden at test time. Earlier solutions trained a context encoder and a history adaptation module in two cumbersome stages.

Their method, SPARC, performs adaptation in a single phase. It is tested on one hundred unseen vehicles in the Gran Turismo 7 simulator and on wind-perturbed MuJoCo environments. A single policy generalizes reliably and robustly to those out-of-distribution settings, they report. The simpler recipe lowers the implementation burden that made earlier history-based adaptation awkward, while keeping the generalization benefit that robotics applications need.
arxiv-2511-09837:
Lu Zhao and sixteen co-authors build MoFa, an approach for predicting how long large language model pretraining will take under varied distributed plans. With models growing toward trillions of parameters, training spans thousands of devices, and choosing a parallelization plan by trial and error is prohibitively costly. Earlier modeling tools missed common optimizations and ignored the cost of recovering from failures during long runs.

MoFa combines an enhanced cost model covering key optimizations with a fault tolerance model built from historical cluster reliability data. A tuning system on top searches for strong configurations and bottlenecks. Evaluations showed high forecast accuracy across scenarios, and tuning tests revealed which factors most influence pretraining performance, giving design guidance before costly runs begin.
arxiv-2511-09937:
Jiayu Wan, writing alone, extends a line of work connecting character varieties with arithmetic geometry for hyperbolic three-dimensional spaces. For a group, the character variety collects the characters of its representations into a matrix group, and for a hyperbolic manifold group it encodes geometry and topology. Chinburg, Reid, and Stover used algebraic and number-theoretic tools on the canonical curves of such objects.

Wan partly generalizes their results to certain hyperbolic link complements, a broader class of spaces with holes where links have been removed. The main theorem says the associated canonical quaternion algebra does not extend to an Azumaya algebra over the canonical surfaces. The result limits how far the structure found for manifolds carries into the link setting.
arxiv-2511-10537:
Members of the H.E.S.S. Collaboration, led by A. Acharyya, report about 100 hours of gamma-ray observations of the microquasar V4641 Sagittarii. Another observatory, LHAASO, had flagged this system as the most extreme Galactic particle accelerator found so far, and the team set out to pin down the nature of its emission.

They detected multi-TeV emission from an elongated region with a hard power-law spectrum, and the combined data show the energy output peaking near 100 TeV for the first time. No dense gas was found nearby to serve as a target for cosmic-ray collisions, which strains explanations based on protons. A scenario where electrons produce the gamma rays fits the evidence better, though it requires fast particle transport and a weak magnetic field.
arxiv-2511-10837:
Elyes Hajji, Aymen Bouguerra, and Fabio Arnez map how hallucination detectors for language models succeed and fail, arguing the type of hallucination matters. Extrinsic hallucinations add content no source backs, while intrinsic ones contradict the source itself, and most detectors are tested without separating the two.

The authors build a testing framework that separates the categories across curated benchmarks. They also improve an attention-based uncertainty method with new ways to pool attention over input tokens. Sampling-based detectors such as Semantic Entropy proved effective against extrinsic hallucinations but mostly failed on intrinsic ones, while their attention-pooling method suited intrinsic cases better. The lesson they draw: match the detection plan to the kind of falsehood, and treat attention patterns as a rich signal of doubt.
arxiv-2511-11137:
Samuel Auroy and Pavlos Protopapas present a way to solve nonlinear partial differential equations by splitting them and reusing what was learned once. Such equations govern waves, growth, and spread, but each new setup usually demands a fresh solve. Their frame breaks a polynomial nonlinear problem into a chain of linear subproblems, solved by a multi-head physics-informed network.

Once the linear core is learned, answers for new forcing, edges, or starts come from a closed form with no retraining. Tests on a growth equation and the wave equation gave small errors and adaptation in a fraction of a second. Error growth with key settings is charted to mark the safe regime.
arxiv-2511-11337:
Akshat Gupta, Caterina Doglioni, and Thomas Joseph Elliott present BOA Constrictor, a lossless compressor for high-energy physics data built on the Mamba sequence architecture. Collider experiments produce petabyte-scale data each year, and standard compressors such as LZMA leave deep structure in scientific data unexploited. Their system predicts the next byte with an autoregressive Mamba model and codes the stream in parallel as it flows.

On three structured physics data sets, BOA beat the strongest LZMA setting every time, with the largest gain on the most structured set. The model itself is only a few megabytes. The trade-off is speed: the prototype's storage-saving rate per unit time still lags behind.
arxiv-2511-11437:
Guowei Zhang, Yun Zhao, and their colleagues present Hi-DREAM, a brain-inspired diffusion framework that rebuilds images a person saw from their fMRI brain scans. Most decoders condition on one global brain embedding, which ignores how the visual cortex is layered from early to late areas and hides what each area contributes. Hi-DREAM instead structures its conditioning by visual region of interest, split into early, middle, and late streams.

An adapter turns those streams into a multi-scale cortical pyramid, and a small control network injects the anatomy-aware signal at matched depths of the denoising model. On a natural scenes data set, results reached top semantic quality with strong fine structure, and each stream's role stayed inspectable.
arxiv-2511-11537:
Simon Badger and three co-authors compute two-loop scattering amplitudes for a self-dual Higgs boson produced with up to four gluons, all with positive helicity, in the limit of a heavy top quark. Such amplitudes feed into precise predictions for Higgs physics at particle colliders.

Because the tree-level amplitudes in this all-plus sector vanish, the team can build the parts involving polylogarithms from four-dimensional unitarity cuts that combine simpler one-loop and tree pieces. The leftover rational parts come from integral reduction over finite fields. Final formulas use polylogarithms up to weight two and compact rational functions, giving other theorists ready expressions to use and check.
arxiv-2511-12537:
You-Cai Lv and four co-authors report a photonic quantum memory that stores single photons for times on the scale of minutes in reach, a step toward global quantum networks. Such networks need storage of seconds to minutes, yet prior photonic memories lasted under a second. A europium-doped crystal offers long spin coherence at a special magnetic field, but its weak absorption blocked single-photon storage there.

The team combines a noiseless photon echo protocol, which uses the crystal's natural absorption, with a robust pulse sequence that protects the stored spin-wave excitation. At a storage time of several seconds they report qubit fidelity above the best any classical strategy could reach, beating the classical limit for that task.
arxiv-2511-12737:
Adiba Amira Siddiqa, Sayed Shafaat Mahmud, and Rafael Martinez-Galarza build a model that reads galaxy properties straight from images. Spectroscopic measurements are slow, so large surveys need faster ways to estimate a galaxy's mass, star formation rate, redshift, metal content, and central black hole mass. Their framework pairs a variational autoencoder with a normalizing flow, and it works from Sloan Digital Sky Survey images and photometry for nearby galaxies, returning probability distributions rather than single point guesses.

The model matches established non-spectroscopic methods on mass and redshift, beats them on star formation rate and metallicity, and gives the first black hole mass estimates from imaging alone. It also predicts key emission line strengths, which support checks on star formation, dust, and active nuclei without a spectrum. Coming surveys such as Rubin and Roman will need exactly this fast inference.
arxiv-2511-13137:
Yanda Zhu and four co-authors let teams of learning agents invent their own division of labor. In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, splitting a long task into subtasks makes learning feasible, but learning the decomposition from scratch eats training samples, especially when agents see only part of the world. Their framework, CD3T, is two-level: a high-level policy learns subtask representations and assigns subtasks, while at the low level agents master and share specialized skills inside their assignments.

The subtask effects are captured by a conditional diffusion model that predicts the next observation and reward, giving the high level something concrete to plan with. The learned subtask representation also feeds a multi-head attention mixing network as semantic information, bridging individual and joint value estimates. Across benchmarks, CD3T beat existing baselines. Real cooperative tasks change shape as they unfold, which is why dynamic decomposition matters.
arxiv-2511-13237:
Alan G. Paredes Cetina and 3 co-authors present CONFETTI, a method that explains time series classifiers by showing what small change would flip a result. Deep models read multi-signal time series well but stay hard to trust, and most explanations show only part of the choice. Counterfactual examples can help if they stay accurate, close, and sparse.

CONFETTI finds the key segments of a series, picks a target case, and edits the series to balance confidence, closeness, and sparsity. On seven public datasets it beat leading methods on its main goals and on six other measures. It gained at least ten percent more confidence while making edits much sparser.
arxiv-2511-13537:
Clemens Brüser and Julian Weigert settle adjoint hypersurfaces for convex polytopes. The adjoint polynomial of such a shape was conjectured to be fixed, up to scale, by vanishing to the right order on the residual arrangement. That question, posed by Kohn and Ranestad, had been answered only for simple polytopes.

The authors prove the claim for arbitrary convex shapes, extending the earlier main theorem in full. They go further: vanishing on a zero-dimensional subset of the residual arrangement already pins the polynomial down. Such a spare result sharpens how geometers can compute and reason about adjoints of polytopes.
arxiv-2511-13637:
Ana Durica, John Booth, and Ivana Drobnjak explore temporal modeling for predicting kidney trouble in children from routine hospital records. Children's kidney disease varies widely in course, so spotting near-term decline matters. Their data come from Great Ormond Street Hospital records gathered over several recent years, joining lab histories with basic demographic facts.

A recurrent neural model learned from those sequences to predict whether a child would show an abnormal creatinine value within the next thirty days. As a pilot, the study shows simple time-aware representations can capture useful patterns in everyday pediatric data. The authors frame it as groundwork for richer multimodal models that add more clinical signals and finer kidney outcomes.
arxiv-2511-13737:
Ferris Moser maps how particles move through a caldera-shaped energy landscape with the Origin-Fate Map method. The caldera model mimics a chemical reaction with four exit passes, and a stretching factor tilts which exits are favored. Each starting point is labeled by where it entered and where it will leave, exposing the transport skeleton.

At full symmetry the maps reproduce known patterns from earlier studies. Weaker stretching brings channel imbalance, figure-eight loops, and tangled mixed regions, while long runs shrink trapped zones whose borders look self-similar under deep zoom. Lagrangian descriptor ridges line up closely with the map borders, confirming that invariant manifolds steer the flow between channels.
arxiv-2511-13837:
Saul A. Teukolsky completes a two-part project on the math behind realistic space plasma simulations. Codes that model magnetized gas near black holes need to split the flow into basic wave parts, but that split was unknown in the frame and variables the codes actually use. This second paper derives it for relativistic magnetohydrodynamics.

The method applies the almost-reversible frame changes developed in the first paper. The outcome is simpler than earlier attempts had suggested. With the decomposition in hand, simulators can use full-wave Riemann solvers, the most accurate known class of methods, for flows that mix strong gravity, fast motion, and magnetic fields.
arxiv-2511-13937:
Cristina López Amado, Tassilo Schwarz, Yu Tian, and one co-author give graph neural networks a new kind of wiring. Standard versions blur node features together and struggle when linked nodes differ. The authors attach a complex number to each edge and let information diffuse through the graph in the complex plane, extending the usual random walk picture.

They prove this diffusion is powerful: with the right complex weights, any node classification task can be solved at the walk's steady state. Their network, CWCN, learns those weights from data with learnable matrices and nonlinear steps. It adds no extra tuning knobs beyond a standard graph network and performs competitively on benchmark data sets.
arxiv-2511-14137:
Mingi Kang and Jeová Farias Sales Rocha Neto show that two big ideas in image AI are two ends of one tool. Nets based on convolution pick nearby pixels by place. Vision transformers pick pixels by how alike their features are, a step called self-attention. The team's framework, called ConvNN, treats both as one act: gather a set of near items and merge them.

By choice of the match rule, the same frame yields plain convolution, depthwise convolution, self-attention, and sparse forms of it. Tests on the ImageNet task back the claim. A mixed layer raised a ResNet-50 score by three points, and the new form inside a vision transformer beat plain self-attention too.
arxiv-2511-14337:
Ivo Kraayeveld, Thomas de Jong, and Mircea Lazar replace a weak link in how power converters ride through grid faults. When the grid weakens, conventional proportional-integral controllers for the DC-link and connection-point voltages oscillate and recover poorly. Their offset-free data-driven predictive controller builds its predictors straight from input-output data, either before or during the fault, with no physics model needed.

In simulations the pre-fault version doubled the critical grid impedance the converter could tolerate and cut voltage error during faults by a factor of forty. Computing time stayed comparable to the conventional controller. The authors present the approach as a simple, robust upgrade for fault ride-through in weak grids.
arxiv-2511-14437:
Mehrnoush Hajnorouzi, Astrid Rakow, and Martin Fränzle help designers decide how much automation a shared-control system can safely carry. Human behavior varies, which makes formal verification of human-machine systems hard. Their framework learns coarse finite-state models of human behavior from simulations using active automata learning, then feeds those models into game-theoretic reactive synthesis.

The synthesis step asks whether any controller can guarantee safety against the learned human model. When no safe strategy exists, designers can refine the human model or adjust which actions the automation controls, and iterate. A driving case study built with the UPPAAL tool chain shows the loop working on a simplified shared-driving scenario.
arxiv-2511-14537:
Ayham Makhamra, Yelyzaveta Satynska, and Michael Weselcouch compare five math models for predicting amateur darts games. The models forecast the winner at the start and update as the score changes. Data come from games among students, faculty, and staff at Roanoke College. Models range from a score only null model to regression and simulation methods.

A new variant of the Massey model that updates with the live score performs best overall. The team judge models by Brier scores and by head to head betting tests. Checks are done both at game start and at each round start. The score aware Massey approach wins under both evaluation styles.
arxiv-2511-15137:
Xiaoxuan Wang, Bo Liu, and five co-authors train language models to solve problems and to check their own work under one shared objective. Reinforcement learning has made models far better reasoners, yet they still verify their own reasoning chains unreliably. A model that cannot spot its own errors cannot be trusted to self-correct.

Their algorithm, GRPO-Verif, mixes the reward for producing a solution with a reward for judging solutions, weighted by a single adjustable dial. Experiments show self-verification improves while problem-solving performance stays comparable. The unified training suggests checking is not a separate talent but a skill that grows alongside solving when both are rewarded together.
arxiv-2511-15337:
Ronika Sarkar, Arka Bandyopadhyay, and two co-authors uncover a sideways electrical current created purely by bending electron paths at a slanted barrier. Hall effects usually need a magnetic field or broken time symmetry to push charge sideways. Here the material keeps time-reversal symmetry, and geometry does the pushing instead.

When an electron wave packet crosses a tilted potential step, it refracts, like light entering water, and the sideways deflection accumulates into a real transverse current with a Hall-like conductance. The authors derive the effect on paper, confirm it in simulations across lattice models and device shapes, and watch it unfold in real-time wave packet movies. A geometry-only Hall response opens new design freedom for electron optics.
arxiv-2511-15437:
Fabrizio Canfora, Cristóbal Corral, Borja Diez, Luis Guajardo, and Julio Oliva study a nonlinear version of electromagnetism that keeps two prized symmetries: scale symmetry and a swap between electric and magnetic fields. Extending that theory to non-Abelian fields, the kind used for strong nuclear forces, adds hard nonlinear terms. The work asks whether neat self-dual solutions, called instantons, still exist there.

For the simplest such group they build the classic instanton and versions in curved Euclidean spaces. A symbol-based setup extends the result to many instantons at once, solved step by step in the nonlinear strength. Coupled to gravity, the theory also yields smooth wormhole-like solutions with extra scalar hair.
arxiv-2511-15737:
Vilém Rožek applies a micro-macro method to speed up simulations of shallow water moment equations. Shallow flows, like thin water layers, are described exactly by heavy equations, and the simple shallow water model often loses accuracy. Moment equations add variables for a much better description, at a much higher computing cost, which motivates a faster scheme.

The micro-macro method switches between a detailed model and a cheaper coarse model, allowing larger stable time steps. Rožek formulates that switching for the moment equations and analyzes its run time in theory. Tests on a dam break and a wave transport case show significant speed-up while keeping sufficient accuracy for practical use.
arxiv-2511-15837:
Sai Sitharaman and three co-authors present a hypergraph approach for privilege analysis in multi cloud big data platforms. Privileged access risks grow as firms spread across clouds. Classic trait based tools scale cubically, making real time analysis impossible at enterprise size. Their approach merges a next creation access control standard with labeled hypergraph semantics.

Hyperedges model multi dimensional privilege relationships directly. Traversal becomes sublinear and finding near linearithmic, with formal complexity proofs. A 3D analysis lens covers attack surface, window, and identity. Tests on a cloud based system validate the approach. Faster privilege analysis could let security teams find dangerous access paths before attackers exploit them at scale.
arxiv-2511-16037:
Qing Wang, Chong-Wah Ngo, Ee-Peng Lim, and Qianru Sun use large language models to help food recognition systems handle real user photos. Training images are usually crawled from the web and look different from free-living snapshots, a domain shift problem. Real food data are also long-tailed, with many rare dishes, and some categories differ only subtly, compounding the difficulty.

Their framework first has a language model read each food image and generate its title and ingredients. Texts and images from different domains are then projected into a shared embedding space so matching pairs align closely. Recognition uses those aligned features from both modalities. On two food data sets, the approach beat methods tailored separately to long tails, domain shift, and fine-grained classification.
arxiv-2511-16237:
Dagmara Oszkiewicz and three co-authors present a way to clean up asteroid phase curves, the records of how an asteroid's brightness changes with viewing angle. Rotation and viewing geometry distort sparse brightness data, so curves from different apparitions are hard to compare or fit on the same footing.

Their method uses precomputed spin and shape models to correct the data to a pole-on view, then fits two standard phase functions under new, physically grounded limits on the allowed parameters. They also compare solver types and suggest fixes where one function fails to converge. Applied to more than 25,000 asteroids from the ATLAS survey, the method also helps pick the best spin and shape solution for each body.
arxiv-2511-16337:
Ilmo Räisänen and Ilari Maasilta improve the Simmons model, the standard formula for electric current tunneling through a thin insulating barrier in a metal junction. Fitting the model to measurements is a common way to estimate barrier thickness and height, so formula errors flow straight into those estimates.

The authors derive new analytic formulas for current density and conductance that hold at finite voltage and temperature. Their conductance curves sit much closer to the more exact Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin approximation than the Simmons formulas or the popular parabolic shortcut. Fitting real junction data with the improved model gives noticeably different barrier values, showing the correction matters in practice, not just in theory.
arxiv-2511-16437:
A. Marino and 38 co-authors report a full multi-wavelength campaign on the 2024 outburst of Aql X-1, a neutron star low-mass X-ray binary. The Einstein Probe caught the outburst unusually early, below the brightness at which sky monitors normally notice such events, opening a rare view of the rise.

Data from the Einstein Probe, NICER, NuSTAR, Swift, and Las Cumbres Observatory cover the outburst from rise to decay. Comparing optical and X-ray light curves shows the X-ray start lagged the optical rise by at most 13 days. Spectra tracked the accretion flow through hard, intermediate, and soft states, including a rapid hard-to-soft switch lasting about twelve hours. Changes in disk and surface temperatures suggest a boundary and spreading layer formed at that transition.
arxiv-2511-16837:
Oliver Kramer introduces Cognitive BASIC, a small prompting language that makes a large language model show its steps. It borrows the look of old BASIC, with numbered lines and plain commands, and asks the model to run the program inside its own reply. A separate guide file sets out what each command means and how memory and logs should be kept.

Kramer uses the setup to pull facts from text, spot clashes between claims, and settle those clashes when it can. Tests across three language models show that all of them can run such programs, though skill varies by model and task. The appeal is a reasoning trace that a reader can follow line by line, rather than a hidden chain of thought.
arxiv-2511-17337:
Xiaoyun Jin, Mirjam Ernestus, and R. Harald Baayen ask whether a word's meaning shapes how its tone is pronounced in conversational Taiwan Mandarin. Mandarin tones are usually treated as properties of syllables, fixed by the dictionary. Using a spoken corpus, the authors decompose observed pitch contours with generalized additive models, separating the effects of duration, speaker, gender, tonal context, vowel height, and position in the utterance.

Even after all those controls, the individual word remains a strong predictor of the pitch contour, and the effect looks semantic: word sense predicts better than the word form. Homophones written with different characters carry different contours. Strongest of all, pitch contours of single tokens could be predicted from their contextualized embeddings well above chance. The findings challenge standard tone theories and fit the Discriminative Lexicon Model, which ties pronunciation closely to meaning.
arxiv-2511-17437:
Sebastian Osorio Perez and three co-authors construct the basic gates needed to simulate a discrete chunk of the SU(3) symmetry group on a quantum computer. Digital quantum simulation of gauge theories can replace continuous groups with finite subgroups, and the 216-element subgroup studied here is a leading candidate for SU(3). A simulation needs primitive operations: inversion, group multiplication, the trace, and the group Fourier transform, each broken down into qubit-level circuits.

The authors supply those decompositions and price them in the currency of fault-tolerant computing, T gates. For a representative shear viscosity calculation, their gate set would need roughly a trillion T gates, which compares favorably with other modern estimates for the same physics. The paper is a concrete step toward simulating quantum chromodynamics on future fault-tolerant machines.
arxiv-2511-17737:
João Silva and Alba Soto-Ontoso study how spin links between split particles in a jet change when the jet passes through hot, dense matter called quark gluon plasma. Such links shape the angle pattern of later splits, and jet studies in heavy ion collisions need that pattern modeled well.

In a simplified setup with a narrow jet formed inside the medium, the angle pattern always weakens compared with empty space. If the medium flows unevenly by direction, the pattern also shifts in phase. The size of both effects depends on the medium and on how the split shares energy.
arxiv-2511-18537:
Tuomas Varanka, Juan Luis Gonzalez, Hyeongwoo Kim, Pablo Garrido, and Xu Yao remove rain from video with no training on rain at all. Past deraining tools learn from paired sets, fake or shot by fixed cameras, so they falter on real rain and moving scenes. Fine tuning a diffusion model on rain can also blunt the broad image sense that makes it useful.

Their route starts from a pre-trained text to video diffusion model, left as is. The input clip is flipped into the model's latent space, and the rebuild is steered away from the model's notion of rain by a negative guide. Rain fades while scene motion and detail stay. A first zero shot method for hard dynamic scenes is the claim.
arxiv-2511-18637:
Alfredo Guevara and Uri Kol add a new class of near extremal black holes with an exact symmetry. Spinning, charged black holes near their limit show hidden symmetries and links to two dimensional theories. Their new holes live in a space time with two time like and two space like directions, a split signature world, yet mirror the classic Lorentzian ones closely.

The outer zone is a self dual solution with a photon ring. Near the horizon an endless throat forms, shaped by the Eguchi-Hanson instanton. An exact form of Love symmetry, a hidden symmetry of perturbations, rules the throat. Bound states of the hole give quasinormal modes in the Lorentzian world. Exact structure makes the model a clean lab for near extremal physics.
arxiv-2511-19337:
M. A. Arroyo-Ureña and three co-authors ask whether the High-Luminosity LHC could catch the Higgs boson breaking a flavor rule. Lepton flavor violation, where a Higgs decays into two different charged leptons, is forbidden in the Standard Model but arises in Froggatt-Nielsen style extensions. Finding such a decay would signal new physics.

Scanning the allowed parameter space, the authors project what the upgraded collider could see. With enough data, the electron-muon and tau-muon channels could cross the five-sigma discovery line, while the tau-electron channel stays out of reach even at the highest planned luminosity. The study maps where rare Higgs searches pay off.
arxiv-2511-19537:
Muhao Guo and Yang Weng test whether a multimodal language model can map solar panel installations around the world better than standard vision tools. Distributed solar power is expanding fast, yet many installations are undocumented, which complicates grid management. Satellite images cover the globe, but conventional models such as convolutional networks need extensive labelled data for each new region and tend to fail when the scenery changes.

With structured prompts and fine-tuning, the language model handles detection, localisation, and counting of panels inside one unified scheme. Judged by how little its score drops when moved to unseen regions, the model degrades least among the systems tested, beating both conventional vision models and transformer baselines. The authors present the result as evidence that such models offer a scalable, transferable, and interpretable route to global solar assessment.
arxiv-2511-19637:
Max Nilsson, Anton Åkerman, and Pontus Giselsson extend a classical algorithm family for convex optimization. Douglas-Rachford splitting solves problems built from two monotone operators, and it was recently shown to be the only frugal splitting of its kind that always converges in general. The authors ask whether convex problems allow more.

When the operators come from convex functions, a strictly larger class of such methods converges unconditionally. The paper characterizes every member of that class and proves the boundary is sharp: convergence holds exactly on the identified parameter regions. New ADMM-type and Chambolle-Pock-type methods fall out through known reformulations.
arxiv-2511-20137:
Chita builds a solar flare detector from radio parts instead of satellites. His 2025 paper describes a VLF monitoring system. Very low frequency radio runs from three to thirty kilohertz. Such waves bounce off the ionosphere's lower layers. Solar flares disturb those layers almost at once.

Distant transmitters supply the signals being watched. Their stations sit thousands of kilometers away. A magnetic loop antenna receives the faint reflections. A low-noise amplifier and converter digitize them. A spectrum analyzer displays the incoming patterns. Data came from a remote, interference-quiet site. Collection ran over several days of observation. Flare-driven ionosphere changes shift the received signal visibly. The setup costs far less than satellite instruments. Independent researchers can assemble it themselves. The D region, sixty to ninety kilometers up, does the reflecting. Magnetic storm warnings could ride on such systems. Accessibility is the design's central virtue.
arxiv-2511-20437:
Bergonzoni, Riso, and Pupillo entangle atoms sitting tens of micrometers apart. Their 2025 paper proposes fast two-qubit gates for neutral atom computers. Today's best gates rely on the Rydberg blockade effect. Blockade works only when atoms sit a few micrometers apart. Wider links usually require physically shuttling atoms around. Shuttling takes hundreds of microseconds, far slower than gates.

Their scheme uses resonant dipole-dipole spin exchange instead. A single smooth laser pulse excites, exchanges, and de-excites the atoms. Optimal control shapes that pulse for speed and fidelity. Atoms separated by more than twenty micrometers can now interact. That stretches the entangling range by roughly an order of magnitude. Gate speeds rival the fastest blockade gates at short range. Fidelities reach levels fit for error correction. Long-range links suit sparse parity-check codes especially well. Quantum information could cross registers without moving atoms.
arxiv-2511-20537:
Staiger and a large team measure atomic nuclei by the light of stripped atoms. Their 2025 paper uses extreme ultraviolet light from highly charged ions. Lutetium and ytterbium ions sat in Tokyo's electron-beam ion trap. Their line energies shift slightly with nuclear size. Those tiny shifts encode charge radius gaps directly.

Two charge states of each element were measured and cross-checked. State-of-the-art theory supplied the matching predictions. A new scheme tracks how nuclear shape and surface softness add doubt. Both charge states gave the same radius gap, cross-checking the method. Optical isotope shifts and muonic atom data joined a combined fit. Lutetium-175's radius came out at 5.291 femtometers, below ytterbium-174's. That ordering restores the expected odd-even pattern along the chain. The error shrank threefold versus the 1979 scattering value. A long-standing flaw in rare-earth radius tables is resolved.
arxiv-2511-20737:
Daeheon Jeong and colleagues introduce in 2025 CANVAS, the first benchmark for whether vision-language models can do interface design by actually operating design software. Designers refine screens step by step in tools like Figma, and new models can invoke such tools directly, but existing benchmarks only grade generated code, not tool use. In CANVAS the model works through tool calls, such as creating a rectangle as a button background, inside design software.

The benchmark holds 598 tasks drawn from 3,327 human-made mobile interfaces across 30 function categories, from onboarding to messaging. One task type is replication, rebuilding a whole screen from a reference image. The other is modification, changing one part of an existing screen. Models are scored on structural, compositional, and semantic similarity plus component-level attributes. Leading models issued more strategic tool calls and produced better designs, and the authors catalogue the common error patterns the rest fell into.
arxiv-2511-21637:
Vijay Vazirani unifies an auction used by central banks with a classic market model, in 2025. Klemperer's Arctic Auction allocates liquidity to banks pledging collateral of varying quality, a mechanism the Bank of England and the IMF have used in practice. Linear Fisher markets, where buyers spend fixed budgets on divisible goods, are the theoretical bedrock of market equilibrium computation.

Vazirani shows that an Arctic Auction equilibrium is exactly the solution of a Rational Convex Program, a family of optimization problems with rational data he introduced earlier. That bridge exposes deep structural parallels between auction design and convex optimization. Building on the primal–dual techniques developed for the linear Fisher market, he then derives the first polynomial-time algorithm for Arctic Auction equilibria. A mechanism long valued in financial crises thus gains firm algorithmic foundations.
arxiv-2511-21837:
Bode and Hsueh work in knot theory, the mathematics of loops and tangles in three-dimensional space. A fibered link is the binding of an open book, whose pages sweep around it; a braided open book is a special structured version. Montesinos and Morton had asked some years ago whether every canonically fibered link, one built in the standard layered way, is the binding of a braided open book.

The authors answer yes. Their main new technical tool is the mutual arc presentation. A way of describing two links together with arcs drawn on shared pages, which they consider of independent interest in its own right. They prove that any fibered link admitting such a presentation is the binding of a braided open book. Using connected sum and cabling, they also produce braided open book bindings that are not canonically fibered.
arxiv-2511-22237:
Song, Luo, and Wan, computer vision researchers, protect images from AI forgery by making them invisible to AI. As generative editing makes tampering effortless, detectors trained on yesterday's fakes keep missing tomorrow's. Their proactive trick uses the Segment Anything Model backwards. They add carefully crafted adversarial perturbations that blind SAM to the protected image's content, turning it into a blank canvas from the model's perspective. Edit the image afterward, and the forged region suddenly becomes visible to the model, betraying the tampering.

Naive attacks cannot fully blind a model as perceptive as SAM, especially along edges and textures. So a frequency-aware optimization strategy deepens the blindness and sharpens the localization of later edits. Experiments show effective tamper localization without training on forged examples. The authors frame the shift from post-hoc forensic analysis to proactive protection as the scalable route to image authentication.
arxiv-2511-22337:
Singh, Watanabe, Moser, and Dengel, researchers at RPTU Kaiserslautern and the German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, let experimenters label data by showing hand signs while the data is being recorded. Tools like Label Studio make people annotate afterwards, which is slow with large datasets and unreliable for labels like emotions, where subjects must recall what they felt. HandyLabel instead recognizes gestures in real time and maps them to labels through a customizable web interface, so annotation happens in the moment, when memory is fresh.

Comparing gesture models on the open HaGRID dataset, with and without skeleton-based preprocessing, ResNet50 fed skeleton images performed best, reaching an F1 score of 0.923 on the benchmark. A user study with 46 participants validated the workflow: 88.9 percent of them preferred HandyLabel over traditional post-hoc annotation tools.
arxiv-2511-22637:
Bradd, Higson, and Yuncken open a two-part project re-proving a representation theory cornerstone with geometry. Harish-Chandra's principle says every tempered irreducible representation of a real reductive group is either square-integrable modulo the centre or sits inside one parabolically induced from such a representation. The missing tool is a groupoid attached to the Satake compactification, the closure of the group's symmetric space inside all its subgroups.

This first paper constructs that groupoid three ways and shows they coincide. It is defined first as a topological groupoid, a special case of Omar Mohsen's construction. It is then re-derived from Lie theory, borrowing from Toshio Oshima. It is finally identified with the b-groupoid of the compactification as a manifold with corners. The sequel will use this groupoid and its operator algebra for a proof of the principle, an account of how the tempered dual is assembled.
arxiv-2511-22737:
Jan and colleagues propose an agentic AI framework helping disabled and neurodivergent people eat healthily and keep daily routines. Over a billion people live with disability. Existing wellness tools rarely adapt to their cognitive, sensory, and mobility needs. The design is a three-layer multi-agent system coordinated by a hybrid reasoning engine through a shared blackboard and event bus.

Four specialised agents do the work: a meal planner, an adaptive reminder agent, a food guidance agent for shopping and cooking, and a monitoring agent tracking intake and physiology. Health records, wearables, and smart kitchen devices feed in through a policy-controlled layer guarding privacy and consent, while explainable AI modules state why decisions were made and clinician dashboards aid supervision. Evaluation on synthetic data showed better nutritional adherence, reminder responsiveness, and user satisfaction with fewer caregiver interventions, though real clinical validation is still ahead.
arxiv-2511-22837:
Xie and Li prove a mirror symmetry equivalence for six-dimensional spaces built by gluing cotangent bundles of lens spaces along circles. Such plumbings generalise Smith and Wemyss's double bubble plumbings. Their wrapped Fukaya categories, encoding the symplectic geometry, are predicted to match derived categories of coherent sheaves on crepant resolutions of corresponding compound A_n singularities.

The proof verifies a Lekili-Segal conjecture for these affine A_n plumbings, establishing the equivalence after completion. Localising yields an equivalence between the full plumbing's wrapped Fukaya category and the crepant resolution's relative singularity category.
