The analysis reveals strengths and limits in how potentials capture local minima, saddle points, and overall surface topology, giving benchmarks for future model work.
arxiv-2602-02937:
Cooling a single trapped ion far below the usual laser limit is demonstrated by Brian J. McMahon and 1 co-author in a 2026 paper. Their ion is calcium, held in a compact Penning trap with a strong magnetic field. Three modes of motion, the ways the ion can oscillate, all need cooling.

Retuning the same lasers used for ordinary cooling creates a narrow two-photon dark resonance. The axial mode's thermal occupation dropped sharply in under a millisecond. A parametric drive swaps motion between the axial and radial modes, so all three cool in three dimensions. Measurements matched a semiclassical model well. The result matters for precision experiments with trapped ions outside the usual confinement regime.
arxiv-2602-03037:
Rough interfaces may explain why quantum devices vary, according to Yu Zhu and 2 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Superconducting qubits rely on Josephson junctions, thin sandwiches of aluminum and its oxide. Even minor geometry changes in the tunneling layer can shift results substantially, a growing problem as processors scale to many qubits in large systems.

The authors model how interface roughness changes the Josephson energy. Roughness is described as a Gaussian random field with an amplitude and a correlation length, drawn from literature and molecular motion runs. Transport calculations use the Ambegaokar-Baratoff relation with a local thickness approximation. Simulations of five thousand junctions show a log-normal energy spread. Both roughness settings raise the variance, with direct relevance for junction design.
arxiv-2602-03337:
Counting how DNA words share a fingerprint is tackled theoretically by Florian Ingels, together with 3 colleagues, in a study of XOR-based minimizers. Bioinformatics handles short fixed-length words from sequencing by assigning each a minimizer, its smallest sub-word under some order, as a fingerprint for sampling, storage, and partitioning. Lexicographic order is known to produce badly unbalanced partitions, pushing the field toward hash-based random orders in practical tools.

Their family replaces the order key with an XOR against a fixed key, an exponentially large family of hash functions. For each sub-word they count how many full words admit it as minimizer, giving the maximum bucket size under complete partitioning. Combinatorial equations adapted from the lexicographic analysis allow dynamic programming computation in efficient time and space.
arxiv-2602-03537:
One stored model that can serve at several precisions would simplify deploying language models on varied hardware. Maximilian Kleinegger and 2 co-authors deliver that with MatGPTQ in a 2026 paper. In nested quantization, a low-precision model is read out of a high-precision one by using fewer bits per weight. Building such models usually needs expensive training, though.

MatGPTQ reframes the job as multi-precision error compensation, done in a single pass using one small calibration set. It also refines the storage format so an r-bit model reads exactly r bits. And it ships the first dedicated inference kernels, integrated into the vLLM serving system. The pipeline beats earlier nested methods and reaches speedups up to three and a half times in the low-bit regime.
arxiv-2602-03637:
Subash Chandra Behera and Arvind Khuntia measure how electric charge balances itself inside jets from proton-proton collisions. Their 2026 paper uses the PYTHIA8 event generator at a collision energy of 13.6 teraelectronvolts. The balance function tracks opposite-charge partners in the jet frame, for all charged hadrons and separately for pions, kaons, and protons.

As a jet's charged multiplicity rises, the balancing width narrows, so particles crowd into a narrower momentum range. That trend resembles collective expansion effects usually tied to heavy-ion collisions. Gaps between particle species show how strangeness and baryon number redistribute during string fragmentation and color reconnection. The authors argue such measurements constrain models of hadronization and small-system collectivity.
arxiv-2602-03737:
A petroleum well's bottom-hole pressure guides production and safety decisions, but the gauges that measure it downhole are costly and failure-prone. M. A. Fernandes and 2 co-authors build a software replacement in a 2026 paper. Their soft sensor estimates flowing bottom-hole pressure from wellhead and topside measurements alone.

A long short-term memory network does the estimating, benchmarked against a multilayer perceptron and ridge regression. The authors also pioneer transfer learning for this task, adapting models between different operational environments. On real offshore datasets from Brazil's pre-salt basin, the method's error stays consistently below two percent, beating the benchmarks. The result is a cheaper, dependable stand-in for physical gauges across varied reservoirs.
arxiv-2602-03837:
David P. Woodruff and 35 co-authors collect case studies of researchers solving open problems with Google's Gemini models. Their 2026 paper documents collaborations across theoretical computer science, economics, optimization, and physics. The models helped solve problems, refute conjectures, and generate new proofs. The focus is expert-level discovery, not routine assistance.

From the cases, the authors distill common collaboration techniques: iterative refinement, problem decomposition, and cross-disciplinary knowledge transfer. Some episodes go beyond chat. In one, the model acts as an adversarial reviewer hunting subtle flaws in existing proofs. In another, a neuro-symbolic loop lets it write and execute code to verify derivations autonomously. The collection argues AI can serve as a genuine partner in creative research.
arxiv-2602-04037:
A robot policy trained in one world often fails in a slightly different one. Pengcheng Wang and 6 co-authors present DADP, a domain-adaptive diffusion policy, in a 2026 paper. Learning a compact description of the domain should help, but naively chosen context mixes stable domain traits with passing dynamics.

Their fix predicts future states from a lagged, historical context. Widening the time gap filters out transient details, leaving a clean domain representation. That representation then conditions a diffusion policy through domain-aware injection. The goal is zero-shot adaptation: walk into unseen dynamics and perform anyway, a requirement for robots leaving the lab.
arxiv-2602-04437:
Dormant seeds are a bet hedged against bad years, and Alison Etheridge and 1 co-author model when that bet evolves. Their 2026 paper modifies the Wright-Fisher model with a seed bank, contrasting wild-type plants making only nondormant seeds against mutants whose seeds can wait.

Changing population size drives the surprising result. Seed banks are favored in declining populations and disfavored in constant or growing ones, even when size changes crawl over evolutionary timescales. Short-term fluctuations like annual rainfall variation add further structure. The mathematics reduces to a stochastic system forced onto a manifold by strong drift, converging to a diffusion under scaling.
arxiv-2602-04837:
Zhaotian Weng and 5 co-authors let groups of AI agents evolve together in a 2026 scheme called Group-Evolving Agents. Self-improving agents that redesign themselves can escape fixed designs, but past approaches evolve lone branches in a tree, wasting the value of varied tries.

Their scheme treats the whole group as the unit of evolution, with explicit sharing and reuse of experience throughout. On hard coding tests, the method beat leading self-evolving systems by a clear margin and matched or beat top human-designed agent schemes. Study showed the group turns early varied tries into sustained long-term progress more effectively. It also transferred across coding models and stayed robust, fixing scheme-level bugs far faster than rival methods.
arxiv-2602-05537:
Two kinds of particles move over a surface whose shape keeps changing, and each kind pushes the surface in its own way. Chandradip Khamrai and Sakuntala Chatterjee study this coupled driven system, which also contains empty sites called vacancies. A species that pushes the surface along its own motion has an aligned bias, which promotes order, while a push against its motion is a reverse bias, which destroys order.

Earlier work without vacancies explained the phases as a contest between those two biases. Vacancies were expected to change nothing, since they push neither way. Instead, they weaken the reverse bias, and new ordered phases appear. In two of them, one species separates out while the other stays mixed with the vacancies, under a broad hill of a surface. Mean-field calculations give the new phase boundaries, and long-range order can survive even when the aligned bias is weaker.
arxiv-2602-05637:
Interfaces between spins and photons are building blocks for quantum computers and networks, but simple models of them often leave out physics that matters. Tejas Acharya, Loïc Lanco, and 4 co-authors solve the full Hamiltonian dynamics of a solid-state spin-photon interface, without the usual single-mode or open-system approximations. They cover three protocols: making superpositions of photon number, a controlled gate between two photons, and producing photonic cluster states.

By deriving exact fidelities, the authors identify the fundamental performance limits of each protocol. Realistic imperfections, they find, severely limit the photon-photon gate, while cluster states suffer only slightly and photon-number superpositions are nearly unharmed. That ranking tells experimentalists where this hardware is strongest today. The work serves as a benchmark for solid-state interfaces in quantum computation.
arxiv-2602-05737:
Living neurons can compute, and Luca Ciampi, Ludovico Iannello, and 5 co-authors put that claim to work in a reservoir computing system. A network of cultured cortical neurons, grown in vitro, serves as the physical reservoir instead of a simulated recurrent network. Patterns enter through chosen electrodes of a high density array, while hundreds of other channels record the resulting neural activity.

A simple linear readout, a single layer perceptron, is trained to classify the reservoir states. Tasks grow harder in sequence: point stimuli, oriented bars, clock digit shapes, and finally handwritten digits from the MNIST data set. Despite the noise and drift of living tissue, the neural responses formed rich representations that supported accurate classification. The authors present the system as biologically grounded feature extraction for visual pattern recognition. The work speaks to neuromorphic computing researchers who question whether artificial reservoirs are needed at all.
arxiv-2602-05837:
Synchrotron light sources produce torrents of data from beamline experiments, and user groups face scarce access time plus terabytes of files to manage. Aashish Panta and 13 co-authors describe a framework built for the Cornell High Energy Synchrotron Source, known as CHESS. It tackles data acquisition, remote monitoring, and quality checks in one system.

Deployed on a secure CHESS server, the framework gives researchers real time web tools to watch experiments and assess data quality from afar. It ran across three beamlines in late 2024, handling up to a hundred terabytes and over ten million files. Testing covered dozens of research groups and dashboards. The authors report reduced overhead, better accessibility, and smoother workflows. The paper was accepted at an IEEE big data workshop. It should interest facility operators who run shared scientific instruments at scale.
arxiv-2602-06237:
Flags flapping in wind are a classic case of a flexible sheet coupled to unsteady flow. Gaétan Raynaud and Karen Mulleners measured how flag shape changes the motion and the drag. They varied the aspect ratio, the length-to-height balance, and the mass ratio across many flags.

Bending waves ran from the fixed root to the free tip at about the flow speed, with wavelengths set by flag length. Narrower flags felt weaker local pressure, so waves slowed and tip motion eased. Two length scales captured how much swirling motion each flap cycle shed into the wake. A simple motion-based model predicted the average drag with no fitted constants, across a wide scatter of values.
arxiv-2602-06837:
Naoya Takeishi works on hybrid modeling, which pairs a machine learning model with a scientific model so predictions stay partly explainable. The danger is that the flexible learning part simply ignores the scientific part, leaving its parameters unmeasured. Standard fixes add penalties, but those depend on the design and the domain.

Takeishi proposes a design-free alternative based on sharpness-aware minimization, which favors flat minima of the loss as a stand-in for simplicity under Occam's razor. Adapted to the hybrid setting, the method keeps the scientific part genuinely involved in prediction while still fitting the data. Numerical tests show it measures the scientific parameters more accurately than naive hybrid training, demonstrating that a flatness prior can discipline a flexible learner.
arxiv-2602-07437:
Stiff matrix differential equations with Sylvester-type structure resist naive time stepping, but splitting methods can handle them if the pieces are treated right.  Carmen Scalone and one co-author analyze a second-order Strang splitting that treats the stiff linear part exactly with matrix exponentials.

The non-linear part is integrated by a second-order dynamical low-rank scheme. The paper proves the combined method achieves second-order accuracy under stated assumptions, with numerical tests confirming robustness and efficiency.  Numerical analysts get a proven, useful integrator for a class of stiff matrix equations that shows up across control and quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2602-07537:
When many particles interact, each one feels the crowd, and propagation of chaos describes how the crowd's average action becomes predictable.  James Vuckovic studies that phenomenon for non-linear Markov chains of McKean type and their interacting particle systems, in the 1-Wasserstein metric.

The first part systematizes quantitative, non-asymptotic figures with Lipschitz regularity as the main tool, including uniform-in-time results and faster rates under stronger assumptions.  The second part applies the theory to an Euler-Maruyama scheme for McKean-Vlasov diffusion and to particle filtering via Feynman-Kac flows.  Probabilists get a unified treatment plus concrete applications of abstract chaos figures.
arxiv-2602-07737:
Molecular clocks need very steady terahertz rates, but crowded spectral lines clash with the usual control tricks. Kohei Eguchi and three co-authors show a made FM triplet method that removes tuning side band overlap for high-density lines.

Applied to spinning shifts of acetonitrile, the method yields clean slope signals and a fractional frequency wobble of one part in a billion at one second of averaging. The team also sees Lamb dips, narrow traits prized in fine spectroscopy. Acetonitrile emerges as a strong option for agile molecular clocks, and the method offers a robust tool for compounds with complex hyperfine structure.
arxiv-2602-07837:
Training robots in the real world cannot be sped up, reset cheaply, or copied at scale the way simulation can. So online policy learning is as much a systems problem as an algorithms problem. Hongzhi Zang and sixteen co-authors present USER, a unified and extensible system for real-world online policy learning in embodied AI.

On the systems side, USER abstracts diverse robot hardware and provides an adaptive cloud-edge communication plane. On the learning side, it runs fully asynchronous training with a persistent, cache-aware replay buffer and extensible reward, recipe, and policy interfaces. Tests show multi-robot coordination, varied manipulators, cloud-edge training with large models, and long asynchronous runs. Robot learning teams gain infrastructure for learning directly on physical hardware.
arxiv-2602-08037:
NASA's SPHEREx mission needs asteroid brightness histories, and a dedicated ground survey can supply them. Bumhoo Lim and ten co-authors present SOLO, the Solar system Objects Light curve Observatory, a wide-field, high-cadence optical system installed at Sierra Remote Observatories in California in July 2025.

SOLO delivers absolutely calibrated asteroid light curves in the Gaia G-band system across an 11.6-square-degree field, reaching magnitude about 17.5 at ten sigma in 180 seconds. Multi-night sample curves show consistent photometry at the same rotational phase, validating the pipeline. The system will feed the SPHEREx Solar System Object Catalog, giving planetary scientists reliable rotation and shape data for many asteroids.
arxiv-2602-08337:
Turning motion into discrete tokens lets generators work with compact codes, but more tokens mean harder learning. Sheng Yan and four co-authors propose LG-Tok, a tokenizer that uses language to guide motion coding, so a few high-level tokens carry the meaning of a movement. Their 2026 arXiv paper pairs that idea with a Transformer tokenizer whose attention can link words and motion across the whole sequence.

A language-drop trick during training also lets the decoder work without language at generation time. On two motion benchmarks the method tops prior work on both match accuracy and realism scores, and a mini version using half the tokens stays competitive. Readers get a neat trade: richer tokens, fewer of them, and easier learning for the generator downstream.
arxiv-2602-08437:
Chomsky famously dismissed large language models as pattern predictors unable to grasp impossible languages the way humans supposedly cannot learn them. Ziyan Wang and Longlong Ma test that critique with experiments on GPT-2 small and LSTM models, training on English transformed into impossible variants by reversal and parity-based negation. Their arXiv paper blends linguistics literature with new empirical work.

GPT-2 small learns natural language faster and better than the impossible variants, with reversal showing the largest gap, while LSTMs show little difference. The authors are careful: each condition ran only once, so the results are descriptive and cannot support formal statistical claims. Readers get a nuanced update to a famous debate, plus a proposal to move from rationalist to functionalist frames.
arxiv-2602-08937:
Campus disability offices write alt text so blind students can use course and research materials, but complex research figures strain staff who are not subject experts. Muhammad Raees and four co-authors study how generative AI can help. First they watch 12 disability-services professionals write alt text for human-computer interaction figures with AI support. Then they ask 11 experts to judge the results.

AI-assisted descriptions scored higher than those written alone, and staff worked faster and with more confidence. Yet staff also found the back-and-forth with the AI inefficient at times. The study maps where AI help genuinely lifts accessibility work, and where the interaction itself still needs design attention.
arxiv-2602-09037:
A microwave cavity that supports helical modes are usually designed by intuition. Emma Paterson and two co-authors turn helicity maximization into a boundary-shape search problem, systematically exploring complex shapes that heuristic rules would miss. Families include twisted cavity shapes with control-point cross-sections in linear and ring forms, intersecting prisms, sphere-subtracted cylinders, and parameterized surfaces.

Two gradient-free search methods, a genetic algorithm and Bayesian optimization, explore compact sets of design parameters on their own, scoring a scaled-helicity figure for the top helical mode via finite-element analysis. Toughness to factory error is tested with Gaussian shape perturbations. The search reveals clear physical rules for building high-twist cavity designs.
arxiv-2602-09137:
How does a smooth laminar flow over a wall break down into churn? Dušan Božić and two co-authors build a nudge-based rate-response setup for the below-threshold route, growing input-output motion in forcing size to connect linear response analysis with curved effects. At second order, wobbly oblique waves mix so effects square to generate steady streamwise streaks through the lift-up route.

Those streaks match the second output key function of the streamwise-constant response tool. At higher orders, wave-streak coupling acts as shaped forcing, boosting or damping the streaks based on relative phase. A critical forcing size marks where the weakly curved picture breaks down, matching secondary instability, the classical trigger of transition.
arxiv-2602-09237:
Santiago Camara asks whether foreign effects of central-bank policy hinge on the way of the move. Using high-rate spotting of pure money-policy shocks from the Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank across 44 rich and rising economies. He records sharp lopsidedness in cross-border spread that straight-line models hide.

Tightening shocks sharply worsen money conditions, business life, and trade abroad, while loosening shocks bring little to no gauged gain. The pattern holds across samples, spotting plans, and a second setup. For policy chiefs abroad, the lesson is sobering: tightening abroad hurts more than easing abroad helps.
arxiv-2602-09537:
Quality-of-life results in groups with high death rates face a thorny problem: quality of life is not defined for people who die before a check, so death cuts the result. Torben Martinussen and three co-authors propose a joint quality-of-life and living-on design in their 2026 paper that models both spreads jointly without pushing quality of life beyond death. From multistate models, it extends joint binary-health and death-rate accounts to graded quality-of-life results.

Since treatment effects cannot be fairly squeezed into one number without strong guesses, the approach weighs living on and the joint spread jointly, the latter displayed in a simplex. Guess-light flexible estimators built on efficient influence functions yield steady root-n figures, using machine learning while stating its rules plainly. Test runs and two real-data uses illustrate the method.
arxiv-2602-09637:
Hateful content in online videos threatens individual well-being and social harmony, but existing video hate detection leans on large human annotation or lacks fine-grained time precision. Yueming Sun and three co-authors propose LELA, the first training-free framework for hate video localization built on large language models, in their 2026 paper. Unlike supervised pipelines, LELA uses language models and modality-specific captioning to detect and time-locate hateful content without training.

The method splits a video into five modalities, image, speech, OCR, music, and video context, and uses multi-stage prompting to compute fine-grained hateful scores per frame. A composition matching mechanism strengthens cross-modal reasoning. Tests on two hard benchmarks, HateMM and MultiHateClip, show LELA beating all existing training-free baselines by a large margin. Extensive ablations and qualitative visualizations position LELA as a strong, scalable, interpretable foundation for hate video localization.
arxiv-2602-09737:
Matthaios Chouzouris and five co-authors study fracture in pre-cracked three-sided beam-grids whose bars carry failure stresses drawn from a Weibull spread. Their 2026 paper uses stat analysis and number sims to find and verify three distinct failure regimes. Mess is nearly damped, mess shows locally near the crack tip and changes crack shape, or mess shows wide with at first diffuse failure.

The model reveals the key ruling knobs: the Weibull modulus, sizing spread in failure thresholds, and a shape value called the Slenderness Ratio. Mess-induced toughen seen in prior lab and number studies is remade, with its strength varying evenly on mess. Key, toughen cannot be tied simply to damage amount in the grid, doubting readings that credit higher fracture energy solely to crack winding or diffuse failure. Shape emerges as a strong control for how mess shows during fracture.
arxiv-2602-09837:
Grasping the earliest stage of star and planet birth needs close looks at the link among infall, outflow, and disk growth. A 2026 paper led by Mayank Narang presents looks at the low-glow, low-mass Class 0 young star IRAS 16253-2429 from eDisk ALMA and JWST cycle-1 IPA. Looks reveal a wide hourglass-shaped smooth cavity traced in spread light, with a brighter northern side, plus fifteen spinning H shifts showing a wide gas outflow.

Outflow width at the star spot exceeds dust and Kepler disk widths and the smaller jet width. The opening angle narrows from forty to thirty-five degrees for low-energy H lines and cold gas to twenty-eight to nineteen degrees for high-energy lines. Place-speed diagrams show higher speeds for higher energy levels. The nested energy and speed structure of narrow jet and wide-angle wind suggests a magnet wind as the launching engine.
arxiv-2602-10037:
Black-box combinatorial optimization must find good solutions with few costly evaluations. A 2026 paper led by Tetsuro Abe, with two co-authors, examines a popular method that builds a quadratic stand-in from samples, then optimizes that stand-in on an Ising machine. That method needs binary variables, so structures beyond binary, like permutations, depend heavily on their binary encoding.

A poor encoding breaks neighbor structure, so small bit flips mean nothing in the original space and constraints spawn dead-end candidates. Using a small traveling salesman problem, the authors show a binary autoencoder learns codes that reconstruct feasible tours, align tour distances with latent distances, smooth neighborhoods, and cut local optima. Those shape traits explain its faster, feasible gains.
arxiv-2602-10237:
Eco-friendly service options aim to cut personal carbon emissions, yet their green framing may license extra consumption that weakens the intended effect. A 2026 paper led by Albin Zeqiri, with two co-authors, investigates that rebound effect in ride-hailing through an online within-subjects experiment with seventy-five participants. Each participant completed ten trials across five conditions, choosing fifty times between walking and ride-hailing for trips from half a mile to two miles.

Options without clear eco-feedback numbers raised ride-hailing uptake relative to a no-option baseline, and qualitative responses suggest eco-friendly options make convenience-driven choices feel more permissible. The paper closes with design implications for eco-friendly options that begin to account for rebound effects. It warns against assuming green framing alone reduces consumption.
arxiv-2602-10337:
The online bisection problem keeps n nodes split into two equal clusters as pair requests arrive, paying unit cost for cross-cluster pairs and per-node migration. A 2026 paper led by Mateusz Basiak, with three co-authors, studies the variant where requests follow edges of a ring network, modeling ring-allreduce patterns in distributed machine learning. Even with that restriction, the problem stays challenging, with a linear deterministic lower bound.

The authors present a randomized algorithm with a competitive ratio depending on an augmentation parameter, allowing clusters up to about three-quarters plus epsilon of nodes. Framing it as a metrical task system with a narrowed state space, they cap cut-edges at a small multiple of an inverse-epsilon parameter, shrinking the state space from exponential to polynomial. The key technical contribution proves that restriction raises cost only by a factor linear in that parameter.
arxiv-2602-10437:
Seonglae Cho and two co-authors give language-model steering a sharper instrument in a 2026 paper. Sparse autoencoders break model activations into clear traits, but they only show which traits fire, not which ones change outputs when strengthened. The new method, Control Reward-based Learning, closes that gap by training a policy to pick steering traits token by token.

The learned policy yields readable intervention logs and new diagnostics. Branch-point tracking finds tokens where a feature choice decides correctness, and layer comparisons show syntactic traits early and meaning traits later. Tests on a small Gemma model show the approach can steer conduct while keeping each intervention clear. That is a step toward models whose thinking can be inspected as it happens.
arxiv-2602-10637:
Weilong Chen and three co-authors scale Boltzmann generators to larger molecular systems in a 2026 paper. Sampling equilibrium shapes from the Boltzmann spread is a long-standing challenge. Boltzmann generators combine exact-likelihood models with importance sampling, but they scale poorly, while coarse-grained surrogates lack the reweighting needed for correct statistics.

Their coarse-grained Boltzmann generators work in reduced coordinates with a flow-based model, reweighting samples through a learned possible of mean force. That possible can be learned from rapidly converged paths via aided sampling force matching. Tests show the approach reaches larger systems with asymptotically correct statistics, bridging the gap between scalable coarse-graining and rigorous equilibrium sampling.
arxiv-2602-10737:
Nikhil Ken studies a counting stable for matrix varieties with unitary balance in a 2026 paper. The Hermitian distance degree counts key points of the squared Hermitian distance function, a real enumerative quantity. For varieties stable under left and right unitary actions, that count should reduce to something simpler.

Ken proves it equals the real Euclidean distance degree of the associated absolutely symmetric variety of single values. For a generic data matrix, Hermitian key points lift from Euclidean key points on the single-value slice. A Hermitian slicing theorem, paralleling a known principle, reduces the count to a diagonal slice. As a motivating example, the theory recovers a shaped Hermitian analogue of the Eckart-Young theorem.
arxiv-2602-11137:
A base model that looks weak may still adapt best. Tessa Han and three co-authors study plasticity, the ability of a pretrained language model to improve under further training. They focus on weight decay, a key regularizer during pretraining, and test its effect in systematic runs.

Larger weight decay raises plasticity, giving bigger downstream gains after fine-tuning. That creates a counterintuitive trade: models worse at pretraining end can win after adaptation. Inner checks link the effect to cleaner separable forms, steadier focus, and less overfitting. The paper warns against judging pretraining choices by checks loss alone.
arxiv-2602-11437:
Cooperative robot teams train centrally but act separately, relying on value factorization. Chengrui Qu and four co-authors address the sim-to-real gap with Distributionally robust IGM, a principle requiring each agent's robust greedy action to match the robust team-optimal joint action. Environmental doubt from model mismatch and noise otherwise breaks the standard recipe.

They define robust individual action values compatible with decentralized greedy execution, with a provable toughness guarantee for the whole system. Robust variants of standard factorization designs train on robust targets, preserve scalability, and integrate without bespoke reward shaping. Tests on high-fidelity simulators and a StarCraft setting steadily improve out-of-spread results.
arxiv-2602-11537:
Precision quark decay forecasts need structure functions at very high order. Long Chen and three co-authors report the first complete calculation of five heavy-to-light hadronic structure functions at third order beyond leading order in perturbative QCD, achieved by a hybrid computer strategy. That advance enables precision forecasts for triple differential decay rates.

Uses include a state-of-the-art forecast for an inclusive B decay width, crucial for a percent-level determination of a quark mixing element. They also include first third-order results for lepton-energy moments in charm decays, vital for other mixing elements. Large higher-order corrections appear at large momentum transfer, offering insight into a persistent tension between inclusive and exclusive determinations.
arxiv-2602-11637:
In an ultracold mix of atoms and molecules, tuning molecular energy through a Feshbach resonance normally drives a smooth, second-order phase change. Bougas and four co-authors map what happens when coherent three-body recombination joins the picture. The smooth change gives way to a sharp first-order one. A double-well shape in the free energy landscape drives the shift.

The new transition brings atom-molecule entanglement, bistability, and molecular metastability with it. The authors present three-body recombination as a powerful knob for quantum state engineering. It offers a way to steer reaction dynamics in ultracold chemistry rather than merely observe them. By charting the full phase diagram of the two-mode condensate, the work links a subtle few-body process to large, controllable changes of state in quantum matter.
arxiv-2602-11837:
The Antezana-Pujals-Stojanoff theorem says iterated Aluthge transforms of any matrix converge to a normal matrix. Masaki Izumi introduces a family of matrix flows with the same limit property, defined through ordinary differential equations. The family includes a smooth analogue of the Aluthge transform, as well as a formula discussed by Haagerup in the context of type II-one factors.

The same type of flows is also studied for Hilbert space operators equipped with unitarily invariant norms. By placing discrete stepping inside a smooth family, the work connects a famous limit result to smooth motion and operator theory. Flows, in this view, extend step methods: where stepping moves forward in jumps, a flow moves smoothly toward the same normal limit.
arxiv-2602-11937:
Longer reasoning traces lift answer quality but inflate serving cost, so inference cost matters as much as raw capability. Akhiad Bercovich and a large team extend Puzzle, a post-training search framework, to gpt-oss-120B, producing the deployment-tuned gpt-oss-puzzle-88B. The recipe mixes expert pruning in mixture-of-experts layers, window attention replacing full-context focus in selected spots, FP8 quantization of the key-value cache, and reinforcement learning to win back quality.

On eight H100s, per-token throughput rises about 60 percent for long contexts and about 20 percent for short ones. A single H100 runs nearly three times faster. But per-token speed alone misleads, since longer traces can erase the gain. Judged by request-level efficiency, which normalizes for tokens generated, the new model beats its parent across the whole accuracy-speed frontier, by up to about 29 percent, while matching or beating parent accuracy.
arxiv-2602-12037:
Catalytic surfaces host a tangle of reactants and structural shifts that standard rate theories struggle to capture. Caitlin A. McCandler and three co-authors extend Markov state models to coarse-grain atom-motion data for hydrogen on rhodium catalysts, in slab and nanoparticle shapes across surface loadings. With machine-learned force models making such runs feasible, the models retain motion complexity while yielding readable kinetic processes.

Oddly, particle corners and edges slow joining and splitting rather than speeding them. Cooperative hydrogen-hydrogen interactions produce a non-monotonic concentration dependence of rates, a pattern standard transition state theory would not predict. For mixed systems, the message is that surface geometry and joint effects must enter kinetic models together, not as afterthoughts.
arxiv-2602-12137:
Local council meetings shape daily life, yet their written minutes have rarely been used to train language tools. CitiLink-Minutes fills that gap with 120 meeting minutes from six towns in Portugal, written in European Portuguese and stripped of personal names. Ricardo Campos led the work with 15 co-authors.

Each minute was read by two trained readers and checked by a skilled linguist, giving over 38,000 notes in all. The notes cover basic facts about each meeting, the topics raised, and how votes went. With over one million words in total, the set also comes with first test results for pulling out facts, sorting topics, and labelling votes. It is meant to help tools make local decisions easier to find and check.
arxiv-2602-12237:
Training a language model means choosing how much data to take from each domain, and that mix is often set by guesswork. Mayee F. Chen led this work with seven co-authors, presenting Olmix, a frame for data mixing across the whole life of a model. First, the team maps the design space, testing which choices actually make a strong mixing method, including limits set by available data.

Second, they tackle a real-world twist: domain sets change as data sets are added, removed, split, or revised. Their mixture reuse method keeps old ratios where possible and recomputes only for affected domains. Over five updates that mirror real development, reuse matches full recomputation with 74 percent less compute, and beats no mixing by 11.6 percent on downstream tasks.
arxiv-2602-12437:
Reconfigurable intelligent surfaces promise better wireless links, but tuning them optimally adds overhead that can eat the gain. L. Yashvanth led this work with five co-authors, testing an in-house surface integrated with a real-time 5G New Radio system built on OpenAirInterface. First, they measure the throughput gain from adding the surface to a 5G system.

Next, they show that setting the surface phases at random, combined with 5G's proportional fair scheduler, can reach near-optimal throughput, if the scheduler's averaging window is chosen well. In each slot, the scheduler favours the user with the best channel, namely the user the random surface happens to align with. Tests of received power, block error rate, modulation and coding, and throughput confirm that a random surface with negligible overhead rivals optimised designs in real 5G systems.
arxiv-2602-12737:
Stacked graphene sheets aligned with boron nitride have become a rich playground for topological phases driven by electron interactions. Jiannan Hua and three co-authors review the quantum anomalous Hall effect in these rhombohedral multilayer systems, where Hall currents flow without an applied magnetic field. Experiments have grown from early Chern insulators in three layers to fully quantised states in thicker stacks.

Theory points to a team effort between the moiré pattern and electron interactions, and raises the prospect of an anomalous Hall crystal, a phase where interactions alone build the topology. The review covers the experimental signs, the continuum and many-body models, and how displacement fields and moiré potentials fit the picture. It closes with open questions, placing these stacks at the front of topological quantum matter.
arxiv-2602-12937:
Arabic dialect identification has long been treated as choosing one label per sentence, but many sentences fit several dialects at once. Ali Mekky and four co-authors argue for multi-label framing and tackle the lack of multi-label training data. Analysing single-label models, they find the core problem is negative sampling: sentences marked negative for one dialect may be perfectly acceptable in others.

The team builds a multi-label dataset with automatic annotations from GPT-4o and binary acceptability classifiers, aggregated using the Arabic Level of Dialectness. A BERT-based classifier trained with curriculum learning keyed to dialectal complexity and label count then reaches 0.69 macro F1 on the multi-label leaderboard, up from 0.55 for the previous best system. Code and data are public, giving the field a realistic multi-label benchmark.
arxiv-2602-13037:
Graph colouring with two kinds of sets, independent sets and 2-independent sets, was recently introduced by Choi and Liu. Thomas Delépine studies the problem's complexity and extremal behaviour for planar graphs. He proves the problem is NP-complete even on restricted planar classes, so efficient exact algorithms are unlikely in general.

On the extremal side, he investigates how many 2-independent sets are needed when the number of independent sets is fixed, in colourable classes. Results include bounds showing k-degenerate graphs, triangle-free planar graphs, and planar graphs are colourable with a square-root number of 2-independent sets alongside fixed independent sets. All upper bounds are tight up to a constant factor, giving a sharp picture of the trade-off.
arxiv-2602-13137:
Double white dwarfs are the Milky Way's most common compact binaries, future gravitational-wave sources, and possible Type Ia supernova progenitors. Yet none has been found through relativistic Doppler beaming alone, even though beaming amplitude tracks radial velocity directly. Gautham Adamane Pallathadka and four co-authors run binary population synthesis with SeBa, embedded in a three-part Galaxy model, to forecast what the Rubin Observatory's LSST should find.

Simulations show LSST reliably recovering fairly bright, unequal-mass binaries in compact orbits of about 10 to 600 minutes at moderate to high inclinations. At least 287 short-period double white dwarfs should appear, 47 of them detectable by LISA. Light curves readily yield periods and full orbits, unlike spectroscopic searches. Because unequal-mass short-period formation hinges on mass-transfer assumptions, the observed beamed population will test binary evolution models.
arxiv-2602-13437:
Convolution powers of a function, repeated self-convolutions, govern random walks and numerical schemes, and sharp bounds for them matter. This paper proves generalized Gaussian estimates and local limit theorems with cumulants. Accuracy extends to any order, with sharp Gaussian-type error, for convolution powers of certain complex-valued functions on integer lattices in d dimensions.

The global space-time bounds are phrased through Legendre-Fenchel transforms of positive-homogeneous polynomials, mirroring bounds for heat kernels of a related class of partial differential operators. Applications run to the analysis and stability of difference schemes for partial differential equations, extending recent work of Diaconis, Saloff-Coste, and others. Pedro H. Alves leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13637:
Video generation often looks good frame by frame yet fails on consistency: worlds shift within a clip, cameras jump between clips, and elements change across shots. DCDM tackles all three with a system-level divide-and-conquer design sharing one video generation backbone. Within clips, a language model parses prompts into structured semantic representations that a diffusion transformer turns into coherent content. Between clips, a temporal camera representation in noise space enables precise stable camera motion control, aided by text-to-image initialization.

Across shots, a holistic scene generation approach with windowed cross-attention and sparse inter-shot self-attention preserves long-range narrative coherence efficiently. Validation on the CVM Competition test set at AAAI 2026 shows the strategies effectively address the three consistency challenges. Haoyu Zhao leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14337:
Yukang Feng and 18 co-authors introduce a 2026 arXiv benchmark for long-horizon coding agents that work through command lines. Existing benchmarks suffer short task horizons, contamination from GitHub scraping, and coarse evaluation, failing to test the long-horizon planning real software engineering demands. LongCLI-Bench fills that gap.

Twenty high-quality, long-horizon tasks were curated from over 1,000 computer science assignments and real workflows, spanning from-scratch builds, feature addition, bug fixing, and refactoring. A dual-set protocol measures requirement fulfillment through fail-to-pass tests and regression avoidance through pass-to-pass tests, with step-level scoring to pinpoint failures. Even state-of-the-art agents scored below 20% pass rates, showing how far long-horizon agentic programming still has to go.
arxiv-2602-14437:
Adel Ali and one co-author present a 2026 arXiv minimal tunable many-body system: fermions coupled to quantum magnetic flux. The system is analytically diagonalizable and exhibits Stoner orbital instability and a Dicke-like quantum phase transition. Unlike standard cavity QED, where electric fields couple via electric dipoles, here the quantized magnetic field of an LC resonator couples to particle angular momentum.

Adding a Josephson junction to the linear LC circuit opens new flux-matter phases and selective photon clothing, in settings apt for circuit QED and tiny rings. Tight-binding setups with a tunable non-linearity standing in for a fake Josephson junction, but with no real junction, are also weighed. The platform offers a clean, tunable setting for many-body phenomena driven by magnetic coupling.
arxiv-2602-14637:
Tunnel junctions sit at the heart of many chip-scale devices, from sensors to quantum circuits. Juho Luomahaara, with seventeen co-authors, presents a scalable normal-metal junction technology. It replaces superconducting aluminium with a titanium-tungsten alloy and aluminium oxide barriers.

The process is CMOS-compatible and was shown at wafer scale. Junctions were tested in Coulomb blockade thermometers down to 20 millikelvin, holding normal-state behavior. That range suits cryogenic, quantum, and nanoelectronic systems. The design avoids magnets, doping, and proximity tricks that hurt integration. Wafer-scale fabrication shows the process can grow beyond single devices.
arxiv-2602-14737:
T. Matulic and D. Sersic build a parameter-minimal neural solver for rate laws by forcing trial answers into Horner form. That form gives a smooth, trainable answer with just a few free numbers, and start values hold exact by design, since low-order freedoms are set in advance.

Training then chases only the gap between the law and the trial at grid points. To cut error without adding bulk, a split form trains small Horner models on short spans, with smooth joins and smooth slopes at each seam. Small, exact, and trainable: that is the solver's pitch.
arxiv-2602-14837:
Lorenzo Mur Labadia and colleagues improve short-term object interaction anticipation from egocentric video: finding the next active object, its noun and verb, and time to contact. Their STAformer and STAformer++ architectures integrate frame-guided temporal pooling, dual image-video attention, and multiscale feature fusion, working from an image-input video pair.

A second contribution, detailed in the paper, extends the anticipation framework further for wearable assistants and human-robot interaction. Predicting what a wearer will touch next, and when, lets assistance arrive in time rather than after the fact. Egocentric vision gains a sharper sense of imminent action.
arxiv-2602-14937:
Anusorn and colleagues build two lattice filters from laterally excited bulk acoustic resonators in thin-film lithium niobate. One uses a direct lattice layout. The other uses a layout-balanced form. Both are made in periodically poled piezoelectric film. At about 20 GHz they reach fractional bandwidths near 27 percent and 39 percent. Insertion losses stay under one decibel, in footprints smaller than one and a half square millimetres.

The wide bands come from strong electromechanical coupling joined to the broad nature of lattice design. The team presents the devices as a path to compact, low-loss, wideband filters for next-generation wireless front ends and sensing. They also note work that remains on tuning and refinement.
arxiv-2602-15037:
Ravishankara introduces CircuChain, a benchmark that separates following instructions from doing physics in circuit analysis. A numerically right answer still fails if it breaks rules such as mesh direction or polarity assignments, mistakes that can spread in safety-critical systems. It is unclear whether frontier models reason from first principles or lean on training priors that clash with explicit orders. The benchmark uses paired control and trap problems across five standard layouts, varying sign rules, current directions, and polarity rules.

A multi-stage pipeline combining symbolic solvers, SPICE simulation, and an error taxonomy pins each failure to rules, physics, arithmetic, or hallucination. Across 100 tasks per model, the strongest model reasons nearly perfectly yet breaks rules often under trap conditions, while weaker models follow orders better despite weaker physics. Capability, the paper warns, does not guarantee constraint alignment.
arxiv-2602-15637:
Dolatpour Fathkouhi and colleagues expose a bias hiding in time-series imputation benchmarks. Standard tests use uniform random masking and shape-blind scores such as MSE and RMSE, weighting evaluation by how common each regime is. In regulated systems with a dominant attractor, that setup flatters simple methods. Stable physiology, nominal industrial operation, and steady network traffic all show the pattern: most test cases sit in the easy, low-entropy regime where simple methods trivially succeed.

Their stratified stress test splits evaluation into stationary and transient regimes, using continuous glucose monitoring as a test bed, where meals and insulin give precise regime markers. Linear interpolation matches the state of the art in stable intervals. But its shape fidelity collapses during transients, a pattern they call the RMSE mirage, where low pointwise error hides destroyed signal shape. Deep models preserve shape during transients, making them essential for safety-critical uses.
arxiv-2602-15737:
Jariwala and colleagues lay out a roadmap for AI-enabled statistical channel modelling built on NYUSIM, a simulator from NYU WIRELESS dating to 2016. AI channel models need large, accurate, physically consistent data sets from real measurements, spanning frequencies and environments. NYUSIM generates realistic spatio-temporal channel data from extensive outdoor and indoor field data between 28 and 142 GHz.

To support 6G research and scale, the team migrated the full NYUSIM frame from MATLAB to Python, adding new model generation from field measurements in the 6G upper mid-band at 6.75 GHz and 16.95 GHz. Migration was validated with Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests, moment analysis, and end-to-end testing under unified randomness control, confirming consistency with MATLAB NYUSIM version 4.0. The Python version also adds a standardised 3D antenna format, Ant3D, and is built for parallel data generation in modern AI workflows.
arxiv-2602-16137:
Xintong Yu leads a team of three researchers designing experiments to learn how people choose among items. The question is which subsets, or assortments, to offer so data can pin down a choice model over many items. Their structured, non-adaptive design needs only a logarithmic number of distinct assortments. Each is offered repeatedly. It beats randomized and heuristic designs across a broad benchmark with varied ground truths, including misspecified ones.

The team then turns to Nested Logit models, which group close substitutes into nests. Prior methods assume nests are known. Their new algorithm identifies nests from collected data. Paired with the design, it guarantees correct identification under any Nested Logit ground truth. Deployed at Dream11, an Indian fantasy sports platform, the design gathered data from tens of millions of users. The learned nests predicted choices out of sample better than clusters built from contest features in advance.
arxiv-2602-16537:
Jiadong Liang, Zhimei Ren, and Yuxin Chen study online conformal prediction, a method that wraps a model's forecasts in sets meant to cover the truth at a chosen rate. Their focus is data streams that drift over time, judged by cumulative regret tied to the training data rather than by average coverage gaps alone. Two drift shapes are treated: sudden change points and smooth, gradual drift.

For scores trained in advance on separate data, the authors give a split-conformal method that uses drift detection to refresh its calibration sets and prove it reaches the best possible regret. For scores trained online, they give a full-conformal method that leans on the stability of the fitting method rather than on symmetry, with matching guarantees under limits on the prediction sets. Tests back the theory, and practitioners get principled tools for prediction under drift.
arxiv-2602-16837:
Hanna Herasimchyk and co-authors build a structural theory of position bias in transformers. Transformers tend to favor certain token spots, yet the design roots of that bias stay poorly known. The bias ties closely to the Lost-in-the-Middle effect, where models underuse info placed mid-context. Causal transformer designs are shown to induce a systematic position-bias prior that helps explain Lost-in-the-Middle influence profiles.

The theory builds on cumulative attention rollout with layerwise residual mixing. At finite depth, competing positional drifts from causal masking, residual mixing, and positional encoding interact to yield broad, often U-shaped profiles. At infinite depth, prior attention-only theory predicted inevitable collapse, an open puzzle. Residual-aware study replaces collapse with a split ruled by cumulative attention mixing. Across thirty model-dataset settings, the adaptive rollout closely matches gauged token influence and cuts profile mismatch sharply.
arxiv-2602-17037:
Rahul Nanda and co-authors present Wink, a system for fixing coding-agent misbehaviors. Coding agents powered by large language models are increasingly used in software to automate complex engineering tasks. Those agents are prone to a wide range of misbehaviors, such as straying from user instructions, getting stuck in loops, or failing to use tools right.

Those failures disrupt development workflow and often require costly manual intervention. Wink is a lightweight, async self-fix system for fixing agentic misbehaviors at scale. A taxonomy of misbehaviors grounded in analysis of production traffic identifies three primary categories, found in about thirty percent of trajectories: Specification Drift, Reasoning Problems, and Tool Call Failures. Wink observes agent trajectories and provides targeted course-correction guidance to nudge the agent back on track. Tests on over ten thousand real-world agent trajectories found it resolves ninety percent of misbehaviors requiring a single fix.
arxiv-2602-17237:
Tannaz Zameni led a three-author paper on merging behavior-driven development cases for model-based testing. In behavior-driven development, system conduct is written as textual scripts, which this approach turns into transition systems for testing. The paper defines disjunction composition, a way to combine these systems for alternative cases.

Merging lets testers model and test the merged whole while keeping the testing power of the first cases. That keeping is proved through symbolic rules, under which such equivalence of two systems ensures they fail the same test cases. A real-world case study shows the method's promise, showing the merge working on real work items rather than toy cases.
arxiv-2602-17337:
Antoine Legouhy led a five-author team offering Polaffini, a feature-based system for robust medical image matching. Matching usually relies on brightness-based methods using proxy matching scores, while feature-based methods that match stated body matches fell out of favor because reliable feature mining was hard. Deep learning splitting models now deliver fine-grained body outlines at once, opening the feature-based route again.

It takes split regions and extracts body-grounded feature points with one-to-one matches simply by taking their centroids. Those points enable fast global and local affine matching via closed-form answers, yielding mappings from affine to polyaffine with tunable smoothness. These transforms offer finer matching with more degrees of freedom, and log-Euclidean setup keeps them fold-free. Tests show it beats popular brightness-based methods on structural fit and lifts the start for downstream nonlinear matching.
arxiv-2602-17637:
Sujoy Bhore and Konrad Swanepoel study monochromatic shapes in point sets where each point is colored red or blue. The classic Motzkin-Rabin theorem guarantees a monochromatic line, and Green and Tao's work on Sylvester-Gallai sets the stage for sharper counts and structure. The paper asks how many such shapes must appear, and when they can vanish.

If no line holds more than three points, the authors prove a lower bound on monochromatic lines that grows with the square of the point count. They also prove a converse of a Jamison theorem on conics. They settle a small case of a Milićević conjecture. They show that a near-pencil layout minimizes the expected monochromatic line count under random coloring. Families with no monochromatic circles or conics round out the picture.
arxiv-2602-17737:
Upasana Biswas and team propose NestRL, a nested training regime for mutual adaptation in human-AI teaming. Humans naturally adjust their strategies to an AI partner's conduct, yet standard training partners stay static and miss that adaptive quality. Joint training, meanwhile, often yields opaque coordination strategies that work only with co-trained partners and generalize poorly.

The team frames human-AI teaming as an interactive partially observable Markov decision process. NestRL learns its finite-level solution by training agents at each level against adaptive agents from the level below. Theory shows NestRL agents avoid partner-specific strategies, and tests in the Overcooked domain back that claim. NestRL beats leading baselines with unseen adaptive agents and real human teammates, showing markedly greater adaptability over the course of interaction.
arxiv-2602-17937:
Xiaotang Du and team present the first full comparison of instruction optimization for tabular fact verification, using the DSPy tuning frame. Instruction tuning offers a light, model-neutral way to lift reasoning. The study tests four out-of-the-box prompting methods covering text-only prompts and code use: direct prediction, Chain-of-Thought, ReAct with SQL, and CodeAct.

Across four benchmarks and three model families, the team studies COPRO, MiPROv2 and SIMBA. Instruction optimization lifts verification scores throughout, with MiPROv2 giving steady Chain-of-Thought gains and SIMBA giving the largest ReAct gains, above all at large scales. Checks show SIMBA pushes more direct reasoning paths by applying rules of thumb, improving number comparison in Chain-of-Thought reasoning and curbing needless ReAct tool calls. Chain-of-Thought stays effective for tabular fact checking, above all with small models, while large-model ReAct agents need careful tuning.
arxiv-2602-18037:
Johannes Ackermann and colleagues confront reward hacking, where a policy exploits reward inaccuracies and learns unintended behavior. Reinforcement learning from human feedback and verifiable rewards are key post-training steps for modern language models. Past work mostly limits policy updates with a penalty toward a reference model.

The authors reframe the problem: train so updates drift where the reward is more accurate. They link reward accuracy to the flatness of an optimum at convergence. Gradient regularization then steers training into flatter regions, preserving accuracy. In feedback training, gradient norm and reward accuracy move together. Reference resets of the penalty also land in flatter regions. Explicit gradient regularization with an efficient finite-difference estimate beats the penalty across diverse experiments. It earns a higher GPT-judged win rate in feedback training, fixates less on format in rule-based math rewards, and stops judge hacking in judge-based math tasks.
arxiv-2602-18337:
Sayantan Chakraborty proves new Sobolev-type inequalities for a class of curved complex spaces with positive Ricci curvature. His 2026 paper treats compact Kähler manifolds, a setting where analysis and geometry intertwine. Sobolev inequalities in this context bound a function's size by the size of its derivatives, a workhorse tool for partial differential equations.

The new inequalities extend what is known for these manifolds, giving analysts sharper control in the positive-curvature case. Chakraborty also revisits an existing Sobolev inequality through the classical approach of Bidaut-Véron and Véron, laying out its proof in that frame. The paper thus both advances the theory and clarifies an established route to it, serving geometers and analysts working on Kähler spaces.
arxiv-2602-18537:
Yiran Wang and three co-authors predict and diagnose crashes in machine learning notebooks before execution. Their 2026 paper notes Jupyter notebooks are popular for early machine learning development. ML notebooks are prone to bugs, crashes most disruptive, yet crash prediction and diagnosis remain unexplored.

The team presents CRANE-LLM, a runtime-augmented approach giving large language models runtime information from the notebook kernel, plus source code, to predict and diagnose target-cell crashes before execution. Evaluation on JunoBench, a benchmark of one hundred eleven Kaggle ML notebooks with crashes across libraries and types, shows runtime information greatly improves crash prediction and diagnosis. Gains reach seven to ten percentage points in accuracy and eight to eleven in F1-score, compared with source code alone across models: Gemini, Qwen, and GPT-5. Gains are larger when diagnosis is required, indicating runtime context matters more for crash causes than merely predicting their presence.
arxiv-2602-18637:
Alejandro de Miguel and two co-authors decode rat walking speed from brain waves. Their 2026 paper notes accurate neural decoding of locomotion promises advances in rehab, prosthetic control, and neural correlates of action. New studies decoded locomotion kinematics across species on treadmills, but decoding self-paced speed naturally remains scarce, modest in accuracy, and reliant on implants.

The team introduces an asynchronous brain-computer interface processing thirty-two-electrode EEG to decode speed from a non-motorized treadmill in self-paced walking. Using recurrent neural networks and over one hundred thirty-three hours of recordings, decoders map EEG activity to speed. They achieve a correlation of zero point eight eight for speed, driven by visual cortex electrodes and slow oscillations under eight hertz. Pre-training on a single session allowed decoding on later sessions from the same rat, suggesting shared neural signatures generalizing across sessions but not animals.
arxiv-2602-18737: Duc Duong, writing alone in 2026, studies elliptic equations through Green representations. These are functions that rebuild a solution and its derivatives from the source term. The work constructs those representation functions on a domain. It examines global Hölder continuity, a form of controlled smoothness, for solutions of this class of equations.
arxiv-2602-19137:
How much reasoning does answering a question really take? Siyuan Qiua, with two co-authors, answers with derivation depth in 2026. It is a computable metric of reasoning effort from a given premise set. Information is modelled in two layers. Abstract knowledge links to physical carriers. Core facts separate from operational shortcuts.

For any finite premise base, derivation depth is defined and proved computable. Reasoning traces are encoded, and incompressibility arguments yield fundamental bounds. Depth ties to descriptive complexity of queries. For frequent, information-rich queries, minimal description length grows with depth times log knowledge-base size. A practical tradeoff follows. Beyond a critical access threshold, caching beats recomputing. Optimal cache allocation becomes an optimisation problem with approximation guarantees. Noisy and incomplete bases are handled too.
arxiv-2602-19337:
Fix a unitary operator U on a complex Hilbert space, then conjugate it by every conjugation on that space. Javad Mashreghi and two co-authors study the resulting set, called the conjugate orbit of U. The adjoint operator always belongs to this orbit, they show. U itself belongs only when a unitary map matches it to its adjoint, making that membership uncommon.

The paper gives a full account of the conjugate orbit for the classical bilateral shift. It also treats unitary multiplication operators on the Lebesgue space of the unit circle. Higher-multiplicity shifts connect to translation and dilation maps on the real line. Finite unitary matrices supply many cases, including which diagonal matrices join the orbit.
arxiv-2602-19837:
People adapt to new tasks by reusing prior knowledge, a skill standard machine learning still struggles to match. A 2026 arXiv paper by Björn Hoppmann and Christoph Scholz surveys meta-learning and meta-reinforcement learning, tracing the path toward DeepMind's Adaptive Agent.

The survey gives a rigorous, task-based formalization of both fields, then chronicles the landmark algorithms that led to the Adaptive Agent. By consolidating the concepts needed to understand that generalist system and its relatives, it serves readers who want the lineage in one place. It shows how models learn to learn. It shows how they adapt fast from little data. And it shows how they move toward agents that handle many tasks rather than one.
arxiv-2602-19937:
Neural implicit fields represent three-dimensional shapes at arbitrary resolution, and they promise dense links between camera space and an object's standard space, even for regions the camera never sees. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yifei Shi and three co-authors improves pose estimation with such fields through better point sampling.

Predicting standard coordinates for unseen regions is hard without direct signals. Dense sampling across all of camera space can yield inaccurate results that hurt learning. The authors pair a rotation-equivariant convolutional network with a positive-incentive point sampling strategy. That strategy picks locations from the input itself. That combination boosts accuracy and training speed, beating prior methods on three pose data sets, with notable gains for unseen poses, heavy occlusion, novel geometry, and severe noise.
arxiv-2602-20037:
In five dimensions, the Curtright field is the dual graviton, and its asymptotic charges extend the familiar BMS algebra. A 2026 arXiv paper by Federico Manzoni, working alone, studies those charges in Minkowski spacetime.

Working in Bondi coordinates at future null infinity, the author imposes radiation fall-offs and fixes a de Donder-like gauge with an on-shell traceless condition, paralleling linearized gravity. Surface charges for residual gauge transformations are built as boundary integrals from Noether's two-form. In five dimensions, Hodge decompositions on the three-sphere split the charge into scalar, vector, and transverse-traceless sectors, parametrized respectively by a scalar function, a vector field, and a transverse-traceless tensor. The charge algebra closes only under a restriction on the vector field, yielding an abelian extension of a BMS-like algebra with a higher-spin-like supertranslation sector.
arxiv-2602-20137:
Chart rules distilled from decades of design and perception research keep visual communication trustworthy. Whether language models can enforce those rules directly has been unclear. A 2026 arXiv paper by Martin Sinnona and three co-authors tests language models against visualization rules, with ground truth verified by answer set programming.

Systems such as Draco encode rules as logical constraints, enabling precise automated checks. Maintaining symbolic encodings takes expert effort. That burden motivates language models as flexible rule validators instead. The authors turned part of Draco's constraint set into plain-language statements. They built a dataset of two thousand Vega-Lite examples, each marked with its rule violations. Models were tested on accuracy in detecting violations and on prompt adherence, whether outputs follow the required structured format. Frontier models achieve the strongest results, though remaining gaps are reported.
arxiv-2602-20237:
Two cosmic puzzles might have one source: the decay of a heavy neutrino that is its own antiparticle. Such decays could make both the surplus of matter over antimatter and the dark matter we observe. A 2026 arXiv paper by Henry G. F. McKenna and two co-authors studies a minimal model. In it, complex couplings break the symmetry between matter and antimatter in both the known sector and a dark sector.

Two paths are mapped. In wash-in, an early dark surplus is handed to known leptons through scattering. In co-genesis, a ranked coupling pattern boosts the asymmetry while keeping the seesaw mechanism at a low scale, around two teraelectronvolts. That ties light neutrino masses to the heavy neutrino's mass term and puts lepton-number breaking within reach of experiments. For dark matter heavier than ten gigaelectronvolts, co-genesis predicts scattering rates that current direct searches can test.
arxiv-2602-20337:
Erdem Sucu and İzzet Sakallı study a quantum probe of strong-field gravity: the gravitomagnetic Aharonov-Bohm effect for Cooper pairs in Kerr spacetime. Frame dragging from a spinning black hole creates an effective vector potential through an off-diagonal metric part, coupling to the phase of the superconducting condensate. The authors derive a gauge-invariant phase shift for a test setup with arms at two radii.

The phases reach huge values for Sgr A* and even larger ones for M87*, showing the huge gravitomagnetic flux near supermassive black holes. The analysis covers the test setup and shows tidal breakup of Cooper pairs is tiny at a range of at least ten Schwarzschild radii. The effect also connects to the Berry phase. Direct tests remain beyond current tools given the vast distances, but the method links quantum coherence to spacetime curvature in numbers.
arxiv-2602-20437:
Quantum diamond microscopes are strong but optics-heavy, and Ioannis Varveris and eight co-authors report progress toward a compact alternative: a CMOS-based quantum diamond biosensor. It pairs nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond with a custom forty-nanometre CMOS single-photon avalanche diode array. The system joins on-chip active quenching and digital readout with outside photon counting, compact microwave feed, and usable optical schemes for widefield optically detected magnetic resonance.

Design analysis covers glow pickup, sensor count-rate limits, and even fields, with bio fit and scale-up in mind. Using tagged human kidney cells as a test case, simple dipole math shows sub-microtesla response is needed to resolve resonance shifts within typical ensemble widths. The planned design reaches an estimated ninety nanoteslas per root hertz per pixel, mapping a usable path to compact sensors for measured imaging in complex biology.
arxiv-2602-20637:
The incompressible Navier-Stokes equation governs fluid flow, and Haithem Taha proves a match between it and the principle of minimum pressure gradient. The paper proves that a trial flow field solves the equation exactly when its instant-by-instant change minimizes the pressure force needed to enforce incompressibility. The principle is the minimum form of the Leray-Helmholtz projection.

Any allowed instant change from it hits the pressure-gradient minimum, while any other motion-allowed change needing a larger pressure force fails it. The principle thus offers a variational lens for intricate flow behavior. In a finite-mode setting with divergence-free modes, it matches classic Galerkin projection motion, and it extends that map beyond linear modal expansions to nonlinear and non-modal forms. The paper closes with guesses on balance and on Navier-Stokes flows moving to Euler flows as viscosity vanishes.
arxiv-2602-20837:
Spain voted in two general elections only months apart, in December 2015 and again in June 2016, giving researchers a rare near-repeat of a political contest. Samuel Martin-Gutierrez, Juan Losada, and Rosa Benito mine millions of Twitter messages from both campaigns in this 2026 arXiv paper. They ask which patterns of online behavior repeat when the context stays nearly the same.

Daily activity in the two campaigns correlates strongly, and the daily counts of tweets, retweets, and mentions follow a power law against the number of users taking part. The networks of mentions and retweets also keep the same shape from one election to the next. The authors conclude that collective online behavior has recurrent, robust patterns that survive a change of social context.
arxiv-2602-21137:
Urban traffic scenes challenge video-language models with unscripted multi-agent dynamics. Joseph Raj Vishal and nine co-authors introduce a benchmark for that challenge in this 2026 arXiv paper. UDVideoQA is built from sixteen hours of traffic footage at city intersections under varied traffic, weather, and light. An event-driven blur technique protects privacy without degrading scene fidelity.

Twenty-eight thousand question-answer pairs span eight hours of densely annotated video, about one question per second, across a hierarchy from basic understanding to counterfactual inference. Tests on ten leading video models expose a perception-reasoning gap: strong abstract reasoners still fail basic visual grounding. Fine-tuning a smaller model on the dataset closes much of that gap.
arxiv-2602-21337:
Teamwork needs common ground: shared beliefs, premises, goals, and alertness that let partners sync and fix mix-ups. Christian Poelitz, Finale Doshi-Velez, and Sian Lindley build a yardstick for that skill in human-AI teamwork in this 2026 arXiv paper. The yardstick rests on theories and observed studies of human-human teamwork.

A joint puzzle task demands round-by-round exchange, joint action, pointing sync, and repair under varying situation alertness. A check user study with humans teaming with an AI backs the yardstick: it echoes known human-human findings while showing clear splits in human-AI exchange. Workers get a tool for gauging whether AI partners can truly share ground with people.
arxiv-2602-21837:
Estimating gas traits from observed line emission often requires working out how light moves via emission and absorption, so-called radiative transfer. In radio and infrared astronomy, the Fortran code RADEX is a popular tool for non-LTE radiative transfer of a uniform medium in a simplified shape. The package on offer comes from Gianni Cataldi, who rebuilt RADEX from scratch in Python.

Users get a friendlier front end, quicker execution, and capabilities RADEX lacks, among them continuum effects plus lines that overlap. Every geometry the code supports, spheres included, gets its total flux worked out in one internally coherent calculation.
arxiv-2602-21937:
Tomer Adar studies how many samples it takes to estimate the L2 norm of a probability distribution, a quantity also called the collision norm. Earlier work by Batu and Canonne mapped the problem in depth, but their estimator did not always meet the best bound known for each specific distribution. The open question was whether any sampling method could match that per-instance bound.

Adar answers yes, with an unbiased estimator whose sample cost matches the instance-specific second-moment bound. He then proves that no estimator, biased or not, can do better on a given instance: the same bound is also a lower bound. The paper thus closes the gap between what was known to be possible and what was shown to be necessary for this core estimation task.
arxiv-2602-22337:
Cataclysmic variables pair a white dwarf with a companion star, and their boundary layers glow in X-rays in two distinct components: hard and soft. Nazma Islam and three co-authors study UU Aqr, a non-magnetic system with deep optical eclipses, hunting for its X-ray eclipse. A short Chandra exposure had hinted at one; new observations with NuSTAR and XMM-Newton settle the question.

Total eclipses appear in the hard X-ray band with both observatories, while the soft band shows no eclipse at all. The split pattern suggests hard emission comes from a compact region near the white dwarf, while soft emission comes from a more extended region that escapes eclipse. The split eclipse behavior thus maps where each X-ray component is born.
arxiv-2602-22937:
Suresan Pareth introduces bend-aware Sobolev tuning for neural networks on curved spaces. Standard training checks flat-space slopes, but networks living on curved spaces need geometry-aware learning. MSINO swaps in a matching Sobolev loss that aligns slopes through shifted carry, plus a Laplace smoothness term for steadiness.

Curved-space tuning theory yields shape-dependent constants behind three promises. First, a descent lemma with a curved-space smoothness constant. Second, a Sobolev Polyak-Lojasiewicz rule giving straight-line landing for curved-space gradient descent under plain step bounds. Third, a two-step Newton-Sobolev method with local squared shrink in bend-ruled zones. Unlike flat-space Sobolev training, MSINO gives promises that plainly track bend and carried Jacobians. Uses span surface imaging, physics-informed learning, and robotics on Lie groups. The setup joins value- and slope-based learning with bend-aware landing promises.
arxiv-2602-23137:
Raluca M. Balan and one co-author prove Gaussian fluctuations for the hyperbolic Anderson model with Lévy coloured noise. The work studies the asymptotic behaviour of the spatial integral of the solution in one dimension, driven by Lévy coloured noise. The spatial colouration kernel is either integrable or a Riesz kernel of order between zero and one. The Lévy measure has finite moments of order p and twice p for some p between one and two.

Applying a recent result of Trauthwein, the authors prove that the normalized spatial integral converges to the standard normal distribution as the radius tends to infinity. They give an estimate for the convergence rate in Fortet-Mourier, 1-Wasserstein, or Kolmogorov distance. A corresponding functional limit result is also provided, extending the central-limit picture to the full process.
arxiv-2602-23437:
Moyi Tian and three co-authors model how information spreads through networks of language-model agents linked to offline events. Online information increasingly feeds real-world instability, as automated accounts and language-model agents spread and amplify news. The paper asks how offline event types and assigned model 'personalities' shape online spread dynamics.

Two models are introduced: a stochastic agent-based network model, and differential equations from a mean-field approximation to it. Fitted to simulations of armed-conflict news spreading on social media, with agents carrying one of 32 personality trait profiles on k-regular random networks. The models perform surprisingly well.
