Despite the complexity of news events, personalities, and model behaviors, overall dynamics follow a Susceptible-Infected type model with just two transmission rates. Simple laws thus govern even agent-driven information spread.
arxiv-2602-23537:
Alyssa M. Guzman and one co-author track sink pixels in the Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys Wide Field Channel from 2015 to 2021. Sink pixels sit at least 10 electrons below the local background of LED-flashed short darks and trap significant charge during readout, corrupting science frames.

Over seven years, 5,430 sink pixels formed in WFC1 and 5,649 in WFC2. Creation rates ran about two point one five and two point two three pixels per day. By end of 2021, 44,068 sink pixels were detected, roughly zero point two five percent of the science frame. Return to normal values is rare. More flagged pixels sit near the serial register than the chip gap. Y-positions skew with a 'bounce-back' peak near the gap. Charge transfer losses steepen the gradient over time, worse farther from the register.
arxiv-2602-24037:
Vanya Priscillia Bendatu and Yao Lu present a portfolio reinforcement learning method that uses macro-conditioned scenario rollouts to survive market regime shifts. The 2026 paper notes that regime changes shift return distributions and degrade rebalancing policies trained on past markets, while history alone cannot show what would have happened under stress.

The proposed scenario-context rollout generates plausible next-day return scenarios under stress events. The authors analyze a subtle flaw: scenario-based rewards create a reward-transition mismatch in temporal-difference learning, destabilizing critic training toward a mixed evaluation target. Their fix builds a counterfactual next state from rollout continuations and augments the critic's bootstrap target, stabilizing learning with a workable bias-variance trade-off. Out-of-sample tests across many US equity and ETF universes show large gains in risk-adjusted return and smaller worst drawdowns over classic and RL baselines.
arxiv-2603-00237: Hook, Mondal and Mukherjee show friction between the thermal bath and axion strings drastically changes axion string network behaviour in DFSZ-like models with tree-level fermion-axion interactions, for lower axion decay constants. Friction delays scaling onset and raises axion energy density. Including friction, the standard mass near one milli-electronvolt still reproduces dark matter density, and a mass near 0.1 electronvolts also reproduces it.
arxiv-2603-00337: Fu, Kang, and Vazquez-Corral propose a conditional diffusion setup for low-light image enhancement, built around a Structured Control Embedding Module. The module splits a low-light image into light levels, light-invariant features, shadow priors, and color-invariant cues, which steer a U-Net diffusion model trained with a simple noise-prediction loss. Trained only on the LOLv1 set, the method is tested without fine-tuning on five other benchmarks. It achieves top quantitative and perceptual results, showing strong generalization.
arxiv-2603-00437: Fu tackles hallucinations in large vision language models with an internal self correction layer that needs no outside feedback. As models grow stronger, old bias and overthinking patterns fade, blunting earlier fixes. Her ICLA design lets each layer pull from all earlier layers through diagonal cross layer attention, refining hidden states during generation. Training only tiny added parameter counts on two current models, the method lifts visual grounding across several hallucination benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-00837: Poster, Chadwick, and Baker tackle transient drift in surface code correction, where noise rates vary over time rather than staying constant. They use transient surface code information to predict logical error rates live, mapping detector fire rate to logical error rate from real hardware samples. This predicts without usual characterisation overhead, and the prediction should stay accurate yet conservative, giving an upper estimate so responses run ahead of time. They pair the predictor with remapping drifted logical qubits to fresh tiles while their original tiles are recalibrated.
arxiv-2603-00937: Ishihara, Roga, and Takeoka show that device-independent conference key agreement works with W states as well as the usual GHZ states. The method lets several parties share a secret key without trusting their devices. They build Bell inequalities strongly violated by W states and work out the detection efficiencies needed for finite keys. A long-distance protocol using single-photon interference then stretches secret keys farther than GHZ-based versions, opening a second route to multipartite key distribution.
arxiv-2603-01037: Mohan and Dhir develop a quark-diquark effective mass formalism for heavy-baryon spectra across singly, doubly, and triply heavy sectors. One scenario treats all diquark channels dynamically, while a second restricts dynamics to scalar and axial-vector diquarks for a cleaner physical picture. Masses and couplings extracted from known baryons, with no sector-by-sector tuning, yield predictions matching experiment and lattice results in both charm and bottom sectors, giving a symmetry-constrained baseline.
arxiv-2603-01137: Ramachandran and five colleagues forecast day-ahead heat demand for district heating with deep learning on time-frequency pictures of decomposed demand and weather factors. Wavelet transforms let convolutional networks learn layered time patterns that plain time-domain models miss. Tested on multi-year data from Danish districts and cities in Denmark and Germany, the method cuts mean absolute error by 36 to 43 percent against the strongest baselines. It reaches accuracy up to 95 percent.
arxiv-2603-01237: Demni and three colleagues extend three robust tools from the line to the circle, giving steadier spread figures for direction or cyclic data that resist odd points. They study toughness through influence functions and scaled bias curves. They then derive robust gauges for circular distribution values, including the von Mises focus and wrapped normal spread values. Breakdown values and power are compared in tests. The best estimator yields a robust circular anomaly spotting tool, shown with a circular violin plot on three real data sets.
arxiv-2603-01337: Tan and Syrgkanis study tuning gauging in ill-posed inverse problems from given moment rules. Old methods like Regularized DeepIV need smoothness known in advance, often a beta rule, and wrong settings can slow settling or wobble. They offer a gap-principle plan picking settings, weighing bias-variance without knowing smoothness. It covers Regularized DeepIV and the Tikhonov Regularized Adversarial Estimator, with the same weak and strong rates. It also supports an adaptive doubly robust gauge for linear functions at the optimal better primal or dual rate.
arxiv-2603-01837:
Hongkun Dou, Zike Chen, Zeyu Li, and colleagues solve inverse problems with diffusion models and no gradient steps. Their 2026 work covers tasks like rebuilding an image from partial or noisy measurements. Most diffusion solvers need full knowledge of the measurement process to compute guiding gradients, which many real cases lack.

Their method, Constrained Particle Seeking, searches actively among candidate samples, called particles, for the best one. Constraints steer the search toward high-density regions of the learned prior, where plausible answers live. Only forward passes through the observation model are needed, so no gradient of that model is required. On image and scientific problems, results match gradient-based solvers in quality. Gradient-free rivals trail by a wide margin in the same tests, which makes the method handy where measurement models are opaque.
arxiv-2603-01937:
Vitalii Vertogradov proves universal size bounds for spherically symmetric black holes in this 2026 work. He assumes the weak energy condition, a rule that matter energy density never goes negative for any observer. The bounds cover event horizon radius, photon sphere radius, and shadow size.

All three measures reach their largest values for the Schwarzschild black hole, the simplest uncharged case. Any added matter that obeys the energy condition can only shrink those radii. Schwarzschild thus sets an absolute ceiling on observable size for static round black holes. For two-horizon cases, he bounds where the merged extremal horizon can sit, hinging on the lapse function tail. He also proves pressure at the outer horizon is never negative, which bars strong-energy-condition violation outside the hole.
arxiv-2603-02037:
F. Laytimi and W. Nahm extend a positivity result for vector bundles to three weaker positivity notions. Their 2026 work studies Schur functors, which build new bundles from a given bundle via partition data. Positivity here means forms of ampleness, a bigness trait that drives many geometry theorems.

Earlier, the pair showed ampleness of one Schur bundle forces ampleness of another when partitions compare by dominance. Dominance is a partial order that ranks partitions by their cumulative part sizes. The new proof covers k-ample, semiample, and nef bundles in one sweep. It exploits the shared algebraic nature of all three properties at once. Littlewood-Richardson rules, which govern how representations combine, supply the key combinatorial input for the argument.
arxiv-2603-02237:
Laziz Abdullaev, Noelle Wong, Ryan Lee, and colleagues refine how language models are steered in this 2026 paper. Steering nudges a model's inner signals at run time to change its behavior. Most methods use one global direction, found by averaging two contrasted data sets. That works only if a concept sits in one uniform cluster, which often fails.

Their method, CHaRS, views steering as moving mass between clustered groups. Concepts are modeled as mixes of clusters, each with its own center and spread. A transport plan between source and target clusters yields a steering shift per input. The shift is a smooth blend of cluster-level moves. Across many test settings, this input-aware steering controlled behavior better than one global direction.
arxiv-2603-02337:
Shadab Ahamed, Eshed Gal, Simon Ghyselincks, and colleagues fix a training bias in generative models in this 2026 paper. Flow and score models learn a vector field that morphs noise into data. The shape of the midway distributions steers how training unfolds. When that shape is stretched unevenly, some directions train fast and others stall.

High-variance directions get fitted quickly, while low-variance modes lag behind. Training then plateaus at weights that are far from optimal. The authors formalize that bias in simple settings they can solve exactly. Their fix reshapes the midway geometry with reversible maps that keep the final model unchanged. Condition labels guide the reshaping. Across image data sets, reshaped training avoided plateaus and produced better-trained models.
arxiv-2603-02437:
Cole Monnahan, Kasper Kristensen, James Thorson, and Bob Carpenter speed up Bayesian sampling in this 2026 paper. Hierarchical models are workhorses for understanding natural processes. The no-U-turn sampler explores them well but slows under strong correlations. High dimensions make that slowdown worse and cap practical model complexity.

Their Sparse NUTS reshapes the posterior before sampling, using a sparse precision matrix. That matrix comes cheaply from an approximation at the posterior's peak. The reshaped problem then goes to standard software for sampling. Across seventeen varied case studies, sampling converged ten to a hundred times faster. Gains vanish for funnel shapes, wide tails, or multiple modes, they note. Huge models with sparse, correlated structure benefit most.
arxiv-2603-02537:
Yunxiang Su, Tianjing Zeng, Zhongjun Ding, and colleagues organize language-model database operators in this 2026 paper. Databases now embed language models inside operator-like parts. Such parts filter with semantic rules, fill gaps, match entities, and more. Definitions and builds vary wildly, and benchmarks lag behind practice.

Their taxonomy sorts these operators into five types: Select, Match, Impute, Cluster, and Order. Operands and build variants are cataloged for each type. A new benchmark holds hundreds of single and multi-operator queries across many databases. Tests derive practical design lessons and best practices for each type. End-to-end tests compare existing multi-operator systems against a suite built on those practices. Future directions close the analysis.
arxiv-2603-02737:
Yiqi Liu, Yudong Pan, Mengdi Wang, and colleagues design a whole-wafer chip for running large AI models. Their 2026 system, Ouroboros, does its math inside the first memory layer itself. Normal designs waste time and power shuttling data back and forth between memory tiers.

Three ideas make the wafer-scale layout work. A token-level pipeline keeps cores busy when input lengths vary. A split cache scheme stores key-value data in spare scraps of memory. A placement method maps model blocks to nearby cores and routes around defects. In tests, Ouroboros ran more than four times faster than leading rival systems. It also used far less energy per task. The work shows in-memory chips can scale to full wafers.
arxiv-2603-03237:
Abhinav Natarajan, Thomas Chaplin, Joshua Bull, and colleagues map how multiple species share space, and how that sharing changes. Spatial patterns matter everywhere, from tumor growth to coral reef survival, but the standard topological toolkit reads one species at a time. Their 2026 framework extends persistent homology to genuinely multi-species data.

The method separates four kinds of shape features: those shared by several species, those erased by another species' presence, those visible only jointly, and those that persist regardless. Two demonstrations show the range. A synthetic tumor model falls into distinct behavioral regimes under the analysis, and colorectal cancer samples reveal which interspecies spatial interactions shift most as disease progresses. The scalable approach brings interaction-aware shape analysis to spatial biology.
arxiv-2603-03437:
Anas Zafar, Leema Krishna Murali, and Ashish Vashist check whether medical question-answering models actually look at the images they discuss. A worrying clue came first: text-only training sometimes matched image-based training on medical benchmarks, suggesting the tests never forced real visual dependence. Their 2026 framework swaps images behind the model's back, using real, blank, and shuffled pictures across four established benchmarks.

New scores measure visual reliance, image sensitivity, and a hallucination rate for visual claims made despite image-proof answers. Training with accuracy-only rewards improved scores while degrading grounding: models answered nearly as well with blank or wrong images, and made visual claims in most responses, a large share of them ungrounded. One model even scored better with mismatched images on a pathology benchmark. The authors demand grounding-aware tests and training goals that require true visual dependence.
arxiv-2603-04337: Qi and colleagues let language model CAD generation select faces and edges for real editing. Command sequences alone cannot pick entities, so chamfer or fillet work stays out of reach. Discretizing continuous sketch values can also break topology. Pointer-CAD folds B-rep geometry into pointer commands, building each step from text plus prior shape. A pointer picks the best matching candidate when an entity is needed, cutting quantization error, and about 575,000 annotated models train the system.
arxiv-2603-04437: Meng and colleagues split federated learning adaptively with ASFL on wireless networks. Weak clients face high delay and energy costs when training alone. ASFL offloads part of the model to the server and adapts the split and resources during training. Convergence analysis supports a joint performance and allocation problem solved by online block descent. Against five baselines, ASFL converges faster, cutting delay by up to 75 percent and energy by up to 80 percent.
arxiv-2603-04537: Jiang and colleagues survey 378 professional visual artists on generative AI at work. Artists face heavy critique of generative AI in media and scholarship, but workplace and career impacts need direct study. Most artists strongly oppose generative AI in any form, and negotiate its workplace inclusion through varied refusal strategies. Client, boss, and peer pressures shape use, alongside other environmental factors. Artists report overwhelmingly negative workplace impacts, with added stress and fewer job opportunities. The authors urge researchers to take artists' refusal wishes seriously.
arxiv-2603-04737: Yue and colleagues propose Interactive Benchmarks, a unified frame for testing model thinking. Fixed benchmarks grow full and stale, while taste-based scores lean on gut judgment. Smarts, they argue, includes choosing which facts to gather and how to apply them. The tests assess thinking through capped multi-turn chats. Two settings are tested: Interactive Proofs, with judge feedback on logic and math tasks, and Interactive Games, paying long-horizon play. Results show these tests give a more robust test, with big room for gains in interactive tests.
arxiv-2603-05037: Remi Petitpierre builds generalizable semantic splitting models and ontology for mixed historical map collections, which vary widely in style, scale, and geographic focus. Most map spotting work targets specialist models for homogeneous series. The author presents Semap, an open benchmark of 1,439 by hand annotated patches reflecting the variety of historical map documents. A method mixing procedural data synthesis with multiscale joining reaches state-of-the-art scores on HCMSSD and Semap, with scores largely stable across collections, scales, regions, and publication contexts.
arxiv-2603-05137: Leonardo Zambrano builds a robust classical shadow rule for quantum tests whose rounds are not independent and identically distributed. Real setups drift, suffer noise, and adapt to feedback, so successive states or channels depend on history. His truncated mean estimator predicts features of the averaged state or channel over time with the same sample hardness scaling as the standard independent case, governed by the shadow norm. The result stretches the shadow method well beyond its usual independence premise.
arxiv-2603-05437: Ye-Chan Kim and team offer SAIL for dense video captioning. Prior work used Gaussian masking. Current methods make non-overlapping masks without semantic consideration. SAIL constructs masks via alignment. A similarity-aware objective guides masks to emphasize regions similar to event captions. An LLM-based plan makes synthetic captions for sparse annotations. Synthetic captions enter through an inter-mask mechanism. ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 tests show state-of-the-art scores.
arxiv-2603-05937: Pham and team propose a Residual Masking Network for facial feeling reading, mixing deep skip and U-Net-like architectures. Auto facial feeling reading matters for human-computer contact, and focus tools offer one gain path. The novel masking idea boosts conv scores: a splitting network sharpens feature maps, letting the network focus on key information for correct calls. The method holds state-of-the-art score on the FER2013 and private VEMO data sets.
arxiv-2603-06237: Krishnaswamy and his team tackle witnesses for nonclassical light in photon counting devices. Their criteria rest on generalized counting statistics and moment matrices, with witnesses from half integer powers of click counts and moments. That gives an exponential rise in tests one can build for such light, noting even and odd parity states that need distinct witnesses. The method covers spatial and time multiplexing, where modes use on-off detectors and partial quasi photon number detectors. It reaches multimode cases, where nonclassical correlations and coincidences can be read straight.
arxiv-2603-06337: Assanioussi and colleagues ask whether length, area, or volume as seen by different observers Poisson commute or not. They compute the Poisson bracket of two lengths for a rigid rod measured by two different geodesic observers, one at rest and one moving relative to the rod. The calculation shows such observables generically fail to Poisson commute, even in Minkowski spacetime. That finding informs questions about a fundamental scale in quantum gravity.
arxiv-2603-06637: Boumali and Jafari study the Klein-Gordon oscillator under doubly relativity, where a Möbius-type Casimir tweak deforms the mass-shell condition. An arrow controls the (1+1)-dimensional deformation, giving different timelike, spacelike, and lightlike forms with spectra and answers for both branches. Time-like and light cases share identical spectra with a Planck-damped displacement breaking exact energy symmetry through a term linear in energy. The space case is same-toned to the plain one, though with complex-shifted waves and an operator that is non-Hermitian.
arxiv-2603-06837: Amaro and colleagues claim the first sighting of negative ion drift at surface pressure, measured at Gran Sasso with an optical time projection chamber in a helium mix. They give the first PMT waveform analysis in this regime, reading light patterns through a model joining track geometry with charge transport. Drift speeds imply mobilities matching negative ion transport. Time extension grows linearly with drift distance, revealing a faster minority carrier group beside the main species. The work opens a path toward large, low-diffusion optical chambers for rare event searches.
arxiv-2603-07337: Du carries Khovanov homology over from links in the three-sphere to links in spaces formed as connected sums of interval bundles over surfaces. He cuts each space along a separating sphere and builds two tangle invariants, one of type D and one of type A, for the two halves. Gluing the pair along their shared edge gives back the homology of the whole link. The half-space invariants follow Roberts.
arxiv-2603-07537: Kim presents the Kerr-Newman two-twistor particle through an all-orders worldline effective action in twistor particle theory. Working to all orders means the action is not truncated at any finite order of approximation. In self-dual backgrounds, exact hidden symmetries turn up. The contribution is that complete action plus the symmetry identification.
arxiv-2603-07737: Jang, Carrington and Begel argue assistive tools should aim at sovereignty, not just autonomy. Social access research pursues independence, yet disabled people's lives show rich tastes for leaning on others. Their 90 papers from 2011 to 2025 trace the tension through self-determination theory, meaning-making, and post-human tech science. They propose shared self-rule: choosing between going solo and leaning on others. They offer the Relational Sovereignty Matrix and four design moves, from a reframe of self-determination theory to weighing power in assistive tools.
arxiv-2603-07837: Miehling and colleagues present an open toolkit that lets users steer large language models in a planned way. It covers four levers: the prompt, the model weights and shape, the inner states, and the way text is drawn out. A shared pipeline lets several steering methods be joined, while task and test classes help compare them on the same job. The aim is to make new steering ideas easier to build and to judge fairly.
arxiv-2603-08237: Nabi and colleagues report heat and neutron scattering data on the spin-3/2 antiferromagnet Cs2CoI4, a member of the well-studied frustrated magnet family Cs2MX4. Unlike earlier members, Cs2CoI4 undergoes a structural phase transition, and the authors pin down its low-temperature crystal structure. This symmetry drop strongly affects both magnetic exchange interactions and single-ion anisotropy. Despite the large parameter space, they propose a spin Hamiltonian that captures the magnetic behavior of this compound.
arxiv-2603-08837: Ruijia Chen and colleagues help blind and low vision people mark places by voice on the move. GPS-based tools drift by meters and were never tested for making notes. NaviNote pairs vision-based precise positioning with an agentic design, and tests with 18 participants show better navigation and a richer sense of place.
arxiv-2603-08937: Cezar-Mihail Alexandru and colleagues improve unit interval selection in random-order streams. An algorithm sees unit-length intervals arrive in random order and must output a largest disjoint set using space proportional to the optimum. Their one-pass method reaches an expected approximation factor of 0.7401 with space proportional to the optimum, and factors above 8/9 demand at least input-size space.
arxiv-2603-09237: Neil Janwani and colleagues present MO-Playground, pairing a fast GPU-native algorithm for multi-objective reinforcement learning with a kit of GPU-run environments. Older methods fail to use large-scale parallel simulation, so training on hard robotics problems stays slow. Their MORLAX algorithm approximates Pareto sets within minutes, with large speed-ups over CPU approaches and better front quality. A custom BRUCE humanoid setup shows strong locomotion trade-offs across six objectives such as smoothness and efficiency.
arxiv-2603-09337: Yang Li and colleagues introduce the STAR Benchmark, which tests language models as agents in one-on-one zero-sum contests rather than on static puzzles. It frames reasoning as repeated, adaptive choice under time pressure, in both turn-based and real-time modes. A modular design with a standard API and full execution engine keeps runs reproducible and tasks customizable. A scoring suite grades not just wins but how well the agent plays, including how fast and cleanly it acts.
arxiv-2603-09837: Shang-Jie Liou and Herbert F. Fotso ask whether disorder can help a many particle quantum system change more gently. They pulse the interaction strength up and back down, then measure the energy left behind. Across rectangular, triangular and Gaussian pulse shapes, more disorder and longer pulses both leave less extra energy. Triangular pulses are gentlest, and the team also tracks how effective temperature shifts.
arxiv-2603-09937: Guy Hay and Nir Sharon build a framework for extrapolating a function past the region where it was sampled. Standard fits are tuned for interpolation, and small in domain errors can blow up outside it. Their anchor functions certify an upper bound on distance to the unknown target, defining a set that must contain it. Projecting any baseline fit onto that set provably never worsens the outside error.
arxiv-2603-10537: Gaishan Li and co-authors present an event-driven electronic skin that senses touch and classifies it with a spiking neural network. A piezoresistive array is scanned with an event-based binary search, which slashes scan counts and leaves the data stream almost entirely sparse. That stream feeds a spiking network on an FPGA, using far less compute and storage than a plain CNN. The system still read handwritten digits in real time with high accuracy.
arxiv-2603-10737: V Gelfreich and A Vieiro develop a theory of discrete averaging for systems that evolve by iterates of a map. Weighted averages over a segment of trajectory yield an autonomous vector field that approximates the map, a tool for finding adiabatic invariants. The method skips two steps classical averaging needs, and so can strengthen classical theorems. Applications cover near-identity maps and maps near a resonant fixed point, with explicit uniform bounds on the error.
arxiv-2603-10837: Juliann Geraci, Alexander B Kunin, and Alexandra Seceleanu study adjoints of morphisms between combinatorial neural codes. A code is a collection of subsets of an index set, and a morphism is a map between codes whose image coordinates are products of domain coordinates. Representing morphisms as binary matrices, they show each sits in a Galois connection, with its adjoint given by boolean multiplication by the matrix. This characterizes morphisms that factor a boolean matrix. Morphisms also order codes; the authors pin down covering relations via free neurons.
arxiv-2603-10937: Rajdeep Pathak, Amit Basak, and Sayantee Jana propose a practical way to measure how much membership information tabular synthetic data leaks about the real records behind it. Their method uses kernel density estimators on nearest-neighbor distances between synthetic and training records. It turns membership inference into a probabilistic score that ROC curves can judge. Tests across four datasets and six generators beat a prior baseline. A realistic attack variant needs only auxiliary data, sparing custodians expensive shadow models.
arxiv-2603-11137: Jongwoo Ko and coauthors stabilize on-policy distillation. It is the route for moving reasoning skill from teacher models into students. But it can wobble or transfer negatively. They show the process acts like policy optimization. The teacher-student log-likelihood ratio serves as a token-level reward. They build REOPOLD on that view. It uses mixture-based reward clipping, entropy-guided token sampling, and an exploration-to-refinement schedule. A 7B student matches a 32B teacher in visual reasoning, with far better sample efficiency.
arxiv-2603-11437: Bartusek and Goldin build unclonable encryption inside the Haar random oracle model. In that model, all parties can query a Haar random unitary and its related forms. Their scheme meets the standard unclonable indistinguishability notion of safety. It also allows secret key reuse and messages of any length. The result gives first evidence that such encryption can live in microcrypt, where even one-way functions might be absent. A unitary reprogramming lemma, built with path recording, does much of the heavy lifting.
arxiv-2603-11737: Gil and co-authors present the design of EPOS, a stellarator built to confine electron-positron plasmas. New tools shape both the plasma shape and the superconducting coils, with HTS strain kept in view. The design meets its targets for buildability and confinement at the same time. Coil robustness and quasisymmetry both reach good levels. Eight candidate designs pass all engineering checks. A final study tunes the candidates over radius and current, and picks the best EPOS design so far.
arxiv-2603-11937: Goubault and Médioni develop homological algebra for modules over non-unital rings and algebras. Dropping the unit changes the standard theory, so the basic machinery must be rebuilt for this setting. Their main use of the theory is directed homology for (∞,1)-categories and directed spaces. Relative homology and its exact sequence come with the package. The work lays groundwork for studying directed systems, where direction matters, with homological tools.
arxiv-2603-12337: Abaroa, Romero, and Bosch-Ramón cast dead microquasars as reservoirs of PeV cosmic rays. LHAASO found Galactic sources shining past 100 TeV whose engines stay unidentified. In their picture, mass transfer onto a stellar-mass black hole has already stopped for good. Jets once inflated a hot cocoon packed with cosmic rays from termination shocks. That cocoon then lives on as a vast store of PeV particles. Relic rays striking dense gas near star-forming regions yield delayed gamma rays, a match for some mystery sources.
arxiv-2603-12937: Tianwei Ye and co-authors match points between non-rigid 3D shapes with help from semantic cues. Hard cases bring non-isometric warps and topological noise that geometry alone cannot settle. Their SGMatch feeds geometric descriptors with features drawn from vision foundation models, guided by semantics. A local cross-attention module keeps structure continuity while doing so. Conditional flow matching then regularizes feature transport over time for coherent recovery. Benchmarks showed top results near isometry and steady gains on harder warps.
arxiv-2603-13037: Steven Motta and Gioele Nanni run federated few-shot learning on real neuromorphic edge hardware, a setting not tried before. On-chip plasticity gives binary weight updates, not the float gradients standard methods assume. Their two-node system uses BrainChip Akida processors across about 1,580 trials. Neuron-level joining of weights kept accuracy, while plain averaging destroyed it. Tuning the feature extractor drove most gains. Wider features helped federation more than solo learning, which points to shared prototype effects.
arxiv-2603-13137: Mahdi Najafi and co-authors constrain a model where dark energy switches on late, through a phase transition. In this critically emergent picture, dark energy is absent early and matters only after a set epoch. They fit it to microwave background, baryon acoustic oscillation, and supernova data. Several data mixes favor a nonzero transition point over the standard model. Statistical gauges back that edge in those mixes. The model does not fully ease the Hubble tension, though.
arxiv-2603-13237: Nasim Abdirahman Ismail and Enis Karaarslan propose a dual-path generative framework for zero-day fraud detection in banking. Fast checks must still meet GDPR demands for clear explanations, a hard trade-off. One path uses a Variational Autoencoder to model normal transactions and flag anomalies in under 50 milliseconds. A parallel Wasserstein GAN builds high-entropy fraud cases offline to stress-test the detection bounds. A Gumbel-Softmax estimator handles discrete banking data, and SHAP explanations run only on high-uncertainty cases.
arxiv-2603-13437: Eman Ouda and co-authors present a fully automated way to check paintings and write expert reports. Experts now read thermographic output by hand, in bespoke ways, so results are hard to compare across collections. Pulsed Active Infrared Thermography can show voids and past repairs under the surface, but its artifacts are often misread. Their pipeline runs three thermal methods and fuses the anomaly masks into one consensus map. A vision-language model then writes a structured report on each anomaly, its thermal behavior, and likely causes, with uncertainty stated.
arxiv-2603-13637: Jingxu Wu, Liangyu Luo, and Jie Shi derive how a phase transition can cause long-term dephasing near a Kerr black hole. Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals are a prime target for space-based gravitational-wave observatories like LISA. They model a first-order QCD phase transition in a neutron star that orbits a supermassive Kerr black hole. The transition sharply changes the tidal deformability of the star. With the Teukolsky formalism and Post-Newtonian expansions, they get a strict scaling law for the dephasing.
arxiv-2603-13737: Thinula De Silva and Pu Gao introduce a non-uniform notion of spread for the Kahn-Kalai framework. Building on Park and Vondrak's generalization of the Park-Pham theorem to non-uniform measures, they define spread in that setting. The framework yields 1-statements about subgraph containment for inhomogeneous random graphs, with forced edges allowed or not. They derive conditions for perfect matchings in the Stochastic Block Model and the Chung-Lu model. Those conditions are not tight in general but capture thresholds across broad regimes.
arxiv-2603-13837: Dixit and co-authors read out a superconducting transmon qubit with millimeter waves instead of microwaves. Their cavity runs at 34.7 GHz while the qubit sits at 3.1 GHz, a gap of more than ten times. The wide gap blocks unwanted state flips, even under strong drives. The team drives the cavity with over 100 photons and sees no stray transitions up to 1,000 photons. Readout fidelity passes 99% without a quantum-limited amplifier.
arxiv-2603-14137: Singh and co-authors track the nebular phase of the Type II supernova SN 2023ixf from day 150 to day 750. Optical and near-infrared data join published early photometry and JWST spectra. An early infrared excess and a later rebrightening trace echoes from dust around the star. The red wing of the H-alpha line fades from about day 132, the first direct sign of new dust forming inside the ejecta. Modeled dust mass stays tiny, between roughly one and sixty millionths of a solar mass.
arxiv-2603-14637: Conradt and Furst map self-assembly in paramagnetic colloidal suspensions under toggling magnetic fields. Strong steady fields arrest the particles. Switching the field on and off drives a dissipative route to dense, dynamic steady states. Shape and separation measures feed a k-means phase study. Six structural regimes emerge, from a structureless phase to sheets, ribbons and a spiky phase. Domain spread and alignment are charted as well. A mean-field energy model predicts the odd, stretched shapes that confinement produces.
arxiv-2603-14837: Yang and co-authors arbitrate disaster damage grades from street-view images with DamageArbiter. Vision models grade damage fast but act as black boxes. Their frame arbitrates fights between model types instead of trusting one. Image-only, text-only and CLIP-style multimodal models vote first. A light logistic meta-classifier settles cases where the votes clash. Tests use 2,556 post-disaster street images with written descriptions. Accuracy reaches 75.85%, past image-only and CLIP baselines. Overconfidence errors also shrink under arbitration, they report.
arxiv-2603-15037: Nallaguntla and co-authors release PhonemeDF, a dataset for audio deepfake detection split at the phoneme level. Real speech comes from LibriSpeech, while fake speech comes from four text-to-speech and three voice conversion systems. Each clip has phoneme-aligned TextGrid files from the Montreal Forced Aligner. The team measures the Kullback-Leibler divergence between real and synthetic phoneme distributions. They find this gap tracks how well classifiers spot the fakes, which flags the most telling phonemes.
arxiv-2603-15337: Khatab and Totzeck propose a consensus-based optimization method that uses Gaussian processes for problems posed in Sobolev spaces. Consensus methods let a swarm of points drift toward a shared best guess. Here, Gaussian processes supply sample functions that already meet initial values, boundary rules, or state limits. Known marginal properties of these processes make the infinite-dimensional scheme computable. Tests cover nonlinear boundary value problems with state constraints. They also cover optimal control of a system of ordinary differential equations, with sound results in both.
arxiv-2603-15437: Truter trains a deep reinforcement learning agent to hunt for Fano hypersurfaces in a vast integer lattice. Rewards are sparse, so a feedforward network learns to steer the search toward rich ground. Fano varieties with terminal singularities are core building blocks in algebraic geometry, yet their classification stays far from complete. The method found thousands of previously unknown examples. Hundreds of them lie beyond the reach of known search methods. The work shows learning-guided search can crack combinatorial spaces that resist brute force.
arxiv-2603-15637: Meyer and co-authors test a wave energy converter built from linked buoys. The buoys share one closed hydraulic circuit that drives a turbine. A 1:40 scale model ran in the wave tank at the University of Oslo. The team compared an eight-buoy layout with tight spacing and a four-buoy layout with wide spacing. The eight-buoy layout gave the most power per buoy. It also reacted more to wave period and heading. Wider spacing cut harmful buoy clashes.
arxiv-2603-16037: Chadjiconstantinidis and Bozikas define a new entropy for doubly truncated variables. Interval data, cut at both ends, need their own uncertainty gauge. Their cumulative residual interval entropy builds on residual entropy ideas. It generalizes two earlier entropy forms in one stroke. Hazard rate traits and truncated mean life results support the build. Several forms express the measure through reliability tools. Covariance and relevation routes give alternate readings of it. Bounds and monotonicity rules round out the study. Rising transforms connect the measure across scales.
arxiv-2603-16137: Zhai, Chen, and Zhang ground e-commerce search models in product facts safely. Shop search models hallucinate when product knowledge shifts fast. Jailbreak attacks add a compliance risk on top. Their SIA frame runs synthesize, inject, and align stages. Stage one builds text from knowledge graphs and behavior logs. Safety-aware data and reasoning chains enrich the corpus. Depth up-scaling then injects domain knowledge with few moved weights. Dual-path alignment tunes tasks and adversarial safety together. Live A/B tests at JD.com lift core search metrics.
arxiv-2603-16337: Roga shows that the friendship paradox vanishes under degree biased sampling. The paradox says your friends have more friends than you do, on average. He works on an undirected graph with this biased sampling rule. Under it, the expected degree of vertices equals that of their neighbors. So the paradox gap closes to zero. The result matches a random walk reaching its stationary state. It also matches flow conservation on the graph.
arxiv-2603-16537: Ng designs front-end guardrails for robots that hand out scarce help. People can fairly disagree about who gets helped first. Language model policies also shift with prompts and context. Ng proposes bounded calibration with contestability. Help modes come only from a governance-approved menu. The active mode stays legible at the point of deferral. Users get a path to contest one outcome, not the whole rule. A public-concourse robot story illustrates the pattern.
arxiv-2603-16737: Xiong, Sinha, He, and Zhang improve visual in-context learning by retrieving counterfactuals. Vision-language models often tangle fine visual traits with outcomes. In-context learning adapts them, but demo choice decides the gain. Similarity search picks correlated, non-causal examples and deepens spurious links. Their CIRCLES framework builds demo sets by composed image retrieval. Attribute-guided queries fetch counterfactual-style contrasts for the target. Models then reason about causes, not surface correlations. Gains were broad, largest for small models under scarce information.
arxiv-2603-17037: Halloran and co-authors probe how magnetic field direction affects Kondo hybridization in the superconductor UTe2. Neutron scattering had shown that the main low energy response sits along Brillouin zone boundaries. The team applies fields along the a axis, up to 13 tesla. They find the peak of the inelastic neutron signal rises in energy, with a change in slope near 7 tesla. This mirrors features in the resistivity tied to Kondo hybridization. They suggest fields near 7 tesla change the mixing between f electrons and the conduction band.
arxiv-2603-17237: Guo and co-authors study ultralight scalar dark matter that couples off diagonally to down type quarks. Such dark matter acts as a coherent background field that can shift Standard Model parameters over time. Working in an effective field theory, the authors diagonalize the quark mass matrix in this background. They derive formulas for wobbling shifts in quark masses and CKM parameters. They then use flavor measurements, nuclear beta decays, atomic clocks, and pulsar timing to bound the couplings.
arxiv-2603-17937: Gholap and co-authors name overdamped gauge phonons as a fresh route to non-Fermi-liquid behavior. These phonons couple to electron currents, not densities, in Dirac materials. That mimics transverse gauge-field effects with no quantum critical point nearby. Two numbers, orbital susceptibility and a damping ratio, set the low-energy story, they show. Strong damping bends quasiparticles far from Fermi-liquid form. Twisted bilayer graphene is a prime place to look.
arxiv-2603-18137: Xu, Matar, and Kee explain odd magnetothermal transport in frustrated magnets by splitting shear and compression phonons. They derive a spin-phonon Hamiltonian where each phonon type couples to distinct spin operators. In the strong spin-orbit limit, this mode-selective coupling is set by symmetry. Compression and shear modes then carry spin heat in different field ranges. Landauer transport plus exact diagonalization yields a peak-dip-peak field pattern seen in Mott insulators.
arxiv-2603-18237: Wang and Zhang propose gradient-informed temporal sampling for training PDE surrogate models. Uniform sampling may not give the best data under a fixed budget. Past samplers collapse into dense regions or keep diversity without model focus. GITS joins pilot-model gradients with set-level temporal coverage for balance. It cuts rollout error across PDE systems, backbones, and sample ratios, with ablation support for both parts.
arxiv-2603-18437: Song, Yang, and Ouyang study how hypothetical exomoons would shape planetary thermal phase curves. No exomoon is confirmed yet, though over 200 moons exist in the Solar System. They simulate phase curves with mutual transits and occultations across many orbital periods. Close airless moons add strong day-night contrast and phase-dependent transit depths. Occultation signals reach about 20 ppm for long-period systems and up to 100 ppm for short-period ones.
arxiv-2603-18837: Halder, Hajisharifi, Bakhshaei, and Rozza shrink brain blood flow simulations with reduced order models. Full 3D flow runs on an idealized basilar artery split are costly. Proper orthogonal decomposition first compresses flow snapshots into a small latent space. A POD-Galerkin model projects the Navier-Stokes equations onto that basis. A rival POD-reservoir model learns coefficient dynamics from data with a recurrent net. A rich training signal with many harmonics speeds learning. Both models run 100 to 1,000 times faster than full runs while tracking wall shear stress well.
arxiv-2603-19537: Ma and Zhu present U-Discovery, a tool that finds the laws behind how cities change over time. City systems lack the fixed first principles that physics has. Their setup splits change into two parts: a steady spatial interaction part and a self-driven part. A language model proposes draft laws, drawing on past studies. A neural fit scores each draft on fit error and simplicity. On made-up data, the tool found the true law. Tests on real activity data from Hennepin County, Minnesota, also went well.
arxiv-2603-19737: Liu, Gao, and Niu propose a magnon-driven anomalous Hall effect in altermagnets. It comes from coupling between chiral magnons and chiral electron motion. Using density-matrix perturbation theory and symmetry checks, they find a sharp rule. The Hall signal depends only on the chirality of the Néel-order precession. That sets it apart from the Hall effect of the static Néel order. It can appear even where the static effect is banned by symmetry. They show it in a lattice model with the symmetry of CrSb.
arxiv-2603-19837: Wei, Tang, and Tao use the structure function to sort variability in active galactic nuclei. They draw samples from OVRO, ASAS-SN, and Fermi data. A normalized structure function is fit with a power-law model in three bands. Two parameters from the fits separate the radio, optical, and gamma-ray samples well. The same split also separates BL Lac objects from flat-spectrum radio quasars. The authors link optical variability to accretion disk fluctuations. Radio and gamma-ray variability is tied to relativistic jet radiation instead.
arxiv-2603-20137: Farahmand Bafi, Evans, and Maciolek study two kinds of colloids mixed in a near critical solvent. One colloid type alone in such a solvent already shows rich phase behavior. Their lattice model treats the full four component mixture in three dimensions. Both colloid types are hard spheres of equal size. They differ only in how much they favor one solvent species. Small shifts in the mix ratio reshape the phase diagram topology. The paths of two lines of triple points stand out as especially intricate.
arxiv-2603-20237: Muhammad shows how careless panel building distorts financial data from the Dhaka Stock Exchange. Researchers often align stocks to one calendar, as if all had traded from the start. Securities listed later then gain fake early price history. His coverage-aware framework stores each instrument's true observation window as metadata. An availability matrix enforces those windows during panel construction. Data cover 486 instruments from 2012 to 2026. Forward-filling alone cut measured volatility by about 20 percent on average. Variance distortions passed 26 percent in most tested instruments, a lower bound on the harm.
arxiv-2603-20437: Padovani and Fiore present yProv4DV, a library for reproducible data visualization in Python. Plots often circulate without the code and data needed to rebuild them. Existing tools focus on pipelines, not the short scripts researchers write. Their library tracks inputs, outputs, and source files in one call. Provenance records then let others rebuild a figure exactly. The design stays lightweight to fit minimalist plotting habits. It fills a real gap in reproducible research workflows.
arxiv-2603-20537: Siboni and co-authors study how language models can synthesize control policies as readable code. Industrial control needs policies that stay interpretable and auditable. Their testbed is hot steel rolling, simulated with hard equipment limits. A language model proposes and refines Python controllers from simulator feedback. Across 52 runs, moderate run lengths matched the best budget split. Luby-style restarts reached that regime without problem-specific tuning. A small per-job portfolio beat the single best heuristic. An audit pipeline then proved key safety properties automatically.
arxiv-2603-20637: Fang and co-authors present AEGIS, a multi agent system that hunts code flaws with grounded proof. Past tools let agents debate with no fixed evidence base. That freedom leads to made up links between code parts. AEGIS starts from suspect code spots, called clues. It then traces each clue's data flow on a graph of the whole repository. One agent argues both sides of exploit risk. An audit agent can veto claims the trace does not support.
arxiv-2603-20837: The ATLAS Collaboration searches for invisible particles in photon induced collisions with tagged forward protons. Two photons can fuse to make a visible particle plus an unseen partner. ATLAS forward proton detectors measure the outgoing proton energies. Subtracting the visible system's momentum gives the missing mass of the unseen part. They scan this spectrum from 100 to 900 GeV for a narrow resonance. The data come from 2017 running at 13 TeV. No significant excess appeared over Standard Model expectations. Limits on cross sections follow for three signal models.
arxiv-2603-21337: Nekrich and Rahul design an optimal-cost algorithm to build shallow cuttings for 3-D dominance ranges in the I/O model. Shallow cuttings are a core tool for range searching in computational geometry and spatial databases. An optimal internal memory algorithm existed, but no efficient I/O construction was known. Their method performs a number of I/Os that matches the optimal bound, given block and memory sizes. As applications, they give fast algorithms for offline 3-D dominance reporting and approximate dominance counting.
arxiv-2603-21437: Gao and co-authors argue that pooling, not text length alone, drives a key flaw in text embeddings. When a model pools diverse sentences into one vector, meaning gets diluted and vectors crowd together. They prove this effect in a unified framework and define semantic shift, the drift of meaning inside a text. Controlled tests show semantic shift best predicts severe embedding crowding. Retrieval tests add that anisotropy hurts mainly when strong semantic shift causes it.
arxiv-2603-21537: Ogawa and co-authors design large fixed-frequency superconducting qubit systems around a gate called siZZle-CZ. Fixed-frequency transmons are simple and long-lived, but frequency collisions cut fabrication yield as systems grow. Cross-resonance gates restrict drive frequencies, which shrinks the design space. The siZZle gate allows arbitrary drive choices, and simulations show wide windows with controlled-Z fidelity above 99.6 percent. Using those windows, they lay out lattices of over 1,000 qubits. Even with fabrication spread, zero-collision yields reach 80 to 100 percent.
arxiv-2603-21737: Hvozd and co-authors extend scaled particle theory to hard-sphere fluids trapped in messy porous media. The porous matrix itself is made of hard spheres with a spread of sizes. Their fully analytic formulas cover the fluid's thermodynamic properties, including chemical potentials. The treatment reaches higher matrix packing fractions than earlier versions. It also handles varied matrix density, size spread, and particle size distributions. Results match Monte Carlo simulations and integral-equation theories well across a broad range of settings, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-21837: Hu and co-authors compare two galaxy formation simulations that start from the same initial conditions but use different subgrid physics. The APOSTLE and AURIGA runs thus isolate how baryonic recipes shape Milky Way-like galaxies. AURIGA galaxies end up with higher stellar masses and surface densities, driven by faster gas cooling from the halo. Both runs form clear disks, but AURIGA disks form earlier and show stronger bars and spiral arms. Satellites differ too: AURIGA makes heavier ones, while counts above a million solar masses stay similar.
arxiv-2603-21937: Tian and co-authors release MultiBind, a benchmark for a sneaky failure in multi-subject generation: traits landing on the wrong person. Users feed several subject photos plus long per-person prompts, and models often swap attributes. MultiBind is built from real multi-person photos, with ordered subject crops, masks, clean references, and an inpainted background. Its scoring matches generated people to the true slots and checks identity, appearance, pose, and expression separately. Subtracting true similarity patterns splits quality loss from real mix-ups: drift, swaps, and blending.
arxiv-2603-22137: Ono builds a route to nonlinear response functions, which encode how systems react to fields. Such functions also underpin nonlinear transport and optical effects. Direct evaluation gets costly fast, since multipoint correlators scale combinatorially. Ono's method takes a Gateaux derivative in field space. That yields a closed set of tangent equations of motion. Running them beside the base dynamics isolates each response order cleanly. He demonstrates fifth-order response in a solid-state electron model. In a Duffing oscillator, he reaches the 49th order accurately.
arxiv-2603-22237: Sahasrabuddhe and Lambiotte extend information theory for compositional data. A concave diversity index can induce a measure of collection spread. Shannon entropy and mutual information form the classic pair. The authors add category similarity into the alpha-logarithmic entropy family. They disprove a claimed general concavity result. For alpha equal to 3, they prove the strict concavity region is always convex. The new tools compare compositions much faster than optimal transport. Tests cover jobs across England and Wales, plus ecological data.
arxiv-2603-22537: Desai and co-authors check how well lab models of scalar vortex coronagraph masks match reality. Such masks must dim starlight by ten orders of magnitude so future telescopes can image Earth-like planets. The scalar design keeps both polarizations in one path, which simplifies the optics. The team measures mask defects with phase metrology and feeds the results into their control model. They test how errors in angle or wavelength degrade the wavefront control. Lab results from the JPL testbed agree well with the model.
arxiv-2603-22637: Saha, Chan, and Sultana analyze data protection law in Bangladesh. Fast growth in digital services, finance, and telecoms has raised the amount of personal data collected. The state replied with three ordinances in 2025, covering personal data, cyber security, and data governance. The authors review all three as one legal regime. They map how the rules fit together and where they fall short. Key barriers include weak institutional independence and uneven enforcement capacity. The laws also assume lone, self-reliant data subjects, hiding informal data flows and human helpers.
arxiv-2603-22837: Aizaz and Nguyen analyze personas that language models generate for Palestinian and Israeli identities. Five models are tested across 640 conditions, varying war context and assigned role. In war settings, Palestinian profiles often get lower status and survival-focused roles. Israeli profiles mostly keep middle-class status and specialist jobs. Prompts that warn against harmful assumptions change the outputs in varied ways. The deeper status gap often stays, though. Reasoning traces mention fairness, yet final personas do not mirror those ideas in a steady way.
arxiv-2603-22937: Saha reports the first direct measurement of radial flow in heavy-ion collisions with ALICE. The probe is an observable that tracks transverse momentum, called v0. Data come from lead-lead collisions at high energy. Results cover charged hadrons, pions, kaons, and protons across centrality ranges. A pseudorapidity gap cuts short-range nonflow effects. At low momentum, a clear mass ordering appears, matching hydrodynamic hopes. At higher momentum, protons show larger values than pions and kaons. That fits quark recombination models, Saha notes.
arxiv-2603-23037: Impraimakis, Vazquez, and Zhou build an interpretable layer over YOLOv10 object detection. Detectors give confidence scores that users cannot easily judge. A Kolmogorov-Arnold network acts as a post-hoc surrogate for trust. It models detection trust from seven geometric and semantic features. Its additive spline form shows each feature's effect directly. A BLIP model adds scene captions for a light multimodal interface. Tests on COCO and campus images flag low-trust predictions under blur or occlusion. The system supports review and risk choices downstream.
arxiv-2603-23237: Santini and fifteen co-authors report a way to count photons inside a working nanowire laser. Such lasers are tiny, tunable light sources prized for integrated optics. Their inner behavior is hard to probe because light diffraction blurs the nanoscale view. The team pairs near-field electron microscopy with far-field photon counts. On a gallium nitride nanowire laser, they read the absolute photon number above threshold. Their time resolution reaches below a picosecond. They also map the lasing mode's shape at the nanometer scale.
arxiv-2603-23637: Xu and five co-authors rebuild 3D Gaussian splatting on stochastic ray tracing. Ray-traced splatting dodges the limits of raster views, like fake shadows and stiff cameras. Its cost sits in sorting every Gaussian a ray touches. Their method samples a few Gaussians per ray instead of sorting them all. A Monte Carlo estimator gives clean gradients from that sample. For plain scenes it matches raster quality and speed, and beats sorting tracers. For lit scenes it traces true shadow rays and tops prior fidelity.
arxiv-2603-23737: Wei and co-authors study a risk-aware form of linear-quadratic regulation. Their control problem runs in discrete time over a finite horizon. It penalizes both temporal swings and random swings in the state path. They extend a risk measure called predictive variance to states that are coupled across time. This lets a controller trade steady regulation against lower variability, with clear sensitivity to risk. Numerical examples show how temporal coupling changes both risk-aware and risk-neutral control.
arxiv-2603-24237: Perrin and co-authors turn correlated atom loss into a resource for quantum error correction. Atom loss is a top error source in neutral-atom processors, and its errors come correlated. Their decoder builds a loss graph for a surface code with teleportation-based loss detection. It updates loss probabilities as data arrive, in a form that runs in parallel and in real time. Versus a decoder that assumes independent loss, logical errors drop by up to ten times. The loss threshold rises from 3.2 to 4 percent.
arxiv-2603-24437: The Belle and Belle II Collaborations report a search for the rare decay of a B meson into a kaon and two tau leptons. The search uses electron-positron collision data with about 1.2 billion Upsilon(4S) mesons. One B meson is fully rebuilt from its hadronic decay, and the rest of the event is scanned for the signal. No significant excess over background appears. The team sets an upper limit on the decay rate at 90 percent confidence, four times tighter than the only prior result.
arxiv-2603-24637: Damele studies the multiplicative group of a two-sided skew brace whose additive group is solvable. A skew brace carries two group operations linked by a compatibility law. Damele proves that every finite quotient of the multiplicative group is solvable. In particular, the result recovers Nasybullov's theorem in the finite case. It also extends that theorem to arbitrary two-sided skew braces of solvable type, with no finiteness assumed on the brace itself. The work connects brace structure with classic solvability questions in group theory.
arxiv-2603-24737: Nowicki-Koth develops a low-regularity global well-posedness theory for the generalised Zakharov-Kuznetsov equation. The Cauchy problem is posed on the plane and on a mixed domain of a line times a torus. Using Strichartz-type estimates within the I-method, he proves global well-posedness at low Sobolev regularity. Thresholds differ by case: above 11/13 for the standard equation on the mixed domain, and above 2/3 or 36/49 for the modified equation. He also shows higher Sobolev norms of smooth solutions grow at most polynomially in time.
arxiv-2603-24837: Lekssays introduces codebadger, a server that bridges code property graphs and language models for program analysis. Language models cannot load whole repositories, and code embeddings miss inter-procedural data flow. Codebadger exposes Joern's graph engine through high-level tools for slicing, taint tracking, data flow analysis, and semantic navigation. The model explores large codebases in a targeted way instead of reading files exhaustively. Demonstrations include auditing an 8,000-method codebase, finding a new buffer overflow in libtiff, and patching an integer overflow in libxml2 correctly on the first attempt.
arxiv-2603-24937: Mohov and Lyutikov simulate magnetised bubbles blown by active galactic nuclei into galaxy cluster gas. The bubbles quickly relax to a spheromak-like state with plasma beta near one. Rising through the cluster medium, they are magnetically stabilised against interface instabilities and stay coherent for a long time. Internal kink instabilities tilt the bubbles only slowly. The results explain the observed longevity of cluster cavities. Slowly rising bubbles deposit roughly their injected energy in their wake, reheating cluster cores gently.
arxiv-2603-25037: Qi and co-authors pack twenty years of Earth scans into a queryable neural cube called GeoNDC. Satellite archives sit as stacks of raster files, which are heavy to store, move, and search. GeoNDC instead learns a smooth field over space and time that can answer point queries on plain hardware. On the global MODIS record it shrinks the archive about 95 to 1, down to 0.44 gigabytes, with high fidelity. On Sentinel-2 views it rebuilds clear scenes through fake cloud gaps. Plant trait products come back with near-perfect scores.
arxiv-2603-25337: Matsuoka shows that linear lambda terms can express any multiple-valued function. The terms are typed in a second-order polymorphic system. He gives two styles of encoding. One mimics switching circuits, gate by gate. The other builds the function by induction, in a classic math style. He also discusses ways to shrink both forms. A case study then shows where the approach could apply. The result links a typed lambda calculus to a basic question about finite functions.
arxiv-2603-25637: Takahashi presents Conchordal, a tool that makes music through artificial life. Its sound agents act in a field built from how consonant tones sound to the ear. No scales or chord rules are built in. Agents shift pitch by small local steps. They gain or lose energy based on consonance. They also lock their timing through phase coupling. In tests, consonant search gave rich polyphony. Selection effects died out when recharge was off. Guided respawn built more structure over generations.
arxiv-2603-25837: Bečirević and co-authors reexamine recent BESIII results on the decay D to K mu nu. The measured rate and forward-backward asymmetry sit a bit off Standard Model values. A proposed fix turns on a complex new-physics coupling. The authors show this fix clashes with LHC bounds from Drell-Yan tails. Other scenarios fit both low- and high-energy limits, they find. But their couplings look too small to see in most integrated measures. Angular data from two other decay modes may still reveal them.
arxiv-2603-25937: Guerrier and co-authors test whether vision foundation models can truly navigate in the real world. They evaluate five visual navigation models on two robot platforms. The trials span five indoor and outdoor settings. Beyond success rate, they score path quality and vision-based goal recognition. They also probe robustness with motion blur and sunflare. Three flaws stand out, they report. Models collide often, which shows weak grasp of geometry. They confuse look-alike places in repeating scenes. Performance also drops when conditions shift.
arxiv-2603-26637: Rogenmoser and co-authors close the gaps in fault protection for chips exposed to radiation. Guarding cores and memories alone leaves voting logic and interconnects as single points of failure. Their plan overlaps several component-level defences so the whole system-on-chip stays covered end to end. They show the design on a RISC-V microcontroller, tested by simulation-based fault injection. The chip tolerates over 99.9% of injected upsets in both RTL and netlist form. It also cuts implementation overhead by 22% versus one global scheme.
arxiv-2603-26737: Guo, Lu, Feng, and Sun propose SSV-CoT, a visual reasoning method that looks at an image in a planned order. Multimodal models usually freeze the image into static tokens and reason only in text. Human sight instead shifts focus from the most telling region to weaker cues. A saliency map first ranks the regions that matter for the question. Reasoning then follows that order, building a curriculum-like path from primary to secondary evidence. Trained end to end, the method gains across varied visual reasoning tests.
arxiv-2603-26937: Patra and co-authors model how climate variables and ice volume moved together over late Pleistocene glacial cycles. They build a five-variable stochastic model from reconstructed paleoclimate records. The variables are ice volume, carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, and temperature. Coupling terms let each variable influence the others. Multifractal analysis separates near-red-noise behavior below the 100,000-year cycle from white noise above it. Response functions computed from the model match the empirical data. Ice volume, carbon dioxide, and temperature stabilize each other in the model.
arxiv-2603-27137: Basti and co-authors frame evolutionary clustering as a quasi-stationary mean field game. Each cluster is a probability density moved by a Fokker-Planck equation. A stationary Hamilton-Jacobi equation supplies the velocity field for each density. The setup fixes the number of clusters but not their shapes. For Gaussian clusters, affine rules reproduce classic expectation-maximization paths exactly. Time-averaged likelihood goals improve smoothness when clusters overlap or noise intrudes. A density-based version handles non-Gaussian parts as well. Tests compare against snapshot and smoothed EM rivals.
arxiv-2603-27237: Marmoret and co-authors test whether pre-trained deep learning models can predict musical groove ratings from audio. Groove spans several dimensions that people rate by feel. Seven state-of-the-art models supplied audio vectors for the task. The team sets them against handcrafted audio features. Outputs from source-split tracks isolate what each part adds. Results split clearly by musical style across funk, pop, and rock tracks. Deep vectors caught style-bound groove cues that classic features missed. The findings support vector learning for music research.
arxiv-2603-27437: Zhang and co-authors improve how vision-language models judge 3D space. Most models fuse shape data only at deep layers. That habit wastes rich cues from early layers. SpatialStack aligns sight, shape, and words at many levels. Local shape detail and broad scene sense both survive. Their model, VLM-SpatialStack, tops several 3D reasoning tests. Extra checks show the layered fusion helps across tasks. The method also transfers well to new scene types.
arxiv-2603-27937: Pan surveys locally analytic vectors in modular curve cohomology. Completed cohomology of modular curves holds these vectors. His works map their structure across several papers. The survey gathers those results in one place. It serves readers tracking the p-adic Langlands area. Key constructions and outcomes are summarized. Links between papers are made explicit. The piece is a guide to his research line.
arxiv-2603-28237: Hacker and nine co-authors weigh the exoplanet LHS 3844 b, an Earth-size world on a very short orbit. Its mass had never been measured, though it is a prime target for the Webb telescope. They analyze 25 ESPRESSO radial velocity measures under 15 rival noise and drift models. The planet's signal holds up in every model. The mass comes out at 2.27 Earth masses, with a density that fits a dry, rocky body like Earth.
arxiv-2603-28337: Wang, Wei, and Huang extend a model of K-star Sigma photoproduction to cover spin data as well as cross sections. Their effective Lagrangian fit already matched CLAS data, with a Delta(1905) resonance playing a key role. Adding LEPS spin density data gives two fits that work equally well. They differ on how much kappa exchange matters, which undercuts older claims that it dominates. Predictions at higher photon energy may settle the question.
arxiv-2603-28437: Laurent, Munthe-Kaas, and S generalize aromatic trees to design integrators that keep divergence at zero on manifolds. Aromatic Butcher series already help build volume-preserving methods in flat space. The new planar aromatic trees fit curved settings and group integrators. The authors prove these trees span the free tracial post-Lie-Rinehart algebra. From them they derive fresh Lie-group methods that hold geometric divergence-free traits to high order. The work links combinatorics, algebra, and numerics.
arxiv-2603-28537: Šindelář and four co-authors build large training sets for automatic grading of short student answers, starting from a small private one. The work ties to PISA, where grading must dodge language gaps and rater bias. Their methods recast the secret data into simple derived formats that hide its content. Three surrogate sets came out closer to the real one than plain prompt-made text. Early tests hint one method may also train better grading models.
arxiv-2603-28637: Flin and co-authors give a distributed algorithm for vertex coloring with a near-optimal number of colors. For a graph with maximum degree Δ, they define a threshold based on the largest valid k. Given any smaller k, their LOCAL algorithm finds a valid coloring with Δ minus k colors, if one exists. It runs in a time that is close to the known lower bound. For small Δ, it improves on the prior best time. For very large Δ, it runs in log-star time.
arxiv-2603-28937: Ugail and Howard present a neural tension operator for curve subdivision in spaces of constant curvature. Classic schemes use one global tension value and need apart forms for Euclidean, spherical, and hyperbolic spaces. Their shared network predicts a per-edge insertion angle from local features and a geometry embedding. A safety bound keeps each new vertex in a valid angular range. On 240 held out curves, the method cut bending energy and angular roughness below fixed tension baselines. On an orbital ground track test, bending energy fell by 41 percent.
arxiv-2603-29037: Whalley and co-authors introduce Singing Materials, a project that turns phonon spectra into sound. Solid materials vibrate at the atomic scale, and those vibrations set key traits like strength and heat transport. Their Python package, SingingMaterials, turns materials data into sound. It links to the Materials Project database and can extend to new sources. Three approaches are supported: spectral, synthesised, and sample based. A user study tested if listeners can tell material properties apart from sound. Sound gave a clear, added way to explore vibrational data.
arxiv-2603-29137: Ramani and Kumar present a minimal axiom basis for BCH-algebras. The standard setup uses three axioms: two equations and one quasi-identity. Using automated theorem proving, they replace both equations with a single 14-symbol equation. The quasi-identity stays unchanged. They then prove that this replacement is strictly minimal. An exhaustive machine-assisted search with finite countermodels shows no equation of 12 or fewer symbols works. Derivations were checked with Prover9, and countermodels came from Mace4.
arxiv-2603-29437: Li and co-authors present SeGPruner, a method that trims visual tokens for 3D question answering. Multi-view images create huge token sets that slow inference. Most pruners target 2D inputs or use weak geometry cues. SeGPruner first keeps tokens tied to key objects by attention scores. A second step adds tokens that widen spatial coverage. It weighs semantic relevance against 3D distance. On ScanQA and OpenEQA, token budgets fell by 91 percent. Latency fell by 86 percent, with accuracy kept competitive.
arxiv-2603-29637: Dengler derives the phase diagram of the Poland-Scheraga model of DNA melting in closed form. The model describes how a long DNA molecule denatures. He works through a field theory twin of the lattice model. For a wider model with excluded-volume effects, he runs a one-loop renormalization calculation. Two stable fixed points appear. Excluded volume matters at both of them. At one fixed point the transition is continuous. At the other, the transition is first order.
arxiv-2603-29937: Kuntur and co-authors trace how news agencies reuse each other's sentences across languages. Their weakly supervised method spots sentence-level reuse without full translation. They compare Slovenian Press Agency articles with reports from 15 foreign agencies. The corpus spans two time windows and over 237,000 foreign articles. They find 1,087 aligned sentence pairs from earliest likely sources. Reuse appears in 52 percent of Slovenian articles. Most reuse is paraphrase, not copy, and sits mid-article.
arxiv-2604-00137: Dang, Dao, and Jiang offer OpenTools, a community-run toolbox for tool-using language models. Earlier work stressed how well models use tools, while the tools' own correctness, stability, and safety went largely unexamined. The toolbox gives all tools one interface shape, turns documented Python functions into reviewable bundles, and pairs risk checks that run no code with optional model review. Task-specific tools from the community beat an existing toolbox by 6 to 22 percent in relative gains across several agent designs.
arxiv-2604-01037: Shao tackles an open problem in eigenvalue work: pulling rough pairs from a given subspace. Mapping the target vector onto the subspace works well, but matching that closing speed with a rough pair has resisted a fix. The Rayleigh-Ritz method is used yet may suffer weakened Ritz value closing and may fail to produce settling Ritz vectors. Shao presents a random Rayleigh-Ritz method whose output settles at a rate similar to the map. His work needs only a simple target value and extends to nonlinear eigenvalue problems.
arxiv-2604-01237: Grinberg presents a way to read Helly's theorem, and a route into it, fit for the first years of undergraduate study. The presentation aims to be easy for teachers and students to follow, and the piece is pitched at teachers and students alike, not only specialists. It also links to current work on data privacy and to sampling methods used in epidemiology.
arxiv-2604-01637: Halder and colleagues introduce SecLens-R, a multi-user scoring method for LLM-based security vulnerability finding built around 35 shared axes grouped into 7 measure groups. Current benchmarks compress model results into a single metric, missing distinct user needs. The method defines five role-based weighting sets. Results show large spread across user views, with Decision Scores apart by as much as 31 points for the same model. For instance, Qwen3-Coder scores 76.3, an A, under the Head of Engineering profile but a D under the CISO profile.
arxiv-2604-01937: Shelby maps how the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill forces a redesign of security architecture, not just new paperwork. The Bill, the biggest UK cyber-law reform since the 2018 NIS rules, widens scope to managed providers, data centres and key suppliers. It demands dual incident reports within 24 and 72 hours, plus supply-chain duties and ministerial direction powers, which make perimeter-first defenses structurally non-compliant. Shelby argues Zero Trust design offers the most coherent base, adding a reference design, a staged path, and finance mappings for DORA and NIS2.
arxiv-2604-02237: Mizuyama builds a microscopic metric for nuclear collectivity from Jost RPA pole residues. A rank one Takagi split divides the scattering residue into a single particle overlap scale, multi channel coherence, and operator phase alignment. The metric is set to unity for a pure single channel excitation and yields decay widths and branching ratios with no artificial broadening. Tests on oxygen span giant dipole, quadrupole and isovector channels, separating truly collective peaks from trapped single particle resonances.
arxiv-2604-02537: Zhao and two colleagues present PolyJarvis, an agent-run tool that automates atom-level motion simulations for disordered single-unit plastics. Given a repeat-unit structure and target traits, a planning agent drafts a checked run plan that scripts carry out with standard simulation tools. Across seven plastics, 13 of 19 graded checks meet acceptance, with failures clustered in PCFF systems such as under-dense polystyrene.
arxiv-2604-02637: Fan and three colleagues offer LLMimic, a game-like lesson in which players act as a language model. Players move through pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and learning from human feedback. In a trial with 274 players, the lesson raised AI literacy and cut persuasion wins across charity, scam, and hotel cases. It also raised truthfulness and social care in the hotel case.
arxiv-2604-02937: Kelly and Chockler propose transferability analysis for audio classification models: if one model accepts a minimal sufficient signal for a classification, do other models accept it with the same classification? Across music genre, emotion recognition, and deepfake detection tasks, transferability varies by task, with music genre signals transferring about 26 percent of the time.
