Some deepfake models behave distinctively as flat-earther models, revealing information-theoretic differences beyond accuracy and precision.
arxiv-2604-03037: Mao and seven colleagues propose Advantage Reward Modeling for long-horizon manipulation, where sparse rewards starve credit assignment. Dense progress rewards cost much and handle backtracking poorly, so ARM estimates relative advantage instead of absolute progress. Tri-state labels of Progressive, Regressive, and Stagnant cut human effort while keeping annotator agreement high. Trained on these signals, ARM annotates progress automatically and reweights actions and rewards adaptively in offline reinforcement learning. It reaches a 99.4 percent success rate on a towel-folding task with near-zero human intervention during training.
arxiv-2604-03337: Qin and colleagues present GxEStat, an interactive R platform for studying genotype performance across varied trial sites. The workflow tests which effects matter and how steady each type stays, covering adaptability and site fit. By automating model setup, estimates, tests, and plots, it makes multi-site trial analysis faster and easier to repeat.
arxiv-2604-03637: Pal and colleagues build SAGE-GAN, a two-step system for cutting out nanoparticles in EM images and making lifelike fake image-mask pairs. First, a self-focus U-Net learns to cut out nanoparticle features from real images. It focuses on physical and shape details while skipping background and noise. Then the trained U-Net sits inside a cycle-true GAN framework, making fake pairs that mirror learned shape patterns and augment training data without human input.
arxiv-2604-03837: Meilun Zhou and Alina Zare replaced fixed loss weights in multi-task triplet learning with task-guided triplet selection. Static weights need tuning and ignore how tasks shape a shared representation. Their method picks triplets by mutual information, choosing samples that inform across tasks rather than rescaling losses. On an aerial wildlife set, the guided selection improved classification and regression and built a stronger shared representation.
arxiv-2604-03937: Vishesh Jain and Clayton Mizgerd proved a sharp form of Fill's spectral gap result for the adjacent-transposition chain on the symmetric group. Greaves and Zhu had shown the uniform parameter vector minimizes the spectral gap among regular vectors. Jain and Mizgerd showed the gap is minimized exactly when the vector has a neutral label, a coordinate set to one half against all others. The multiplicity of the second eigenvalue then equals the neutral-label count, except in two edge cases where it is n minus 1.
arxiv-2604-04037: Nilesh Sarkar and Dawar Jyoti Deka argued that knowledge distillation hits a geometric loss floor, not just a training limit. Students pack many more features than dimensions via superposition, and a student of a given width can encode only a bounded feature count, losing the rest for good. Tests on a toy model and on Pythia-410M confirmed the predicted floor ordering across five student widths. Coarse concepts survived even 88 percent feature loss, showing the floor comes from fine-grained features in the long tail.
arxiv-2604-04537: Li probes tracking for underactuated sea craft in a polar frame. Two polar coordinate transformations cut the first two-input-three-output second-order flat-frame model to a two-input-two-output feedback set. The new model may not meet the strict-feedback rule for backstepping. To dodge likely controller-design singularities, Li offers exponential modification of orientation, a new idea for taming angle snags. While the shifts ease structure, they also bring built-in limits, most of all angle snags. Tests show the new control plan works.
arxiv-2604-04637: Pae presents a minimal architecture giving artificial agents a history-shaped perspective on the world. A slow perspective latent feeds back into sight and updates through work, so the same observations encode in new ways with stance, as tested in a minimal gridworld. First, the perspective latent reorganizes encoding, with five of 16 gating parts shifting across 30 runs. Second, only self-modulation yields growth-then-stabilization. Third, perturbation history leaves reduced plasticity after normal times return. Conduct stays stable, hinting reorganization is sense-based rather than action-based.
arxiv-2604-05137: Hajizadeh and Jana introduce differential execution feedback for raising code speed. Large language models can generate correct programs that differ in speed. Current tuning methods usually refine each entry using pointwise runtime or timing feedback. That feedback shows how costly it is or where cost arises, but gives limited guidance on how it should change. It compares implementations in program space but separated in speed. It turns their differences into evidence. They show the method in EffiPair, a tool pairing similar programs with speed gaps.
arxiv-2604-05537: Capelli and four colleagues introduce Tree Decision Diagrams, a Boolean-function model generalizing ordered binary decision diagrams. TDDs keep the same tractable operations, counting, enumeration, conditioning, and apply, while staying more succinct. Formulas of treewidth k fit in fixed-parameter tractable size, which ordered diagrams cannot match, and the authors map bottom-up compilation cost to factor width.
arxiv-2604-06037: Low examines a 2020 method by Brückner and colleagues for inferring the dynamics of underdamped stochastic systems. The method works from noisy measurements of systems where friction is weak and random kicks matter. While calling the method a notable achievement, his 2026 comment identifies a number of significant errors in the original paper. He explains and corrects them in this short note.
arxiv-2604-06237: Cloitre studies a perturbed Hofstadter recursion introduced by Mantovanelli, proving it well-defined for every positive integer. He shows the ratio of its terms to their index tends to one half, with optimal error order n over the square root of log n. He also bounds the corresponding normalized limsup explicitly from above and below. The argument runs combinatorially: a parity split recasts the recurrence as two exact interleavings of binary words, whose Dyck paths define plane forests, with Catalan numbers arising in the enumeration.
arxiv-2604-06737: Wu and six colleagues present LuWen, an open-source Chinese legal language model built on Baichuan. Legal work taxes general models with specialized terms, tangled reasoning, and fast-changing knowledge. LuWen combines continual pre-training on a large legal corpus, supervised fine-tuning on curated legal instructions, and retrieval-augmented generation over a legal knowledge base. Tests on five tasks, from judgment prediction and judicial exams to summarization, article questions, and decision reasoning, show it beating several strong baselines.
arxiv-2604-06837: Yang, Lim, and Lee align Bellman residual minimization with contraction geometry for Markov problems. The Bellman operator shrinks in the max norm, yet projected value iteration and residual minimization usually rely on squared-error forms, creating a shape mismatch. Their soft residual form, spread to a broad weighted Lp norm, aligns the goal with contraction geometry as p grows. The work yields error bounds and a clean link between residual minimization and Bellman contraction, cutting error growth while staying usable in practice.
arxiv-2604-07037: Alonso-Monsalve and four colleagues build a vision model learning patterns from mixed tiny sensor data. Self-taught pre-training mixes auto-coder rebuild with linked voxel goals, and the shared encoder is fine-tuned across sorting and fitting tasks. On FASERCal events, pre-training lifts flavour and charm-quark ID, push and vertex rebuild over training from scratch. With about a thousand labeled events, the encoder matches flavour sorting of a model trained on ten times as much data. Patterns transfer to benchmarks.
arxiv-2604-07137: Wisinski and six colleagues probe what a multi branch beta variational autoencoder learns about coupled tropical Pacific climate swings. The model is trained on a five hundred year control run, using ocean heat content, outgoing long wave radiation, and sea surface temperature by month. It rebuilds the fields well, keeps their main basin scale shapes, and loses only a little skill from training to test data. Latent checks show sea temperature bunched in fewer latent slots, while heat content and outgoing radiation spread more widely.
arxiv-2604-07237: Kitsios adds a broad form of diagonal dimension, a size-like number for sorting operator algebras. He shows how it extends an earlier form from Li, Liao, and Winter, and when the two match. He proves it keeps key traits under usual constructions, and sets it beside nuclear dimension. As a test case, for a Cartan piece in the algebra of finite-spread operators on a well-spaced metric space, his size equals the space's asymptotic dimension.
arxiv-2604-07437: Gregory and seven colleagues present ASTRAFier, a transformer-based classifier for stellar variability that works directly on light curves with no feature engineering. It combines bidirectional long short-term memory layers with convolutional networks to sort variability types from Kepler and TESS data. Trained and validated on both missions, it reaches 94.26 percent accuracy on Kepler and 88.22 percent on TESS. The team then scales it to about 2.8 million TESS light curves from TESS sectors 14, 15, and 26, releasing the resulting stellar variability catalog.
arxiv-2604-07537: Telikicherla and nine colleagues present SEUSHI, a solar tool joining multi-pinhole soft X-ray imaging with grazing-incidence UV spectroscopy on a shared camera. It maps heat and emission measure at fine resolution and 5-second cadence to spot Hot Onset Precursor Events that warn of flares. High-cadence 100-hertz readouts of picked rows allow photon-counting spectroscopy over 1.1 to 6.8 keV, tracking element mix change in active regions. High-resolution EUV spectra across 16.1 to 33.8 nm at 5-second cadence support coronal dimming studies and early coronal mass ejection alerts.
arxiv-2604-07837: Zhi and 12 colleagues propose SPARD, a self-paced curriculum for aligning language models with reinforcement learning. Post-training now spans complex, open-ended tasks with multi-objective rewards covering many skills and settings. Fixed reward weights ignore how learning shifts over time and struggle with uneven data across dimensions. SPARD watches learning progress and dynamically adjusts both reward weights and data importance. That synchronization of learning intent with data value aims for better performance across the full capability spectrum.
arxiv-2604-08137: Maciala and three colleagues study the Drazin index of anti-triangular block matrices. The Drazin index is a basic invariant for singular matrices and generalized inverses. Sharp results exist for block triangular matrices, but the anti-triangular case is less developed. The paper studies matrices with blocks A, B, C, and zero under set constraints. Using additive splits with von Neumann inverses, the team links the matrix's Drazin index to invariance properties of related indices. This link gives a practical way to control the index via factorizations and block products.
arxiv-2604-08437: Tellili, Epperson, and Akrout rebuild power sharing for radios to account for amplifier distortion instead of assuming a clean linear chain. With a statistical linearization of the amplifier's hard limit, they derive a gradient method that also picks a spatial back off. They also give a closed form threshold that separates noise limited from distortion limited work. Tests show clear capacity gains when the amplifier saturates, over classic water filling.
arxiv-2604-08537: Nan and fourteen colleagues decode vision from brain scans for new people with no retraining, tackling the wide variation in neural patterns across individuals. Conditioning on a few image brain examples from a new person lets their meta trained model infer that person's encoding patterns and invert them in layers. The approach generalizes across people, scanners, and visual backbones, needing neither anatomical alignment nor shared stimuli.
arxiv-2604-08837: Hsu and Wood cut the training budget for Meanflow models with a Discrete Meanflow training curriculum built on a discretization of the Meanflow objective with a consistency property. Flow models train stably but need multi step sampling, while one step models sample well yet train unstably, and strong Meanflow models have demanded extremely large budgets. Starting from a pretrained flow model, the curriculum reaches one step FID 3.36 on CIFAR-10 in only 2000 epochs, pointing toward efficient training of future one step models.
arxiv-2604-09037: Huang and eleven colleagues introduce SiMing-Bench, a benchmark for judging procedural correctness in full-length clinical skill videos. Current video benchmarks test event recognition, temporal ordering, and long-context recall, but miss a harder expert skill. That skill is tracking how ongoing interactions change the procedural state and decide whether later actions are correct. The benchmark targets rubric-based process-level judgment, and finds step errors persist even when overall scores look acceptable. The bottleneck is modeling how interactions update procedural state over time, not finer scoring or localization.
arxiv-2604-09337: Li, Jolly, and Waintal tailor tensor network techniques to the quantics representation for inhomogeneous and few-body problems. Tensor networks solve partial differential equations in quantics form, with resolution depending only logarithmically on grid point count. First-generation techniques used out-of-the-box algorithms designed for settings like quantum magnetism, where degrees of freedom play equal roles. In quantics form, however, degrees of freedom correspond to physics at different scales. By tailoring algorithms to this case, the authors obtain faster and more robust convergence.
arxiv-2604-09437: Tsingalis, Kotropoulos, and Briat introduce AdaCubic, an optimizer that tunes the weight of the cubic penalty inside Newton's cubic-regularized method through a separate auxiliary problem with cubic constraints. Hutchinson's method approximates the Hessian cheaply, keeping costs down, while the local convergence guarantees of the cubic-regularized Newton method carry over. Across vision, language, and signal tasks it matches or beats standard optimizers without any per-task hyperparameter tuning.
arxiv-2604-09537: Tayebi Arasteh and four colleagues argue that decisions must hinge on evidence, not just retrieved text pasted beside a prediction. Their case-grounded verification framework hands a model a local case, external evidence, and a structured claim. It asks whether the evidence supports that claim for that case. Support and controlled non-support examples are generated without hand annotation, including wrong-state counterfactuals. A radiology verifier trained this way beats case-only and evidence-only baselines, and falls apart when evidence is removed or swapped.
arxiv-2604-09637: Nikolopoulos, Eden, and Muntean study a reaction-diffusion model for colloid deposition in porous matter across two scales. Large-scale flow follows an effective equation with pore-scale cell-problem values. Pore shape evolves as particles deposit or detach. Growing cores may meet and clog local pore space. The authors prove weak solvability for the nonlinear parabolic system in the non-clogging regime. They propose a two-scale finite-element scheme for computing weak solutions. Tests show local clogging shifting the dispersion tensor, trading flow speed against storage room.
arxiv-2604-09737: Fodeh and seven co-authors present a method for ontology-constrained prediction, where outputs stay label-accurate, structurally valid, and evidence-grounded. A design combining XML-style structure, chain-of-thought reasoning, and a self-validation gate targets format drift and ambiguity. Their STaR-DRO method upweights hard groups without suppressing easier ones, unlike DRO. On EPPC Miner, prompt engineering lifts label F1 about 14 points and span F1 about 17 points. STaR-DRO lifts label F1 and cuts cross-entropy about 21 percent against fine-tuning and about 15 percent against standard DRO.
arxiv-2604-09837: Hen presents planted-answer benchmarks for SAT and Ising tuning from integer factoring. Given two primes, the build encodes their product's math as an AND normal form formula whose picks match factors. The known prime pair serves as ground truth for clear checks of solver output. For two d-bit primes, carry folds number about the fourth power of bit-length. Benchmarks show median runtime explodes in factor bit-length over the range tested. The build gives a scalable, ordered, solid benchmark family with one knob and open making software.
arxiv-2604-09937: Bedi and 14 co-authors present HealthAdminBench, a benchmark for computer-use agents on healthcare administration, a field with over 1 trillion dollars yearly. Four realistic interfaces, an electronic health record, two payer portals, and a fax system, host 135 expert-defined tasks across prior authorization, appeals and denials, and durable medical equipment orders. Each task splits into verifiable subtasks, giving 1,698 evaluation points. Seven agent setups were tested; the best agent reaches only 36.3 percent end-to-end success, while another tops subtask success at about 83 percent, showing a gap to real-world reliability.
arxiv-2604-10337: Derrazi and Sharami test whether SAINT embeddings help tree models predict employee leaving. SAINT uses focus to model feature links, but one-hot coding creates gaps and loses meaning links between groups. They compare solo SAINT, XGBoost, and LightGBM with hybrids mixing SAINT vectors and tree models. Solo tree models beat solo SAINT and the hybrids in scores and reach. The hybrids did not improve results, likely because trees use dense vectors poorly, and the approach also reduced clarity.
arxiv-2604-10437: Wang, Dai, Liu, Li, and Batmanghelich tighten where CT report models point in space. Old training pairs a whole scan with a whole report, leaving fine sites and disease spots unmarked. Their DCP-PD method distills fine cues from report text and steers writing with them, dropping prompts at times to block shortcuts. Scores lift by 20 percent in relative terms on CT-RATE and by 89 percent on Rad-ChestCT. A staged question test then probes site grounding from presence down to lobe.
arxiv-2604-10537: Gyaprasad and Joshi steer light pulses in voltage tuned liquid crystal cells. Their shared frame covers spread and tunable split refraction for quantum light states. Treating photons as short packets yields group speed, walk off, and phase drift for split polarizations. Voltage tuning then shifts arrival times, polarization links, and photon sameness. The work points to tunable quantum links for secure light based messaging.
arxiv-2604-11137: Zhan and five colleagues establish a framework for trustworthy clinical reasoning. Language models in decision support are obstructed by weak reasoning. In healthcare, correct answers alone are not enough; practice demands clarity for safety and duty. A weakness is correct answers through flawed reasoning. This signals grasp and risk of errors. The authors propose Curriculum Goal-Conditioned Learning, training models to generate diagnostic arguments following Toulmin structure. Its three-part curriculum builds by listing facts and diagnoses. It backs an idea while denying alternatives, gives a verdict.
arxiv-2604-11237: Nath and three colleagues identify vibration modes of truss structures from output-only data with UResVGAE, a physics-aware graph autoencoder with a variational latent code. Treating each structure as a graph of spectral and geometric node data, it predicts natural frequencies and damping ratios. It also rebuilds full mode shapes, enforcing physical consistency through rebuilding and orthogonality terms. The tests vary noise levels and sensor counts to stress the method. Tests on simulated trusses show accurate, well-calibrated results under noise and sparse sensing.
arxiv-2604-12037: Mamo shows a photon profile fixed by the two-point function yields the hard kernel for deeply virtual Compton scattering and its double, in a fixed-spin Witten diagram. For a near-boundary vertex, the diagram yields the Gauss-hypergeometric Wilson-kernel family, with the Mellin exponent from a power count, not an ansatz. The lower vertex matches the nonperturbative conformal moment, not a new kernel or skewness profile. Fixed-scale matching gives the parton basis a second ultraviolet origin, from the QCD expansion and the AdS vertex.
arxiv-2604-12137: Stoumpou and three colleagues infer a hidden prognostic factor from survival-time gaps between similar patients who received the same treatment but fared differently, then balance it with observed traits. Across three observational cohorts with trial benchmarks, balancing the hidden factor improved agreement with trial hazard ratios in every comparison, cutting log-error roughly tenfold at best. The approach also narrowed cross-center differences in multicenter cohorts.
arxiv-2604-12737: Gustavo de Carvalho Bertoli tests differential privacy as a shield for federated learning models. Federated models hide raw data yet leak membership through their outputs. The study uses the 2025 NIST genomics red team event as test bed. A stacking attack ensembles seven black-box estimators into a meta-model. It trains on prediction scores and losses. Three tiers are tested: no protection, low privacy, and high privacy. The attack beats all baselines without protection and at low privacy. Leakage persists even at that tier where a single-signal baseline collapses.
arxiv-2604-13237: Fosco and Guntsche work out the effective action for the moving Casimir effect for a real scalar field in d plus 1 dimensions. They use the worldline picture of quantum field theory. The field couples to a spacetime-varying mass term playing the role of a moving medium, imposing imperfect boundary conditions on time-varying surfaces. Expanding around a planar setup, the worldline path integral splits into simpler lower-dim pieces, giving the Dirichlet result at strong surface coupling with orderly inverse-power fixes.
arxiv-2604-13437: Choi, Jang, and Yoon introduce small covers built as pullbacks from the simplex, going beyond pullbacks from the linear model. Their central result offers multiple equivalent ways to characterise this class. These include torsion-freeness of odd-degree integral cohomology, vanishing of the first Steenrod square on even-degree mod-2 cohomology, and links between integral and mod-2 Betti numbers. The characterizations tie the geometric pullback construction to algebraic invariants, giving multiple routes to recognize and study this class of small covers.
arxiv-2604-14037: Ramakrishnan classifies all symmetries of shallow ReLU networks, settling which distinct parameters give the same function. Earlier full lists needed smooth activations, leaving out ReLU. By using ReLU's kink head-on, he maps the full symmetry structure of the shallow case. That shows the neuromanifold shape that shapes training dynamics.
arxiv-2604-14137: Itzhak and three colleagues study vibe-testing, the informal way users judge language models through hands-on trials tied to their own work. Drawing on a survey and on public comparison reports, they formalize the habit as two personal choices: what to test and how to judge answers. A trial pipeline built on that framing pairs tailored prompts with user-aware scoring. It shifts which model wins on coding tests, suggesting formalized vibe-testing can bridge benchmark scores and lived experience.
arxiv-2604-14237: Song and eight colleagues turn transistor topology search into a generative task for large language models with TOPCELL. Fine-tuned with group relative policy optimization, the model aligns its topology choices with circuit logic and layout space. In an industrial flow aimed at a 2nm node, TOPCELL beats foundation models at finding routable, physically aware topologies. Plugged into a state-of-the-art flow for 7nm library generation, it generalizes with no examples and matches exhaustive solvers on layout quality while running about 86 times faster.
arxiv-2604-14637: Liu, Qu, Bagaoisan, Lee, and Gilpin build Touching Space, a system helping blind and low-vision people map unfamiliar places before travel. Most navigation tools guide users in real time but do little for pre-travel spatial understanding. A fountain south of a tower, west of a hotel, is one example. Touching Space pulls target-place map data into an interface for exploration, combining touch feedback with spoken questions to a conversational agent. It runs on commodity hardware and supports cognitive map building through audio-haptic conversation.
arxiv-2604-14737: Gu and six colleagues used scanning tunnelling microscopy to view bound states in nanostructures patterned into a two-dimensional molecular film with a parabolic band and partial gaps. The lowest states split off from the band bottom and mimic the s and p orbitals of real atoms, even bonding the same way. Yet the gapped vacuum around them also breeds wholly new orbitals with no natural counterparts. These quasi-one-dimensional states widen the orbital vocabulary of chemistry, shaped chiefly by the surrounding electronic vacuum.
arxiv-2604-14937: Krajczok and Sołtan continue the study of the braided compact quantum group SUq(2) for complex q with magnitude between 0 and 1. They address existence of the Haar measure, construct the scaling group, the antipode and its polar decomposition, and describe the related braided Hopf algebra. They also study when the braided flip extends to a completely bounded map. They establish equivalence between two approaches to bosonization and braided tensor product in the literature.
arxiv-2604-15737: Kim and three colleagues test whether Bayes limits on jet quenching travel across centrality, energy, and measure kinds in LHC hits. A JETSCAPE model, tuned to ALICE, ATLAS, and CMS hadron and jet data in PbPb hits at 5.02 and 2.76 TeV, gives the limits. Centrality splits agree, while energy and measure-kind splits shift a bit inside shared zones, so overlap alone does not vouch for all-round foresight. Fresh tests with no refit give mixed foresight, and unlike probes catch unlike sides of jet-medium play.
arxiv-2604-15837: Landais and four colleagues add a repulsive Stein mechanism to estimation-of-distribution algorithms for high-dimensional black-box combinatorial optimization. The repulsion pushes search points apart, so the search covers several promising regions instead of collapsing onto one. It counters early settling on complex, multi-peaked landscapes. Across varied benchmarks, the method matches or beats leading rivals, especially on large instances. That points to Stein variational gradient descent as a good fit for costly discrete search.
arxiv-2604-15937: Pagan and three colleagues audit bias in large language models used to curate and rank social media content. Through 540,000 simulated top-10 picks from pools of 100 posts, across 54 conditions and six prompting styles, they map biases across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google models. Polarization grows in every setup, toxicity handling flips between engagement and information prompts, and sentiment skews negative. On Twitter/X, left-leaning authors are over-represented even though right-leaning authors form the plurality, a pattern that mostly survives prompt changes.
arxiv-2604-16537: Bertsimas and colleagues challenge the idea that external calibration guarantees transfer. Using six surgery cohorts from top centers, they test whether fit depends on cohort similarity. Calibration worsened as mismatch grew, with KL gap and the Calibration Index. From the builder side, they tune a model toward a meta-analysis target spread. From the user side, they propose a cohort-outcome similarity measure to pick the model for a cohort. Weighting improved fit in most settings without hurting ranking, and similar-cohort models gave lower error and greater care value.
arxiv-2604-17137: Patil and Christensen introduce BOIL, a process for mining environment structure for useful signals to guide long-term agent behavior. Using PageRank and shared-signal maximization, it builds plans for tasks such as coverage, patrols, and random reachability. Experiments show BOIL beats simple rules in complex settings over long runs.
arxiv-2604-17637: Shafter and Hornoch catalog recurrent novae in M31, comparing positions of over 1,300 nova eruptions recorded through 2025. The work extends a 2015 study that found 12 confident cases plus four candidates from 964 novae before 2014. Seven more appeared in the past 12 years, one candidate was confirmed, and another proved a foreground dwarf nova. Today 79 eruptions belong to 20 known cases, with four more from two unconfirmed candidates. They prove fainter and faster than novae generally, though their spread and light-curve traits match other novae.
arxiv-2604-17937: Rishav and two colleagues introduce ContraPrompt, a prompt optimizer that learns from a model's own failed and successful retries on the same input. Because model, input, and base prompt stay fixed, differences between the two reasoning traces expose strategy and feedback effects, which the method turns into routing rules in an input-aware decision tree. It beats GEPA on all four reasoning and compliance benchmarks, gaining 8.29 points on HotPotQA, and on 53 black-box problems it wins 11, ties 41, and loses 1.
arxiv-2604-18637: Zador and 30 colleagues name three gaps in today's AI: no real-world touch, fragile learning, and wasteful power and data. Fixes they urge run from body-control design, learning by acting, and multi-scale learning to layered nets with sparse, event-led computing. They lay these ideas out as a plan with near, middle, and far stages. Carrying it out needs researchers schooled across brain science and engineering, plus training, kit access, norms, and ethics. Brain-led AI could beat today's limits while deepening insight into neural computing.
arxiv-2604-18837: Kakavand, Strohmeyer, and Schlotter benchmark quantum kernel support vector machines against strong classical baselines on tabular data, in 970 experiments with strict nested cross validation. Statistical testing finds none of 29 pairwise comparisons significant, and learning curves show steeper quantum slopes that still trail the best baseline. Hardware checks on IBM Heron show kernel fidelity of at least 0.976 across six tests. Dataset choice drives performance variance, while kernel type accounts for only 9 percent.
arxiv-2604-19037: Covey and Maslov study energy relaxation when single phonon scattering is forbidden but two phonon scattering is allowed. Above the Bloch-Gruneisen temperature, two phonon scattering beats single phonon scattering, whose rate falls as temperature rises while the two phonon rate rises linearly. This breaks the usual energy diffusion picture; rare thermal events relax energy instead. Below that temperature, the rate scales as the cube of temperature for soft phonons. For anisotropic bands, an intermediate regime appears where both processes scale as the square of temperature.
arxiv-2604-19337: Rao and colleagues present POLAR-PIC, a jointly built tool for large-scale particle-in-cell plasma work, which often scales poorly because of particle-grid choke points and reshuffle costs. It recasts field interpolation into a matrix-unit-friendly outer-product form. It keeps particles in a physically ordered layout to preserve tight memory placement. It pairs data exchange with deposition to hide reshuffle cost. The design targets three flaws at once: idle matrix units, jagged memory access from particle motion, and lost nearness from lockstep reshuffling.
arxiv-2604-19537: Tost and colleagues design and evaluate InvestChat, a multimodal tablet app for stock market exploration. It offers multiple coordinated views and a language-model-powered chat. They test the app with 12 novice investors. Combining natural language, touch, and pen input facilitates user engagement. Participants use the modes in complementary ways and find natural language most effective. Choice across modes is part of the appeal.
arxiv-2604-19637: Jimenez Marti and colleagues present a general potential model for dust and ion wake systems under PK-4-like settings. Dusty plasmas, made of electrons, ions, neutral gas, and charged dust grains, exhibit self-organization like string patterns seen in microgravity tests. Those patterns are shaped by ion wakes from streaming ions under outside electric fields, plus time-shifting plasma patches like ionization waves. Current ion wake models often rely on setup-bound parameters, curbing general use, while the new model uses a small set of numbers from computer simulations.
arxiv-2604-19837: Xie presents Forage V2, a system for autonomous agents in open-world tasks where the finish line is not given in advance. Such agents suffer denominator blindness, systematically underestimating the scope of the target space. Version 1 answered this with co-evolving evaluation, where an independent Evaluator discovers what complete means, and method isolation, where neither side sees the other's code. Version 2 grows from a single run into a learning organization, with experience accumulating across runs, transferring across model capabilities, and guards against knowledge degradation.
arxiv-2604-20337: Biswas and ten colleagues probe the frustrated magnet Sr3CuNb2O9 with muon spin relaxation and niobium-93 nuclear magnetic resonance. Muon relaxation rates diverge as a power law with temperature and with applied longitudinal field, matching a random singlet phase. Niobium spectra resolve two parts with distinct local magnetic settings, and inverse Laplace analysis splits them into fast and slow channels. The fast channel looks random singlet like and the slow channel looks quantum spin liquid like, with exponents 0.6 and just over one, proving microscopic coexistence of the two phases.
arxiv-2604-21237: Chiang-Mei Chen and three colleagues trace the late-time fate of an anisotropic Bianchi-I universe filled with radiation under asymptotically safe gravity. In the radiation era, evolution creeps toward isotropy through log terms, while quantum effects soften anisotropy further mid-way. With magnetic fields and no cosmological constant, the universe drifts to a Kasner-like state with lasting anisotropy and faster magnetic decay. A nonzero value instead drives it to an isotropic de Sitter phase, and Hodge duality extends the findings to electric fields.
arxiv-2604-21637: Lester James Miranda and colleagues survey the last mile where multilingual language models meet edge deployment, the small-device settings common across the Global South. Reviewing 232 papers across the full pipeline, from data collection to deployment, they map how linguistic diversity and tight hardware limits pull in opposite directions. They also explain why the two research fields have stayed largely separate. The paper closes with open questions and practical recommendations for building fairer, more inclusive language technology.
arxiv-2604-21837: Piccininni and Stensrud show that effects tied to post-treatment events can sometimes be found without measuring all shared causes of the event and the outcome. Simple comparisons tied to dropout, nonadherence, or truncation by death usually have no causal meaning, even when treatment is assigned at random. If treatment and other unmeasured outcome causes generate the post-treatment event through independent mechanisms, then conditional separable effects and survivor average causal effects can be found with no such adjustment. Examples cover truncating events, uneven nonadherence, and the birth weight paradox.
arxiv-2604-22037: Sole introduces a third quantitative descriptor for portamento in string performance: the spectrographic gradient of the slide, measured in Hz per second. The gradient captures what duration misses: how steep the pitch path is. The method yields gradients near 600 Hz/s in late-period recordings and above 4,000 Hz/s in performances from the early twentieth century. Across 22 recordings spanning 1930-2012, Sole tests whether gradient steepness correlates negatively with tempo: slower performances yield steeper, longer slides, while faster ones yield shallower slides or none. Results support this hypothesis.
arxiv-2604-22337: Jacob and three colleagues present TabSCM, a generator for realistic tabular data that preserves causal structure. Most generators match marginal statistics yet ignore causes, so later models learn spurious patterns. TabSCM starts from a causal graph, orients its edges, fits root distributions, and learns assignments in topological order. Ancestral sampling then yields valid records and exact counterfactual queries. On seven public datasets it matches or beats leading baselines, while running up to 583 times faster than diffusion-only models.
arxiv-2604-22437: Ferreira, Herdeiro, Radu and Zilhão study resonant-hair black holes, static spherical charged Einstein-Maxwell-scalar solutions. Scalar self-interactions are needed for their existence. Earlier spherical-only studies suggested stability, but recent non-spherical studies revealed instabilities, now studied in detail with a different decay channel. A second model suggests instabilities may be generic across classes. They conclude the solutions are unstable, splitting by fission into a bosonic lump and a bald black hole, or collapsing into it. Non-spherical dynamics, they stress, is key.
arxiv-2604-22737: Emam, Martens, Rottmann, and Gerdts set out the Electric Mobility Dial-a-Ride Problem, which builds on electric dial-a-ride service with a human focus. A mixed fleet of battery cars must serve rider trips under dial-a-ride and mobility needs, with charging stops woven in between trips. The authors cast the task as a mixed-integer linear program and solve test cases that show real-world use.
arxiv-2604-22837: Miao and five colleagues extend a SAM-based dense tracker to survive long occlusions, fast motion, viewpoint changes, and distractors. The weakness is worst for small objects. Their occlusion-aware version of DAM4SAM adds a reliability state machine, branch-based recovery, delayed memory promotion, and selective memory choice. Memory is committed only after a candidate branch is reconfirmed, and the first conditioning frame is preserved. The design keeps easy cases efficient while improving recovery after long gaps.
arxiv-2604-23137: Hasnain and four colleagues fuse a SqueezeNet-style CNN branch with a MobileViT-style transformer branch to classify brain tumors in MRI scans. An Adaptive Attention Gate weights each branch per sample and per feature, so the merge adapts to each scan. On the Brain Tumor MRI Dataset, the hybrid reaches 97.60 test accuracy and beats single CNN and ViT baselines plus rival fusion methods. The result backs dynamic feature weighting as an effective route for medical image classification.
arxiv-2604-23437: Panth and Nigam design a federated learning system that lets banks jointly detect fraud without sharing raw transaction data. Their sharded scheme splits participants into small short-lived clusters and uses integrity tags so the server can check that updates are consistent without decrypting them. A recovery protocol handles banks dropping out mid-round. Tests show far lower aggregation delay than an encrypted baseline and fraud recall well above locally trained models.
arxiv-2604-23837: Ross and Lo study heuristic collapse in language-model money advice. Complex multi-factor choices shrink to a few main inputs. Using simple stand-in models on model outputs, they find asset picks rest largely on stated risk comfort. Other key factors add little. Web search partly softens the collapse but does not resolve it. The findings suggest advisor use needs audits of how inputs sway outputs, not just output quality.
arxiv-2604-23937: Dong, Qin, and Xu model offshore wind turbine wakes under surge-pitch motions with two deep methods, physics-informed neural networks and Fourier neural operators. Data come from large-eddy simulations with an actuator line model. Both methods capture large-scale meandering patterns. But the Fourier operators win on speed, with eightfold faster computation and 40 times faster convergence, plus better long-term forecasts. The neural-network outputs smooth away fast patterns and miss turbulent swings, while they resolve the meandering frequency, its higher harmonics, and the energy cascade.
arxiv-2604-24237: Pawlowski and Froese study the interval ordering problem from bioinformatics: order intervals to minimize a cost on each exposed part. Their dynamic programming approach solves the problem with exponentially many oracle calls and arithmetic operations. When a cost function's shift from zero is subadditive or superadditive, the approach yields polynomial-time algorithms, settling an open question for the exponential cost function. A lower bound shows no oracle-only algorithm can beat that in general, and NP-hardness holds for some simple function classes, closing the complexity gap.
arxiv-2604-24737: Joshi, Magen, Srebro, Tsilivis and Vardi study learning from chain-of-thought supervision by multiple thinkers, all correct but in set ways. Some classes are easy to learn from one thinker's chain of thought but hard from end results alone. Under cryptographic assumptions, chain-of-thought data can make learning hard by two or a few thinkers in passive settings. An active learning algorithm learns well with little chain-of-thought data per thinker, independent of target accuracy, plus a moderate number of thinkers and enough end-result data.
arxiv-2604-24937: Kumar and five colleagues report dielectric spectroscopy of single-crystalline NdMgAl11O19, a magnetoplumbite hexaaluminate. The real permittivity along the c axis rises as temperature falls from 275 K to 30 K, staying flat across 4 Hz to 50 kHz. High-frequency permittivity follows a Barrett formula plus a two-level term, yielding a robust gap of 25.85 K consistent with the lowest Nd3+ crystal-field splitting. Isothermal tests reveal a repeatable low-field crossover, linked to a contest between antiferromagnetic links and splitting of the ground-state Kramers doublet by the Zeeman effect.
arxiv-2604-25137: Wang solves the time-dependent Schrödinger equation by learning the score function along Bohmian trajectories. The score is the gradient of log-probability density, and Bohmian paths are deterministic tracks shaped by classical plus quantum potentials. He models the score with a neural network and minimizes a self-consistent Fisher divergence. The zero-loss minimizer recovers Schrödinger dynamics for nodeless wave functions, and tests cover wavepacket splitting in a double well plus anharmonic vibrations of a Morse chain.
arxiv-2604-25237: Shulman proposes GC-LPR, a generalized context-aware local polynomial regression method, decoupling fitting coordinates from weighting context. Old LPR suffers a Euclidean tautology: local values are the same as fit values, limiting it on graphs or categories. The new method projects and smooths, isolating a data slice via a product kernel and fitting polynomials within that slice. Theory shows it keeps the bias-reduction properties of standard LPR while non-Euclidean contexts modulate local estimation. Tests on map and network data sets show it works.
arxiv-2604-25637: Dimca and Pokora study a Ziegler pair of plane arrangements: two cases with matching intersection lattices, yet Jacobian algebras whose minimal resolutions have unequal Betti numbers. They define several traits for such pairs and relate them to cones over Ziegler pairs of line arrangements. The work shows matching lattices do not force matching resolutions.
arxiv-2604-25737: Tarshish and six colleagues propose SAFEdit, a multi-agent system for instructed code editing that splits the work into specialized roles. A planner drafts an explicit edit plan, an editor applies minimal literal changes, and a verifier runs real tests. When tests fail, a failure abstraction layer turns raw logs into structured feedback for another editing round. On the EditBench benchmark of 445 editing instances in five languages, SAFEdit reached 68.6 percent task success. That beat the single-model baseline and a ReAct single-agent baseline.
arxiv-2604-26037: Ramakrishnan and Motamarri speed up large-scale density functional theory with GPU-centred methods inside a finite-element projector augmented-wave code. Their solver uses Chebyshev filtered subspace iteration with an approximate inverse overlap matrix. Mixed-precision arithmetic and low-precision communication cut cost while keeping the method robust. Reported gains reach eightfold on Intel graphics chips and twentyfold on AMD hardware. Solutions run close to eightfold faster than plane-wave methods for ten-thousand-electron systems, with scaling shown to one hundred thirty thousand electrons.
arxiv-2604-26637: Stanovcic, Sliwowski, and Lee introduced ATLAS, a tool for long-horizon robotic action segmentation. Existing tools favor vision-only data, lack synchronized robot time-series views, or resist new dataset formats. ATLAS synchronizes multi-view video with proprioceptive signals, annotates boundaries, labels, and outcomes, and reads ROS bags and RLDS formats through a modular layer. Its keyboard-centric design cut annotation time per action by at least 6 percent versus ELAN, improved expert alignment nearly 3 percent with time-series data, and cut boundary error fivefold against vision-only tools.
arxiv-2604-26837: Zhao and ten colleagues present SPIN, a framework unifying sparse attention for long-context language-model serving. Sparse attention reads only a small query-dependent slice of stored key-value state, but varied granularities and GPU-CPU transfers usually erase the gains. SPIN maps varied patterns onto one page store, manages cache budgets by locality, and sizes metadata to the active set. Built on vLLM, it beats plain vLLM on throughput and first token time, cutting token time by up to 58 percent.
arxiv-2604-27037: Eichholtz and four colleagues reproduce the Hypencoder, a framework swapping inner-product scoring for a query-specific neural net whose weights come from a hypernetwork. Their rerun confirms it beats a matched bi-encoder baseline in-domain and out-of-domain, with fast search cutting latency at little cost. On hard tasks support is partial: it wins on DL-Hard and FollowIR but not TREC TOT, where checkpoint issues and tuning quirks block full checks. Extensions find encoder gains, bi-encoders still faster, and nonlinear scoring gives no robustness penalty.
arxiv-2604-27237: Bellenbaum and ten colleagues present xDAVE, a code to predict and read X-ray Thomson scattering experiments in warm dense matter. Such scattering estimates plasma density, temperature, and charge state. The measured spectrum blends the dynamic structure factor with the source-instrument function. The Chihara split divides the spectrum into bound- and free-electron parts, enabling fast structure-factor calculation for large-scale parameter tuning. Few such codes exist, so this open checking tool fills the gap.
arxiv-2604-27637: Sadjoli and four colleagues investigate whether prompt optimization changes large language model rankings. Current frameworks use one static prompt template for every model, unlike industry practice, which optimizes the prompt per model for best results. On public academic plus internal industry test sets, optimization greatly affects final model rankings. The authors urge practitioners to optimize prompts per model when choosing the best model for a task.
arxiv-2604-27737: Chraibi, Konya, and Üsten revisit the 1919 Amritsar massacre through agent-based modeling and social psychology. Even under cautious assumptions, their simulations yield death estimates well above the official count of 379. They explore how early twentieth-century talk, shaped by Le Bon's crowd theory, cast the crowd as irrational and threatening, justifying excessive force. The study argues that seeing crowds as socially built explains today's parallels and framing risks, and shows why mixed methods matter for historical accountability and crowd safety.
arxiv-2604-27837: Jiang, Qingqing Zhang, and Yiying Zhang study insurance deals under doubt about loss odds, inside a Bregman-Wasserstein ball. First, a demand model where the buyer weighs worst cases under alpha-maxmin tastes and Value-at-Risk gives the best payout rule in closed form. Next, a robust design curbing the worst-case bent risk score under a promised Value-at-Risk cap. It pins down the best payout and the worst loss shape. They trace how lopsidedness bends payouts, and close with a Tail Value-at-Risk example.
arxiv-2604-27937: Taye offers a thermodynamic account of why primates live far longer than similar-sized mammals, with a macaque reaching decades where a cat rarely passes eighteen years. He argues that devoting more energy to the brain lowers entropy produced per bodily cycle, stretching a fixed lifetime budget of cycles. Predictive regulation, repair and behavioural buffering together supply the effect, yielding testable links between brain energy, entropy and lifespan.
arxiv-2605-00037:
Shao-Wen Wei and Yu-Xiao Liu review the topology of black hole thermodynamics, a young approach that sorts black holes by topological numbers. Recent work has shown that different black hole systems fall into distinct universality classes under this scheme, above all in thermodynamic limits. The classification promises insight for any future theory of quantum gravity, and this brief review gathers the latest progress.

The authors outline the fundamental topological frameworks for black hole solutions, critical points, Davies points, and the Hawking-Page phase transition. For each case they calculate the associated topological numbers and analyze their physical significance. They also explore the practical implications of the approach, giving readers a compact map of a fast-moving field.
arxiv-2605-00437:
Gábor Kasza and György Wolf ask how heavy a neutron star can be, using the spread of possibilities rather than a single answer. The physics of matter at neutron-star densities is uncertain, so they build families of equations of state from two trusted low-density baselines, extended upward until they meet quantum chromodynamics results. Each family member is causal and spans a range of stiffness.

Real observations then weight the possibilities in a Bayesian scheme: the famous neutron star merger of 2017, X-ray timing measurements of pulsars, and candidate objects in the low-mass and mass-gap ranges. The heaviest allowed star lands near 2.2 to 2.3 solar masses under the firmest constraints, barely sensitive to the baseline chosen. Its radius sits near twelve kilometers, with more dependence on the baseline. Together, the endpoint distributions form a sharp diagnostic for dense-matter physics.
arxiv-2605-00537:
Sumanta Mukherjee offers a study in theory of the Griffiths phase, a curious magnetic regime, across three families of magnets. In a Griffiths phase, rare ordered regions inside disordered matter produce unusual magnetic effects above the usual ordering point. The effect is best understood in ferromagnets, which align the same way. Antiferromagnets, whose moments alternate, and ferrimagnets, whose opposing moments are unequal, have been less charted.

Mukherjee develops a framework for how the Griffiths phase behaves in 3D spin-half Ising-type systems, and extends it from the ferromagnetic case to the other two kinds. Within that framework, the antiferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic cases behave more oddly than the usual ferromagnetic one. The study's practical promise is diagnostic: it offers a possible way to recognize Griffiths phase behavior in those less-studied materials. The work stays at the level of theory, setting out the framework rather than fitting one experiment.
arxiv-2605-00637:
Kaviru Gunaratne, Stephen Kobourov, and Jacob Miller introduce a quality metric for dimensionality reduction that judges how honestly a projection arranges its clusters. Reduction methods are praised for preserving global shape or local neighborhoods. But a plot can show tidy clusters whose relative placement is arbitrary or misleading, a known hazard of popular tools. Existing cluster metrics test separability alone, or assume clusters are round blobs.

Their Class Angular Distortion Index uses angles inside triples of points to measure whether the organization of classes survives projection. On real and synthetic data, they show cases where older metrics fail while theirs gives an interpretable verdict. Because the index is built from angles, it is differentiable. That bonus turns the metric into an objective: the authors demonstrate a reduction technique that optimizes it directly, so the judge becomes the coach.
arxiv-2605-00737:
Qinyuan Wu and 7 co-authors build a decision-theoretic framework for a question every AI agent faces: should I call a tool, or answer on my own? Tools add capability but cost money and time, and redundant or low-utility calls can actively harm performance. The authors analyze tool decisions along three factors: necessity, utility, and affordability.

Two lenses are combined. A normative lens infers the true need and utility of each call, while a descriptive lens infers what the model itself seems to perceive, from its behavior. Across seven models, two tools, and six tasks, perceived and true values were misaligned. The gap was worst under budget constraints, producing wasteful overuse and harmful calls. The fix is a set of light estimators read from the model's hidden states. They predict true need better than the model's self-reports. They also improve budgeted tool allocation across scales and tool types.
arxiv-2605-00937:
Shihang Zhao, Martín Saravia, Haokui Jiang, Zhiyang Xue, and Shunxiang Cao propose a machine learning framework for fluid-structure interaction on deforming meshes that respects the arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian formulation. A graph neural operator combined with a vision transformer predicts fluid dynamics over space and time. A lightweight memory network predicts structural motion at the interface. The two parts are coupled through a standard partitioned procedure.

Compatibility at the moving interface is enforced by a correction step. That step updates the fluid-side speed with the predicted structural speed at each coupling update. Two-stage training moves from single-step supervision to long-term autoregressive fine-tuning to limit error growth. On a flexible beam in a cylinder wake, predictions stay phase-consistent over long rollouts and generalize across inlet profiles.
arxiv-2605-01037:
Alan L. McCann presents a certified purity design that turns rule enforcement in cognitive workflow systems from a runtime convention into a structural boundary. Earlier rule results depended on the assumption that step executors cannot perform effects, enforced only by checking module imports. That check is not enough against adversarial bypass on the BEAM virtual machine, so McCann closes the gap with four mechanisms.

Executors compile to a restricted WebAssembly target where effect instructions are absent. They carry cryptographically signed purity certificates, pass a runtime checking gate, and support portable credentials through remote attestation. Four theorems cover purity by construction, bypass removal, certificate integrity, and gate completeness. Tests show verification is fast with minimal extra cost.
arxiv-2605-01137:
Gaoyi Chen and six co-authors introduce metric-normalized posterior leakage, a privacy measure designed for systems consumed under joint observation. Metric differential privacy scales noise to semantic distance, but per-record guarantees can miss leakage when learned aggregators combine evidence across correlated items. Their measure is attacker-aligned and distance-calibrated. It tracks the shift in posterior odds induced by releases.

For single or independent releases, bounding the new measure is equivalent to metric differential privacy, but under joint observation the older guarantee can still leave leakage high. A version bounded in probability limits how often leakage may exceed a budget, and an adaptive trust-and-verify framework perturbs, audits with a learned attacker, and adjusts parameters. A word-embedding case study shows substantial reduction in violations with low utility loss.
arxiv-2605-01237:
Deep Ghoshal and Sabyasachi Chatterjee study total variation denoising, a curve-fitting method that cleans noisy data while keeping sharp jumps, in the harder setting of quantile regression. A full pointwise picture of the fitted values was known only for the mean case, and quantile fits can have many valid answers.

The pair prove an exact formula that gives the fitted value at each point as a balance of local data summaries over nested ranges. The set of valid values at a point forms a closed interval, and the whole solution set is closed under taking pointwise highs and lows, so top and bottom envelope fits exist. A side result shows quantile fits at different levels cannot cross when they share one tuning value. The formula also yields sharp error bounds that hold even under very heavy-tailed noise.
arxiv-2605-01637:
Gorgi Pavlov defines a new invariant for Boolean functions, functions that take bits in and one bit out, tuned to how much each input matters. The construction dresses the Walsh-Hadamard transform, the Fourier analysis of bits, in a Banach geometry whose exponent at each layer is set by that layer's influence.

The invariant contracts in a way that is strictly Schur-convex in the influence pattern, so it rewards concentration of influence. Its size sorts famous families: parity at one extreme, majority in the middle, dictatorship at the other. It also splits functions that share a total influence score. Exact certificates over full small universes, every function on four bits and a vast census at five, test it as a guide to minimum support. The link holds at four bits and reverses at five, so the author reports it honestly as a concentration invariant, not a universal predictor.
arxiv-2605-01737:
Sushovan Mondal rings anisotropic neutron stars and listens to their spacetime tones. The axial w-modes are vibrations of spacetime itself around the star. Mondal builds the stars from two realistic equations of state. He lets pressure point unevenly, stronger along the radius or across it, under two standard recipes for that split.

Frequencies come from solving the linearized ripple equations by a continued-fraction method. Along the stable branch, tones fall steadily as mass grows, with the ordering between radial-led and tangential-led stars flipping between low and high masses. Frequency tracks compactness almost linearly, with anisotropy bending the line's slope and offset, and one recipe spreads values wider than the other. Damping times grow with mass, spiking near the branch's top, and tangential-led stars ring down faster. Fit formulas in terms of compactness and anisotropy close the study.
arxiv-2605-02037:
Zijian An and colleagues present VILAS, a low-cost robot platform for learning manipulation from vision, language, and action together. The system pairs a collaborative arm and electric gripper with two cameras, all linked by a messaging layer that handles teleoperation, data collection, and policy use in one framework. Keeping the hardware cheap makes the setup easier to copy.

For fragile objects, they add a kirigami-based soft gripper extension that bends in a predictable way under pressure, giving gentle contact without force sensing. Three leading vision-language-action models are fine-tuned from public checkpoints on the same demonstration set and tested on the platform. The work supplies a shared testbed for accessible robot learning.
arxiv-2605-02737:
Romain Valabregue and five co-authors present SIAM, a model that segments whole-head MRI scans after training on just six hand-labeled templates. Synthetic training has advanced brain segmentation by letting models learn from generated data in any contrast. Most methods, though, need hundreds of auto-labeled templates, which bake in biases and make adding new structures awkward.

SIAM randomizes both image intensity and shape, so synthetic scans vary in contrast and in anatomy, including cortical thickness and deep nuclei form. It labels sixteen structures at once, covering brain tissue plus fluid, vessels, membranes, skull, and skin, with no preprocessing step. Across eight varied datasets with hundreds of scans, spanning common contrasts and a wide age range, SIAM matched or beat leading methods on brain structures and extended coverage beyond them.
arxiv-2605-02937:
Fang Wu and twenty-eight co-authors introduce Proteo-R1, a protein design system that reasons before it builds. Deep learning can now design new proteins with atomic-level fidelity, but most models jump straight to geometry. They never state which residues or contacts are functionally essential, so design choices tangle with sampling, and the result is hard to interpret, control, or reuse.

Proteo-R1 splits the job between two experts, mirroring how human engineers work. A multimodal language model studies sequence, structure, and text to pick the key functional residues for binding and specificity. Those choices become hard constraints for a separate diffusion generator, which designs the molecule around the fixed interaction anchors. Understanding and geometry stay apart, so each can be checked and steered on its own terms.
arxiv-2605-03037:
Kanato Goto, Alexey Milekhin, Herman Verlinde, and Jiuci Xu show that de Sitter space can emerge from a pair of one-dimensional theories. De Sitter space is an expanding vacuum with positive energy. The pair they use matches the low-energy limit of the SYK model.

They use large N methods, conformal symmetry, and a split form for Green functions. Inside the two theories, they find a set of operators. That set acts as a free field on a timelike path in de Sitter space. For the three-dimensional case, their map matches the standard bulk rule, adjusted for de Sitter space.
arxiv-2605-03237:
Dhruv Gulwani, Basem Suleiman, Aditya Joshi, and Sonit Singh present TeamUp, a system that matches students to projects and builds diverse teams at course scale. Hand allocation and preference surveys cannot reliably place students at the right challenge level or mix skills well, and visible projects tend to go to already strong students.

TeamUp uses language model embeddings plus rules for difficulty, domain taste, and demand balance to recommend placements. Teams are formed for skill spread rather than sameness. In a virtual trial with hundreds of profiles, match quality, difficulty fit, and team diversity all rose sharply over baselines, at low cost and sub-second speed.
arxiv-2605-03437:
Haibo Xiao, Hanzhe Liang, Jie Zhou, Jinbao Wang, and Can Gao detect anomalies in 3D point clouds by learning a discriminative signed distance function from multi-scale features. Point clouds are large and sparse, so per-point representations accurate enough to flag defects are hard to learn directly.

A noise generation module creates varied abnormal points to sharpen feature learning. A multi-scale level-of-detail module then mixes fine local and coarse global cues, and a surface discrimination module trains the distance function to separate normal from abnormal points. On two benchmarks the method beat the prior best on object-level scores by clear margins.
arxiv-2605-03637:
Zhiyuan Li and six co-authors address the data bottleneck in robot learning: human videos are plentiful, but robots move differently from people. Their framework edits a human demonstration video into a robot execution video. The key is separating what the task is from how a particular body performs it.

The method factorizes a video into two independent latent spaces, one for task content and one for embodiment, enforced by a dual contrastive objective. A small adapter feeds those codes into a frozen video diffusion model, producing a coherent robot version from a single human demonstration, with no paired human-robot data needed. Experiments show temporally consistent, morphologically accurate robot demonstrations.
arxiv-2605-03837:
Grigory Solomatov and Derya Akkaynak ask when the true colors of a scene can be recovered from images taken inside a scattering medium, such as water or fog. The problem is intrinsically ill-posed: many color and medium combinations explain the same observation, so error cannot be controlled without understanding the candidate solution space. Two sources of trouble are the projection of spectra onto pixel values and the unknown medium parameters.

The authors show sensor improvements alone cannot fix medium-induced distortion without extra constraints. They identify recovery patterns, cross-pixel relationships that occur naturally in images, and prove that for an ideal hyperspectral camera these patterns restrict the solution to a unique candidate. The result opens a first-principles route to quantitative imaging in scattering environments.
arxiv-2605-03937:
Jingyao Gong reports MiniMind-O, an open small-scale omni model built on the MiniMind language model at about a tenth of a billion parameters. The model accepts text, speech, and image inputs and returns both text and streaming speech. The release includes model code, checkpoints, and the main training datasets, making the complete interaction loop directly inspectable.

Architecturally, a full MiniMind backbone acts as the Thinker, while an independent four-layer Talker built from MiniMind blocks produces speech, reading a middle-layer Thinker state together with an autoregressive codec buffer. Frozen speech and image encoders feed lightweight projectors, and speaker control is handled inside the audio-code context rather than by a separate synthesis module. Dense and mixture-of-experts variants reached similar consistency scores in Thinker-Talker evaluation.
arxiv-2605-04037:
Giulia Sambataro and Virginie Ehrlacher work on model order reduction for time-dependent parametrized variational inequalities. They focus on discrete contact problems. Their prototype is an agent-based crowd model. In it, agent speeds come at each time step from a least-squares problem with constraints. Parameter changes create strong spread in positions and contact forces. So the solution manifold's complexity decays slowly, and linear reduction struggles. The aim is speed: smaller models that still track the full one.

Their nonlinear approach pairs a linear reduced-order model with a deep-learning-based fix. A greedy algorithm compresses the Lagrange multipliers. Proper orthogonal decomposition is applied to velocity snapshots. Hyper-reduction is explored through the empirical interpolation method and empirical quadrature. The two are compared on cost and accuracy. The method is shown on a complex, highly congested crowd scene with many agents. The paper is a methods paper.
arxiv-2605-04137:
Yuval Grossman, Zoltan Ligeti, and Yosef Nir study CP asymmetries in the decays of charged B, D, and K mesons into a charged pion and a neutral pion. These asymmetries are commonly said to vanish in the isospin limit, the approximation where up and down quarks are treated as identical. The authors set out to clarify what that term actually means in this context, where loose usage can hide real effects.

They provide a unified formalism for discussing the three asymmetries. They build an understanding of how various suppression factors distinguish them qualitatively. Their Standard Model estimates span three orders of magnitude. The B meson asymmetry sits at a few parts in a thousand. The D meson sits near one part in a hundred thousand. The K meson sits near one part in a million.
arxiv-2605-04437:
Yu Zhong and three co-authors study how a fast magnetic wave steepens as it approaches a null point in the Sun's corona, a place where the magnetic field vanishes. The setting connects to sympathetic flares, where one eruption seems to trigger another nearby.

The null is modelled with a simple potential field and uniform plasma, and the wave is launched from a point source outside the region where sound and magnetic wave speeds match. Refraction bends the wave, and the falling wave speed near the null amplifies its nonlinear deformation. The authors find the wave can dissipate before reaching the null itself.
arxiv-2605-04537:
Jianfei Liu and Zhimin Zhou use survey data to study how bars, the elongated stellar structures crossing many disk galaxies, relate to star formation and activity at a galaxy's centre. Their sample holds more than thirty-three thousand nearby disk galaxies, classified by citizen-science volunteers.

Strong bars are more common in massive, redder, metal-rich galaxies, while weak bars favour bluer, lighter disks. Strong bars boost central star formation in low-mass galaxies but suppress it in massive ones, suggesting bars first funnel gas inward and later help exhaust it. Barred galaxies also host active central black holes more often, with the most powerful cases most frequent where bars are present.
arxiv-2605-04737:
Edoardo Giusto and seven co-authors run a graph classification task on a real quantum simulator. It has two hundred fifty-six neutral atom qubits. On this platform, atoms held by optical tweezers natively encode graph structure. Public access to such machines is rare, and hardware restrictions make implementation nontrivial.

They compute a quantum evolution kernel. It turns each graph into features, based on how a quantum state evolves on it. The graphs come from a standard protein data set. Classical machine learning then performs the final classification. Benchmarked against classical kernels, the quantum features performed slightly better, showing the method works even on a noisy analogue simulator.
arxiv-2605-05337:
The quantum Fourier transform is a workhorse of quantum computing, defined for groups. Ben Foxman, Barak Nehoran, and Yongshan Ding extend it to a broader algebraic setting, finite-dimensional semisimple algebras. They give efficient transforms for three families: the partition algebra, the Brauer algebra, and the walled Brauer algebra.

These algebras matter for duality theory, statistical physics, and many-body problems. Their transforms need not be unitary, but for large parameters a unitary operator approximates them well. The circuits run in time that grows only polynomially in the key parameters, keeping the construction practical.
arxiv-2605-05437:
Eye contact quietly runs most face-to-face teamwork, deciding who speaks and who is heard. Markus Wieland, Phillip Koch, and Michael Sedlmair interviewed seventeen people with visual impairments about such mixed-ability settings. Their question was how eye contact feels when the visual signal itself is not accessible.

Three patterns stood out. When gaze cannot hand over the floor, being named directly becomes essential. Unclear turn cues and constant access work tire people out, sometimes to withdrawal. Norms around eye contact also skew how participation is judged. The authors turn these findings into five design challenges for fairer collaboration tools.
arxiv-2605-05537:
The space antenna LISA will one day hear a hum from countless distant black hole pairs. Ran Chen and four co-authors ask how orbital eccentricity changes that stochastic background. Pairs born through some channels start on stretched orbits, and their combined signal differs from the circular case.

With a fully Bayesian analysis, they find highly eccentric populations would stand out clearly from circular ones. For thermal eccentricity patterns, formation height decides whether confusion arises. They also show environmental effects like gas friction could be told apart from vacuum evolution, but only in fairly dense surroundings.
arxiv-2605-05937:
Jifei Wang and eight co-authors examine wave like patterns in the disk of the Milky Way. Large surveys from LAMOST and Gaia show complex ripples in how stars move and in their chemical makeup. The team set out to map the shift between the inner and outer thin disk and test one physical reading of the pattern.

They built a simple model of two radial waves moving in opposite directions and fitted it to the observed motions. Both survey samples show the known wave pattern, plus a clear shift in spin speed and metal content. N-body simulations backed the model. The results point to a disk shaped by more than one past disturbance.
arxiv-2605-06037:
Amy Searle and five co-authors test a virtually connected probabilistic computer on hard combinatorial problems. Such problems often must be reshaped to fit fixed hardware layouts, and steps like embedding or quadratisation degrade solution quality. The design studied here uses fast photonic random number units and virtual connections, avoiding those reshaping steps.

The authors run heuristic solvers on problems whose geometry would suffer most on physically wired hardware. Greedy graph coloring supports parallel operation and favorable scaling. Simulations predict the photonic machine would beat the times set by digital annealing units on spin glass ground state problems by a wide margin. They also show how much problem size would grow under the reshaping that rival hardware requires.
arxiv-2605-06137:
Bowen Zheng and four co-authors add a short learned preface to autoregressive image generation. In such systems, visual tokens must serve both faithful reconstruction and smooth generation, and those demands pull against each other. Their design separates the two jobs instead of forcing one token set to do both.

Prologue generates a small set of prologue tokens placed before the visual sequence. Only those tokens train on the generation loss, while visual tokens stay dedicated to reconstruction. On ImageNet, the base version more than halved a key generation error score with reconstruction almost unchanged. The prologue tokens also developed emergent semantic structure on their own, and fixing them while resampling kept the broad layout of the scene.
arxiv-2605-06537:
Bodong Du and ten co-authors introduce MedHorizon, a benchmark for understanding full-length medical procedure videos. Clinical review often needs a whole procedure, not a short clip. Decisive evidence inside these videos is sparse, subtle, and spread out, while most views are repetitive, and earlier benchmarks hand models pre-located evidence instead.

MedHorizon keeps 759 hours of full procedures and asks over a thousand evidence-grounded multiple-choice questions. Evidence frames average a tiny fraction of each video, so models must search before reasoning. The best model tested reaches only about forty-one percent accuracy, showing robust full-procedure understanding remains far off and retrieval is a key bottleneck.
arxiv-2605-06637:
Lei Tan, Yingshi Luan, Pincong Zou, Pingyang Dai, and Liujuan Cao tackle person re-identification when bodies are partly hidden behind obstacles. Occlusion removes identifying cues and adds clutter, so matching a partial view against a whole-body representation is unreliable. Earlier methods estimate visible parts with extra models or fake occlusion through augmentation, without one unified learning scheme.

Their DPM++ framework learns a masked metric that adapts per sample, selecting identity features that stay visible and suppressing unreliable ones. A CLIP-based two-stage supervision transfers text-side identity knowledge into the matching space. Saliency-guided patch transfer synthesizes realistic occluded training samples, and benchmarks show consistent gains in both occluded and normal settings.
arxiv-2605-06837:
Jozef Kratica, Mirjana Čangalović, and Vera Kovačević-Vujčić determine metric dimensions for two classic graph families, the Johnson and Kneser graphs. A metric dimension counts how few landmark vertices suffice to identify every vertex by its distances to them. The strong version demands unique identification along shortest paths, and the doubly version strengthens the separation requirement further between vertex pairs.

For Johnson graphs the exact strong metric dimension is obtained from known literature results. For Kneser graphs it is settled whenever the ground set is at least roughly triple the subset size. Both families, in the case of two-element subsets, share the same doubly metric dimension, a rounded two-thirds of the vertex count parameter.
arxiv-2605-07037:
Atsushi Takagi and three co-authors improve robot teleoperation, where a follower robot copies a human leader's movements. A spring-like pull keeps tracking accurate only at high stiffness, which can be dangerous near people or fragile objects. Their controller instead estimates where the leader intends to move, and sends that target to the follower.

Because accuracy no longer depends on stiffness, users can soften or stiffen the follower as the task demands. Tests on two seven-joint arms covered free tracking, touching a balloon, inserting a peg, and polishing a table. The new control raised tracking accuracy, improved completion rates, and shortened task times compared with an earlier approach.
arxiv-2605-07237:
Hyeon Hwang, Jiwoo Lee, and Jaewoo Kang teach language models to do their reasoning in code rather than alongside it. Tool-using models usually reason in words and call code only to check calculations, which leaves error-prone mental arithmetic and muddled roles. Their ThinC framework starts with a brief written plan, then reasons entirely through code blocks linked by execution results.

Trained on thousands of distilled code-centered solutions, the larger ThinC model beat every tool-using baseline on five competition math benchmarks. It even surpassed a far larger thinking model. Almost all final answers were grounded in interpreter output, and the model recovered well from code failures without falling back on written reasoning.
arxiv-2605-07537:
Brice and four colleagues study decision making under uncertainty when the agent cannot see the full state of its world. Their setting is multi environment partially observable Markov decision processes, where the starting environment is unknown and chosen adversarially. The paper focuses on finite horizon goals, asking for the optimal value and policy over a fixed number of steps.

Computing the optimal value and policy was already known to be PSPACE complete for ordinary partially observable processes. The authors prove the same PSPACE completeness holds in the broader multi environment setting. They also present a practical algorithm for the problem and test it on classical benchmarks. It significantly outperforms the only previously known algorithm for this setting. The result pins down the problem difficulty while giving practitioners a working method that beats the prior state of the art.
arxiv-2605-07637:
