Tests use teams of up to ten agents on navigation tasks. Their fronts beat baselines trained at fixed reward mixes. The method also scales where central control fails.
arxiv-2606-02537:
Laber and Klein write a guide to homophily in higher-order networks. Homophily means similar individuals interact more than chance suggests. Heterophily is the reverse pattern. Social systems are now often modeled as hypergraphs. There, one edge can join many people at once. Pairwise measures do not carry over cleanly.

The guide offers two complementary views. First, it surveys measures of homophily and heterophily in hypergraphs. Conceptual gaps versus pairwise measures are stressed. Each measure is taught through deep examples. Second, it reviews hypergraph models for higher-order mixing patterns. Model families are split by use case. The synthesis lays a base for sound method choices. It also points to future work in this young field.
arxiv-2606-02637:
Hernández and co-authors solve an inverted oscillator model in relativistic quantum theory. The starting point is the Dirac-Moshinsky oscillator, a standard solvable model. A change in the momentum term turns it into its inverted twin. The team works in one space and one time dimension. The upper part of the spinor obeys a Weber equation with a complex parameter. Solutions are parabolic cylinder functions of complex order.

The spectrum is purely continuous, with energy above the rest mass. No bound states exist. Three schemes fix state normalization. Sharp resonances, of Gamow type, appear as poles of the resolvent. The negative-energy sector holds mirror resonances for antiparticles. Their math signals an unstable vacuum, where pairs can form on their own, much as in the Schwinger effect. The algebra is the principal series of SU(1,1). The Hamiltonian is PT-symmetric, with symmetry intact in the physical range.
arxiv-2606-02737:
Michail and co-authors fix a position bias in dense text retrieval. Dense retrieval packs a passage into one vector. Early content dominates that vector. Relevant spans near the end get short shrift. A prior method equalized the pooling token's attention across segments. It used fixed strength and a fixed self-attention mass. Its effect on retrieval was never tested. The new work adds control.

A strength coefficient blends raw and fully equalized attention. A lean implementation cuts calibration memory from gigabytes to under a megabyte. A variant keeps the pooling token's self-attention mass intact. Tests span three embedding models and two pooling schemes. Moderate calibration beats full equalization as a trade-off. On a benchmark across 10 languages and 31 domains, one setting cuts position sensitivity in all 16 test combinations. Gains reach 43 percent in relative terms. Retrieval quality also improves slightly. Calibration runs at indexing time, so queries stay fast.
arxiv-2606-02837:
Brunello and co-authors audit two datasets used to test translation from natural language into first-order logic. The datasets are FOLIO and MALLS. Such benchmarks support neurosymbolic AI and natural language inference. Yet the authors note that no one had checked them with care before.

The team inspected the FOLIO validation split and part of the MALLS test set by hand. They report that about 42 percent of entries in each set hold wrong logic formulas. Many source sentences were also vague, and some FOLIO inference labels were wrong. The group then released corrected ground truths. Three large language models gained 11 to 23 points in accuracy on the fixed data. The authors also built a tool that points human reviewers to the entries most likely to be wrong. With that help, 90 percent dataset accuracy took review of under 20 percent of entries.
arxiv-2606-02937:
Wang and co-authors present BEAST3D, a framework for reading animal behavior from multi-view laboratory video. Cameras now record animal motion in three dimensions. Rich 3D features are still hard to extract. Supervised pose tools need heavy manual labeling, and generic reconstruction models fail on sparse lab views.

BEAST3D learns from unlabeled, calibrated video in a self-supervised way. A vision transformer predicts 3D Gaussian splats that rebuild held-out views through differentiable rendering. It also separates the animal from the background. The method needs as few as four views because it uses known camera settings directly. Tests span four species. The learned features transferred to three tasks: new view synthesis, multi-view pose estimation, and neural encoding. Neural encoding links the 3D behavior features to brain activity recorded. The authors present BEAST3D as a versatile base for behavioral analysis.
arxiv-2606-03037:
Liu and co-authors report James Webb Space Telescope observations of a distant quasar. The quasar J1512+4422 sits at redshift about 6.2, roughly 900 million years after the Big Bang. It comes from the Aether survey. NIRSpec integral field observations reveal a black hole of about 8.9 times ten to the eighth solar masses.

It already lies on the local black hole mass to velocity dispersion relation. The measured dispersion is about 288 kilometers per second. The team detects a nuclear outflow moving near 478 kilometers per second, extending about 3.2 kiloparsecs. Its mass outflow rate exceeds the current star formation rate. Its kinetic energy rate meets the threshold that simulations set for negative feedback. The outflow's timescale matches the host's quenching timescale from its star formation history. The authors suggest the outflow is suppressing star formation. The host also resembles later quiescent galaxies.
arxiv-2606-03237:
Trivedi, Jaques, Cross, Vezhnevets, and Leibo argue that a lone-wolf path to superintelligence will not yield cooperation. Most AI research builds agents that treat the world as a fixed source of feedback. The authors call this stance solipsistic. A system built that way, they claim, is unlikely to cooperate once deployed.

Deployment itself shifts the world the system acts in. Past data then diverge from the live context, a gap the authors name the self-undermining property of unilateral optimization. Closing the gap needs AI that takes part in cooperation: the process by which actors pick equilibria while bound to each other. The team calls for a fresh research stance. Interdependence should be a core design rule, not a task to solve later. They urge testbeds with adaptive partners and institutions as design parts.
arxiv-2606-03437:
Sanz-Guerrero, Mager, and von der Wense show that chat models trust their own answers too much. Instruction-tuned models are known to be worse calibrated than their base versions. What the chat format itself adds to that flaw was unclear. The team separates the effect of post-training from the effect of the chat template.

A clear ownership bias appears in the tests. Models rate their own answers as more likely right than the same answers from a user. The gap reaches 26 percent higher confidence for self-made text. Six recent open-weight models, three benchmarks, and three ways of asking all agree. A simple fix follows from the finding. When a model's answer is fed back as if a user wrote it, overconfidence drops. Calibration improves by up to 26 percent, with no retraining needed. The trick narrows the gap between base and tuned models.
arxiv-2606-03637:
Rõõm and co-authors probe vortex-core states in a thin-film iron-based superconductor. The film is FeTeSe, a multiband material with no gap nodes. Bound states, named for Caroli, de Gennes, and Matricon, sit inside its vortex cores. The team reads their decay with terahertz Faraday spectroscopy. Light tuned by polarization picks out each state's helicity and band of origin.

Long-lived peaks show up with opposed circular polarizations. Electron-like and hole-like bands give split signals. That split lets the team gauge lifetimes band by band. Vortex mass, coherence length, and upper critical field also come out per band. All shift in step with changes in the film's mix. The work proves terahertz optics can probe these helical core states head-on. It gives hard proof of multiband core states in iron-based materials.
arxiv-2606-03837:
Sträter and Doughty ask where temporal context is truly needed when adapting video models with little data. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning and probing adapt foundation models cheaply. Video versions usually adapt image-pretrained models. Standard methods can also run on video representations directly. The two settings are rarely compared head to head. Both also confine temporal reasoning to a single model part.

This study compares adaptation plans across settings in a systematic way. Appearance-focused, motion-focused, and spatially dense tasks are all covered. Low-data scenarios get special focus, since efficiency matters most there. How temporal context spreads across backbone, adapter, and probe is the central variable. Results show that allocation choice drives adaptation quality. Teams adapting video models on small budgets get direct guidance. Not every stage needs time context, and the study maps which do.
arxiv-2606-03937:
Jin and co-authors question a common trick in training visual reasoning models. In text-only training, token entropy helps assign credit for good or bad steps. In image tasks, key visual tokens can have low entropy by nature. An entropy-only rule can thus skip the tokens that carry sight. Past multimodal methods felt this strain but lacked a shared fix.

Their VEPO method joins visual sensitivity with token entropy in one score. Credit flows to tokens that are both grounded in the image and rich in signal. Tests show clear gains over the entropy-only base. The gain was 2.28 points at the 7B scale and 3.15 at 3B. Extra tests back the design choices, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-04037:
Thanh Luong Tuan and Sanyal tackle pre-release checks for business AI agents. Bench tests of skill do not show if an agent is safe to run. Checks after launch, and human review, give weak proof once an agent is live. Their frame builds test cases from an ontology instead. It aims to form a clear gate before release.

An Agent Operational Envelope sets the test space first. It spans access rights, field limits, safety traits, rules, and levels of self-rule. A pipeline then turns the ontology into rule-based and hostile test cases. A Trust Certificate that machines can check records graded verdicts. A pilot in four tightly ruled fields built 1,800 cases. Ontology-based cases beat persona-based ones on rule coverage, 48.3 to 33.1 percent. Cross-checks spanned three model families and 5,400 cases.
arxiv-2606-04237:
Sam Rosen and Jason Xu extend in 2026 the weighted Bayesian bootstrap, a fast method for sampling from an approximate posterior distribution, to problems where the posterior must obey constraints. Constrained estimates are common in finance and engineering, where optimizers give a point answer but no uncertainty.

Their algorithm leans on fast convex optimization tools. Under regularity conditions, they prove the samples' spread matches that of an efficient restricted estimator, so the uncertainty quantification is honest, not decorative. Tests on varied constrained problems showed broad applicability and advantages over rival methods. As a case study, they imposed the no-arbitrage constraints that European-style option prices must satisfy and derived uncertainty bands for an entire option pricing surface.
arxiv-2606-04337:
Jiayue Han and co-authors review Floquet nonadiabatic dynamics in 2026. This is a framework for molecules and materials driven by repeating light fields. Periodic driving can reshape electronic states. It can also open reaction paths that the standard field-free picture misses.

The review surveys recent methods for closed and open quantum systems. It then shows what the framework has explained. Cases include electron transfer where molecules meet metals, and quantum transport through molecular junctions. Carrier motion in crystalline solids is covered, as is driving with several light colors at once. The authors close with the hurdles between today's model demos and predictive simulation of real light-driven processes.
arxiv-2606-04737:
Wang and colleagues inject physical knowledge into AI video generators so the motion they produce obeys real-world physics, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Large video models look convincing, but pixel-level training does not teach the regularities governing motion and interaction, so physical plausibility lags visual quality. Their framework, PILA, adds physics-structured latent guidance into the frozen flow-matching dynamics of a pretrained video model, leaving its visual prior intact while correcting its dynamics.

PILA first estimates anchored physical fields from the frozen generator's latents, mapping observable motion into an attribute bank of less directly observed physical proxies. The refined proxies are decoded into a correction of the flow-matching vector field. Trained in stages on the Wan 2.1 model, the adapter transfers directly to the larger Wan 2.2, achieving state-of-the-art results on three benchmarks in both visual quality and measured physical plausibility.
arxiv-2606-04837:
Cunden, Cuppone, Gramegna, and Vivo solve a spacing puzzle. Given random points on a line, choose a subset that keeps the chosen points as evenly spread as possible, in a 2026 arXiv probability paper. From an initial configuration of random points, the goal is to select a smaller set maximizing the minimal spacing between consecutive chosen points. For general gap distributions and all valid sizes, they derive exact distributional identities for the optimal spacing and its asymptotic behavior.

The problem reformulates as a threshold-resetting random walk. The walk advances by random increments and resets to the origin whenever it exceeds a fixed threshold. The probability that the optimal spacing exceeds a given value equals the probability that the walk completes the required number of reset cycles within the allotted steps. This yields an exact representation through first-passage functionals of the walk, and a numerical scheme for the large regime.
arxiv-2606-05337:
Haorui Ni, Sunil Bhave, and Mengyue Xu demonstrate a push-pull acousto-optic modulator on non-suspended thin-film lithium niobate in this 2026 arXiv paper. Acousto-optic modulators convert between microwave and optical signals and serve quantum transduction, where chip-scale devices need high efficiency, broad bandwidth, and low optical loss. Their device keeps the film attached to its silicon substrate and builds the push-pull action in, aiming for efficiency and bandwidth.

The team mapped how electromechanical coupling depends on orientation in X-cut lithium niobate by fabricating devices with different propagation directions, identifying the orientation that maximizes acousto-optic transduction. The low-loss device reached a half-wave voltage-length product of 1.004 volt-centimeters at 0.842 gigahertz with an interaction length of 400 micrometers, and a modulation bandwidth of 132.5 megahertz, wide for this device class. The authors present the results as a step toward integrated photonic-phononic links.
arxiv-2606-05437:
Simegnew Yihunie Alaba and Yuichi Motai present an uncertainty-aware sensor fusion method for autonomous navigation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Each sensor fails differently: inertial units drift over time, while cameras suffer under poor lighting, occlusion, and scarce visual features, so a fusion rule is fragile.

Their hybrid model pairs a Vision Transformer, which reads patterns in the inertial data, with a multiscale convolutional network that extracts optical-flow motion cues from images. An adaptive fusion module then weights the two streams dynamically according to estimated uncertainty, trusting whichever sensor is currently more reliable. A new uncertainty-aware loss function builds prediction uncertainty directly into training. Evaluated on the KITTI driving dataset, the method outperformed baselines on absolute trajectory error and relative pose error. It ran at 155 frames per second on a high-end GPU, fast enough for deployment on resource-constrained autonomous systems.
arxiv-2606-05737:
Yitong Chen and colleagues show robot policies can act in one generation step in a 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models often borrow diffusion tricks from image tools. They refine an action through many denoising rounds. The authors note an asymmetry: robot inputs are rich, but action chunks are small and low-dimensional. Heavy few-step machinery from imaging may be needless here.

Their recipe keeps plain velocity training and skips teachers, distillation, and extra losses. The one change biases training toward high-noise states. A toy grid task first isolated the effect cleanly. Robot tests on the LIBERO suites followed, plus a real two-armed robot check. One-step policies generally matched ten-step decoding under the same recipe. On the long-task suite the one-step policy scored about ninety-six percent. Simpler training, the authors argue, already buys fast action generation.
arxiv-2606-05937:
Lerner and Yvon measure political fairness in language models by how surprised the models are in a 2026 arXiv paper. Perplexity gauges how unexpected a text feels to a model. A fair model, they propose, should find all parties' texts equally unsurprising. They tested ten models on three datasets spanning thirty-seven languages. Party manifestos and speeches supplied the texts.

The models were systematically more perplexed by far-right and nationalist parties than by social-democratic ones. The pattern held across the language collection. It also tracked earlier translation-fairness results, and perplexity correlated with downstream translation quality. Base models and their instruction-tuned versions scored almost identically. That correlation finger-points pretraining data, not later fine-tuning, as the bias source. Instruction tuning barely moved the numbers. The authors offer perplexity as a cheap fairness audit for any model. Political leaning, they conclude, is baked in early.
arxiv-2606-06037:
Ceccatelli, Jeon, and Adelani probe whether audio assistants keep their safety training when harmful requests switch languages mid-sentence in a 2026 arXiv paper. Safety testing for large audio language models leans on monolingual text prompts. Real speech mixes languages freely, and attackers exploit the seams. SpeechJBB is an audio jailbreak benchmark spanning multiple top models. An augmented setting inserts plausible pseudo-words around safety-critical terms to mimic casual obfuscation.

Code-switched harmful audio produced high jailbreak success rates. Non-English monolingual prompts and non-English code-switched pairs attacked most successfully. Pseudo-word wrapping lowered refusal rates further. Natural-sounding disguise, not exotic hacking, defeated the policies. The results expose a generalization gap: alignment trained on tidy text does not transfer to messy multilingual speech. Voice interfaces are deploying fastest where such mixing is normal. The benchmark gives safety teams a concrete test where the weakness lives.
arxiv-2606-06237:
Luca Cirfeta stress tests a machine learning pipeline that hunts for gravitational wave glitches in this 2026 arXiv paper. Glitches are short noise bursts in LIGO data that can mimic or mask real cosmic signals. The pipeline embeds spectrogram images with the DINOv2 vision model and flags outliers. Cirfeta asks how faint a glitch it can catch, and what its alert threshold should be.

He injected synthetic glitches from eight shape families into real LIGO O4a data, in one thousand four hundred seventeen valid trials. A shifting dynamic threshold recovered the broad Butterfly and ZSweep shapes perfectly at strong signal levels, but its false positive rate drifted. A fixed threshold set at zero point eight seven four for strict false positive control missed every morphology, even at signal to noise ratios up to four hundred thirty. Background scores across one hundred eighty eight thousand segments were strongly non Gaussian.
arxiv-2606-06437:
Archisman Panigrahi, Vladislav Poliakov, and Leonid Levitov describe a ghostly interference effect in superconductors in this 2026 arXiv paper. In optics, a mirror beside a light source creates a second, virtual source, and the two interfere. The authors find the electronic version: quasiparticles in a superconductor scatter from a single impurity and also reflect from a nearby boundary, such as a terrace edge. The direct and reflected waves interfere as if a ghost impurity sat behind the mirror.

The pattern mixes the familiar Friedel oscillations, rings around the impurity, with extra hyperbolic fringes from the ghost. Crucially, the effect appears at first order in the impurity's strength, making it parametrically larger than the two impurity interference studied before. The fringes stretch beyond half the Fermi wavelength and encode the paired state's structure, including how its gap varies around the Fermi surface. Scanning tunneling microscopes should see them directly.
arxiv-2606-06637:
Tianyi Zhang and co-authors write a photonic molecule with light, erase it, and write it again in this 2026 arXiv paper. A photonic molecule couples two resonators so their modes hybridize, splitting apart in frequency, which is useful for filters, lasers, and transducers. Normally the coupling is fixed at fabrication, or tuned with a constant electrical bias that scales poorly. Here one lithium niobate racetrack resonator hosts both modes. A photorefractive grating, written optically by interfering bright and dark modes, couples them.

The hybrid mode splitting reaches gigahertz scale across a seven hundred gigahertz bandwidth. The gratings persist for hours with no power applied. Their strength is set by the writing pump, and selective pumping drives repeated write, erase, and rewrite cycles. As a demonstration, the team built a single sideband millimeter wave transducer near one hundred seven gigahertz, with five gigahertz of tuning range.
arxiv-2606-06837:
Job interviews now come with a new worry: is the candidate reading a script? Vsevolod Kovalev and Pranay Manocha build a detector for that problem in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system, SEAM, listens for the difference between scripted and spontaneous speech. It is meant as a guardrail that flags suspicious stretches for human review.

The hard part is honesty in testing. Models can cheat by memorizing recording conditions instead of speaking style. SEAM fights that with uniform preprocessing and sampling that hides corpus identity. It also adds non-speech sounds during training. The compact model scored near the top on an outside interview test set. Removing the anti-shortcut parts raised internal scores but hurt outside performance badly. A compressed version shrank the model to about forty two megabytes. It kept almost all of its external accuracy.
arxiv-2606-07037:
Cruttwell and Lanfranchi generalize a classic geometry tool in this 2026 arXiv paper on tangent categories, which are abstract frameworks that capture how tangent spaces behave without requiring smooth surfaces. Their subject is the Ehresmann connection, a rule that splits movement along a surface into vertical and horizontal parts. The authors ask whether that splitting can be defined purely through category theory, the branch of mathematics that studies structures and maps between them.

The paper gives several equivalent definitions, contrasting full connections with more abstract versions built from vertical lifts. It proves these definitions recover the older Koszul connections, which describe how vectors change along curves. The authors also define parallel transport, meaning how vectors are carried along paths, and curvature for their setting. They prove the structural equation and the Bianchi identity, two standard consistency checks for curvature.
arxiv-2606-07137:
Magnets usually lose their order as they warm up; these crystals do the opposite. Qin and co-authors report inverse melting in magnetic perovskites in this 2026 arXiv paper. The materials are columnar ordered quadruple perovskites with sodium, a rare earth, manganese, and titanium. At the coldest temperatures their spins show only two dimensional correlations, no true long range order.

Neutron powder diffraction tracked the spin patterns as temperature rose. Warming carried the disordered state into a fully three dimensional antiferromagnetic structure. Only later did further heating destroy order into the usual paramagnetic state. The authors blame built in chemical disorder on one crystal site. That disorder couples to competing exchange forces between the rare earth and manganese sublattices. The result is order created by heating, an order by disorder twist. Such behavior reshapes how phase diagrams of frustrated magnets are read.
arxiv-2606-07237:
Mahdi Alkaeed examines whether medical chatbots give consistent advice when a clinical question is merely reworded, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The models studied include general systems such as GPT-3.5 and Llama3 alongside medical ones such as BioBERT and ClinicalBERT. All were tested on MedMCQA, a benchmark of medical examination questions. The worry is practical: a tool that changes its diagnosis after simple rephrasing cannot be trusted at a patient's bedside.

The study separates natural rewordings, such as synonym swaps and paraphrases, from adversarial prompts designed to mislead. Models handled simple word substitutions fairly well but broke down under sentence reordering and misleading context. Accuracy slipped from near ninety-eight percent on clean inputs to roughly ninety-four percent under syntactic changes in the reported comparisons. Adversarial prompts sometimes produced dangerous outputs, including wrong dosages and omitted findings, even from models trained specifically for medicine.
arxiv-2606-07337:
Zhentao Huang and colleagues introduce a way to represent three-dimensional shapes that captures both surface and inner skeleton, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their method, Skeletal-Anchored Dual Harmonics, tiles a shape's surface with compact patches rooted at anchors inside the object's volume. Each patch uses spherical harmonics, mathematical wave patterns on a sphere, in two channels: one describes the local surface shape, the other controls how far the patch reaches. Unlike round blob primitives, these patches stretch directionally to fit ridges and flats.

Starting from a raw point cloud, the system jointly optimizes patch geometry, anchor positions, orientations, and connections in stages. A graph linking neighboring anchors along the surface preserves the shape's structural organization. Experiments on complex shapes showed accurate reconstruction with a compact, coherent skeleton. The representation also supports grouping patches into meaningful regions, within one shape or across several, helping downstream tasks like part segmentation.
arxiv-2606-07437:
Shinde and co-authors rework the automotive safety standard ISO 26262 for vehicles with no driver, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard grades hazards by severity, exposure, and controllability, assuming a human can grab control and mitigate danger. At autonomy levels 4 and 5 that assumption collapses. The authors decompose the controllability placeholder into two parts. Transferability captures how well the system hands control to fallback mechanisms, while predictability captures how other road users can predict the vehicle's behavior.

Predictability is defined from human-robot interaction research, with a framework for measuring it. A designed-versus-achievable gap separates what a fallback design claims from what it can achieve in a scene. The metrics align with ISO 26262 and the SOTIF standard for intended functionality, making fallback and interaction claims testable and traceable across slices of the operating domain. It complements rather than replaces the standards, and keeps their structure.
arxiv-2606-07537:
Md Sadi, Tasin, and Naeem trace hallucination in language models to three architectural decisions rather than to bad data, in this 2026 arXiv analysis. Hallucination, fluent confident falsehood, persists across models, and existing schemes sort it by output type without naming the mechanism behind it. The authors argue three choices form a failure system. Self-attention learns word pairings, swapping proximity for meaning and causing mix-ups and misattribution. The training objective rewards plausible next tokens without factual constraint. Autoregressive decoding commits to each token, pushing errors forward.

Each mechanism maps to a hallucination category in a taxonomy: attention produces intrinsic cases, the objective produces extrinsic ones, and decoding yields logical inconsistency. Dataset flaws like long-tail coverage, bias, and synthetic pollution amplify the harm but exploit them rather than causing them alone. The paper contrasts output checks with model-layer fixes: fixes must target the cause behind a falsehood.
arxiv-2606-07637:
Bertolami proposes flying a proton accelerator as a weather control instrument, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The basis comes from CERN's CLOUD experiment, which showed cosmic rays help seed cloud condensation. A proton beam would act as a steerable cosmic ray source. Low-altitude clouds reflect sunlight and cool the surface, while high-altitude cirrus clouds trap radiation and warm it. One device, flown on a plane, airship, or rocket, could enhance the cooling kind and, at higher flux, trigger the warming kind to precipitate.

Bertolami argues the tool could mitigate droughts, regularize rainfall, and bleed off storms before they grow harmful. Satellites are excluded for reasons developed in the paper. The proposal is speculative, reviving older discussions of weather modification with a mechanism tied to aerosol physics. It invites assessment of feasibility and governance rather than reporting experiments, and frames cloud seeding by accelerator as an alternative to chemical methods.
arxiv-2606-08437:
Seyedmohammadi and colleagues release a dataset for identifying people by their palm prints across very different cameras, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Palmprint recognition offers a privacy-preserving biometric, since palms are less exposed than faces. Deployment is hindered by a domain gap: sign-up usually happens under controlled conditions, while sign-in must work in unconstrained settings. Existing datasets are largely restricted to controlled setups, so algorithms trained on them disappoint in practice.

Their dataset, X-Palm, contains just over six thousand palm images from one hundred three people. It is the first palmprint dataset with paired-identity acquisition designed to bridge controlled enrollment and unconstrained smartphone sign-in. The same identities appear in both domains, letting researchers measure cross-domain performance directly. Both hands of each person are included in the set of images used for the tests in this work.
arxiv-2606-08537:
YanYan Li, Nguyen, and Bo Wang construct new solutions to a classical problem in conformal geometry in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Nirenberg problem asks which functions can arise as the scalar curvature of a sphere after a conformal change of metric, a rescaling that preserves angles, not distances. The authors revisit the axisymmetric case for prescribed curvature functions whose critical points include the north and south poles. The solution set was known to be compact when certain parameters stay away from a critical hypersurface.

For dimensions at least four, they construct two-bump axisymmetric solutions for parameter points close to that hypersurface from one side. A two-bump solution concentrates curvature in two separate peaks rather than one. This gives a one-sided refinement of the known blow-up phenomenon. Non-compactness near the critical surface is realized by two-bump solutions from this side only.
arxiv-2606-08637:
Taşkıran and colleagues predict a new flat magnetic material from theory alone in this 2026 arXiv paper. Altermagnetism is a recently recognized phase. It combines the best of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets, such as spin-split bands with no net magnetization, and is promising for spintronics. Using density functional theory, the authors identify a monolayer of vanadium oxide in a buckled Lieb lattice as a promising altermagnet. They verify the crystal's stability through formation energy and phonon checks.

The crystal also shows auxetic behavior, a negative Poisson ratio, meaning it widens when stretched. Calculations indicate an antiferromagnetic ground state with a large local magnetic moment on each vanadium atom. The band structure shows spin splitting above one electronvolt in the reported results, the hallmark of the phase. A stable monolayer with such strong splitting would be a good platform for spin-based devices.
arxiv-2606-08837:
Chen studies the long-run fate of Kähler-Ricci flow solutions on a noncompact complex space, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The flow deforms a Kähler metric in proportion to its Ricci curvature, smoothing it over time. Self-similar solutions, called solitons, are the expected endstates because they rescale over time. Chen works on an expanding soliton and asks whether every solution must settle toward one such profile.

The answer is no. He shows a solution's asymptotic profile can depend on which sequence of times one follows. A solution can approach infinitely many self-similar solutions along different time sequences and under different rescalings. The behavior traces back to how the initial data look at spatial infinity under dilations. Framing rescaling as a dynamical system, he proves it has infinitely many non-soliton fixed points: non-trivial Ricci breathers, solutions that pulse without being self-similar.
arxiv-2606-09237:
Czubarow, Terpin, and D'Andrea balance an inverted pendulum using one of the cheapest, blurriest depth cameras available, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Time-of-flight cameras time reflected light pulses to measure distance. Compact, cheap, and lighting-robust, they are still believed too coarse for precise feedback control. The inverted pendulum is the canonical test of fast, unstable dynamics: hesitate, and it falls.

With the camera mounted beneath the pendulum, raw depth became angle estimates with a root-mean-square error of 3.4 thousandths of a radian. Feeding those estimates to a standard LQG controller, a linear-quadratic-Gaussian design, stabilized the pendulum reliably and precisely, no motion capture or high-end encoders needed. The setup ships as a compact, open-source platform for replication. Since the controller was deliberately ordinary, the result is a lower bound: better sensors or controllers should improve on it, opening cheap depth sensing to serious control.
arxiv-2606-09837:
Yue Zhao and his co-authors give chatbots a planner that picks the feeling before the words in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spoken agents now stream speech as text is born, token by token. Warmth lags, since no part of the chain owns the choice of mood. Their Self-EmoQ module slots in front of the speech stage and calls the emotion first.

The module is a small add-on built from a pretrained language model. Reinforcement learning trains it with feelings as its moves. Its reward blends copycat cues with scores from Plutchik's wheel of emotions, a classic map of how feelings mix and clash. On four chat sets, from DailyDialog to MELD, the planner beat prompt-only and fine-tuned rivals. It won on both mood calls and reply quality. A full live pipeline then spoke the results. Listeners rated the speech high on fit, flow, and flair.
arxiv-2606-09937:
Sekar presents a training-free method for speeding up multi-step reasoning in language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on inference efficiency. Reasoning pipelines often run several branches sharing the same prompt prefix, yet each rebuilds the same key-value cache, the stored attention data for shared text. Verification passes add more wasted work. His framework, RKSC, attacks both redundancies without retraining.

One part computes the prefix cache once and broadcasts it to branches whose hidden states look similar, generalizing exact prefix caching used by serving tools like vLLM. A second part exits early when branch confidence is decisive or when layer entropy settles, skipping needless verification work. Across five model families, four benchmarks, and one thousand problems, RKSC averaged a speedup slightly above threefold over a no-sharing baseline. Its early-exit errors stayed tiny, at six mistakes among more than sixteen hundred verification calls.
arxiv-2606-10537:
Xiong and colleagues speed up diffusion language models in this 2026 arXiv paper, a newer kind of language model that writes by denoising a whole draft at once. The cost problem is that every denoising step re-reads the entire input prefix, so work grows quadratically with context length. Prefilling-dLLM splits the prefix into chunks, caches their representations once, and retrieves only the most relevant chunks during decoding. The approach needs no retraining.

On LongBench and InfiniteBench the method reaches the best quality among acceleration techniques tested. Its attention kernel delivers speedups between 9.1 and 28.0 times at context lengths from eight to thirty-two thousand tokens. Tokens placed at the start of each chunk act as attention anchors, removing the lost-in-the-middle failure where models ignore mid-context facts. Multi-chunk prefilling even extrapolates to 128,000 tokens with over ninety-two percent exact-match accuracy on retrieval questions.
arxiv-2606-11037:
Le Goff, Smith, and Hart evolve robot bodies for variety as well as performance in this 2026 arXiv paper. Evolutionary searches often collapse onto a few decent designs and stop exploring. The team encodes the robot chassis with superquadrics, smooth tunable shapes described by few parameters, and pairs the encoding with MAP-Elites, an algorithm that archives the best design in each behavioral niche.

Across two test environments, superquadrics plus MAP-Elites earns the highest quality-diversity score, beating network-based encodings and plain evolution. Each factor helps on its own, but the pairing wins: a compact, readable shape language makes the space easier to search. One run archived nearly four thousand distinct functional robots.
arxiv-2606-11137:
Deepthi, Kumar, and Lather count special trees and parking functions in a 2026 arXiv combinatorics paper. Parking functions are classic objects counted by a famous formula. Spherical G-parking functions are a distinguished subset arising from skeleton ideals, with explicit counts known for few graph families. The authors study graphs built from the complete graph on n plus one vertices by deleting some edges at vertex one.

An uprooted spanning tree of the reduced graph has no root edge at vertex one. The authors count those trees where vertex one avoids a forbidden neighbor set. The count is a clean product of powers, with factors n minus one, n minus two, and n minus the set size minus one. They derive the formula combinatorially, then recover it from the matrix tree theorem, gaining identities as byproducts. Finally they count the spherical parking functions: another closed product, squaring the last factor.
arxiv-2606-11337:
Jung and seven co-authors test whether AI agents can synthesize scientific conclusions in a 2026 arXiv paper. Scientific AI agents increasingly retrieve evidence, reason across sources, and synthesize conclusions used in key decisions, yet their ability in high-stakes domains like health is unclear. The team introduces SciConBench, a live benchmark of 9,110 questions with expert-written conclusions from systematic reviews.

Their evaluation pipeline decomposes conclusions into atomic facts and measures correctness and coverage through factual precision and recall. A clean-room harness, SciConHarness, gives agents controlled web interaction to prevent data leakage from boosting scores. Evaluating eight frontier models and deep research agents, factual quality remains low: the best agent reaches a factual F1 of only 0.337 under clean-room settings. Clean-room scores are always lower than open ones, suggesting leakage inflates estimates. Audits of consumer agents like Google AI Overview and OpenEvidence find frequent incomplete and sometimes contradictory conclusions.
arxiv-2606-11537:
Abdallah and five co-authors replace multi-agent debate with a market in a 2026 arXiv paper. Financial and tabular question answering demands exactness: answers must be grounded in the precise facts, formulas, units, signs, and scales behind them. One misread cell can silently yield a plausible but wrong result. Their MoCA-Agent decomposes each question into typed atomic claims.

Specialist traders buy or sell those claims; the market clears orders into confidence-weighted accept or reject decisions. A synthesizer then builds an executable Python program from market-supported evidence only. A code-aware verifier checks the program's execution, structural consistency, and common financial reasoning errors, with at most one repair round. Across ten public benchmarks it scores 78.3 percent on FinQA and 86.9 percent on ESGenius, among other strong results. The authors argue aggregating evidence at claim level, rather than whole answers, improves robustness for high-stakes numerical reasoning.
arxiv-2606-11637:
Kailin Lyu leads a large team building touch-based reasoning for robots in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tactile commonsense reasoning means drawing physical conclusions from touch signals, such as judging softness or slipperiness. Earlier systems were held back by small datasets and by wasteful ways of encoding touch, which is repetitive and depends on the action being performed.

The team's framework, TouchThinker, attacks both problems. They build TouchThinker-1M, a dataset of about one million tactile examples covering 415 objects, eight scenarios and seven sensor types, plus a benchmark for open-world tasks. Their encoder is action-aware, meaning it represents a touch signal in light of the movement that produced it, trimming redundancy. Tests across several datasets show competitive results against the strongest existing models, with more reliable physical reasoning. The authors present the work as a step toward robots that handle unfamiliar objects and settings.
arxiv-2606-12237:
Belchior and Maluf extend a theory of spin three-halves particles across distance, in this 2026 arXiv paper. It describes such fermions, particles with spin one and a half, including the gravitino of supergravity. Nonlocal versions smear the field's response through form factors, weighting functions that soften interactions over a scale. Two kinds are studied: factors on the wave operator and factors on the Dirac operator, the spin equation.

For the massless theory, a covariant gauge fixing lets the propagator, the field's response function, be written with the spin three-halves projector. In the massive theory, free-field constraints survive for form factors, so the unphysical spin one-half sector never becomes dynamical. Wave-operator factors deform only the pole equation; Dirac-type factors give modified dispersion relations, written explicitly for exponential factors. The authors state when the theory stays ghost-free and flag what must be fixed before interactions.
arxiv-2606-12637:
Filatov and Auzinsh present a geometric account of pure two-qubit entanglement in this 2026 arXiv paper. A qubit is the basic unit of quantum information, and entanglement links two qubits so their measured results stay correlated. Entanglement is usually summed up by concurrence, one number for its strength. The authors argue the link also has a shape, visible in the Pauli correlation tensor, a table of correlations between measurements on the two sides.

Seen through local Bloch spheres, which picture one qubit's states, maximally entangled states act as roto-reflections. A roto-reflection combines rotation with a mirror reflection, so it reverses handedness between the spheres. For partly entangled states, the same geometry returns once the shrinkage tied to concurrence is factored out. That plane orders the directions of strongest correlation and changes consistently when either qubit is rotated alone.
arxiv-2606-12737:
He and colleagues present PI-Hunter, an auditing framework that hunts for prompt injections in language-model agents before deployment, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A prompt injection plants malicious instructions inside external content, such as web pages, emails, or retrieved documents, so an agent follows them as if they were commands. Such injections stay dormant until user requests or retrieval paths activate them, which red-teaming tends to miss.

PI-Hunter maps the agent's tools, retrieval links, and external sources. It then builds source-aware test cases and evolves them through feedback, steering the agent into retrieving the planted instructions and giving them away. Auditing the traces pinpoints which source and tool admitted each injection. Across the AgentDojo and AgentDyn benchmarks, PI-Hunter discovers more ingestion paths than red-teaming baselines. It remains effective under defences such as Spotlighting, MELON, and PIGuard, showing that latent injections still slip past them.
arxiv-2606-12837:
Zhao and colleagues present LoHoSearch, a benchmark built to stay difficult for long-horizon search agents after earlier benchmarks topped out, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Benchmarks such as BrowseComp climbed from 30 percent to over 90 percent accuracy in about 10 months, losing their edge. Because their questions are human-written, humans pick familiar entities with direct links, setting a difficulty ceiling that more capable models quickly reach.

LoHoSearch instead builds questions automatically from a knowledge graph covering over 7 million Wikipedia entities. By design it selects relations with large search spaces and assembles them into structurally complex questions whose unique answers are verified against the graph. The result is 544 human-verified questions across 11 domains. Even the strongest model tested posts only 34.74 percent accuracy. Existing context-management tactics, which help a lot on earlier benchmarks, add at most 6.8 points here.
arxiv-2606-12937:
Dyer and Gimenez extend the basic theory of Brink-Howlett groupoids, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They were introduced in the study of normalisers of parabolic subgroups of Coxeter groups. The authors develop their root systems and associated cones. A Coxeter group's reflections are organised by its root system, and the groupoid version aims to linearise the study of reflection subgroups the same way.

These root systems have properties analogous to those of Borcherds-Kac-Moody Lie algebras; in particular, some contain imaginary simple roots, a phenomenon absent from Coxeter root systems. The paper extends the properties of the Tits cone and the imaginary cone from Coxeter groups to cones defined for Brink-Howlett groupoids. As an illustration, the classical Tits theorem says that a finite subgroup of a Coxeter group lies in a finite parabolic subgroup. It generalises to finite-index overgroups of a parabolic subgroup.
arxiv-2606-13537:
Zhu, Huang, and Kan study mixed-language search queries in this 2026 arXiv paper. In multilingual communities, users blend languages inside a query, yet the sensitivity of dense retrievers, search systems that match meaning through embeddings, to mixing is not well understood. The authors run a ratio-controlled study on the mMARCO benchmark. They construct mixed queries by interpolating between the embeddings of translations of the query, varying the mixing proportion. Experiments use the BGE-M3 retrieval model across language pairs and collections.

An optimal mixing ratio beats the best monolingual query in the large majority of cases. An asymmetry emerges, driven by English dominance: mixing is beneficial when searching non-English collections, while collections containing English are best served by English queries. English is the strongest mixing partner for every non-English language. When English dominance is controlled for, the mixing gains follow clearer patterns.
arxiv-2606-14037:
Kim and Flanigan show that language models accept user pushback blindly on moral questions, even when they filter it well on factual ones. When users nudge a model toward or away from a right answer, selective updating is the safe behavior. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines compliance asymmetry: beneficial change under helpful nudges over harmful change under misleading ones. Nine models produced nine hundred seventy-two thousand nudge responses.

On factual questions the ratio reached one point five eight: models followed helpful nudges far more than harmful ones. On moral questions it collapsed to one point zero four, near blindness to direction. The pattern held across families, capability levels, and nudge types. Chain-of-thought prompting amplified helpful and harmful compliance together. Identity-based prompting suppressed both by similar margins. Alignment, the authors argue, should target directionally calibrated updating, not just lower compliance.
arxiv-2606-14537:
Boudjemaa models dark matter as quantum liquid droplets in a 2026 arXiv paper. Dark matter is the unseen mass shaping galaxies. One idea treats it as a Bose-Einstein condensate, a cold quantum fluid. Boudjemaa instead explores self-bound droplets. They would form from ultradilute Bose mixtures. Small quantum fluctuation effects, called Lee-Huang-Yang corrections, hold them together at zero temperature.

He derives an extended equation of state. That is the rule linking pressure and density. He uses self-consistent quantum theory plus a fluid approach. The results show halo traits depend on two things. They depend on the interaction between the mixture's parts. They also depend on fluctuation strength. Halo density, mass, and radius all shift with these. He checks stability through small perturbations. He then compares droplet halo predictions with observed galactic rotation curves.
arxiv-2606-14737:
Geng and co-authors describe protein motion with shape math in a 2026 arXiv paper. Proteins work by changing shape. But most models learn from still sequences and structures. They miss the motion. The authors test a shape tool called persistent homology. It tracks shapes across scales. The goal is descriptors that keep global shape, fine wiggles, and timing cues.

They add a masked Flood complex. It stresses links between residues at low cost. They run the shape tool on structures drawn from motion sims. Diagrams become compact vectors learned from time-lagged views. State models built from them capture the kinetics. Using those models to guide a recent image-style maker improved several ensemble stats. After fine-tuning on colder data, the model carried over well to fast-folding proteins.
arxiv-2606-15037:
Shi and coauthors evaluate radiology reports by asking questions about them in a 2026 study. Standard scoring metrics reward word overlap with a reference report, which says little about clinical correctness. Efficacy metrics check named findings but cover few entities and need costly hand labels. The team instead treats a report as a context that should answer clinical questions.

ReportQA builds knowledge trees of clinical entities and attributes with radiologist guidance. Language models extract structured facts from free-form reports, and templates turn them into question-answer pairs. Filtering keeps about six hundred sixty thousand pairs, near one hundred per report. A judge model answers the questions from the report text, and accuracy becomes the QAScore metric. On a radiologist-judged benchmark, QAScore aligns with expert opinion better than prior metrics. Tests across vision-language models show current systems miss fine-grained attributes, while question-driven inference works better.
arxiv-2606-15137:
Chowdhury builds uringscope, a tool that makes Linux io_uring traffic visible in a 2026 study. io_uring moves input-output requests through shared-memory rings, so syscall tracers like strace see nothing. Kernel tracepoints expose the flow, but they are not stable interfaces across versions. Existing tools therefore work only on narrow kernel ranges.

uringscope is a single binary built on compile-once-run-everywhere eBPF. A model of the request lifecycle lets it rebuild per-request flows from kernel events. BTF-probed program variants and portable field reads handle the shifting tracepoint surface. On device-bound NVMe workloads, its aggregate mode costs under ten percent of throughput, beating rivals. A correctness mode reuses the reconstruction to catch submission-boundary hazards. A built-in doctor turns measurements into problems with evidence for operators. The tool runs on kernels across a version span and is open source.
arxiv-2606-15237:
Kalman and Moscovich speed up ensemble classifiers by quitting early, in a 2026 statistics paper. Ensembles like random forests average many models by majority vote. Bigger ensembles are more accurate but costlier to run on every input. The authors evaluate base models one at a time instead of all at once. Once a majority emerges, the remaining models are never run. They formalize three notions of an optimal stopping rule for this process.

For each notion and each allowed disagreement rate, a linear program yields the optimal strategy. The program runs efficiently, so strategies are cheap to compute. On datasets, the methods gave speed-ups of four times or more on most tasks. Disagreement with the full ensemble stayed controlled at a tenth of a percent. Prediction runtime fell by eighty percent in the random forest tests. The trick applies to other majority-vote ensembles, including language model voting.
arxiv-2606-15337:
Jana and coauthors build a hybrid density functional that predicts band gaps across dimensions in a 2026 electronic structure paper. The band gap decides whether a material conducts, and cheap theories underestimate it. Accurate many-body methods cost too much for large or low-dimensional systems. Dielectric-dependent hybrids fix bulk materials by tying exact exchange to screening. But in thin materials the screening estimate depends on the simulation box, not the material. The authors define an intrinsic screening drawn from the material's electron density.

Their functional folds it in self-consistently, with no per-geometry tuning. Benchmarks cover one hundred materials: bulk, two-dimensional, one-dimensional, and systems. The functional reached near-GW accuracy at Kohn-Sham cost. A pattern emerged linking weaker screening to stronger exchange and gaps. Lower dimensionality weakens screening, which explains thin gap openings. The result gives designers a tool for gap prediction across classes.
arxiv-2606-15437:
Alpay and coauthor turn questions about modal logic countermodels into GPU experiments in a 2026 paper. Modal logic reasons about necessity and possibility across possible worlds. A false formula is refuted by a countermodel, a set of worlds with an assignment making it fail. Theory guarantees a finite one but bounds its size only exponentially. The authors encode worlds as bits in an integer, making the modal operators into fast bitmask operations on a graphics processor.

Their census checks over five thousand formulas across four logics, performing an enormous number of evaluations in about forty-five minutes and emitting checkable countermodels. Every refuted formula in the weakest logic fails on at most two worlds. A synthesized pair of formulas agrees on all frames up to five worlds yet provably splits on a six-world path. The accelerator proposes candidates, but a small checker certifies every claimed witness, keeping brute force honest.
arxiv-2606-15637:
Vadhavkar and colleagues build digital twins of the heart's electrical activity in 2026 that adapt to a patient and predict forward, using HAPI-EP. A patient twin promises personalized medicine, but mechanistic and data-driven models each fall short, and reconstruction-only fitting leaves models unidentifiable. HAPI-EP couples a mechanistic backbone with a neural part that models the leftover mismatch.

Rather than pre-encoding every variation, the twin adapts on the fly to a few live measurements, via meta-learners that infer all its parameters in one pass. That adaptivity makes the twin a conditional generative model, giving its parameters theoretical identifiability. In synthetic and real-data studies, the hybrid twin performs best across parameter values. Gains are largest for repolarization features, hardest for other approaches to recover, and for out-of-distribution prediction. The work is a proof of concept for twins that stay identifiable while they adapt.
arxiv-2606-15737:
Benedikt surveys how Craig interpolation and Beth definability can rewrite database queries in 2026, in a chapter connecting logic to data management. Rewriting translates a source query into a target language that obeys interface restrictions, such as restricted access methods. It generates exactly the middle formulas such rewrites need.

The chapter stresses algorithms that consume a proof and output the needed formula, not mere existence theorems. It ties the methods to preservation theorems, model theory's semantics-to-syntax results. Cases range from vocabulary renaming of first-order queries to access-method plans, nested relations, and Datalog via uniform interpolation. For database readers, the survey reframes rewriting in a logical language with decades of tools behind it, and flags the forms practice actually needs.
arxiv-2606-15837:
Pal and Awate present VarDeepPCA in 2026, a lightweight plugin that repairs distribution shift damage in medical image segmentation. Networks trained at one hospital often fail on scans from another, since scanners and protocols differ, and retraining is costly. Their framework learns valid anatomy from a tiny in-distribution dataset of segmentation maps alone, then restores maps on out-of-distribution images.

A reinterpretation of the softmax mapping lets the variational method model the geometry of anatomy exactly, without sampling, so learning and inference stay cheap. It also attaches uncertainty estimates to each restored map. Across four clinical applications, fourteen datasets, and fifteen comparison methods, it consistently improves the realism and accuracy of segmenters' outputs. The model is small, between one and three million parameters, and modality independent. For hospitals facing scanner changes, it offers repair without new training data or access to the target images.
arxiv-2606-15937:
Lingam, Sulake, and Machara present GOOSE-M2F in 2026, an adaptation of Mask2Former for fine-grained segmentation of unstructured outdoor terrain, built for the GOOSE challenge at ICRA 2026. The benchmark spans 64 fine-grained classes with a severe long tail: rare classes can occupy fewer than fifty pixels per image. Off-road robots need exactly this parsing, for locomotion, navigation, and rescue, yet urban-trained segmenters assume balanced, coarse classes.

Three changes target the tail. Two hundred object queries end representational saturation. A feature refinement module mixes multi-scale context with dual attention. An auxiliary supervision head gives rare classes per-pixel gradients. Training adds balanced losses, rare-class copy-paste, and dynamic re-weighting. Inference uses sliding windows with Gaussian blending and four-scale augmentation, worth over ten points alone. It scores about seventy percent mean IoU, sixty-four fine and seventy-seven coarse, third on the leaderboard.
arxiv-2606-16137:
Li and colleagues build explanations for speech deepfake detectors in 2026 that a person can actually check. Detection systems flag synthetic speech, but users need trustworthy reasons, not just a verdict. Classic explainable AI gives low-level signals tied tightly to the model, which people find hard to read. Language-model explanations read smoothly but often stay generic and ungrounded.

Their training-free framework feeds evidence from classic explainable AI methods into multimodal language models as guidance. The model then writes explanations anchored to that evidence instead of improvising. Working with the PartialSpoof dataset, the team also builds a grounded explanation dataset. Methods using the XAI evidence raise inside accuracy by over 45 percent in the reported evaluation, backed by human evaluation and faithfulness checks. Explanations become more specific and better located in time, with less hallucination.
arxiv-2606-16237:
Meng and Zhang establish in 2026 the basic theory for a class of backward stochastic equations that mix partial differential operators with jumps. Backward stochastic partial differential integral equations arise when a system evolves under noise and sudden jumps, and a terminal condition must be met. Proving that solutions exist, are unique, and respect ordering is the paper's task.

The authors first solve a backward stochastic evolution equation with jumps in the Gelfand triple framework, a standard setting for such problems. They then obtain well-posedness of both weak and strong solutions to the full equation, with specific Sobolev spaces replacing the abstract triple. Finally, they prove a comparison principle: ordered terminal data and drivers yield ordered solutions. That principle ensures uniqueness of value functions in stochastic control. In finance, it supports consistent pricing equations and the absence of arbitrage.
arxiv-2606-16737:
Valorani shows how to discover dimensionless groups from data in a 2026 paper on the algebra of units. Engineers combine measurements with different units into a few pure numbers, like the Reynolds number in fluid flow. A classical theorem of Buckingham guarantees such groups exist, but finding them has always needed expert knowledge of the physics.

The key move is to log the measurements and watch how the data change when an experiment is rescaled in size or speed. Rescaled data lie on a low-dimensional surface whose shape is fixed entirely by the hidden dimensionless groups. Singular value decomposition, a workhorse of linear algebra, finds that surface directly. A final search over integer exponent combinations, filtered by the machine's own scales, recovers the named groups. On a fan example the method rediscovers the standard flow coefficient, head coefficient and Mach number with no physics input at all.
arxiv-2606-16837:
Nezhad and Karimian improve spoofed speech detection in a 2026 audio security paper. Fake speech from synthesis, voice conversion and replay attacks threatens speaker verification in banking and phone authentication. Detectors trained on one dataset often fail on another, since each attack leaves different traces.

Their model adds a Temporal Pyramid Adapter to a self-supervised speech encoder. Parallel convolutions with different receptive field lengths watch the signal at several time scales at once, catching both tiny local artifacts and broad prosody oddities. Front-end variants based on Mel features, sinc filters and the pyramid itself are compared across six benchmarks, including multilingual and partial-spoof sets. On the PartialSpoof database the pyramid model reaches the best ranking scores and a far lower error rate than named earlier systems. Spoofing artifacts appear largely language-independent, though accuracy still drops under domain and language shifts.
arxiv-2606-16937:
Amsalem and colleagues build examples of covering properties in uncountable spaces in a 2026 paper on set theory and topology. Covering properties, named for Hurewicz and Menger, plus the gamma property, describe how well covers of a space can be thinned in controlled ways. They are usually studied for sets of real numbers.

The authors ask whether these properties still make sense, and admit rich examples, when the space is uncountable. Their constructions adapt classic countable examples: one splitting the Hurewicz property from sigma-compactness, one splitting Hurewicz from Menger, and a nontrivial set of reals with the gamma property. Each step, when scaled up, exposes new difficulties rather than routine changes. Several open problems emerge, quite unlike their countable counterparts. The work maps where the classical theory ends and a theory for larger cardinals must begin.
arxiv-2606-17037:
Yıldırım tests what image classifiers actually encode in a 2026 paper on neural representations. A classic result says natural images stay recognizable when rebuilt from Fourier phase alone, while magnitude carries little identity. The question is whether trained networks reproduce that asymmetry inside their hidden layers.

The test is causal: transplant one image's phase onto another's magnitude at a chosen layer, then see which image the prediction follows. In three architectures, the prediction follows the phase or sign donor, and deleting image-specific magnitude barely dents accuracy. A convolutional network seems to break the pattern, but a fair intervention before its rectifiers reveals a strong latent sign code in late blocks. So all the models share a phase-based identity code, exposed in different bases set by rectification and readout shape. That single mechanism helps explain the known texture-versus-shape gap between convolutional and attention models.
arxiv-2606-17137:
Iacovelli and colleagues speed up the first analysis of neutron star-black hole mergers in a 2026 gravitational-wave paper. When such a merger is detected, telescopes need fast answers: how far, how tilted, where to look. Low-latency pipelines usually fit only the dominant quadrupole harmonic, leaving distance, inclination and masses degenerate.

Mode-by-mode filtering instead tracks the signal-to-noise time series of three harmonics separately. That structure lets the pipeline marginalize over higher-mode information in about a second, quadrupole-only cost. On simulated detections, constraints on distance, viewing angle, localization volume and the secondary's mass all tighten. Better numbers mean better judgments about whether a light counterpart exists and which galaxies to target. The method is validated on real past events, with the largest gain on the asymmetric, loud event GW190814. A public implementation accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2606-17337:
Mujtaba and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on screening for tuberculosis from cough recordings, a cheap and non-invasive triage route. Their framework, COBALT, rests on the idea that two kinds of audio features complement each other well. Spectral descriptors keep fine short-time detail in the cough sound, while foundation model embeddings capture broader patterns learned from large-scale pretraining on speech and audio data.

COBALT fuses the two through codebook-aligned hyperbolic prototypes, which place class representatives in a curved space suited to hierarchical patterns. A bandit-style weighting scheme judges how reliable each representation is and adjusts its influence on the final call. On the CODA TB DREAM Challenge benchmark, the fusion beat each single representation and a plain concatenation baseline. The best pairing, combining MFCC features with a PaSST audio model, set a new state of the art.
arxiv-2606-17437:
Gou and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on automatically classifying the standard views in echocardiographic videos, a first step in heart ultrasound workflows. Three obstacles stand out: public data sets are small, modern video architectures are barely tested on this task, and some views look so alike that single frames cannot separate them. Frame quality also varies within a clip, which complicates any attempt to fuse information across time reliably.

The team releases a data set of nine standard views with thousands of videos and close to a million frames, the largest public set of its kind. Their model pairs a dual-stream convolutional and recurrent design, capturing anatomy in space and heart motion in time together. Uncertainty-aware training samples representative segments, and evidence-based fusion weights frames at test time. Results were competitive across diverse video models benchmarked on the new set.
arxiv-2606-17637:
Qian and colleagues present a 2026 conference paper on Brick-DICL, a system that maps building management points onto the Brick schema, the standard vocabulary for smart building data. Vendor metadata arrives in clashing formats, the schema holds hundreds of classes, and language models lack the niche knowledge to choose among them. Manual checking of every suggested label is the bottleneck the authors aim to cut for building onboarding teams working through large estates.

Two retrieval stages do the heavy lifting: one fetches examples that teach the model the domain, one narrows the candidate classes before classifying. A multi-model filter compares several models' answers and flags only the shaky labels for human review. The approach is presented as the first dynamic in-context learning method for this task. Experiments across building data sets show clear accuracy gains and less manual verification work.
arxiv-2606-18237:
Li and colleagues turn GitHub complaints into a scalable exam for research reproducibility, in a 2026 paper from Carnegie Mellon University. Checking whether a paper's results can be reproduced normally takes scarce human effort, so benchmarks stay small. Their framework, ReproRepo, instead mines the issues that users already filed on code repositories, treating each as a naturally occurring report of a real reproduction blocker.

Built over more than eleven hundred recent machine learning papers, the benchmark asks model agents to find the blockers without running any code. The best configuration, Codex driving a frontier model, surfaced at least one semantically matching human-reported problem for about ninety percent of papers. Agents excelled at visible failures and at naming the right repository area, while subtler statistical mismatches remained harder, charting where AI auditing of science already helps.
arxiv-2606-18337:
Cheng and colleagues propose calibrating a giant neutrino detector with two free beams nature already provides, in a 2026 particle physics paper. The DUNE far detector will watch for the electron neutrinos of a galactic supernova, a unique window on the explosion. Reading the burst's spectrum, though, depends on how neutrinos interact with argon, and that cross section is poorly known. Nuclear models used in its place can bias the extracted spectral parameters severely.

The stand-ins are standard candles. Boron-8 solar neutrinos pin down the low-energy part of the cross section, while neutrinos from muons decaying at rest cover the high-energy part. Together they constrain both ends of the range a supernova probes, cutting the reliance on nuclear theory. The authors note the calibration data could even discriminate among rival nuclear predictions, QRPA calculations and event-generator evaluations among them, independently of any burst.
arxiv-2606-18437:
Nguyen, Blake, and Macpherson test whether the universe's lumpiness biases a standard way of measuring how fast cosmic structure grows, in a 2026 cosmology paper. The usual framework assumes a smooth spacetime, so brightness fluctuations of distant objects are read as pure Doppler shifts from their motions, yielding the growth rate.

Using simulations run in full general relativity, the team measured how inhomogeneous curvature and gravitational lensing distort the brightness correlation pattern across angle and redshift. At low redshift the standard treatment proves adequate: the systematic offset in the inferred growth rate stays below one percent, well under the statistical noise of peculiar velocity surveys. By redshift around a third, though, the relativistic contributions become visible and keep growing with distance. The authors conclude that today's experiments can safely keep the simpler model, while future datasets reaching farther out will need theory that includes lensing and uneven curvature.
arxiv-2606-18737:
Lang, Roughan, and Ye model Australia's internet as a stack of interacting provider networks, to test how it survives failures, in a 2026 network science paper. National infrastructure depends on multiple long-haul networks owned by different providers. Peering between them may supply redundancy. But shared physical plant creates hidden common risks. Links of different firms fail together, because they share a conduit or a similar tie.

The authors present a broad multilayer network model. It has one layer per internet service provider, plus an exchange-point layer for link hubs. They build it with six major Australian providers. Running failure analysis on the model, including simultaneous failures of shared-risk link groups, they found provider diversity does provide redundancy, even with shared risks present. The result argues for the resilience value of a diverse network system, over merging onto fewer physical paths.
arxiv-2606-19037:
Zhong and colleagues present Querit-Reranker in 2026, a family of compact rerankers that work across many languages. A reranker reorders search results as a second stage, so it must be fast and still adapt to new domains. Such adaptation usually needs costly hand-labeled relevance data for each new task. The team builds a data-centric pipeline that adapts with far fewer labels.

Training first learns general relevance from large ranking data. It then mines synthetic queries and uses teacher scores as soft labels to fit the target mix. Checkpoints are merged by spherical interpolation into one deployable model with no ensemble cost at run time. Two sizes are released, one compact and one larger. The compact model lifts ranking scores a great deal on BEIR and MIRACL tests. It also beats larger embedding baselines on a multilingual reranking test, showing small models can adapt well.
arxiv-2606-19337:
Lonappan and colleagues constrain cosmic strings in 2026 using the curl-mode lensing power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background measured by ACT DR6. A network of cosmic strings is a well-motivated source of vector and tensor perturbations. Such perturbations imprint a curl component in the deflection of microwave background photons. That curl vanishes for ordinary density fluctuations.

The team uses the ACT DR6 curl-mode reconstruction, built from five seasons of temperature and polarization data over a wide sky area. Modeling the string signal in a standard framework, they bound the dimensionless string tension and the reconnection probability. The combined bound on tension over probability reaches a few parts in a hundred thousand. Adding older Planck curl data tightens the limits further. The null result presses string models toward ever lower tensions, narrowing the space left for such relics of the early universe.
arxiv-2606-19537:
Hongwei Xu sets out a formal model of mesh inference in 2026: joint reasoning with no centre. Independent agents each hold private state and swap only admitted, typed observations. No agent shares weights, gradients, or hidden state, and the group may span rival teams and networks.

Xu models the mesh as coupled free energy that each agent relaxes on its own. One admission and emission policy then governs three key properties. First, the mesh settles on a unique answer under any admission rule, since the coupling is always an M-matrix. Second, it matches the centralised optimum exactly when contributing views stay carrier-connected. Third, nothing internal ever leaves a node, so privacy follows from the same rank condition as recovery. In the linear-Gaussian case, answers arrive within a latency set by the square of the network diameter. Xu leaves open when asking improves the group rather than corrupting it.
arxiv-2606-19637:
Priyanshi Garg, Ishita Rao, Jieqiong Ding, and Amandalynne Paullada warn in 2026 that suicidality datasets bake in hidden choices. Clinical language tools mine health records to detect suicidal behaviour. Records look like solid ground truth, unlike messy social media posts.

Their case study dissects the ScAN dataset, built over MIMIC-III clinical notes. Governance limits, code-based cohort selection, and single-annotator labelling shape its labels. Aggregation at the hospital-stay level frames suicidality as one bounded episode. Labels thus record clinician-written judgments, not raw patient states. They also assume intent can be read reliably from documentation. A linguistic study shows identical labels covering unlike framings of time, negation, and uncertainty. The authors urge clinical language work to audit dataset construction before trusting labels as truth.
arxiv-2606-19737:
Adway Wadekar and Jake Soloff ask in 2026 whether error claims in mass hypothesis testing can be trusted as probabilities. Large-scale testing assigns each hypothesis a local false discovery rate, an error chance for that single claim. Such numbers act like forecasts, yet the true labels never arrive to check them.

Calibration in forecasting leans on observed outcomes, which testing lacks. Wadekar and Soloff build pseudo-labels from the spacings of ordered p-values. Those pseudo-labels carry the local false discovery rate as their regression target. Standard calibration tools then apply to multiple testing at last. Post-hoc calibration also becomes possible on the same footing. A survey of published psychology and neuroscience work delivers a warning. The popular q-value, they find, can be badly miscalibrated in practice.
arxiv-2606-19837:
Jeremy Mould asks in 2026 whether dark matter might be decaying away. Decaying dark matter would leave a fingerprint: less matter today than the early universe held. The cosmic microwave background pins the early matter budget tightly.

Testing decay needs an equally precise audit of the present-day inventory. Local counts of normal and dark matter carry stubborn systematic gaps. Warm-hot gas between galaxies, diffuse cluster media, and low-mass halo profiles all blur the ledger. A firm verdict on late-time decay stays out of reach for now. Cosmic rays, the diffuse gamma-ray background, and reionization history already hem in decay channels hard. Coming surveys promise sharper mass maps and baryon counts. High-resolution spectroscopy, new X-ray missions, and weak lensing campaigns could turn the audit into a clean test within a decade.
arxiv-2606-19937:
Johannes Wilson, Mikael Asplund, and Niklas Johansson present AutoTam in 2026, a language-first route to verified secure protocol code. Checking cryptographic protocols with provers such as Tamarin is powerful but demands rare modelling skill, and results seldom transfer back to real implementations. AutoTam instead starts from a domain-specific language for writing the implementation itself, then generates the Tamarin model automatically.

The team proves that verified trace properties of the model carry back to the implementation, and adds symbolic execution to check memory safety. Case studies cover a signed Diffie-Hellman protocol and WireGuard, whose AutoTam version interoperates with existing ones at acceptable speed. Both are proven secure through the generated models.
