Choosing the right sample type matters for judging exposure. Forty-two Swedish first-time mothers gave breast milk, blood and urine two to three weeks after delivery. Collection used special pumps and treated glassware to avoid contaminating samples with phthalates from equipment.

In milk and blood, phthalate compounds sat near the detection limit when found at all. In urine, most breakdown products were detectable at levels comparable to general populations in the United States and Germany. Urine levels did not correlate with milk or blood levels for any single compound. The authors conclude urine is far more informative for monitoring. Milk levels also cannot estimate an infant's intake from breastfeeding.
europmc-pmc2409737:
Forrest and colleagues pitted a blood score against doctor-rated fitness in lung cancer in 2004. The patients, 109 in total, had inoperable non-small-cell lung cancer and were getting platinum-based chemotherapy. The blood score, the Glasgow Prognostic Score, combines an inflammation marker with a nutrition protein.

Doctors also rated each patient's fitness on the standard ECOG scale, which grades how active a patient remains. When both measures entered the same survival model, only the blood score predicted survival on its own. Its hazard ratio was 1.88, with a significance value of 0.002 in the analysis, while fitness and white cell count dropped out. The authors argued that an objective lab score beats a subjective fitness grade for these patients. That matters when deciding who is strong enough for harsh treatment.
europmc-pmc2531137:
Thun and a large group of collaborators pooled data in 2008 on lung cancer in people who never smoked. Such cancers are puzzling, and claims about sex and race differences needed checking on firmer numbers. The team combined 13 cohort studies, covering over 630,000 people for incidence and 1.8 million for deaths, plus registry data from ten countries where few women smoked.

Men died of lung cancer at higher rates than women in every age and racial group, though new-case rates were similar once age was standardised. Asians living in Korea and Japan, and African Americans, died at higher rates than people of European descent. Rates among American women barely changed from the 1930s to today, arguing against claims that risk is rising. Rates in East Asian women were high and varied widely.
europmc-pmc2600337:
The WHO/OIE/FAO H5N1 Evolution Working Group proposed in 2008 a single naming system for the highly pathogenic H5N1 bird flu virus. The virus had appeared in more than 60 countries and kept diversifying, but laboratories used different names for the same emerging lineages, confusing comparisons. Convened in Toronto in 2007 with backing from the three agencies, the group set out to fix the chaos.

They analysed 859 nearly complete haemagglutinin gene sequences, the gene that has stayed in the lineage since its 1996 ancestor in Guangdong. Family trees from three methods supported grouping the circulating viruses into clades. These branches are designated by a hierarchical numbering system, not by place names. The scheme removes stigmatising geographic labels, and the authors urge its adoption worldwide and its extension to other influenza lineages.
europmc-pmc2603037:
Ho and Gruswitz presented a program called HOLLOW in 2008 for cleanly visualising the inside surfaces of protein channels. Channels and cavities matter for understanding how molecules travel through proteins, but standard viewers bury the inner surface under the outer one. Researchers had to clip views or hand-pick residues, and both tricks left stray surface fragments behind.

HOLLOW instead fills the interior volume of a protein with dummy atoms, casting the empty space like a mould. The surface of that cast closely matches the channel's true inner surface and can be displayed alone, free of superfluous pieces. The authors demonstrate it on channel proteins such as the ammonia channel. The program is written in Python and released freely for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc2633437:
Cunningham and colleagues reported in 2009 on what happens when a body-wide infection strikes a brain that is already failing. They used mice with early prion disease, a fatal illness that slowly kills nerve cells. In these mice, brain immune cells called microglia sit primed, ready to react, yet stay fairly quiet.

The team injected a bacterial toxin fragment that mimics infection into the mice. Diseased mice, unlike healthy ones, produced far more brain inflammation signals, such as interleukin-1 beta. They burrowed and moved much less, grew cold, and showed new problems with thinking. A later, larger dose hurt coordination and muscle strength only in the diseased group. After those mice recovered, the same problems returned earlier than expected, so a single infection had sped the disease itself.
europmc-pmc2661137:
Moraes and colleagues reported in 2009 that a fatty diet can kill nerve cells in the part of the brain that controls hunger. In rodents, rich diets dull the brain's response to leptin and insulin, two hormones that curb appetite. The dulling involves local inflammation, and inflammation can switch on cell death programs, so the team looked for dying cells.

Rats on the fatty diet showed clear signs of neuron death in two hunger centers, the arcuate nucleus and the lateral hypothalamus. Surviving neurons also held fewer connections. The harm tracked the diet's makeup, not just its calories: animals fed the same calories of lean food were spared. A sensor called TLR4 played a double role. It helped start the inflammation, yet its presence also limited further cell death. The findings suggest obesity may partly reflect lost brain cells, not only weak signals.
europmc-pmc2680737:
Saisho and colleagues measured in 2007 the size of the human pancreas across the whole lifespan, from birth to age 100. The pancreas makes insulin, and its size might matter for diabetes, but basic reference data were lacking. The team measured organ volume on scans from 135 children and 1,886 adults without pancreas disease, and checked fat content in 47 organs after death.

The organ grows steadily through childhood, levels off between ages 20 and 60 at about 72 cubic centimeters, then shrinks in old age. Obesity enlarged every part: total volume rose by about a third, and fat volume by about two thirds. Fat inside the pancreas also climbed with age. Surprisingly, people with type-2 diabetes carried no more pancreas fat than others of the same age and weight. Fatty pancreas, the data say, follows age and body size, not diabetes itself.
europmc-pmc2687937:
Stamatovic, Keep, and Andjelkovic reviewed in 2008 how the blood-brain barrier, the sealed lining of brain blood vessels, gets pried open in disease. The barrier's tightness comes from junction complexes that glue neighboring lining cells together, blocking leaks between cells. Almost no traffic crosses by bubbles through the cells either, so the brain stays chemically sheltered.

In many brain disorders this seal fails. Inflammation, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, and epilepsy can all loosen the junctions. Blood cells then slip into brain tissue, and fluid follows, swelling the brain. At the same time, the cells' bubble transport wakes up and ferries large molecules across. The review maps the routes of opening and the signal pathways that control them. Knowing the locks, the authors argue, is the start of learning to close the barrier again, or to open it briefly for drugs.
europmc-pmc2688237:
Sokka and colleagues, with the QUEST-RA Group, compared in 2009 how rheumatoid arthritis plays out in women and men across 25 countries. Their registry held 6,004 patients seen in ordinary clinics, not trials. Whether the disease, an immune attack on the joints, runs worse in one sex had long been disputed.

On every standard activity measure, women scored worse than men. They reported more swollen and tender joints, more pain and fatigue, and stiffer daily function. Their composite activity scores ran clearly higher. Yet the gaps were small to middling, and for swollen joint counts the sex difference was the smallest of all. That pattern raises a caution: measures heavy on patient report may rate women's disease as worse than the joint damage itself warrants. Treatment use, including steroids and biologic drugs, was broadly similar between the sexes.
europmc-pmc2689237:
Johnson, Greaves, and Repta reported in 2009 on a primer they wrote to help health researchers handle sex and gender properly. The two words are often confused or ignored, though biology and social roles both shape illness, behavior, and treatment response. Sloppy use weakens studies and hides inequalities that better design could expose.

Their primer defines sex as the biological side and gender as the social side. It then shows how such an analysis can be woven into research at each stage, from question to reporting. They offer three workable approaches at different depths, so teams can start where they stand. The authors also describe spreading the primer to funders, journals, and research groups, and the pushback and confusion they met. Their closing plea is simple: keep asking, in every study, whether sex and gender could matter.
europmc-pmc2696037:
Johannes and a large team tested in 2009 whether chemical marks on DNA, inherited without any change to the DNA letters themselves, can shape visible traits. Such epigenetic marks can pass from parent to offspring, but separating their effects from ordinary gene differences had blocked the field. The team bred plant lines from two parents with nearly identical DNA but contrasting mark patterns.

The resulting lines differed in flowering time and height, and about 30 percent of that variation was heritable, passed down faithfully. The mark differences themselves stayed stable for at least eight generations without any selection. That stability means mark variants, called epialleles, can in principle be hunted with the same mapping tools used for genes. Population genetics, the authors argue, must stop treating DNA letters as the only inheritance in town.
europmc-pmc2779337:
Hall and Garthwaite asked in 2009 what concentration of nitric oxide, a gas signal used across the body, tissues actually experience in life. A decade earlier, about one micromolar looked plausible from electrode readings and receptor potency guesses. Since then, direct electrode measurements in cells and tissues had produced an irreconcilable spread of values, leaving experiments hard to calibrate.

They weigh four alternative lines of evidence. These include quantitative study of the enzyme nitric oxide activates. They include computer models built from the amount and activity of nitric oxide synthase in cells. New biosensors watched single cells release the gas. The target enzyme itself served as a built-in sensor in challenged tissue. All converge far lower than once thought: from about one hundred picomolar up to roughly five nanomolar. Real signaling, they argue, works at these trace levels.
europmc-pmc2782137:
Tsuda, Sato, Stoddard, Glazebrook, and Katagiri mapped in 2009 the network behind robust plant immunity. They used Arabidopsis mutants that knock out hormone signaling sectors. Some mutants lost one sector, others lost all together. Plants fight biotrophic pathogens, which feed on living tissue, with two recognition modes. Three hormone sectors shape the response. Single mutants barely dented either immunity mode.

A quadruple mutant missing all the sectors lost almost all immunity of both kinds, and suffered badly against a necrotrophic fungus too. They fit measurements from every mutant combination to a model. Each hormone sector, they found, can help against both pathogen types. That runs contrary to the usual split. The two immunity modes share one network but use it differently. Sectors amplify each other in the pattern-triggered mode. In the effector-triggered mode they back each other up. That backup explains its robustness.
europmc-pmc2784037:
Rajilić-Stojanović and co-authors built in 2009 the Human Intestinal Tract Chip, a phylogenetic microarray for profiling the microbes of the human gut. The gut hosts thousands of microbial types that aid digestion and health, but counting them well was hard. They designed over forty-eight hundred probes from two variable regions of the ribosomal RNA gene, covering eleven hundred forty distinct microbial types drawn from over sixteen thousand gut sequences.

The chip proved highly reproducible, with repeat readings matching almost perfectly. It measured mixtures faithfully down to types forming a tenth of one percent of the community. Tracking stool samples from ten adults, five young and five elderly, showed each person's gut community was individual and fairly stable over time. Its stable core, shared across people, consisted of members of three great bacterial groups: Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Firmicutes.
europmc-pmc3039637:
Smith, Devane, Begley, and Clarke set out in 2011 how to review whole sets of systematic reviews, using maternity care as their working example. Single reviews already gather many trials, yet decision makers now face stacks of overlapping reviews of uneven quality on the same topics. A review of reviews lets readers compare their findings side by side.

The paper walks through finding reviews, judging their quality, and presenting results so the strength of each conclusion is clear. Quality checks cover how widely each review searched, how studies were chosen, and whether bias and disagreement between studies were handled. The authors flag common pitfalls at each step and offer practical fixes. Their aim is to help clinicians and policy makers trust, or discount, summaries built on summaries.
europmc-pmc3041737:
Bacon and Aphramor argued in 2011 that health care should stop making weight loss its main goal for heavier patients. Standard advice tells people classed as overweight or obese to diet and exercise, which reliably sheds weight for a short time. Most people regain it, and the authors say the weight focus itself can cause harm, from shame and eating disorders to endless loss and regain cycles.

They present an alternative called Health at Every Size, which targets health habits and outcomes directly, without a weight goal. Trials of that approach improved blood pressure, blood fats, eating and activity habits, and self esteem, the authors report. In their reading, it matched or beat dieting programs on health gains without the downsides. The paper makes the ethical case for shifting care toward weight neutral goals.
europmc-pmc3052437:
Szanto and colleagues uncovered in 2010 a teamwork trick that lets two immune cell switches control far more genes together than either could alone. One switch, called PPARγ in short, is turned on by fats and calms inflammation in macrophages and dendritic cells. The other responds to a calming signal molecule. Inflammatory signals suppressed the fat switch, while the calming signal boosted it.

The boost worked because the two switches meet on the control regions of shared target genes and help each other grip the DNA. With both present, more genes responded and each responded more strongly. The partnership differed between cell types, helping explain why the same signal does different things in different immune cells. The authors present this as a general way that inflammation signals tune fat sensing switches. It may matter for diseases where both systems are involved, such as artery disease and diabetes.
europmc-pmc3154137:
Chris Cotsapas and colleagues tested how widely genetic risk is shared across autoimmune diseases in a 2011 paper in PLoS Genetics. Genome studies had flagged many risk variants for diseases such as Crohn disease, lupus, and type one diabetes, with some variants appearing in two diseases. The team built a new statistic to catch variants tied to several diseases at once, without requiring all of them.

Applied to just over a hundred known risk variants across seven diseases, the method found nearly half linked to multiple diseases, each in its own subset. Proteins coded near variants sharing the same disease subsets also interact with each other, hinting at shared disease machinery. Borrowing strength across diseases, the authors argue, can reveal mechanisms no single-disease study would show.
europmc-pmc3160337:
Silvia Cermelli and colleagues tested tiny RNA molecules in blood as markers of liver disease severity in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Four such molecules are often disturbed in liver scarring and liver cancer. The team first watched their release from infected liver cells in the lab, then measured them in patients with chronic hepatitis C or fatty liver disease.

Three of the molecules ran high in patient blood, and two of them climbed in step with scarring stage and inflammation in both diseases and in a repeat patient group. Their levels also tracked standard liver enzyme measures, while virus amount in hepatitis C showed no link. The authors propose the pair as gentle blood tests for staging liver disease without biopsy.
europmc-pmc3241537:
J. L. Villano and colleagues analyzed three decades of United States registry data on primary central nervous system lymphoma, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. This rare lymphoma arises in the brain and related sites without disease elsewhere. Using the national SEER datasets for 1980 to 2008, they tracked incidence and survival by age, sex, and race.

Overall the disease stayed rare, affecting well under one person in a hundred thousand each year, and struck men more than women. Incidence dipped in the late nineteen-nineties, then rose slightly, with the sharpest climb in people over seventy-five. Among younger patients, incidence ran higher in Black than in white Americans, while the pattern reversed at older ages. Five-year survival favored white patients in the younger group, driven by white women. The authors stress that survival remains poor overall.
europmc-pmc3316137:
Küllenberg, Taylor, Schneider, and Massing reviewed the health effects of eating phospholipids, a class of fats found in every cell membrane. Claims for their benefits date back to the early nineteen hundreds, spanning heart disease, inflammation, and cancer. Phospholipids carry fatty acids into the membranes of body cells, and changing that membrane mix can change how the cell behaves.

The review surveys phospholipids from soy, egg yolk, milk, and sea sources, since the attached fatty acids decide much of the effect. Across studies, eating them seemed to help in several diseases with few serious side effects, and they sometimes softened the side effects of drugs. The authors caution that most evidence comes from cell and animal work, with only limited proof in people, and call for stronger human trials.
europmc-pmc340937:
Papagno and a large team reported in 2004 that HIV wears out killer T cells by pushing them toward old age before their time. Why infection ends in immune collapse was still unclear, though chronic immune activation tracked with poor outcomes. The team studied virus-specific CD8 cells from patients and modeled first encounters in the lab.

Acute infection massively activated CD8 cells, far beyond those aimed at HIV itself. That activation drove cells into later, worn stages of development. Patients whose disease advanced carried more of these highly aged cells, which copy themselves poorly. The authors argue that relentless stimulation spends the immune system's reserves, a mechanism that may explain how activation turns into deficiency.
europmc-pmc3531337:
A placenta that grows too deeply into the womb wall can kill, and Kathryn E. Fitzpatrick and six colleagues measure its frequency and risks in the United Kingdom in 2012. Using the national UK Obstetric Surveillance System, they compare 134 diagnosed women with 256 controls over one year.

Overall incidence is 1.7 per 10,000 maternities. In women with both a previous caesarean and a low-lying placenta it jumps to 577 per 10,000, roughly one in twenty in the discussion's terms. Previous caesarean multiplies odds about fourteenfold; placenta praevia found before birth, about sixty-fivefold. IVF pregnancy and other uterine surgery also raise risk. The message is vigilance and delivery planning for the high-risk group.
europmc-pmc3541537:
One wild data point can fake a correlation, and Cyril R. Pernet, Rand Wilcox, and Guillaume A. Rousselet hand psychologists a defense in 2012: a free MATLAB toolbox for robust correlation. Pearson's coefficient assumes straight-line relations and crumbles under outliers, yet it dominates the field.

The toolbox computes percentage-bend and skipped correlations, which down-weight or set aside outliers while handling significance testing honestly. Simulations with clean and contaminated data show robust methods estimate true associations well, keep false positives at their promised rate, and lose little power. With perfectly normal data Pearson still wins narrowly. The authors advise which method fits which data situation, with code on SourceForge.
europmc-pmc3542737:
RNA viruses cheat the protein-making rules, and Andrew E. Firth and Ian Brierley catalogue the cheats in 2012. A virus depends entirely on its host's ribosomes, yet its messages often lack the usual start cap, carry blocking structures, or must squeeze several proteins from one message inside a compact genome.

The review walks through seven workarounds: internal ribosome entry, leaky scanning, non-standard start codons, ribosome shunting, reinitiation, frameshifting, and stop-codon readthrough. Each trick packs more coding into less sequence. Fresh examples discovered recently get special attention. For virologists, the paper is a field guide to how compact genomes buy complexity with translational ingenuity.
europmc-pmc3543237:
Nerve growth factor keeps neurons alive, and Luigi Aloe, Maria Luisa Rocco, Patrizia Bianchi, and Luigi Manni review its long road from 1950s discovery toward the clinic in 2012. First mapped in sensory and autonomic nerves, NGF's roles extend to the central nervous, endocrine, and immune systems, in development and adulthood alike.

Trials have targeted Alzheimer's disease through the brain's cholinergic neurons and peripheral neuropathies through sensory neurons, among many attempts the review catalogues. Results have been sobering: NGF's own actions on pain and autonomic systems limit doses, and benefits proved hard to win. The authors give a comprehensive account of trials so far and a perspective on smarter delivery.
europmc-pmc3607137:
Masahiko Matsumoto and colleagues improved a mouse model of fatty liver disease in the International Journal of Experimental Pathology in 2013. Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, or NASH, scars the liver toward failure, and its workings remain murky. The standard mouse model starves the diet of two nutrients, which scars the liver but also wastes the animal, unlike human patients. Pure high-fat feeding gives fat without scars. Their fix blends both: a choline-free, high-fat diet with a measured trace of methionine.

Two mouse strains reacted differently to weight, one holding or gaining, the other losing up to a fifth. Both, though, showed liver enzyme rises and fat in the liver from the first week. By week six the weight-stable strain had an enlarged, fatty liver with clear scarring, confirmed by stains and chemical assay. A fast, faithful fibrosis model, the authors conclude, is ready for testing NASH therapies.
europmc-pmc3686737:
Ray and colleagues asked whether crop yields are rising fast enough to double food production by 2050, as demand projections require. Drawing on roughly two and a half million statistics from some thirteen thousand reporting units worldwide, they tracked yield growth for maize, rice, wheat, and soybean.

All four crops were growing too slowly. Yearly gains ran near one to one and a half percent, while doubling output by mid-century would need growth closer to two and a half percent a year. At current rates, production would rise by well under the required amount. The authors argue that yield growth, not just more farmland, must accelerate.
europmc-pmc3692137:
McWilliam and colleagues describe the analysis tool web services offered by the European Bioinformatics Institute. Since 2004 the institute has exposed its databases and software through interfaces that other programs can call directly. Analyses can then be built into pipelines and websites instead of being run by hand.

The services cover searching across databases and fetching entries in standard formats. They also run similarity searches with tools such as BLAST and FASTA, sequence alignment programs, and protein function analysis. Both REST and SOAP interfaces are provided, together with sample client code in several programming languages and tutorials for building custom clients.
europmc-pmc3708837:
Schär and colleagues mapped the global spread of Strongyloides stercoralis, a soil-transmitted threadworm they describe as among the most neglected of the neglected tropical diseases. They gathered two decades of prevalence studies, 354 from seventy-eight countries, and combined them in a Bayesian meta-analysis that accounted for how sensitive each diagnostic method was.

Infection rates ran high in parts of Africa, Asia, and South America, though data are missing for many poor countries. Risk was clearly raised in people with HIV and in people with alcoholism, with odds roughly doubled and multiplied several-fold respectively. The authors press for more surveys and for including the worm in global helminth control.
europmc-pmc3713237:
Ken Lee and Zdenka Pausova wrote a review in Frontiers in Genetics in 2013 on cigarette smoking and DNA methylation. Methylation is a chemical mark on DNA that can switch gene activity up or down without changing the DNA code itself. The marks are set early in life, stay fairly stable, and are shaped by both genes and the world a person lives in.

Smoking stands out as a strong force on these marks, both for people who smoke and for babies exposed before birth. Large studies have found genes whose marks shift with smoking, and some of those genes play roles in diseases that smoking causes. The authors present methylation as a possible link between smoking and later illness, including cancer and long-term disease in adult life.
europmc-pmc3801437:
Cheon and co-authors reported in The EMBO Journal in 2013 how interferon beta keeps antiviral defenses switched on long after the first alarm fades. Interferons are the alarm proteins cells release when a virus invades. The signal raises the amounts of three proteins, STAT1, STAT2, and IRF9, inside the cell.

Together these proteins form a complex called ISGF3, and in its unphosphorylated form it keeps a set of antiviral genes active for days rather than hours. Cells treated this way resisted virus infection longer, and the same state also made them harder to kill with DNA-damaging agents. The authors frame the complex as a memory of past interferon exposure stored in protein levels.
europmc-pmc3900837:
Shinya Kimura, Toshihiko Sato, Shunya Ikeda, Mitsuhiko Noda, and Takeo Nakayama build a claims database in the Journal of Epidemiology, with the record dated 2010. Health insurance receipts record every treatment and cost, a rich research source. The same patient's hospital, clinic, and pharmacy receipts sit apart, and disease names vary in style.

Working with insurers, the team gathered all receipt types and built two fixes. A dictionary-based program restyles disease names to the international coding standard after entry. An encryption code, built from hash values and stream ciphers, links one person's receipts without exposing identity. Tests on two identifier sets compared match rates to prove the linkage works. The system opens claims data to research while guarding privacy.
europmc-pmc3919437:
Clemencia M. Rojas, Muthappa Senthil-Kumar, Vered Tzin, and Kirankumar S. Mysore review in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2014 how a plant's everyday metabolism changes when microbes attack. Plants under attack often slow photosynthesis and growth processes, and one common reading is that the saved energy is simply redirected into defense.

The authors argue the picture is more active than that. Attacked plants also switch on genes for making and breaking down sugars, amino acids, and fats, and genetic studies confirm those pathways help defense work. On their reading, boosting parts of primary metabolism helps run the signal chains that launch defense, not just pays for them. The review reframes growth metabolism as a working part of plant immunity.
europmc-pmc3944437:
Alexandra Naba, Karl R. Clauser, John M. Lamar, Steven A. Carr, and Richard O. Hynes profile the protein scaffolding around breast tumors in eLife in 2014, hunting for what helps cancer spread. The extracellular matrix is a major part of any tumor and a driver of its growth. Using protein mass spectrometry on human breast tumors grown in mice, the team compared tumors with weak and strong spreading ability.

Matrix makeup differed between the two, with contributions from both tumor cells and surrounding support cells. The team defined matrix signatures for poorly and highly spreading tumors, and several signature proteins, LTBP3, SNED1, EGLN1, and S100A2, proved to actively drive spread at different steps. High levels of LTBP3 and SNED1 also matched worse outcomes in patients with hormone-receptor-negative breast cancer.
europmc-pmc3983037:
Peter M. Visscher and colleagues work out the statistical power of a popular genetics method in PLoS Genetics in 2014. The method, GREML, estimates how much of a trait's variation is captured by all measured DNA markers together, and how strongly two traits are genetically linked, using unrelated people. It had spread fast, but users lacked formulas for how precise its answers would be in a study of a given size.

Using mathematics and simulation, the team derived the sampling error of both estimates. Precision grows with the number of person-to-person contrasts and with how varied the genetic relatedness in the sample is. For two traits measured together or apart, the error also depends on each trait's marker-captured share and on their genetic and visible correlations. The formulas let researchers size studies before spending on genotyping.
europmc-pmc3986937:
Hai-tao Zhu and colleagues test curcumin against inflammation after brain injury. Their paper appeared in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2014. Curcumin is the yellow compound of turmeric. A blow to the head sets off an inflammatory cascade. That cascade adds its own neuronal damage. The sensor protein TLR4 helps drive it. Mice that lack TLR4 fared better after injury. They showed less swelling and fewer inflammatory signals. Their loss of function was milder too.

Curcumin was given to normal mice after a weight-drop injury. The dose came fifteen minutes after the blow. At the higher dose, activated TLR4-bearing immune cells fell in number. Inflammatory mediators dropped as well. Neuron death was reduced. TLR4 and its partners MyD88 and NF-kappaB were dialed down. Cell-culture tests echoed the protection. The authors present TLR4 blockade as curcumin's route of benefit.
europmc-pmc4013237:
Lindsay G. Carter, John A. D'Orazio, and Kevin J. Pearson review animal and human evidence on resveratrol and cancer, in Endocrine-Related Cancer in 2014. Resveratrol is a natural compound in grapes, peanuts, and berries. Lab dish studies had shown strong anti-cancer effects, which raised hopes for its use in people.

Work in living animals tells a mixed tale. The review covers breast, bowel, liver, pancreas, and prostate cancers. Results ranged from gain to no effect to harm, shifting with dose, route, tumour model, and the strain, age, and sex of the animals. A core snag is that the body absorbs resveratrol poorly when it is swallowed. Cell studies thus promise more than body studies deliver. The authors argue that dose, delivery, and model choices must be fixed before the compound can be judged for cancer prevention or care in humans.
europmc-pmc4016637:
Thomas Brinker, Edward Stopa, John Morrison, and Petra Klinge offer a fresh view of how fluid moves through the brain, in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS in 2014. The classic account says most cerebrospinal fluid is made by one tissue, flows one way through the brain's chambers, and drains into the blood through small villi. That view has guided care for decades.

New cell and imaging work paints a busier picture: a pulsing back-and-forth motion through the whole brain, with steady local exchange among blood, tissue fluid, and spinal fluid. Star-shaped support cells and water channels in cell walls run much of this exchange, which outpaces the classic production rate. Flow around vessels also drains brain waste and lets body and brain immune systems meet. Sleep repair may ride on this system.
europmc-pmc4022337:
Brennan C. Kahan, Vipul Jairath, Caroline J. Doré, and Tim P. Morris measure the gain from adjusting trial results for patient traits, in Trials in 2014. Randomised trials can sharpen their findings by accounting for baseline traits that predict the outcome. In practice, many trial reports skip the step.

The team ran simulations on twelve outcomes from eight real studies across varied disease areas. Adjusting for traits known to predict outcome raised power a lot for most outcomes. Trials sized for eighty percent power reached a median above ninety percent after adjustment, and several passed ninety-five percent. Adjusting for traits with no predictive value cost almost nothing: the worst dip in power was slight. The authors urge routine adjustment for known predictors. For a few traits that might predict, the likely gain far outweighs the small risk, at least in trials of fair size or larger.
europmc-pmc4024737:
Nicolas Sierro and eight co-authors report the genome sequence of tobacco, in Nature Communications in 2014. Common tobacco is a major crop and a workhorse plant for lab study. It carries a doubled genome from two wild parents, and only broken sequence scraps were on hand before this work.

The team produced sound draft genomes for the three main tobacco types. The drafts show tobacco split only lately from its ancestors, and its gene layout still matches kin such as tomato and potato block by block. More than ninety thousand gene models were picked out. The team also traced where tobacco's resistance to two virus diseases came from in its ancestry. With full drafts in hand, tobacco's use as a model for gene function and for plant-made products should grow stronger. The paper sets the new sequence beside tomato and potato to show shared and split traits.
europmc-pmc4052137:
Stephen Burgess provides the maths for planning Mendelian randomization studies with a yes-or-no outcome, in the International Journal of Epidemiology in 2014. The method uses genetic variants as natural instruments to test whether a risk factor truly causes a disease. Such studies often need very large samples.

Burgess gives formulas first for measured outcomes, then adapts them to binary ones. The instrument can be a single variant or a score built from several. Charts show the sample needed for a standard power level across plausible effect sizes. Required size swings hard with how much of the risk factor the instrument explains. Binary outcomes demand more people than measured ones at the same power. Adding variants to a score helps, but invalid variants can bias the result. R code and an online calculator come with the paper.
europmc-pmc4204637:
Cristina Tecchio, Alessandra Micheletti, and Marco A. Cassatella reviewed cytokines made by neutrophils in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. Neutrophils are the first immune cells to reach an infection, where they swallow germs, poison them, and cast out sticky traps. That fighter image long hid a second role.

Neutrophils also make and release a wide range of cytokines, including chemokines that call in other cells, and through them they fine-tune inflammation and immunity. Better cell sorting and analysis kept lengthening the list of these products. The review covers how production and release are switched on and timed, and gives examples from human and animal studies where neutrophil cytokines changed the course of disease. The authors argue these cells are regulators, not just foot soldiers.
europmc-pmc4228337:
Manon Ragonnet-Cronin, Samantha Lycett, and five co-authors released two analysis tools in BMC Bioinformatics in 2013. Health teams use family trees of virus genomes to spot transmission clusters, groups of infections linked by spread. As HIV data sets swelled to tens of thousands of sequences, picking clusters by eye stopped being practical.

Their Cluster Picker pulls clusters from a tree automatically, under set rules for statistical support and genetic distance. The companion Cluster Matcher then lines up clusters between separate runs, so teams can watch clusters grow or shrink over time. Tested on public HIV sequences, the tools showed clusters spanning several UK locations were more likely to grow than single-place ones. The pair makes cross-study comparisons of transmission patterns feasible.
europmc-pmc4273437:
Yoshinori Aso leads a second team paper that maps every neuron type in the fruit fly mushroom body, the brain center for learning from odors. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. Knowing the full wiring is the first step to seeing how the center links a smell with a reward or a shock.

The map shows output neurons divided into types that each cover one of fifteen zones across the mushroom body lobes. Dopamine neurons each reach just one or two of those zones. This tidy layout means a dopamine signal can stamp value onto one smell channel at a time. The anatomy gives a clear logic for how simple associative learning can work.
europmc-pmc4321437:
Igor Allaman, Mireille Bélanger, and Pierre J. Magistretti review methylglyoxal, a toxic byproduct made whenever cells burn sugar. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2015. The brain runs on glucose, and star shaped astrocytes process much of it by fast glycolysis, which inevitably leaks this reactive compound.

Methylglyoxal feeds into advanced glycation end products, damaged proteins tied to diabetes, aging, and brain degeneration. Cells defend themselves mainly through the glyoxalase system, which detoxifies it. The review explains that defense chain, where it can fail, and how the byproduct may injure neurons when it builds up. The topic connects everyday brain fuel use to slow diseases of aging.
europmc-pmc4321537:
Haitao Shi and seven co-authors tested whether melatonin, sprayed on bermudagrass, helps the grass withstand salt, drought, and cold. Their study appeared in the Journal of Experimental Botany in 2015. Bermudagrass is a common turf and pasture grass, and melatonin had shown protective effects in other plants.

Treated grass kept better growth under stress. The team traced the gain to stronger antioxidant defenses, steadier internal chemistry, and wide reprogramming of gene activity, including shifts in how the plant handles light energy, sugars, and nitrogen. The three layer comparison, covering body measures, small molecules, and gene readouts, shows melatonin acting as a general stress shield rather than a single pathway tweak.
europmc-pmc4348437:
Konstantina Kourou, Themis P. Exarchos, Konstantinos P. Exarchos, Michalis V. Karamouzis, and Dimitrios I. Fotiadis review machine learning methods for predicting cancer outcomes. Their review appeared in Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal in 2015. Cancer splits into many subtypes, and sorting patients into high and low risk groups early shapes every treatment choice that follows.

The review covers neural networks, Bayesian networks, support vector machines, and decision trees as used in cancer studies, and weighs how each handles the complex, high dimensional data of modern oncology. These tools can surface key features that human review misses. The authors also note the validation gaps that keep many models out of clinics. The paper maps a fast growing corner of medical computing.
europmc-pmc4362737:
Manjit Jaiswal, Rupesh Dudhe, and P. K. Sharma reviewed nanoemulsions as a drug delivery method in 3 Biotech in 2015. A nanoemulsion mixes two liquids that do not normally blend, such as oil and water, into one stable system using emulsifying agents. Its droplets are tiny, typically in the range the review gives as 20 to 200 nanometers across. The aim is to carry drug ingredients better than older delivery forms.

The review lays out what nanoemulsions are, how they differ from plain emulsions in droplet size and shape, and how they are made, including high-pressure methods. It covers how such systems are described and tested, and what measures judge their quality. Uses discussed include carrying drugs more effectively while limiting side effects, with roles in infection, cancer, and vaccine work among the areas surveyed.
europmc-pmc4374537:
Hannah Snyder, Akira Miyake, and Benjamin Hankin argued for joining two research traditions on executive function, in Frontiers in Psychology in 2015. Executive function covers the mental control skills, such as holding information in mind, stopping impulses, and switching tasks, that guide daily life. Weakness in these skills appears across most mental disorders. Yet clinical researchers and cognitive researchers have mostly worked apart, using different tasks and models, which slows progress in both camps.

The authors first review what is known about executive weakness across disorders, judged against newer, sharper models of the skills themselves. They then give concrete advice for better testing in clinical studies, such as using tasks that cleanly separate the component skills. Their closing plan links modern skill models with layered models of mental disorder, aiming at findings clinics can actually use.
europmc-pmc4407537:
Daniel Zerbino, Steven Wilder, Nathan Johnson, Thomas Juettemann, and Paul Flicek described the Ensembl Regulatory Build in Genome Biology in 2015. Most genome variants tied to traits or disease fall not in genes but in regulatory regions, the switches that control genes, which makes them hard to interpret. The team gathered public data on epigenetic marks and transcription factor binding across human cell types and distilled it into a plain summary of regulatory regions genome-wide.

The build was checked against independent assays for sensitivity, to confirm it catches real regulatory DNA. It is free through the Ensembl browser, a database server, and a track hub for other browsers. More cell types and marks will be added as data appear. A trusted regulatory map turns anonymous variant lists into testable hypotheses about gene control.
europmc-pmc4489237:
Alexander Rose and Peter Hildebrand built the NGL Viewer, a web application for viewing molecular structures, in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Structural biologists inspect three-dimensional models of proteins and other large molecules to understand how shape drives function, for instance at a drug binding pocket. Browser-based viewing once depended on plug-ins such as Flash and Java applets, which were being retired.

The NGL Viewer instead uses WebGL, a graphics standard built into modern browsers, so nothing extra must be installed. It can display very large molecular complexes interactively and reads common structure formats such as PDB and mmCIF. Users can switch among representations, from cartoon ribbons to space-filling spheres, through a graphical interface aimed at working scientists. The viewer can also be embedded in other websites, letting databases and calculation services show structures inside their own pages.
europmc-pmc4653637:
Nadeem O. Kaakoush wrote a solo 2015 review of the Erysipelotrichaceae, a bacterial family in the human gut whose role is only starting to surface. Gut microbiome studies often mention this family in passing. Its members seem strongly immune-stimulating and can bloom after broad antibiotic treatment. The review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology.

Kaakoush gathers reports linking the family to normal gut function, gut disease, and effects beyond the gut. One member stood out in a sorting study as heavily coated by the antibody IgA, a sign the immune system watches it closely. Because deep sequencing keeps revealing these organisms in new contexts, the review argues they deserve direct study rather than footnote status in microbiome papers.
europmc-pmc4669737:
How blood cancers resist the BCL-2 blocking drug ABT-199 is the subject of a 2015 study by Gaurav S. Choudhary and colleagues. The drug frees cancer cells to die by disabling one survival protein, but it cannot touch two relatives, MCL-1 and BCL-xL. The team bred resistant lymphoma cell lines by long exposure to the drug. The work appeared in Cell Death and Disease.

Resistant cells showed strong AKT signalling and higher MCL-1 and BCL-xL, which captured the death signal BIM. Blocking the PI3K, AKT, or mTOR pathways lowered MCL-1, freed BIM, and restored drug killing. Silencing the survival genes one by one confirmed their roles. The findings support combining ABT-199 with pathway blockers to outflank resistance in leukaemia and lymphoma.
europmc-pmc4704737:
Glen M. Chew, Tsuyoshi Fujita, Gabriela M. Webb, and a large team flagged the receptor TIGIT as a marker of worn-out T cells in HIV infection, in PLoS Pathogens in 2016. In chronic infection, killer T cells gradually lose function, a state called exhaustion, marked by rising brake receptors on their surface. The team measured TIGIT on T cells from people with HIV and monkeys with the related SIV virus.

TIGIT ran high, stayed high even when virus was controlled, and tracked with disease progression markers. Virus-specific cells carrying the most TIGIT and PD-1 worked worst. Blocking TIGIT, alone or with the PD-1 pathway, revived those cells' responses in the lab. TIGIT levels on helper T cells also tracked with hidden virus stores. The authors propose TIGIT as both a gauge of exhaustion and a drug target for restoring immune control.
europmc-pmc4706937:
Eileen Uribe-Querol and Carlos Rosales reviewed neutrophils in cancer for the Journal of Immunology Research in 2015. Neutrophils are the most common white blood cells and the first to reach infections. They also pour into many tumors, where their role cuts both ways. Some evidence casts them as tumor killers; other studies link their presence in tumors with worse outcomes for patients. The review's title names the puzzle: two sides of one coin.

Signals from the tumor's surroundings recruit neutrophils and set their behavior. Once inside, they can attack cancer cells directly or summon other attackers. Just as often they help the tumor grow, spread, and hide. The authors sort recent work on recruitment, on tumor-supporting actions, and on ways to switch neutrophils into their anti-tumor mode. The goal is practical: keep the helpful side of the coin facing up.
europmc-pmc4707437:
Sheng Wang, Jian Peng, Jianzhu Ma, and Jinbo Xu presented a deep learning method for predicting protein shape in Scientific Reports. Knowing a protein's local folds, its secondary structure, is a key step toward its full three-dimensional form. For a decade, the best predictors using sequence data alone stalled near eighty percent accuracy. Their system, DeepCNF, stacks deep learning layers over a model that also tracks how neighboring positions in the chain depend on each other.

On standard test sets, DeepCNF reached about eighty-four percent accuracy for three-state prediction, clearly beating popular tools. It also scored well on harder eight-state and shape-quality measures. The framework is general: the same design can target contact numbers, disordered regions, and how exposed each residue is to water. The result shows deep architectures can crack a problem that had resisted a decade of tuning, with sequence alone as input.
europmc-pmc4712337:
Steve Horvath and Beate R. Ritz tested whether the blood of Parkinson's patients ages faster than it should, in Aging in 2015. Their tool was the epigenetic clock, which reads age from chemical tags on DNA. Two sample sets were used, one of 508 Caucasian participants and one of 84 Hispanic participants, each mixing patients and controls. Two flavors of age acceleration were scored, one independent of blood cell mix and one tied to it.

Parkinson's blood ran old on both measures. Cell counts differed strikingly too: patients carried more granulocytes but fewer helper T cells and fewer B cells than controls. The granulocyte excess was the strongest signal in both ethnic groups. The authors argue the immune system itself ages faster in Parkinson's, not just the brain. Blood clocks and cell counts, they suggest, may help catch the disease's long silent phase.
europmc-pmc4755737:
David Tse Shen Lin, Elizabeth Conibear, and Philip A. Cole report a new enzyme family in eLife in 2015. Cells tag some proteins with palmitate, a fat that anchors them to membranes. Tags come and go, and only two enzymes were known to strip them off. The authors doubted those two handled every case.

A pulse-chase test showed the known pair could not explain tag loss on two key proteins. Screening drug-blocked enzymes then pointed to the ABHD17 family. These enzymes sped tag removal from both test proteins. On N-Ras, a growth signal protein, their action pulled it off the cell surface toward inner membranes. The result widens the known set of tag strippers and hints that cells assign them by target.
europmc-pmc4773137:
Anna Herland leads seven authors in PLoS ONE in 2016 with a lab-grown model of the blood-brain barrier. The barrier is the tight wall that guards the brain, and its role in brain swelling and immune attack is hard to study in a dish. The team built a tiny vessel on a chip: a hollow gel tube lined with human brain vessel cells, fed by flowing fluid.

They then added the barrier's two support cell types, astrocytes and pericytes, one at a time. When an alarm signal hit, the mix of defense proteins released differed by which support cell was present, so each plays its own part in the response. The chip also answered more strongly than flat dish cultures. The model offers a human test bed for barrier disease.
europmc-pmc4816837:
Marc Noguera-Julian leads a team of many co-authors in EBioMedicine in 2016 re-examining the gut microbes of people with HIV. Early studies blamed HIV itself for a gut shift from one microbe group to another, but those studies rarely matched patients by how they likely caught the virus. The team studied two cohorts, in Barcelona and Stockholm, totaling 240 people with and without HIV.

A gut type rich in Prevotella microbes tracked not with HIV but with being a man who has sex with men, whatever the HIV status, while the other type dominated in others. Once that factor was set aside, no solid HIV-specific gut disorder remained. HIV did track with fewer kinds of gut bacteria, worst in patients whose immune recovery lagged their virus control. The authors urge future studies to control for transmission group.
europmc-pmc4861537:
Robert S. Lanciotti and co-authors traced the family tree of Zika virus in the Western Hemisphere in a 2016 letter in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Zika, spread by Aedes mosquitoes, causes fever, rash, headache, and eye redness. First found in 1947 in a monkey in Uganda's Zika Forest, it stayed a sporadic African and Asian infection for decades, easy to confuse with dengue.

Gene comparisons place the American strains within the Asian lineage, matching the virus's Pacific spread before it reached Brazil. The short letter sums up early isolates and the route debate, and urges work on how the virus crossed oceans. Knowing the path, the group argues, is the base for prevention.
europmc-pmc4881937:
Carmen Haro and a large team studied gut microbes by sex and body weight in 2016. Obesity links to gut microbe shifts, but human studies clash, since diet, age, and hormones vary. The team read microbe marker DNA in 39 men and 36 post-menopausal women of like diet and age, split by body mass index.

One genus, Bacteroides, ran lower in men than women at high body mass, and it fell as men's weight rose, while women's levels held steady. Another genus, Veillonella, showed up far more often in one group. Gut answers to weight thus differ by sex, which may explain clashing past results and argues for sex-split analysis in microbe studies.
europmc-pmc4929537:
Jun Zou and Christopher J. Secombes review what fish cytokines actually do. Their review appeared in Biology in 2016. Cytokines are signal proteins that run immune responses. Most work so far covers teleost fish, the largest fish group. Studies add lab made cytokine proteins to fish cells, or turn cytokine genes off or up in zebrafish, and watch what changes.

The review walks through the main families, from interleukins and interferons to tumor necrosis factors. Fish hold all the major families, and many genes come in extra copies that mammals lack. So far the functions look much like those in mammals, with few surprises. The authors stress that gene presence alone proves little. Each protein's job must be tested in its own species. They frame the work as a base for improving fish health in aquaculture.
europmc-pmc4931237:
Tetsuya Saito leads a large team tracing how a protein called p62 helps liver cancer tied to hepatitis C grow and resist drugs. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. The protein, also named Sqstm1, handles cell survival and waste cleanup. Its gene is often copied extra times in tumors, and the protein builds up in cancer tissue. The team focused on liver cancer cells that carry the hepatitis C virus.

They found that a phosphate tag on p62 at one site switches on a factor called Nrf2. That switch reroutes sugar and glutamine in ways that shield the cell and fuel its growth. Tagged p62 piled up in virus positive tumor areas. A drug that blocks the pathway slowed cancer cell growth and weakened drug tolerance. The authors propose the blocker as a way to make liver cancer easier to treat.
europmc-pmc4931337:
Dawn M. Dudley leads a large team testing Asian lineage Zika virus in rhesus macaques. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. This virus lineage had been linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome and birth defects, but how it behaves in the body was poorly known. Animal models were urgently needed. The team infected eight monkeys, two of them pregnant, under the skin with a strain close to those then spreading in the Americas.

Virus RNA showed in blood one day after infection in every animal. It also appeared in saliva, urine, and spinal fluid. Nonpregnant monkeys carried virus for 21 days, while pregnant ones carried it for at least 57 days. Protective antibodies appeared by day 21. A second dose ten weeks later caused no new infection. The authors offer the model for studying the disease and testing vaccines or drugs.
europmc-pmc4987937:
Kornel Labun, Tessa G. Montague, James A. Gagnon, Summer B. Thyme, and Eivind Valen present CHOPCHOP v2, an update of their CRISPR design web tool. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. CRISPR editing spread through biology in three years, and new enzymes and design rules kept arriving. CHOPCHOP helps users pick guide RNA targets that cut where intended and nowhere else. The update adds support for the Cpf1 enzyme and for Cas9 nickases, which cut one DNA strand at a time.

Users can now set custom guide lengths. The tool scores the whole guide sequence and its neighborhood using models pooled from large studies. A refreshed interface and a growing organism list widen its reach. The authors aim to serve novice and expert users in one place. They argue design tools must move as fast as the editing methods they support.
europmc-pmc5004837:
Maria Lucia Carneiro Vieira, Luciane Santini, Augusto Lima Diniz, and Carla de Freitas Munhoz review microsatellite markers in Genetics and Molecular Biology in 2016. Microsatellites, also called simple sequence repeats, are short bits of DNA repeated many times in a row. They vary a lot between plants, which makes them handy tags for telling plants and plant lines apart.

The review covers what these repeats are, where they sit in the genome, what they may do, and how labs find and read them. It then surveys their uses as markers in plant studies. Two counts back the survey: about 930 papers on the topic from 2010 to 2015, and 87 marker-building notes in one plant journal over three years. The authors show the markers remain in wide use across plant science.
europmc-pmc5037537:
Aleksandra Niedzwiecki, Mohd Waheed Roomi, Tatiana Kalinovsky, and Matthias Rath review polyphenols against cancer in Nutrients in 2016. Polyphenols are plant compounds found in foods such as green tea and grapes. Lab studies credit them with slowing cancer cell growth, blocking new blood vessels and spread, and triggering cancer cell death, while shielding normal cells from free-radical damage.

Most past work tested single compounds. The review argues that blends act more strongly, and it reports the authors' own mixtures. A five-polyphenol blend slowed several cancer cell lines and their invasion through lab membranes. Blends adding vitamin C, amino acids, and other micronutrients shrank ovarian tumors and limited lung spread in mice. The authors frame diet-level combinations as a safe, low-cost partner to standard therapy and call for wider testing. All of the cited blend results come from lab and animal work, not patient trials.
europmc-pmc5041037:
Florian Fischer, Kerstin Lange, Kristina Klose, Wolfgang Greiner, and Alexander Kraemer review barriers to putting clinical guidelines into practice, in Healthcare in 2016. Guidelines sum up the best evidence for doctors, yet they are often not followed. The team screened 1,659 articles in PubMed and kept 69 for a close qualitative synthesis of what blocks uptake and what helps.

The barriers fall into three groups: personal factors in the clinician, such as knowledge and attitudes; features of the guideline itself; and outside factors in the workplace and system. Working strategies share five elements: spreading the guideline well, education and training, social interaction among staff, decision support tools, and standing orders. Publishing a guideline alone changes little, the authors stress. Each setting should first name its own barriers, then build a plan fitted to its people and place, with the stakeholders at the table.
europmc-pmc5091637:
Eloise J. O'Donoghue and Anne Marie Krachler reviewed how tiny sacs shed by bacteria enter human and animal cells, writing in Cellular Microbiology in 2016. These outer membrane vesicles pinch off from Gram-negative bacteria and carry a mixed cargo of proteins, fats, toxins, and genetic material to nearby cells.

The review gathers what is known about how host cells take the vesicles in, comparing entry routes such as uptake through caveolin-lined pits or other membrane pathways. It also weighs how the entry route shapes what happens to the cargo inside the cell. The authors compare the lab methods used to track uptake and point out where studies disagree, since the same vesicle can seem to enter by different doors in different tests.
europmc-pmc5097837:
Liqing Li, Chunmei Wu, Yong Gan, Xianguo Qu, and Zuxun Lu pooled long-term studies on sleep and mood in BMC Psychiatry in 2016. Their question was whether insomnia, trouble falling or staying asleep, raises the later risk of depression in people who were not depressed at the start.

Their meta-analysis covered 34 cohort studies with 172,077 people, followed for about five years on average. People with insomnia had more than double the pooled risk of later depression. The studies differed a lot from each other, and the team found signs that some results may go unpublished, yet correcting for that gap did not change the overall finding. They argue that treating insomnia may help prevent depression.
europmc-pmc5105237:
Oren Zusman, Miriam Theilla, Jonathan Cohen, Ilya Kagan, Itai Bendavid, and Pierre Singer studied feeding in intensive care in Critical Care in 2016. How much energy and protein very ill patients should get is hotly debated, and most studies rely on rough formulas. This team used measured resting energy use in 1,171 patients treated between 2003 and 2015.

They compared calories given against calories measured. Survival improved as feeding rose toward about 70 percent of measured need, then worsened beyond that point, so both underfeeding and overfeeding looked harmful. More protein tracked with lower death rates, while feeding above the 70 percent mark meant longer stays and longer time on a ventilator. The authors argue for measuring each patient's energy use directly rather than guessing.
europmc-pmc5113837:
Stefanie Widder and a large group of co-authors set out challenges for microbial ecology in The ISME Journal in 2016. Microbe communities drive Earth's soil, ocean, and air chemistry and affect plants, animals, and people, yet science can barely predict what a given community will do or how it will change.

The authors argue that prediction needs experiments, new methods, and math models built together, not in sequence. They give cases where tight model-experiment loops already revealed how communities are structured and what they do. They also list open questions that still block progress. And they offer practical steps, such as shared study designs. Such steps could help labs forecast community behavior, for uses from waste treatment to gut health.
europmc-pmc5136137:
Anna Grimsrud and a broad team of co-authors argued for reshaping HIV care in the Journal of the International AIDS Society in 2016. New World Health Organization guidance says treat everyone with HIV, which shifts the challenge from deciding who qualifies to delivering good care to about 37 million people.

Their answer is differentiated care: fitting services to each client group instead of one standard model. Stable patients might collect medicines in the community with fewer clinic visits, while those who are ill or struggling get more intensive support. Drawing on ideas such as simplification, task shifting, and decentralization, the authors say tailored models free health system capacity, reach underserved groups better, and keep quality up. The piece defines the approach across the whole path from prevention to viral suppression.
europmc-pmc5189937:
Mohammad Mojtahedi and his co-authors treat a cell's choice of fate as a critical state transition. Blood progenitor cells must pick between the erythroid and myeloid lines. Before the choice locks in, the cell's stable state weakens, a pattern the authors liken to an attractor losing its hold. Using single-cell data, they built an index that tracks this approach to the tipping point.

Near commitment, correlation between cells falls while correlation between genes rises. The index flags the moment of instability without needing to know the outcome in advance. Rare "rebellious" cells that took the opposite fate fit the model rather than breaking it. The authors offer the framework as a general way to spot decision points in development, where intervention might still redirect a cell before its fate is sealed.
europmc-pmc5209637:
Jocelyn V. Hull, Lisa B. Dokovna, Zachary J. Jacokes, Carinna M. Torgerson, Andrei Irimia, and John Darrell Van Horn reviewed resting-state brain scans in autism in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2016. Resting-state functional MRI records brain activity while a person lies still and does nothing in particular, letting researchers measure which regions rise and fall together. In autism, studies have reported both stronger and weaker links of this kind, with no settled pattern.

The review compares the published studies side by side to see why their results clash. Autism itself varies widely from person to person, and studies also differ in the age and sex of participants, scan design, and analysis method, all of which can shift the findings. The authors close with ideas for sorting patients by connectivity, testing scans as a diagnostic aid, and making better use of shared data sets.
europmc-pmc5210537:
Cornelia M. Hooper, Ian R. Castleden, Sandra K. Tanz, Nader Aryamanesh, and A. Harvey Millar introduced SUBA4 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2017, a database of where proteins sit inside cells of the plant Arabidopsis. Knowing a protein's location inside the cell helps explain what it does. SUBA4 gathers published large-scale proteomics, fluorescent tagging, and interaction data, plus location predictions from 22 computer programs, all checked and organized by hand.

The new version holds more than 60,000 experimental location claims and adds 37 finer categories for parts inside cell compartments. Its interaction set grew to 26,327 protein pairs. A rebuilt interface lets users combine filters on location, protein traits, interactions, and source to form complex queries across more than a million annotations. A sequence search tab matches a fragment from any species to its closest Arabidopsis protein, and toolbox services estimate compartment shares and closeness among partners.
europmc-pmc5229937:
An unsigned article in The Hospital dated July 17, 1915 reviewed lessons from open-air wards, drawing on the Cambridge experiment at the 1st Eastern General Hospital. Fresh-air treatment had been little encouraged outside surgery and tuberculosis sanatoria, even though small trials suggested gains. The piece asks why wards open to the air were not used more for infectious fevers such as measles and scarlet fever.

Results in fever cases were described as good, with fewer complications and shorter stays. Even the limited open-air setup at the London Fever Hospital in Islington helped children with the chest infection that follows measles. Public interest had been stirred by a pamphlet on the Cambridge hospital, The Open-Air Treatment of the Wounded, drawn from articles by Dr. Shipley. The reviewer finds the pamphlet lively and persuasive for lay readers, if thin on the technical detail a hospital expert would want.
europmc-pmc5234437:
Ilias Lagkouvardos, Sandra Fischer, Neeraj Kumar, and Thomas Clavel presented Rhea, a free pipeline for microbial profiling, in PeerJ in 2017. Sequencing the 16S rRNA gene is now the standard way to survey which microbes live in a sample, and cheap sequencing has drawn in many new users. The analysis steps that follow, though, involve choices that can daunt non-specialists and skew results if made badly.

Rhea is a set of scripts in the R language that walks through the standard downstream steps for unit tables from such sequencing. These include normalization, diversity measures within and between samples, taxonomic breakdowns, statistical comparisons, and correlations. Each choice is documented, and a filter drops units too rare to test soundly. The authors pitch Rhea as an easy entry point for beginners and a frame that experts can extend, designed to track best practice as the field's standards evolve.
europmc-pmc5263237:
Katharine Askew and fifteen colleagues measured how fast microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, turn over in Cell Reports in 2017. Adult microglia were widely assumed to live long and renew themselves slowly. Using label-chase studies, live brain imaging in mice, and mouse models with disturbed cell death, plus human data, the team timed the population's birth and death directly.

Turnover proved remarkably fast: the whole population can be renewed several times across a lifetime. Yet cell counts hold steady from late development into aging. The balance comes from tight coupling in place and time, where a dividing cell is matched by a nearby dying one. Models in which blocked cell death swells the population confirm this. The authors conclude the microglial population is not a fixed crew but a constantly remodeled one, which reframes how it guards brain balance.
europmc-pmc5421437:
Kyrgiou and co-authors grade the evidence linking body fat with cancer. Their umbrella review appeared in The BMJ. Many past reviews tied obesity to many cancer types. Not all of those claims rest on firm ground. An umbrella review rechecks whole reviews at once. The team gathered 204 meta-analyses on fat measures and cancer. They then graded each claim by strict tests.

Only a small share earned the grade of strong evidence. Higher body mass index held up for nine cancers. They include colon, rectum, pancreas, and kidney cancers. Endometrial cancer and multiple myeloma also held up. Risk rose with each five-point gain in body mass index. The rise ranged from 9 percent to 56 percent by cancer type. Weight gain linked firmly to breast cancer after menopause. The authors say most other claimed links stay uncertain. Firm cases can guide targeted prevention.
europmc-pmc5436437:
Kuo and Chen review blood and urine markers that could sharpen osteoporosis care. Their mini-review appeared in Biomarker Research. Osteoporosis thins bone until it breaks. About 200 million people live with it worldwide. Hip fractures kill up to a quarter of patients within a year. The standard test measures bone density by X-ray scan. That test gives only part of the strength picture. It cannot show bone quality or turnover speed.

Bone constantly rebuilds itself. That cycle releases marker molecules. Some mark bone formation. Others mark bone breakdown. A third group regulates the cycle. Paired with density scans, markers can flag disease earlier. They can also track how treatment works. The review sorts the main markers by role. It then surveys new measurement techniques. The authors note that lab methods still vary too much. Standard assays are the next step for clinic use.
europmc-pmc5550537:
Cheng wrote a review article in Current Psychiatry Reports. The subject is the burden carried by family caregivers of people with dementia. As dementia spreads with global aging, most care falls on relatives at home. Many report stress, depression, and poor health.

The review asks which care demands weigh most on caregivers. Symptoms that disrupt behavior, such as agitation and aggression, predict burden best. Delusions and mood changes matter too. Effects differ by dementia type. In frontotemporal dementia, cold behavior toward others adds strain. In Lewy body dementia, visual hallucinations distress caregivers. Readers get an updated, critical map of what drives caregiver strain.
europmc-pmc5555437:
Faivre-Finn and co-authors present a phase 3 trial report in The Lancet Oncology. The CONVERT trial enrolled 547 patients with limited-stage small-cell lung cancer. All got chemotherapy plus radiation at the same time. The open question was the best radiation schedule.

One group got 45 gray in twice-daily doses over 19 days. The other got 66 gray once daily over 45 days. Median survival was 30 months against 25 months. That gap was not statistically significant. Side effects were alike and milder than expected in both groups. The authors say twice-daily treatment should stay the standard. Readers get firm evidence for a long-debated care choice.
europmc-pmc5739437:
Banks, Kuper, and Polack review the link between poverty and disability in low and middle income countries. The two are widely said to feed each other in a cycle. Firm proof for that claim has been thin. The team searched ten databases for studies with direct data.

They kept 150 studies, most from China, India, or Brazil. About 81% found a clear link between disability and a poverty marker. The link held across sex, poverty measures, and types of impairment. It was strongest for working age adults. The authors urge action to break the cycle, plus more research.
europmc-pmc5748737:
Wessels, Maywald, and Rink review zinc as a gatekeeper of immune function. Zinc is vital for both innate and adaptive immune cells. Importers, exporters, and binding proteins keep its levels in tight balance. Lack of zinc is common, above all in poorer countries and among the elderly.

The review sets out how zinc signals work on three time scales. Fast fluxes, mid length waves, and late steady signals each play a role. Low zinc pushes cells toward an inflammatory state. Links to diseases such as diabetes and arthritis are traced. The authors show why zinc supplements can help a faulty immune system.
europmc-pmc5753537:
Sato and co-authors test whether a diabetes drug shrinks fat around the heart. The drug, dapagliflozin, makes the body pass sugar in urine and aids weight loss. Epicardial fat is a harmful depot linked to coronary disease. The team followed 40 diabetes patients with coronary artery disease for six months.

Half took dapagliflozin and half took standard care. The drug group lost weight and cut blood sugar more, they report. Heart fat volume fell clearly in the drug group, while it rose slightly in the other. Falls in heart fat tracked falls in weight and in TNF-α levels.
europmc-pmc5765637:
Franc and co-authors argue that brucellosis, a livestock disease that also infects people, stays neglected across the developing world. Their commentary in BMC Public Health calls for joint action across medicine, veterinary work, and public policy.

Infected herds lose fertility, milk, and work power, and abortions are common. In people the illness brings recurring fevers, long illness, lost workdays, and heavy costs for families and health services. The authors say fear of officials and false beliefs let the disease smoulder unchecked. They urge public education, better disease reporting in both fields, control campaigns in livestock and wildlife, and planning that counts social as well as money costs.
europmc-pmc5816037:
Mahmood and co-authors review the uPA system in cancer spread. A protein-cutting system helps cells move through tissue. Its key pair is uPA and its receptor uPAR. When cancers hijack the pair, tumors invade and seed new sites.

Bound uPA switches on plasmin, another cutting enzyme. Plasmin chews through the matrix around cells. That clears a path for cancer cells to travel. Many common cancers show altered levels of the system's parts. Those levels can flag diagnosis and outlook. Drugs aimed at the pair are in study. Readers get a tour of a prime target in metastasis research.
europmc-pmc5827537:
Lamaoui and co-authors review heat and drought stress in crops and ways to soften it. Both stresses cut yields and threaten food supply. Climate change is making each worse and more common. Even mild stress trims harvests, sometimes by half.

Plants answer stress at the shape, function, and chemistry levels. Signals, hormones, and gene switches coordinate the reply. Grain-forming stages are the most fragile of all. Farm practices can shield crops from part of the harm. Breeding and biotechnology promise hardier varieties. The authors sort progress across physiology, genetics, and field methods. Readers get a status report on farming under a hotter sky.
europmc-pmc5831537:
Edwards and co-authors review how computers can guess which bacterium a bacteriophage infects. Their review appeared in FEMS Microbiology Reviews. Metagenomics now finds phage genomes without growing them. That leaves the basic question open, since sequence alone names no host.

The authors test prediction signals against 820 phages with known hosts. Plain sequence matching proved the strongest signal. Word-use patterns and shared abundance across samples also carried real signal. CRISPR records in bacterial genomes add another clue. Combined, these tools let researchers assign likely hosts to the flood of new phages from wild samples.
europmc-pmc5833737:
Volpe and co-authors review how high blood sugar kills cells and scars organs in diabetes. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. Lasting hyperglycemia sparks oxidative stress and inflammation. The fallout lands on eyes, kidneys, nerves, and the heart.

One route takes center stage in their account. Sugar feeds diacylglycerol, which wakes protein kinase C and NADPH oxidase. That pair pours out reactive oxygen species. The stress then pushes cells toward apoptosis and faulty autophagy. The authors walk the route step by step. They mark each point where a drug might cut in.
europmc-pmc5913237:
Wistrand-Yuen and co-authors trace how low antibiotic levels breed high resistance. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. They exposed Salmonella to streptomycin below killing levels. Weak drug levels are common in polluted water and soil. How resistance evolves under such pressure was poorly known. Lethal doses were known to select one gene only.

Low-level exposure built resistance by other routes, they report. Several small-effect mutations combined to give high resistance. Some changed the drug target in ribosomal RNA. Others cut drug uptake or switched on a modifying enzyme. Weak pressure thus follows distinct paths to strong resistance. The finding matters for drug pollution policy.
europmc-pmc6006237:
Finotello and Trajanoski review methods for quantifying tumour-infiltrating immune cells from transcriptomics data. Their review appeared in Cancer Immunology, Immunotherapy. Immune cells inside tumours can help or hinder growth. Their counts may predict therapy success or failure. RNA sequencing of bulk tumours offers a data source. Software methods infer cell mix from the gene signal. The review describes the current state of the art.

Open challenges for accurate counts are discussed in depth. Bulk samples blend many cell types into one signal. Better methods could reveal escape routes tumours use. They could also flag patients likely to answer immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6050737:
Couronné and co-authors benchmark random forest against logistic regression. Their study appeared in BMC Bioinformatics. Random forest has become a default classification tool. Logistic regression is the older standard in many fields. Fair, large comparisons between them were rare.

The team gathered 243 real data sets. They ran both methods in their standard forms. Random forest won on accuracy in most data sets. The edge was about 69 percent of cases. Gains also appeared in curve and error scores. Results depended on which data sets were included. That dependence itself is a key warning. The authors call for more neutral benchmark studies. Readers get a careful verdict on two everyday tools.
europmc-pmc6168937:
Atkin and co-authors report a randomized trial in The Lancet on one-time bowel screening and its effects after 17 years. Colorectal cancer is the third most common cancer worldwide. A short scope exam, flexible sigmoidoscopy, can find growths before they turn deadly. Earlier reports followed patients for at most 12 years.

The UK trial enrolled 170,432 men and women between 1994 and 1999. One group was offered a single screening exam; the other was not contacted. After 17 years, the team compared cancer cases and deaths. Screened participants showed lower rates of both. The study shows how long the benefit of one exam lasts, a key fact for national screening programs.
europmc-pmc6277637:
Bennett and co-authors argue that inflammation is the shared root of most chronic disease. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Medicine.
