Standard medicine treats diseases as separate items in separate boxes. The authors say the body answers harm in one main way. Blood flow rises, white cells gather, and cleanup begins. Healing then follows as the response winds down.

When that response fails to switch off, chronic disease can follow. The trigger may be injury, infection, or stress. Neural and mental pathways feed into the same loops. The paper traces several common conditions through that lens. It calls for care of the whole person over care of single diseases. System design, they argue, favours the simple shared response. Overloading it has system wide costs.
europmc-pmc6323937:
Amberger and co-authors describe OMIM, a knowledge base linking genes and inherited traits. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. For over fifty years it has chronicled medical genetics. Each gene and phenotype gets its own stable entry. Experts write structured summaries from the literature. By late 2018 the base held over 24,600 entries.

Its Morbid Map ties 6,259 phenotypes to 3,961 genes. The website supports searches by genome position. Phenotypic Series views show how one trait can stem from many genes. Clinical summaries can be compared side by side. A strong programming interface serves computational queries. Update lists and a matching service track new entries. Links reach out to many genome resources.
europmc-pmc6355837:
Braun and co-authors test whether blood or saliva can stand in for brain DNA methylation. Their study appeared in Translational Psychiatry. Brain methylation patterns link to psychiatric disease. Living brain tissue is almost never available for study. Surrogate tissues are therefore widely used. The team had a rare chance to check them directly.

They sampled 27 epilepsy patients during brain surgery. Each gave live brain, blood, saliva, and cheek samples. Genome-wide methylation was measured on two chip types. Patterns were compared within each person. Some peripheral tissues tracked brain patterns fairly well. Others diverged in region-specific ways. The results tell researchers which stand-ins to trust. They also warn where blood-based findings may mislead.
europmc-pmc6384237:
Deacon reviews DPP-4 in Frontiers in Endocrinology, writing alone. DPP-4 is a protein found across the body, on cell surfaces and loose in blood. It cuts many active molecules, but few cuts matter in normal body use.

One key target is GLP-1, a gut hormone that keeps blood sugar steady. DPP-4 breaks GLP-1 down fast, so blocking DPP-4 extends its action. Drugs that block it now treat type 2 diabetes. The review covers how these drugs work and where they fall short. It also tracks other roles of DPP-4 in the body.
europmc-pmc6445137:
Gan and co-authors build a tough, sticky, antibacterial hydrogel inspired by plant catechol chemistry, using silver-lignin nanoparticles to keep the glue chemistry alive. Ordinary adhesive hydrogels lose their grip quickly, tear easily, and cannot fight bacteria. The nanoparticles run a continuous redox cycle inside the gel, constantly regenerating fresh catechol groups.

That cycle gives long-term, repeatable sticking to glass, steel, rubber, and even Teflon, plus strong adhesion to organs and skin in tests. The particles also spark self-gelation at room conditions and kill bacteria, while the mix of covalent and loose bonds makes the gel hard to tear. Soft-tissue repair is the target use.
europmc-pmc6449537:
Koelmans and co-authors grade the proof on microplastics in freshwater and drinking water, checking fifty surveys for data quality before trusting their counts. No standard way to sample or name these particles exists, and reported levels spanned ten orders of magnitude, from 0.01 to 100 million particles per cubic meter.

Only four of the fifty studies passed every quality check the team proposed, covering stray-plastic control, blank fixes, and naming rigor. Polyethylene and polypropylene topped the finds, roughly matching global plastic demand, with fragments and fibers the commonest shapes. The authors supply best-practice protocols and warn that estimates of human exposure rest on shaky ground.
europmc-pmc6470737:
Rabbee and co-authors gather what is known about Bacillus velezensis, a soil germ that forms spores, helps plants grow, and holds back the germs that sicken them. Recent name reshuffles moved several named Bacillus species into this one, scattering its papers. Genomes show strain-by-strain clusters of genes for making weapons and helpers.

Its ring lipopeptides, surfactin and fengycin among them, plus compounds such as macrolactin, attack germs, fungi, and tiny worms. Other products grab iron or drift off as scent signals, and the germ can wake the plant's own body-wide defenses. As the first joined resource on the renamed species, the review aims at people building living pest control.
europmc-pmc6510537:
Sullivan and co-authors measure nutrient levels inside mouse tumours. Their study appeared in eLife. Cancer metabolism depends on what nutrients reach tumour cells. Blood plasma levels may not match levels in the fluid around those cells.

The team used quantitative metabolomics on plasma and tumour interstitial fluid. They measured absolute concentrations of more than 118 metabolites. Samples came from mouse models of pancreatic and lung adenocarcinoma. Nutrient levels in tumour fluid differed from levels in circulation. The authors also compared tumour types and transplant models. Tumour type, body location and animal diet all shaped local nutrient supply. The data form a reference for work on tumour metabolism.
europmc-pmc6527037:
Falk, Yi and Hiller-Sturmhöfel analyse co-occurring alcohol and tobacco use in the United States. Their article appeared in Alcohol Research & Health. It draws on the 2001–2002 National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions. That survey sampled the adult population at large.

Drinking rates peaked among young adults and fell with age. Smoking and co-use showed the same pattern. So did alcohol use disorders and nicotine dependence. Whites were most likely to drink. Native Americans and Alaskan Natives had the highest smoking and disorder rates. Tobacco use rose with heavier drinking and with alcohol disorders. The authors draw lessons for prevention and treatment planning.
europmc-pmc6539237:
Srikantha and Mohajeri review a possible link between gut microbes and autism spectrum disorder, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Many autistic children suffer gut problems at about four times the usual rate. The authors gather the human studies on whether an unbalanced gut flora helps explain that overlap.

Studies report lower microbial diversity in autistic children and more of some groups, such as Clostridia. A leakier gut barrier may let bacterial products — short-chain fatty acids, indoles and others — reach the blood and brain. Blood and urine tests show shifted levels of such compounds, hinting at future biomarkers. Cause and effect remain unproven, the authors stress. They weigh probiotics, prebiotics and stool transplants as gentle ways to restore gut balance.
europmc-pmc6541037:
Molenaar and co-authors present LION/web, a free web tool for reading meaning into lipid data, writing in GigaScience. Lipidomics studies list thousands of fats at once, and making sense of such lists is hard. The team first built LION, a knowledge base tying over 50,000 lipid species to their traits.

Each lipid is linked to its class, chemistry, physical traits such as membrane thickness and fluidity, function and usual cell location. LION/web then tests which of these terms are enriched in a user's dataset. Tests on macrophage membrane samples recovered the right terms, and a cell feeding study matched measured rises in membrane fluidity. The tool runs in a browser and needs no programming skill.
europmc-pmc6543837:
Orecchioni and co-authors test a common shortcut in macrophage biology, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. Papers often treat M1 and M2 — labels drawn from mouse strain responses — as the same thing as classically and alternatively activated cells grown in dishes. The team compared the gene patterns behind both usages.

They set in vivo signatures from LPS-treated mouse abdominal macrophages against published dish data for classical activation (LPS plus interferon-γ) and alternative activation (IL-4). The matches were only partial. Many genes moved in opposite or unrelated ways across the two settings. The authors conclude the labels are not interchangeable. That mismatch, they argue, is why dish-found surface markers keep failing in the body, and true in vivo M1/M2 markers remain to be found.
europmc-pmc6554437:
Hu and co-authors review natural killer cells as a cancer treatment platform, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. NK cells kill tumor cells on contact, without prior training, and also help steer the wider immune response. The review gathers four ways researchers are turning that talent into therapy.

First, stimulants such as cytokines and antibodies can sharpen NK killing. Second, NK cells grown outside the body can be infused in bulk. Third, NK cells can carry engineered receptors that lock onto tumor targets, borrowing the CAR approach from T cells. Fourth, tiny vesicles shed by NK cells show early anti-tumor promise. The authors weigh the obstacles honestly: NK cells reach solid tumors poorly, and the tumor's suppressive surroundings can blunt them.
europmc-pmc6566837:
Mazini, Rochette, Amine and Malka compare fat-derived stem cells with their bone marrow and umbilical cord cousins, writing in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Adipose tissue tops the source list for practical reasons: it is plentiful, reachable, and far less painful to harvest than marrow. Its stem cells, ADSCs, expand in culture for long stretches without losing their power to become other tissues.

The review sets the three sources side by side — yield, growth speed, differentiation range and trial results — across nerve, heart and autoimmune disease. It then turns to what clinics must standardize before routine use: purification, storage, dose and delivery route, plus the shift from a patient's own cells to donor cells.
europmc-pmc6592937:
Yang and co-authors show that an RNA demethylase helps melanoma grow and dodge immunotherapy, writing in Nature Communications. The enzyme is FTO, which erases m6A marks from messenger RNA. It runs high in human melanoma, speeds tumor growth in mice, and is itself switched on by starvation stress through autophagy and NF-κB signaling.

FTO's erasing protects three pro-tumor genes: PD-1 itself, CXCR4 and SOX10. Knocking FTO down restored their m6A marks, and the reader YTHDF2 then destroyed those messages. Melanoma cells grew more sensitive to interferon gamma, and tumors in mice responded far better to anti-PD-1 blockade. The authors propose pairing an FTO inhibitor with checkpoint therapy to crack resistance.
europmc-pmc6593637:
Palmqvist and co-authors test whether a simple blood test can flag Alzheimer-related amyloid in the brain. Their study appears in JAMA Neurology. Brain amyloid is now found by costly PET scans or spinal fluid tests. A cheap blood screen could widen access a great deal. The team used fully automated plasma assays from Roche. They measured amyloid beta 42, amyloid beta 40, and tau.

The main cohort held 842 people from the Swedish BioFINDER study. A second cohort of 237 people served for validation. The plasma amyloid 42 to 40 ratio predicted brain amyloid status well. It held up across all disease stages in both cohorts. Adding APOE genotype raised the accuracy even further. The authors propose the test for prescreening in primary care and trials.
europmc-pmc6656537:
Blacklow and co-authors build a wound dressing that actively pulls wounds closed. Their study appears in Science Advances. Embryonic skin heals by contraction, like a purse string. Adult skin largely lost that ability. The dressing copies the trick with materials. A PNIPAm-alginate hydrogel shrinks at skin temperature. Chitosan bonding glues it firmly to tissue. The contraction then draws wound edges together. Silver nanoparticles inside add antibacterial action.

Tests showed tough, stretchy mechanics in the gel. Adhesion on porcine skin beat a standard bandage product. Bacterial growth dropped sharply with the silver version. The approach uses no drugs or cells. The authors call it a mechanotherapy for slow wounds.
europmc-pmc6692637:
Barbier and co-authors review tau, the protein that steadies microtubules in nerve cells. Their review appears in Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience. Tau holds microtubule bundles steady inside axons. It supports neurite growth and axonal transport. Phosphorylation mainly regulates that steadying role. In Alzheimer's disease tau becomes overloaded with phosphate tags. The changed protein loses its grip on the tubes. Bundle breakdown may drive neuronal toxicity. Tauopathies gather around this failure mode. Tau is disordered by nature as a protein. That disorder makes its structure hard to pin down.

Lab methods anchor the review's approach. Binding sites and tag sites are mapped. Mutations shift both binding and clumping. The authors argue molecular detail is essential. Tau-targeted therapies depend on such understanding.
europmc-pmc6765137:
Callahan and co-authors present a way to sequence the full 16S rRNA gene at single-letter accuracy. This gene is the standard barcode for profiling microbe communities. Sequencing only fragments of it blurs close relatives together. Long-read machines can read the whole gene but make more errors. The team paired PacBio circular consensus reads with the DADA2 inference method.

In two artificial communities of known makeup, the method recovered every expected sequence variant with no leftover errors. Abundances matched the ratios expected from real gene copies. It sorted E. coli strains into the right sub-species groups, O157:H7 and K12. Human fecal samples replicated strongly. Fine microbial detail is now within reach.
europmc-pmc6792437:
Delmont and co-authors found abundant nitrogen-fixing bacteria in surface ocean water that are not cyanobacteria. Nitrogen fixation feeds the ocean's supply of usable nitrogen, which powers plankton growth. Cyanobacteria were thought to be the main fixers at the surface. Gene surveys hinted at other fixers, but counts suggested they were rare. This study says otherwise.

From the TARA Oceans data, the team recovered nearly a thousand population genomes. Some belonged to Proteobacteria and, strikingly, Planctomycetes, a group never before tied to nitrogen fixation. Read counts showed these fixers were widespread in the Pacific and northwest Atlantic. One population alone reached 0.3% of all reads. Decades of survey results need revisiting.
europmc-pmc6844537:
Alexander and co-authors introduce the Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 2019/20, in the British Journal of Pharmacology. The guide is a reference work on drug targets, the proteins drugs act on. This edition, the fourth in a series issued every two years, opens with background and a set of protein targets that fit no other section.

Across its parts, the guide gives short profiles of nearly 1,800 human drug targets. Each stresses selective drugs where they exist. Entries link to the Guide to Pharmacology website, which holds fuller data. Though the print version runs to about 400 pages, it is a fixed, citable snapshot. That record survives later updates to the online database.
europmc-pmc6863137:
Xu and co-authors review relapse after CAR T-cell therapy, in Frontiers in Immunology. The treatment engineers a patient's T cells to hunt B-cell leukaemia by its CD19 marker. It can rescue patients who failed all standard care. Yet 30 to 60 percent of patients relapse afterwards. Understanding why is urgent.

Two failures dominate. Sometimes the engineered cells fade too soon and the cancer returns still bearing CD19. Sometimes the cancer sheds or hides CD19 and escapes unseen. The review details each route and the countermeasures in study. Dual-target cells that hunt CD19 and CD20 together worked better in animal tests. Other fixes aim to make the cells last longer.
europmc-pmc6992637:
Papadimitriou and co-authors use genetics to test whether physical activity truly cuts breast and colorectal cancer risk. Their analysis appeared in Nature Communications. Observational studies link activity to lower risk, but such links can be confounded by other habits. Mendelian randomisation treats gene variants as natural random assignment.

Drawing on UK Biobank and consortium data, the team tied measured movement, by wrist acceleration, to cancer outcomes. One standard unit more of average movement linked to lower breast cancer risk, with an odds ratio of 0.51. Colorectal cancer risk also fell, at 0.66. Similar patterns held for hormone-positive breast cancer and for colon cancer. The results, the authors say, support a true causal effect. Promoting activity, they argue, is likely a sound prevention strategy.
europmc-pmc7020037:
Teleanu and co-authors review tumour blood-vessel growth in the Journal of Clinical Medicine. Tumours need new vessels to grow, progress, and spread. That process is called angiogenesis. Stopping it has long been an attractive idea for cancer therapy.

The review first explains how vessels form in health and in disease. It then covers drugs that block the signals driving vessel growth. Their benefit is still debated, the authors note. Newer plans pair such drugs with chemotherapy or immunotherapy. Nanotechnology is also covered, as a way to carry drugs straight to tumour sites. The survey gives the reader the main mechanisms first. It then maps the treatment strategies now being tried against them.
europmc-pmc7077337:
Schwartz and Graham assess coronavirus infection in pregnancy in the journal Viruses. In December 2019 a pneumonia cluster in Wuhan, a city of 11 million people, was traced to a new coronavirus, later named SARS-CoV-2. It spread quickly through China and abroad. The early case fatality rate was estimated at approximately 2 percent, with most deaths in special populations. Experience with coronavirus infections in pregnancy was very limited, yet pregnant women were certainly being infected.

To judge the risks to mothers, fetuses, and newborns, the authors review what SARS, MERS, and other human coronaviruses did in pregnancy. Earlier outbreaks produced serious maternal illness and poor obstetric outcomes in a share of cases, including deaths, even when some patients improved briefly under treatment. The review organises that record so obstetric teams could plan. It is an early-warning document: borrowing evidence from sister viruses because direct evidence did not yet exist.
europmc-pmc7083237:
Harrison, Vyse, and Huang review rare EGFR mutations in non-small cell lung cancer, in Seminars in Cancer Biology. Two common mutations in the EGFR gene predict good responses to EGFR-blocking drugs. Rarer changes in the same gene, spread across exons 18 to 25, respond less well and are less understood.

The authors describe the shape and mechanics of these rare mutations, then weigh lab and clinical evidence drug by drug. Complex mutations, carrying two changes at once, get separate treatment. Trial data stay scarce because few patients carry each variant. The review closes with open questions and the steps needed to give these patients better options.
europmc-pmc7098037:
Li and co-authors describe how mental health services in China responded to the COVID-19 outbreak, in the International Journal of Biological Sciences. Patients, health workers, and the public all faced heavy strain. Anxiety, fear, depression, and poor sleep were common.

China's National Health Commission called for emergency psychological crisis work. Expert teams wrote guidelines and public education materials. Online mental health services opened, and specialists were sent into isolation hospitals. Experts also agreed rules for admitting patients with severe mental illness during the outbreak. The authors note that fast viral spread still strained these services hard. Readers get an account of crisis mental health care built at speed, and where it fell short.
europmc-pmc7105737:
Zheng and co-authors review the pharmacological actions of Astragalus polysaccharide, a key active compound of the herb Astragalus membranaceus, in Frontiers in Pharmacology. The plant, called Huangqi in China, has a long history in traditional Chinese medicine and food use. Its polysaccharide is its most important active ingredient.

Reported effects are wide-ranging. They include strengthening immune organs and cells, slowing ageing signs, and fighting tumors by raising immunity and driving tumor cells to self-destruct. Antiviral, blood-sugar, fat-lowering, anti-fibrosis, antibacterial, and radiation-protecting actions are also surveyed. The review covers how the compound is prepared and analysed, and offers a base for work on its structure, mechanisms, and clinical use.
europmc-pmc7126537:
Tiku, Tan, and Dikic review how mitochondria shape infection and immunity, in Trends in Cell Biology. Mitochondria do far more than make energy: they influence cell death, metabolism, and immune signalling. Many bacteria and viruses bend mitochondrial shape and function to survive inside cells or dodge immune attack.

Host defences against infection, in turn, depend heavily on mitochondrial activity. The review covers both directions of this contest, for bacterial and viral invaders alike. Changes in mitochondrial networks, which constantly split and merge, are a recurring theme. Placing mitochondria at the centre of the infection story, the authors argue, explains much about how microbes cause disease and how cells resist.
europmc-pmc7146037:
Mobasseri and co-authors systematically review the worldwide prevalence and incidence of type 1 diabetes, in Health Promotion Perspectives. They searched major databases for English-language studies from January 1980 to September 2019. From 1,202 located articles, 193 studies entered the final review.

Their pooled analysis put global incidence at 15 per 100,000 people and prevalence at 9.5%. Both measures are rising worldwide, they conclude. Growth in cases means insulin demand grows with it, and the authors warn insulin will be hard to reach and afford in poorer countries. The paper offers a global baseline for health planners tracking an illness that requires lifelong daily treatment.
europmc-pmc7179937:
Dai and co-authors describe two drug candidates built to block the main protease of SARS-CoV-2. Their report appeared in Science. The main protease is an enzyme the virus needs to copy itself. Blocking it could stop the virus from maturing. At the time, no proven antiviral drug existed for COVID-19. The team designed compounds around the shape of the enzyme's active site.

The authors made two lead compounds, called 11a and 11b. Both bound tightly to the protease in lab tests. Crystal structures showed each compound linked to a key cysteine in the enzyme. The compounds also fought virus infection in cell tests. Compound 11a showed low toxicity in animal tests. Both showed good drug-like behavior in the body. The authors present them as promising starting points for COVID-19 treatment.
europmc-pmc7196837:
Duan and co-authors test convalescent plasma in patients with severe COVID-19. Their study appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Plasma from recovered patients carries antibodies against the virus. No specific antiviral drug existed at the time. The team gave one 200-milliliter dose to 10 severely ill adults.

The transfusion was well tolerated by the patients. Neutralizing antibody levels rose or stayed high afterward. Virus disappeared from the blood within 7 days. Symptoms and lab measures improved rapidly, within about 3 days. Lung scans showed lesions being absorbed over the following week. The authors call plasma a promising rescue option. Larger controlled trials would still be needed to prove the benefit.
europmc-pmc7198537:
Wang and co-authors report a human antibody that blocks SARS-CoV-2 infection in cell culture. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Vaccines and targeted drugs were still lacking when the work was done. Antibodies from human sources can neutralize a virus directly. The team found one that works against two related viruses.

The antibody, called 47D11, also neutralizes the earlier SARS virus. It binds a shared spot on the spike protein's receptor-binding region. Its blocking action does not rely on stopping receptor binding itself. Such cross-reactive antibodies could serve for prevention or treatment. They could also anchor new diagnostic and blood tests. The authors present 47D11 as a candidate for further development.
europmc-pmc7314537:
Rivett and co-authors screen health care workers without symptoms for SARS-CoV-2 in a large UK teaching hospital. Their study appeared in eLife. Testing programs in many countries focused on staff who felt ill. Over 3 weeks in April 2020, 1032 asymptomatic workers gave nose and throat self-swabs, and symptomatic staff and household contacts were tested too.

Three percent of the asymptomatic group tested positive. Of those positives, 17 of 30 had truly minimal or no symptoms, while 12 of 30 had felt ill more than a week earlier and mostly recovered after isolating. Sequencing showed most infections were the dominant local lineage, and clusters appeared on two wards. Comprehensive screening, the authors argue, is critical to protect patients and staff from silent spread.
europmc-pmc7319437:
Wolff and co-authors present version 3 of Galaxy HiCExplorer, a web server for analyzing three-dimensional genome data. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Hi-C methods measure how chromosomes fold and touch inside the nucleus, revealing compartments, domains, and loops that help control genes. The data are heavy, and analysis needs many steps.

The server supplies tools and computing power to preprocess, analyze, and visualize Hi-C, capture Hi-C, and single-cell Hi-C data through the standard Galaxy web interface. New tools deepen capture Hi-C analysis and support single-cell data. Ready workflows, documentation, and tutorials aim to serve novices and experts alike, and to make results reproducible. The service runs on a public Galaxy site anyone can use.
europmc-pmc7356137:
Ni and co-authors present a review in Critical Care on the ACE2 receptor in COVID-19. ACE2 is the door the virus uses to enter human cells. It sits in many organs, not just the lungs. The review draws on past SARS work and new COVID-19 studies.

The authors explain how ACE2 normally balances a hormone system that affects blood pressure. After infection, ACE2 levels fall and that balance tips. They argue this shift adds to harm in the heart, kidneys, and other organs. The virus spike protein, which locks onto ACE2, is a target for drugs and vaccines. Restoring the lost balance may also ease organ injury. Readers get a clear account of one receptor's role in a whole-body disease.
europmc-pmc7382537:
Flach and co-authors track stroke recurrence in a south London population register, reported in Stroke. A first stroke leaves survivors at risk of another, and older studies suggested about 11 percent recur within a year. The register, running since 1995, let the team measure long-term risk and prevention in a real community of 6,052 patients.

During follow-up, 650 people had at least one recurrence. Five-year recurrence risk fell from 18 percent for strokes in the late 1990s to 12 percent for later periods, then leveled off. Blood pressure treatment, statins, and anti-clotting drugs can cut secondary events by roughly a fifth to a third. Rising diabetes and patchy uptake of prevention worry the authors. Readers get two decades of evidence on a second stroke.
europmc-pmc7441837:
Tzotzos and co-authors survey global studies of acute respiratory distress syndrome in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. ARDS is a life-threatening form of lung failure. Its rate in COVID-19 was unknown early in the pandemic.

The team searched PubMed for studies from January to the end of July 2020. From over 1000 publications, 17 studies covering 2486 hospitalized patients in five countries fit their rules. The studies reported ARDS rates, intensive care use, breathing machine use, and outcomes. Rates differed a lot between studies. Many studies were small, and seven did not define ARDS. Only one sorted patients by mild, moderate, or severe disease. The survey still gives planners a clearer view of the burden on hospitals and critical care.
europmc-pmc7489837:
Ettman and co-authors compare depression symptoms in United States adults before and during COVID-19. Two survey groups anchor the check. One answered during the pandemic, the other before it.

The pandemic group held 1441 respondents, and the earlier group held 5065 respondents in the comparison set used here. Depression symptom prevalence ran more than 3-fold higher during the pandemic. Lower income raised the risk of symptoms. Having less than $5000 in savings did the same. Facing more stressors also tracked with more symptoms. The authors say the burden falls hardest on people already at risk. Support should aim first at those with thin money buffers and high stress loads in a crisis.
europmc-pmc7527737:
Kuang, Liu, Tang and Kang review oxidative damage in ferroptosis. Ferroptosis is a regulated form of cell death. It involves iron buildup and damage to cell fats.

The review maps systems that push or block the process. Reactive oxygen species drive fat damage in cells. Enzymes such as lipoxygenase help that damage along. Defense systems use glutathione and coenzyme Q10. Another defense uses tetrahydrobiopterin. Gene control by NRF2 shapes these defenses. Membrane repair also matters once damage starts. Readers get a full picture of how cells resist or undergo ferroptosis. That picture may guide precise disease treatment.
europmc-pmc7653537:
Janelidze and co-authors present a cohort study in JAMA Neurology on blood tests for early Alzheimer disease. They focus on tau protein changed at one site, called P-tau217, in blood plasma. They compare its levels with spinal fluid tests and with brain scans that show tau buildup.

Blood tests are cheap and simple to take, unlike scans or spinal fluid. The study asks how soon in the disease course plasma P-tau217 tracks tau seen on scans. The authors report links between the blood marker and scan results in early disease. Such a test could help select patients for trials and care.
europmc-pmc7681237:
Kinuthia and co-authors review immune cells that drive damage in diabetic eye disease. The cells are microglia, the retina's resident immune guards. At rest they clean tissue and keep mild inflammation in check. Long exposure to high blood sugar primes them to overreact.

Once primed, microglia pour out signals that keep the retina inflamed. This chronic state helps drive vessel leak, cell death, and vision loss. The authors present animal models that mimic the human disease well. They also discuss ways to calm microglia as a route to new treatments for patients whose sight is at risk.
europmc-pmc7688437:
Møller and co-authors set out reporting rules for a widely used DNA damage test. The test is the comet assay, which detects DNA strand breaks and repair. Results for the same samples vary a lot between labs. Thin method details make the cause hard to pin down.

The statement splits reporting items into essential and desirable groups. Essential items are the details needed to judge the quality of the work. Desirable items cover tech points that arise when others repeat the test. The authors say full reporting will let results be checked and compared with trust across labs.
europmc-pmc7778937:
Frankish and co-authors report the 2021 state of GENCODE, the project that annotates genes and transcripts in the human and mouse genomes. GENCODE builds its annotation from experimental data and computer analysis. Its output is a core reference for genome biology and clinical genomics.

The team completed a first pass of manual annotation for the mouse reference genome. They improved annotation of genes linked to SARS-CoV-2 infection. They also worked with other databases to align protein-coding gene annotation. A first manually checked automated annotation of long non-coding RNAs is included. Readers can reach the annotation through Ensembl, the UCSC Genome Browser, and the GENCODE website.
europmc-pmc7779037:
The RNAcentral Consortium presents RNAcentral in 2021, a single access point for non-coding RNA sequences. RNAcentral gathers data from 44 RNA resources. It covers over 18 million sequences from many organisms and RNA types.

Secondary structure data are the big addition. Over 13 million sequences now carry 2D structure information. That makes RNAcentral the largest RNA structure database in the world. Diagrams use R2DT, a method that draws related RNAs in matching layouts. The sequence search is faster and can filter by RNA type, organism, or source. All sequences now carry Sequence Ontology terms for finer typing. The search tool also ships as a reusable web component for member databases.
europmc-pmc7782737:
Chen and co-authors present a tool that corrects errors in nanopore reads and assembles genomes from them. Long nanopore reads help build genomes from scratch. Their errors are wide-ranging, and some stretches carry very high error rates. Older tools trim those stretches, which shortens reads and breaks up assemblies.

The new method picks reads adaptively and corrects them in two steps. Accuracy rises while full read length is kept. A two-stage assembler then uses those full lengths. The authors report a 2.47-fold gain in NG50 over prior tools. Their assembly of the human WERI cell line reached an NG50 of 22 Mbp. Cleaner assemblies also cut false signals in structural variant detection.
europmc-pmc7791137:
Štorkánová and co-authors measure the heat shock protein Hsp90 in blood of patients with systemic sclerosis. Their earlier work found more Hsp90 in patient skin. The team recruited 92 patients and 92 matched healthy controls. A follow-up group held 30 patients with related lung disease. Those patients received cyclophosphamide.

Blood Hsp90 was higher in patients than in controls. Higher levels tracked with more inflammation. They also tracked with worse lung function test results. In diffuse skin disease, levels rose with the skin score. Treatment did not change Hsp90 over 12 months. Starting levels did predict the 12-month change in gas transfer capacity. The authors propose Hsp90 as a marker of disease activity.
europmc-pmc7801737:
Song and co-authors link the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio to death rates in the US general public. The ratio reflects the balance of inflammation and immunity in blood. It predicts outcomes in many diseases. Its role for the public at large was untested.

The team used national survey data from 1999–2014, with deaths tracked to 2015. Adults over 30 with blood counts were included. A higher ratio tracked with higher overall mortality. The hazard ratio was 1.14 per quartile step. Links also appeared for heart disease deaths. Lung disease, flu and pneumonia, and kidney disease deaths rose too. Cancer mortality linked only in the first follow-up year.
europmc-pmc7810037:
Wajnberg and co-authors show that neutralizing antibodies to SARS-CoV-2 last for months. The cohort held more than 30,000 infected people. Most had mild to moderate illness. How long antibody defense lasts was a key open question.

The team measured antibodies that can block the virus. Levels held up well over the months of follow-up. This pattern applied to most people in the cohort. The finding counters fears of a very fast fade. It also informs hopes for lasting protection after infection. Vaccine planning can draw on the same picture. Durable responses in mild cases are a hopeful sign for broad immunity.
europmc-pmc7847437:
Attems and co-authors build shared rules for judging Lewy pathology in post-mortem brains. Lewy body disease can be staged by several systems. Braak, McKeith, and later variants are all in use. Each scores Lewy bodies and neurites in set brain zones.

Some systems suffer from rater disagreement. Others cannot classify every case cleanly. The new rules, called LPC, build on McKeith. Scoring is simple: each zone is marked absent or present. Two extra stages cover amygdala-led and smell-only patterns. Sixteen raters tested the systems on 34 cases. Slides came from brain banks in Newcastle and Pennsylvania. The aim is one reliable standard for labs worldwide.
europmc-pmc7861537:
Papa and co-authors test whether the enzyme furin is required for SARS-CoV-2 infection. The virus fuses with host cells after its spike is cut. A multi-part cut site sits where the spike halves join. Furin was thought to prime that cut.

Knocking out furin with CRISPR cut output of infectious virus. It did not stop production outright. Spike splitting fell a lot without furin, but still occurred. Cell-to-cell fusion also dropped, yet persisted. Mutating the cut site, by contrast, blocked fusion fully. The authors conclude furin boosts spread but is not essential. Furin-blocking drugs may thus slow the virus without halting it.
europmc-pmc7881137:
Huang and co-authors report a surveillance study from New Zealand on flu and other respiratory viruses. New Zealand used lockdowns and border closures to wipe out COVID-19 in its first wave. The team asked what those same steps did to other infections that spread through the air.

Using several surveillance systems, the authors tracked influenza and other respiratory viruses through 2020. They report a parallel and unprecedented drop in these infections while the strict measures held. Flu cases fell far below their usual seasonal levels. The authors say the finding supports using such measures against pandemic flu and other severe respiratory threats. The study offers rare real-world evidence on a question usually argued from models alone.
europmc-pmc7908437:
Fabbri and co-authors present a review of questionnaires that measure how people rate their own sleep quality. Poor sleep is a common complaint and a symptom of many disorders. Lab sleep studies are costly and hard to run at scale. Self-report scales fill the gap in clinics and research. The review judges how well those scales hold up.

The authors searched the literature from 2008 to 2020 and analysed 49 articles. They report the measurement traits of eight scales, led by the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. That index proved sound overall. But its internal structure varied between samples, which clouds its single total score. Other scales for insomnia and sleepiness also showed strengths and flaws. The review helps researchers pick a scale with open eyes.
europmc-pmc8065437:
Fiorentini and co-authors review magnesium from its chemistry to the social cost of lacking it. Magnesium serves many roles in the body, yet intake often runs low. The modern western diet is a chief reason. Low magnesium quietly shifts body chemistry toward chronic disease. Judging a person's true status is the hard part. Blood levels, the usual test, barely reflect total body stores.

The body holds between 20 and 28 g of magnesium in total. Half to two-thirds of it sits in bone. Less than 1–2% circulates in blood and fluids. The review covers how the mineral works in cells and enzymes. It then gives food strategies to reach the daily targets. Detection methods across body tissues get a full survey. The authors close with the diseases tied to shortage. Their burden lands on whole health systems, not just patients.
europmc-pmc8159237:
Pérez-Jiménez and co-authors weigh the gains and trade-offs of surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy. The method reads fine molecular fingerprints with very high sensitivity. It can detect targets down to single molecules.

This mini review asks why the method is still not a routine lab tool. It reviews the physics of the signal boost and the surface rules that shape it. It then weighs ways to lift performance and fix weak points. Nanotechnology advances have widened what the method can do. The authors map steps that could move it into daily practice.
europmc-pmc8201837:
Orakov and co-authors present GUNC, a tool that spots mixed or tainted prokaryotic genomes. Genome quality checks remain hard in microbiology. A chimera blends pieces from more than one lineage into one record.

GUNC judges each contig by the lineage of its genes. The authors estimate that 5.7% of GenBank genomes are hidden chimeras. The share was 5.2% in RefSeq and far higher in metagenome assemblies. Existing tools missed these cases. GUNC runs fast and flags the bad records. Cleaner genome sets should follow from its use. The tool complements, rather than replaces, current checks.
europmc-pmc8248937:
Su and co-authors assess PLGA-based biodegradable microspheres for drug delivery. Such spheres can carry many kinds of drugs by many routes. They allow low doses with low side effects.

PLGA is a widely used material that the body breaks down safely. Its mix of lactic and glycolic acid can be tuned per drug. Release speed follows that choice. Uses span cancer drugs, proteins, and DNA from bacteria or viruses. The review gathers recent lab advances and real applications. It shows why this carrier stays a field favourite. New uses keep joining the list as methods improve.
europmc-pmc8360537:
Graves and co-authors study gender gaps in perceived stress and coping among college students. Students juggle study, personal, and work pressures each term. Poor stress skills make that load hard to carry.

The study surveyed 448 undergraduates in three exercise science courses. It ran in the twelfth week of term. Two standard tools measured stress and coping styles. Men and women differed on both scales. The authors sort which coping routes each group favoured. Findings can shape campus support near term's end. Stress peaks then, and help should match how students actually cope.
europmc-pmc8431537:
Yanai and co-authors review hyperuricemia, the state of high uric acid in the blood. Uric acid forms in the liver, gut, and vessel walls as purines break down. The kidney clears about 70 percent of daily output, and the gut clears the rest.

When output outruns clearance, levels rise. High uric acid ties closely to metabolic syndrome. Transport proteins and sugar handling faults driven by insulin resistance may drive that link. Uric acid was once blamed only for gout. Basic research now points to a direct role in kidney and heart disease. The review covers causes and treatments in both lab and clinic terms.
europmc-pmc8691037:
Dai and co-authors review how epigenetic drugs can boost anti-tumor immunity and improve cancer immunotherapy. Chemical marks on DNA and its packaging shape gene use. These marks guide immune cell growth and action. They also set how visible cancer cells are to the immune system.

Key immune genes and checkpoint proteins are under epigenetic control. Drugs that shift these marks can reprogram cells in the tumor. They may curb suppressor cells and wake killer T cells. They can also raise tumor antigens and display machinery in cancer cells. The review sums up this fast-moving field. Its aim is stronger and wider immune attack on tumors.
europmc-pmc8767537:
Gruell and co-authors show that mRNA booster shots restore strong serum activity against the Omicron variant. Omicron carries an unusual load of mutations in antibody target sites. The team tested blood from vaccinated and recovered people over time. Lab-made virus assays measured how well each sample blocked Omicron.

Two doses of the Pfizer vaccine left near no blocking activity against Omicron. Blood from recovered people also failed in most cases. Several lab antibodies in clinical use lost their effect too. Booster shots changed the picture. Both vaccinated and recovered people gained strong blocking activity after an mRNA booster. The authors call boosters critical against this variant.
europmc-pmc8820737:
Weaver and co-authors report a hidden housekeeping job in the bacterial cell wall. Bacteria build and remodel a mesh called peptidoglycan. Old material must be cut away as new material arrives. The cutting enzymes here are lytic transglycosylases. Their exact role in cell survival was unclear. The team studied these enzymes in Vibrio cholerae.

Mutants with weak enzyme activity built up defects and grew poorly. The harm came from low total activity, not from losing one enzyme. A foreign enzyme from another species could rescue growth. The mutants also filled their inner space with loose wall chains. The authors conclude that these enzymes stop toxic crowding. They clear stray wall polymers before the polymers harm the cell.
europmc-pmc8982737:
Unoh and co-authors describe the discovery of S-217622, an oral drug candidate against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. Vaccines alone left a need for easy antivirals. Pills suit patients outside hospitals best. The target enzyme, 3CL protease, cuts viral proteins into working parts. The team screened a compound library virtually, then in cells. A hit emerged and was refined. Structure-based design sharpened it step by step. The result is noncovalent and nonpeptidic, a first for its class.

The candidate fought current variants in cell tests. Its blood profile in animals suited once-daily pills. In mice, it cut virus growth in the lungs. The effect rose with dose. The authors present it as a clinical candidate. Oral dosing is the practical prize. Hospital-only drugs miss the early window. This one aims at that window.
europmc-pmc9382837:
Singh reviews how astrocytes and microglia steer brain inflammation in Alzheimer's disease. These two glial cell types form the brain's front-line immune defense. When they misfire, inflammation turns chronic and toxic. Failed clearance of amyloid-beta plaques sits at the center of the story.

Plaque material switches both cell types into harmful states. They release nitric oxide, reactive oxygen, and inflammatory signals that can kill neurons. Gene variants in glial genes, including APOE4 and TREM2, raise disease risk. Bad cross-talk among glia and neurons then erodes memory circuits. The review argues that calming these cells' pathways could slow the disease. It also notes that brief inflammation can help after injury. Timing and dose of any intervention will matter.
europmc-pmc9607737:
Amaria and co-authors test neoadjuvant relatlimab plus nivolumab in resectable melanoma. The drug pair had already beaten nivolumab alone in unresectable disease. This trial moved the pair before surgery for stage III or limited stage IV cases. Patients got two doses before surgery, then ten more after.

Among 30 patients treated, the pathologic complete response rate was 57%. The overall pathologic response rate reached 70%. Scan based response also came in at 57%. No grade 3 or 4 immune side effects arose during the pre-surgery phase. Recurrence-free survival at two years was 92% for pathologic responders. It was 55% for those without a pathologic response. Dense immune cell presence at baseline tracked with response. Falls in M2 macrophages during treatment tracked with it too.
franklin-commission-animal-magnetism-183:
Benjamin Franklin and fellow commissioners test Mesmer's claims in their famous report of 1784, here in an 1837 printing. Bailly and Lavoisier join Franklin in blindfold trials at Paris. Imagination, not magnetic fluid, proves to work the seeming cures when patients cannot tell real passes from sham ones.

Controlled tests turn here, perhaps for the first time, on a medical craze. The verdict has stood ever since in the judgment of science. Mesmer's empire of fashion cracked under one careful, polite inquiry. The report remains a model of how to test a wonder: fair in form, firm in method, and deadly in its calm conclusions.
frus-1861-d137:
William Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 July 1861. The dispatch is document 137 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The printed order puts Dayton's 5 July report after Seward's of the 6th. Dates, not file order, give the true sequence here. Dayton wrote from a Paris still calm about the war, unaware of the clash that would come in Virginia within the month. True sequence matters in this file, since the mails often crossed in transit. True sequence, once restored, lets the Paris story read as it was lived.
frus-1861-d237:
Seward heard from James Shepherd Pike on 12 June 1861, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 237 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. It belongs to the opening months of the Civil War, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d37:
Thomas Corwin, the American minister to Mexico, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 29 May 1861. The dispatch is document 37 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Corwin reported from a capital torn by its own recent civil war. Mexico's debts to Britain, France, and Spain raised fears of European troops near Texas. His May letter gave Washington a close view of a weak neighbor at a risky hour. European fleets would in fact land in Mexico within the year, which gives his fears a sharp point. His fears were not idle, as the landings in Mexico soon proved to all.
frus-1862-d137:
A dispatch dated 4 September 1862 carried word from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward in Washington. Congress received it as Document 137 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the summer of 1862, the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d237:
Document 237 is the second Seward letter to William Stuart dated 11 September 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to the British legation's acting head on the same day.

The habit of splitting business across same-day letters makes the printed file look repetitive, yet each sheet had its own purpose. For a reader now, the pairs are a gift. They show the exact order and shape of work in the week before Antietam. Every office in Washington knew a decisive battle was near. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d337:
William L. Dayton reported from Paris on 21 October 1862 in a letter printed as Document 337 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It went to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Dayton wrote as the European question of the fall neared its answer: Britain was backing away from joint action. His reports in late October traced the French reaction to that retreat. For the Union, the news was the year's best from abroad, and the Paris file records the moment it became clear. Dayton, a former senator from New Jersey, held the Paris post from 1861 until his death in 1864.
frus-1862-d37:
By the date of 25 March 1862, Seward had new word ready for Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Congress received it as Document 37 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d437:
On 11 September 1862 Gabriel García Tassara wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Washington. His note is Document 437 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Tassara wrote six days before Antietam, in the tensest week of the autumn. Whatever its formal subject, a Spanish note that week landed on a desk waiting for battle news from Maryland. Spain's attitude mattered to the Union because of Cuba and because Madrid's voice counted in Europe. The note belongs to the small set of Washington exchanges through which Seward kept Spain informed and correct. Above all, he kept it neutral while the war hung in the balance.
frus-1862-d537:
Roest van Limburg addressed this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 July 1862. It is Document 537 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

A month had passed since the June cluster. The Dutch minister's July note took up the standing business between the two governments. It did so in a harder season. Union armies had fallen back in Virginia, and foreign legations in Washington were revising their estimates. The Netherlands, a commercial power, cared most that the war's rules at sea stay predictable. Van Limburg's note is part of the quieter middle file of the Dutch correspondence, where routine and principle were usually mixed in the same page.
frus-1862-d637:
Townsend Harris sent this dispatch from Japan to the Secretary of State on 7 June 1861. It stands as Document 637 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

In June 1861 Japan still knew nothing reliable of the American war. Harris's business was entirely Japanese. It covered the treaty ports, the exchange of officials, and the safety of the small foreign community. His letters home traveled for months and arrived as history. For the reader, the Japanese file is the volume's most exotic strand. It records America's first embassy in Edo. That embassy ran on its own clock while the republic fought at home. The dispatch sustains that parallel story into the war's first summer.
frus-1863p1-d137:
This dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward, dated 28 March 1863, sits among same-date sheets from both men. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 137 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, set among a cluster of same-date sheets from both men.

Adams wrote on the last day of a crowded month at the legation. His March mail had tracked the ship question to its hottest point yet. This dispatch is the London half of the 28 March cross in the file. It shows the envoy's steady craft: facts first, heat last, in a city where the South's friends made plenty of both.
frus-1863p1-d237:
The State Department's mail for London dated 15 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 237 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d337:
A formal note dated 12 December 1862 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 337 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d37:
Judah P. Benjamin, the Confederate secretary of state, sent this letter to John Slidell on 17 October 1862. Slidell was the South's envoy in Paris. The letter is document 37 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Slidell's brief was the hardest the South gave any man: bring France, and with it Europe, to back the new republic. Benjamin's letters fed him the arguments and the news from home. This one came a month after Antietam, as the South's hopes of foreign aid began to thin. It stands in the Union's printed record as a piece of the foe's own file, kept for all to read.
frus-1863p1-d437:
The date 2 April 1863 heads a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d537:
A 27 May 1863 dispatch from F. W. Seward, the assistant secretary reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d637:
Document 637 in the volume is a letter of 9 October 1863 from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. The value of the London file is its view from inside Britain: cabinet moods, press talk, and opinion's turn after Gettysburg and Vicksburg.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d137: Roosevelt wrote to General Dwight Eisenhower, commanding Allied forces in North Africa, on November 17, 1943. The letter is Document 137 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president was then in Eisenhower's theater, on his way to Cairo, and the theater commander stood close to the journey's route. The record names the two men and the date. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d237:
Joint Staff Planners drafted a proposed agenda, marked Enclosure C, for President Roosevelt's first meeting with Marshal Stalin at Tehran. Prepared aboard the Iowa between 15 and 19 November 1943, the secret paper went straight to the President and was not approved by the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

Only two items are listed for the Americans to raise. One is Soviet help in strategic bombing, including the use of Soviet bases by American forces. The other is zones of military responsibility if Germany collapsed completely under the Rankin C plan. Three more items are held in reserve, to be answered only if Stalin raised them: Turkey and Sweden, the Italian fleet and shipping, and Soviet entry into the war against Japan.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d337:
James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, telegraphed President Roosevelt from Washington on 27 November 1943 with a fresh landing craft idea. It builds on the production argument running through the Cairo conference papers, where landing craft supply set the limits for every planned operation.

Shipbuilder Francis Gibbs advises Byrnes that, if authorized at once, forty to fifty extra ships could probably be delivered in the time allowed. They would be nearly identical with the infantry landing craft but make twelve knots. They would be converted from army cargo vessels under contract in Gulf yards. Their service would be in MacArthur's theater, with first deliveries inside sixty days. Even if unfit for every landing craft duty, they could free true landing ships from non-combat work. Byrnes asks Roosevelt to wire back authority to proceed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d37: Churchill answered Roosevelt on October 5, 1943, a day after the president's letters to London and Moscow. His message is Document 37 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The autumn exchanges between the two men were near daily as the Moscow foreign ministers' meeting neared. The catalog record gives the date and the names and nothing further. The text itself, in the Foreign Relations series, carries whatever business the day required.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d437: Historians at the State Department drafted the editorial note listed as Document 437. Notes of this kind sit between the wartime papers in the Cairo-Tehran volume. They explain background that the papers themselves assume. They also identify officials and point readers toward related records. The conferences behind the volume met in late 1943. Allied leaders used them to align strategy for 1944. The note helps a modern reader follow that crowded record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d537:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote directly to President Roosevelt from London on January 3, 1944, bypassing the State Department channel he also used. Winant's standing with both governments made his direct line to the President a working part of the alliance. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The volume's later pages follow the conferences' business into 1944, and this message belongs to that follow-through. Winant reported on Britain as it turned from summit decisions to the invasion year. For readers, a direct ambassador-to-president report shows how much Roosevelt governed through personal channels laid over the formal diplomatic machine.
frus-1944-quebec-d137:
Civil affairs in the Balkans is the subject of this State Department briefing paper prepared for Quebec in September 1944. American planning covered only Greece, Yugoslavia, and Albania, the countries expected to be liberated territory. A combined Anglo-American military headquarters would run relief, but American participation was tiny: sixty-three officers against several thousand British personnel.

The paper's sharpest point concerns UNRRA, the relief agency. Washington wanted it given maximum responsibility and insisted relief be distributed without discrimination by race, creed, or politics. Supplies must not become a political weapon in Yugoslavia's civil strife, the authors warn. They also wanted the Russians fully informed, to allay suspicion and set a useful precedent.
frus-1944-quebec-d237:
Hull sent Roosevelt a department study on September 11, 1944, about British chiefs of staff proposals for Italy's overseas territories. The Joint Chiefs saw no direct objection from narrow national security, since American postwar military interests were not affected. From the broader view, though, they held America should not support the proposals before learning Russian views.

Hull added that the proposals had never been considered by the British War Cabinet and did not represent British government policy. The enclosed experts' memorandum preferred giving all Eritrea to Ethiopia, under obligations to the future international organization: ports and airfields open to United Nations forces in an emergency, and technical personnel employed. That would satisfy Ethiopia's claim and give her an outlet at Massawa.
frus-1944-quebec-d37:
Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on August 30, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It sits in the last run of letters before the September conference.

By August 30, the German retreat in France had become a rout. The leaders' business was turning toward the war's end. At issue were Germany's treatment and aid to Britain. The Pacific war also demanded attention. Roosevelt's letter belongs to that pivot from campaign to conference. For readers, it shows the President in writing. He set out his positions days before hosting Churchill in Canada.
frus-1945-50-intel-d137:
Souers, the director of central intelligence, sent a memorandum to the National Intelligence Authority on 2 February 1946. The new director reported upward to the board that owned his group, days after its creation. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Early reports from a first director set the pattern of an office: what it tells its masters, and how often. Souers wrote as the group stood up its staff and took its first tasks. Readers can place this paper beside the January directive that created both board and group. The directive promised a servant. This memorandum shows the servant's first accounting. It began the reporting habit that bound the central system to the secretaries above it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d237:
The Assistant General Counsel, Central Intelligence Agency (Pforzheimer) addressed a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 6 January 1949. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 237, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Three men — Dulles, Jackson, and Correa — were touring the CIA's work for the Council and taking notes for a report.

A memo of this kind was the basic tool of office work at the top. It put a matter before a senior man and asked for a choice, a signature, or a view. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d337:
Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter addressed a memorandum to the Intelligence Advisory Committee on 27 January 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 337 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. By then the National Security Council met often, and questions about secret operations abroad were moving to the center of its work.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d37:
Appleby of the Budget Bureau wrote to Attorney General Clark on 31 October 1945. A budget official writing to the head of the Justice Department marks a question that crosses money and law. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

The FBI's foreign intelligence work raised exactly such questions: it cost money, and its legal footing in peacetime was open to doubt. Appleby's letter brought the bureau's scrutiny to the Justice Department's door. Readers can see the net widening here. The intelligence fight was no longer only about who spied where; it was about authority and appropriations, the two things that make agencies real. This letter is an early sign of that harder phase.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d137:
American control of Bremen is the sticking point in this top secret cable of 5 January 1945. Secretary of State Stettinius writes to Ambassador Winant in London about the ports that would feed the American zone in Germany. The cable is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Formal action had been stalled to avoid a sharp clash. On 4 January a formula was worked out in Washington. War Department officials and Joint Chiefs men sat with Lord Halifax and General Macready. The British said they would recommend it to London. Under the formula, the Bremen and Bremerhaven enclave sits under complete American control, military government included. It would still be run, on paper, as a subdistrict of the larger British area around it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d237:
London was thinking of putting Iran on the Big Three agenda, Winant reported on 9 January 1945. His one-paragraph cable from London, number 296, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It came out of a general talk on Iranian matters at the Foreign Office that day.

The official who handles Iranian affairs directly, Winant writes, said serious thought is being given to one step. At the next Big Three meeting, the general question of Iran should be raised. The focus would be Soviet pressure in connection with the recent incidents over oil concessions. The short cable shows the Iran quarrel moving from embassy channels toward the leaders' table at Yalta.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d337:
Two records of the same Yalta plenary survive, and this one, kept by H. Freeman Matthews, covers February 5, 1945, on Germany. Roosevelt opened by saying the leaders should talk of the broad aims of peace, not Dakar or China. Zones of occupation came first, since matters there were coming to a head.

He showed a map and linked it to his Quebec talks with Churchill. Then he corrected himself: the map in fact came from the zones protocol drawn up by the European Advisory Commission. Matthews catches a small human slip that the smoother Bohlen record leaves out. Reading both versions shows how minutes differ.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d37: The president turned back to the Moscow channel on 31 December 1944, writing to Ambassador Harriman that day. The message is document 37 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Instructions sent to Harriman at year's end helped him prepare the Soviet side of the coming summit, where his local knowledge would matter throughout the Yalta meetings.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d437:
Hiss's notes of February 10, 1945, catch Molotov haggling over one phrase in the Polish formula. Stettinius said the Americans would withdraw the final sentence Molotov disliked. The President would stay free to speak to the American people about reports from his ambassador. Molotov proposed a small amendment to the previous day's text.

His condition: the United States and Britain would establish diplomatic relations with the new government as soon as possible, as the Soviet Union had done. Eden objected that this would be a new government. Molotov answered that their situations differed, since Moscow had already recognized the present one. The shorthand preserves the last inch of the Poland bargain.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d137:
Acting Secretary Grew settled a timing question with London in a telegram to Ambassador Winant on July 12, 1945. The message is document 137 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Lord Halifax had asked, for Churchill and Eden, on which day the President and Secretary Byrnes would arrive at Terminal.

The British leaders wanted to time their own departure so as to arrive the same day. Grew answers that the present schedule allows the President and the Secretary to reach Terminal about 3 p.m. local time on Sunday, July 15. He notes that Halifax has been informed. The synchronized arrivals were partly courtesy and partly tactics: neither Western leader wanted the other to have a head start with Stalin.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d237:
Acting Secretary Grew gave Rome its green light in a letter to Ambassador Tarchiani dated July 7, 1945. The letter is document 237 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Tarchiani had told him the day before that the Italian government had decided to declare war on Japan.

The news will be greeted with approval by the American people, Grew writes. The timing of the announcement is for Italy to decide. The British, French, and Soviet governments have already been informed of American approval and have raised no objection. The American government naturally hopes the announcement will come at an early date. The letter closed the diplomatic round that let a former enemy state join the war's last campaign as a gesture of good faith.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d337:
McCloy answered Clayton on June 21, 1945, with a first, informal reaction on paying for German civilian supplies. The hard point, he wrote, was justifying Army funds once the armies sat in separate zones. Army money spent on supplies would aid civilians in liberated countries, not American troops. That was hard to defend in Congress.

Yet McCloy conceded the other side of the case. An American commander, as a Control Council member, acted as an agent of his government. Government policy included using German resources for the freed areas. He promised the War Department would study the matter and reply formally.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d37: No objection to the Berlin area: Truman's extract to Churchill of May 28, 1945, is a single sentence of substance. Stalin had informed him through Hopkins that he would like the three-party meeting held in the Berlin area. Truman would reply that he had no objection to the Berlin area. The first two paragraphs of the message, omitted from this printing, appear elsewhere in the volume. The extract's brevity is its meaning: the place of the next summit was settled almost as an aside, while Hopkins was still in Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d437:
British draft instructions on Czechoslovakia are shared with Washington in a British Embassy paper dated June 28, 1945. It paraphrases a Foreign Office telegram of June 22. The Foreign Office's next telegram would contain the text of instructions it proposed to send Mr. Nichols, its ambassador in Prague. Before despatching them, London was anxious to know the State Department's views.

The Embassy is told to discuss the draft with the Department and send comments as soon as possible. The matter, London notes, concerns the Americans more closely in its immediate aspect. American troops occupied a large part of Czechoslovakia, and the American zone in Germany marched for many miles along the Czech frontier.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d537:
Phase II commitments to Britain are recalled in a briefing book paper on lend-lease after Germany's defeat. At Quebec in September 1944, President Roosevelt agreed to Prime Minister Churchill's proposal. Britain should go on receiving lend-lease aid after Germany's defeat. The basis would let her shift some work from war goods to civilian output.

A memorandum of November 25, 1944, reported the Phase II program to Roosevelt. Its authors were the American committee of Morgenthau, Stettinius, and Crowley. The program set 2.7 billion dollars for war goods and 2.8 billion for other goods, for the British Commonwealth. Such a program, they stated, would let Britain and America free manpower for reconversion. It would ease living standards, and partly revive exports.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d637:
An extract from Grew's memo of his June 25, 1945 talk with Ambassador Bonnet forms document 637 here. Printed in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam, it covers the same talk as document 616. The extract kept here gives the first sore point in full: the Levant.

Bonnet said France felt it had won little satisfaction on a string of issues. On Syria, he charged, the United States was backing the British position. Grew cut in to correct him. U.S. policy, Grew said, rested in no respect on Britain's stand. It followed Washington's own view of the matter, which the ambassador knew very well. The sharp little exchange shows how raw Franco-U.S. feeling ran that summer. It also shows Grew refusing to let France frame the Levant clash as an Anglo-U.S. plot.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1037:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the Secretary of State from London on July 24, 1945. The European Advisory Commission had met the night before to finish two outstanding documents. One snag was a matter of translation in the additional requirements agreement for Germany.

Soviet delegate Saksin said his government approved a title ending certain additional requirements to Germany. The English text reads requirements to be imposed on Germany. The gap arose when the Soviet team first cabled the title home, unaware the English and French texts carried the stronger phrase. Saksin would seek fresh instructions. Winant suggests Mosely might see Gusev at Potsdam to speed those instructions along.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1137:
A second memorandum from Poland's deputy premier Mikolajczyk bears the same date, 24 July 1945. Two formal papers in one day show how hard he pressed his country's case while the summit sat. He could not wait for a better moment; the decisions were being made that week.

Poland's western border and its future vote were the stakes. Mikolajczyk spoke for the part of the Polish government that had not come from Moscow's camp. His papers asked the Western powers to hold to their pledges. This one is the middle piece of the day's trio, and the urgency in it is plain.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1237:
The Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State on 16 July 1945. Grew held the department in Washington while Byrnes traveled to the summit. His message of the day before the opening kept the chief abroad in touch with the home office.

Such eve-of-summit cables carried last news, pending files, and the state of affairs at home. The department's two halves had to act as one through the talks. This note is an early link in that daily circuit. It shows the machine starting its Potsdam rhythm: Washington reporting, the team abroad reading, both sides writing back.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1337:
Ambassador Wallace Murray in Iran cabled the acting secretary of state again on 30 July 1945, his third message from Tehran in four days. By then the Potsdam Conference, where Truman, Churchill, and Stalin met outside Berlin in July and August 1945 was nearing its close. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

A third cable in a short run tells readers the Tehran post saw no pause in its work as July ended. Murray's messages form a small run within the volume, and each one adds a piece to the picture Washington held of Iran. They reward readers who want to see diplomacy as daily reporting rather than as treaties alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-137:
