On July 30, 1945, Bohlen again kept the minutes of a Potsdam meeting. The conference was in its last three days. Charles Bohlen's Russian fluency made his records central to the American file. This set was printed in the second Potsdam volume with his other minutes.

Late-stage minutes carry the feel of a race to finish. Points once debated at length now get short, sharp treatment. Bohlen's account preserves that pressure on the page. Readers can trace the final shaping of agreed lines. The record shows both the substance of the talks and the strain of their closing days.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-37:
A rapporteur's report, in translation, records Molotov's account of the foreign ministers' meeting of July 20, 1945. It is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The report is frank about how little the morning had settled.

On German economic principles, the authorized commission had not finished its work. The question was not in fact discussed, and the commission was told to finish by July 21. The Polish question met the same fate for the same reason, with the same deadline set. On the peace settlement, the drafting commission had also failed to produce a text. Its members were busy in other commissions, Molotov explains. The ministers therefore resolved to meet at 3:45 that afternoon themselves. At that sitting an amendment to paragraph 3 was adopted, and the report quotes its new opening words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d737:
Charles Yost of the Central Secretariat wrote this memorandum on August 9, 1945, a week after Potsdam closed. Document 737 belongs to the conference's aftermath. The secretariat had managed the flood of texts for three delegations. Its work did not end when the leaders left. Yost's memo entered the second Potsdam volume.

Aftermath papers settle the record while memories stay fresh. They chase missing copies and fix the order of texts. Readers gain a clerk's-eye view of a summit's remains. The document shows history being filed, literally, by the men who ran the paper. That filing is why the conference can still be studied in such depth.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d837:
The British delegation tabled this proposal at Potsdam on July 19, 1945, as document 837. It dates from the conference's third day. British drafts in the first week stated London's aims while Churchill still led the team. The proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An early British text shows the alliance's second voice in full confidence. Readers can compare it with the drafts London tabled after the election changed its team. The document marks how much of Britain's line survived that change. It also shows the conference's three-way drafting race at its start: each side writing, each side reading the others overnight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d937:
American staff wrote this undated paper on valuing removable equipment in the Ruhr, filed with the July 25, 1945 papers. Much talk at Potsdam turned on what Ruhr gear was worth, and what share might go to the Soviet Union. The paper argues that the whole valuation fight is a dead end.

Value shifts with method: cost minus wear, replacement cost, or worth as a going concern. Turning marks into dollars adds a second dispute. The only realistic answer, the paper says, is a percentage of equipment, not a price. A share means the same thing to both sides, whatever values each side computes.
frus-1964-68v06-d37: An editorial note in the 1964-1968 Foreign Relations series, Volume VI, on Vietnam, presents a phone call from the morning of January 31, 1968. President Johnson asks Secretary of Defense McNamara to judge the Tet offensive, which had just begun. McNamara says the attacks show more strength than many had credited. He expects heavy losses for the attackers but no quick knockout. He doubts that area bombing of Hanoi would help. Johnson presses for more public statements from General Westmoreland and from McNamara himself.
frus-1969-76v37:
Volume XXXVII of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, carries the energy crisis from 1974 to 1980. Early chapters cover the talks at which oil-buying states organized in reply to OPEC. The rising price of oil fills the next chapter. Strategies to cope with high prices follow, for 1977 to 1979. The final chapter covers the Iranian oil shortfall of 1979 to 1981.

Cables from Caracas report OPEC meetings and price votes. A message from President Carter thanks King Khalid for Saudi restraint on prices. The records span three presidencies. They show stockpiles, saving drives, and joint plans among buyers.
gao-gaoreports-b-295737:
USA Fabrics, Inc., won in part in GAO files B-295737 and B-295737.2, dated April 19, 2005. Federal Prison Industries had sought T-shirt fabric under a total small business set-aside. The firm said the buy should have been reserved for HUBZone small businesses. On that point GAO sustained the protest. The agency's file lacked facts enough to support its finding that two or more HUBZone firms were not interested, or that the price would not be fair.

A second claim failed. A term requiring set stock levels held by the contractor was fairly drawn to make sure the government's needs would be met.
gao-gaoreports-b-297137:
Testek protested a Defense Logistics Agency award for test stand work in GAO decision B-297137, dated October 28, 2005. The winner was Avtron Manufacturing. The work was to upgrade test stands for plane power units. The buy was sole-source in form. The firm pitched a new path to meet the need. That path was ruled not fit.

GAO denied the protest. The new path did not meet the tests in the call. A sole-source need can still set clear tests for a rival path. A path that misses those tests can be cut. The firm did not show its path met the bar. The sole-source award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-297537:
MMI-Federal Marketing protested a Defense Logistics Agency award for bednets in GAO decision B-297537, dated February 8, 2006. The winner was Iguana. The nets pop up round a bed and hold a bug spray coat. The count was 25,000 nets. The Berry Amendment sets home-made rules for such goods. The firm said the winner would not meet them.

GAO sustained the protest. Facts known before award cut against the winner's claim of fit. The agency still took that claim at face. That take was not sound. When pre-award facts clash with a vow of fit, the agency must check. A blind take on a home-made vow cannot stand.
gao-gaoreports-b-299037:
Margni, Inc. protested a sole-source Veterans Affairs award to Native Contractors, Inc. The contract covered cemetery maintenance at the Georgian National Cemetery in Canton, Georgia. The award ran through the section 8(a) program. GAO ruled in B-299037 on January 26, 2007.

The fight turned on harm to small firms. Moving the work into the 8(a) program needed a check for adverse impact. The Small Business Administration made that check. It found no harm to a single firm, a local group, or other small-firm programs. GAO found those findings sound on the record. The sole-source path could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299237:
Hawkeye Glove Manufacturing, Inc. protested an Army award to Hatch Worldwide Imports. The contract covered combat gloves. Half the need was set aside for small firms. The set-aside half carried set counts of pairs. GAO decided B-299237 on March 6, 2007.

The firm, itself a small business, called the winner's price too high. GAO tested that claim against the price record. The winning price fell below the government estimate. It also sat within the range of small-firm prices sent in. A price inside that range is not too high on its face. The claim lacked a firm base. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299737:
HealthStar VA protested a Veterans Affairs award to Valor Health Care. The contract covered a community based outpatient clinic in the Hot Springs area of Arkansas. The clinic gives primary care to assigned veteran patients. GAO ruled in B-299737 on June 22, 2007.

The case turned on what a bid must hold. The terms asked for all facts the agency sought. A firm must place those facts inside its own bid. That duty falls on prior holders of the work as well. Incumbent status does not fill gaps by itself. GAO found the firm's bid fell short on that duty. The award to the rival could stand. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-307137:
A uranium deal between the Energy Department and a firm it once owned is judged in this GAO decision, B-307137, dated July 12, 2006. The United States Enrichment Corporation sold Russian-origin uranium for the department. A December 2004 pact set the terms. Sale cash was to cover the firm's costs to clean the uranium for use.

GAO split its ruling. The 1996 privatization law did let the department hand the uranium to the firm for sale. But the setup broke a second law. The firm held and spent sale cash for the department before Congress allowed that in November 2005. That use broke the miscellaneous receipts law and swelled department funds.
gao-gaoreports-b-308037:
A legal aid group's spin-off landlord is upheld in this GAO opinion, B-308037, dated September 14, 2006. The Legal Services Corporation set up Friends of Legal Services Corporation in 2001. The aim was to cut rent costs in Washington. The group then leased its office space from Friends. A senator asked if the setup was lawful. He also asked if a 10-year lease broke the funds law.

GAO held the setup lawful. Congress made the group a private nonprofit firm with broad powers. Those powers cover both the spin-off and the lease. The Antideficiency Act does not bind the group. So the long lease stands, as would a later take of Friends' assets.
gao-gaoreports-b-311137:
Two event firms lost their protest; the GAO decision is B-311137, dated April 25, 2008. National Conference Services, Inc. and a peer had bid to plan a yearly meet. The agency killed its call for quotes once bids were in. It chose to keep its past co-host for the meet. That co-host is a known pro or trade group. A Defense ethics rule lets such joint meets run.

GAO denied the protest. The men in charge said they used the buy path in good faith. They did not run the race to squeeze the past co-host. The joint path was judged best for the government. Good faith and a real gain can back a kill.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-537:
Policing U.S. trade deals as they multiply is the problem in GAO report GAO-05-537, dated June 30, 2005. Most U.S. exports fall under at least one trade agreement. Four agencies share the watch: the U.S. Trade Representative and the departments of Agriculture, Commerce, and State. GAO asked how the work has grown, how agencies track compliance, and how resources are shared out.

World Trade Organization membership has grown over 30 percent in 10 years. New deals reach into harder fields, such as intellectual property and technical standards. Agencies act on complaints from firms or on issues they spot themselves. Steps over 5 years have sharpened their response. Still, staff told GAO messages between Washington and overseas posts can be slow. Commerce staff may lack full word on cases abroad. Training is thin at the posts GAO visited. No joint plan steers resources to the work. GAO urged a coordinated strategy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-637:
Contractors who dodge federal taxes fill GAO-05-637, dated June 16, 2005. About 33,000 firms hired by civilian agencies owed over $3 billion in unpaid taxes as of September 30, 2004. GAO probed 50 of them and found abusive or possibly criminal conduct in every case. Many withheld payroll taxes from workers' wages and kept the money, a felony. One person ran about 20 firms owing taxes on over 300 returns. Some bought costly property while debts grew.

A levy scheme that skims federal payments barely dents the debt. Legal bars, tax agency policy choices, and weak payment oversight all blunt it. GAO lists fixes for each gap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-737:
GAO issued GAO-05-737 on July 28, 2005, on private security firms in Iraq. U.S. teams rebuilding Iraq faced an insurgency that hit troops, workers, and Iraqis. Guard work fell to private firms. GAO checked how agencies and builders hired those firms. It also checked ties with the U.S. military and what the guard work cost.

GAO found that agencies and builders had obligated over $766 million for private guards as of December 2004. Builders often found their first firm fell short. On over half the 2003 contracts GAO reviewed, the first firm was replaced. Lack of clear agency guidance was one cause named. GAO said joint work with the military was sound but could be made stronger. It also faulted weak cost checks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-137:
The Internal Revenue Service's books are audited in GAO-06-137, a report issued on November 10, 2005. GAO audits the tax agency's statements each year, since its collections drive federal receipts. GAO judged whether the fiscal year 2005 and 2004 statements were reliable. It also tested internal controls and compliance with key laws. Systems compliance with a 1996 financial improvement law came under review as well.

GAO found the statements fairly presented in all material respects. But the agency again leaned on heavy manual workarounds to close its books. Serious control flaws meant it did not keep effective controls over financial reporting. Material weaknesses remained in areas such as unpaid assessments, refunds, and information security. The agency did launch the first phase of a new financial system in fiscal year 2005. That system is still years from full use. The audit credits real progress while naming the flaws that persist.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-237:
Electric power's shift toward competition is summed up in GAO-06-237, a report dated November 15, 2005. The industry is moving from strict regulation toward market rivalry. That shift plays out across local, state, and federal rules. Demand is set to climb steeply by 2025, which demands new plants and lines. Two shocks frame the study: the vast 2003 East Coast blackout and the 2000 and 2001 California energy crisis. At Congress's request, GAO gathered its past work on the change.

The report traces what the federal government has done to reshape wholesale power markets. It shows how those markets have changed since the shift began. It then gives GAO's view of the hard problems that remain. Fair markets need watchful referees and sound market rules. Wires and plants must be built before demand outruns them. The report is a briefing book for a debate that touches every power bill.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-337:
A crop disease that luck and weather held at bay is revisited in GAO-06-337, dated February 24, 2006. Asian soybean rust is a fungus whose spores ride the wind. In 2005 it menaced the U.S. soybean crop. Growers in 31 states planted about 72.2 million acres worth some $17 billion. Kind weather kept 2005 losses low. GAO examined the agriculture department's strategy that year. It drew lessons for the seasons ahead.

The department must build on the 2005 experience, GAO urged. It should guide states on how often to report the disease's spread. Sentinel plots and advanced tests need clear rules for their use. A detailed action plan should be ready before the growing season. Strong national coordination in 2005 won praise worth keeping. The report treats a quiet year as borrowed time. Rust will return; the question is whether the watch does.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-437:
Egypt has long bought U.S. weapons with U.S. grant money. On April 11, 2006, report GAO-06-437 reviewed the Foreign Military Financing program for Egypt. Since 1979, Egypt has received about $60 billion in military and economic aid. About $34 billion came as financing grants. Those grants let Egypt buy U.S. military goods and services.

GAO describes the types and amounts of aid given. It assesses the financing arrangements used to provide it. It then judges how the United States checks the program's value. GAO said State and Defense need to assess how the aid serves U.S. foreign policy and security goals. Readers get amounts and arrangements.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-537:
A new satellite network was meant to link soldiers and systems without seams. In GAO-06-537 (May 24, 2006), GAO reviews the Transformational Satellite Communications System. The Defense Department began the program in January 2004. GAO reported in 2003 that it was starting without mature enough technology. This report follows up at a congressional request. It tracks how the program is progressing.

GAO also judges the buying approach. The test is whether that approach yields the knowledge needed before product development. More knowledge is needed as the department starts its new approach, GAO said. Readers get a progress check on a key space program. The focus is readiness to build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-737:
Staffing at embassies and consulates is reviewed in GAO-06-737, which GAO issued on June 30, 2006. In 2001, the administration made rightsizing the overseas presence a management priority. Rightsizing means matching staff to policy goals and security limits. It can also mean moving support work to regional centers and cutting needless posts. GAO checked how far these approaches had spread after almost five years.

GAO found that the government still lacked accurate data on its overseas presence. Estimates of total staff ranged from 66,000 to 69,000 people. The State Department separately estimated about 78,000 government positions. Without a firm count, agencies cannot judge whether posts are staffed right. GAO said rightsizing was slowly taking hold, but more action was needed to coordinate efforts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-137:
Health professions schools get federal grants to draw disadvantaged students into health careers. GAO reviewed how those grants were awarded in report GAO-07-137, dated February 2, 2007. The Health Careers Opportunity Program sits inside the Health Resources and Services Administration. About $34 million was available for the program each year. GAO covered fiscal years 2002 through 2005. It checked both the award process and who applied and won.

The agency first renewed existing projects without competition, GAO found. It then awarded the funds left over through a competitive round. Independent reviewers scored the applications and applied a funding preference for broad partnerships. From $4 million to $15 million a year went out as competitive grants. The agency followed the reviewers' ranking in every case. Of 439 applications over four years, 99 won grants. Minority-serving schools sent about 25 percent of applications and won about 30 percent of grants.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-237:
Offshore tax schemes hide income behind foreign accounts and shell firms. GAO studied the time crunch they create in GAO-07-237, a report dated March 30, 2007. The tax agency has 3 years to assess tax in most cases. Offshore cases take far longer to build than normal audits. GAO compared the two kinds of cases. It weighed the gains and losses of giving offshore cases more time. Tax experts and agency officials gave views.

Offshore audits that finish tend to yield larger assessments, GAO found. But the clock forces hard choices. Agents said they sometimes drop cases early or never open them. Some 1,942 offshore cases ran past 3 years by consent or agency choice. Over 700 of those closed with no added tax at all. GAO suggested that Congress carve out an exception to the 3-year limit. The tax agency said a longer clock makes sense.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-37:
The national recycling rate has barely budged since 2000, and cities hold most of the levers. GAO collected their best moves in GAO-07-37, a report dated December 29, 2006. GAO interviewed recycling chiefs in 11 large cities. It asked what raises participation. It reviewed what the environment and commerce agencies do. It also listed federal policy options.

Convenience tops the cities' list, GAO found. Curbside pickup, weekly service, and free bins drive use. Money talks as well. Austin charges by garbage can size, rewarding light trash. Outreach through mail, web, and ads ranks third. Food scraps and yard waste form almost a quarter of the waste stream. Shops and offices add 35 to 45 percent more. The environment agency cannot show its programs work. It keeps no performance measures. One grant program faces an 81 percent funding cut.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-737:
Data breaches and identity theft are examined in GAO-07-737, a report GAO released on June 4, 2007. Lost or stolen personal data can let thieves misuse card numbers or open false accounts. Many states now force firms to tell victims of breaches. Congress weighed a national rule of the same kind. GAO counted how often breaches occur and under what conditions. It studied 24 large breaches in depth. It also weighed the gains and costs of notice laws.

Over 570 breaches hit the news from January 2005 through December 2006. A House survey found over 788 breaches at 17 federal agencies in a longer span. Banks and schools, shops and hospitals all appear in the lists. Proof that breaches led to identity theft was thin, though. The full scale of harm stays unknown. GAO made no recommendations in the report. It frames the choice Congress faces on a national notice rule.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-837:
Federal computer security is graded again in GAO-07-837, a report GAO issued on July 27, 2007. The Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002 sets security duties for agencies. It also tells GAO to report to Congress on how agencies fare. Recent incidents put data on millions of Americans at risk. GAO read reports from agencies, watchdogs, and the budget office. It judged policies and practices across the government. It also weighed how agencies carry out the act.

Almost all 24 major agencies had flaws in one or more control areas. User access checks were often weak or missing. Agencies failed to limit access to what each user truly needs. Network borders, encryption, and event logging all showed gaps. Patching of key systems lagged in many places. Physical access to data assets was not always tight. GAO urged the budget office to sharpen its reporting measures. The office said it would weigh the advice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-37:
Grants management at the Legal Services Corporation (LSC) is the focus of GAO report GAO-08-37, dated December 28, 2007. LSC is a nonprofit that funds legal aid for low-income people. In 2006 it handed out most of its $327 million as grants. GAO tested its controls and checked practices at 14 grantees.

GAO found weak controls that left grant funds open to misuse. Duties among LSC's oversight units were unclear, and management shared fiscal review work with the inspector general in ways that confused staff. Site visits were not chosen by risk, and feedback to grantees was slow. At some grantees, GAO found poor fiscal practices and improper spending that better oversight could have caught. LSC's board and management agreed with GAO's recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-437:
The National Flood Insurance Program is examined in GAO report GAO-08-437, issued June 16, 2008. GAO placed the program on its high-risk list in March 2006. By December 2007, the Federal Emergency Management Agency owed over $17.3 billion to the Treasury for hurricane losses.

Policies in force rose 36 percent from 1997 through 2006, yet most at-risk homeowners still had no cover. Loss payments peaked at more than $17.7 billion in 2005, and 79 percent of payouts across the decade were for hurricane claims. Claims from repeat-loss properties grew from $3.7 billion to nearly $8 billion. Data gaps kept GAO from counting how many flooded properties were bought out to cut risk. GAO recommended live tracking of buyouts and tighter checks on contractors. The agency agreed on contractor oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-837: GAO-08-837, dated June 23, 2008, is a progress report on securing, stabilizing, and rebuilding Iraq. The hosted text holds the summary only. Congress has given about $640 billion for the global war on terrorism since 2001, most of it for Iraq. The report grades the January 2007 New Way Forward strategy on five goals: better security, stronger Iraqi forces, key laws, capital spending, and basic services. GAO drew on staff in Baghdad and more than 130 past Iraq audits. Its title verdict: some gains made, and an updated strategy needed.
hawthorne-twice-told-tales-1837:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published Twice-Told Tales in 1837, the story collection that made his name in America. The book is a founding text of the American short story as a serious art. Hawthorne had burned or buried early tales, and friends urged these into print at last.

Tales like The Minister's Black Veil and Wakefield probe hidden sin and quiet obsession in New England. Sketches of streets, inns, and old customs sit beside the darker moral fables in this volume. A hooded minister, a man who leaves home for twenty years, and gray champions fill its pages. The tone is gentle on the surface and unsettled below, Hawthorne's mark from the very start. Poe praised the tales' unity of effect, a standard the short story still chases.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley opens his History of the United Netherlands with the murder of Orange, in these first two chapters. William the Silent was killed by a single obscure fanatic, Motley writes, after twenty years of growing authority. Protestantism's extension and Spain's vast power frame the scene. The Estates of Holland show their courage at once.

A provisional council of state governs while sovereignty is offered abroad. Holland and Zeeland stand firm; Flanders weakens, and Ghent falls to the adroit Alexander Farnese. The second chapter turns to France and Elizabeth's severity toward the Dutch envoys. Motley's sympathies are declared from the first page: a small republic against the greatest empire on earth. These chapters are the foundation of a famous nineteenth-century history, dramatic in style and liberal in judgment.
irish-constitution-1937:
Ireland adopted a new constitution in 1937, approved by the voters in a referendum that July. Éamon de Valera, head of the government, shaped the text himself. Bunreacht na hÉireann, its Irish name, replaced the Free State charter of 1922. It cut the last cords binding Dublin to the Crown, while stopping short of the word republic.

The charter names the state Ireland, claims the whole island as the national territory, and gives the president a direct election. It promises strong rights for citizens and the family, with a Catholic coloring that marked its age. Courts gained the power to strike down laws that broke it, a lasting change. The document that finished the work of Irish independence still rules the republic today, amended many times but sound in its frame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abendana-237:
Abendana is the name of a group of Sephardic families of Amsterdam and London. The first to take it was Francisco Nuñez Pereyra, a Marano who fled Spain at the start of the seventeenth century. He settled in Amsterdam and took the name David Abendana. He was one of the founders of the first synagogue there, and died on February 14, 1625.

His son Manuel served as hakam of the Amsterdam congregation and died on June 15, 1667. The entry then lists more of the house by name and post. Isaac Hayyim de Brito Abendana, hakam of the Portuguese community, died at the age of one hundred, on April 5, 1760. He had led the academy 'Ez Hayyim and helped ready a nine-volume set of rabbinical rulings, printed in 1732 and 1733.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ablitas-ezmel-s:
Ezmel (Samuel) de Ablitas, son of Don Juceph, was born in the village of Ablitas near Tudela. He died in 1342 and was known as the rich Jew of Ablitas. Kings of Navarre and Aragon did business with him.

Those kings and Navarre nobles borrowed large sums from him and failed to repay. He then could not meet his own duties to the state. After his death, the Queen of Navarre seized his whole estate in 1343. Records cite one royal debt to him of £53,000. His sons Funes and Judah are also named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-achzib-called-a: Achzib is a name borne by two towns. One lay in the lowland of Judah, as Joshua xv. 44 shows. Micah links it with Mareshah in a play on the word for deceit. Genesis calls it Chezib, and Chronicles calls it Chozeba. The second town was a Phenician port claimed by the tribe of Asher. Asher never took it, as Judges i. 31 says. It is now the village Ez-Zib. It sits nine miles north of Acre, on the shore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aha-of-difti-93:
Aha of Difti was a Babylonian amora of the sixth generation, in the fifth century. He is often found in halakic debate with Rabina II. For a time he served as counselor to the exilarch Mar Zutra I., who held office from 441 to 450.

After Nahman b. Huna died, the academy at Sura moved to elect Aha as rector. His friend Mar b. Ashi wanted the seat once held by his own father, Ashi. While the members waited inside for the set hour of voting, Mar had himself elected outside. Aha thus lost the post by strategy, not by open vote.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-akiba-ha-kohen-:
Akiba ha-Kohen lived in Hungary and Bohemia in the second half of the fifteenth century. He died at Prague in 1496. His learning, wealth, and kindness won him the title Nasi, or Prince. About 1480 he held high standing at the court of King Matthew of Hungary.

Envious nobles slandered him to the king, and he had to flee the country. At Prague he founded a large Talmudic college and lectured there himself. Enemies pursued him there too, and even tried to take his life. In thanks for three escapes, he gave three Prague synagogues costly curtains for the Ark. He had twelve sons and thirteen daughters. With his sons and sons-in-law he could muster twenty-five priests, enough to give the priestly blessing in its full literal form.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexander-bernh:
Bernhard Alexander was a Hungarian writer and professor of philosophy and esthetics. He was born at Budapest on April 13, 1850. He studied at home and then at German universities. His fields were philosophy, esthetics, and pedagogy. Back in Hungary he taught at a Budapest real-school. In 1878 he joined the philosophy faculty of the University of Budapest. He became a full professor there in 1895.

Since 1892 he has also lectured at the National Theater Academy, on drama and esthetics. His chief books include a history of philosophy from 1878. His life of Kant, crowned by the Academy of Science in 1889, is another. With Professor Banoczi he edits a series of philosophical writers. Its volumes hold his versions of Descartes, Hume, and Kant. He has also edited journals on teaching, in 1882-86 and again in 1891.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alushta-1337: Alushta is a village on the southeast shore of the Crimea. It lies in the district of Yalta in Russia. Ruins there mark a fort of Justinian. That fort, Aluston, rose in the sixth century. The place shows up in the same Chazar letter as Alupka. There it is called Aluss, a town bound to pay the Chazars. In the middle ages Genoa held the village. Its names then were Lusta, Austa, and Alusta. Few Jews live there now, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amram-ibn-salam: Amram ibn Salameh ibn Ghazal was a Samaritan prayer poet. His full name adds the titles ha-Kohen ha-Levi. A set of his prayers stands in a prayer book. A part of that book is kept at Oxford. The part sits in the Bodleian Library there. His hymns serve the ten days of repentance. They serve both the dawn and the eve rites. Poems for the Feast of Tabernacles are his as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-animal-worship-:
Animal worship needs a careful definition, the entry warns, before any history can start. Serving an animal as a god differs from merely seeing it as divine. Using an animal as a symbol of the true object of worship differs from both.

In the strict sense, the entry doubts that animal worship ever held a large part of the Hebrew community. In a wider sense, it finds real cases worth close study. It sorts them into three forms. The lowest is awe of animals thought to hold demon powers, a notion the entry calls common among early peoples and still alive in modern lands. Other forms grow from symbol and cult practice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aphraates-the-p:
Aphraates, called the Persian Sage, was a Syrian writer of sermons in the fourth century. His homilies, written between 337 and 345, matter greatly to Jewish historians. The entry claims that no church father was ever so strongly shaped by rabbinic Judaism as this defender of Christianity against the Jews.

Bishop Georgios, about 780, already noted his debt to Jewish teaching. Modern scholars cited here match his Bible comments line by line with rabbinic parallels. On the soul, on God, and on reward and punishment, he proves a docile pupil of the Jews. His teaching on God's two traits, justice and mercy, is called decidedly Jewish. The entry then works through his homilies topic by topic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-archite-1737: Archite names an inhabitant of a town or district on the southern border of Judah. It is probably linked with the Erech, called Archi in the Authorized Version, of Joshua, chapter 16, verse 2. Hushai, David's friend, came from that region, as Second Samuel, chapter 15, verse 32, shows. The place seems to lie near Ataroth. The short entry closes with a limit: it has not been identified with any certainty.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arton-leopold-e:
Leopold Emile Arton, born Aaron, was a French adventurer born at Strasburg in 1849 who settled in Paris in 1871. He handled the bribes of the Panama Canal Company, paid to statesmen to win chamber approval for the company's money plans. For over four years his name filled French debate, shook cabinets, and drew stormy scenes in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

He fled in 1892 and was caught in London on November 16, 1895, then handed back to France. In 1896 one court gave him six years at hard labor for cheating a dynamite company; a second court changed the sentence to eight years of seclusion. In prison he produced his famous Notebook, the Carnet des 104, naming 104 deputies and senators he claimed to have bribed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asher-b-meshull:
Asher ben Meshullam was a Talmudist who flourished at Lunel in the second half of the twelfth century. His father was the noted scholar Meshullam ben Jacob. His teachers were Joseph ibn Plat and Abraham ben David of Posquieres, whose ascetic bent he shared. Benjamin of Tudela reports that Asher lived in complete seclusion, wholly given to Torah study, and never tasted meat.

Seclusion did not mean hostility to learning. Judah ibn Tibbon praised Asher's love of science in a letter and urged his own son to keep the man's friendship. Two Talmudic works of Asher are cited by title, on holiday rules and on priestly gifts, but neither seems to survive. A small Midrash on the Ten Commandments is also laid to his name in a manuscript note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asshurites-2037: The Asshurites were a nation the Bible traces to Abraham and Keturah, in Genesis xxv. 3. Prophetic writing shows them making benches of ivory for Tyre. The entry notes a problem in II Samuel ii. 9, where the name cannot mean this people or the Assyrians. Scholars cited there read it as a copying error for Geshurites, or explain it through Targum Jonathan as the Asherites. Rabbinical writers read the name as a word for merchants who travel with their wares from place to place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asylum-12637:
Asylum is the right of a hunted person to find safety at a sacred place. The entry opens with the custom in the wider world. Altars, temples, and graves could shelter slaves, debtors, and offenders. The safety grew with the holiness of the spot. Athens limited the right by law, and Rome curbed it under Tiberius in the year 22.

In Israel the right appears first in the days of Solomon. Adonijah fled to the altar and won his life. Joab, who would not leave the altar, was killed on the spot by Solomon's order. Later parts treat the cities of refuge set apart in the law of Moses. The entry follows their rules in Talmudic sources and asks where such cities could stand after the exile. Changed borders and lost Levitical towns forced hard choices, which the rabbis debated at length.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-b-nai-b-rith-or:
B'nai B'rith, Sons of the Covenant, is the largest and oldest Jewish fraternal order. In 1902 it counted about 30,000 members. They were spread over more than 330 lodges and 10 grand lodges, in the United States, Germany, Rumania, Austria-Hungary, Egypt, and Palestine. German Jews in New York founded it in 1843, with Henry Jones at their head.

The founders aimed to unite Jews of the Mosaic faith on ground all could share, whatever their views on doctrine or ritual. They barred talk of politics and religion from the lodge room to keep the peace. Charity and brotherly love stood as the highest virtues. The order grew fast. By 1857 it reported 2,889 members and a fund of $78,000. A new constitution in 1868 gave it a more open, representative shape. Later parts tell of its orphan homes, its aid in disasters, and its work for Jews abroad.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baer-dob-of-mes:
Dob Baer of Meseritz, known as the Maggid or Preacher of Meseritz, was born in Volhynia in 1710 and died on Dec. 15, 1772. He was the first apostle of Ḥasidism and its chief spreader. Trained in Talmud and drawn to Lurian Cabala, he first lived as a strict ascetic. A visit to Besht, the movement's founder, changed his course and restored his health.

After Besht died in 1760, Baer led the movement without rival. He sent out emissaries, brought in the Lurian prayer-book, and drew strong young scholars to his side. The entry sets out his teaching at length: God is present in all things, and prayer in deep rapture can join man to God. It also tells of the ban at Wilna in 1772 and of his sayings, kept by pupils since he left no writings of his own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bandoff-benjami: Benjamin Bandoff, also spelled Bendoff or Bendorff, was an English prize-fighter born in the first quarter of the nineteenth century. He died after 1865. The entry is a bare record of his fights. He entered the ring against Jerry Duggan on Sept. 20, 1853, for £10 a side. Darkness stopped that match at seventy-five rounds, drawn. George Sims beat him twice, in 1854 and 1858. He beat Hopkinson in 1862 and Jackson in 1863, fought Callaghan to a drawn eighty-six rounds, and lost his last fight, to John Smith, on Feb. 14, 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-barnay-ludwig-2:
Ludwig Barnay, a German actor, was born at Budapest on February 12, 1842, son of the secretary of the Jewish congregation there. Destined for the building trade, he persuaded his father to send him to Vienna to study under Adolf Sonnenthal. At eighteen he made his début at Trautenau under the name "Lacroix" and failed. He then led a troupe of barnstormers through Moravia and Austrian Silesia until the tour collapsed.

From 1875 to 1880 Barnay directed the Stadttheater in Hamburg while starring at Stuttgart, Munich, Frankfort, and Berlin. In 1883 he co-founded the Deutsche Theater in Berlin. Two years later he converted the Operetten-Walhalla into his own Berliner Theater, keeping it until 1894. In 1872 an address signed by four thousand actors thanked him for his work for the profession. German critics acclaimed him a genius of the first order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bassani-hezekia: Hezekiah Mordecai Bassani was rabbi of Verona, Italy, around the turn of the seventeenth century. He wrote on divorce and on levirate marriage, two works printed together at Mantua in 1744 under one title. He also wrote a book of prayers for visiting the sick, printed at Verona in 1710. That book drew in part on Aaron Berechiah and on Isaiah Horwitz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beer-alexander-:
Alexander Beer was a religious teacher and author in Munich who wrote a German catechism of the Mosaic religion in 1826. He worked under the rabbi of Würzburg and with approval from rabbinic courts in Bavaria. The king endorsed the book, and the state paid to print it for Jewish schools.

The book sets Hebrew quotes beside its German text. Its parts treat the thirteen articles of faith, duties to God, to self, and to others, plus marriage law. A rabbinic note on circumcision draws note. Critics of reform attacked the book in a pamphlet of 1827.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-belmonte-franci: Francisco de Ximenes Belmonte was a Dutch diplomat who lived at Amsterdam in the first half of the eighteenth century. He was a nephew of Baron Manuel de Belmonte. In 1706 he followed his uncle as resident of the king of Spain in the Netherlands. That office of resident came to an end when the Bourbon line took the Spanish throne. The entry gives no birth or death dates for him and names no other post that he held.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benet-mordecai-:
Mordecai Benet, a Talmudist and chief rabbi of Moravia, was born in 1753 in Hungary and died at Carlsbad on Aug. 12, 1829. Poor parents sent him at age five to his grandmother at Nikolsburg, where a patron paid for his schooling. His gift showed early, and at his bar mitzvah guests saw three works in his own hand.

He studied at Fürth and Prague, then settled at Nikolsburg in 1773. In 1789 he became its rabbi and chief rabbi of Moravia, refusing calls from Presburg and Cracow. His few books rank as classics of Talmudic writing, praised for keen logic and a strict, clear method.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berechiah-ii-r-:
Berechiah the Second was a Palestinian amora of the fourth century, cited in the Midrashim as Berechiah ha-Kohen. Though likely born in Babylonia, he came to Palestine young and learned under Palestinian masters, chiefly Ḥelbo in the Haggadah. His sayings fill the Palestinian sources.

One count finds him cited sixty-eight times in a single Midrash set, and eighty-five times in another. He worked in law as well, but the Haggadah was his main field. A specimen teaching of his holds that dreams, though partly fulfilled, are never fulfilled in full, a point he draws from Joseph's dream.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-isaiah-b:
Isaiah Berlin, also called Isaiah Pick, was the leading critic among German Talmudists of the eighteenth century. Born in Hungary about October 1725, he died as rabbi of Breslau on May 13, 1799. He came of a famed line of scholars and learned first from his own father.

After years in trade at Breslau, he joined its rabbinate in 1787 and became rabbi in 1793, after a hard-fought election. He slept only on Sabbaths and feasts, the entry says, and gave all other time to study. His lasting fame rests on keen notes to the Talmud and many classic texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bernstein-elsa-: Elsa Bernstein, a German dramatist who wrote as Ernst Rosmer, was born at Vienna. She was a daughter of Heinrich Porges, a friend of Richard Wagner, and was schooled at Munich. A short time on the stage ended when an affliction of the eyes forced her to retire. She turned to writing plays instead. Her first, after her marriage in 1892, stirred wide debate. Four later plays fell rather flat, but her dramatic fairy tale of 1895 won boundless praise for its beauty and poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bezah-egg-3237:
Beẓah, meaning "Egg," is a Talmudic treatise. It belongs to Seder Mo'ed, the second Talmudic order. Its place in that order is not fixed. It is often called "Yom-Ṭob," or Holy Day. That name fits its contents better. The treatise has five chapters. They treat work rules for holy days.

Chapter one covers muḳẓeh, things set aside from use. Chapter two treats cooking for an adjoining Sabbath. Later chapters bar hunting and buying tools on holy days. Chapter five lists acts banned as precautions. The entry also names two special commentaries. One is by Bezalel Ashkenazi. The other is by Menahem Meïri.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bismarck-prince:
Otto Eduard Leopold Bismarck was a Prussian statesman. He was born at Schönhausen on April 1, 1815. He died at Friedrichsruh on July 30, 1898. He led Prussia, then the North German Federation. From 1870 he was chancellor of the German empire. He held that post until March 1890.

The entry traces his shifting stance on Jews. In 1847 he opposed Jewish emancipation in the Diet. He championed a Christian state there. Yet in 1868 he defended persecuted Rumanian Jews. At the Berlin Congress he pleaded their rights. Later he let Stöcker's anti-Semitic movement run. Political alliance with conservatives explained that tolerance. Still, he blocked stripping Jews of legal rights.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boniface-ix-pie:
Boniface IX, born Pietro Tomacelli at Naples, was the two hundred and eighth pope. He was elected on Nov. 2, 1389, and died at Rome in 1404. His rule was very favorable for Jews in general and for Roman Jews in particular.

At the Roman Jews' request, Boniface ordered city officers to guard them from drudgery, cheating, and violence. The Jewish badge was repealed under his bull. Jews were to be treated as Roman citizens, the bull said. He also made two Jewish physicians his own doctors. Angelo di Manuele and Solomone de Sabalduchio both won his special favor in those years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brandes-marthe-:
Marthe Brandès, born Marthe Josephine Brunschwig, was a French actress born in Paris on Jan. 31, 1862. She studied design, sculpture, and music before the drama. Success in private theatricals led her to the Paris Conservatoire.

Dumas the younger engaged Brandès for the Vaudeville after her prize years. From 1884 she was a Paris favorite in modern roles. She joined the Comédie Française in 1887 and excelled in classical parts too. She returned to the Vaudeville in 1890, then rejoined the Française in 1892. Voters made her a sociétaire in 1896. Her specialty, the entry says, was the self-willed modern woman of the world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brokers-jew-373:
Jew brokers were the Jewish merchants allowed to trade at London's Royal Exchange. The entry dates the wider use of the word broker to the time of Edward III. It says the term joined with Jews after their resettlement in England in 1656. Jewish traders faced strong opposition, yet their links with the East and West Indies made them hard to ignore.

Solomon Dormido gained admission to the Exchange in 1657, and a special Jews' Walk was later set aside. A reorganization in 1697 capped broker numbers and required a medal. Only twelve Jew brokers were allowed, and medals sold for large sums. The entry ends with the cap removed in 1828 and city freedom extended to Jews in 1832.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-calmer-liefmann:
Liefmann Calmer, baron of Picquigny, was a leading figure in eighteenth century French Jewry. Born in Aurich, Hanover, in 1711, he settled first at The Hague, then in France, where he won naturalization papers. His full synagogue name was Moses Eliezer Lipmann, son of Kalonymus, and the entry traces both his names to it.

In April 1774 a stand in buyer took the barony of Picquigny and the viscounty of Amiens for him. The price was 1,500,000 francs, paid to the duke of Chaulnes' creditors. The buyer soon declared the purchase was for Calmer himself. He thus became a Jewish baron in old regime France. Two of his three sons died on the guillotine in the Terror. He died at Paris in 1784.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chao-yng-cheng-: Chao Yng-Cheng was a Chinese mandarin who flourished about 1653. After the sack of K'ai Fung-Foo, which followed the fall of the Ming dynasty in 1642, the synagogue there was destroyed. The Jews fled across the Hoang-Ho river, saving scrolls thrown into the water. Chao, a Jewish mandarin sent to restore the city, brought the Jews back with his brother's help. They rebuilt the temple in 1653. One full scroll of the Law was pieced together from the saved fragments. A stone stele dated 1663 later recorded his action.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-christiani-pabl:
Pablo Christiani was a Jewish convert of Montpellier and a contemporary of Nahmanides. After baptism he joined the Dominicans and tried to convert his former coreligionists. Failing in Provence, he pushed for forced debate in Aragon. Through Raymond de Penyaforte he won King James's consent, and Nahmanides was summoned to Barcelona in 1263.

The disputation ran four days, July 20-24, before the whole court. Christiani tried to prove the Christian faith from the Talmud itself. The entry says Nahmanides answered firmly and won, even receiving a royal gift. Christiani then denounced the published account, and Nahmanides was exiled for two years while his pamphlet was burned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohnheim-julius:
Julius Cohnheim, a German pathologist, was born at Demmin, Pomerania, on July 20, 1839, and died in Leipsic on Aug. 15, 1884. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1861, served as a surgeon in the war against Denmark, and joined Virchow's pathological institute at Berlin in 1864.

His 1867 essay on inflammation and pus formation made his name. In it he proved that white blood cells, by emigrating, form the origin of pus, a finding that reshaped pathology. Chairs took him to Kiel in 1868, Breslau in 1872, and Leipsic in 1876. The entry also credits him with first freezing fresh tissue for study and with showing nerve endings in the muscle areas that bear his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crehange-alexan: Alexandre ben Baruch Créhange was a French Hebraist. He was born at Etain, in Meurthe-et-Moselle, in 1791. He died in Paris on Jan. 7, 1872. He served as secretary to the Hebrew United Charities. His life's work was spreading religious books in French. He issued a modern family Bible study in 1846. He translated the Passover Haggadah in 1847 and the Psalms in 1858. Prayer books for French and Sephardic Jews followed, in Hebrew and French. From 1870 he put out a Paris almanac.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crime-4637:
Crime is an act banned by human law and punished by human authority. It stands apart from sin, which offends God rather than the state. In Mosaic law the chief crimes against person and property were handled by the injured party or his kin. The avenger of blood pursued the murderer. Injuries were paid for in money. A thief had to repay double, and was enslaved if he could not pay.

Other offenses struck at the whole nation: idolatry, Sabbath-breaking, blasphemy, and adultery. Witnesses had to prosecute them and even help carry out the sentence. The article then turns to Mishnah law. There the avenger of blood has dropped out. Fathers and sons no longer suffer for each other's guilt, a change the sages read back into the texts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-bonet-bon:
Bonet David, also called Bonjorn or Bongoron, lived in Catalonia in the second half of the fourteenth century. He is believed to have been a son of the astronomer Jacob Poel. In the persecutions of 1391 he converted to Christianity and took the name Maestre Bonet Bonjorn.

David was a close friend of Profiat Duran, who had also been forced to convert. David persuaded Profiat to flee abroad with him so both could return to Judaism. On the eve of departure David changed his mind and stayed. Profiat left Spain alone, then wrote David the famous satirical letter "Al Tehi ka-Aboteka," aimed at converts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deckingen-judah: Benjamin's son Judah ben Benjamin Deckingen was a German lexicographer of the sixteenth century, and the entry on him is brief. He studied under Isaac of Ahrweiler and worked as a tutor at Wendersheim in 1555, at Rüsselheim, and elsewhere in southern Germany. In 1556 he compiled a Hebrew-German glossary of five quarto pages. It was meant to help in translating German into Hebrew. The entry notes that N. Brüll later published the glossary from a manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-deutsch-david-5:
David Deutsch was a German rabbi born at Zülz, Silesia, in 1810. Raised by a relative at Breslau, he studied Talmud under Mordecai Benet and Moses Sofer. He became rabbi of Myslowitz in 1838 and of Sohrau in 1845, serving there until his death on July 31, 1873.

Like his older brother Israel, Deutsch championed Orthodoxy. He led the protest against naming Abraham Geiger rabbi of Breslau. With his brother he answered Geiger's pamphlet in print in 1843. He also protested the Reform rabbinical conferences of 1844 and 1845, and opposed the synagogue organ. He translated Isaac Troki's defense of Judaism into German, with critical notes, in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-drunkenness-in-:
Drunkenness in Jewish law turns on one Talmud passage, a baraita in Erubin 65a. The Talmud speaks only once, the entry says, on drink and legal blame. It asks when a drunk man's acts still count. Its answer is strict.

A drunken man's purchase is a purchase, and his sale is a sale. If he commits a capital crime, he is put to death. Lesser crimes still earn their stripes. He counts as sound of mind for all purposes, save prayer. Rabbi Hanina sets one limit: a man drunk as Lot was is free from all blame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elijah-ben-abra: Elijah ben Abraham was a Karaite scholar. He lived in the twelfth century at the latest. His book sets out the split between Karaites and Rabbinites. Its title names that split in plain terms. Pinsker printed the work in a larger Karaite collection. Elijah stands out for one odd fact. He was the only Karaite to quote a book by Saadia. That book was Saadia's reply to Anan, the Karaite founder. One view holds Elijah only copied the work. In that view the true author was another man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elles-elis-isaa: Isaac Elles was a Polish rabbi of the sixteenth century. The entry names two books from his hand. The first treats the core dogmas of Judaism. It bears the title Yesod Emunah, Ground of Faith. Cracow printed it in the year 1582. The second book treats the theme of repentance. It draws its matter from older works on the topic. A book by Eleazar of Worms feeds into it most. That volume came out at Cracow the same year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-errera-giorgio-: Giorgio Errera was an Italian chemist born at Venice on October 26, 1860. He studied at Padua and Turin and took his doctorate in chemistry at Turin in 1882. He then lectured there and assisted the professor of chemistry. In 1892 he became professor of chemistry at the University of Messina. The entry lists many essays by him in chemical journals, in Italian and German. His one named book is Lezion di Polarimetria, printed at Turin in 1891. No later career facts are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-father-6037:
Father first means the begetter of a child, and the entry opens by widening the word step by step. It can mean a grandfather or any forebear. It can mean the head of a house, family, or clan. It can name the founder or patron of a craft, or a helper and guard. Used of God, it points to his bond with Israel.

Titles of honor follow: Moses as father of wisdom, Hoshaya as father of the Mishnah, and the court's second judge as father of the bet din. The father held supreme power over his children, the entry then shows. Old cases include Isaac's binding and Jephthah's daughter. Later law curbed that power: a stubborn son had to be brought before the elders, not dealt with at home.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fornaraki-affai:
The Fornaraki affair was a charge of ritual murder made in Egypt in 1881. It stirred the European press for nine months. On May 18, 1881, a Greek child, Evangeli Fornaraki, vanished in Alexandria. After some time the body was found on the seashore. A world commission of thirty-four doctors and consuls' delegates studied the case. All but two Greeks agreed the child had died by accident. Sand in the lungs showed the child was alive when it fell into the sea.

Still, a Jewish family named Baruch was accused of a ritual crime by the Greeks. Protest came from Patriarch Joachim III and from medical men at Paris. None of it freed the family at once. They were shipped to Corfu, jailed, and ill-treated there. On Jan. 4, 1882, the Corfu tribunal set them free. Two short source lines close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-free-will-6337:
Free will is the doctrine that man's choosing is self-started and cannot be foretold. That man is free to choose his course was held by rabbinical Judaism as a basic rule of the faith. Philo taught it, and Josephus reports the Pharisees holding it. They stood against the Sadducees, who gave all to chance. A Talmudic saying runs that all is in God's hands except the fear of God.

Thinkers then faced a hard knot: if God knows all beforehand, how can man choose freely? Saadia answered that God's knowing does not cause the act. Man's choice comes first, and God knows things as they are. Later writers split God's knowledge into kinds, or set fate in the stars. Maimonides held that free will must stand, or reward and punishment would fail. God's knowledge, he said, is not like ours at all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-furstenthal-jac:
Jacob Raphael Furstenthal, a German poet and Hebrew writer born in Glogau in 1781, died at Breslau on February 16, 1855. He worked chiefly to modernize Jewish worship. Toward that end he rendered key prayer books into German. Those versions stayed popular among German Jews for years. He added Hebrew notes to some of them.

His wider fame rests on Hebrew verse with a classic ring. Critics praised its fine diction, rich thought, and plain national feeling. His Song on Zion, printed in 1810, counts as his best poem. He also translated Maimonides and Bahya into German with Hebrew comment. A large Hebrew comment on the whole Bible shows his range.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gascon-abraham-: Abraham Gascon is named as a scholar of the sixteenth century, and the entry records little beyond his link to one book. He owned a copy of Samuel of Sarsah work Miklal Yofi. To that copy he added notes in the margins. He also brought the index of the work to completion. The entry gives no place, no dates, and no other writings for him. Its one source is a Bodleian catalogue note on the manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geba-pausal-for: Geba was a city of Benjamin set among towns on the northern border, in Joshua xviii. 24. Geba and its open lands went to the priests. Second Kings names it as the northern mark of Judah, against Beer-sheba in the south. In Saul days Philistines held Geba. Jonathan drove them out, and the armies faced each other across a ravine. Geba on the south faced Michmash on the north. The site is matched with the village Jeba.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gems-12337:
Gems are precious stones cut or polished for dress or other uses. None came from Palestine itself. Ships brought them from Ophir under Solomon. Traders brought them from Arabia and Phenicia. The Queen of Sheba gave gems as gifts. With gold they ranked as the costliest goods a house could hold. A restored Zion is pictured as built and decked with them.

Twelve stones sat in the high priest breastplate, and two more in his ephod. Exodus lists them in four rows of three. Scholars find the exact stones hard to name with care. Greek, Targum, and Josephus accounts each shed light of their own age. Gems also served for signet rings, seals, crowns, and fine robes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gold-6737:
Gold gets a word study first. Six Hebrew terms denote it, four of them in Job xxviii alone. They range from the common word tied to its yellow color to poetic words meaning "hidden" and "treasured." Gold was known from the earliest times. It served first for ornaments. Only by the days of the Judges does it appear as money.

The metal covered the Tabernacle's walls and the Ark. It covered the Temple's floor and ceiling as well. It dressed the high priest and crowned kings. The entry names its source lands: Havilah, Sheba, Ophir, Uphaz, and Parvaim. In biblical imagery gold stands for purity, nobility, and great worth. Isaiah calls Babylon the "golden city." Daniel figures its empire as a head of gold.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goudsmit-joel-e:
Joel Emanuel Goudsmit was a Dutch jurist. He was born in Leyden on June 13, 1813. He died there on March 17, 1882. He graduated in law on May 12, 1842. Leyden University made him professor of Roman law in 1858. His fame rests on his "Pandect System." Its first volume came in 1866 and its second in 1880. The work was never finished.

It was the first Dutch treatment of that system, the entry says. It reached French, English, and Russian versions. In 1873 Goudsmit toured the United States and wrote up New York for "De Gids." He was active in Jewish affairs too. He wrote an open letter on the Jewish question in 1863. He also worked for the Jews of Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gumperz-aaron-s:
Aaron Solomon Gumperz was a German scholar and physician. He was born on Dec. 10, 1723, and died in 1769. In March 1751 he took his medical degree at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. He was the first Prussian Jew to earn a doctor's degree. History knows him best as Mendelssohn's teacher of philosophy. He kindled Mendelssohn's love of literature.

Gumperz wrote a calendar for the year 5509. His "Megalleh Sod" comments on Ibn Ezra's work on the Five Scrolls. Only the Ecclesiastes part was printed, at Hamburg in 1765. An essay on religion and philosophy follows it. Mendelssohn praised the work warmly in his "Bi'ur Millot ha-Higgayon."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haggith-7037: Haggith was one of David's wives and the mother of Adonijah. She seems to have married David after he took the throne. Adonijah is often called simply "the son of Haggith," and he was born at Hebron. In the lists in II Samuel, Haggith and her son stand fourth among David's wives and sons. The entry draws on II Samuel iii. 4, I Kings i and ii, and I Chronicles iii. 2, and tells nothing else of her.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-haphraim-7237: Haphraim was a city of Issachar. Joshua xix, 18, 19 sets it between Shunem and Shihon. The "Onomastica Sacra" still knew it as "Affarea." It placed it six miles north of Legio. The entry matches that distance with the village of Al-'Afulah. The village stands about two miles west of Sulam, the ancient Shunem. It may stand for Haphraim today. The entry adds one more possible link. Haphraim may be the Aphærema of I Maccabees xi, 34. Beyond the verse and these identifications, the entry records nothing of the town.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hauser-carl-fra:
Carl Frankl Hauser, born on Dec. 27, 1847, at Janoshaza in Hungary, was an American humorist and writer. He won a free place at Vienna's Theater Academy and acted in Vienna and Berlin. Late in 1875 he moved to the United States and settled in New York. There he joined the German edition of "Puck" in 1876.

Hauser stayed with "Puck" for fourteen years as associate editor. He also acted at the Thalia Theater and founded a German comic weekly called "Hallo." His books include a comic account of twenty-five years in America. He wrote a libretto and pieces for six burlesques, and he took part in reform politics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heller-jehiel-b:
Jehiel ben Aaron Heller, born in 1814 in the Minsk government, was a Russian rabbi. He came from the line of Yom-Tob Lipmann Heller. He held rabbinates at Glusk, Volkovisk, Suwalki, and Plungian in turn. He was a noted preacher who gave sermons in pure German on state occasions.

His books include a work on patriotism, printed at St. Petersburg in 1852. A German version came out for the government. His answers on all four parts of the Shulhan Aruk appeared in 1856. He also commented on the Passover Haggadah and the Song of Solomon. He died on Nov. 14, 1861.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herzfeld-jacob-:
Jacob Herzfeld, the chemist born at Mülheim on June 17, 1859, should not be confused with the actor of the same name. He studied at Charlottenburg and Berlin, taking his doctorate in 1886. In 1885 he directed dyeing at the royal weaving school at Mülheim. He became its chief in 1892.

Herzfeld later joined a Berlin publishing house, founded an electrochemistry journal, and entered a Cologne chemical firm. From 1900 he lived at Fürth doing research. He was an authority on weaving, dyeing, and printing. His many books treated textile testing, bleaching agents, dyes, yarn bleaching, and rare earth chemistry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-huna-b-nathan-7: Huna ben Nathan was a Babylonian scholar of the fourth and fifth centuries. He studied under Amemar the Second and was a senior companion of Ashi, to whom he repeated Amemar's sayings. He was wealthy and learned, yet ranked below Ashi. He had access to the Persian royal court. King Yezdegerd once adjusted Huna's belt with his own hands, a mark of high favor. Sherira names him as exilarch in Ashi's time. The entry warns of a second Huna ben Nathan, a companion of Raba and pupil of Nahman.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-wakar-wakka: Judah ben Isaac ibn Wakar of Cordova was tax collector for the infante Don Juan Manuel about 1320. He also served as that prince's agent and traveling companion. Don Juan Manuel wrote the book Conde Lucanor. Judah was a very pious man. He admired Rabbi Jehiel ben Asher of Toledo. The entry says he punished all moral and religious offenses without mercy. No works are credited to him, and the notice rests on responsa of Asher ben Jehiel and one history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-immanuel-5737:
Immanuel is a name that occurs only three times in the Bible, all in Isaiah. In the last verse the English versions render it as a sentence, God is with us. A Targum note takes the word as a proper name in the first two places and as two words in the third. The Talmud and Midrash never use the name at all.

Nor does the name stand among the many names for the Messiah in Jewish lists. A Greek Baruch book calls Jesus Christ Immanuel, marked here as a Christian addition. The absence in Jewish lore suggests, the entry argues, that applying the word to the Messiah was unknown in Jewish circles. Three modern studies are named for the question.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-issachar-dob-be: Issachar Dob ben Jacob Joshua was rabbi of Podhajee, in Galicia, born at Lisko in 1712. His father wrote the "Pene Yehoshua" on the Talmud, and Issachar Dob studied under Hirsch of Halberstadt. In 1741 he approved the printing of the Hoshen Mishpat with its commentaries. In 1744 Metz called him as head of its yeshibah, but he fell sick on the way and died at Berlin on Oct. 28. Though young, he was known as a fine Talmudic scholar, and his responsa survive in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-javal-leopold-8:
Leopold Javal, a French politician, was born at Mülhausen on Dec. 1, 1804, as the son of a wealthy merchant. He served as an army officer in the Algiers campaign of 1830, then left the army for finance in France. He helped start the first Paris omnibuses, directed a bank, ran a model farm, and aided the Alsatian railways.

In 1857 the Yonne department elected him to the legislature, where he backed free trade and voted with the Left. He won his seat again in 1863 and 1869 and helped proclaim the republic. He also spoke for the Jews of Alsace at the Central Consistory of Paris. He died at Paris on March 28, 1872.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-hazzan-b: Joseph Hazzan ben Judah of Troyes was a French Talmudist and cantor who flourished at Troyes near the middle of the thirteenth century. Quotes in Minhat Yehudah show he wrote a commentary on Ecclesiastes and a grammar called Sefer Yedidot. A few of his Masoretic notes stand in a Pentateuch manuscript. He also wrote a treatise on the calendar. A like work, Mozne Zedek, by a gaon of Troyes, may be his as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-zabara-j:
Joseph Zabara, or Joseph ben Meir Zabara, was a Spanish doctor, satirist, and poet of the start of the thirteenth century. He was born and died in Barcelona and studied at Narbonne under Joseph Kimhi. His one known work is the Sefer Sha'ashu'im, printed at Constantinople in 1577.

The book is a set of stories and fables on the model of Kalilah wa-Dimnah. A giant named Enan Manatash is said to tell them to the author over a run of visits. Many tales turn on the slyness of women, and one retells the story of Tobit. The book ends with the author's return to Barcelona and its great prince, Sheshet Benveniste.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joy-hebrew-simh:
Joy, in Hebrew carried by words such as simhah, sason, and rinnah, is the feeling of gladness and rejoicing. One source counts ten Hebrew terms for it, and the entry says no tongue has as many. That fact is read as a sign of a cheerful cast in Jewish life. Poets and prophets spread the feeling outward, picturing heaven, earth, fields, and trees breaking into joy.

The Bible, the entry argues, joins joy to a sober life. Lawful pleasures count as gifts from God, while pleasures that end in sorrow are warned against. In rabbinic writing, joy in a duty well done is the state in which the divine presence rests on a person. Cheering the downcast is praised as a deed that can win a share in the world to come.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kaiser-alois-91:
Alois Kaiser was a cantor and composer. He was born on Nov. 10, 1840, at Szobotist, in Hungary. From the age of ten he sang in Solomon Sulzer's choir. He trained at schools in Vienna. He then served as assistant cantor at Fünfhaus. From 1863 to 1866 he was cantor at the Neusynagoge in Prague.

In June 1866 Kaiser reached New York city. The next month he became cantor of Oheb Shalom in Baltimore. He still held that post in 1904. He led the Society of American Cantors for some years. He also helped compile the music of the Union Hymnal, issued in 1897. The entry lists his service music, hymn books, and cantatas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-katz-ludwig-923: Ludwig Katz was a German doctor of the ear and throat. He was born at Loslau on Jan. 1, 1848. He took his medical degree at Berlin University in 1872. From 1878 he worked as a specialist in Berlin. In 1892 he became a lecturer at the university there. He is known for two atlas works on the ear. One shows the ear in health and disease. The other gives see-through views of the organ. Both came out at Berlin, in 1890 and 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kiralfy-imre-93: Imre Kiralfy was a musical composer born in Budapest on Jan. 1, 1845. He studied music at Budapest, Vienna, and Paris. He began composing at the age of twelve. Kiralfy created and produced a series of spectacular exhibitions. They were given in the United States and in England. His shows included "America" at the Chicago Columbian Exposition of 1893. Others were "Venice in London" and "Paris in London." He also published compositions such as "Nero" and "Columbus." In 1904 he resided in London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kuba-9537:
Kuba, chief town of its district in the government of Baku, counted 15,346 people in 1897, about 7,000 of them Jews. Most local Jews were Caucasian Jews, called Mountain Jews there. They live in a suburb by the River Kubinka. Dress follows the Caucasian Muslim pattern, with quilted coats and high caps.

Daily life gets close attention. Families of ten to fifteen share small earthen huts lit from a roof window. Work centers on farming and trade, above all carpet export to Constantinople. Pay for labor runs at 20 to 30 copecks a day. The entry calls the group strict in religion, notes that polygamy is not barred, and says they write in Rashi script.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-laqueur-ludwig-: Ludwig L. Laqueur, a German eye doctor born at Fürstenberg in Silesia on July 25, 1839, studied at Paris and Berlin. His medical degree came in 1860, with teaching at Berlin the same year. From 1863 to 1869 he assisted at an eye hospital in Paris. Strasburg called him in 1872 as assistant professor. Full professor of eye medicine followed there in 1877. His works treat fellow-eye disease, drug action on the eye, and the early stage of glaucoma, in French and German journals from 1869 on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lekah-dodi-come:
Lekah Dodi is the first words of the refrain of a hymn sung to welcome the Sabbath. Solomon ha-Levi Alkabiz wrote it about the mid-sixteenth century. He signed eight of its nine verses with his acrostic. Much of its wording draws on Isaiah's prophecy of Israel's return.

The hymn pictures Israel as a bride on the great Sabbath of deliverance. It is among the last Hebrew poems taken into regular worship, in both southern and northern rites. Sephardic congregations chant it to an old Moorish tune older than the words. Northern congregations use old German and Polish airs at set seasons. The entry traces those tunes and their folk roots.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-catellani-: Enrico Levi-Catellani, an Italian lawyer, was born at Padua on June 12, 1856. He studied at the university there. In 1885 he became assistant professor of international law at Padua. In 1890 he rose to full professor. He belongs to law bodies in Padua, Venice, and London. His books treat colonies and the Berlin Conference, the history of private international law, and peace as fact and as hope. He also wrote on citizenship and on Plato's doctrine of ideas.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-litthauer-issac: Issachar Bär Litthauer was a Polish-German Talmud scholar who flourished at the start of the nineteenth century. He wrote Iggeret Yissakar, a work on morals and religion cast as a letter to his son, printed in 1826. He also wrote Da'at Yissakar, notes on Rashi's commentary on the Pentateuch and the Five Megillot, printed in 1827. Both books appeared at Budapest, the first also at Lemberg. The entry gives only these brief facts and a short list of sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-low-samuel-call:
Samuel Löw, known also as Samuel Kollin or Kelin, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Talmudist born at Kolin, Bohemia, about 1720, he was the son of Nathan ha-Levi. For nearly sixty years he presided over a yeshivah at Boskowitz, Moravia. He died there on May 20, 1806.

The entry centers on his writings, above all Mahazit ha-Shekel, a large subcommentary on the Magen Abraham section of the Shulhan Aruk. That work was printed at Vienna in 1807 and 1808 and reprinted several times. Two shorter works on ritual law appeared later at Lemberg. The article also notes his son Wolf Boskowitz, who preached at his funeral. As a period reference, it preserves the publishing history of a commentary that later scholars kept reprinting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maccabees-books:
Books of the Maccabees, four works bearing one name, are surveyed in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article of 1906. Four scholars share the writing. The entry states at once that only the First Book counts as a reliable historical source. The others are treated with more caution.

The article gives the first book a close reading. It covers forty years, from Antiochus's rise in 175 to Simon's death in 135 years before Christ. Sections treat the revolt's start, the wars of Judas, and the rule of Jonathan and Simon. The style is praised as simple, terse, and modeled on the Old Testament histories. The entry argues the book was written in Hebrew, though only the Greek survives. Origen and Jerome are cited for the lost original. For readers, the piece sorts four confusing books by value and date.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-malter-henry-10:
Henry Malter, an American rabbi and scholar, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Zabno, Galicia, on March 23, 1867, he studied at Berlin and Heidelberg, taking his doctorate in 1894. He also trained for the rabbinate at Berlin's Hochschule. In 1899 he served as librarian of Berlin's Jewish community library.

The article follows his move to America. In 1900 he became professor of medieval philosophy and Arabic at Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati. Two years later he also took the pulpit of that city's Sheerith Israel congregation. His publications joined Hebrew bibliography to Arabic philosophy. He produced a Hebrew edition of Steinschneider's Jewish Literature with fresh notes. He also edited a treatise of the Arab thinker al-Gazzali, printed at Frankfort in 1896. The entry catches a Galician scholar remaking himself as an American professor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mecia-matthew-d:
Mecia de Viladestes, a Jewish mapmaker of Majorca at the opening of the fifteenth century, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Richard Gottheil. His surviving work is a chart dated 1413, once kept in the convent of Val de Cristo near Segorbe and in the encyclopedia's day held by the Bibliothèque Nationale at Paris. The map gives special prominence to the African coastal voyages of Jacme Ferrer, another Majorcan.

The entry places Mecia in the Judaeo-Catalan school of chart-makers and names his model: the chart rests on the work of Jaffuda Cresques, probable maker of the atlas of Charles V. It also records a permit of January 20, 1401, found in the Majorcan archives, allowing "the convert Macia" to land in Sicily, probably this same man. Six sheets of the chart were reproduced at Paris in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menahem-b-micha:
Menahem ben Michael was a Karaite philosopher and poet of Babylon. Kaufmann Kohler and A. Biram profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A contemporary of Saadia, he corresponded on philosophy with the Rabbanite thinker David al-Mukammas, whom he had met in Babylon. Later, poor and displaced, he wrote from Alexandria. He wrote to the Karaite community of Cairo, begging aid. Even after moving to Cairo he kept up the correspondence from a distance. He was too conscious of his poverty to approach so prominent a man directly.

In one letter, answering a reproach, he affirmed his belief both in the creation of the world and in the heavenly bodies. What survives is slight: verse rules for ritual slaughter, three poems in the Karaite prayer-book, and citations as a grammarian by later Karaite authors. The entry closes by warning against confusing him with another Menahem of Saadia's circle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-millaud-arthur-:
Albert Millaud, born in Paris in 1836, was a French journalist and playwright, the son of the press magnate Moïse Millaud. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He published a book of poems at eighteen to considerable success, an early sign of the wit that made his name.

In 1869 Millaud joined the Figaro and created the light feuilleton style the paper kept ever after, writing under the names Baron Grimm and La Bruyère. For the stage he turned out a string of sarcastic successes, many built around the actress Madame Judic, from Madame l'Archiduc in 1874 to Mam'zelle Nitouche in 1883. His own papers, the Revue de Poche and Gazette de Hollande, both failed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moscato-judah-a:
Judah Aryeh Moscato, called Leone in Italian, was a rabbi, poet, and philosopher of sixteenth-century Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Osimo near Ancona, he moved to Mantua after the Jews were expelled from the Papal States in 1554. There he studied with leading scholars and became chief rabbi in 1587.

Moscato was a child of the Renaissance, at home in the classical languages and in philosophy. His fifty-two sermons, printed as Nefuzot Yehudah in 1588, opened a new epoch in Jewish preaching. They follow the rules of rhetoric yet treat their subjects in a natural way. His Kol Yehudah, printed after his death, was the first commentary on the Cuzari of Judah ha-Levi. It has been printed with that work ever since.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-of-pavia-:
