Severity rewired metabolism step by step. The chemical distance from healthy grew steadily across the groups. Early and moderate disease centred on disturbed fatty acid handling. The severest group shifted toward pyrimidine metabolism, the chemistry of building DNA letters. That fits frantic virus replication and immune cell multiplication. One amino acid pathway stayed disturbed across nearly all stages. Fine-grained staging like this could eventually match treatments to the metabolic phase a patient is actually in.
plos-pone-0352937:
Liangliang Jiang and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One remote-sensing study of how Central Asia's vegetation withstands and recovers from drought, season by season. Western Central Asia suffers frequent spring droughts, while the Aral Sea basin gets fewer but harsher summer and autumn droughts. The team measured two qualities: resistance during drought and resilience afterward, across croplands, grasslands, forests, and sparse vegetation.

Croplands in northern Kazakhstan tended to bend but bounce back, while sparse lands downstream of the Aral Sea resisted yet recovered poorly. Rainfall and dryness of the air together drove over half of the variation in resilience. Spring vegetation was both toughest and quickest to recover, and spring also accounted for the largest share of vegetation loss. Long summer droughts hit grasslands hardest. The authors say seasonal detail like this sharpens drought planning.
plos-pone-0353137: Fan, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on safe ways to test tax-risk software. Real tax records are private, so Fan built a simulation that makes fake but realistic data. Rules check that the fake data obey set limits, and the setup can be rerun the same way each time. Shared test data of this kind let tax offices and researchers compare detection tools fairly.
plos-pone-0353237:
Yulin Li and three co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a simple blood ratio in critically ill bowel disease patients. The ratio compares hemoglobin with the spread of red cell sizes. It tracks inflammation in the body. The data covered an unusual subgroup. These were intensive care patients with bowel disease who all died within thirty days. The question was whether the ratio related to sepsis during the stay.

Patients who developed sepsis had lower ratios on arrival. Each step up in the ratio came with notably lower odds of sepsis. The pattern was steady and straight-line. The authors are candid about the limits. This hand-picked subgroup cannot speak for patients in general. They frame the result as a hypothesis about end-stage bowel disease. Future studies in broader groups should test it.
plos-pone-0353837:
Zeyu Zhang and three colleagues develop a questionnaire for gauging how ready trainee teachers in China are for artificial intelligence, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Five hundred and twenty-eight pre-service teachers answered the draft survey, which the team split into halves to discover and then confirm its structure. The finished tool has fourteen items across three themes: how well teachers understand AI, how risky they judge it, and how confident they feel academically.

Statistical checks showed the three-part structure fit well and each theme measured consistently. Trainees who had already used AI scored higher on literacy and confidence, but slightly lower on caution. Teacher educators now have a tested yardstick for a fast-moving part of training.
plos-pone-0354037:
Henry Mensah and three colleagues soak cowpea seeds in a mutation-causing chemical to breed better varieties, in this 2026 PLOS ONE experiment. Cowpea is a staple protein crop in West Africa, and creating fresh genetic variety is the first step in improving it. Seeds of one cultivar were treated at three strengths of the chemical, grown out, and scored for flowering, pod, seed, and yield traits.

Counter to expectations, germination and survival rose with the chemical dose. The lowest dose gave the best average yield, and two standout plants produced roughly double the control's harvest. Those two mutants advance to the next generation of trials, where their advantage must prove stable and heritable.
plos-pone-0354137:
Krokovsky and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, ask what happens when two mosquito-borne viruses infect the same cells. Zika, West Nile, and Mayaro viruses now overlap in parts of the world, thanks to trade, travel, and a warming climate. A mosquito or a person could carry two at once, or catch one after another.

The team infected monkey kidney cells with Zika plus West Nile, or Zika plus Mayaro, either together or one after the other. When the viruses arrived together, Zika's output fell, a pattern called interference. When Zika arrived first, it held its ground. When Zika arrived second, it was shut out. The partner viruses, by contrast, grew just as well whether Zika was present or not. Six days after infection, the team measured viral RNA and cell damage. The authors frame these dish results as a first step toward understanding double infections in real hosts.
plos-pone-0354237:
Yevusiak and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial called REST, about stopping the weight-loss drug semaglutide. The drug helps many people with obesity lose a large amount of weight and improves heart and metabolic health. Yet most people regain weight after stopping suddenly, and the health gains fade.

The trial will enroll people who have already lost at least a tenth of their body weight on the drug and whose weight has leveled off. Half will taper the dose slowly over sixteen weeks before stopping, and half will stop at once. The main measure is how much weight each group regains. Blood pressure across a full day and levels of a hunger hormone will also be tracked. The team expects that a slow taper will soften regain. Their design speaks to a common real-world problem: how to come off a drug many patients cannot take forever.
plos-pone-0354337:
Wei and colleagues, in a 2026 study, model how blue honeysuckle branches shake when a harvest machine vibrates them. Mechanical shaking can knock ripe berries loose, but the trunk and roots soak up much of the energy, weakening the force at the fruit. The team simplified a forked branch into a Y shape and wrote the equations of its motion.

Their math shows that when the branch sits at a small angle to the shaking direction, a certain shaking speed can trigger parametric resonance. That is a runaway wobble that could shake fruit free or, if uncontrolled, harm the branch. The unstable zone depends on shaking strength, speed, and branch size. Computer models of the branch and real shaking tests on branches matched the theory well. The authors offer the model as a design basis for honeysuckle harvesters that shake hard enough to pick, but not to damage.
plos-pone-0354737:
Jiafeng Zhang and co-authors compare in 2026 two Chinese made tests that count HIV virus in blood against a leading imported reference test. Counting the virus guides treatment and diagnosis, but cost and speed limit use in poorer settings. Plasma samples from several hundred infected people were run through all three tests.

Both local tests found slightly more positives than the reference and agreed with it closely on counts across virus subtypes. Small average biases stayed within a narrow range. The authors say the local tests meet needed standards while costing less and returning results faster, helping close a monitoring gap where resources are tight.
plos-pone-0354837:
Qi Liu, Yang Liu, and Yumei Zhang present a 2026 trial plan for people who lose language after a stroke. The plan tests magnetic stimulation aimed at the right side of the cerebellum, a rear brain area now linked to speech. Participants in the subacute stage would receive either real or sham stimulation alongside speech therapy.

Follow-up stretches to one year, with a standard aphasia battery as the main measure. Brain scans and a test of nonverbal thinking add detail on how any change happens. Because recruitment was still under way, the document sets out methods and hopes rather than results, and it records any side effects tied to stimulation.
plos-pone-0354937:
Abdelmuhsen Abusneina and Soad Elwirfli published a cautionary analysis in 2026 about cancer gene signatures built around the loss of a gene called PTEN. Researchers often read a tumor's pattern of gene activity as a signature of some process, here glutaminolysis, the cell's use of the amino acid glutamine. The authors show that when PTEN is deleted, neighboring genes are often deleted along with it, as passengers.

Those passenger deletions can distort the signature, making it look as if glutamine use changed when the true cause sits nearby in the genome. Their case argues for location aware signature design: checking what else a deletion drags with it. The lesson reaches beyond one gene, to any study that reads meaning into cancer's copy number changes.
plos-pone-0355437:
Xiaomin Lin and Xudong Huang examine in 2026 whether a simple index built from blood sugar and blood fat relates to early kidney damage in a very large Chinese sample. The damage sign is a raised level of a protein in urine. Tens of thousands of adults from eight centres were included, with many health factors accounted for in the models.

Higher index values linked steadily to higher odds of the urine sign, in a straight line pattern. The link held for people with and without diabetes, but was stronger where diabetes was present. Because the data are a single snapshot, the authors say follow up studies must show whether the index comes before damage.
plos-pone-0355737:
Giulia Tomasetig and seven colleagues scan the brains of professional artists as they judge their own paintings, in this 2026 study. Twenty artists rated artworks by themselves and by others inside an MRI scanner, and in a second task they mentally relived the moment they had conceived each of their pieces. The design tests whether the physical act of making art stays embedded in how its maker later experiences it.

Judging their own work, compared with others', engaged brain regions tied to action and to the emotional feel of movement. Reliving creation recruited a network involved in motor thinking. Artists who showed stronger activity in a movement-planning region during that reliving also judged their works more favorably. The authors read this as support for an embodied view: for painters, the gestures of creation remain part of the finished artwork's experience.
plos-pone-0355937:
Jianfan Zhou and colleagues test whether two simple blood-based scores can flag adults at risk of poor mental health. One score mixes blood sugar and fat measures, and the other compares two blood cell types tied to inflammation. Several hundred adults at a hospital in Shandong, China, completed a standard symptom checklist and gave fasting blood samples for both scores.

Higher values on either score tracked with higher symptom totals across most areas, including low mood, anxiety, and body complaints. Adults high on both scores fared worst. Among several machine learning models, a regularized regression sorted risk best, though modestly. Zhou and colleagues suggest routine blood scores could help flag patients who deserve a closer mental health check.
plos-pone-0356237:
Suzanne Ablard and seven colleagues evaluate community hubs designed to keep urgent-care patients out of hospital in England, in this 2026 qualitative study. The hubs help paramedics and other clinicians route people with pressing but non-emergency needs into nearby community services instead of an ambulance trip. The team interviewed twenty-one staff working in, or referring into, hubs at three locations and analyzed the conversations thematically.

Staff said the hubs genuinely improved integrated working, giving clinicians rapid access to community support for patients. But three brakes limited their impact. Fuzzy eligibility rules created a tension between easy access and consistent decisions. Ambulance services engaged unevenly. And hiring and keeping staff with the right skill mix proved hard. The authors conclude the model can simplify access and prevent needless hospital trips if referral processes, ambulance buy-in, and workforce planning are fixed.
plos-pone-0356837:
Jiyan Zhang and co-authors build a math method for picking the most useful features from data when no labels exist to guide the choice. Feature picking cuts noise and cost in machine learning, but common tools can flatten the hidden shape of a dataset. Their method uses a curvature-aware penalty to keep complex shapes intact, a compression step to drop repeated features, and a filter that resists stray outliers.

Across nine standard test datasets, the method chose feature sets that performed better than rival approaches, and the team proves their solving routine settles properly. Zhang and colleagues aim the tool at tasks such as image and gene analysis. Those datasets are wide, messy, and unlabeled. Keeping true structure matters more than raw size.
plos-pone-0357037:
Qi Zhang and colleagues used advanced eye imaging to document what near-sightedness does inside the eyes of rats, in a model where lenses placed before the eyes drive them to grow myopic. Their 2026 study scanned the animals after eight weeks with a technique that measures both tissue thickness and blood flow without contact, comparing them against normally sighted controls.

The myopic eyes were longer, as expected, but also showed thinner choroid and retinal layers and reduced blood flow in the inner retina, differences clear at most measurement points. Those three changes mirror what doctors fear in severe human myopia, where stretched, underfed tissue can tear or degenerate. The imaging markers give researchers a way to track candidate treatments in animals over time.
plos-pone-0357737:
Mina Hwang and Yeji Hwang published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on depression in people with cognitive impairment, asking whether who provides their daily care matters. Using a national sample of older adults, they analyzed just over five hundred people needing help with everyday activities. Care networks were sorted by who helped: spouses, children, extended family, friends and neighbors, paid carers, or public services.

Five network types emerged, the largest centered on children and the smallest on friends and neighbors. Compared with child-centered care, people whose networks centered on public services, and those with mixed networks, scored higher on depression, even after adjustments. Pairwise tests showed the same two types also exceeded spouse-centered and friend-centered networks. The overall shape of a care network, not just its size, relates to mental health, they conclude, so assessments should map the whole configuration.
plos-pone-0357837:
Vasileia Karasavva and Amori Yee Mikami published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a systematic review of research on short-form social media videos about autism and ADHD. Most young adults now get mental health information from social media, and neurodiversity content is hugely popular, yet professionals worry about unvetted claims spreading as fact. No one has synthesized studies of these videos' accuracy or effects on viewers.

The review will search three major databases for peer-reviewed work in English, with paired reviewers screening independently. Three questions organize it. What does this content look like, and how popular is it? How closely does it follow clinical guidelines? And what does watching it do to stigma, to seeking diagnosis or treatment, and to how people read their own symptoms??? Descriptive and thematic analyses will combine findings. The registered protocol aims to give clinicians and platforms an evidence base.
plos-pone-0358137:
Fizza Ghulam Nabi leads a team of six studying how weather drains the power of industrial gas turbines in Pakistan, in PLOS ONE in 2026. At the Nandipur plant, three large turbines ran at full load for a year while the team logged output against temperature, humidity, and dew point. Hot air is thinner, so turbines swallow less of it, and operators need forecasts that price the weather in rather than discovering shortfalls at peak demand.

Ambient temperature dominated: as it climbed, output and efficiency fell in a strong, tight relationship. Humidity and dew point mattered too, but more weakly. The team built prediction models three ways, classical regression and two machine learning methods, and validated them on operating data. Their best models give plant managers a practical tool for scheduling generation and maintenance around Pakistan's summers, and for estimating the fuel and emissions cost of each hot day.
plos-pone-0358337:
Rebecca T Brown leads a team of eight tracking when everyday abilities start to fail in middle aged Americans, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Struggling to bathe, dress, shop, or cook is rising in this age group, yet the long view is missing. The team followed more than fourteen thousand Health and Retirement Study participants, all entering between ages fifty and fifty-six without difficulties. They fall into four birth cohorts spanning 1935 to 1959.

Group based models sorted the paths that difficulty counts followed before age sixty-five. Regression then tied cohort membership to those paths. Even the starting gate told a story: the share already impaired at entry ran near fourteen percent in the earliest cohort. It sat near ten percent in the middle cohorts and twelve percent in the youngest. Whether later generations are aging worse is a policy question this machinery was built to answer.
plos-pone-0358537:
Md Mamunur Rashid leads a team of eight mapping where rice neck blast disease strikes hardest in Cumilla District, Bangladesh, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The fungal disease can shrivel the rice neck just before harvest, and Cumilla is among the country's most intensive rice regions. Using field records from 2017 to 2025, the team hunted season specific hotspots separately for the rainfed and irrigated growing seasons, with clustering statistics and interpolation methods.

One subdistrict, Nangalkot, burned as a hotspot in both seasons. Rainfed season severity there averaged roughly half the crop's potential damage range, while irrigated season peaks in several subdistricts ran higher still. Weather trends around the rice's reproductive stage tracked the intensification. Probability mapping pinpointed zones likely to exceed a fifth severity, giving extension services a target list. The prescription is local: resistant varieties and forecasts tuned to each hotspot, not a blanket national spray calendar.
plos-pone-0358737: Wu and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a plant compound and wound healing in rats. The compound, ligustroside, was tested on open wounds cut into the skin. The title reports that it softened the scar-like remodeling that fibrosis brings and quieted fibrosis signals. Wounds that heal with less scarring stay more flexible, so such compounds interest skin researchers.
plos-pone-0358837:
Anneke Olson and six colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It tackles a methods problem in research on child maltreatment: contamination bias. The question is what happens to effect estimates when studies try to replicate how maltreatment affects children's behavior problems.

Contamination occurs when comparison groups are not as unexposed as researchers assume, quietly shrinking measured effects. If replication studies inherit that bias, real harms of maltreatment can look smaller than they are. Child welfare researchers and the policymakers who read their work are the audience for a warning about hidden bias in replication.
plos-pone-0359337: Barrio and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on deaths from heart and vessel disease in a Brazilian capital. The city lies in the Central-West region. They mapped where deaths cluster, how they changed over time, and what area traits link to them. Area-level maps can show city leaders which districts need clinics, prevention, and cleaner living conditions most.
plos-pone-0359437:
Laura Vancer and seven colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It standardizes wrist X-rays by designing a positioning tool around the people who will use it, and then evaluating that tool. Where a patient's wrist sits during imaging changes what the radiograph shows, so inconsistent positioning undermines diagnosis.

Human-centered design builds the tool around the technologists and patients who will actually use it. A positioning aid that staff find awkward will be abandoned, however sound its geometry. Radiology departments and orthopedic teams reading wrist films are the readers for a tool meant to make every image comparable.
pmc-10158837:
The Gene Ontology Consortium's 2023 update describes the state of the Gene Ontology knowledgebase, a shared reference for what genes and their products do. The resource organises gene functions into a structured vocabulary used by labs worldwide. It links those terms to the evidence behind each assignment.

Updates reported for 2023 cover new terms, improved annotations and better tools for searching the base. Almost every large gene study leans on this vocabulary to make sense of gene lists. A careful annual update keeps that common language accurate as biology moves.  Users can browse it freely through the consortium's website.
pmc-10657637:
Rau and coauthors seek a brain scan mark for a fluid-linked brain illness. In this illness, fluid builds up and harms gait and thought. It can look much like Alzheimer or Parkinson disease. Right diagnosis matters, since a drain can help true cases.

They scanned brain sugar use in 11 confirmed patients. A math method drew out one shared brain pattern. Healthy adults of like age gave the contrast set. The team then scored that pattern in mixed patient groups. Groups held the illness, Alzheimer disease, and Parkinson disease. A clear score gap could help doctors sort hard cases.
pmc-10670437:
Ziyang Chen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three mouse study linking early-life separation to adult gut pain through brain mast cells. Separating newborns from mothers produced lasting visceral hypersensitivity. Whether immune mast cells in a stress hub of the brain drive that pain was unknown.

Separated mice grew into adults with lowered pain thresholds and stronger reflexes. Mast cells and stress-hormone neurons in the hypothalamus switched on together. Histamine from mast cells rose, and its receptors multiplied on the neurons. Stabilizing mast cells calmed the neurons and the pain, while histamine did the opposite, proving the chain.
pmc-10696837:
Wertheim and colleagues present a study protocol, published in 2023, for a randomized trial of EMDR therapy in irritable bowel syndrome. The trial, called EMDR4IBS, will run at a city hospital in the Netherlands.

Adults with considerable abdominal pain will be assigned to EMDR therapy or a waiting list. The protocol aims to include thirty-four participants, and the therapy arm receives seven weekly sessions of about ninety minutes. The reasoning is that unresolved traumatic and pain memories may increase abdominal pain through flashbacks and stress. Readers get the full trial design before results exist, including eligibility and treatment structure.
pmc-10699637:
Kupila and coauthors use twin pairs to split the effects of weight and genes. Weight and mood link in complex ways shaped by age, sex, and home life. Twins share genes and early home life, so twin gaps help isolate weight effects. The team studied pairs where one twin was much heavier than the other.

They drew on 74 pairs of same-egg twins and 77 pairs of fraternal twins. All took surveys on mood, stress, self-worth, and life quality. Heavier twins in same-egg pairs still showed some gaps in well-being. That hints weight itself plays a role past genes. The team weighs what those gaps mean for care.
pmc-10713137:
Liexiang Zhang and colleagues show bone marrow stem cell parcels suppress a human glioma cell line. Their study from twenty twenty-three identifies a microRNA as the active cargo. Glioma outcomes remain poor despite improving standard therapies. Stem cell based approaches offered a new angle on treatment.

Tiny vesicles from the stem cells carried the microRNA into tumour cells. Tumour cell growth slowed and death increased in the tests. Invasion through barriers also fell with the treatment. Migration assays confirmed the anti-spread effect separately. Overproducing the microRNA strengthened the vesicles' impact. Marker proteins confirmed the vesicle identity in the work. A defined molecule may replace whole-cell therapy eventually.
pmc-10725837:
Necmiye Şengel and nine co-authors test two protectors against organ harm in diabetic mice, in this twenty twenty-three study. When blood flow to a limb is cut and then restored, the liver and kidneys can be hurt by the surge. The team asked whether a carbon-based antioxidant, a common sleep gas, or both could shield those organs.

Forty-six mice were split into six groups, covering healthy, diabetic, and harmed states, with each protector alone and paired. The carbon compound was injected before the blood flow test. Tissue checks then showed how much harm each route prevented. Such work may point to ways of guarding organs during limb surgery in diabetic patients.
pmc-10737037:
Christina Mu, Alisha Thompson, Bailee Brekke, and Patricia D'Antonio set out health points for research on aging in 2023. They start from a growing older group that is more mixed than in the past. Health gaps by race and by pay still last. Black Medicare users and low pay users face higher risks of stays in care, returns to care, and urgent care visits.

Their talk looks at three linked themes: health gaps, how forms of bias overlap, and climate change. Mu tells of work on bills and of reading reports on steps to make health fair for all. The team says new work should fill gaps on health gaps and on climate change. Both will shape the health of older adults in the years ahead.
pmc-10740337:
Jinye Lu and colleagues probe a long noncoding RNA in cow udder cell inflammation. Their study from twenty twenty-three models mastitis in cell culture. Bacterial toxin triggers the inflammation in the model. The RNA called ANRIL is linked to many diseases elsewhere.

Silencing tools located and reduced the RNA in cells. Toxin treatment suppressed cell growth significantly in tests. Growth, division, and death were measured several ways. Inflammatory factors and oxidative stress markers were assayed. A central inflammation pathway, NF-kappa-B, framed the analysis. ANRIL levels shifted how cells answered the toxin. Udder inflammation costs dairy farmers heavily worldwide.
pmc-10747337:
Helgadottir and Bjornsson review sex differences in response to acid blocking drugs, in work from twenty twenty-three. Proton pump inhibitors are widely used for reflux. They raise levels of gastrin, a gut hormone, by cutting stomach acid.

Long term gastrin rise can thicken stomach lining, grow small polyps, and cause rebound acid when the drug stops, which drives overuse. Past studies found women release more gastrin on these drugs and may need distinct doses. Since women often get higher doses per body weight, they may face more overuse risk. The review urges dose care by sex and weight.
pmc-10757137:
Shogo Wada leads a team on melanoma spread to the brain in Japan. Their study from twenty twenty-three looks back at one center's cases. Brain spread of this skin cancer has a poor outlook.

New drugs have raised hopes, but may work less well in Asian folks. The team reviewed more than a decade of cases in Tokyo. Mean life span after brain spread was under eight months. Traits linked to longer life are named in the work. Rates at six months and one year are also given. The work guides care for this group.
pmc-10797237:
Grgur Salai and colleagues survey people who reported muscle twitching and migraine aura without headache after the BNT162b2 vaccine. Their 2023 web-based survey follows an earlier case report describing similar symptoms.

Eleven participants completed the survey, and ten reported muscle twitching after immunisation lasting a median of fourteen days. Half also reported migraine auras without headache. Participants named triggers such as anxiety and caffeine that changed symptom intensity. Among those later infected with SARS-CoV-2, half saw muscle symptoms intensify during illness. The authors stress that no causal relationship between vaccination and these phenomena can be inferred from the survey.
pmc-10828037:
Davide Clemente and four colleagues systematically reviewed forest therapy delivered through virtual reality for older people. Real forest visits can improve mental and physical health, but many older patients are bedridden or frail. Virtual reality could bring the forest to them. Following PRISMA guidelines, the team searched three databases plus gray literature. Only studies using virtual forest settings with participants aged sixty-five or older qualified.

Seven articles survived the screening process. That small number itself signals how young this research area is. The authors call for more work to standardize procedures that actually help. Effective virtual forest programs could support the health of older people and their caregivers. They could also cut social costs by reaching patients who cannot travel to real woodland.
pmc-10910037:
Guo, Jin, Chen, and co-authors review NF-kB, a protein system known to science for nearly forty years. When found, it was seen mainly as a switch for inflammation, the body's response to harm. Long study since then has widened that picture a great deal.

The review gathers fresh insight into the many roles this system plays across biology. It then turns to drugs that aim to block or tune it, and to what that could mean for patients. Because the system touches inflammation, immunity, and cancer, a clear summary helps both basic researchers and drug developers.
pmc-11438937:
Anna Crepaldi and eight co-authors pilot two exercise programs for kidney transplant recipients, in a two thousand twenty-four rehabilitation study. Structured exercise helps these patients, but hospital-based programs are hard for many to reach.

Seventeen recipients chose their program: nine took low-intensity interval walking at home, eight took supervised gym training mixing aerobic and resistance work; two gym participants later dropped out. After six months the home walkers improved their six-minute walking distance far more, though they had started older and weaker. Oxygen capacity improved significantly in both groups. The authors suggest home walking as a practical option for frailer recipients, with gym training as the fuller alternative.
pmc-11545937: Isabel Lara and Josep Puche Fontanilles give an overview of a special issue of a journal, titled Biochemical and Molecular Approaches to Postharvest Research, from 2024. The piece sets out the issue as a whole, in place of a report on one test or one set of data. Its theme is postharvest research through biochemistry and molecular methods. Readers can use the overview as a first step in, as it frames the theme of the collection, how wide it runs, and its place in postharvest science publishing.
pmc-11567837:
Francesco Paolo Panei and six colleagues published a computational study in two thousand twenty-four on predicting how tightly RNA strands bind a disease protein. TDP-43 clumps in several neurodegenerative diseases, including ALS. RNA aptamers that grip it could block that clumping, but measuring each candidate is slow.

The team designed aptamers computationally, docked them onto the protein, and simulated the complexes' motion. They hypothesised that interface residues moving in sync signals stable binding. Across six RNA molecules, that synchrony score correlated strongly, about zero point nine, with measured binding strength. The authors propose motion covariance as a cheap screening metric. The method could speed aptamer hunts for other targets too.
pmc-11585737:
Qi Qin and his team test a good germ and the goods it leaves behind for help with stiff, sore joints in mice. Their 2024 study looks at Lactiplantibacillus plantarum strain BX sixty-two as a fresh way to treat the ill.

Lab tests first showed the strain could stand acid, could stand bile salts, and could stick to gut walls. Live germs then cut joint scores, cut paw swell, and cut leak through the gut in mice with the joint ill. Dead germs and the broth they grew in helped too. They cut harm to joints, change in the gut, self-aimed blood goods, off-track cell-talk goods, and stress from air-based harm. Gene-based checks showed the mix of germs in the gut shift back toward the sound mix seen in plain mice once the mice were treated.
pmc-11593337:
María Beatriz Álvarez Flores and co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-four on a flow probe that may speed the diagnosis of a fast, lethal leukemia. The probe, FLAER, binds a cell anchor that some blood cells lack. In one leukemia kind, the sick cells must be found in hours to dodge clot or bleed deaths. Their cells showed no or weak probe binding. Healthy core cells bound it strong.

The team read the probe across dozens of blood cancers and healthy marrows. The weak signal in the fast leukemia held in all cases. It ran lower than in kin cancers too. In follow up, the probe's return to normal matched clean checks for left over disease. Its loss flagged relapse.
pmc-11593737:
Ana Torres and a large team track COVID-19 among healthcare workers in a Brazilian primary care unit. Their cohort study from twenty twenty-four spans before and after vaccination. Health workers face higher infection risk than the general public. Watching infection patterns helps protect staff and patients alike.

The unit serves a disadvantaged community in the Federal District. Workers gave interviews and samples across eight months in twenty twenty-one. Swabs tested workers showing flu-like symptoms for the virus. Blood samples every month checked vaccine-driven antibody conversion. Infection and reinfection rates were tracked through the rollout. The study shows how vaccination changed worker risk over time in a frontline setting.
pmc-11602437: Hiromasa Tanino, Ryo Mitsutake, and Hiroshi Ito report a fractured artificial hip liner in a single patient after total hip replacement surgery. The liner was made from vitamin E-blended, highly crosslinked polyethylene, and the authors present theirs as the first such case report. After dislocation, a fracture fragment became lodged between the joint surfaces. That interposed fragment blocked successful reduction of the joint. The case warns clinicians to consider liner fracture when a replaced hip will not reduce after dislocation.
pmc-11602537:
Leonardo Volpato, Evan Wright, and Francisco Gomez fly drones over bean fields in this two thousand twenty-four phenotyping study. Breeders track dry bean maturity, stand count, and plant height by hand. The authors tested whether RGB drone imagery with deep learning could speed it. A hybrid convolutional and recurrent network estimated relative maturity from image time series. A Faster R-CNN detector counted early-stage plants, and height came from surface models and point clouds via a quantile method.

The maturity model proved highly accurate across conditions and beat traditional image preprocessing, improving when growing degree days were added under stress conditions. The detector identified young plants more accurately and consistently than manual methods across flight altitudes. Height estimates correlated moderately with ground truth from both sources, with the better one depending on conditions. The authors present drone phenotyping as higher-throughput, cheaper measurement for breeding trials.
pmc-11603237:
Feng Shan and ten colleagues published a physics study in two thousand twenty-four on gold nanoparticles sitting on metal mirrors. Tiny metal particles concentrate light into hot spots, boosting sensing and light-based tools. The gap between particle and mirror is where the action concentrates.

Using computer simulation, the team compared gold ellipsoids standing upright versus lying flat on the mirror. Both formed hot spots under the right light. The flat orientation produced a far stronger local electric field, over ninety-four hundred volts per metre, against twenty-two hundred for upright. The authors say the coupling design could serve plasmonics, sensors, and light control. Orientation, they show, is a powerful tuning knob.
pmc-11612437:
Chunxiao Dang and his team test for cause links between inflammation and cancers in women. Their gene study from twenty twenty-four uses Mendelian randomization. Cervical, ovarian, and womb cancers all give inflammation a part. If inflammation in fact causes these cancers was not settled.

Public gene banks gave the study its tools for the tests. Scores of blood-borne inflammation factors were tested at one time. Bayesian methods made the cause calls more exact. One growth factor tied to one cancer kind, and four factors tied to a second kind. Checks of trust probed pleiotropy and which way each effect ran. Gene proof helps rank which inflammation paths drugs should hit first.
pmc-11613337:
Cheng Xue, Chenchen Zhou, and Zhiguo Mao wrote a letter to the editor in twenty twenty-four about minimal change disease, a leading cause of nephrotic syndrome in children. For decades the cause was debated, with most suspicion falling on T cell problems. The letter discusses a recent study that found autoantibodies against nephrin, a key protein in the kidney filter, in patients with this disease and related conditions. Antibody levels tracked with how active the disease was.

The writers argue that the finding reframes the disease as driven by antigen and antibody complexes, which also explains why treatments that deplete B cells help. They puzzle over why such complexes are not seen in kidney tissue, suggesting that severe damage to the filter may prevent them from being retained. A mouse model copying the disease strengthens the case, and they see antibody tests and targeted treatments as promising next steps.
pmc-11613937:
Mai Sherif Hafez, Carolin Sherif Mounir, and Laila Othman El Zeini published a statistics study in two thousand twenty-four on domestic violence in Egypt. Both violence and its cost are layered ideas that no single question can measure. Past Egyptian work relied on simple counts.

The team built a latent trait model from a national two thousand fifteen survey on the cost of gender-based violence. Thirty-five observed items fed measures of violence and of its cost. Psychological abuse weighed as heavily as physical abuse in the violence measure. Cost combined lost quality of life with money losses for women and children. Ages, schooling, and the husband's job all shifted violence levels in the model.
pmc-11617537:
Lan Huang and six co-authors review the two-way talk between mouth microbes, gut microbes, and breast cancer, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Breast cancer is a varied disease and a major public health burden. Microbe communities are now known to sway many parts of health, and the mouth-gut link has been tied to colon cancer through immune and inflammation paths.

Whether the same axis shapes breast cancer is far less studied. The review gathers the latest ideas on how mouth and gut microbes may affect each other in this disease. It weighs their possible roles in tumor growth, response to treatment, and patient outcomes. The authors frame microbe ecology as a fresh angle that could open a breakthrough in breast cancer research.
pmc-11639937:
Enrique Almanza-Aguilera and co-authors looked for blood markers of diet that foretell prostate cancer, in twenty twenty-four. The team drew on a large European cohort study of cancer and nutrition. Plasma samples from eight hundred fifty-one matched pairs of cases and controls were profiled for a wide panel of metabolites, and links to cancer risk were tested, overall and by tumor type.

Thirty-one metabolites showed links to risk, most of them traces of food intake or gut microbe activity. None of the links held up once the many tests were corrected for. The strongest single leads were a raised risk of advanced cancer with one compound and a lowered risk of fatal cancer with another. The authors say the leads hint at early metabolic shifts and diet traces, but larger studies must confirm them before any use.
pmc-11640437:
Anestis Tsitsos and co-authors published a meat science study in twenty twenty-four on feeding oregano oil to Holstein bulls. Dairy-breed calves are usually an afterthought for beef, yet careful feeding might make their meat a quality product. The team asked whether the aromatic oil improves the meat itself.

Fifty bulls around a year old were split into two groups for ninety days: plain feed, or feed carrying oregano oil. The supplemented beef kept better color and formed far less malondialdehyde, a marker of fat oxidation. Tasters scored its flavor and color higher, and the meat carried more of several amino acids. The oil looks like a simple route to better dairy-beef.
pmc-11644037:
Rey Jalbuena and three colleagues improve estimates of near-surface air temperature from satellite data, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Air temperature drives urban heat and climate analysis. Satellites measure surface temperature well, but converting it to air temperature is error-prone.

Earlier methods largely ignored season and time of day. The authors built an ensemble that treats them explicitly. Weather station data from 147 South Korean sites across two thousand twenty-two trained the models. Random forest regressions were fitted separately per season. Thirteen candidate variables, led by land surface temperature, were ranked for importance. Seasonal tailoring sharpened accuracy. City heat studies stand to gain from better temperature maps.
pmc-11649337:
Adrian Cookson and eight colleagues catalog the Campylobacter bacteria living in three New Zealand freshwater catchments shaped by farming and towns. Genome sequencing of one hundred isolates found the familiar food-poisoning species jejuni and coli, plus two entirely novel lineages making up eleven percent of samples.

Some jejuni types matched human, cattle, and environmental sources, and swapping of toxin genes between strains was evident. Resistance genes were scarce. The data suggest two kinds of waterborne Campylobacter: persistent strains shed by waterbirds, and new environmental species apparently not linked to human illness. Telling them apart matters for honest water-quality risk assessment, the authors argue.
pmc-11666637:
Justyna Borowiec, Monika Papież, and Sławomir Śmiech published a 2024 study of environmental rules and carbon emissions. They compared countries at high, medium, and low emission levels. Two accounting methods tracked the emissions carefully. One counted production at home. The other counted consumption, including imports.

Stricter policy generally meant lower emissions per person. Effects were stronger for production-based counts. Low-emission countries responded most to tightened rules. Market-based tools worked best overall. Combining market and non-market tools helped clean countries further. The results suggest policy mixes should match national starting points.
pmc-11668637:
Xiaowei Qin and others studied antiviral control in mandarin fish in 2024. STING protein switches on interferon guard duty. Too much interferon harms the host though. A regulator protein tags STING for disposal. Mammal work showed one tagging site. Fish ways were still unknown here.

The fish protein used two new sites. Tagging sent STING to the proteasome. Virus-fighting action weakened after that clearing. Interferon signals fell as a result. The pathway is held down overall. Findings clarify fish immune control. Fish farming disease work may benefit later. Further teleost research is invited.
pmc-11668737:
Daza Prieto and co-authors read gene spread in gut germs from Montenegro foods. The germ, E. faecium, lives in soil, men, and beast webs alike. It helps make old foods, like brine cheese and dry meats. Yet drug-proof strains of it pose a world health threat. That threat keeps its clan off the safe list for foods. Kin germ E. lactis joins the read set in the work.

In sum, 39 of the first germ and five of the kin came out. Bits came from craft cheese and dry meats of 21 makers. A set world way, ISO 15214, drove the germ pulls. Full gene reads ran on all pulls in the lab work. Core gene type reads showed high spread cross the pulls. Drug hold genes rode in the pulls in those reads.
pmc-11672637:
Seongyeon Lee and colleagues published a drug chemistry study in two thousand twenty-four on reviving an antibiotic against a stubborn germ. The germ Pseudomonas aeruginosa can destroy many antibiotics with enzymes and pump others out. The drug aztreonam fails when both defences run at once.

Earlier plant-based compounds blocked both defences but only at near-toxic doses. The team reasoned that a more water-friendly tweak would let the blocker gather where the defences sit. Their new compound blocked the enzyme and the pump together. Paired with aztreonam at modest doses, it stopped most resistant strains tested. Kill curves over time backed the pairing. The authors present it as a lead for further drug design.
pmc-11672837:
Patricia Osta-Ustarroz and colleagues review the microbial city living inside the modern washing machine, in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Bacteria colonize the machine's metal, plastic, and rubber, and ride the fabrics themselves, building biofilms that shrug off detergent. The visible result is fouling; the smellable one is malodour, microbes exhaling into clean laundry.

The review connects the biology to our changing habits. Consumers wash cooler, quicker, and greener, and detergents have evolved under environmental pressure, both trends plausibly letting more microbes survive the cycle. Sweat, skin flakes, and soil feed the residents between washes. The authors argue that the next detergent generation must be designed against biofilm reality, sustainable and antimicrobial at once, informed by how organisms actually live in these warm, wet, complex machines.
pmc-11675437:
Xiangyun Zhu and colleagues assemble and annotate the genome of the endangered red-wing fish at chromosome level. Their 2024 study concerns a Yunnan species endemic to Chenghai Lake whose wild numbers fell sharply after alien fish invaded.

Long-read sequencing and chromosome contact methods produced a genome of about one billion bases. Assembled pieces were anchored into twenty-four chromosomes, with high gene coverage completeness. Roughly half the genome consisted of repeat sequences, and over thirty thousand protein-coding genes were identified. Artificial breeding of the fish has succeeded locally. The genome provides essential data for evolution and conservation research on the species and its genus.
pmc-11675737:
Xiangqin Xu and five colleagues sequence soil microbes after fumigation plus a feed of herbal medicine waste, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Chemical fumigation holds soil diseases down in the field. But it wrecks the microbial communities. Farmers as a rule follow it with organic fertilizer; Chinese medicine residue is a quality one.

Five fertilization treatments were set side by side. The soil was that around continuously cropped peppers. Metagenomics tracked diversity in the samples. It also tracked keystone species and functional genes in the soil. Fumigation followed by the residue raised rhizosphere nutrient content by a marked amount. It also raised the available nitrogen in the ground. To rebuild a helpful microbiome after the soil has been sterilized is the agronomic puzzle. Waste from medicine production has become the material for that rebuild. That gives the study a satisfying circularity for growers with tired soils.
pmc-11675937:
Rhondene Wint and Michael Cleary read how carrier RNA counts are tuned as fly brain cells split to nerve cells. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Nerve birth needs a wide shift in gene use, and these small carriers fine tune the protein yield. Counts were taped in first-cell bent and nerve bent fly brains and set with chain death and full gene reads.

Counts held flat in whole, but ten genes and eight code-key packs split true. Counts tied to how codes steer chain death in both cell kinds, though not in full. Count shifts backed the move from growth to split in code use.
pmc-11676737:
Madeline Schwarz and four co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-four on tests for a deep lung fungus infection that preys on weak immune systems. Death rates in this illness are huge, and slow diagnosis is a chief cause. Early finds cut deaths by a wide share. The team tours the lab and scan tools in use, from culture and PCR to flow tests and mass spectra.

Each tool gets a frank grade: what it does well, and where it lags. Speed and sensitivity, in the lab sense and the clinic sense, are the axes. The call is for faster, keener tests that can flag the infection in days, not weeks.
pmc-11680237:
Rita Carmona and colleagues traced non-polio enteroviruses in São Paulo, Brazil, across twenty-one years in a 2024 study. With wild poliovirus nearly gone worldwide, other enteroviruses that can also cause acute flaccid paralysis need closer attention. Stool samples from children under fifteen in the paralysis surveillance programme were the source material.

More than fifteen hundred children sampled between the early two thousands and the early twenty twenties were covered. One virus group, species B, made up the largest share, followed by species A and then C. Thirty-one distinct types were found, and one type was recorded in Brazil for the first time. Genotyping, the authors argue, keeps paralysis cases correctly classified.
pmc-11689837:
Sara Moorman and Saber Khani asked whether what students study in high school is linked to thinking skills late in life. Their paper, published in twenty twenty-four, follows Americans who attended high school around nineteen sixty and were tested again near age seventy-five. The team looked at whether students took a college preparatory track and how many semesters of math and science they completed. They accounted for early ability, grades, family background, and school traits.

Students who took harder tracks and more math and science showed better word recall and verbal fluency in old age. Much of that link ran through later schooling: those students earned higher degrees, and higher degrees tracked with better late-life cognition. The authors suggest that the content of high school courses, not just years spent in school, may help protect the aging mind.
pmc-11889437:
Hajar Arfaoui and eight co-authors present a case report from twenty twenty-four on a collapsed lung that hid a rare airway tumor. Links between a sudden lung collapse and a bronchial tumor are rare, and rarer still with this tumor kind. The patient was a woman in her early fifties with a long past of secondhand smoke. She had been treated for thyroid, lung, and heart ills in past years.

She came to emergency care with a left lung collapse out of the blue. Scans and a scope of the airways found an atypical carcinoid tumor as the cause. The left lung was removed, with follow up after. The team urges doctors to hunt the cause of such collapses with a scope.
pmc-11897737:
Mineyuki Yokoyama and colleagues tested a plant growth signal in 2024. The signal is a fat-derived molecule called KODA in short. Plants make it from the same starting fat as jasmonic acid. Its effects differ from that hormone. Past work linked it to flowering and rooting. The team grew young white poplar shoots in glass culture. Paired shoots were cut from the same parent growth. One shoot was dipped in the signal solution. The twin shoot got water instead.

A month later, treated plants grew more strongly. Roots grew much longer than in controls. Leaf growth drove most of the above-ground gain. Certain stem segments stretched longer after treatment. Total segment counts stayed the same, though. The authors read the effect as system-wide growth activation. Young tissues in roots, stems, and leaves all responded. The signal seems to boost growth quality rather than part counts.
pmc-11905937:
Hui Guo and eight colleagues show that a gene switch slows breast cancer by cutting its blood supply, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Growth of new vessels feeds tumors. The vessel growth factor VEGF drives that supply. The team hunted for changes in the gene's control region.

A short deletion in that region turned up often in patients. The deletion wipes out the docking site for the switch protein, GABPα. That protein is scarce in breast tumors. Raising it slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and vessel building. It also sped cancer cell death. Mouse tests matched the dish results both ways. The switch acts as a brake on the tumor's plumbing.
pmc-12662137:
Almouwlid and co-authors catalog Gram-negative bacteria in ICU chest infections in Saudi Arabia. Hospital pneumonia is a lead cause of ICU illness and death. The team reviewed 271 isolates from 2020 to 2022. Samples were sputum, tracheal aspirates, and throat swabs. Sputum gave 46 percent of the isolates.

Sex split was near even across the patient set. Resistance classes covered multi, extensive, and pan-resistant grades. Local resistance data guide first drug choice in such units. The authors say their map aids stewardship work. Species and drug patterns are charted per sample type.
pmc-12663337:
Quintana-Quintana and coauthors build a shared data set on breast cancer return. Cancer spread ends the lives of many breast patients. Most spread occurs years after the first diagnosis. Teams need early marks of who faces high return risk.

The new data set is the first open set of its kind. It holds 47 whole-slide tissue images from patients. It also holds 677 light spectrum images of the same tissue. Clinical facts on return join the image files. Mixed data may train tools that guess return risk. Such tools could guide closer checks for high-risk patients.
pmc-12696137:
Rodrigo G Dias and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five study on boosting a natural germ-killing compound. Streptococcus equinus HC5 makes bovicin HC5, which slows harmful and spoilage microbes. Low output has limited its use.

The team first found the strain grows best at a warm temperature and stops above a higher one. They then evolved it for hundreds of generations under heat stress. Two resulting variants made much more bovicin, up to well over double. The best variant also grew faster and resisted heat better. Food and feed researchers get a route to hardier producer strains.
pmc-12700737:
Rinrada Worapongpaiboon and three co-authors report a rare stomach finding in this twenty twenty-five case paper. A woman in her early seventies, checked for long-term reflux, was found to have a lump under the stomach lining. The lump turned out to be pancreas tissue growing in the wrong place.

Such misplaced tissue is usually harmless. Here it held a cyst-like growth of a type that can turn into cancer, with some cells already far changed. Doctors removed the lump in full through a scope. The case warns that even rare misplaced tissue needs care and follow-up checks.
pmc-12706037:
Jieyi He and eleven colleagues test a phone app for preventing injuries among rural Chinese preschoolers, in a trial report from twenty twenty-five. Unintentional injury burdens young children in resource-limited areas. Twenty-four preschools joined a twelve-month cluster trial. Nearly four thousand children and caregivers enrolled.

Preschools were randomized to injury-prevention app education or general app content. Injury incidence fell significantly in the intervention group. Caregiver safety attitudes improved as well. Supervision behaviors and home environment scores also rose. About eighty-seven percent of participants finished the study. The authors say the app could spread widely across China. It could also adapt to other low-resource settings.
pmc-12706237:
Swastika Poudel and six colleagues measured financial catastrophe among dialysis patients in Kathmandu, Nepal. Even where dialysis itself is free, travel, medicines, and lost work can crush household budgets. The study covered patients treated under the government's Deprived Citizen Support Programme. One hundred twenty patients on regular haemodialysis for at least six months answered interviews. Nine patients joined a qualitative strand in twenty twenty-five.

Financial catastrophe meant health payments eating at least forty percent of a household's disposable income, following the World Health Organization definition. The team assessed how common catastrophe was despite free treatment. They also asked patients how effective they found the government support. Mixed methods let numbers on hardship sit beside patients' own accounts. The findings can guide better financial protection for kidney patients.
pmc-12707237:
Haiqing Xie, Xueting Deng, and Quanpeng Li review a cell death type in bowel cancer. Their review from twenty twenty-five deals with pyroptosis. Bowel cancer is a top cause of cancer death world wide.

This death type bursts cells through pores cut by enzymes. It can start through a few distinct paths in the cell. Some sensor groups link it to finds and outlook in cancer. The team sets out how each path works in detail. They also weigh how it could shape new cures. Old cures leave much room to do better.
pmc-12712737:
Kalyani Parvathy and colleagues reported two unusual patients in 2025 whose recurring fevers turned out to be a children's syndrome appearing in adults. PFAPA brings periodic fever with mouth sores, a sore throat, and swollen neck glands, and it is usually diagnosed in young children. The two patients, a woman of twenty-four and a man of twenty-eight, reached a tertiary care center in India after repeated episodes.

Both were diagnosed clinically and responded well to corticosteroid treatment. The authors warn that adult PFAPA is under-recognized because recurrent fever in adults usually triggers hunts for chronic infection. That hunt often means repeated antibiotics that were never needed. Adding PFAPA and similar auto-inflammatory syndromes to the adult differential can spare patients pointless antimicrobial courses. The paper frames the cases as a lesson in antimicrobial stewardship.
pmc-12723037:
Junsha An and six co-authors review the drug-like works of the glue proteins of mussels, and where they may serve. Their review is from two thousand twenty-five.

These proteins let the shell fish grip rocks and hulls in harsh seas. They are rich in a rare build block that does the grip. That grip draws the health field: wound heal, drug loads, frame builds for flesh, and skin care. Made-by-gene forms add more gifts: they fight rust-like cell harm, calm flare, kill germs, and shield cells. Snags stay: how to make them at scale, curb harm, and grip well under water. Gene craft and protein design push past them.
pmc-12729937:
Erika Rask and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five retrospective study of strangles, a horse disease, on one farm. A new horse arrived the same day most resident horses got their first vaccine dose. An outbreak followed soon after.

Blood tests tracked exposure to the bacterium that causes strangles. One vaccinated horse later tested positive and showed cough, fever, and nasal discharge. Two other horses ran fevers. The case shows how timing of arrival, exposure, and vaccination can overlap awkwardly. Horse owners and vets get a real farm example for planning quarantine and vaccination schedules.
pmc-12743837:
Do and coauthors check if a web quit-smoking program reaches rural smokers fairly. The free program has served United States smokers for years. Rural smokers face more blocks to quit aids than city smokers. Fair reach by place is key to fair health gains.

User zip codes were mapped to rural and urban classes. Reach rates compared program share to national smoker share. National survey data from 2018 to 2020 gave those shares. Trend tools checked reach shifts from 2013 to 2020. Rural non-metro users were under-served in the set. The team urges outreach tuned for rural smokers.
pmc-12747437:
Christopher Bohrer and Daniel Larson give a post fix way to cut place error in multi-spot scope reads of genome sites. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Spot scope ways map many DNA sites in fixed cells, but place error can cloud true spots. Their way, LEAR, uses the fact that error puffs the spread of gaps twixt sites.

With a gauge of that error, true spread can be got back and spots nudged right step by step. Games and lab tests proved the fix. On past data for a key gene, LEAR found a link twixt booster closeness and gene bursts that error had hid. Loop pull shifts in multi-way meets also came clear.
pmc-12750737:
Tinland, Haddadi, and Dann study the ethics of a watch-and-wait leukemia diagnosis. Stage A chronic lymphocytic leukemia often shows no harsh symptoms. No treatment starts at once for these patients. Instead, doctors track the disease for signs of decline. About half will never need treatment at all.

The team built a survey with a French patient association. It held 46 questions on diagnosis, follow-up, and support. Replies came from 235 patients, 46 percent of them women. Mean age was 66 years. Results probe how a cancer label can weigh more than the disease itself.
pmc-12785137:
Daci Fu and colleagues fed a protected supplement to beef cattle in 2025. The supplement is beta-alanine, shielded so the rumen cannot break it down. Beta-alanine is known to raise nitrogen use in cattle. Its growth effects were less clear. The team used thirty-six young Simmental crossbred bulls. Half ate a plain diet, and half got the daily supplement. The trial ran five weeks, including one week to adjust. Weight, digestion, rumen microbes, and blood chemistry were all checked.

Treated cattle tended to gain faster each day. They digested protein better and needed less feed per gain. Those edges fell just short of firm statistical proof. Rumen microbes shifted toward helpful groups, raising acid output and nitrogen use. Treated cattle showed better antioxidant capacity and lower inflammation signals. Harmful microbe groups and their byproducts fell. The authors credit better energy supply and calmer body stress.
pmc-12822337:
Burhan Dost and seven co-authors review a newer family of pain blocks that numb the chest wall without threading needles near the spinal cord. Surgery on the breast, chest, or heart leaves severe, mixed pain that slows breathing and recovery. Epidural and paravertebral blocks work but are technically demanding and riskier.

Ultrasound-guided fascial plane blocks instead flood the tissue layers where nerves travel. The review covers the interpectoral, pectoserratus, serratus anterior, erector spinae, and parasternal techniques, explaining anatomy and mechanism for each. Across breast, thoracic, and cardiac operations their pain relief often matched conventional methods, with a friendlier safety profile and possible opioid sparing. The authors close by calling for stronger trials.
pmc-12830837:
Lloyd Hopkins and a large team hunt genetic variants behind learning and memory differences. Their genome-wide study from twenty twenty-five uses a deeply tested healthy cohort. Memory ability is heritable yet varies widely between people. Most genetic signals found so far explain little individually.

Six hundred thirteen unrelated adults took twenty-one cognitive tests. Scores merged into combined measures through statistical reduction. Genome scanning then searched for associated variants. New signals landed in smell-related gene pathways. Vitamin A and vitamin B pathways appeared as well. Cell-adhesion cadherin genes also carried associations. Unexpected pathways may hold real cognitive biology worth following.
pmc-12836937:
Hao Fan and three co-authors test an artificial intelligence teaching helper in anesthesia training, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. Anesthesia packs a huge body of knowledge into a small slice of medical school. Lectures alone struggle to meet each learner's needs or check what stuck.

The trial split forty-eight learners, half medical students and half resident doctors from other fields, into two groups. One group got standard teaching only. The other also got round-the-clock help from a helper built on the DeepSeek system, with tailored study plans and live feedback on performance. That group scored higher on the theory test right after the course. A month later, the edge had faded. Students in the helper group also reported stronger engagement and faster answers.
pmc-12849537:
Seila Llorente-Pulido, Estefanía Custodio, and Laura Otero-García report a two thousand twenty-five longitudinal study of exclusive breastfeeding on Tenerife, Spain. Spain's six-month exclusive rate sits below the world target for two thousand thirty. The team followed pregnant women to find what helps or hinders.

Over eighty women were tracked from pregnancy through six months after birth. Check-ins happened at several set points. Pacifier use in hospital and in the first weeks strongly cut exclusive breastfeeding. Women's gynaecological problems also hindered it. Midwives get clear, early warning signs to support mothers who want to breastfeed exclusively.
pmc-12872737:
Li, Ling, and Yang study how iron helps sugarcane seedlings recover from manganese poisoning. Too much manganese in acid soils turns seedlings yellow and stalls growth. Fields often green up again with the seasons, but the cause was unclear. The team tracked 78 field sites and followed recovery over time. They also ran water-culture and field trials with added iron.

Leaf green color tracked closely with leaf iron levels, with a strong statistical link. Excess manganese cut a key pigment gene's activity by 60%. Iron treatment restored enzymes that build green pigment. Sprays of iron sulfate on leaves eased the yellowing. The work supports iron sprays as a cheap fix for affected cane fields.
pmc-13171037:
Jeong-Yoon Lee and a large team of colleagues report a 2026 study of clot-removal treatment for a blocked artery at the base of the brain. Two major trials had shown the treatment works, but only in tightly picked patients. The team asked how it performs in everyday care, using a nationwide stroke registry.

Of more than forty-nine thousand stroke patients, about one thousand had this blockage. Most of them, nearly three quarters, would not have qualified for either trial. Treatment rates were highest in those who matched trial rules. Still, treated patients died less often at three months, even among those the trials would have excluded. Bleeding rates did not differ between groups. The authors argue the strict trial rules shut out many patients who could gain from treatment.
pmc-13182337:
Clarissa Sagi and her team put out the plan for a trial that puts a hub for care of old folk in knife care at a sick bay in Australia. Their 2026 BOOST plan tests if care led by a doc for old folk lifts ends for old sick folk.

Old sick folk stay in care for long spans and face risk of lost work skill and side ills. The trial spans rush and picked knife work in broad care, pee care, and blood path care, and looks for more than two thousand sick folk through two years. The hub checks old sick folk in full, step-first and through their stay. Checks take in sick bay ends with span of stay at the top. They run through three spans of six months: prior to, in the midst of, and in the wake of roll-out.
pmc-13186237:
Hyeonji Kim and a team of co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on dosing a myeloma drug in patients whose kidneys work poorly. The drug, lenalidomide, leaves the body through the kidneys, so dose must fall as kidney work falls. Thirty patients gave blood samples at steady state. Both total drug and free drug in blood were read.

A two room model with plain protein binding fit both read kinds. Free drug clearance rose with kidney score and body size. Fake patient runs test dose plans against the mark set by healthy kidneys. Label doses mostly hold, but body size tweaks sharpen the aim: cuts for small frames, hikes for large ones.
pmc-13202437:
A natural cyclic peptide is re-engineered for cancer in a 2026 study authored by Yujun Bao, which modifies Sansalvamide A by flipping one amino acid into its mirror-image form. The research article uses a light-driven cyclization method to build five analogs with a rigid isoindolinone unit built into the ring.

Cell tests showed the analogs inhibited tumor cell growth to varying degrees, with the multiply modified compound performing best among them. Target prediction and docking pointed to BCL2, a protein that helps cancer cells avoid death, as the key partner. Further cell assays showed the lead compound lowered mitochondrial membrane potential, consistent with triggering apoptosis, and predicted drug properties looked workable.
pmc-13208237:
Javedh Shareef, Sathvik Sridhar, Sanah Hasan, and Mohammed Karattuthodi test how well three drug databases agree on risky drug pairs. Patients on blood thinners often take many drugs at once, so clashes are a real risk. The team ran 130 real prescriptions from a hospital in the United Arab Emirates through three widely used databases. The tools flagged more than three thousand possible clashes.

Only 107 pairs showed up in all three tools. The databases also split on how severe each clash was and what to do about it, though two agreed more on proof strength. The paper warns that the choice of tool can shape care.
pmc-13211137:
Juan Valdiviezo-Campos and his team test the calm and mood-lift acts of a herb from the Andes used in old care for nerve ills in Peru. Their 2026 study joins beast tests with screen dock builds and a chem set-out of the herb.

The scent oil of the herb held fifteen named goods that fly off in air. Two known scent bits led that set. Its water draw showed mid strength to fight air harm and a phenol share that could be gauged. In beast tests, the oil made beasts roam more in the open arms of a maze. That roam is a stock sign of low fear. It cut still time in a stress swim test by more than a third. That cut was less than with stock drugs used as a check. Dock work showed good binds of herb goods to brain marks that count here.
pmc-13212937:
Magnus Reulbach and colleagues test in 2026 a gentler way to rescue loosened artificial hip stems without the destructive cement removal that revision surgery usually demands. Heating the metal stem should soften the surrounding plastic cement enough to lock the stem back in place.

Three simple metal samples were cemented, loosened, then reheated by induction to 95 degrees and pressed with a set force. Fresh fixation resisted pulling out far more strongly than loosened fixation did. Refixation barely improved average pull-out strength, though one sample fully recovered. Sounds emitted during twisting loads added another check on grip. The concept shows promise, the authors say, but needs testing in models closer to real hips.
pmc-13215437:
Anita Fjærestad and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study of anger among parents who lost children in the 2011 Utøya terror attack in Norway. Anger is a common grief response that research often overlooks.

Twenty-two bereaved parents were interviewed nine years after the attack, and their accounts fell into three patterns. Some felt no anger at all, some treated anger as a natural part of grieving, and some found anger complicated and hard to carry. Anger aimed at oneself stood out as a sign of deeper distress. The authors suggest that Norway's collective response, which stressed love over anger, may have shaped what parents felt allowed to express.
pmc-13216137:
Andrew Wang and co-authors present a 2026 resource paper rating how useful it is to know more than 80,000 English words and multiword expressions. The idea, borrowed from economics, is that people keep words that pay off and drop words that do not.

Participants judged usefulness through best-worst comparisons, and raters agreed strongly with one another. Words scored as more useful tended to be frequent, widely known, learned early, and central in the meaning network, while abstract words outscored concrete ones. Usefulness predicted which words first- and second-language speakers actually know, though not how fast known words are recognized. The full ratings are released freely for research and teaching.
pmc-13218937:
Sina C. Rosenkranz and a team show that the exercise hormone irisin protects tissue in a model of multiple sclerosis, in a 2026 study. Exercise is one of the few interventions known to slow decline in multiple sclerosis, but the molecules carrying that benefit were unknown. Irisin, released from muscle during activity, was a candidate.

Mice with the experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis model of the disease ran on wheels and were protected against nerve damage, yet mice unable to make irisin lost protection. Injecting irisin raised its blood levels and reduced clinical symptoms and neuron loss in animals. The hormone did not change immune responses in the body or the nervous system. Instead it switched on a protective gene program inside spinal cord neurons, preserved their synapses and energy production, and appeared to bind motor neurons directly. They propose irisin, or a drug mimicking it, as a therapy for multiple sclerosis.
pmc-13220337:
Takuma Yokosawa and colleagues discover a memory effect working backwards in yeast regulation in a 2026 study. Genes tucked in heterochromatin, the genome's packed silent zones, are easier to switch on a second time once opened. The team tracked one gene, IMD2, which sits near a chromosome end and wakes when cells run low on GTP, a fuel and building block.

Using single-cell tracking, they watched the region around IMD2 flicker open and shut as GTP fell. Population looked uniform, but histories diverged: cells that had expressed IMD2 before the shortage were less likely to fluctuate and re-induce it. A first expression made the region more resistant to reactivation, the opposite of the expectation that experience loosens chromatin. They call this expression memory, and tie it to cell-to-cell differences in heterochromatin structure. The result reframes cellular memory as able to suppress as well as prime a gene.
pmc-13220637:
Yi-Hung Yeh and colleagues solve the structure of an antibody locked onto the brake CD33 in a 2026 study. Hepatitis B virus persists partly by engaging CD33, a receptor on myeloid immune cells whose sugar-binding surface, grabbed by viral proteins, triggers an off signal. The monoclonal antibody 10C8 blocks that suppression, but nobody knew how.

The structure, at 3.2 angstroms, shows two receptor molecules clasped by two antibody fragments, an assembly whose weight matched measurements. The antibody grips the receptor's outer domain next to, not inside, the sugar-binding pocket, covering surface to bar the virus protein from docking. Binding squeezes the receptor pair into a tighter angle than its relaxed state, a geometry preventing the clustering the off signal needs. The authors frame 10C8 as a clamp that holds the brake in a signaling-dead pose, restoring antiviral activity, and offer the structure as a template for designing antagonists.
pmc-13220837:
Lihua Wang and colleagues examine two blood proteins as signals in lymphoma patients who develop infections after chemotherapy in a 2026 study. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma patients are fragile, and post-chemotherapy infection can turn fatal. The receptor AXL and its partner Gas6 help clear dead cells and calm inflammation, and their levels might reveal which patients are headed downhill.

One hundred two patients at one centre were followed for a year after infection was diagnosed; seventy-nine survived and twenty-three died. Respiratory infections were commonest, and Gram-positive bacteria supplied most of the 108 pathogens. The patients who died carried higher rates of risk markers and higher levels of AXL, Gas6, and the marker procalcitonin. In models, B symptoms and elevated AXL and Gas6 predicted death, and the two proteins discriminated survivors from non-survivors with accuracy around 0.82. The authors label the study exploratory and propose the pair as prognostic markers.
pmc-13222137:
Jocelyn N Kuate and co-authors make copper sulphide nanoparticles from single-source precursor compounds, in a 2026 chemistry study. Olive oil and castor oil served as green capping agents during heat treatment at two temperatures. The particles were then checked with diffraction, microscopy, and spectroscopy, and tested as light-driven catalysts against methylene blue dye.

Particle shapes ranged from spheres to irregular forms, sized between five and over one hundred nanometers. Crystal phase shifted with precursor choice and temperature. Under visible light, the best samples broke down roughly sixty percent of the dye within two hours. Reaction settings strongly shaped performance, marking these particles as candidates for cleaning dyed wastewater.
pmc-13222637:
Bin Hou, Qiang Liu, and Zhi Li map a regulatory RNA circuit that drives colon adenocarcinoma growth, in a 2026 study of a copper-driven cell death pathway called cuproptosis. A long non-coding RNA, a microRNA, and a transport gene form the axis under study. Expression analysis, cell experiments, and rescue tests were used to pin down the mechanism.

The long RNA sponges up the microRNA, freeing the transport gene SLC6A6 to rise. That rise promoted tumor cell growth, movement, and survival. Suppressing SLC6A6 instead raised copper levels and reactive oxygen, triggering cuproptotic death. Rescue experiments confirmed the microRNA's effect partly depends on this gene. The circuit offers fresh diagnostic and treatment targets for colon cancer.
pmc-13223837:
Saleh and coauthors map gene diversity in native Spanish chicken breeds. Local breeds hold rare traits that farm stocks may lack. Guarding that pool needs clear facts on breed ties and inbreeding. The team used a dense gene chip for the tests.

They sampled 114 birds from seven local breed groups. Data from two more breeds joined the set for context. Breed groups split into two main clusters in the tests. Long matched gene runs showed past inbreeding in each breed. Some breeds held more diversity than the rest. The maps can guide mating plans that keep diversity high.
pmc-13224037:
Shumin Xu and colleagues introduce a 2026 brain-age tool for children with beta-thalassemia major, a serious inherited blood disorder that can harm thinking and development. Their model, SurfGNN, reads the shape of the brain's outer surface from MRI scans to estimate brain age. The gap between estimated and actual age becomes an index of delayed development.

Scans came from 25 affected children and 40 matched healthy controls aged six to fifteen. Affected children scored lower on intelligence testing and showed more delayed brain age.
