The index also tracked haemoglobin and ferritin levels and statistically linked those blood measures to cognition. The model beat standard machine-learning baselines while highlighting which cortical regions drove its estimates.
pmc-13227537:
Yunxiao Li and colleagues test a 2026 exercise-lab measure as a warning sign for flare-ups in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The measure, called EqCO2 at the anaerobic threshold, captures how much carbon dioxide a patient exhales for each unit of oxygen used at the point where breathing hardens during exercise testing. Seventy-nine patients with baseline lung and exercise tests were grouped by later flare frequency.

Patients who flared had worse lung function, less exercise capacity, and higher values of the measure. Each step up in the measure raised flare risk, and the link survived adjustment for age, weight, and lung function. Alone it predicted moderately well, and the authors built a simple scoring chart to make the index usable in clinic.
pmc-13229937:
Simone Murchio and colleagues propose in 2026 a cheaper way to predict fatigue failure in printed metal lattice parts. Tiny struts made by laser powder bed fusion carry small surface flaws that make lifetime hard to forecast. Detailed X-ray scans capture those flaws well but cost too much for routine design work.

Their method builds digital twins from microscope images, recreating bumpy surfaces and partly fused particles in computer models. Computer stress tests combined with a statistical energy rule then point to likely failure spots and lifetimes. Models matched X-ray based versions closely and placed failures inside accepted scatter ranges. Designers could screen lattice designs earlier, before costly scanning or testing begins.
pmc-13230637:
Michael Ishida and colleagues model in 2026 a walking pattern shared by many fishes that move on land. Distant fish species with very different bodies use strikingly similar steps, hinting at shared mechanics. The pattern pairs a wavy body motion with alternating front contact points, like a moving tripod.

High-speed filming of the grey bichir set the basic timing and angles for the model. Values matched those of other walking fishes well enough to treat the pattern as general. Computer runs then varied body shape and joint motion to see what speeds travel most. Best performance landed near the settings the bichir actually uses. A robot built on the same simple plan also walked, which supports the model.
pmc-13230837:
Kristian Kniha and colleagues compare in 2026 germ growth around ceramic and titanium dental implants in the lower jaw. Their prescription pairs gene silencing of Rho switches with mitochondria-blocking repurposed antibiotics, aiming to collapse the partnership outright.
pmc-13261637:
Yu Chen and colleagues present a 2026 textual analysis of Chinese local tobacco control laws against the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control. China ratified the treaty in 2005, but with no national smoke-free law, cities and provinces wrote their own rules unevenly. The team compared legal texts with the treaty's Article 8 on smoke-free environments.

They compiled 38 dedicated subnational regulations enacted or amended between 2006 and 2024, totaling 100,635 substantive Chinese characters. Only 10 regulations (26.3%) met the Article 8 compliance criteria, while 28 (73.7%) did not. Compliant texts were longer, with a median 3,249 versus 2,572 characters, and had more clauses. They more often banned e-cigarettes and required quitting services. The 10 compliant jurisdictions cover about 121.6 million residents, 8.6% of mainland China's 2020 population. The authors stress these are features of legal text, not proof of real-world enforcement.
pmc-13262137:
Kawtar Lahlali and a large team presented in 2026 a stroke case blamed on the hyoid bone pressing against the carotid artery, joined with a review of similar reports. Carotid dissection usually follows trauma or tissue disorders, yet bones near the artery can injure it mechanically. Their patient was a forty-six-year-old woman with no notable medical history.

She arrived two hours into a stroke with left-sided heaviness and facial weakness. Scans showed a fresh blockage of the right middle cerebral artery and a tear in the right internal carotid artery. That artery touched the rear horn of her hyoid bone directly at the tear site. A literature search found twenty-five articles on strokes from this bone-artery conflict since 1999. The authors urge imaging teams to check bone contact when dissection lacks an obvious cause.
pmc-13262937:
August Myers and colleagues follow one vaccinated monkey's B cells as they learn to neutralize an HIV vaccine construct. The BG505 SOSIP trimer mimics the virus's envelope spike, and protection in earlier work tracked with antibodies against a glycan hole. Their 2026 study sequences over four thousand seven hundred targeted B cells over time.

Three expanded families produced the neutralizing antibodies, all aiming at the same glycan hole. Structures show each family grabbing the hole differently, one even shoving a sugar aside to reach the CD4 docking loop. Some relatives bound the spot without neutralizing. Repeated vaccination drove the expansion and sharpening behind the strong serum response.
pmc-13263137:
Videha Sharma and colleagues build an open data model for gene-based prescribing in a 2026 journal article. Pharmacogenetics uses genetic tests to make drug choices safer and more effective, but results often arrive as documents that computer systems cannot easily share. The team drafted a standard format from literature and existing specifications, then refined it in expert workshops.

Twenty-four experts from ten countries reviewed the model in two rounds. The final version keeps test results separate from advice on treatment and uses standard medical and gene vocabularies. It is published on an open clinical knowledge platform. Tests of conversion to the FHIR health data standard showed information could flow both ways, with automated mapping making reuse easier at scale.
pmc-13263337:
Guanzhao Wen and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how light energy splits into free charges in graphene nanoribbons, atom-thin carbon strips. Such splitting, called exciton dissociation, is needed for solar cells and light sensors. The team used ultrafast terahertz measurements, which track charge movement, on ribbons of different lengths.

They found that hot excitons, still carrying extra energy, do most of the splitting. A critical length of about twenty nanometers decides the outcome. Ribbons shorter than roughly twice that length form bound excitons within picoseconds instead. Longer ribbons with strongly spread energy bands moved charges faster and split excitons more efficiently, offering design rules for future devices.
pmc-13263537:
Tiffany Arista Sutanto and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on gluten-free, low-glycemic cookies made from fruit seed waste. The flours came from durian and papaya seeds, normally thrown away. The team tuned the recipe in two stages: first the amount of lecithin, a fat-based emulsifier, for texture, then a sugar replacement mix.

Half a percent of lecithin gave the best texture. The winning sweetener blend used erythritol and a trace of stevia. The finished cookies had improved texture and appearance, a low glycemic index of about thirty-three, and a low glycemic load. Tasters still accepted them well. The authors see potential for a functional snack aimed at health-conscious buyers.
pmc-13263637:
Jia Yang and co-authors review a 2026 survey of mesenchymal stem cell therapy for type 2 diabetes. These versatile stem cells, found in tissues such as bone marrow and fat, can calm inflammation and release healing signals. The review examines how they might regenerate insulin-making beta cells and how their tiny secreted packages, exosomes, may steady blood sugar.

Standard drugs control sugar only temporarily and can bring side effects, while islet transplants face donor shortages. Stem cells offer a cheaper, more available option, and studies suggest combined benefits across beta-cell repair, immune modulation, and tissue healing. The authors warn that long-term clinical data are still lacking, so their conclusions are a starting reference, not firm guidance.
pmc-13263737:
Chenqing Wang and colleagues correct a diagnosis in two children whose sun-sensitive skin hid an ultra-rare porphyria. Both had blistering, scarring, and raised red-cell protoporphyrin, pointing doctors to a more common cousin disease. Their 2026 report shows why the chemistry's fine print mattered.

The protoporphyrin was mostly zinc-bound rather than free, an unusual tilt that prompted a full gene panel. Each child proved homozygous for a brand-new variant in PPOX, the variegate porphyria gene. A plasma fluorescence scan in one case flashed the signature peak for that disease. Test the genes, they urge, whenever zinc dominates the porphyrin pattern.
pmc-13263937:
Jakob Lindskog and co-authors present a 2026 scoping review of artificial intelligence and machine learning in sports medicine. They mapped which clinical tasks the tools target and judged how close each is to real clinical use. Their February 2026 search across three databases screened 8,677 papers and included ninety-seven.

Most work sat in orthopedics, about seventy percent, and neurology. Prediction and estimation models dominated, covering injury risk, image diagnosis, and recovery forecasts. Reported accuracy was often high, but most studies used old data and tested only within their own sample. Calibration was rarely reported, and only one study tried an actual prevention intervention. The authors advise treating these tools as support, not decision makers.
pmc-13264037:
Xinyun Che and co-authors report a 2026 brain study linking physical activity to rhythmic visual attention in humans. Attention was once pictured as a steady spotlight, but evidence now shows it pulses several times per second in the theta range. Using magnetoencephalography, which records magnetic signals from the brain, the team tested whether a short bout of activity changes that rhythm.

After activity, discrimination accuracy improved and theta patterns in behavior grew stronger. Frontal theta power rose after cues, and fast visual activity locked more closely to a useful theta phase. Target responses also fluctuated more clearly in the theta range. The findings suggest movement tunes a built-in sampling rhythm, offering a brain-level account of sharper attention after exercise.
pmc-13264137:
Lidia Maeso and a large team develop ready-to-use printed scaffolds for chronic skin wounds in a 2026 study. Lasting wounds need support structures that also deliver biological signals matched to the patient. Their scaffold prints from a gelatin and alginate ink chosen for flow and strength, then is crosslinked, freeze-dried for storage and rehydrated at use with the patient own platelet-rich growth factor preparation.

The rehydrated matrix held its shape, swelled and broke down at favorable rates, and released active factors over two days. Skin support cells grew well on it in culture. In lab-grown human skin, damage and inflammation markers fell while matrix rebuilding improved, with more mature collagen and elastin. The design targets personalized wound care that clinics can stock in advance.
pmc-13264237:
Leila Satarian and colleagues test stem cell vesicles for protecting vision nerve cells after crush injury in a 2026 mouse study. Tiny vesicles released by mesenchymal stem cells can carry protective factors to retinal ganglion cells, whose death causes vision loss. Vesicles were collected from three stem cell sources and split by spinning speed into two size fractions, then given in a model where the optic nerve is crushed.

All vesicle types improved visual behavior somewhat. Fractions from a clonal bone marrow stem cell line performed best, keeping more target retinal cells alive. One fraction also raised survival signaling and lowered cell death proteins in retina and nerve. That fraction is easier to produce, which helps future clinical translation.
pmc-13264337:
Patrick H. Waring, Fred DeFrancesch and Kathryn Grace set out an emergency protocol for oversedation during pain procedures in a 2026 society document. Sedation for spinal and pain work ranges from light oral calming to moderate vein sedation. Breathing depression is the central danger when drugs push deeper than planned, notably as several common agents, including benzodiazepines, opioids and propofol, can stack effects in older or sicker patients.

First steps run from early recognition and airway support to reversal drugs such as naloxone or flumazenil when fitting. Steady monitoring and readiness to follow basic and advanced life support steps are required throughout. Prevention through dosing care and patient choice frames the protocol. Clinics gain a shared checklist for a rare but serious event.
pmc-13264437:
Dražen Domijan wrote a 2026 review that contrasts two views of how the seeing part of the brain works. One view, predictive coding, says the brain tests guesses about what the eyes receive and tracks errors. The other says the brain builds a picture of surfaces through loops that boost figures and mute backgrounds.

Domijan weighs brain recordings on contour linking, false contours, figure-ground split, predictability, and attention. Many studies fit the second view, with loops across early visual areas lifting the whole figure. Some studies on false contours and figure-ground did show error signals, as the first view predicts. He concludes the data do not clearly back either view on their own.
pmc-13264637:
Thomas M Vollbrecht and colleagues wrote a 2026 heart imaging study on spotting a stiffening of the heart sac in pericarditis, inflammation of that sac. When the sac stiffens, it chokes heart filling, and scan judgment today rests mostly on the eye. The team tested number-based measures from standard moving heart scans.

They re-read scans from 103 patients, of whom 42 had the stiff pattern. Pumping strength did not differ between groups, but heart stretch measures and blood force measures were clearly worse in stiff cases. Two measures each sorted the groups fairly well, and together they did best. Both stayed predictive when other factors were counted. The authors say these measures add hard numbers to routine scans at no extra scan cost.
pmc-13264937:
Joyce Ong and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of modern preoperative assessment for bowel surgery. A careful check before major surgery has long rested on history, examination, and selected lab tests. As patients grow older and sicker, this step has become a key chance to cut risk and improve recovery.

The review covers risk scores that help explain danger to patients and families, plus checks of nutrition and frailty. Modern additions include iron given by vein, bowel cleaning paired with antibiotics, and blood biomarkers. Teams now span many specialties to fix fixable risks and manage other illnesses. Patient teaching and prehabilitation, training before surgery, prepare people for the strain. The authors argue that thorough assessment and tuning before surgery make the whole course safer.
pmc-13266037:
Changsheng Jiang and the team review the gut microbiota-brain axis (2026). Gut microbes and the brain talk through nerve, hormone, immune, and body routes. Upsets in this network are linked with metabolic, autoimmune, and mental disorders. Much human evidence remains correlative, and causal links are still being tested.

The review sorts the parts of the axis and the signals microbes send. Microbial products affecting mood, cognition, and stress answers receive attention. Treatments discussed include live germ doses and stool transfer. Diet plans such as fibre and live-culture foods are treated as add-on. Gaps for tailored care are flagged.
pmc-13266837:
Chunhui Zhang and Yu Liu explore in 2026 whether a large scaffold protein called AHNAK helps drive chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The protein was predicted to be plentiful in this lung disease, but its role was unclear. They studied human blood samples, lung cells exposed to cigarette smoke extract, and mice exposed to smoke plus a bacterial component.

AHNAK levels were high in patients and in the smoke-treated cells. Turning the protein down eased oxidative stress and inflammation, and it lessened lung injury in mice. The benefit ran through the Notch signaling pathway, since reactivating that pathway undid the protection. Blocking AHNAK may offer a fresh treatment direction for a disease that current drugs only slow.
pmc-13266937:
Maximilian Roca Jungfer and others forced a rare bond onto technetium in two thousand twenty-six. Technetium is a radioactive metal used in health care. Its alkyne complexes had defied all attempts to make them. Math hinted the ligand setting was to blame. A custom pincer ligand gripped the metal tightly. Arsenic arms held the triple bond side-on against it.

Several stable crystal compounds were made and mapped. Two oxidation states of technetium were reached. Rhenium cousins were made as a match too. Analysis showed classic two-electron alkyne binding. Ligand design, not the metal, caused past misses. Basic chemistry gains a new compound class.
pmc-13268037:
Malka Korenblit and co-authors analyze in 2026 the personal statements of 298 applicants to one plastic surgery residency program, hunting for language patterns tied to matching and to bias. Statements were scored by word-analysis software for tone, reasoning style, and self-presentation, then compared with outcomes and applicant backgrounds. Of the group, about six in ten matched into a program.

Matched applicants wrote with more analytical thinking and richer vocabulary, and they addressed the reader far less often. Statement length itself did not matter. Language patterns differed by race even after accounting for grades and scores: Asian applicants wrote more analytically, while Black and Hispanic applicants used less positive and certain language. The authors warn that uniform standards can still favor majority writing styles.
pmc-13268637:
Yu Zhu and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of deep learning for detecting age-related macular degeneration in eye images. This disease is a leading cause of permanent blindness. The team searched four databases through 2025 and pooled 28 studies, covering about 77,000 samples for detection and about 29,000 for separating wet from dry disease.

The algorithms detected the disease with very high sensitivity and specificity, near the top of the scale. For wet-versus-dry separation, performance was slightly lower but still strong. The authors warn that mostly retrospective designs and internal testing may inflate results; they frame the tools as triage helpers needing local checks, not replacements for doctors.
pmc-13269437:
Vesta Brauckmann and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 measuring how emergency workers apply pressure dressings to stop severe bleeding. Pressure that is too low fails to stop blood loss, while too much can cause harm. Sensors under the bandage recorded the true pressure in a training setting.

A total of 124 providers took part, and 116 records were used in the final analysis. Average peak pressure was about 169 units, but values ranged widely from 50 to 412. Doctors pressed significantly harder than other groups. A short-tug method was the strongest predictor of high pressure, followed by bandage type. Israeli bandages gave the highest pressures. Pressures classed as excessive, above 250, occurred in 28 percent.
pmc-13269837:
Quanyou Wu and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on how the human immune system ages, using several layers of molecular data at once. Blood samples from 69 people aged 23 to 75 were measured for genes, proteins, and gene splicing, the cutting and rejoining of gene messages. Single-layer studies had missed how these layers interact.

One key translation gene's faulty splicing reshaped the protein mix of aging white cells. Those protein shifts matched a gradual weakening of T-cell function, the immune cells that kill infected cells.
pmc-13270237:
Erinn D'hulster and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on children's doctors in Belgium using rapid CRP testing, a finger-prick test for inflammation, in community practice. A prior trial had shown the test helps cut antibiotic overuse in acutely ill children. Fifteen experienced paediatricians were interviewed about real-world use.

Doctors viewed the test positively but faced missing payment schemes and unclear supply routes. Many also used it beyond diagnosis, to reassure parents or back up treatment choices in conversation. Confidence grew through repeated use and informal peer exchange rather than formal training. The authors map what helps or hinders lasting uptake of the test outside trial conditions.
pmc-13270337:
Jessica C O'Neil and co-authors published a survey study in 2026 on how infectious disease doctors who specialize in bone and joint infections are paid in the United States. These doctors give long-term, team-based input for infections such as those around artificial joints. Much of that work cannot be billed directly, so its funding was mapped.

Fifty-two doctors replied, 94 percent from United States academic centers. Their median clinical effort was 70 percent, with a median of 55 percent of that spent on orthopaedic infections. Pay was most often salary plus productivity incentives, at 53 percent. Coordination, informal advice, and teaching were near universal, yet 83 percent got no protected time or funding for them.
pmc-13271337:
Huldah Pearlin Sarah Lazarus and Nalini Easwaran report a 2026 computer-based study of small bacteria-killing proteins. These proteins are carried in membrane vesicles from a plant-helping bacterium, Priestia megaterium. Earlier work showed these vesicles can inhibit Pseudomonas syringae, a plant pathogen. The authors asked whether the proteins could bind its virulence proteins, the tools it uses to attack plants.

Because all evidence here is computed, not from live tests, the authors frame the proteins as promising candidates. They build on earlier laboratory findings.
pmc-13271937:
Umberto Zanini and colleagues present in 2026 three cases where ulcerative colitis, a chronic bowel inflammation, narrowed the airways of the chest. Lung involvement in this disease is uncommon, and narrowing of the windpipe or main bronchi is rarer still. Airway symptoms can also appear years apart from bowel symptoms, which delays recognition.

One improved quickly on high-dose steroids during a bowel flare, while another needed a scope procedure with balloon widening after steroids failed. The varied courses show treatment must match how active or scarred the airway has become.
pmc-13273037:

They merged four datasets with 364 tumors and 99 normal samples, using a shared method across two test platforms. Hundreds of sites differed in the same way in every cohort. Added methylation clustered on control regions for nerve and development genes. Machine learning models, checked strictly across cohorts, narrowed the signal to a compact set of 18 sites that separated tumor from normal tissue. The authors offer this set as a candidate marker for further testing.
pmc-13273437:

She had neurofibromatosis type 1, a genetic condition that can distort the spine, with progressive kyphoscoliosis causing a rotatory dislocation at T2 to T3, but no nerve deficits. Standard fixation was not feasible at the distorted levels.

Surgeons performed a posterior-only fusion with bone grafting, using screws anchored between ribs and vertebrae as the sole thoracic fixation. A CT at eight months confirmed solid fusion, so no front approach was needed. At 21 months she was symptom-free, and at eight years she needed no further surgery, reporting only mild intermittent pain.
pmc-13274037:
Faeezah Patel and a large team report a 2026 journal article on routine vaccines in young children exposed to drug-resistant tuberculosis at home. The data come from a South African trial of preventive treatment held at five sites. Children under five need vaccines on time to gain full protection.

Coverage passed eighty percent for every vaccine except measles, where two-dose coverage was about seventy-one percent and eleven percent had none. Delays were linked to the sick parent being the child's main caregiver and to lower household income. The COVID-19 lockdown months showed no extra delay.
pmc-13274137:
Siqiao Gong, Chen Yang, and Huafeng Liu present a 2026 journal article on a glowing reporter mouse that lets scientists watch cells eat their own fat stores. That cleanup process is called lipophagy, and its failure is linked to fatty liver, diabetes damage, and artery disease. Until now it could not be watched live in a whole animal.

Their tfLiveDrop mouse carries a two-color tag on fat droplets that changes with acidity as droplets are digested. Using it, the team found cleanup rates differ sharply by organ. They also found one organ's cleanup blocked in type 2 diabetes, and a timed cleanup surge that helps kidneys mature after birth.
pmc-13275537:
Mahesh Mathur and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a skin infestation that first masqueraded as eczema. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old farmer with an intensely itchy, scaly patch on top of his left foot, treated for ten days as eczema with steroid cream and antihistamines.

When a raised, snake-like red line then crept from the foot toward his ankle, the true diagnosis became clear, helped by his habit of working barefoot in soil. The culprits are dog and cat hookworm larvae in contaminated ground. Treatment with albendazole, a worm-killing drug, resolved the lesions. The authors warn that early lesions mimic eczema in many cases.
pmc-13276137:
Chiranjib Majumder and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review on eye scans in amblyopia, often called lazy eye. In this condition one eye sees poorly despite glasses, usually starting in childhood. Light-based scans called OCT can measure the retina, the eye's light-sensing layer, in fine detail.

The team searched four major databases plus reference lists and trial records, with two reviewers screening studies. Thirty studies comparing lazy eyes with partner eyes or healthy controls were included. Most found a thicker nerve fiber layer and central retina in the type caused by unequal focus between the eyes. Findings for the type caused by eye misalignment were mixed. Scans of tiny blood vessels often showed lower density in untreated eyes. The authors want standardized long-term studies to settle cause and effect.
pmc-13277437:
Yang Shao and colleagues present PhenoRob-P, an autonomous robot for measuring potted plants, in a 2026 paper. Breeders need repeated, traceable measurements of many plants to link genes with growth under stress. Greenhouse aisles are narrow, satellite positioning fails indoors, and pot layouts vary.

The robot pairs a compact two-wheel base with laser and camera navigation that works row by row. A six-axis arm positions cameras for repeatable close-up views from several angles. In greenhouse trials it scanned hundreds of pots per hour with positioning errors mostly inside three centimetres. Wheat drought and recovery were tracked through colour indices, and maize height estimates matched hand measurements closely.
pmc-13277537:
Tianjing Wang leads a 2026 study of a new class of bacteria-killing polymers, plastics-like chains built to attack bacterial membranes. It binds a fat found in bacterial membranes, breaks the membrane, and acts fast with little sign of breeding resistance. It also blocked and broke up bacterial biofilms, slimy colonies that resist drugs. In animals, it showed promise against drug-resistant lung infection and abdominal infection.
pmc-13278237:
Metasebia Worku Abebe leads a 2026 study of long hospital stays and costs after burn injury in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Burns burden poorer countries heavily, and long stays are common where burn centers are few. The team followed 196 patients at a tertiary burn center from January 2023 to 2025 and compared costs with catastrophic spending thresholds.

The average stay was about thirty-three and a half days. Electrical and flame burns dominated in adults, while scalds dominated in children. The number of procedures and infections were tied to longer stays in every group, and longer stays drove higher costs. Family out-of-pocket spending neared or passed catastrophic levels. Prevention and age-specific care paths could cut both stays and costs, the authors say.
pmc-13278437:
Hina Hashmi leads a 2026 study of a hybrid quantum-classical neural network for detecting faults in power grids in real time. Modern grids with renewable sources produce variable, noisy signals that fixed thresholds handle poorly. The model pairs a classical feature extractor with a quantum circuit to classify faults such as line-to-ground and three-phase faults.

Accuracy reached about ninety-six percent on simulated data and about ninety-five percent on real events, beating standard deep learning models, with detection under three milliseconds. Removing the quantum layer hurt performance. Hardware limits and quantum noise remain open issues.
pmc-13278837:

The team analyzed more than forty-two thousand visits by nearly twenty-eight thousand patients at one academic center from 2018 to 2022.

A language model sorted chief complaints and social factors, such as substance use and home environment, from free text with strong accuracy. Adding those features to a standard model improved prediction modestly. A hybrid explanation framework, blending the model with language-based context, made risk outputs far easier to interpret at patient and population levels.
pmc-13280537:
Iris Lin and colleagues published a 2026 review of miR-150-5p, a regulatory RNA with a double life in cancer and immunity. MicroRNAs fine-tune gene activity, and this one can suppress tumors in some settings yet promote them in others. The outcome depends on cancer type and surroundings. The review covers blood cancers and solid tumors, tracing how the molecule influences cell growth, death, and spread.

Special attention goes to copies packaged into extracellular vesicles, the parcels cells use to message each other. Through them it reshapes the tumor neighborhood, blood vessel growth, and immune escape. The authors detail its governance of macrophages, dendritic cells, T cells, and natural killer cells, central to anti-tumor defense. Therapeutic ideas run into delivery problems and off-target risks, which the review weighs. Their bottom line: miR-150-5p has value as a biomarker and as a drug target, provided context is respected.
pmc-13280637:
Helmi Sulaiman and colleagues published a 2026 study of how piperacillin and tazobactam behave in critically ill patients with sepsis in Malaysian intensive care. Forty-five adults gave blood samples on the first and third days. The team modeled drug behavior and simulated schedules.

Kidney function, captured by creatinine clearance, was the main driver of how fast the drugs cleared. About half the patients hit the therapeutic exposure on day one, and fewer, 44 percent, on day three. Those who hit it tended to be older with weaker kidneys. Cure and survival differences between exposure groups were numerical only, not significant in this sample. Simulations favored a loading dose, then continuous infusion, for mid-range kidney function. The authors name continuous infusion the most reliable route to target levels.
pmc-13281237:

In their group, germs of one broad class caused two thirds of cases that could be checked. A single germ, Staphylococcus aureus, still ranked first on its own. Most of those cases were the drug-sensitive form, not the drug-proof form. The authors compare two other large studies and find the same rise of the sensitive form. They say local germ maps must guide care.
pmc-13281337:
Nicolas Chardon and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter on airway surgery in intensive care. The surgery makes a breathing hole in the neck for patients who cannot leave a ventilator. The letter writers push back on dropping the scope for so small a gain.

They argue the key choice is not scope or no scope. A sound scan can map the soft tissue in front of the windpipe, which the scope cannot see. That map helps dodge blood vessels and the thyroid gland. The scope, in turn, guards the steps once the airway is entered. Used together, the tools cover unlike risks. The authors urge teams to pair them, not pick one.
pmc-13281637:
Dandan Wei and colleagues built a two-in-one bird flu vaccine for chickens in a 2026 study. Two bird flu strains, H5 and H7, circle the globe and wreck poultry flocks. Both can also threaten people. The team tested it in lab-raised chickens free of germs.

Shots raised strong antibody defenses, and more dose gave more response. Blood from the birds blocked the matched viruses and partly blocked kin strains. At the two high doses, every bird survived lethal doses of both flu types, matched or not. The vaccine also curbed virus growth in lungs and largely stopped its spread. Gene reads showed a broad immune wake-up. The authors call it a hopeful guard for flocks.
pmc-13282337:

That surgery diverts urine through a piece of small bowel to a skin opening, after bladder removal. Problems can hit the joins, the conduit, the opening, or the belly wall. The authors show four narrated operations, each matched to a distinct failure pattern.

Cases covered a one-sided and a two-sided narrowing where urine tubes join the conduit, a twisted conduit with a hernia, and crossed urine tubes. Techniques used dye tests to confirm tube identity, widening cuts, stents, and fresh joins on healthy tissue. One case needed a longer new conduit, another a mesh repair of the hernia. The authors organise revision around spotting the defect, confirming tubes, preparing healthy tissue, and tension-free rebuilding.
pmc-13283237:

A weighted score summed risk across all five lobes for each person. The right upper lobe high-risk group had higher cancer rates than its low-risk group. The total score linked to cancer risk after checks for genes and habits. The link held most clearly in long-term smokers in the cohort.
pmc-13283837:
Seongyeon Lim, Suh-Yeon Dong, and Tzyy-Ping Jung measured forehead brain signals in 2026 during a fast image-stream task. The team used a fifteen-channel light-based brain scanner on fifty people, recording blood oxygen changes in the prefrontal cortex, the front brain area tied to attention.

Deoxygenated signals differed in shape-related features instead. Connections between channels also shifted by condition, and answers came slower when no target appeared. pmc-13306937:
Umar Iqbal surveyed self-driving systems through their sensors in a 2026 review. Cameras, LiDAR, radar and satellite plus motion units each fail in distinct ways, and drift in timing or alignment can make later decisions overconfident.

A sensor-centred frame links what each device truly measures to how doubt spreads through fusion, safety checks and risk-aware control. Uncertainty styles covered include probability, evidence and conformal methods, while fusion designs range from filters to transformer models. Aviation integrity ideas are reshaped for road use to force graceful failure. The frame ties each doubt source to a clear safety claim that teams can test.
pmc-13307037:
Xuan Wang catalogued sugar transporter genes in the endangered timber tree Phoebe bournei in a 2026 study. SWEET carriers move sugars for loading into veins and stress replies, yet this species had no family map before.

Twenty-one genes split into four subfamilies, with one branch expanding through tandem and segmental copying in reported analysis. All duplicate pairs showed ratios under one, signalling strong purifying selection on the family. Under hormone ABA stress, one gene spiked at once while another answered late, and sugar outweighed proline as a protective solute. Such gene maps may guide care of this rare tree in a warming world.
pmc-13307237:
Ngawang Norbu analysed niches and species links in white birch forests of Tibet's Niyang River Basin in a 2026 ecology study. Forty-eight plots recorded 71 woody species, mainly from rose, heather and honeysuckle families in the survey counts.

White birch plus three partners held the broadest niches, showing strong resource use and wide spatial fit in index results. Several niche and association measures, plus a stability method, tested how dominant trees share space and resources. Findings describe which species build the forest and how stable the whole community stands. The maps may guide tree care and grazing rules on the high plateau in years to come.
pmc-13307337:
Mathilde Cochonat and Ronny Lopes set out an arthroscopic repair in 2026 for a freshly torn medial ankle ligament in a complex sprain. Conservative care is usual, yet some patients develop lasting medial instability. Their technique works through standard keyhole portals plus one small extra opening below the inner ankle bone.

The bone tip is cleaned, and a soft anchor is placed where the ligament tore away. Suture loops pass twice through the ligament in a U-shape to grip it firmly. With the foot bent fully upward, the ligament is pressed and locked against its original footprint. The authors call the method reliable and reproducible for acute proximal detachment. A linked video shows the full procedure on a right ankle for surgeons learning the steps.
pmc-13307837:
Tinglian Lai and colleagues present ViroBioTree in 2026, a system that organises evidence about viral proteins as a tree of linked facts instead of chopped text passages. Standard retrieval tools fragment relationships between gene regions, domains, motifs, and annotations. Their framework converts sequence, structure, and model attention evidence into typed nodes with traceable connections.

Retrieval then runs through deterministic recall, evidence-aware reranking, balanced selection, and rule-based checks before writing cited reports. Demo tests scored perfectly on structure explanation tasks, though the authors stress those scores measure agreement with expected tags, not biological truth. A full SARS-CoV-2 index held nearly two hundred thousand nodes. Against a vector retrieval baseline, performance varied by task. The system works offline and avoids claiming wet-lab validation it has not done.
pmc-13308537:
Kirstin Gaffney, Megan E Bartlett, and Theresa Rueger test in 2026 whether anemonefish help their hosts to pay for a place to stay, apart from any kin benefit. In these fish, helpers are often unrelated to the breeders they aid, which makes them a clean test of the pay to stay idea.

The team blocked helping in three species, then watched for punishment from breeders or for extra effort from helpers to make amends. Both patterns showed up in all three species, with mix shifts tied to local and social limits on each reef. Help can thus grow from rent like pressure alone, and body size trades off with effort in that bargain.
pmc-13309137:
Sophie M Weiss and co-authors lay out in 2026 what lecanemab, an antibody drug for early Alzheimer disease, means for care in Canada, where it won approval in January 2026. The drug binds loose amyloid in the brain and helps clear it, which slows the disease at its root in the amyloid view.

Gains are modest, a slower slide in thinking that may not feel real to all who take the drug in clinic. Use is heavy work: proof of amyloid by spinal fluid or scan, shots each two weeks, and repeat brain scans for safety. Brain swelling or bleed marks are the main risk, though most stay silent. Two review bodies urged no public pay for it.
pmc-13309237:
Yi and co-authors offer a safer way to use outside control data in drug trials. Outside controls can cut trial cost and free more spots for new drugs. But outside patients were not randomized, so hidden gaps can bias results. Their first tool gauges how much hidden bias would flip a result. Their second tool runs two tests at once.

One test uses trial patients only and stays unbiased. The other adds the outside controls for extra power. A small error budget is spent on the second test. If outside data help, power gains can be large. If they do not help, the power loss stays small. Tests on a real trial show the method works.
pmc-13309537:
Xing Tao and co-authors report a 2026 cell study on how HIV triggers a fiery form of cell death in macrophages, a type of immune cell. A chemical tag on RNA, called m6A, and a protein that reads it, TRA2A, were the focus. The protein was scarce in macrophages from people living with HIV.

Lowering TRA2A in lab cells boosted virus copying and switched on a death pathway that spills inflammatory signals. The protein normally grips tagged RNA for a partner protein and shortens its life, which keeps that pathway quiet. Raising TRA2A or blocking the partner reversed the effect. The authors name TRA2A as a brake that balances virus control against harmful swelling.
pmc-13309837:
Taslim UDDIN and co-authors describe daily-life limits after spinal cord injury in Bangladesh in a 2026 survey. Such injury reshapes movement, self-care, work, and social life, and surroundings can ease or worsen each limit. A shared world framework, the ICF, sorts those limits and their drivers.

Face-to-face interviews reached 789 people living in the community, as the Bangladesh arm of a world survey run in 2023 and 2024. Most respondents were men, over half were aged 18 to 40, and about a third lived with tetraplegia. People with higher injuries reported greater limits in every domain. Male sex, younger age, low schooling, rural home, and severe injury each tied to poorer outcomes.
pmc-13310237: A 2026 correction adds a section to the retraction notice for a study in Ibrain comparing two triple-therapy regimens for neuropathic pain. After the retraction appeared, co-author Vennila Jaganathan told the journal they had not known of the problems behind the decision. Their part was limited to data analysis. The retraction call, they said, was made solely by corresponding author Nithya Raju without proper notice to co-authors. The journal notes messages went to all listed contacts. The item adds no new data; it records that disagreement.
pmc-13310637:
Eugen Mengel and co-authors report a trial substudy of a drug for a rare lipid storage disease in infants in a 2026 article. Niemann-Pick disease type C harms the brain and organs from early life, and arimoclomol is approved in the United States from age two, paired with miglustat. Safety and handling in babies under two were untested.

Five infants aged 14 to 23 months at screening received arimoclomol beside standard care for up to 36 months, all also taking miglustat. Safety led the outcome list, with development scores, biomarkers, and drug levels behind. Most of the 108 reported side events were mild or moderate, though 15 serious events fell in two patients. Exposure ranged widely, from 72 to 1109 days across the small group.
pmc-13310737:
Jiaxi Yao presents a 2026 case of a rare kidney cancer type in a man aged 39 years from China. The cancer links to a fused gene that switches on growth signals. Fewer than many cases are known, so each well checked case adds useful detail for doctors and lab staff.

Surgeons removed part of the left kidney for a small tumor found on exam. Lab stains supported a kidney origin and ruled out close mimics. Gene testing found a fusion joining KIF5B with the ALK gene, which names this subtype. Care is hard due to few cases and few drug choices, though drugs aimed at ALK may help some patients.
pmc-13310837:
Amedeo Chiefa and co-authors build a math frame for how neural networks learn proton structure in a 2026 theory paper. Maps of quarks and gluons inside protons guide collider tests, and modern fits train neural networks on data to draw those maps. Knowing how training moves and how doubt spreads is vital as tests grow sharper.

Work uses the neural tangent kernel to write training steps in closed form under clear premises. The frame shows how network shape and data steer the fit, and how doubt flows from data to the final map. Tools can compare fit methods on equal ground. Results guide checks, not replace full fits.
pmc-13311137:
Modibo Diallo and colleagues prove a common gene variant harms pigment making in albinism in a 2026 study. Albinism stems from faults in melanin building genes, and most known faults are rare and sit in coding parts. A patient carried one rare coding fault plus a common intron variant in the OCA2 gene, whose role was doubted.

Blood RNA tests showed the intron variant made the gene skip two blocks, dropping 78 building units from the protein. Modeling showed the loss breaks a key fold and strips sugar tags, which likely traps the protein. The variant was classed as likely harmful. Common intron variants deserve functional tests.
pmc-13311637:
Jackie Zhanbiao Li and co-authors trace how hospital-centered management took root in China's health system in a 2026 history study. The pattern has aided control and growth but starved primary care of resources.

The authors follow seven phases from 1835 to today, from missionary hospitals through socialist planning to market reform and digital management. Four self-reinforcing forces kept hospitals on top: steering from above, growing roles, standard management, and market shifts. Sources span past studies, policy papers, and institutional records. The long view is offered as a guide for health reform debates beyond China.
pmc-13311837:
Shan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 study identifying a type IV interferon in chickens, and the two receptor parts it uses. Interferons are signaling proteins that organize antiviral defense. Type IV is a recently recognized family whose role in poultry was unclear. The team located the chicken gene, compared its setting across species, and charted where the interferon and its receptors are expressed. They also tested a lab-made version of the protein.

The chicken protein carries the family's conserved structural marks. It clusters firmly within type IV, apart from types I, II, and III. It appears in many tissues, with higher levels in immune and mucosal organs, and rises after a viral mimic challenge. In cell tests the protein switched on interferon-stimulated genes. It strongly suppressed Tembusu virus replication and softened viral damage. Chickens thus run a working type IV defense worth factoring into poultry antiviral research.
pmc-13311937:
Elvan Wiyarta and co-authors present a 2025 network meta-analysis comparing first thrombectomy methods for major front-brain artery strokes. Aspiration, stent retrievers, their pairing, and balloon guide catheters are the contenders.

Nine databases yielded 44 studies with 19,268 patients. The paired method with a balloon guide ranked best for reopening the artery and for first-pass success, with odds ratios of 2.87 and 7.33 against rivals in this analysis. Outcomes also covered walking independence at 90 days, bleeding in the skull, and death. Rankings give stroke teams a map for choosing a first approach when seconds count.
pmc-13312337:
Yu Zhou and co-authors publish a 2026 protocol for a randomized, double-blind trial on the best dose of liposomal bupivacaine for nerve block pain control in shoulder arthroscopy. Shoulder surgery often causes severe pain that slows recovery. A superior trunk block numbs the area with less risk of diaphragm weakness than the classic block, but the right concentration of the long-acting drug is unknown.

The trial will enroll 282 adults having arthroscopic rotator cuff repair and assign them to 66, 44, or 33 milligrams of the drug, each diluted to 10 milliliters. Main outcomes are pain at rest 48 hours after surgery and total oral morphine use across the first 48 hours. The team will also track shoulder movement and recovery quality, aiming to pin down a dose that eases pain without holding back mobility.
pmc-13312537:
Michael S. Kim and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how technology-assisted knee replacement spread across the United States from 2020 to 2024 and whether it outperformed manual surgery. Computer navigation and robotic help promise better implant alignment and soft tissue balance, but proof of clinical benefit has stayed mixed.

Drawing on the TriNetX network, the team identified 198,263 primary knee replacements and matched assisted and manual groups one to one on sex, body size, and health conditions. Assisted surgery's share climbed from 11.9 percent in 2020 to 27.0 percent in 2024. After matching, assisted cases carried lower risks of fracture around the implant, deep infection, revision surgery, and aseptic loosening across three years of follow-up, in every region studied. The authors back wider adoption while calling for long-term and cost studies.
pmc-13312837:
Nadeem Akhtar and fellow members of a United States Pharmacopeia expert committee report a 2026 safety review of turmeric and curcuminoid supplements after scattered reports of liver injury. The committee routinely watches the literature for ingredients in USP monographs and launched a full evaluation to decide whether turmeric products need a caution on their labels.

Animal studies showed liver harm only at high doses of powder or extract, and the many human trials of these supplements reported no organ toxicity or serious events. Published injury cases usually appeared after one to four months of use, often alongside other medicines, and they generally cleared once the supplement stopped. Rare liver failure has occurred, though. The committee recommends a cautionary label advising people with liver history to consult a practitioner and to stop and seek care if symptoms such as jaundice appear.
pmc-13314437:
Wenbo Bian, Qiaoran Liu, and Zhenyu Yao open a journal topic on the interplay of sugar and fat balance in an editorial published in 2026. Metabolic flexibility, the skill of switching between sugar and fat fuels as food and hormones change, sits at the core of metabolic health.

When that switching fails, extra fuel is shunted toward insulin resistance, fat stored in the wrong organs, faulty mitochondria, and lasting inflammation, the editors write. The frame helps explain obesity, diabetes, fatty liver disease, and kindred disorders. They note that big databases and multi-omics data now let risk be read as a whole pattern rather than lone markers, with combined indexes such as the triglyceride-glucose index in wide use. The topic gathers studies that use that joined view to judge and treat metabolic risk.
pmc-13314537:
Kirsty Hodgson and colleagues give an update on sugar coatings in prostate cancer in their 2026 review. Prostate cancer is common in men. Early detection and new drugs for advanced disease are urgent needs. Yet the sugar side of the disease has lagged behind gene and protein work.

Glycans, the sugar chains on proteins, feed into the classic marks of cancer and serve as signs for tests and as drug targets. In prostate cancer they shift in set ways. They grow more branched complex chains, changed sialic acid caps, and more fucose. Sugar on the PSA test protein also alters, and short truncated chains appear, as listed in the review. The authors trace how these sugars drive growth, spread, and escape from immune attack, and why they may sharpen both diagnosis and therapy.
pmc-13314737:
Jun Wang and colleagues use genetic tools to test whether kidney function and hearing loss cause each other, in work published in 2026. Hearing loss affects a share of 6.1 percent of the world population by the figure cited in the report, and kidney disease has long been suspected as a partner.

Their Mendelian randomization design uses gene variants as natural levers, testing both directions. One marker stood out: the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, a sign of kidney filter leak, acted as a risk factor that raised hearing loss odds when high. Three other kidney marks, two filtration estimates and urate, showed no causal tie to hearing loss, as the authors report. The result singles out early filter damage, rather than filtration rate, as the thread to watch in hearing care.
pmc-13315137:
Yong Lin and co-authors propose, in a 2026 pathology study, a new way aortic dissection can begin in people with hypertension. The classic story starts with a tear in the inner lining. These researchers examined aortic wall samples from 43 participants, comparing hypertensive dissection patients, hypertensive controls, and non-hypertensive dissection patients, with microscopy and mechanical stretch testing.

In hypertensive dissection, the wall's middle layer carried an abnormal growth of tiny vessels, medial neovascularization, concentrated in its outer third. The growth frequently sat where the wall had torn. Inside those regions, elastic and collagen fibers showed fractures, and mechanical testing found exaggerated shear mismatch between layers. Ordinary wall degeneration, by contrast, was milder in the hypertensive dissection group than in the non-hypertensive one. The authors suggest the new vessels rupture and start the dissection from within the wall, while cautioning that a cross-sectional study cannot prove the sequence.
pmc-13315437:
Nena Hilmia and colleagues assembled the full mitochondrial genomes of two native Indonesian chickens in a 2026 study. Pelung, kept for ornamental traits, and Sentul, a dual-purpose bird, are named national genetic resources, but their mitochondrial makeup had not been fully described.

Using next-generation sequencing, the team found both genomes were 16,784 bases long with the usual set of 13 protein-coding genes, 22 transfer RNAs, two ribosomal RNAs, and a control region. They compared the pair with 35 other genomes drawn from Asia's domestic chickens and jungle fowls, and found five single-letter differences of interest. The data support conservation of local breeds.
pmc-13315537:
Amy Avakian and Muhammad Umair describe in 2026 how a dark-blood heart scan found a subtle scar missed by the standard scan. Their patient was a 67-year-old woman with mitral valve prolapse and a 3-millimeter gap at the valve ring. She was sent for magnetic resonance imaging after a heart monitor showed frequent early beats and other rhythm faults.

Standard late-enhancement imaging was read as clear, with normal heart function. A matched blood-nulled sequence at the same slice positions showed a focal stripe of scar in the lower side wall, the classic site in this condition. Such scars can host dangerous rhythms, so sharper imaging may improve risk sorting.
pmc-13317537:
Huizi He and colleagues map, in a 2026 study, human papillomavirus infection across ethnic groups in China's Yili region, using records from 13,915 women screened between 2021 and 2023. Local patterns guide where cervical cancer prevention should aim first.

Overall, 22.0 percent of women carried the virus, and high-risk types made up 87.2 percent of infections in the tallied cases. Rates peaked under age 25, dipped in the late forties, and rose again near sixty. Kazakh women showed the highest raw rate, though the gap vanished after age adjustment. Among biopsied women, infection climbed with lesion severity, and type 16 dominated the worst grades. Hospital sampling limits reach, the authors note.
pmc-13318237: Rebecca Marie Ellul and co-authors published a 2026 correction to their study of virulence factors in the fish bacterium Phocoenobacter atlanticus. The notice is a correction only: it fixes the data availability statement and a methods sentence, giving the correct genome accession JBTTGU000000000 in place of a project number. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13318937:
Sandra Igreja, Constança Paúl, and Soraia Teles present a 2026 mixed-methods study of craft skills passed down in families. The setting is a Portuguese UNESCO Creative City for crafts and folk art. Seventy professional artisans who inherited their practice took part. They walked researchers through their workshops and answered family questionnaires.

Participants ranged from 22 to 88 years old, with a median age of 63. Most were men, and all worked in one of eight craft sectors. Family functioning scores ran high, from 7 to 10 points on the scale used. Older artisans reported slightly better family functioning. Interviews traced eleven themes about how inheritance shapes family ties. Passing on a legacy strengthened solidarity and cohesion, artisans said, though tensions also surfaced.
pmc-13319637:
Annik Steimer and co-authors track how fast swollen joints settle under strong arthritis drugs in a 2026 Swiss registry study. Joint pain from this illness does not hit all joints in the same way, and whether some joints heal slower than others was unknown. Records followed people for two years after they started a new drug.

A first drug group held 598 people with at least one swollen joint, while a wider group held 1942 people across five drug types. Next to the wrist, nearly all joints settled faster, apart from two finger base joints and at times the knee. That slow set held across all drug types. Wrist and those finger joints may need a longer wait before care is judged.
pmc-13319937:
Yujie Liu and co-authors review brain chemicals and balance disorders in a 2026 article on the inner ear system. The balance system in the ear and brain stem keeps us upright and oriented, and its signals are tuned by chemical messengers. How one family of messengers, the monoamines, shapes recovery after balance loss on one side was the focus.

Four messengers are weighed in turn, covering their sites, roles, and drug links in balance care. Each one tracks with balance faults in past work, and drugs that tune them are already used for such ills. Early after injury, shifts in these messengers help the brain rebalance the two sides. Mapping their receptors more fully could point to sharper drugs with fewer side effects.
pmc-13320337:
Lorenzo Titone and co-authors track brain waves as adults learn a made up language in a 2026 study of rhythm and pattern. Speech carries sound rhythms that hint at word edges and count based patterns that do the same job in a hidden way. Past work could not pull the two apart cleanly, so a new stimulus build split them on purpose for this test.

Brain fields from 32 adults were logged while they heard steady syllable streams with both cues set at cross purposes. Distinct brain sources tracked sound, stress beat, and count patterns side by side. Later replies to three syllable chunks showed both pattern types were kept and used to learn new words. Behavior backed the joint need for both cues.
pmc-13320437:
Massimo Filippi and co-authors argue for a wider role for amyloid brain scans in governing new Alzheimer drug care in a 2026 viewpoint. Two lab made antibodies can now clear the sticky brain protein tied to the disease at group level. That shifts clinic work from naming the disease to steering long, costly, risky care for each person. Scans that count the protein could set a start line for that steering.

Repeat scans might guide calls to keep, switch, or stop a drug as care unfolds. Yet a falling scan count does not prove that one person feels or thinks better, and safety, burden, and clinic capacity all press on the plan. Lessons from a high volume European memory clinic ground the call for set care paths.
pmc-13320537:
Myeong Seong Bak and co-authors test gentle ear based nerve stimulation in a 2026 study of healthy adults. The method, called taVNS, sends mild pulses through the skin of the ear to the vagus nerve. The team asked whether it sharpens mental control and what brain wave changes go with any gain.

Twenty-three adults aged 19 to 40 did a Stroop word colour task across three sessions, with real or sham stimulation in between. The real group answered hard mismatched trials more accurately in the last session. Brain waves also differed, as a rise in high beta power seen in the sham group was softened by real stimulation, which hints at lower mental strain.
pmc-13321037:
Sharyu Ikhar, Yogesh Nagargoje, and Ruchita Shrivastava comment in a 2026 letter on a review of machine learning for grading mitral valve leakage. The review, by Eini and others, reported a pooled accuracy curve score of 0.97. The writers argue that the yardstick used to grade leakage in each study shapes that headline figure.

Some studies used measured Doppler methods under society criteria, while others used expert labels or text mined from reports, which carry observer noise. Models trained on soft labels inherit that noise, so pooling them with strict studies inflates apparent precision. The letter also questions frame level models, which sort single images rather than full clinical cases.
pmc-13321637:
Gaurav Sharma and a large team test biochar on wheat land in the Indo-Gangetic Plains in a 2026 field study. Burning crop waste each year fouls air and drains soil carbon and nitrogen. Turning waste into biochar may lock carbon away and enrich soil instead. A two year trial at a Punjab farm compared rice husk and rice straw biochar at several rates.

Biochar at 5 tons per hectare gave the strongest gains. Against non-biochar plots, plant height rose by 12.8 percent and grain yield by 32.8 percent at that rate in the trial, with more tillers, longer spikes, and heavier grains. The authors present that dose as a practical, lasting option for wheat growers.
pmc-13322137:
C. Dwan and colleagues study how pasture type and cow breed shape rumen germs tied to methane in a 2026 trial. Dairy cows grazed three sward systems: plain ryegrass with high nitrogen, ryegrass with white clover at half nitrogen, and a mixed species sward. Holstein-Friesian cows and Jersey crossbreds were compared, with rumen fluid sampled in August and October.

Sward type did not shift overall germ diversity, though several bacterial groups grew more common on clover and mixed swards. Total methane making archaea did not differ by sward, but their mix did, with Methanosphaera up and Methanobrevibacter down on diverse swards. Breed effects were minor. Diverse pasture alone looks unlikely to cut methane sharply.
pmc-13322737:
Ethan J Sack and his team systematically review, in 2026, a rare bone inflammation that mimics cancer. Xanthogranulomatous osteomyelitis is filled with fatty immune cells and can destroy bone like a tumour. Surgeons need clues before biopsy to avoid treating infection as malignancy, or the reverse.

Following standard review guidelines, the team searched three databases and kept thirty-one studies covering thirty-three patients with tissue-proven disease. Cancer was suspected before biopsy in almost every report. Bone destruction, membrane reaction, soft tissue spread and cortical breach were the commonest imaging features. Most reports included biopsy proof and culture results, supporting combined tissue and microbiology testing whenever samples are taken. Care ranged from simple debridement to reconstruction or resection, shaped by diagnostic certainty and structural risk.
pmc-13322837:
Elizabeth Beaulieu and co-authors review computer models of the lower spine in a 2026 article on biomechanical modelling. Such models estimate stress and load inside the spine for conditions from wear and deformity to weak bone and tumours, where direct measurement in living people is not possible.

Finite element models gave useful insight but took much labour, used simple loads and generic anatomy. Newer work uses automated image segmentation for patient-specific shapes, plus neural networks that respect physics and linked body models for more real loads. Uses include planning deformity surgery, judging fracture risk and improving implants. The authors stress weak outcome validation, uneven reporting and uncertain fit across varied patients.
pmc-13322937:
Rosa Di Micco leads a multicentre comparison of imaging after drug treatment for breast cancer, published in 2026, asking which scan best predicts full tumour clearance. The analysis held 143 patients, with 54 node-positive patients from San Raffaele Hospital in a prospective trial and 89 cases from Heidelberg Hospital records.

Ultrasound was judged against FDG PET/MRI, with complete response defined by no visible tumour on ultrasound and by absent tracer uptake plus no contrast enhancement on the combined scan. Accuracy was checked for PET alone, MRI alone, the pair read together and the pair read as agreeing. Subgroup work linked scan response with tumour features, aiming to guide surgery planning after systemic therapy.
pmc-13323337:
Mehmet Umut Capar and colleagues test, in 2026, whether a standard hormone suppression test still works after weight-loss surgery. The overnight dexamethasone test screens for Cushing's syndrome by checking whether cortisol falls after the drug. Surgically altered gut anatomy might absorb the tablet poorly and produce false alarms.

Sixty-eight patients who had a sleeve gastrectomy or a gastric bypass at least nine months earlier repeated the test and were compared with their own preoperative results. Values rose slightly after bypass and barely moved after sleeve surgery, with no significant difference between the two operations. Pre- and postoperative values correlated moderately, and results did not track sex, body mass or weight lost. Most patients still suppressed cortisol properly, so the authors judge the test safe and valid after bariatric surgery.
pmc-13323537:
Zhouyang Li and team studied why a protein-tagging process called neddylation matters in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. This lung illness limits breathing and ranks as a top killer worldwide. Their 2026 paper focuses on alveolar macrophages, immune cells patrolling the air sacs, and on one enzyme in the pathway, UBE2M. Work in patient cells and in mice exposed to cigarette smoke tested whether losing UBE2M drives emphysema, the lung damage that destroys air sac walls.

Mice lacking UBE2M in myeloid cells developed emphysema, and gene profiling pointed to MMP12, an enzyme that breaks down elastin, as the go-between. Losing UBE2M let a factor called HIF-2alpha build up, which switched on MMP12. Blocking HIF-2alpha or deleting both genes eased the damage. The team presents the UBE2M, HIF-2alpha, and MMP12 chain as a new target for drugs that might slow or prevent emphysema.
pmc-13323737:
Liping Sun, Juan Lang and Zhongkui Xiong test paederoside as a shield for nerve cells in a Parkinson's model, in a 2026 cell study. Rotenone, which blocks mitochondrial complex I, damaged mouse Neuro-2A cells in a dose and time pattern used to mimic disease stress.

Pre-treatment with paederoside lifted complex I activity in damaged cells by over forty percent at one dose in their assay, and eased mitochondrial swelling across three doses. The highest dose also curbed caspase-3 activation, a step toward cell death. A co-culture with BV-2 cells let the team watch dopamine-marker cells under the same insult. The authors present paederoside as a candidate for protecting mitochondria in Parkinson's research.
pmc-13324437:
Xiao Wei and colleagues report a 2026 study of bone graft change after sinus lift surgery for dental implants. The team looked back at 80 patients who had a lateral window sinus lift with Bio-Oss graft particles and an implant placed at the same time.

Cone-beam CT scans taken before surgery, right after, and six months later measured graft shrinkage and sinus shape. Width loss and height loss were both recorded, and wider sinuses lost more graft material. A thicker sinus membrane was also linked to greater height loss. The findings can help dentists pick implant sites and judge how much graft material a wide sinus is likely to need.
pmc-13326137:
Zhaoping Li and team found a counterintuitive link between the triglyceride-glucose index and sarcopenia in older Chinese adults. Their 2026 cohort study drew on two China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study subcohorts: 6,033 people for starting index analysis and 5,256 for cumulative and subgroup analyses. Sarcopenia was defined as low muscle mass plus low function. The index, a surrogate for insulin resistance, had shown inconsistent links to sarcopenia, especially over time.

Higher sustained index levels tracked with lower sarcopenia odds in an L-shaped pattern with identifiable thresholds: the upper groups showed adjusted odds ratios of 0.526 and 0.273 against the reference. Associations ran stronger in men, people with lower body mass index, and rural residents, with variation across index measures. The authors propose the index as a possible biomarker threshold for muscle health, while calling for validation in multi-ethnic cohorts and mechanistic studies before clinical use.
pmc-13327537:
Brendan J Gibbs and co-authors follow red drum fish from lab tanks to a wild estuary in a 2026 study. They measured swimming costs in flowing water shaped by shapes mimicking mangrove roots and oyster mounds. Fish riding turbulent wakes used less oxygen and changed their tail beats, above all at high flow speeds.

Outdoor pool tests with motion sensors revealed eight distinct movement states, richer than lab views suggest. Tracking then followed wild fish along a 54 km estuary stretch for three years through 36 listening stations. Wild fish mostly chose slow water under 30 cm per second near complex habitat. Shelter, food, and staying put seem to matter more to the fish than saving energy in fast water.
pmc-13330437:
Smriti Ridhi and six co-authors published a workforce study in twenty twenty-six surveying Georgia's public health staff, in the country rebuilding after pandemic strain. Planning needs hard numbers on who the workforce is, and low-income countries rarely have them. An online survey in twenty twenty-three reached the national disease control center and municipal health centers.

The response rate topped eighty-one percent. Municipal staff were older, with a median age of fifty-six against forty-eight nationally, and women made up over eighty to ninety percent of both workforces. Most held advanced degrees and averaged fifteen to eighteen years of service. Training, career paths, satisfaction, and motivation were also charted. An experienced but aging and feminized workforce is the planning reality the data describe.
pmc-13332337:
Aishwarya S Kadam and colleagues review 2026 evidence on carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, a germ that resists last-line antibiotics. Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella causes severe infections with high death rates and few treatment options, making it a major global health concern. The review covers spread, disease process, resistance mechanisms, treatment choices, and lab detection for isolates from patient samples. Special weight goes to lab tests that show enzyme activity directly, rather than gene tests alone.

Those phenotypic methods include the modified Hodge test, the modified carbapenem inactivation method, the Nordmann-Poirel test, and inhibitor-based assays, each weighed with its strengths and limits. New molecular tests promise faster detection and better infection control, the review notes. Yet in settings with few resources, the older phenotypic assays still carry much of the load. The review helps labs pick the right test mix for speed, cost, and local capacity.
pmc-13333337:
Mark J. Thompson and colleagues study 2026 functional roles for FEN1 phosphate steering residues in multi-step substrate verification. Flap endonuclease 1 cuts five-prime flaps off double-flap DNA junctions while DNA is copied and fixed. Picking the target and the reaction site rests on two intrinsically disordered regions. The alpha4-alpha5 helical arch threads the five-prime flap before catalysis, and the adjacent three-prime flap binding pocket signals arch ordering upon sensing a three-prime flap.

The phosphate steering idea says that conserved positive amino acids in the arch help flaps pass and set the target phosphate diester up for hydrolysis, yet backing evidence has been thin. Using kinetic and spectroscopic methods, the team tested alanine substitutions of Arg103, Arg104, Arg129, and Lys132, finding modest reductions in catalytic rate and stability detailed in the full paper.
pmc-13333437:
Juan Chen and colleagues tested whether advanced diffusion MRI can reveal a prostate cancer's TP53 mutation status without a biopsy of the gene, in a 2026 retrospective study. Tumors carrying the mutation resist hormone therapy and fare worse, so knowing the status before surgery could shape planning.

The study covered 84 men who had their prostates removed, comparing ordinary and advanced diffusion measures between mutated and normal-gene tumors. The mutated group showed lower water movement values across several measures and higher mean kurtosis, a sign of tissue complexity. In adjusted analysis only mean kurtosis stayed an independent predictor, with an odds ratio of 19.329. A model using kurtosis alone reached an AUC of 0.860, close to the best combined model at 0.889, and held up under internal re-checks at 0.858. The authors propose the kurtosis value as a practical noninvasive stand-in for mutation testing.
pmc-13336737:
Ruijia Deng and colleagues built a DNA nanodevice in 2026 that assembles inside cells to cut off energy supply in mitochondria. Artificial clumps of molecules can steer cell fate, but aiming assembly at one cell compartment at the right time has been hard. Their hand in hand tetrahedron uses three functions: navigation, enzyme control, and self assembly.

A chemical tag steers the device to mitochondria, while a telomerase gated latch opens only after the enzyme extends a primer, releasing an assembly trigger. The resulting clumps restrict mitochondrial energy in a timed, local way. Such precise control could aid cancer research and drug delivery, where shutting down energy in chosen cells matters.
pmc-13336837:
Tarek Eid, Maryam Ebrahimiazar, Mohammad Zargartalebi, and David Sinton automate the mapping of how liquids mix in a 2026 methods study. Whether two liquids blend or split governs drug and product formulas, yet checking it by eye is slow and narrow. Their flow-through device senses phase borders by capacitance and reads cloudiness from several angles at once.

The platform sorted diverse liquid pairs, followed separation in real time, and caught partial mixing across recipes and temperatures. With active learning, it mapped three-part phase diagrams in about 2 h on its own, and extracted tie lines in about 5 min each in the reported runs. Self-running mapping could feed the data-hungry work of formula design.
pmc-13337037:
Beibei Zhang and colleagues review the heat shock protein HSP90 as both a cell caretaker and a cancer drug target, in a 2026 survey. HSP90 helps other proteins fold and switch on, supporting growth, division, and stress survival in normal cells. In tumors, that same support network becomes a crutch that cancer cells lean on heavily.

The review links HSP90 to four cancer strengths at once: steady oncogenic signaling, tolerance of protein stress, stem-like flexibility, and shaping of immune evasion. Together these push treatment resistance and relapse. The authors map how HSP90 is controlled and where drugs might break its grip, giving readers a single frame for a scattered drug field.
pmc-13337437:
Yang Zhang and colleagues pool pacemaker rates after a demanding double-valve operation in a 2026 meta-analysis built on a systematic review. The Commando procedure rebuilds the tissue between the aortic and mitral valves, and its known hazard is heart block needing a permanent pacemaker. Estimates varied widely, so the team searched four databases through April 2, 2026.

Twelve studies covering 797 patients gave a pooled pacemaker rate of 22.3% after these operations in the random-effects model. One in five patients, roughly, needs a device. The Chimney modification looked safer at 6.3% against 28.3% for the traditional operation in subgroup results, though small-study effects urge caution. The numbers help surgeons counsel patients and weigh technique choices.
pmc-13337737:
Isaac S. Wheeler and co-authors build computer models of microwave-assisted freeze-drying in a 2026 study. Microwaves can speed drying of medicines in vials, yet weak models risk uneven heating and product damage. Good models are needed to make the process both fast and safe.

A two-dimensional level set model improves on simpler lumped models by using measured pore structure and allowing for poorly placed temperature probes. Results helped simplify the simpler model and set two values from electromagnetic simulation. Tests in microwave drying showed heating of the vial wall and heat flow into the frozen product cannot be ignored. Code is shared openly in Julia.
pmc-13339137:
Xin Yu and colleagues build a hydrogen-making enzyme with selenium swapped for sulfur in a 2026 study. The algal enzyme CrHydA1 uses an iron cluster to handle hydrogen. A selenium version tests how atom identity shapes that machinery.

A selenium-bearing iron complex matured the inactive enzyme into an active form. Spectroscopy showed the new complex takes a rare hydride form, unlike its sulfur twin. Formaldehyde, not serine, supplied a needed bridge piece as reported. Pure isotope versions confirmed the selenium enzyme keeps a similar shape and redox behavior to the natural one, with distinct fine details.
pmc-13339437:
Joachim Almquist and colleagues modelled drug levels in 2026 for anifrolumab in lupus kidney disease, where type I interferon signals drive kidney harm. The drug blocks those signals and is cleared for systemic lupus, and a phase 2 kidney trial hinted that a strong dose plan beats the standard dose. Yet high urine protein raised drug clearance, and the exact link was unmapped.

The team modelled how urine protein shifts drug levels across dose plans, with 900 milligram strong doses first then 300 milligrams. Clear dose rules could keep drug levels in range for patients who lose protein in urine. The work backs more exact dosing in lupus kidney trials and care.
pmc-13340237:
Marcelo Pillonetto and colleagues told of sepsis cases in 2026 where a new germ, Phytobacter, had been misnamed by standard lab tests. These germs are newly seen as human pathogens, and routine tests often mix them up with other gut germs, which delays right treatment. Since 2018, the Paraná state public health lab has used a mix of methods to name them.

Mass spectrometry, API 20E tests, targeted gene tests, and whole genome reads together proved three sepsis cases first labelled as other germs. Right naming matters, since treatment and outbreak response hinge on the true germ. The report urges labs to use mixed methods when close gut germs defy routine tests.
pmc-13341337:
Christine Ljungberg and colleagues compared urinary and genital infection risks in 2026 between two SGLT2 drugs, empagliflozin and dapagliflozin, in adults with type 2 diabetes. Urogenital side effects are common with this drug class and may sway treatment choice, while differences in selectivity and potency could shift safety profiles. The team emulated a target trial with new users on metformin from 2015 to 2022.
