Infections were tracked through antimicrobial prescriptions plus inpatient and outpatient diagnoses, and phimosis through health records. Head to head safety data help doctors pick between closely related drugs. The study gives patients a clearer picture of infection trade offs when starting SGLT2 therapy.
pmc-13341537:
Brain-computer interface training for stroke arm recovery is piloted by Wenjie Jin and collaborators in a 2026 randomized trial. Forty patients with first subcortical stroke in the subacute phase were split evenly between closed-loop interface training and an active control after two days of familiarization.

Both groups got standard care and matched motor imagery practice for 4 weeks; the interface group alone had glove feedback driven by their EEG signals. Arm function was scored with standard clinical scales, and brain rhythm measures were explored alongside. Small pilot trials like this test feasibility and safety before larger studies judge true benefit.
pmc-13341737:
Training quality for UK doctors varies more by site than by region, in a 2026 analysis by Arkadeep Dhali and colleagues of the 2025 General Medical Council National Training Survey. The dataset held 26,190 scored observations spanning 31 medical specialties, 16 deaneries, and 18 indicators.

Mean deanery gaps ran from +3.23 in the North East to −3.13 in the East of England; the North East beat the national average on 17 of 18 indicators, led by regional teaching at +7.34. Study leave in the East of England lagged by −10.17. Such decomposition tells regulators where problems live: whole regions versus single hospitals.
pmc-13341937:
A through-skin hearing implant proves cost-effective in Spain, in a 2026 economic analysis by Serafín Sánchez-Gómez and colleagues. A lifetime Markov model compared the transcutaneous Osia System against the through-skin Baha Connect for adults eligible for bone-conduction implants, from the Spanish health system's viewpoint.

Osia cost €24,555 per patient and yielded 15.94 quality-adjusted life years, versus €20,968 and 15.17 for the comparator, giving an incremental ratio of €4,651 per QALY. At a €30,000 threshold, probability of cost-effectiveness reached 62%. Utility values drove the model's sensitivity most, a caveat the authors disclose alongside the favorable headline.
pmc-13342037:
Climate change as a direct health threat is surveyed by Anna Apetrei-Pandrea and Stefan Dascalu in a 2026 narrative review. Global temperatures have risen about 1 °C since 1880, with warming since 2015 running above 0.35 °C per decade, roughly double the earlier pace.

Consequences span extreme weather, permafrost melt, and biodiversity loss, but the review centers on bodies: heat strain, oxidative stress, and weakened immunity raise infection susceptibility. Vector-borne diseases expand their ranges, while respiratory, cardiovascular, infectious, and psychiatric burdens all grow. Given modeling limits, the authors push proactive policy and adaptation over waiting for certainty.
pmc-13344237:
Boujenah Jeremy, Beddock Richard, and Patrick Rozenberg show that a small-but-normal first baby warns of a too-small second baby, in a 2026 matched case-control study. Subtle growth slowing in a first pregnancy may expose hidden placenta or mother vulnerability, so the team compared women whose second babies came out small against matched women with two normal births.

First babies of cases weighed about 300 grams less on average. A first birthweight below minus 0.5 standard deviations carried fivefold odds of a small second baby, and below minus 1 deviation the odds passed eightfold, a clear dose-response pattern confirmed in a second model. Even within the normal range, the authors argue, low weight deserves a flag for closer watching next time.
pmc-13344637:
Xiaoyun Li and co-authors describe the Big Data Science Center at the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility in 2026. Modern detectors pour out huge, fast datasets, and the center built one platform covering the whole life of the facility, from experiment setup through data archiving and sharing.

The superfacility follows findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable data principles while leaning on AI-enabled big data tools. Instead of wrestling complex operations, users get a single friendly surface that keeps the full data lifecycle compliant and traceable. The design favors the data-centric path over purely experiment-driven control, aiming to speed discovery and widen the facility's reach for outside researchers.
pmc-13346037:
Longyao Cao, Hui Lu, and Dongjie Zhang report a 2026 case of emergency spine bleeding treated through two small endoscope portals. A spontaneous epidural hematoma at the neck-chest junction, confirmed on MRI at levels C7 to T2, was squeezing the patient's spinal cord, a rare crisis usually handled with wide open surgery.

Working under general anesthesia, the surgeons cleared the clot in 90 minutes with about 50 milliliters of blood loss. The patient walked with a frame by day three, and at six months reached the top recovery grade with only slight extra leg stiffness left. The authors present the two-portal route as a gentler option that spares spinal stability and speeds recovery.
pmc-13347637:
XiHui Wang and colleagues engineer the yeast Yarrowia lipolytica to make a citrus flavonoid from waste cooking oil, in a study issued in 2026. The target, (2S)-hesperetin, serves drug, food, and cosmetic uses, so genes for its plant pathway were inserted, precursor paths for key building blocks were tuned. Fat-burning steps were adjusted to free more starting material.

Stepwise gains lifted output until a 5-litre fermenter reached 488.7 mg per litre in the reported run, a strong yield from a waste feed. Turning used frying oil into a high-value health compound at once cuts waste and avoids farming or chemical routes. The plan is offered as a template for other flavonoids.
pmc-13347737:
P. Kaviyarasan and co-authors pilot two hands-on treatments for painful trigger points between the shoulder blades, in a randomised study published in 2026. Fifty patients were split between myofascial release with active stretching and a hold-relax method with the same stretching, each given five times a week for four weeks. Pain and neck movement were scored before and after.

Release work cut pain from 7.28 to 5.28 on the reported scale, clearing the set bar for a meaningful change. While the rival method eased pain by a smaller step that missed that bar. Movement gains also favoured release work, so the pilot points that arm toward a full trial.
pmc-13349037:
Qing Kong and colleagues catch attention in the act of sampling the world in rhythm, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Attention does not shine like a steady lamp; it pulses, visiting spots in turn several times a second. The team asked whether the task at hand retunes that pulse. They used flickering stimuli, each flashing at its own rate, so brain waves could tag which one attention touched.

Volunteers either picked one of two stimuli or merged both into one target. In both tasks attention pulsed in the theta band, four to six times a second. But the timing differed: the two stimuli were sampled out of step when picking, and in step when merging. Brain theta waves seemed to set that phase, and in the merging task the phase gap tracked how well people did. Attention, the authors conclude, bends its rhythm to the job.
pmc-13349837:
ZiAng Wang and ZhengGang Luan reviewed the joint role of bacterial lipopolysaccharide and the protein HMGB1 in sepsis in 2026. Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to infection with high death rates worldwide.

Lipopolysaccharide from Gram-negative bacteria starts inflammation through surface and internal sensors. Outside cells it binds HMGB1, and the pair is pulled inside through another receptor to reach lysosomes, where the membrane leaks and the toxin triggers internal caspases. That cycle releases more HMGB1, driving inflammation, clotting, and organ failure. Blocking HMGB1 has helped in animal models but has not yet reached patient care. The review maps this loop as a target for future drugs.
pmc-13349937:
Yi Yao and co-authors measured tiny retinal blood vessels in people with chronic hepatitis B in a 2026 eye imaging study at Xiangya Hospital. Although the virus mainly attacks the liver, it can affect other organs, and eye vessel changes in patients without cirrhosis were unknown.

Scans of the macula in 24 patients and 24 matched healthy people measured vessel length and perfusion density across central, inner, outer, and full zones, plus the vessel-free centre. Results were compared against liver stiffness and virus markers. Finding vessel loss tied to liver measures could reveal silent circulation harm from long-term hepatitis B and suggest when eye checks are worthwhile.
pmc-13350437:
Stephanie J. Hachey and fellow editors introduced a 2026 collection on image processing for microphysiological systems, the organ-on-chip, organoid, and printed tissue models now used to mimic human biology. These systems copy tissue structure, chemical gradients, and sometimes flow, and can screen drugs at scales real tissue cannot.

Their data, though, are growing faster than the manual methods used to read them, which are slow and hard to reproduce. The collection gathers automated and AI-driven image analysis built for these platforms. Better measurement pipelines decide whether richer models actually yield trustworthy answers for drug testing and disease research.
pmc-13350537:
Lanxin Du and colleagues used contrast ultrasound in 2026 to study kidney size and damage risk in children whose urine flows backward from bladder to kidney. Records covered 261 children seen between 2022 and 2024, 119 with reflux and 142 without.

Kidney volume, calculated from ultrasound measurements, shrank as reflux grade rose. In a subgroup also given a radiation-based kidney scan, the team modelled which factors independently predicted one kidney doing less work and kidney scarring, including urine entering the kidney tissue itself. A radiation-free test that also flags damage risk could spare children repeated nuclear scans during years of follow-up.
pmc-13350637:
Yang Wang and co-authors probed in 2026 contrast-enhanced ultrasound traits for renal cortical blood flow in hypertensive patients. Kidney microcirculation harm often precedes overt failure. Gauging perfusion matters for hypertension care. Yet objective, noninvasive measures of cortical flow remain thin.

Eighty-three hypertensive patients with no renal artery narrowing were studied in look-back at one centre. Scans ran at Beijing Hospital from 2020 to 2023. Perfusion curves from contrast-enhanced ultrasound were quantified. Height, weight, blood pressure, and kidney function estimates were also taken. Perfusion traits charted microcirculation patterns in hypertension. The work gives a quantitative base line for tracking kidney injury and treatment response with no radiation or contrast kidney harm.
pmc-13351937:
Hang Cao, Yang Zhang, Fangqiu Fu, and Haiquan Chen review over- and under-screening for lung cancer in 2026. Low-dose CT screening cuts lung cancer deaths, yet current rules miss much of its promise. The review compares screening results across regions and studies how tumours grow over time.

East Asian programmes find far more early disease, driven by ground-glass nodules in non-smokers. Slow nodules with long natural histories sit at one extreme, and fast cancers with narrow cure windows at the other. Smoking-centred rules mismatch both extremes, causing needless checks for some and missed chances for others. The authors argue for screening plans that adapt to risk and tumour behaviour.
pmc-13354337:
Bhawesh Bhattarai leads a 2026 case of an infected appendiceal mucocele blocked by a giant stone. Mucoceles are rare surgical emergencies, and stones over 2 cm count as giant with high rupture risk. A 25-year-old woman arrived with 12 hours of right lower belly pain, vomiting, and fever with chills.

Ultrasound showed the mucocele with its stone, and CT measured the dense stone at about 24 by 22 mm with appendix width of 22.6 mm. Open appendix removal was chosen to avoid rupture and mucus spread into the belly. Tissue study found no excess mucosal growth or tumour. Scan signs had raised cancer suspicion, but smooth walls argued against it.
pmc-13356637:
Sujan Ravendran and co-authors describe a 2026 platform to make gene therapy viruses in suspension cells, a more scalable route than flat cell layers. Their method grows cells in shaken flasks, adds DNA with a common carrier, and boosts output with sodium butyrate. Quality was checked by several distinct methods, from genome counts to single-particle mass measures.

Vectors made this way matched a commercial kit in genome soundness and gene delivery, in both dish cells and mouse liver and heart. One purification route gave more full virus shells and fewer cell impurities than another. The authors offer the workflow as a robust base for lab-scale virus production.
pmc-13356737:
Biao Yang and co-authors explored in 2026 how long non-coding RNAs tied to migrasomes, small structures shed by moving cells, relate to glioma brain tumors and their outlook. Using cancer atlas data for 674 patients, they screened linked RNAs and built an eight-RNA risk model, then checked it in outside cohorts where coverage allowed.

The risk score tracked survival closely in the main data, with strong accuracy. Partial scores in outside groups also tracked survival, led by one RNA called CRNDE. High-risk tumors showed more immune and stromal content and more of a certain immune cell type. The authors call the findings early leads that need full outside checks and lab work.
pmc-13357337:
Kaimei Zhou and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on lung squamous cell carcinoma, a harsh form of lung cancer. They studied a protein called CNTN-1 and its role in helping tumor cells grow and spread. Little was known about how this protein drives the cancer, so the team tested what happens when it is switched off.

In lab-grown cancer cells, turning CNTN-1 down slowed growth, spread, and invasion, and raised cell death. It also calmed stress inside the cells and a change that helps cancer cells move. Tests in mice backed up these effects. The findings mark CNTN-1 as a possible drug target for this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13358537:
Mengmeng Chen and co-authors map the research field on DNA methylation in lung cancer in a 2026 study. DNA methylation is a chemical tag that can switch genes off, and it plays a part in how non-small cell lung cancer starts. Instead of running lab tests, the team counted and charted the papers themselves.

They reviewed 573 papers from 2008 to 2025, written by thousands of researchers in 174 countries. China and the United States led the output, and seven main themes stood out, including genes being silenced by excess tags. Charts of who works with whom, and which topics are rising, help new researchers see where the field is heading.
pmc-13358737:
Michael Weis wrote a 2026 commentary on cholesterol care after heart transplant. A slow narrowing of the new heart's arteries, called cardiac allograft vasculopathy, is a top cause of late death in these patients. High cholesterol feeds the process, and standard statin drugs already help. Weis asks how far newer, stronger drugs should push cholesterol down.

The newer drugs block a protein called PCSK9 and can cut cholesterol far below what statins reach. The open question is whether that extra drop prevents the artery narrowing, and at what point low becomes too low. The piece weighs trial proof and safety to guide doctors treating transplant patients.
pmc-13358837:
Weibin Lv and co-authors present a 2026 study on a sugar-coated protein that fuels lung adenocarcinoma. The protein, MUC21, sits on cell surfaces. The team found it may drive tumor growth by quieting a receptor for retinoic acid, a vitamin A signal that normally restrains cell growth. They tested the link in patient tissue, lab cells, and mice.

Raising or lowering MUC21 in cancer cells changed how fast they grew, moved, and invaded. Tumors in mice followed the same pattern. Blocking the receptor undid some effects, backing the proposed chain. If the chain holds, MUC21 could serve as a drug target in a cancer that spreads early and often.
pmc-13360837:
Vasilios Pergialiotis led a 2026 study of how recovery pathways are put together in cancer surgery for women. Enhanced recovery programs bundle many steps, from feeding to pain control, to speed healing after surgery. The team asked whether these steps act as one linked system or as separate habits. They drew on the first 300 patients of a multi-center cohort treated at five major hospitals.

Only steps used in a fair share of cases entered the network model, which maps how steps connect to each other. The team measured which steps sit at the center of the web and hold the pattern together. Knowing the load-bearing steps helps hospitals that are just starting such programs. They can build the core first instead of chasing every item at once.
pmc-13360937:
Linfen Wu and co-authors studied licorice as a sweetener for spirits in a 2026 sensory paper. Licorice carries a potent natural sweetener, but its sweetness lingers too long in drinks, which has limited its use. Licorice extract is cheaper and easier to handle than the pure compound. The team measured how trained tasters sensed the extract in two base spirits of different strengths.

They set the levels at which tasters first notice the sweetness, name it, and still find it pleasant. A good dose came out at 30 milligrams per liter for the weaker spirit and 40 for the stronger one. They also tested puerarin, a plant compound, as a way to shorten the lingering sweet tail. The results give drink makers firm guidance for using this natural sweetener.
pmc-13361237:
Ovidiu Samoilă and co-authors review artificial intelligence for spotting a swelling eye condition in a 2026 paper. Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc caused by high pressure inside the skull. It can flag brain tumors, fluid buildup, or clots, so missing it is dangerous. The review covers AI tools that read photos of the back of the eye to find and grade this swelling.

Deep learning systems, above all the image networks called CNNs, matched or even beat expert eye doctors at the task in the studies covered. That level of skill opens doors for early spotting and quick sorting of urgent cases. The authors also see a role in telemedicine, where a photo taken far from a specialist can be read at once. The review weighs promise against the proof still needed.
pmc-13361337:
So Ra Kim and Byung-Wan Lee review a ketone body's double role in diabetes in a 2026 paper. The compound, beta-hydroxybutyrate, is best known as a backup fuel the body burns when sugar runs low. It also acts as a signal that steers stress defense, inflammation, and cell power plants. The authors ask whether its blood level is a helpful adaptation or a harmful load in diabetes.

Studies disagree. Some link higher levels to a healthier metabolic state or a useful compensation, while others tie them to worsening blood sugar control. The same split appears for diabetic heart muscle disease, where results point both ways. The review gathers the clash of evidence so clinicians can judge when ketone levels deserve worry, watching, or even welcome.
pmc-13362537:
Liang Hu and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on adding the rare earth metal cerium to an aluminum-silicon alloy used in cast parts. They tracked how cerium changed the alloy's inner structure, pull strength, and surface hardness. Cerium refined the chunky silicon crystals in the metal and created new cerium-bearing phases inside it.

The change brought an odd split: pull strength rose, reaching its best at a small cerium dose, while surface hardness fell. The team explains the split as a contest between tougher, softer phases and other strengthening effects. Breaks also turned from brittle snapping to a more ductile tearing. The findings help engineers tune cast alloys where strength matters more than surface hardness.
pmc-13364137:
Oluwatoyin Favour Olu-Olusegun and colleagues present a 2026 study on a film-forming antitranspirant, a spray that coats potato leaves and slows water loss, during tuber formation under moderate drought. Two pot trials, in a polytunnel and a glasshouse across seasons, compared drought alone against drought plus the spray, the product Vapor Gard. Leaf water state, stolon growth, and tuber count and size grades were measured.

Drought cut leaf water, stolons, and tuber set in both trials, confirming how touchy this growth stage is. The spray lifted leaf water clearly and more than doubled tuber number under drought in the first trial, with a similar gain in the second, and it shifted sizes toward market grades. Yields still trailed watered plants, so the authors call it a helper beside irrigation, not a swap.
pmc-13364737:
Abeer Omar and co-workers tell a 2026 case of a 45 year old woman whose heart stopped out of care and who woke to a hard heart call. Her heart's main pump showed the tip bulge and weak squeeze of stress heart ill, named Takotsubo. A tight bridge of heart muscle over an artery clouded the call.

Flow tests through the artery showed the bridge did not choke blood flow. Scans showed the weak squeeze heal fast, which fits stress heart ill, not a blocked artery. The case warns teams to weigh both calls when a heart stops.
pmc-13366737:
Kei Terasaki and others matched the Clutch Cutter with the Dual knife for oesophageal endoscopic submucosal dissection by non-expert endoscopists, ran the single-centre look-back cohort study in 2026. The Clutch Cutter is a grasping scissor forceps that cuts tissue like biopsy forceps, maybe making dissection easier and safer than non-scissor knives for less experienced operators.

Results of dissection performed with each device by non-experts were matched in hindsight, with completeness, safety, and procedure time. The study tests whether device design can compensate for limited experience. Endoscopy trainers gain evidence for choosing instruments that help trainees perform complex resections safely.
pmc-13371237:
Amal Khalil Y Mohammed and co-authors describe lung disease care at El-Obeid Teaching Hospital in Sudan in a 2026 study. They tracked people with tuberculosis, a germ that harms the lungs, from April 2023 to April 2026. Those years fell in a time of armed war in the area.

The team counted 2,193 patients, most of them men, and split near half town and half country homes. Many started drugs late, by two to six months. War risk, lack of cash, and thin clinic stock were the main blocks. The work shows how war slows basic care and lets the disease spread.
pmc-13374237:
Hongzhi Wang and others explore why palliative care lags in ethnic minority regions of China in a 2026 focus group study. Palliative care relieves suffering for serious illness, yet its growth is hard in low- and middle-income settings, above all among ethnic minorities. Seven focus groups with 56 people, including providers, policymakers, patients, and community workers, were checked thematically.

Six linked themes emerged. They were care at the margins of local systems, too few trained staff, and policies without local traction. The rest were care seen as giving up, language gaps that strain communication, and families carrying the burden of absent systems. The study turns those barriers into actionable recommendations for policymakers, arguing that palliative care must be built with local language, culture, and family realities in mind.
pmc-13374537:
Souradeep Saha and co-authors probed the daily habits of med students in a 2026 study in India. The students live in hostels at their med school, with hard study loads and loose daily times. That mix can tilt food, sleep, and move habits in poor ways, though they learn health craft each day.

The survey scored food picks, first meal habits, sleep, screen time, and sport. It also asked how much they heed food tags and parts lists. A gap twixt what they know and what they do was the key ask. Schools can use such gaps to build real aids, like sound canteen food and sleep rules.
pmc-13375837:
Wongsa Laoasiriwong and others test talk therapy for drugs follow-through among displaced Myanmar patients in Thailand in a 2026 trial. Displaced people with high blood pressure and diabetes face disease management hurdles plus mental health risks. The trial enrolled adults with poor follow-through, under 70 percent in the prior month, in a Thai shelter community. Weekly Common Elements Treatment Approach talk therapy for 4 to 12 weeks was compared against routine psychosocial support.

Of 650 adults screened, 283 were eligible and 224 consented, split evenly between arms, with about one third reporting elevated mental health symptoms. At six months, follow-through improved in both arms, with greater gains in the talk therapy arm on the MARS-5 scale. The trial suggests that structured talk therapy can lift follow-through where routine support alone falls short.
pmc-13376737:
Songming Tang and colleagues built a software toolkit in two thousand twenty-six. It analyzes DNA methylation in single cells. Methylation marks help control gene activity. Single-cell data contain many missing values by design. Older tools borrowed from RNA studies handle that poorly. The new framework was built for these data traits.

The toolkit blends sequence features with mark positions. A hybrid neural network models links between cells. It rebuilds methylation landscapes with good accuracy. Downstream tools label cell types and merge datasets. It also finds regions differing between groups. Epigenetics researchers gain one unified system. Cell-to-cell variation becomes easier to dissect.
pmc-13377837:
Xiao Tang and co-authors mapped job-ready roots in Chinese students in a 2026 study. A stratified set of 1,279 students took scales on mind stock: trust in self, hope, bounce-back, and bright views. Job read was the end score in the math.

Each part of mind stock fed job read in a clear way. A skill to bend with career change sat in the chain and held the top direct tie. A felt crush of the job hunt weak­ened each tie. Schools that build mind stock and bend skill may lift job read more than drills that teach forms and talks alone.
pmc-13378037:
Anand Sekar G and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of systems-based care for adults who live with several long-term conditions at once. The conditions covered include high blood pressure, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, kidney disease, high cholesterol, and obesity. Such patients often need care from many services that do not always work together.

From 252 records found, 11 studies met the rules for inclusion, and their results were combined in narrative form because the studies differed a lot. The clearest gains were in blood pressure and blood sugar control. Benefits were strongest when care included regular monitoring, careful adjustment of medicines, patient education, and support from pharmacists or nurses, including remote monitoring.
pmc-13382237:
Maurice van Steensel wrote a 2026 commentary titled From pixels to pimples, on screen time as a risk factor for acne. In a large genetic epidemiology study cohort spanning Singapore and Malaysia, the Chinese subgroup showed a clear link between screen time and developing acne. The author argues the link probably extends to other ethnic groups.

Screen time likely bundles several effects: light exposure and disturbed sleep unsettling the skin's daily rhythm, a sedentary lifestyle, and eating more high-energy food, which disturbs metabolism. The commentary suggests that people with moderate to severe acne should probably receive lifestyle advice alongside skin treatment. It frames acne partly as a modern lifestyle condition.
pmc-13383137:
Man Zhang's team traced how a gene pair helps the medicinal orchid Dendrobium officinale tolerate cadmium, in a 2026 study. Cadmium in reused cultivation substrate limits seedling growth, and glutathione transferases are known stress mediators, but their exact roles in this orchid were unclear. The team focused on DoGST18 and its partner DoHSP70.

DoGST18 expression raised cadmium tolerance in yeast, and overexpression lines in Arabidopsis resisted cadmium better by growth and antioxidant measures. Pull-down and mass spectrometry named DoHSP70 as a partner, confirmed by yeast two-hybrid, fluorescence, and co-immunoprecipitation tests. The module offers breeders a target for safer orchid cultivation on cadmium-tainted soils.
pmc-13383637:
Qiaolin Wang and colleagues measure whether gold can accept a hydrogen bond from a carbon-hydrogen group in 2026 work. The question matters for catalysis, where such weak contacts are often claimed but rarely measured well. The team used photoelectron imaging on gas-phase pairs of copper or gold ions with acetonitrile, backed by theory.

Bond strengths came out near 9.9 kilocalories per mole for copper and 11.8 for gold in the reported units. Charge-based attraction supplied about 60 percent of the total pull in both cases. The authors offer these values as benchmarks that settle the physical nature of this debated class of hydrogen bonds.
pmc-13385537:
Hang Wang and a large team build an AI system that drafts whole-body PET/CT reports for lung cancer staging in 2026 work. A single misplaced finding can shift a tumor stage and change treatment, yet drafting stays slow and error prone. Their two-stage system, RIDE, first writes structured stage-focused notes, then expands them organ by organ using retrieved examples.

The test cohort held 1,583 patients from three hospitals, with 520 held-out cases including many from outside sites. RIDE beat comparison systems on drafting quality and staging accuracy, and clinician ratings stayed high across sites. The authors frame the tool as decision support for human checking, not a replacement.
pmc-13386237:
Herrmann and co-authors test a thyroid hormone lookalike drug in mice in this 2026 study. The compound, called TRIAC, is a candidate treatment for conditions where thyroid hormone cannot reach tissues properly. Normal thyroid treatment risks racing hearts and overheating. The team gave TRIAC to healthy male mice for 14 days and checked body and organ responses.

The drug lowered circulating thyroxine and switched on classic thyroid responsive genes in the liver, showing real hormone like activity. Yet heart rate and blood pressure stayed normal, and the heart did not enlarge. Brown fat heat production and body temperature did not change either. Herrmann concludes TRIAC acts unevenly across tissues, sparing the heart and temperature control that standard therapy disturbs.
pmc-13386637:
Yuchan Kim, Kyung Hyun Cho, and colleagues build a self-adjusting control circuit for bacterial chemical production in 2026 work. Their E. coli strain makes 3-hydroxypropionic acid, a platform chemical needing both NADPH and malonyl-CoA in balance. Static settings cannot track shifting cell states, so the circuit senses the product itself.

Once product builds up, the circuit jointly tunes cofactor regeneration and precursor allocation without outside input. The final strain reached a titer near 3 grams per liter, about five times the unregulated control strain. Yield per glucose rose by a similar factor, which supports product-responsive control as a modular tool.
pmc-13387437:
Shinichi Yoshioka and colleagues fix a bowel blockage after hernia repair with an omental patch in a 2026 case report. An 82-year-old man developed early small bowel obstruction when the lining closure split after keyhole hernia repair. Bowel loops had stuck to the mesh through the gap, reoperation on day 21 showed.

The torn lining was too fragile to sew shut, so a flap of fatty omentum covered the defect, topped with an anti-adhesion sheet. Recovery ran smoothly, and a look inside four years later showed full lining regrowth without adhesions. The authors offer the patch as a simple, durable fallback.
pmc-13388237:
A surgical team at Shaoxing Central Hospital weighed a newer thyroid cancer operation against the traditional two-step approach. The comparison covered 352 patients treated between January 2020 and May 2024. The newer method opens a tunnel around the recurrent laryngeal nerve, the nerve that controls the voice box, and removes the tumour together with its surrounding tissue in one block.

Against the older method, the newer group had fewer temporary nerve palsies, more thorough lymph node clearance, and shorter operating times for one-sided surgery, with no recurrences found by May 2026. The authors argue that the tunnel technique protects the nerve and nearby glands while clearing nodes more completely.
pmc-13388637:
Tilottoma Kargupta's team made wound-dressing films from potato starch mixed with curcumin, the yellow compound in turmeric known for calming inflammation and fighting microbes. They tested the films for strength, water behaviour, and breakdown, then tried them on skin wounds in rats.

Adding curcumin made the films stronger, more water-repellent, and slower to dissolve. By day fourteen, rat wounds covered with them had closed almost fully, beating untreated wounds and starch-only films and matching a marketed gel. The authors present the films as a cheap, biodegradable dressing option, with human testing still ahead.
pmc-13389437:
Fereshteh Shafiei, Zahra Jowkar, and Sepideh Eslamipanah compare, in 2026, final rinse fluids used during root canal treatment. The standard rinse removes the smeared layer left by filing but can weaken dentine and does not kill germs, so the team tested chitosan and benzalkonium chloride as alternatives, alone and combined.

Ninety-five extracted human premolars were prepared to a standard root length and file size. Seventy roots were filled and loaded until they broke to test strength, while fifty split specimens were checked for surface roughness. Dentists and materials researchers gain a direct comparison of cleaning benefit against root strength, helping them judge whether newer rinses protect treated teeth from later fracture.
pmc-13390137:
Manju Varshini Bhuvaneswaran's team looked over depth sense in schizophrenia in full, a sensory domain less studied than contrast, colour, and visual linking. Following PRISMA guidance with planned sign-up, they screened major data banks through April 2026 and judged bias with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale.

Six studies compared 200 patients with 167 healthy controls, and all found reduced 3D sight. Pooling four comparable studies gave a large standard deficit, hinting depth sense is truly weakened in schizophrenia. The authors present 3D sight as a core early sensory feature worth probing for its links to daily tasks. The authors call for more work on how this early gap shapes daily tasks.
pmc-13390237:
Yan Zhuang's team used deep learning to split sepsis-induced heart dysfunction into medical phenotypes and to predict short-term life span. The condition is common, heterogeneous, and deadly, so the team analysed intensive-care records from the MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV databases with an autoencoder, dimensionality reduction, and clustering.

Three phenotypes emerged, and the high-risk group, marked by metabolism-linked acidosis and multiorgan failure, suffered 55.1 percent ninety-day mortality in the development cohort. Lactate, bilirubin, clotting indices, and coma scale drove the split, and phenotype-aware models better forecast, giving a route to stratified sepsis cardiac care.
pmc-13390737:
Ana Catarina Angelo and colleagues check, in 2026, whether magnetic resonance imaging reliably shows a newly recognised cause of outer elbow pain. Minor instability of the lateral elbow, from overuse rather than injury, was only recently described, and its imaging signs are still being defined.

Patients who had keyhole surgery between 2021 and 2024 for stubborn outer elbow pain without injury were reviewed. Several specialists scored set imaging features in confirmed cases to test how reproducible those features are between readers. Musculoskeletal radiologists gain a cross-specialty verdict on which scan signs can be trusted, since a feature that readers cannot agree on cannot guide surgery.
pmc-13391137:
Anton Alyakin and a large team test, in 2026, whether artificial intelligence can write neurosurgery board examination questions as well as human experts. Multiple-choice questions are the main format for board certification, but writing good ones consumes scarce expert time.

The team built an automated pipeline using the newest vision-language models to generate board-style self-assessment questions, then had them judged blind against authentic questions. Medical educators gain a quality comparison. It shows where machine drafting can safely save faculty time. It also shows where expert writing still wins. Every specialty that maintains large question banks faces this question.
pmc-13391437: Hulme Rios-Guerra and co-authors are the subject of a short correction notice only, issued in 2026 for their study of anticonvulsant aza-Biginelli compounds. The notice states a single fix: Maria Ines Nicolas-Vazquez should have been marked as a corresponding author, and the original article has been corrected to show this. No data, methods, or findings are changed.
pmc-13392637:
Li and co-authors present a 2026 feeding trial asking whether plant sterols, called phytosterols, can raise milk output while cutting methane intensity in dairy cows. Thirty-four mid-lactation Holstein cows were split into a control group and a group fed 15 grams per day of a phytosterol product over 50 days. The team tracked milk yield and composition, nutrient digestibility, blood chemistry, rumen fermentation, gas emissions, and the microbes living in the rumen.

Cows on phytosterols produced more milk with higher fat and protein percentages, and their energy-corrected milk also rose, all without eating more feed. Digestibility of organic matter, protein, fiber, and fat also improved. Blood glucose increased while total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol fell. Rumen microbe communities shifted as well, and methane emitted per unit of milk dropped, a gain for farm profit and climate goals alike.
pmc-13393237:
Dasha Shamarina, Lina María Cortes Rueda, David Alderson, and Anne T Collins gathered the worldwide evidence on what helps or hinders vaccination during pregnancy. Maternal shots protect newborns in their first vulnerable months, yet uptake lags in many countries. Searching seven databases produced a huge initial haul, and one hundred eighty-four studies from countries recommending whooping cough vaccination in pregnancy survived screening.

The commonest barriers sat with individuals and their circles: gaps in knowledge, pre-existing anti-vaccine beliefs, and worries about safety and effectiveness for the baby. The strongest enablers were direct recommendations from health professionals and health authorities, backed by trust in what those professionals said. The authors call hesitancy a layered problem and argue programmes must fix practical obstacles and perceptions together to lift coverage among pregnant people.
pmc-13393337:
Adrienn Molnár and co-authors profile horse blood plasma in seconds using a laser-based mass spectrometry method, aiming to check plasma quality before it is used as therapy. Plasma products are increasingly used to speed wound healing, but preparing them well is still an open problem. Their 2026 study pairs an automated sampling system with several established measurement methods.

The laser system vaporises tiny plasma samples and reads their lipid and metabolite fingerprints without extensive preparation. Certain phosphatidylcholines and fatty acids changed with centrifugation settings, marking them as candidate indicators of plasma stability and quality. Platelet and particle counts were measured by flow cytometry and light microscopy, and samples were imaged by electron microscopy. Lipid profiles correlated clearly with the density of platelet fragments, but not with vesicle counts, suggesting platelets drive much of plasma composition. The authors present the platform for high-throughput quality control and diagnostics.
pmc-13394037:
Ioanna Zimianiti and five colleagues asked whether a genetic variant tied to multiple sclerosis severity also touches cognition in the general population, using UK Biobank data. The variant, labelled rs10191329A, came out of a genome-wide study of MS disability and pointed toward brain resilience as a driver of outcome. If resilience is the mechanism, the variant might show its hand on thinking tests in healthy people and in other brain diseases too.

Reaction time, fluid intelligence, and prospective memory were the yardsticks. Associations in healthy controls were weak but consistently pointed toward poorer cognition in carriers. Similar trends appeared in MS, Parkinson's disease, and dementia groups without reaching significance. The authors read the pattern as support for their hypothesis: the variant may worsen MS outcomes by eroding general brain health rather than through anything specific to the disease.
pmc-13394637:
Hajar Alawadi and others gauge nerve-linked pain flare in long pelvic pain that spurns hormone care in a 2026 one-time study. Long pelvic pain hits over a fourth of women, oft from womb-lining growth outside the womb, and nerve-linked flare may crank pain up even when hormones fail.

Among 270 first-visit patients in a row at a French top-tier site in 2024 and 2025, pelvic nerve flare was scored with a French rule set, with nerve-like traits scored apart. Pain traits, co-signs, life quality, past harm, and past care were logged. Doctors gain hard rates and linked traits for a pain driver that shifts how they treat these women.
pmc-13394837:
Damian M. Bailey leads a 2026 call for a new kind of training in space medicine, named SpaceMed. Crewed trips now aim past Earth orbit, toward the Moon and Mars. Space strains the body through radiation, isolation, odd gravity, and distance from help. No other setting taxes human health as broadly. The authors argue that future crews need doctors trained across many fields at once.

Their program would blend body science, clinic skills, and mission know-how in deep, hands-on study. Stressors in space act together, so training should treat the body as one system. The piece sets out why such training matters now. It frames space health as a core part of exploration, not an add-on.
pmc-13394937:
Faith C. Adams and co-authors test, in 2026, how two calming drugs affect talk between the brain's two halves. Magnetic pulses can probe how one motor area quiets the other across the corpus callosum. Twenty-four adults took baclofen, lorazepam, or a dummy pill on separate days, with no one knowing which. The team measured short and long forms of cross-brain quieting in a hand muscle.

Baclofen cut both forms of quieting, while lorazepam left them unchanged. The two drugs act on sister receivers of the same calming signal, GABA. Only the B-type receiver drug moved the needle. The authors say the split sharpens drug science for stroke and Parkinson's care.
pmc-13395437:
Pola Kuhn and co-authors show, in 2026, that one DNA tag site steers spore making in a gut germ. The germ, Clostridioides difficile, spreads in hospitals through hardy spores. An enzyme named CamA tags DNA and boosts spore output, but its key target was unknown. The team found one tag site in the control zone of a gene named spoIIE.

That single tag lifts the gene's output and wakes the spore program. Some cells woke the program early, before splitting, yet could call it off and grow again. Cells that woke it after splitting stayed committed. CamA also aided mouse infection beyond spore counts. The authors flag CamA as a drug target.
pmc-13395837:
Ramin Nashebi and co-authors build, in 2026, the first maths model of a mitochondrial carrier that matches how it truly works. The carrier, SLC25A10, swaps succinate, malate, and phosphate across the power plant wall. Old models assumed both cargoes bind at once, but structure shows a ping-pong swap at one site. The new model builds that swap in, with rivalry among cargoes and full reversibility.

Bayesian fitting tuned the model to lab uptake data with honest error bars. Runs showed a fast phosphate-driven uptake phase, then a slow reshuffle between the two main cargoes. Swollen power plants boosted early flow in the model. The authors offer the frame for cousin carriers too.
pmc-13396237:
Jiabo Zhang and others offer LG-Transformer for guessing fuel traits in a 2026 paper. Green fuels are key to clean transport, but tuning engines and smoke needs true guesses of many fuel traits at once.

Unlike old graph nets on atom-bond maps, LG-Transformer builds a fuel-to-fuel link map by contrast learning, steered by shape tags and trait likeness, then spreads trait-aware hints through transformer layers. A file of 1,850 mixed fuel molecules backs training. Fuel crafters gain a clear model that spans many traits in one run.
pmc-13396737:
Mahmoud S. Elkotamy built a computer pipeline to find new blockers of GSK-3β, an enzyme long targeted in Alzheimer's disease, and reports the screen in 2026. A useful blocker must be safe and able to cross into the brain, a combination that defeats most candidates.

The funnel started with shape models built from known blockers and from the enzyme itself, run against a public compound library. Survivors faced docking tests, filters for absorption and brain entry, and toxicity predictions. Two compounds passed every gate. Long simulations of 100 nanoseconds, with energy scoring, checked whether the final pair stayed locked onto the enzyme, marking them for lab testing.
pmc-13397137:
Farbod Ebrahimi and co-authors turned ordinary paper into an ultrasensitive chemical sensor by evaporating silver onto it in a single step, and report the method in 2026. The target technique, surface-enhanced Raman scattering, reads a molecule's fingerprint from laser light, but it needs metal nanostructures that focus light into hot spots.

Paper treated with a fluorine compound repels water so strongly that arriving silver atoms bead into separate islands rather than a film. The islands came out uniform, about 29 nanometers wide. The sheets amplified signals a millionfold and detected a test dye down to 2 picomolar, with readings steady within 10 percent across samples.
pmc-13397637:
Charles O Joseph and Faraja Samwel Makwinja test drought tolerance screening in rice varieties in a 2026 study. Rice output faces growing drought threat, yet breeding for steady tolerance stays limited, chiefly on early-stage performance foretelling later growth.

Six varieties were checked under four mannitol-induced drought levels at sprouting and seedling stages, using factorial and randomized block designs with relative performance and tolerance indices. Stress level and variety interplayed strongly, with trait sensitivity varying across varieties. Breeders gain early-stage indices for picking drought-hardy rice without waiting for full-season field trials.
pmc-13397737:
Simona Neri and others track small genetic variants during mesenchymal stromal cell expansion in a 2026 study. Long use of these cells for therapy raises safety worries, and expansion risks picking genetically altered or senescent cells that harm safety and efficacy.

Stock karyotyping spots large alterations but misses small ones, so the team applied next-generation sequencing to track variants during lab expansion for regenerative uses. Within a genetically steady overall frame, shifting small-variant changes emerged. Manufacturers gain a sensitive quality control approach for cell therapy production in routine cell production.
pmc-13398137:
Junzhi Wang and co-authors reveal the switchboard that lets barnyard grass shrug off herbicides. Their 2026 study targets cytochrome P450 detox enzymes, whose control wiring was unknown despite their central role in resistance. The weed, Echinochloa crus-galli, ranks among the world's worst and threatens rice and maize yields as resistance spreads.

A transcription factor named DOF2 directly switches on detox genes, including CYP81A21 in the weed and CYP81A6 in rice. Resistant grass carries extra DOF2 at rest and makes more when sprayed, while deleting the rice counterpart leaves plants tender. A growth hormone pathway, through the DELLA protein SLR1, normally holds DOF2 back, tying weed resistance to the plant's own growth controls.
pmc-13398837:
Ningning Zheng and co-authors report, in a 2026 paper in Portuguese, early heartbeats sparked from an unusual source: the inferior vena cava. Their case concerns a 78-year-old woman with nine months of palpitations, chest tightness and fatigue, episodes lasting 10 to 30 minutes five or six times a month. Premature atrial contractions usually arise from the pulmonary veins, and the great lower vein is normally electrically quiet.

Holter monitoring counted 15,838 premature beats in 24 hours, and tracings pointed below the heart rather than to the lung veins. Beta-blocker treatment had failed to ease her symptoms, so she chose an electrophysiology study with radiofrequency ablation. The case adds the vena cava to the map of treatable triggers doctors should check.
pmc-13400037:
Daniel Correia and colleagues compared round and anatomical breast implants for reconstruction after mastectomy, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Nine comparative studies met the inclusion criteria, together covering 2,535 patients, with 1,578 receiving round implants and 957 receiving shaped ones.

Pooling the studies with a random-effects model found no meaningful difference in overall problems: the odds ratio was 0.46 favoring round implants numerically, but the confidence interval was wide and the difference not significant at a p value of 0.19 in the analysis. The authors conclude that implant shape should not be chosen on expected safety or satisfaction grounds, because the evidence shows neither. Instead they recommend shared decision-making built around the patient's chest anatomy and preferences and the surgeon's experience with each device.
pmc-13400137:
Reisler and co-authors evaluate a computer support tool that links older adults at fall risk to balance and gait exercise. Falls lead injury and injury deaths among older adults. Decision support may lift referral rates and patient access. The study used the RE-AIM frame to judge the first year of rollout. A three-month wash-in came before the measured year. Clinics sat in an academic health system.

Eligible patients were community-dwelling adults aged 65 and up seen in person. The package paired standard risk screening with an alert for positive screens. Linked order sets and ready-made note text cut clinician effort. The team tracked patient and clinician traits tied to success.
pmc-13400537:
Xianli Xu and co-authors study, in 2026, how castration changes meat quality in black Tibetan sheep raised on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Castration calms rams and eases herd management during grazing. Its effects on the meat itself, and on muscle chemistry, were unclear.

Using targeted and broad chemical profiling, the team compared meat from castrated and entire males. Castrated meat lost less drip but more water on cooking, and tested more elastic, chewy and cohesive. It also held more amino acids, including flavor-linked ones, and more fatty acids across all classes. Thirty-four differing compounds emerged, with several pathways tied to the quality shift. Castration, the authors conclude, measurably reshapes both texture and chemistry.
pmc-13400637:
Ivana Nanevski and a large German team release, in 2026, a synthetic health dataset for training artificial intelligence to assess fall risk in older people. Falls are a leading cause of accidental death in later life, yet real patient data cannot be shared freely. Fake but realistic data offer a way around the privacy barrier.

Their dataset, SynTabFall, holds over 745,000 records with 44 attributes spanning demographics, diseases, mobility and cognition. Models trained on the synthetic data matched the performance of models trained on real records for predicting fall risk. The team also describes the multi-year process, built with data protection officers and clinicians at a major hospital, plus the software used to generate and check the data.
pmc-13401137:
Demi Rianne Vintges, Marina Weerheim and Faiz Karim describe, in 2026, a man whose first clear sign of VEXAS syndrome, a recently recognized inflammatory disorder, was a fungal infection of the gullet. VEXAS arises from acquired mutations in blood-forming cells. It causes fierce, hard-to-treat inflammation with low blood counts. Its infection risks have had little attention.

The 62-year-old had recurrent fever, high inflammation markers, cartilage inflammation and skin features. His marrow showed changes too, and the causal mutation sat in most of his blood cells. Endoscopy confirmed Candida infection of the esophagus. An antifungal course treated it before the diagnosis was made. Steroids alone then failed to control VEXAS, while a weekly injected immune drug brought a good response.
pmc-13401637:
Namrata Singh, Jerry H Gurwitz, and Sarah B Lieber authored a 2026 narrative review of multiple chronic conditions in adults with autoimmune and inflammatory rheumatic diseases. Living with several long-term illnesses at once is the norm in these patients and tangles their care considerably.

The review summarises the epidemiology of multimorbidity across rheumatic diseases. Rates run higher than in age-matched general populations. They reach about 86 percent in rheumatoid arthritis and about 82 percent in lupus cohorts. Heart, lung, and mental health disorders recur often in the patterns. The burden tracks with higher death rates, worse function and quality of life, faster disability, and greater health service use and cost, driven by chronic inflammation, lifestyle, and treatment effects. The authors call for holistic, person-centred rheumatology care using multidisciplinary teams.
pmc-13401937:
Binayak Deb and a large trauma team report their experience with one-lung ventilation during surgery for chest trauma. Their 2026 look-back study comes from the apex trauma centre at AIIMS in New Delhi. Ventilating one lung while the other is operated on is harder in trauma than in planned surgery, because patients arrive short of oxygen, unstable, and inflamed.

Over six years, from January 2020 to December 2025, 117 trauma patients in a row needed one-lung ventilation. The team recorded how injuries happened and their patterns, pre-surgery body state, ventilation technique and settings, surgical approach, and results after surgery. Subgroup checks separated blunt from penetrating injuries. A central aim was finding what predicts acute respiratory distress syndrome, the severe lung failure that polytrauma patients are primed for. Data on technique choice in this group have been scarce, and the series is meant to guide practice.
pmc-13402237:
Sriram Nallamothu and co-authors recount a 40-year-old man whose mild sore throat turned into Lemierre syndrome, a dangerous spread of throat infection into the neck veins. Early signs looked like a viral cold, but within days he had fever, muscle aches, and pain on the right side of his face and neck. Local infections common in his setting could easily have masked the real problem.

Ultrasound and contrast CT, done within 48 hours of that turn, showed a clot in the internal jugular vein with septic emboli, infected fragments breaking off downstream. Treatment with intravenous antibiotics and blood thinners brought a full recovery. The authors press a simple point: a sore throat that worsens with one-sided neck pain and fever needs fast imaging, because early treatment is what keeps this rare syndrome from killing.
pmc-13402437:
Nitesh Sanghai and co-authors introduce borsantrazole, a boron-based pyrazole molecule built to fight oxidative stress on three fronts at once, tested in mice carrying the SOD1-G37R form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The compound showed brain-friendly chemistry, with low efflux ratios near 0.9 and 1.0 at the tested doses and fat solubility in a range suited to reaching the nervous system. No toxicity appeared, even over 120 days of chronic dosing.

Treated mice lived 15.1 days longer on average, with gains in both sexes, and lost far less weight, 18.3 percent against 27.1 percent in controls. Symptom onset slipped by about 24.9 days and disease onset by 25.5 days in the reported figures. Protein surveys found 51 proteins and 29 phosphorylation sites changed, including spots on neurofilament chains. The team calls the result proof of concept for a disease-modifying ALS drug, pending far more development.
pmc-13402837:
Massold and co-authors report, in 2026, the first neutral chiral tellurium catalysts that steer a reaction's handedness using only chalcogen bonding. That bond is a weak attraction between a tellurium atom's electron-poor patch and a substrate. Chalcogen bonding's directionality and the binding patches on one tellurium atom had blocked asymmetric catalysis with neutral donors. Their design pairs two triazole-telluride arms on a chiral cyclohexane backbone for two-point binding.

In the benchmark Reissert-type reaction of quinolines, the optimized catalyst reached enantiomeric ratios up to 11 to 89, strongly favoring one mirror-image product. Yields ran above 99 percent for the best substrate in their optimization. Early backbones gave over 99 percent yield but zero selectivity. The comparable hydrogen-bonding catalyst managed only 15 percent yield at a near-even 47 to 53 ratio, crediting the chalcogen bonds for the selectivity. Chloride binding studies and computation revealed the geometry behind the two-point grip.
pmc-13402937:
Victorine Mulur Ngachangong and colleagues examine what brings men into programs that prevent mother-to-child transmission of HIV in the Bamenda Health District of Cameroon, and what keeps them away. Cameroon has cut HIV prevalence to 2.3 percent by 2024, yet prevention cover for infants lags. Only about a third of children under ten receive antiretroviral treatment, even as transmission to exposed infants at six to eight weeks fell to 1.78 percent.

Male partners shape testing, clinic attendance, and treatment decisions inside households, so their absence from antenatal HIV services weakens every link in the prevention chain. The study hunts the determinants of that involvement, social, economic, cultural, and service-side, in one district where progress has been slow. The authors aim the findings at program designers who need fathers present, not only mothers, to close the last gaps in infant protection.
pmc-13403037:
Shirley N Tang and colleagues use mice carrying the fat-1 gene, which converts omega-6 fats into omega-3 fats inside the body, to test whether fat balance shields spinal discs from obesity-driven decay. Low back pain, largely a disc degeneration story, is a leading cause of disability, and Western diets rich in omega-6 fats feed inflammation. Wildtype and gene-carrying mice ate control or omega-6 heavy high-fat diets.

At 16 weeks the high-fat diet raised body fat while gene carriers gained less weight; disc height ran lower in high-fat wildtypes and higher in carriers, with sex and spinal level differences. At 60 weeks, wildtype high-fat mice carried more inflammatory signals IL-6 and IL-17A in blood, and their discs showed fibrosis, cell loss, and matrix disorder, while carrier discs were protected. The authors pitch diet or gene-based fat rebalancing as therapy candidates.
pmc-13403437:
Li Qi and co-authors charted world research in 2026 on a brain stimulation method first put forward in 2017. Two high-rate signals cross in the head so that only deep spots feel a slow beat. The hope is to reach deep brain areas with no surgery at all.

Counting and mapping published studies showed a shift over time. Early work tested the basic physics in animals, while newer work builds head models tuned to each person. Current hot topics include dose, safety risks, and fair tests against older methods. The field still needs strong human trials before clinics can rely on the approach.
pmc-13403637:
Fernanda de Andrade Ribeiro Ferreira led a team that built a teaching game in 2026 for nursing students learning sterile supply work. Sterile supply units clean and prepare tools for surgery, following a strict flow. Ten expert judges and 38 students checked the game between April and August 2023.

The game, called Rota CME, copies the unit's layout so students can walk its steps in play. Judges gave its content a score near 98 percent for validity. One part, covering game build and display, scored lower and was reworked from feedback. The result is a workable classroom tool for a little-taught topic.
pmc-13403737:
Xiaohui Li led a 2026 materials study that pairs near-zero heat expansion with oxygen ion flow in one ceramic. Hot devices such as fuel cells fail when parts swell at unlike rates. Their test material is a lanthanum-doped crystal built from linked four-sided oxygen units.

Vibrations tilt those units together, which cancels most swelling across a wide heat range. The same tilts open paths for extra oxygen ions to hop between ring spaces. Bulk swelling ranked lowest among oxide ion conductors the team surveyed. The twin trick could ease strain in hot cells, sensors, and water-splitting gear.
pmc-13404037:
Benito D Isaac and colleagues asked health workers in 2026 how electronic medical records can survive in a fragile setting like Haiti. Records promise better care, yet power cuts, weak internet, and thin funding break many systems. The team spoke at length with doctors, nurses, and data staff chosen for their know-how.

Workers tied record survival to the health of the systems around it, from power supply to politics. Old paper habits and clashing software add strain. Their fixes include linking systems so data flows, adding backup routes, and growing local staff skill. Keeping some paper steps lean, they add, helps the shift stick.
pmc-13404637:

pmc-13404937:

pmc-13405837:

pmc-13407037:

pmc-13407437:

pmc-13407937:

pmc-13408837:

pmc-13409037:

pmc-13409337:

pmc-13410137:

pmc-13410437:

pmc-13411437:

Researchers will track how many patients get screened, qualify, join, and finish. Interviews with patients and staff will probe what helps or blocks rollout. pmc-13411637:

pmc-13412537:

pmc-13415537:

pmc-13415637:

pmc-13415737:

pmc-13416137:

pmc-13416837:

pmc-13418537:

pmc-13419137:

pmc-13419237:

pmc-13420137:

pmc-13420237:

pmc-13420337:

pmc-13420437:

pmc-13421237:

pmc-13421337:

pmc-13421537:

pmc-13421837:

pmc-13422637:

pmc-13422937:

pmc-13423937:

pmc-13427137:

pmc-13427237:

pmc-13427437:

pmc-13428037:

pmc-13428737:

pmc-13429137:

pmc-13430437:
