pmc-13430637:
Adolfsson and Seppälä report from the 2026 symposium of the Nordic Association for Clinical Physics, held in Gothenburg, Sweden. The meeting ran from March 24 to 26. Its theme was collaboration and future challenges. The triennial meeting drew medical physicists from four fields. These were radiotherapy, radiology, nuclear medicine, and magnetic resonance. Attendees surveyed emerging technology and its move into Nordic practice.

An opening on history traced the group from its 1962 founding. It covered a twelve-year dormancy and the 2004 revival. The opening also noted early Nordic work that fed into international dosimetry standards. Artificial intelligence led the forward-looking sessions, but with a changed tone. Earlier symposia debated methods. The 2026 meeting focused on implementation and rollout. Plenary talks covered the physicist's role beside AI. The report's recurring message casts the medical physicist as directly serving safe patient care. The role is not only a technical specialist.
pmc-13430737:
João Vitor da Silva Borges and colleagues map how pooled donor antibodies, called polyvalent IgG, calm and steer the immune system across the body. The treatment comes from thousands of donors and has broad immune effects, yet its direct cell targets and genome-wide impact stayed fuzzy.

Blood immune cells from 20 healthy donors were grown for 72 hours with the antibody or with a mock treatment. Flow tests tracked survival, cell types, memory groups, homing receptors, and signalling proteins, while gene, small-RNA, and protein-binding maps were layered on top. Viability held up while immune function shifted, giving doctors a cell-level map for a widely used therapy.
pmc-13431437:
Han-Xing Li and co-authors ran a small crossover trial in 2026 of bright light care for sleep trouble in people with Parkinson's disease. Sleep faults strike most such patients, yet how light care may help the brain stayed unclear. Twenty-seven patients took both a month of strong light and a month of dim light, in mixed order, with a month of rest between rounds.

Strong light cut daytime sleepiness scores more than dim light did. It also lowered a sleep fault in which muscles stay tense during dream sleep. Brain scans at rest showed no clear shift in local activity or in links between watched areas after strong light. The authors read the sleep gains as real but early, with the brain path still unmapped, and they call for larger trials.
pmc-13431637:
Simon A Fromm and Simone Mattei presented a guided setup tool in 2026 for low-dose imaging on frozen-sample electron microscopes, built to work inside a widely used control program. Such microscopes now gather huge streams of sharp data for single-particle work and for views inside cells. Yet setting safe low-dose terms by hand stays a skilled, slow chore.

Beam strength, zoom, focus offset, and camera terms all shift with the machine and with the task at hand, from quick screening to full data runs. Shared labs add strain, since users arrive with wide gaps in skill. The guided flow walks each user through the same set steps, which speeds setup and keeps terms even across visits. The authors frame the tool as a way to make first-rate imaging more routine.
pmc-13432837:
López Ortíz and colleagues report a 2026 study of respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, in older adults in Mexico.  The team searched the national surveillance system for lab-confirmed cases from 2015 through 2023 and mapped patterns by age, illness, place, and time.

Of 7,958 confirmed cases at all ages, about one in eleven occurred in adults aged 50 or older. Six in ten of those patients were women, and over half had more than one long-term condition, most often high blood pressure and diabetes. About one in eight of the older patients died, a fatality share far above that in younger groups. Cases peaked in 2019. The numbers argue for RSV prevention aimed at older adults.
pmc-13433337:
Jay-Bethenny Gallimore and colleagues explore how young Barbadians living with mental health conditions experience stigma and help-seeking. Public concern about youth mental health in Barbados has grown, and stigma stands as a key barrier to seeking help.

Semi-structured interviews in 2022 with 28 Barbadians aged 18 to 24, diagnosed or self-identifying with mental health challenges, were analysed thematically. Culture shaped how mental distress is perceived, while both feared and lived stigma discouraged help-seeking. Social networks cut both ways, sometimes opening doors to help and sometimes closing them. Services get a culturally grounded case for anti-stigma work that enlists families and peers.
pmc-13433937:
Kun Liu and colleagues weigh the cost-effectiveness of adding tumour-treating fields to chemotherapy for locally advanced pancreatic cancer, using data from the PANOVA-3 trial, which showed survival gains from the combination. Novel therapies carry high prices, so clinical benefit alone cannot settle their value.

A three-state Markov model compared the combination against chemotherapy alone from American and Chinese payer viewpoints, with willingness-to-pay thresholds of 150,000 dollars and 40,026 dollars per quality-adjusted life year respectively. Lifetime costs, incremental cost-effectiveness ratios, and net health benefits were estimated, with sensitivity analyses testing the assumptions. Health systems get an economic verdict to pair with the trial's survival result.
pmc-13434637:
Jiyao Han and coauthors forge crowded alcohol molecules with exact shape control in 2026. The targets carry three phenyl rings near one carbon, a layout prized in drug design. Crowding makes twin shape centers hard to set at once. A copper catalyst sorts a mixed starting pair as the reaction runs.

Both shape centers form with strong control across many variants. Later steps turn the products into a known anti tuberculosis drug and into shape twins of a second drug. Models show the catalyst coat plus weak contacts lower the energy hill. The route gives drug chemists a flexible path to dense targets.
pmc-13435637:
Masaru Usui and coauthors speed up drug resistance checks for a cattle germ in Japan in 2026. Mycoplasma bovis causes udder and lung disease, yet culture tests take about two weeks. Their nanopore method reads four genes tied to resistance in just six hours.

Gene codes from 329 isolates were matched to lab drug thresholds for seven drugs. Clear mutation patterns foretold which drugs would fail. Resistance linked mutations surged in recent isolates versus the 2013 to 2016 set. Macrolide linked changes jumped from 1.8 percent to 43.3 percent. Vets can now pick drugs by gene read the same day.
pmc-13436637:
Carmine Nasta and coauthors count surprise tumors found in an Italian emergency ward across 2023 in 2026. Among 35,081 visits, fifty three neoplastic incidentalomas surfaced on scans done for other complaints. That rate is 1.52 per thousand visits.

Most finds came in women and in patients over sixty five. Gut tumors led at thirty one percent, with lung finds next at twenty three percent. CT scans caught about half of the finds. All cases arrived triaged as non urgent, often for belly pain or anemia. Up to a fifth may lack clear follow up paths, the authors warn.
pmc-13439237:
Andrea Doddi and a large team pin down the fungal weapon that strips leaves from cotton and olive trees, in work published in 2026. Certain strains of the wilt fungus Verticillium dahliae cause heavy leaf drop and yield loss, while kin strains do not. Genome comparisons across strains located a DNA region found only in the leaf-stripping types. That region holds two copies of a gene for a secreted effector protein, a molecule the fungus sends into plants.

Deleting both copies at once stopped disease and leaf drop in cotton and olive. Adding the effector to mild strains made them strip cotton leaves, and purified protein alone caused wilting. The protein folds in a shape new to science, shared across two fungus families. Giant mobile DNA pieces called Starships appear to have carried the gene between lineages.
pmc-13439337:
Ayman A Refai's team tested folic acid in 2026 against liver harm in rat pups born to mothers given sertraline during pregnancy and nursing. Sertraline is widely prescribed in pregnancy, yet its effects on fetal liver development were less understood, while folic acid offers antioxidant and anti-death properties as a standard prenatal supplement. Pregnant rats were split into control, folic acid, sertraline, and combined groups, with pup livers examined at birth and day fourteen.

Sertraline pups showed vacuolation, vessel congestion, and portal inflammation at birth, with partial recovery but lingering damage by day fourteen, while folic acid co-treatment eased injury markers. The paper supports folic acid as a mitigator in this animal model, not a human recommendation. Obstetric teams get a detailed developmental liver signal to follow.
pmc-13440337:
Gao, Wang, and Xiao test vagus nerve stimulation against sepsis-related lung injury in this 2026 rat study. Sepsis, a runaway response to infection, often damages the lungs and drives deaths in intensive care. Electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve is known to calm inflammation, but its downstream mechanism was unclear. The team induced sepsis by a standard abdominal procedure and examined a brain-related protein, proBDNF, in the lungs.

Stimulation significantly eased lung injury, cut inflammatory signals, reduced fluid swelling, and lowered protein leakage into the airways, while also restoring barrier-related genes. Sepsis had sharply raised lung proBDNF, and stimulation suppressed it; cutting the nerve raised it further, and blocking a cholinergic receptor weakened the benefit. Forcing proBDNF up in the lungs largely undid the protection, identifying it as a key effector.
pmc-13441237: Fan and Xie comment on a Global Burden of Disease analysis of reflux, peptic ulcer, and gastritis care quality from 1990 to 2021. They praise the scope. But they caution that the quality-of-care index is built from outcome ratios. It is not built from process measures, such as endoscopy access or Helicobacter pylori testing. So quality comparisons across health systems at different development stages may mislead. They also note that striking improvements in some low-income countries could reflect modeling and data changes, rather than real care gains.
pmc-13441337:
Pasche Koo and colleagues report a 31-year-old man who developed severe allergic contact dermatitis from wintergreen essential oil, Gaultheria procumbens, inside a compounded herbal ointment prescribed for a sprained ankle. Two days after starting it, an acute eczematous reaction erupted where the ointment touched, on the applying palm, and in both elbow and knee flexures.

Patch testing produced an extremely strong, triple-plus reaction to the ointment itself on days two and four of the readings. Ingredient-by-ingredient testing isolated the culprit: only the Gaultheria procumbens oil reacted, strongly even at 1 percent dilution, while five control patients showed no reaction to it. Tests on its component chemicals methyl salicylate, salicylaldehyde, and benzyl salicylate were all negative, pointing to another constituent of the whole oil. He also reacted to colophonium, balsam resin, fragrance mix, and lanolin, and a similar ointment had caused dermatitis three years earlier.
pmc-13441537:
MD Wasim Bari's team tested culture media in 2026 on core structure and protein-making RNA in mouse early embryos. Culture media support early embryos in vitro, yet their effects on tiny layout, especially the core that builds protein makers, were partly mapped. Fertilized mouse embryos were grown in two distinct media, CZB or alpha-MEM, with core protein placement and protein-making RNA signal counted.

Alpha-MEM embryos showed more single, enlarged nucleoli per cell but lower protein-making RNA signal than CZB embryos, with similar growth rates yet altered cell-type split. Embryo teams get evidence that medium choice reshapes core biology even when embryos look on track. IVF labs should weigh tiny effects alongside growth rates.
pmc-13442637:
Ekaterina Oleinik and colleagues test how pull patterns shape lab-grown tendon tissue in a 2026 study. Tendons heal poorly and lack good lab models, so the team grew 3D tendon tissue from tendon cells in a custom pull machine. One set of tissues sat under steady pull, while the twin set took pull in cycles.

Cycled pull raised three growth marks, Col1, Tnmd, and Sparc, past the levels in steady-pull tissue. Cells in cycled tissue also stretched long and lined up with the pull path. The authors read cycle pull as a push toward mature tendon form, closer to how real tendons work in the body. Their setup gives labs a shared bench for testing how dose and rhythm of pull steer tendon growth, a step toward better repair plans.
pmc-13442737:
Devaki Kalvapudi and colleagues describe sleep-drug care for a cesarean birth in a woman with Ellis-van Creveld syndrome in a 2026 case report. The rare gene state brings short stature, bone oddities, face and tooth traits, plus heart defects in many who carry it. The patient was 23 years old, pregnant, and set for a repeat cesarean.

Heart, airway, spine, and lung checks came first, since each one can sway the drug plan in this syndrome. The team chose a spinal block over a full sleep path, which kept her airway untouched and eased stress on her heart. A strong local drug gave full surgical numbness, and her blood flow stayed steady through birth and recovery. The authors urge case-by-case plans for rare bone states at birth.
pmc-13442837:
M. B. Izidoro's team modeled Sao Paulo rail mobility in 2026 from anonymized smart card taps in 2019 and 2020, reconstructing origin-destination flows from single-tap records. Daily weighted networks, with stations as nodes and flows as edges, were analyzed for efficiency, distance, and community structure before and during pandemic onset. A transaction sequence method inferred inter-station flows where only entry taps existed.

Early 2020 brought sharp contraction, lower efficiency, longer effective distances, and stronger fragmentation into local communities, matching survey evidence of more localized travel. Transport planners get a network framework for tracking demand shocks and community reorganization. The method should transfer to other single-tap transit systems.
pmc-13443037:
Benjamin Leahy and colleagues review water-pressure therapy for joint pain in a 2026 scoping paper. The method, hydrodissection, uses ultrasound-guided fluid to free stuck tissue near joints. Their search covered four databases and the past 15 years of work, with trials, group studies, and case sets all welcome.

From 138 finds, 21 studies passed the screens for close reading. Pain relief and function gains showed for frozen shoulder, outer hip pain, and knee arthritis in those studies. Harm rates stayed low across the set. Yet methods varied wildly, from fluid mixes to shot paths and outcome picks. The authors call the early signs bright but ask for large, strict trials with shared protocols before clinics adopt the method widely.
pmc-13443337:
Arnout Bruggeman and colleagues weigh stool transplants as care for Parkinson disease in a 2026 review. Gut signs often precede shakes by years, and clumped protein shows in gut nerves, which hints the illness may start low. Swapping gut microbes wholesale is the boldest way to reset that crew.

Animal work gives bright signs, yet human trials so far clash in their results. The review blames much of the clash on method drift: donor picks, prep steps, dose paths, and outcome sets vary trial to trial. Stool swaps also demand strict control at each step to stay safe. The authors sketch tighter trial designs and next-wave microbe goods. Their aim is a fair test of gut care for a brain illness.
pmc-13443937:
Zhenyu Wang and colleagues turn social media chatter into cues for 3D design in a 2026 paper. Posts brim with taste and style wishes, yet their loose, emotive shape reads as noise to design tools. Their frame, CoX-3D, inserts a mediation layer that turns social counts into rendering knobs with clear logic.

Tests drew on 60,500 real posts from social feeds. Stable taste patterns, once pulled out, cut shape rebuild error by more than 50 percent in their runs. Match to the target sense, read by CLIP scores, rose by 13.1 percent with those patterns in play. Factor maps split which cues steer shape and which steer style. The authors cast social text as a modelable design resource.
pmc-13444137:
Hussen Yimer and colleagues assess a 2026 carbon inventory of Sulula Mofa Forest, a dry Afro-montane forest in northern Ethiopia where national carbon records remain thin. The team sampled 42 main plots plus 210 soil and litter subplots across altitude, slope, and aspect gradients, estimating tree biomass with allometric models and lab analysis for soil and litter carbon.

Total carbon stock reached 933.9 tonnes per hectare, equal to a sequestration potential of 3,427.43 tonnes of carbon dioxide per hectare, with trees holding the largest share ahead of soil and litter. Just ten woody species held 91.15 percent of the stock, and western and southern sections plus middle and upper altitudes ran richest. The forest deserves protection as a major carbon sink, the authors argue.
pmc-13445237:
Nathazsha Gande and colleagues track a gene switch during a rare cell change in the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, where a glial cell turns into a neuron, published in 2026. The gene, cki-1, helps hold cells out of division, so its level may mark steps in the change. The authors map when the switch eases as the new neuron takes shape.

Working in the worm's tail sense organ, the team timed the change across late larval stages into adulthood. In males, cki-1 activity fell between forty and fifty hours after hatching as glial shape gave way to neuron traits. In hermaphrodites, the same cells kept strong cki-1 activity and stayed glial. The timeline gives later studies a firm frame for probing how one cell type becomes another.
pmc-13445837:
Songlang Liu and colleagues report a seventeen-year-old student whose ankle dislocated backward and inward during a basketball game, with no broken bone, published in 2026 with a review of past cases. Pure ankle dislocations of this kind are vanishingly rare, since the joint is built stable, and most stem from violent injury. A low-energy sports twist makes the case stand out.

Doctors reset the joint at once under local numbing and vein pain relief, then held it in a splint and later a walking boot. Scans confirmed a clean reset, no hidden fracture, and no vessel harm, and feeling and movement stayed intact. At one year he had full function back, with school and sport resumed without limits, which supports hands-on care over surgery here.
pmc-13446037:
Yupeng Qi and colleagues turn mung bean protein into thread-like fibrils and use them to build a calcium-set emulsion gel that works as ink for 3D food printing, in a 2026 study. Plant inks that flow under pressure yet snap back into shape are scarce. Plain mung bean protein gels too weakly for printing, so the fibril form was the bet.

Acid and heat drew the protein into worm-like fibrils, confirmed under the microscope. With calcium added and heat applied, the emulsion set into a self-standing gel that held more than ninety percent of its water. Flow tests showed the thinning under pressure and firm recovery that printing needs, and printed shapes held their form. The work opens a path to custom printed foods from plant protein.
pmc-13447237:
Kabirullah Lutfy and Marcelo López edit a 2026 collection on stress, brain peptides and alcohol use disorder. Few medicines exist for the disorder, and current ones curb drinking and relapse only modestly. Peptides, small protein-like messengers in brain and body, offer fresh targets because several shape both stress and reward circuits.

One review covered here examines how two peptides interact in a thalamus hub and may drive stress-linked craving after long alcohol use. A mouse study tests whether a pain-related peptide in another brain hub fuels anxiety during early abstinence, using tools that switch specific cells on or off. Rat work shows blocking either of two peptide receptors blunted stress-triggered return to alcohol seeking. The editors present such circuits as promising ground for relapse prevention research.
pmc-13447737:
Dookhuu and colleagues charted in 2026 how the diets of South Korean primary school children changed between 2007 and 2022, using a long-running national health survey. Children's eating shapes lifelong health, and Korea's food culture has shifted fast. The analysis covered more than ten thousand children aged six to twelve, whose one-day food records were grouped into patterns.

Three patterns emerged: a rice-based pattern, a flour-based pattern of breads and noodles, and a varied, diversified pattern. Over the study years the rice pattern shrank from well over half of children to about a third, while the varied pattern grew to nearly half. Flour-pattern children were older, skipped breakfast more, and moved less. Rice-pattern children came more often from poorer homes, and the varied group had the most favorable home habits.
pmc-13448037:
Kotheeranurak and colleagues published a 2026 proposal for a registry built for keyhole spine surgery. Endoscopic spine surgery, done through tiny cuts, has spread fast worldwide. Standard spine registries miss the fine technique details this surgery creates. The team studied global registry models to design a better fit.

Their plan sorts data into four domains, from patient background to long-term outcomes. A lean core set keeps the burden low for busy surgical teams. Extra modules cover imaging checks and surgeon learning curves under tight governance. Patient-reported outcomes, gathered on phones, track recovery from the first days onward. The authors offer the plan as an add-on to existing registries, not a rival. A shared dataset would let surgeons compare results fairly across countries.
pmc-13448237:
Min Hee Lee comments in 2026 on deep learning reconstruction for a special MRI method that pictures bone in spinal arthritis. Zero echo time MRI yields CT-like bone images without radiation, yet its low signal makes subtle joint damage hard to see. A study covered here tested whether artificial intelligence denoising could lift the method past standard MRI sequences for sacroiliac joint lesions.

Fifty-two joint scans from twenty-six patients were read by three readers against CT as the reference. Full-strength reconstruction gave the best image quality for two readers and the clearest lesion visibility for all. Best accuracy for bone hardening sat at mid-strength settings, while erosion detection peaked at full strength across readers. Tuning denoising strength to the lesion sought, and perhaps to body region, is the practical lesson Lee draws.
pmc-13448337:
Jain presents in 2026, as abstract MMDA-19, a national database study of breast cancer that has spread to the brain. It asks whether brain-only spread behaves differently from brain spread accompanied by metastases elsewhere, and whether the answer depends on the cancer's molecular subtype.

From the SEER registry's records of nearly thirty-seven thousand patients with newly metastatic breast cancer between 2010 and 2022, about twenty-seven hundred had brain metastases at diagnosis. Roughly eighteen percent of those had brain-only disease. Brain-only patients lived longer overall, a median of thirteen months against eleven. The gap was dramatic in one subtype: HER2-positive, hormone-negative patients with brain-only disease survived a median of twenty-nine months against eleven with wider spread. Triple negative brain-only patients also benefited modestly, while hormone-sensitive HER2-negative patients showed no difference. Surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy each added survival within the brain-only group.
pmc-13449337:
Benjamin Tengler and co-authors build in 2026 an artificial intelligence pipeline that plans adaptive radiotherapy inside a closed commercial planning system. Daily anatomy shifts during prostate treatment call for fast replanning, yet most planning software shuts outside tools out. Their AutoAdapt system predicts the dose distribution with a physics-aware transformer network. It was trained on 266 magnetic resonance images from 25 patients treated on an MR linear accelerator. The prediction then becomes plan constraints the commercial software accepts.

On ten unseen cases, every plan won a radiation oncologist's approval. AutoAdapt met every clinical objective in seven patients, against ten for manual planning, and it held the rectum's maximum dose significantly lower. Median planning time grew by only 29 seconds. The authors see the pipeline as an assistant that removes routine work from human planners while keeping quality high.
pmc-13449737:
Mingchang Pang and Huayu Yang review in 2026 a chemical tagging system on proteins, S-sulfhydration, as a possible lever against fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. The condition, now the world's commonest chronic liver disorder, runs from simple fat buildup to inflammation, scarring, and cirrhosis. Beyond gene switching, cells tune proteins after they are built, and this tag, delivered by hydrogen sulfide gas, is reversible and redox-sensitive, making it an adjustment dial for metabolism.

The review explains how the tag changes enzyme activity, protein partnerships, location, and signaling. It also explains how three enzymes manufacture the hydrogen sulfide that applies it, each with its tissue pattern and metabolic controls. Because those source enzymes link sulfur amino acid handling to liver fat regulation, the authors argue the pathway deserves testing as a therapeutic target. They frame S-sulfhydration as a regulatory layer the field has barely begun to exploit.
pmc-13449837:
Seyedeh Maryam Hashemi and colleagues tracked new cases of metabolic syndrome in southwest Iran in a 2026 cohort study. Metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors including high blood sugar and lipids, predicts chronic disease and death, yet its incidence in this region was not well measured. The team followed adults from a population cohort.

After exclusions, 1,781 at-risk adults were followed, and the overall incidence reached 102.23 cases per 1,000 person-years. Rates ran higher in women than in men and rose with older age, higher body mass, heart disease history, and abnormal blood sugar and triglycerides. Marital status also showed links. Public health planners gain local rates and risk factors to target prevention where incidence is highest.
pmc-13450237:
Emily Gaven, Sarah Siddiqui, and Molly Stout report in 2026 what they describe as the first use of the itch-blocking biologic nemolizumab injected into lesions of prurigo nodularis. The disease builds intensely itchy nodules through a self-feeding itch-scratch cycle, and scalp disease is especially stubborn. Nemolizumab normally goes under the skin as a systemic drug; it blocks the receptor for interleukin-31, the signal that drives the neuroimmune loop behind chronic itch in this condition.

Their patient, a 56-year-old man, had endured scalp-localized disease for ten years. Oral antibiotics and twenty injections of the steroid triamcinolone into the lesions had produced minimal relief. Faced with disease confined to one region, the team tried delivering the biologic intralesionally, concentrating the drug where the nodules sit rather than dosing the whole body. The authors present the approach as a novel option for localized, treatment-resistant scalp prurigo nodularis.
pmc-13450437:
Alberth Patricio Muñoz-Gualan and colleagues reanalyze in 2026 a brain stimulation trial in schizophrenia to ask whether patients who start more impaired gain working memory from treatment. Cognitive problems here barely respond to medication. The parent trial randomized 173 patients to active or sham prefrontal stimulation across ten sessions. This complete-case analysis covers the 120 who finished testing, split by clustering of their baseline scores into greater- and lesser-impairment groups.

Working memory improved more on active stimulation in both groups, by 3.68 test points in the more impaired and 2.59 in the less impaired. The effect survived statistical correction in both. No other cognitive domain cleared that bar. When the groups were rebuilt without the working-memory score, the test of whether severity changes the treatment effect came back non-significant. The authors conclude stimulation shows a working-memory signal across the severity range, not a severity-specific one.
pmc-13450537:
Ertugrul Cagri Bolek and colleagues tested a hands-on statistics workshop for rheumatology trainees in 2026, using cases from their own specialty. Statistical literacy is essential for reading research and running studies, yet clinically relevant training is scarce in subspecialty programs. The team built a workshop around rheumatology examples.

Fellows and early-career rheumatologists took a fifteen-item knowledge test and an eight-item confidence scale before and after the workshop, with course ratings and open feedback collected. Matched pre-post analysis showed gains in both knowledge and self-efficacy. The study offers a template for teaching statistics through the cases trainees actually face, rather than abstract examples.
pmc-13450637:
Chen Yang and co-authors test in 2026 whether ultrasound can speed up cold brewing of green tea without harming its taste. Cold brews take an hour or more, which slows shops that sell them. The team used sound waves on the leaves and checked the brew with taste tools and chemical scans.

Sound waves wet the leaves fast and cracked their surface, opening paths for flavor compounds to escape. Eight minutes of the treatment drew out key taste compounds at levels close to a full hour of plain cold brewing. Color, floral scent, and sweet-savory taste formed far faster. The authors pitch the method as a way to raise output while keeping quality in check.
pmc-13452237:
Junfei Zhu and co-authors engineer in 2026 a fat-tailed antigen carrier that steers cancer vaccine pieces to lymph nodes and into the cells that show them. Peptide vaccines often fail on weak delivery, so the team varied fat tails and linkers one by one. The winner pairs an oleic fat tail with a lysine linker, a charged piece that grabs albumin and keeps the carrier from clumping.

In mice, the lead carrier drove far stronger killer T cell replies than the bare peptide and triple those of a clinic-used carrier. Tumors shrank in both guard and treatment runs of a skin cancer model. The authors set linker choice beside tail choice as a design rule for peptide vaccines.
pmc-13452337:
Andrew Williams, Ramona Danielson, and Michael Osei mine in 2026 a United States birth survey for what pregnant women lived through in the COVID-19 emergency. The virus years hit mothers hard, with women of color faring worst, yet the daily stressors behind the gap were little logged. Survey data from 2020 and 2021, weighted to near half a million births, were grouped into five stress kinds.

Family and home strain touched over two fifths of women, with worry and job loss the top loads. Housing strain hit about a ninth, and a third could not get hold of guard supplies. Black, Hispanic, and Native women, plus the young and the poor, bore the heaviest shares. The authors urge ready aid plans for mothers in the next crisis.
pmc-13453037:
Xue, Chang, and Du ask whether fatty liver changes how quickly tuberculosis patients clear bacteria from their sputum, in this 2026 retrospective study. Sputum clearance is a standard marker of treatment response. They reviewed newly diagnosed, smear-positive lung tuberculosis patients treated at Taizhou People's Hospital in China between 2022 and 2025, defining delayed conversion as tests still positive after eight weeks of therapy.

Hepatic steatosis, the medical term for fatty liver, emerged as a strong independent correlate of slow clearance. Adjusted odds of delayed conversion were about eleven times higher among patients who had it. A cytokine called interleukin-18 showed a similar association, while a positive T-SPOT immune test pointed the other way, toward faster clearance. The authors suggest patients with fatty liver deserve closer monitoring during tuberculosis treatment, since slow sputum conversion can signal weaker response and longer infectiousness.
pmc-13453737:
Zhiqiang Wang and seven co-authors ask whether thyroid function can predict who gains most from immune plus chemo drugs before stomach cancer surgery. Their 2026 study covers 420 patients at five centers in Hebei from 2019 to 2024, all getting four rounds of a PD-1 blocker plus platinum chemo, then surgery. Thyroid tests were taken before treatment and tracked during it.

A favorable thyroid profile, held by 27.1 percent, came with far more complete tumor wipeouts: 43.0 percent against 16.0 percent. New thyroid trouble during treatment, seen in a quarter of patients, also marked better response and far longer survival. Three year survival hit 99.0 percent in that group against 78.4 percent without thyroid trouble. A chart adding thyroid data beat a staging only chart at forecasting response. The authors back cheap thyroid checks as part of pre treatment sorting.
pmc-13455137:
Aaron M Klepper and others showed in 2026 that dead SaCas9 fires genes harder in Nicotiana benthamiana than dead SpCas9. SaCas9 from Staphylococcus aureus beats SpCas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes for plant gene cuts, but gene-fire systems had leaned on SpCas9. The team built a one-plasmid set that set both dead forms side by side.

With Golden Gate cloning, the team joined parts for a wide-use gene-fire set. For the first time, dead SaCas9 fired reporter genes harder by aimed promoters than dead SpCas9 in plants, with both forms sharing one target site for a fair test. The pNOS promoter and a cut-down form showed fine-tune skill. Plant biotech teams gain a stronger gene-fire tool for gene control.
pmc-13455237:
Luthuli tracked isiZulu-speaking South African adults who were free of depression at the start, in the National Income Dynamics Study. The question was who met the depression cutoff by the fifth survey wave, and which social factors signaled it. At the starting wave, 28.3 percent of participants already met the screening criteria for depression.

Among those free of depression at first, 14.0 percent met criteria at follow-up in the longitudinal cohort analysis. Employment was protective, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.55 for depression at follow-up among working adults in the multivariable model. High income expectations were similarly protective, at an adjusted odds ratio of 0.50, while several other demographic and behavioral factors lost significance after adjustment. Luthuli argues the patterning shows depression risk is socially structured long before symptoms appear, so prevention must address employment and economic security rather than treatment alone.
pmc-13455337:
Zafer Güney Çağış presents a 2026 test for national entitlement, the belief that one's own nation deserves more than others regardless of merit. Group favouritism shapes politics and conflict, yet no full, checked scale had measured this belief at the national level. The author adapted a personal entitlement scale to nations and tried it with 335 young and middle-aged Turkish adults, checking its structure with two forms of factor analysis.

The eight-item scale held together as a single factor with high reliability. Scores rose alongside social dominance orientation, a preference for group hierarchy. Scores fell as a sense of global community rose. That global sense partly carried the link between hierarchy preference and national entitlement. Researchers studying nationalism, prejudice or global identity gain a short, tested tool, while the single-country adult sample counsels care in generalising.
pmc-13456937:

pmc-13457337:

pmc-13457537:

pmc-13457637:

pmc-13458237:

pmc-13458337:

pmc-13459337:

pmc-13459537:

pmc-13460837:

Success came far more often when diagnosis was quick, with a median symptom time of a few hours against eighteen hours in failures. Every child under six in the series fell in the failure group. pmc-13461637:

pmc-13461737:

pmc-13461837:

Other options are dye imaging that lights tissue under special light, and a newer trick using a dent on the lung surface.

Some look hazy on scans, some form solid lumps, and some can be felt or seen during surgery while others cannot. If the tumor can be located during the operation, a rough border method is enough. pmc-13461937:

pmc-13462437:

The proof builds distance patterns node by node and checks that no smaller set can survive a failure. pmc-13463537:

pmc-13463637:

pmc-13463937:

pmc-13464237:

pmc-13465137:

pmc-13465237:

pmc-13465937:

pmc-13466937:

pmc-13467137:

pmc-13468337:

pmc-13469337:

pmc-13469637:

pmc-13469837:

pmc-13469937:

pmc-13470037:

pmc-13471337:

pmc-13472837:

pmc-13472937:

pmc-13473437:

pmc-13473537:

pmc-13473737:

pmc-13474837:

pmc-13474937:

pmc-13475837:

pmc-13478037:
Shiyong Xin and coauthors published a 2026 computational study searching for genes shared by type 2 diabetes and bladder cancer. People with diabetes develop bladder cancer more often than others, which hints at shared biology. The team pulled cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas and diabetes data from a public expression archive.

Overlapping gene lists came from differential expression analysis and co-expression network methods, followed by pathway checks. Machine learning then picked PLAU, a gene involved in breaking down tissue scaffolding, as the strongest shared diagnostic marker. The study goes on to examine how this gene relates to disease progression in both conditions. The authors present the gene as a candidate for joint diagnostic and treatment research, pending laboratory confirmation.
pmc-13479437:
Asiyeh Shojaee published a 2026 review, as sole author, of natural products as helpers in veterinary stem cell therapy. Stem cells in animal medicine serve mostly orthopedic problems such as joint and tendon injury. Their behavior depends on many internal and external signals, and plant compounds can shift several of those signals at once.

Medicinal herbs, plant chemicals, and algal extracts show antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, anticancer, and cell-protective actions in the studies reviewed. Several agents nudged stem cells toward faster growth, better specialization, and stronger migration, the traits regeneration depends on. The author argues these natural products could prove safer and cheaper stand-ins for synthetic growth factors in animal regenerative protocols, while noting that dosing and standardization evidence remains thin.
pmc-13480137:
Anmolpreet Kaur and co-authors present a 2026 case where extreme blood fat levels fooled routine lab tests. A 51-year-old man with diabetes and high blood pressure arrived with chest pain after a recent bout of pancreas inflammation tied to high triglycerides. His blood sample looked creamy, with triglyceride levels in the thousands.

A clotting test before a heart procedure read as endless, suggesting no clot could form. A mixing check showed clotting factors were in fact normal, proving the milky sample had jammed the test rather than the blood itself. Heart imaging confirmed blocked arteries, and once fat-lowering care brought levels down, a stent procedure went ahead with success. pmc-13482337:
Antolí and colleagues use eye tracking in 2026 to separate two childhood conditions that clinicians often confuse, autism and developmental language disorder, by watching how toddlers look at faces. Children viewed paired images, one face and one object, while cameras timed their first glances and measured how long each image held them.

Children with autism turned toward faces just as the non-clinical children did, so basic social orientation was preserved rather than absent in this age group. Where autism stood apart was staying power, with stronger sustained engagement with objects than the language disorder group showed on the duration measure used. Two summary indices, covering first-glance priority and overall preference, separated both clinical groups from the non-clinical group, and the authors suggest the pattern could sharpen early differential diagnosis.
pmc-13483537:

Two variants stood out, one tied to higher odds of malaria and another tied to lower odds and to parasite burden. pmc-13483637:
YaLan Rong presents a 2026 case that widens the known genetic picture of inherited spastic paraplegia tied to the COQ4 gene. One variant had been reported before in this condition, while the second is described here for the first time in complicated spastic paraplegia. Muscle pain triggered by exercise stood out as a notable feature of his presentation. The case supports broad gene sequencing when childhood leg stiffness remains unexplained after routine workup.
pmc-13483837:
Li Mao and co-authors link women's reproductive milestones to later risk of combined heart and metabolic disease in a very large cohort. Timing of first period, menopause, and childbirths, plus number of children, are tested against new multimorbidity.

pmc-13486737:
Vaezi and colleagues analyzed how a crystal doped with erbium ions can pass a light beam's twist from one color to another. The incoming twisted beam handed its full twist to a newly generated beam, preserving both its phase pattern and its twist number in the analysis. An erbium concentration of 3 percent gave the strongest transfer efficiency among the values examined. Adjusting concentration also flipped the beams between fast and slow propagation regimes, since the crystal's bending of light changed sign. Vaezi proposes the crystal as a solid-state platform for twist-based communication links.
pmc-13487337:
Soni and colleagues untangle the evolution of the X chromosome in common marmosets in this 2026 study. These small primates are important for biomedical research, but two quirks, frequent twin births and shared blood systems between twins, distort standard population genetics methods. The team built those factors into their analysis to estimate mutation and recombination rates along the X chromosome and to infer the population's history.

Rescaling the previously inferred population history for those chromosomes fit the X well, and inferred sex ratios were nearly equal. The team also found signs of recent selective sweeps. In a sweep, a favored variant spreads fast. The signs sat at several X-linked genes, including some with significant biomedical relevance.
pmc-13487637:
Marine E Caillaud streamlines the hunt for cancer-reactive T cells in patient material with a dual-marker flow assay. Published in 2026, the T107 method briefly exposes T cells to cancer cells, then catches responders that show both a cytokine flag and a degranulation flag on their surface at once. Live responders can be sorted without prior knowledge of the target antigen.

Melanoma and sarcoma immune cell products yielded reactive cells across several receptor families and helper plus killer subsets, against both private and shared cancer targets. Sorted cells supplied paired receptor sequences, functional clones, and specificity mapping in one pipeline. Rebuilt receptors engineered into fresh T cells recognized several cancer types. Faster procurement of proven receptors could widen cell therapy beyond the few centers that manage older workflows.
pmc-13488237:
Emilie Benoni Kofod and colleagues review stigma toward patients with alcohol use disorder among doctors and nurses in a 2026 systematic review. Western hospital and primary care studies from 2014 to 2024 were screened under standard reporting rules, and eleven studies qualified. Quality was checked with a critical appraisal tool, separately for interview-based and survey-based work.

Stigmatizing views were common across the included studies, shown as stereotyping, moral judgment, avoidance, and a belief that treatment will fail. No clear differences appeared between doctors and nurses, between care settings, or across the decade covered. Interview studies were generally stronger than surveys. The authors ask for research that includes patient voices on how stigma shapes care.
pmc-13488337:
Joshua D. Sackett and colleagues hunt for the machinery that lets a marine bacterium eat electrons from solid surfaces in a 2026 study of Thioclava electrotropha. The process, extracellular electron uptake, lets microbes breathe using minerals or electrodes instead of food, with roles in ocean chemistry and biotechnology. Deleting its gene cut uptake sharply, while restoring it pushed uptake past normal. Related genes appear in thousands of species, often seemingly borrowed between lineages.
pmc-13488837:
Leonardo Peterson dos Santos and a large Brazilian team track muscle shape in rheumatoid arthritis over one year in a 2026 prospective study using ultrasound. Muscle loss drives disability in the disease, and ultrasound offers a cheap bedside way to measure thigh muscle thickness and fiber angle. The cohort held 155 patients, mostly women, with strength, function, activity, and disease activity scored at entry, and 106 people completed the follow-up scans.

Women lost fiber angle in three thigh muscles over the year, while men gained muscle thickness in two muscles in the reported figures. In women, lower disease activity and stronger grip at entry tracked with thickness gains, and disease activity predicted thickness change in the model.
pmc-13489937:
Jo Edward Lewis and colleagues separate brain sites behind gut hormone drug effects on appetite in a 2026 mouse study. Drugs that activate the GIP receptor, a gut hormone sensor, help weight loss. Blocking the same receptor also boosts weight loss when paired with related drugs. The team attacked that puzzle by deleting the receptor in one brain region at a time. Regions tested were the area postrema, a nausea-linked sensing zone, and the hypothalamus, the brain's appetite control center.

Deleting the receptor in the sensing zone dulled appetite suppression by GIP-like drugs and partly protected against diet-driven obesity. Deleting it in the hypothalamus instead removed the extra benefit of receptor blockers paired with standard drugs, while normal appetite effects stayed intact. Distinct circuits explain the paradox, the authors conclude.
pmc-13490337:
Panpan Zhang and colleagues test a second-chance immune combination in advanced solid tumors in a 2026 open-label phase 2 trial. Participants had cancers that progressed despite earlier PD-1 or PD-L1 blocking drugs, a common dead end. The pairing joins surufatinib, a daily pill that blocks blood vessel growth signals, with toripalimab, an infused PD-1 blocker, across several tumor types in separate cohorts totaling twenty-eight patients.

Two of twenty-seven evaluable patients had partial tumor shrinkage, while about two thirds achieved at least disease control in the reported results. Median time before growth was just under four months, and median survival reached thirteen months. Severe treatment side effects affected about four in ten patients, most often raised blood pressure. The authors call the signal worth larger studies.
pmc-13490537:
Nazim and team built an electric sensor tipped with a plastic molded around the drug, the common drug, to catch the drug polluting surface waters. Drug residues feed resistance in the environment, and lab analysis is too slow for routine screening. Their 2026 sensor layers graphene oxide bound to the molded polymer on a carbon probe, reading the drug indirectly through changes in current and resistance.

Spotting limits reached about half a µM in clean standards and about five µM in real environmental water, where other matter interferes. Impedance readings confirmed the molded cavities captured the target selectively over similar compounds. Nazim presents the low-cost device as a field-screening candidate for wastewater and river tracking.
pmc-13490737:

Damage rewired the pattern selectively, raising tagging of one Rab and cutting another, without simply overactivating the kinase overall in the reported data. pmc-13491637:

This common rhythm disorder often travels with diabetes and heart failure. The team measured epicardial fat, the fat layer directly covering the heart, from CT scans taken before ablation procedures.

The study included 348 registry participants whose scans, ultrasound measures, and records were analyzed together. People in the highest third for epicardial fat had roughly fivefold odds of having heart failure after adjustment for age, sex, and race. Epicardial fat also tracked with heavier hearts and higher pressure in the lung arteries. Body mass index still predicted diabetes best, so the authors suggest adding heart fat to risk checks.
pmc-13491737:
Xiangmin Liu and eight colleagues follow in 2026 how insomnia, stigma, social support, and depression move together over time in people being treated for tuberculosis. Depression is common in tuberculosis care and worsens adherence, yet most earlier evidence froze these factors at one moment. The team assessed 266 patients at three Chinese hospitals four times across six months of treatment.

Worse insomnia predicted later depressive symptoms at every step, and depression predicted later insomnia at most steps. Stigma tracked alongside depression throughout, while stronger social support came with a faster decline in symptoms. The authors recommend sleep-focused help and stigma reduction as part of tuberculosis depression care.
pmc-13491837:
Kosar Piri and four co-authors compare in 2026 internet-delivered and face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy for first-time mothers frightened of childbirth. Both therapy formats cut fear scores sharply compared with controls, and the gains held at follow-up. In-person sessions did slightly better on total fear, confidence, and positive expectations about birth, while most other measures improved equally either way. Preference for vaginal delivery climbed in both therapy groups, most strongly after in-person care, and stayed flat among controls. Flexible or blended delivery earns the authors' endorsement for prenatal services.
pmc-13492437:
Riddhi P Patel and five colleagues report in 2026 a case of Takotsubo syndrome, sudden stress-related weakening of the heart, striking after an extensive atrial ablation session. The condition mimics a heart attack with chest pain, alarming blood markers, and electrocardiogram changes. The authors blame a mix of nerve disruption, adrenaline surge, small-vessel dysfunction, and procedural stress. pmc-13493937:

pmc-13494437:
Shank and colleagues wrote guidance for emergency doctors treating patients held in immigration custody, in a 2026 commentary. Emergency departments now host more encounters with federal immigration officers, since long-standing limits on enforcement in and near hospitals were rescinded. Officers who accompany patients may try to control talk, decisions, or access. The authors build on a resource guide from the National Immigration Law Center for clinicians caring for such patients.

It also covers knowing the limits of enforcement power inside a hospital. Shank also names the moral injury clinicians suffer when pressed to bend on privacy or practice, and the treatment delays that harm patients. Its aim is a workable path that defends patient rights and medical ethics while staying within policy and law.
pmc-13494537:

pmc-13495437:

pmc-13495537:

pmc-13495737:

pmc-13499437:

pmc-13499837:

pmc-13500837:

Performance was checked by rotating training and test portions ten times. The authors report precision, recall, accuracy, error rate, and F-measure from the confusion matrix, and state that the combined method outperformed earlier approaches on this dataset.
pmc-13501637:

pmc-13501837:

pmc-13504437:

pmc-13505137:

pmc-13507137:

Four explanation tools confirmed that choices rested on real symptom patterns, not background clues.
pmc-13507337:

pmc-13508437:

pmc-13509537:
Jin and colleagues review in 2026 why cancers stop responding to mTOR inhibitors. These drugs block a central growth-control pathway in cells, and the review asks how researchers are trying to beat that resistance. Tumors adapt through several routes that the review organizes and explains.

pmc-13511437:

pmc-13512037:

The three-decade baseline is offered for health systems bracing for more frequent climate events.
pmc-13512337:

One protein stood out as a bladder-infection candidate with strong shared-cause evidence, and a urine defense protein anchored the urinary pattern. Drug potential notes were added for lead proteins.
pmc-13512537:

pmc-13515837:

pmc-13517137:

The authors sort published findings into adverse outcome pathways: chains that run from a first molecular trigger through cell damage to harm in the whole animal. They annotate how strong the proof is at every link.

Four triggers recur: direct membrane contact, protein coatings forming on particles, surface chemistry spawning reactive oxygen, and particles smuggling other pollutants inside, the Trojan horse route. Downstream, stressed powerhouses, leaky storage sacs, and scrambled cell programmes repeat across water fleas, worms, snails, and shrimp. Multi-omics data point the same way. Berber and Akbulut stress that contradictory results often make sense once particle size, charge, and weathering enter the picture.
pmc-13518237:
Magdalene Y Ho leads a ten-author team building wound materials that let the body's own pull do the dosing in a 2026 study. Stubborn wounds need growth factors, yet today's products flood them in at huge, costly doses that fade within minutes. Their scaffold carries aptamer constructs, short DNA strands that grip specific proteins. When cells tug on the material, the grips release their catch exactly where force signals repair.

The constructs harvest, concentrate, and reactivate several natural growth factors at once, from cells, wound sites, and blood material. Working doses ran orders of magnitude below clinical norms. Tests spanned rat thigh bone, mouse skin, and human skin outside the body, and plain aptamers survived enzyme-rich wound conditions. Ho's team pitches the approach as cold-chain-free and protein-free healing help, especially valuable where cost decides what care exists.
pmc-13518737:
Pei-Yin Liao and four colleagues track what happens when a hot-brewed leaf drink from Chenopodium formosanum, known as Taiwanese quinoa, undergoes kombucha-style fermentation in 2026 work. The leaves are a farm by-product rich in phenolic compounds, which are plant chemicals tied to antioxidant action. Brewing at 90 degrees for 20 minutes gave the starting infusion.

Defined yeasts and bacteria then drove stage-like shifts: early growth, a busy middle phase, and later decline. Acidity rose, sucrose broke down, organic acids built up, and phenolic and flavonoid levels climbed. Fruit fly tests hinted at changed movement and enzyme activity, though the design could not isolate fermentation as the cause. The drink looks promising as a fermentation base.
pmc-13518837:
Steven David and a large team report the AZTEC trial in 2026, a randomized phase II study pairing focused radiation with the immunotherapy drug atezolizumab in advanced triple-negative breast cancer. Lab evidence hints radiation can wake up body-wide anti-tumor responses, though the best radiation schedule was unknown. Fifty-four women received either one large dose or three smaller doses.

Median time without disease worsening was 2.5 months for the single-dose arm and 3.1 months for the multi-dose arm, too close to separate. Neither arm beat the two-month benchmark set in advance. Benefit lasting at least 24 weeks appeared in about a fifth to a quarter of patients, all with limited spread. Side effects were similar.
pmc-13518937:
Hao Liang and five colleagues simulate in 2026 how four-hole propellant grains deform while being squeezed through an extrusion die. Grain shape and hole placement govern how evenly the propellant burns, so crooked holes mean poor quality. The team prepared real grains by solvent extrusion and modeled the process with ANSYS Polyflow software.

Simulated deformation and hole drift matched the experiments closely. Flow ran fastest at the center and slowed near the walls and pins that form the holes. Lowering the inlet flow rate reduced both deformation and hole offset. The redesigned mold, Liang and co-authors report, greatly cut the bad deformation seen in production, giving makers a tested route to steadier grain quality.
pmc-13519537:
Jung and colleagues report a 2026 study building a brain organoid model of inherited Alzheimer's disease. Organoids are tiny brain-like tissues grown from stem cells. The team engineered human stem cells carrying a newly found mutation in the APP gene, named APPSeoul, and grew organoids and flat neuron cultures from them.

Both models showed hallmark disease signs: buildup of amyloid-beta protein and abnormal phosphorylation of tau protein, two changes that mark Alzheimer's in the brain. The cutting enzyme that starts amyloid production also ran higher. A drug that blocks that enzyme, a BACE1 inhibitor, cut amyloid levels and tau changes clearly in both models. A human-cell model that answers to a known drug class gives researchers a testbed for screening new treatments without relying only on animals.
pmc-13520137:
Şenay Kılınçel, Furkan Bulut, and Oğuzhan Kılınçel pool research findings in 2026 on internet addiction and mental disorders in children and adolescents. Heavy internet use is rising among youth, while links to mental illness varied across studies. Their meta-analysis searched four databases for checked studies of people aged 18 or younger from 2015 to mid-2025.

Twenty-two studies with 36,432 young people made the cut. Internet addiction was linked with depression, anxiety, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, with odds ratios ranging from 1.92 to 2.78. Gaps between studies ran moderate to high, yet subgroup checks held the pattern steady. The authors urge routine screening for problem internet use inside youth mental health checkups.
pmc-13520337:
Karin Windsperger and colleagues compare in 2026 pregnancy weight patterns in Austria before and during the COVID-19 pandemic, using the national birth registry. Their question is whether pandemic restrictions changed weight at conception, weight gain in pregnancy, or birth complications.

About 30,800 births from May to December 2020 were compared with about 162,500 births from the same months in 2015 to 2019. Weight and body mass index before pregnancy were slightly higher in the pandemic period, while total gain in pregnancy stayed at 13 kilograms. Shares of overweight and obesity rose, as did very large babies and vacuum-assisted deliveries.
pmc-13521937:
Chen and colleagues investigated in 2026 whether common variants in Wnt signaling genes, a pathway that controls cell growth, affect lung cancer risk in the Chinese Han population. Their case-control study compared 1,143 lung cancer patients with 1,172 healthy controls, focusing on gene variants with evidence they can change gene activity.

Three variants, in the genes Wnt2, Axin1, and Dvl2, were each linked with higher lung cancer risk. The Dvl2 variant also improved risk prediction when added to a model. Risk climbed further when the Dvl2 variant occurred together with exposure to cooking oil fumes, reaching about two and a half times the baseline level in that combined group. The authors say such variants could help flag people who need closer screening.
pmc-13522337:
Simanta Roy and colleagues train in 2026 machine learning models that predict nicotine delivery and blood nicotine rise in e-cigarette users from puffing behaviour, device traits and liquid use. Direct measurement normally needs laboratory replay rigs plus blood sampling, which limits scale.

Data held 259 measurements from users aged 21 to 35 years, pairing recorded puffs with robot-replayed emission tests and blood assays. Six model types competed under repeated split testing. A gradient boosting model won for both outcomes, reaching strong accuracy from puff count or liquid use plus personal and device details. Scalable exposure estimates could support regulation and cessation research.
pmc-13523037:
Ansh Gujral and colleagues report regrowing jaw bone after removing a cyst, using a graft made from eggshell plus the patient's own growth factor concentrate. Eggshell-derived nanohydroxyapatite is a cheap mineral scaffold close in makeup to natural bone.

The cyst sat in the back of the lower jaw and measured about 17.7 by 15.1 millimetres before removal. Surgeons scooped it out and packed the hole with the eggshell graft mixed with concentrated growth factor from the patient's blood. That concentrate is rich in platelets and signals that spur new blood vessels and bone growth. Early results suggest the mix can rebuild bone in such defects at low cost, Gujral says. Larger trials with longer follow-up are still needed to confirm the benefit, the authors add.
pmc-13523437:
Ruiyun Chen, Jianqi Li, and Shuqin Guan examine, in a 2026 study, a simple nutrition score measured before surgery. They ask whether it can warn of leakage where the stomach is rejoined after removal for gastric cancer. The CONUT score combines serum albumin, lymphocyte count, and total cholesterol. Leakage after such surgery can raise illness rates and slow recovery, so an early warning tool has practical value.

Records for 283 patients treated between January 2021 and January 2025 were reviewed, and 39 patients developed a clinically relevant leak within 30 days. Higher CONUT scores, diabetes, total gastrectomy, longer operating time, and greater blood loss each raised the odds in multivariable analysis. The authors built an interpretable prediction model and sorted patients into three risk tiers using predicted probability, with bootstrap and later-period checks.
pmc-13523537:
Swasti Bhatnagar and Deepsekhar Das review how lab-grown skin has advanced from simple grafts toward 3D-printed living tissue. Bad burns, wounds, and ulcers can outgrow what normal healing or donor skin can repair, the authors note.

Substitutes grew from plain scaffolds to cell-seeded builds using skin cells, support cells, and natural matrix material. In animal tests, printed grafts sped up surface regrowth and formed organised collagen plus new blood vessels. Newer ideas include printing that changes shape over time, dressings with built-in sensors, and robots printing skin in place. Bhatnagar cautions that cost, standards, and approval rules still block routine use in patients.
pmc-13526737:
Zofia Książkiewicz and others test, in a 2026 lab study, how microbe food regimes shape early life in a tiny wetland snail, Vertigo antivertigo. Microbes serve animals without backbones not only as partners or pathogens but as food, notably at fragile early stages. The snail is notable for differences in male reproductive anatomy, called phally polymorphism.

Eggs and young juveniles got mixes of litter linked bacteria, soil and litter fungi, and a cyanobacterium. Survival was the steadiest response. Fungal additions plus plant litter supported growth and survival to adulthood, while bacteria alone could not replace the intact litter community. The cyanobacterium caused severe growth stunting and complete death of the young, no matter the bacteria. When the microbes were disturbed, anatomy also shifted, with male organs reduced or absent in some animals.
pmc-13526837:
Feldstein-Bofill and colleagues published a 2026 study on tuning a superconducting qubit's tunneling style. Quantum bits in superconducting circuits rely on paired electrons tunneling across barriers. Whether pairs cross singly or in twos changes the device's behavior deeply. The team built a qubit blending two fixed junctions with a tunable nanowire one.

At a set magnetic point, single-pair tunneling faded by up to a hundredfold. Paired tunneling then ruled, shaping a double-valley energy landscape for the qubit. The team mapped the device behavior across 85 control settings in detail. Such parity control could feed new error-resistant quantum designs ahead. Their simpler build avoids the complex stacks past attempts required. Spectroscopy under magnetic flux mapped the energy shape at each setting.
pmc-13528137:
Noel Vest and thirteen colleagues study why peer support meetings thrive or stall in college recovery programs in a 2026 paper. Such programs help students stay sober on campus. The team interviewed eighteen directors and administrators. They came from five programs across the United States in 2023. A standard framework sorted the findings into themes.

Four themes cut across sites. Recovery-minded leadership helped most. Visible campus space and ties to student success goals helped too. Money and staffing decided what could last. Fit and inclusion shaped who felt welcome. Leaders with lived experience carried special credibility. Barriers included doubt about classic twelve-step access and clashes with fundraising offices. Many campuses barely knew the programs existed. The authors map fixes at each level, from meeting format to funding habits.
pmc-13528337:
Nicole Downes and five colleagues review AI systems that spot and judge bowel polyps during colonoscopy in a 2026 paper. Searches ran to June 2025. Fifty-two studies qualified, forty-three on detection help and nine on characterization. Eight systems were covered. Each detection system was pooled on its own, a stricter approach than most reviews.

Every detection system raised the adenoma detection rate versus unaided scoping. Two systems' gains missed statistical firmness. Some systems also found more advanced growths and flat lesions. Judgment tools gave mixed, weaker proof. Many studies skipped key comparisons or dropped unsure calls. Procedures ran slightly longer with detection help. No safety worries appeared. Nothing is known yet about later cancer or death rates. The authors want judgment tools tested harder and long-term follow-up added.
pmc-13530837:
Serebour and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 70, the first single-nucleus gene atlas of the healthy human patellar tendon. That tendon is the band linking kneecap to shin, whose overuse injury plagues jumping athletes. Tendons are so rich in matrix that ordinary single-cell methods destroy the cells they try to read.

The team froze tendon samples from four young adults undergoing knee ligament surgery and sequenced nearly sixty-one thousand individual nuclei. Eleven cell populations emerged. Fibroblasts dominated and split into three transcriptionally distinct subgroups, one matching a major subgroup recently reported in the quadriceps tendon. The atlas also captured blood vessel and lymphatic cells, wall cells, immune cells including resident macrophages and T cells, nerve-related cells, and fat cells. The authors offer the map as a reference for what healthy tendon homeostasis looks like at the cellular level.
pmc-13531737:
Yatong Shen and co-authors pool in 2026 the trial evidence on remote rehabilitation for arm weakness after stroke. About four in five stroke survivors keep some arm impairment, and travel limits clinic-based therapy. Nine randomized trials with 600 patients compared internet-delivered therapy against usual rehabilitation.

The remote group scored higher on a standard arm function scale, yet the gap fell short of statistical confidence. Measures of stiffness, daily arm use, and task completion showed no clear differences. Shorter programs of four weeks or less hinted at stronger gains. Blinding gaps weaken certainty, so larger careful trials remain necessary.
pmc-13531837:
Daisuke Yokoyama and colleagues test in 2026 a sugar-shaped variant of a hepatitis B surface protein as a forecast tool during antiviral therapy. Patients with one viral genotype starting standard tablets had blood stored for the new marker. Early decliners were those whose surface protein fell by a set amount within one year.

Among 106 tested patients, early decliners kept falling over five years while others barely moved. Standard markers predicted decline overall, yet in the low-protein subgroup only the new marker separated decliners after adjustment. Lower values favored decline, possibly guiding who merits stronger combination therapy.
pmc-13531937:
Vincent Cottin and colleagues mine French national health data in 2026 to see how long lung fibrosis patients stay on antifibrotic drugs in real life. Nearly five thousand adults starting one of two drugs between 2019 and 2021 were followed across diagnosis groups. Staying on therapy matters because the drugs slow scarring only while taken.

About 71 percent persisted at twelve months, with a median treatment span near 14 months. Switching drugs occurred in about one in six patients, mostly early. Regular visits, expert center care, and planned pauses for side effects supported persistence, while sparse lung testing predicted stopping.
pmc-13533437:
Jianfeng Huang and colleagues study in 2026 the layout of cuticular drusen, small deposits in the eye linked to age-related macular degeneration. Where deposits sit in the macula may affect risk of moving to late disease. The study held 87 eyes from 57 people with mid-stage disease and two years of follow-up.

Three layouts emerged, led by a central pattern, then an outer pattern, then a diffuse spread. Five eyes moved to late disease, and four came from the outer group. After adjustments that pattern still linked to higher odds, so layout may refine risk checks.
pmc-13534737:
Sanjeet S Kaintura and colleagues map in 2026 natural radioactivity and potentially toxic elements in farm soils of SAS Nagar, Punjab, India. Fast urban and farm growth makes soil monitoring vital for food safety and health. Lab measures covered uranium, thorium, potassium, and a range of metals across the district.

Average radioactivity levels ran above global means for all three main isotopes. Arsenic and cadmium stood out as the chief pollution drivers, with uranium and chromium adding moderate effects. Cancer risk estimates stayed within allowed ranges, yet arsenic, chromium, and nickel still warrant watch and targeted soil checks.
pmc-13535337:
Birtukan Ahmed and five co-authors study high blood pressure in pregnancy in a town in southeast Ethiopia, in this twenty twenty-six paper. The condition is a leading cause of death for mothers and babies worldwide. The team measured how common it was among women at pregnancy check-ups in Asella Town.

More than eight hundred women past the halfway point of pregnancy took part, picked by a set sampling method across three public health sites. Staff used interviews and chart checks, then sorted which factors could and could not be changed. The findings can guide local care to catch the condition earlier.
pmc-13535437:
Humberto Itriago and Marita Cohn study how yeast survives without telomerase by lengthening chromosome ends another way. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses the yeast Naumovozyma castellii. Without telomerase, chromosome ends shorten until cells stop dividing. Some cells escape by an alternative lengthening route.

This yeast activates that escape route unusually fast and reliably. A subtelomeric element spreads to keep ends short but stable. The authors test which repair genes the route requires. Two related genes, RAD52 and RAD51, proved essential here. Their roles differ from the better-known baker's yeast case. Cancer cells use similar escape routes, so yeast mechanisms inform tumour research.
pmc-13536237:
Iordan and co-authors describe vitamin and mineral status in children treated for anorexia nervosa at a specialist center. More than half of deaths in this illness stem from malnutrition. Low intake of energy and protein is well known, but gaps in micronutrients are less mapped in children. Some gaps, like low selenium, can raise anxiety and suicide risk. The study covered 349 young patients at a referral center for eating disorders.

The team set out to chart the full micronutrient picture in these children. They also asked whether gaps differ between the restricting type and the binge-purge type. Adult studies found frequent selenium and copper gaps. Comparable child data had been missing until now.
pmc-13538637:
Frédéric Thomas and colleagues argued that strong cancer treatments may work by breaking how tumor cells work together. Published in 2026, the essay holds that lasting control often arrives without wiping out every cancer cell. Many therapies succeed, the authors say, by shaking up the tumor's Group Phenotypic Composition, the working layout of linked cell groups.

When that layout collapses, tumors lose their grip and staying power. The authors contrast this view with the kill-the-most-cells model, noting stable disease under light or on-and-off treatment in cases like slow lymph cancers and some prostate and breast cancers. The essay offers one frame for designing treatments aimed at how tumors behave as wholes rather than cell counts alone. Readers get a fresh lens for why modest dosing can hold cancer at bay.
pmc-13540837:
Tomoaki Itaya and eight colleagues ask, in a 2026 study, whether pregabalin, a nerve-pain drug often given to cancer patients, can also feed pancreatic cancer growth. A sister drug had raised that worry in earlier work by the same group.

In dishes, two doses of pregabalin increased the number of mouse pancreatic cancer cells. Genetically engineered mice prone to this cancer received the drug daily by mouth, and their pain scores improved. Survival and tumor size, however, did not differ from untreated mice. Immune cell mixes inside tumors shifted toward attacker types, and several inflammatory signals fell. The authors judge the dish effect real yet not confirmed in living animals.
pmc-13542137:
Bence Tamás Varga and colleagues report a failed model transfer in 2026. The model concerns neurovascular uncoupling in the brain. In that state, blood flow stops answering neural demand. The state features in Alzheimer's disease. A mouse model exists, yet rat models are prized for dementia drug tests. No reliable rat version existed.

Aged Long-Evans rats got the mouse drug cocktail. Dosing ran for thirteen days into the abdomen. The blood flow blunting stayed modest and shaky. Thinking tests barely moved at all. Side effects were plain instead. Rats ate less, lost weight, and showed gut trouble. Kidney harm reached a moderate level.
pmc-13542237:
Oksana Haponova and colleagues report a 2026 materials study on hardening the working faces of impulse face seals, the ring seals used in pumps and compressors under high pressure and speed. Their method is electrospark alloying, which uses short electric sparks to fuse a coating onto a surface. The team applied a molybdenum coating, then a special paste carrying single-walled carbon nanotubes, then repeated the spark treatment on Armco iron and a tool steel.

Adding a small amount of nanotubes, 0.01 percent by weight, refined the coating structure down to the nanoscale. Hardness reached 1650 HV on the tool steel, and wear resistance more than tripled compared with coatings made without the paste. Trials on a real gas seal showed steady sealing, low leakage, and favourable temperatures, suggesting longer service life for heavily loaded compressors.
pmc-13542337:
Catherine Crockford, Roman Martin Wittig, and Cedric Girard-Buttoz wrote a framework paper in 2026 on animal calls. Language was long seen as uniquely human in its complexity. A decade of animal research has challenged parts of that view. The authors argue that progress needs shared, measurable tests. Such tests must separate simple call systems from combined ones. They build their framework from new studies of natural animal signals.

The framework sets out four transitions. First comes flexible combining of signals. Second comes learning and settling those combinations as shared habits. Third comes wider messages through varied combining methods. Fourth comes rules for ordering parts, in lines or in layers. Each step yields testable predictions, the authors say. Chimpanzee and bonobo call sequences now show early combining skill. Only humans clearly show full, meaning-based, open-ended communication so far. That claim must be tested, not assumed, they conclude.
pmc-13542437:
I Abousoliman and colleagues tested gut-guarded choline against summer heat stress in dairy cows. Published in 2026, the study fed Holstein cows gut-guarded choline on warm summer days. Heat cuts feed intake, milk yield, and milk quality, so feed aids that hold cows steady through hot spells are prized.

Choline-fed cows showed a clear drop in eye heat, with muzzle, ear, and neck readings trending lower. Feed intake, water intake, body weight, shape scores, and milk fat yield all rose clearly. The authors present gut-guarded choline as a feed plan to blunt heat harm in dairy cows. Readers get a usable feeding lever for hotter summers.
pmc-13542737:
Zijing Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 chemistry study defining a form of electronic conjugation that runs across silicon-oxygen bonds in ring-shaped siloxane polymers. Conjugation, the sharing of electrons across a structure, is what lets many plastics conduct or emit light. The team built copolymers from a four-membered vinyl-bearing siloxane ring joined with aromatic units, using a Heck coupling reaction, and also decorated rings with side groups including thiophene.

Light measurements showed shifted absorption and emission consistent with the unusual conjugation, with thiophene-bearing versions reaching the lowest-energy excited states. Two distinct emitting states appeared, suggesting more than one mechanism at work. A strong electron acceptor formed its radical anion on contact, a classic sign of conjugation, even in simple decorated rings outside any polymer chain. Computer modelling showed the ring flattens when excited. The authors present them as a new two-dimensional conjugation family.
pmc-13543637:
Chunhui Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study testing whether ordinary eye-tracking equipment can help recognise thyroid-associated ophthalmopathy, the autoimmune eye disease that distorts the tissues around the eye. A total of 229 adults at a specialist centre, 181 patients and 48 healthy controls, completed fixation, smooth-pursuit, and picture-viewing tasks while their gaze was recorded. Machine-learning models were trained on how gaze spread across a nine-zone grid during pursuit.

Fixation steadiness was similar in both groups, though patients' gaze dispersed more widely. The pursuit-based model classified patients well, reaching an accuracy score of 0.903 with age and sex included. Viewing habits also differed: patients looked less at obvious disease features in early-stage images and more at near-recovered appearances in later ones. How eyes move, the authors suggest, betrays both the disease and the patient's attention to it.
pmc-13543737:
Maria del Alamo-Sanza and colleagues published a 2026 study of how much oxygen passes through American oak barrel staves, the slow breathing that shapes ageing wine.
