Cooperage traditionally selects staves by grain width, yet its grip on oxygen transfer was unproven. The team measured 214 staves under barrel-like conditions, wine solution on one face and air on the other, and quantified density, porosity, growth rings, rays, and liquid uptake by image analysis.

American oak proved denser and less porous than French oak, with wider, more variable rings, and let through on average about sixty-eight percent less oxygen. Grain width alone predicted transfer weakly; staves with similar grain differed greatly. No single trait governed the rate, which emerged from anatomy, growth pattern, orientation, and soaking combined. Selecting wood for a target oxygenation profile, the authors argue, needs the fuller structural picture.
pmc-13546837:
Noreen Goldman and colleagues asked in 2026 whether the neighborhoods where children grow up leave a mark on heart health in young adulthood. Their data came from clinics held in 2021 to 2023 with 1,421 young adults, average age 23, drawn from a long-running study of births in large American cities. Heart health was scored on eight behavior and clinical factors, and childhood areas were grouped into three neighborhood profiles.

Schooling, racial and ethnic identity, and neighborhood environment all related to heart health scores. Living in disadvantaged areas during childhood predicted worse scores, though much of that link faded once personal characteristics were counted. At this age the differences ran mainly through behaviors such as physical activity, with clinical gaps expected to emerge later.
pmc-13547237:
Jiacheng Zhou, Gang Wu, and Yong Chen proposed in 2026 a way to judge a fuel's ignition quality from chemistry simulations, skipping the special test engines normally required. Their method matches a fuel's simulated ignition delay against reference blends under conditions that mimic the standard octane test. Several independently built chemical models were tried across a range of pressures.

At 40 bar the predictions matched measured octane numbers best, explaining nearly 99 percent of the variation. A straight-line link then turned predicted octane values into derived cetane numbers, the diesel-side measure, with fair agreement against standard measurements. Accuracy rose and fell with how well each chemical model timed ignition delay, which the authors flag as the lever for improvement.
pmc-13548537:
Kathrin Cresswell and colleagues explore how staff, patients, and caregivers view digital symptom questionnaires in cancer care, in a 2026 qualitative case study across four European clinics. The clinics sat in Brussels, Edinburgh, Oslo, and Valencia, and none yet used patient-reported outcome tools routinely. The team ran 99 interviews and watched thirty meetings and clinic sessions to understand daily work and attitudes.

Everyone valued patient-centered care, yet nobody systematically recorded patients' psychosocial needs. Staff worried a new system could add workload and strain the bond between clinician and patient, and past experience with digital tools colored opinions. Leadership, training, resources, and involving users in design were seen as decisive for adoption. The authors argue that the human setup around the software matters as much as the software itself, in every country studied.
pmc-13548637:
Qi Zhang and colleagues examine an anti-inflammatory drug, sivelestat, in critically ill COVID-19 patients, in a 2026 multicenter retrospective study from China. Severe disease is driven partly by a cytokine storm, and sivelestat blocks an enzyme released by neutrophils. From more than two thousand intensive care patients, the team used matching methods to compare 115 treated patients with 211 similar untreated ones.

Survival at twenty-eight days ran higher in the treated group, at roughly fifty-four percent against forty-one percent. Secondary measures, including days free of the ventilator and complications such as bleeding, shock, and organ injury, did not differ significantly. Giving the drug early appeared tied to lower mortality. Because treatment was not randomized, the authors present the link as suggestive and in need of trial confirmation.
pmc-13548737:
Elbek and Kılınç warn that tobacco giants are moving into cannabis in Türkiye. Their 2026 letter to the editor addresses a new public health challenge. Türkiye published cannabis cultivation rules in January 2026. Tobacco firms have eyed cannabis since the early 1970s. Smokable cannabis both threatens cigarettes and offers new products.

British American Tobacco and Philip Morris lead cannabis investment so far. BAT targets recreational and medical markets alike. PMI focuses on medical and wellness products instead. Altria leans recreational, Imperial Brands medical. BAT bought Türkiye's TEKEL back in 2008. That gives it deep production capacity inside the country. Falling cigarette sales push firms toward cannabis profits. Shared production infrastructure makes the pivot cheap. Frequent co-use of tobacco and cannabis helps too. The letter urges regulators to see the pattern early. Public health safeguards should precede industry entrenchment.
pmc-13550437:
Pingting Zhou and colleagues measure how much neighboring places and past moments help predict the Earth's surface, formalizing a geographer's old rule, in a 2026 study. Tobler's first law says near things relate more than distant ones. Prediction models bake it in without checking how far the helpful neighborhood reaches in space or time. Their framework scores the information gained from each combination of spatial and temporal lag, treating predictability itself as the signal.

Applied to global two-meter temperature records, the most informative context window differed from region to region rather than following one global recipe. The authors frame the method as a principled way to size neighborhoods and memories when building forecast models. Those models serve climate, disasters, and resources. The work refines a foundational law into a measurable design choice.
pmc-13550537:
Yuda Disastra and colleagues sequence the full genomes of three probiotic candidate bacteria and find resistance genes that ordinary drug tests nearly missed, in a 2026 safety study. The strains, two from pigs and one from a chicken, had passed the usual hurdles: surviving acid and bile, fighting gut pathogens, and forming biofilms. Genome reading confirmed dozens of probiotic genes in each and broader metabolic range in the pig strains.

Each strain also carried acquired resistance genes on DNA outside the main chromosome. One pair carried a gene giving resistance to lincomycin but not its cousin drug, matching the test results. The chicken strain carried three resistance genes, one sitting exactly at the safety cutoff for its drug, a borderline call likely reflecting a silent gene. Under European rules, all three would be barred as feed additives, proving genome checks indispensable.
pmc-13550837:
Wang and coauthors review ways to treat breast cancer that has spread to bone. Bone spread is a hard and common late stage of the illness. Drugs can ease pain and slow growth, but too little drug reaches the bone. High doses also hurt the rest of the body.

Tiny drug carriers may fix that gap, the team argues. Such carriers can be built to pile up in bone tumors. They can also shift immune cells near the tumor to fight the cancer. The review sums up new designs, test results, and blocks that still hold back use in care.
pmc-13551237:
Luke A Perry, leading a large trial team, published a 2026 pilot trial comparing two monitoring catheters in cardiac surgery. Pulmonary artery catheters are widely used, yet guidelines advise against routine use and no large randomized trial exists. At three tertiary centers, adults having bypass or aortic valve surgery were randomly assigned a pulmonary artery catheter or a simpler central venous catheter before surgery.

Of 480 patients screened, 206 were eligible and 149 were randomized, and nearly all received their assigned catheter. Data were almost complete, and days alive at home at 30 days looked similar between groups in the figures given. The authors treat the pilot mainly as proof that a full trial can recruit and follow its protocol.
pmc-13551737:
Evans Kofi Obboh, leading thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 field study of malaria mosquito biting in Simiw, a coastal forest community in Ghana's Central Region. Control tools such as treated nets and indoor spraying can shift mosquito behavior, so regular surveillance matters. Volunteers using human landing catches collected mosquitoes in dry and rainy seasons of 2021, and laboratory tests identified species, malaria parasites, and insecticide resistance genes.

Collectors caught 4,173 mosquitoes, surprisingly more in the dry season, and indoor catches of the main vector group exceeded outdoor ones in both seasons. One species, Anopheles coluzzii, dominated the identified specimens, and biting peaked between four and five in the morning. The yearly infective bite rate was substantial, which the authors use to argue for sustained local control.
pmc-13551837:
Xiuping Yin, with eight colleagues, published a 2026 study of a combined test for insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes. The team reviewed 394 patients in hospital. Patients were split at the mid-point of a standard resistance score. The team compared that score with three measures. One was adiponectin, a hormone from fat. The other two were body mass index and waist-to-hip ratio.

The high resistance group had higher body mass and waist ratios. Their adiponectin ran lower. Each measure tied to resistance on its own. The hormone tied in the protective direction. All three together split the groups better than any one alone. The team proposes the combined model for flagging high-risk patients.
pmc-13554137:
Hadi Eslami, Ali Zare, and Mahrokh Jalili measure heavy metals in leafy greens sold in Rafsanjan, Iran, in a 2026 study. Six common greens, from coriander to lettuce, were gathered across all four seasons of 2024. A fine instrument counted eleven metals in each sample. The team then judged health risk for adults and children who eat these greens.

Arsenic ranked highest among the toxic metals, followed by chromium and lead. Leek carried the worst load overall, then lettuce and radish. Risk scores for arsenic in leek passed safe lines for both age groups by a wide margin. Cancer risk estimates peaked for chromium in lettuce and arsenic in leek. The authors urge steady monitoring and hunting down the pollution sources.
pmc-13554237: Kudrin and colleagues published an author correction in 2026 to their 2024 article on a chemical mark that helps move messenger RNA into stress granules. The authors found a typo in the methods section: the amount of an antibody used to pull down stress granules was stated wrongly. The corrected text gives a 1:50 dilution instead of a fixed five-milligram amount. The authors state that the results and conclusions stand unchanged.
pmc-13554337:
Sharon Sanz Simon and co-authors test whether menopause changes how aerobic exercise affects thinking skills in healthy older women. Their 2026 paper is a secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial of two six-month exercise programmes.

Ninety-three women aged 20 to 67, of whom 43 percent were post-menopausal, exercised four days a week in either aerobic training or a stretching and toning comparison group. Seventy-six women finished the programme. Post-menopausal women in the aerobic group improved more in executive functions, the mental skills used for planning and focus, than the comparison group and pre-menopausal women did at three and six months. The authors suggest aerobic exercise may be an especially useful brain-health strategy after menopause, when dementia risk rises.
pmc-13558337:
Elsbet Lodenstein and colleagues report a Dutch design-research project that built a practical guide for social-domain professionals facing gambling problems, publishing the article in 2026. Since online gambling was legalised nationally in 2021, worries have grown for vulnerable groups, yet gambling often escapes the notice of busy professionals in education, neighbourhood work, youth work, and debt counselling. Shame and stigma also keep sufferers from seeking help early.

Through four iterative phases of exploring, defining, developing, and delivering, the team co-created the guide with professionals, prevention and gambling experts, and people with lived experience. The article reflects on what the approach taught, where it opened doors, and where it stalled. It offers other teams a tested route for turning scattered knowledge into usable frontline tools.
pmc-13558437:
Alessandro Verbo and Iacopo Verbo compared in 2026 surgical recovery with and without an enhanced recovery protocol in older patients having keyhole surgery for bowel cancer. Such protocols bundle early feeding, movement, and pain control, yet their benefit in elderly, medically complex patients is debated. The two-centre study contrasted patients treated under standard care in 2016 to 2018 with patients treated under the protocol in 2022 to 2025, using matching to balance the groups.

In 68 matched pairs, major complication rates were nearly identical between eras, as were overall complications, and deaths did not differ significantly either. The headline result is therefore a null one for harm reduction in this population. Length of stay findings and other secondary outcomes complete the comparison. The authors' message tempers enthusiasm: a protocol that helps younger patients may not move outcomes for the old and complex.
pmc-13559137:
Yu Ding and colleagues report a young child with early diabetes, whole-body fat loss, and severe insulin resistance linked to an immune gene variant. Their 2026 case report adds a literature review on related disorders.

The boy, just over three years old, developed type one diabetes, insulin allergy, progressive lipodystrophy, and mild liver problems. Fat tissue biopsy showed immune cells infiltrating the tissue. Sequencing found a damaging variant in the CTLA4 gene, also carried by his father and sister without full disease. His regulatory T cells expressed very little of the protein, and leptin was undetectable. A targeted drug normalised liver function but not blood sugar control.
pmc-13559237:
Xiaochen Meng and Wandi Wu built a machine learning model that predicts confusion after surgery to remove the food pipe in cancer patients. Postoperative delirium means sudden confusion in the days after an operation, and it worsens recovery.

Records from 1,089 patients at one Chinese hospital fed the model, of whom about 34 percent developed delirium, mostly within three days. The best of eight methods, called CatBoost, separated future cases from non-cases with an AUC of 0.930 on held-out patients. Its strongest signals were a blood inflammation ratio, patient age, and another inflammation marker, C-reactive protein. Meng offers the model as a web calculator, while warning it still needs testing at other hospitals.
pmc-13561337:
A team including Dennis Matanda tests whether community programs can shift support for female genital mutilation in Kenya. The practice endures where it is tied to marriage prospects and belonging. The team read survey data from 2,235 people in a high-prevalence county. Some had joined mixed-sex dialogues; some women had also joined women-only reflection circles.

Joining the dialogues went with far lower odds of pro-cutting beliefs and of plans to cut a daughter. It also weakened the belief that uncut girls cannot marry and raised open opposition. The paper gives rare measured proof that layered community work can move norms on this practice.
pmc-13562537:
Mohammed A. Albadrani assembles a harmonised dataset for old building materials and asks whether gentle, non-destructive measures can hint at hidden strength. Historic stone and earth-based materials vary wildly, and drilling samples out of heritage walls is rarely allowed. His 2026 analysis groups materials into seven classes, from stone to earth composites, and lines up their porosity, density, moisture uptake, strength, and heat flow. Simple links are then tested between the easy measures and the hard ones.

Porosity tracked compressive strength moderately, with a fit value of 0.62, while density tracked heat conduction strongly at 0.85. A pattern-finding method grouped the materials along one main axis that carried 82.7 percent of the variation. Albadrani stresses that seven classes make these trends exploratory, not laws. He sketches a five-step path that would feed such measures into building information models, flagging fragile elements for conservation teams.
pmc-13562637:
Jarod L. Roland and twelve colleagues test across datasets whether a small fluid space deep in the brain marks Chiari malformation type 1. The condition is defined by cerebellar tonsils slipping downward, yet reports on the fourth ventricle, a fluid cavity, have disagreed. Earlier work drew on single hospitals. The 2026 team measured volumes with two tools, one classic and one deep-learning based, in a local clinical group. They then repeated the test in a large adolescent brain study, a prospective Chiari study, and a syringomyelia consortium dataset.

Every dataset, time point, and tool told the same story: people with the malformation had a smaller fourth ventricle on average. Such consistency makes the finding hard to dismiss as a quirk. The authors frame the smaller cavity as a group-level feature that may illuminate how the condition develops, while stressing its value for individual care needs more study.
pmc-13562737:
Weiyi Zhang and colleagues built a model that generates retinal angiography videos from a single ordinary eye photograph. Fundus fluorescein angiography, which films dye moving through retinal vessels, is vital for vascular eye disease but invasive and hard to access. Colour fundus photos are cheap and simple, yet static images miss how lesions change over time. Their 2026 model, Fundus2Video, uses a generative network to turn one photo into a moving angiography sequence.

Experts judged the generated videos faithful, and the model transferred across ten external datasets to tasks including vessel segmentation, disease diagnosis, and systemic disease prediction. It also handled new tasks with little or no extra training. The authors present it as a non-invasive alternative to dye angiography and a versatile foundation model for retinal imaging.
pmc-13563737:
Ismail Abiola Adebayo and nine colleagues publish the whole genome of a drug-resistant Escherichia coli strain taken from a pregnant patient in Uganda. The strain, coded KAB-AI-497, came from a 20-year-old woman whose waters broke early, a complication tied to bacterial vaginosis. The isolate was recovered at Kabale Regional Referral Hospital, a resource-limited setting. The 2026 team extracted its DNA and read it on a high-throughput platform, then assembled and annotated the sequence with standard pipelines.

The draft genome spans 5.1 million bases across 153 pieces, with a completeness score of 98.46 percent and low contamination. Annotation found 4,726 protein-coding genes. Closest matching strain analysis confirmed the species identity at 98.43 percent similarity. Most usefully, the genome carries resistance genes against many antibiotic families, tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and penicillins among them. The authors offer the full resistance map so clinicians and researchers can judge which drugs this strain would shrug off.
pmc-13563937:
Xingxin Wang leads a 2026 cross-sectional study of oral frailty in 235 older patients with several long-term conditions at a university hospital in China, surveyed during 2024. Participants completed short scales covering mouth function, family function, nutrition risk, daily living, other illnesses, and general frailty, plus an oral health check.

More than three quarters met the study definition of oral frailty. Missing teeth, repeat hospital stays within a year, heavier illness burden, general frailty, and dry mouth each linked to the problem. General frailty predicted it best among the measures tested. Nurses and dentists get a practical list of warning signs to check in older patients with complex health needs.
pmc-13569137:
Davide Crucitti and colleagues present, in a 2026 study, IrregulAB, a free open-source web tool that helps blood bank staff interpret red cell antibody panels. Panel reading is a manual step where errors and delays persist. The program first applies rule-based screening across several test phases, then searches for the smallest set of antibodies that explains every reaction.

Screening kept the full correct antibody set in over ninety percent of both development and held-out test panels. The solver found a valid explanation in most remaining panels and reports every equally plausible answer. Because every rule is visible, hospitals can verify and adapt the tool, which its makers stress supports trained staff rather than replacing them.
pmc-13569437:
Saptarshi Mandal and co-authors demonstrate, in a 2026 study, tiny upconverting nanoparticles that blink on their own for super-resolution microscopy. This technique locates single glowing molecules to image far below normal limits. By tuning the mix of light-absorbing and light-emitting elements inside ten-nanometer particles, the team found a mix that switches on and off steadily under one infrared beam.

The particles never bleached and located with sub-angstrom precision over tens of thousands of flashes. Blue and red versions enabled multicolor imaging, resolving receptor pairs and clusters on cell membranes at single-protein level with a simple setup and no special buffers. Microscopists get durable probes that simplify very sharp imaging.
pmc-13569737:
Surya P. Bhatt and co-authors present, in a 2026 plain-language summary, pooled results from two phase three trials of dupilumab for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with type 2 inflammation. That inflammation is a pattern of airway inflammation driven by certain immune signals. Patients received the drug or a placebo for up to fifty-two weeks across the BOREAS and NOTUS trials.

The drug, which blocks two interleukin signals, cut flare-ups and symptom severity while improving lung function and quality of life, and patients tolerated it well. Because the summary restates a published analysis in accessible words, patients and general readers can grasp why a targeted biologic now serves a defined subgroup of lung disease.
pmc-13569937:
Chris Meier's team built membrane-crossing prodrugs of a favipiravir-like drug to beat its slow activation, in a 2026 study. The parent compound T-1105 blocks viral RNA synthesis once converted to its triphosphate, but that conversion is rate-limiting and inefficient. The team synthesised three series of diphosphate and triphosphate prodrugs designed to slip into cells and release the active nucleotides.

Release was confirmed in buffer, liver enzyme preparations, human cell extracts, and plasma. Several prodrugs beat the parent nucleoside against influenza A and B in dog kidney cells and against human coronavirus OC43 in human lung cells. The work validates the pronucleotide strategy for raising antiviral potency against flu and coronaviruses.
pmc-13570737:
Mohammad Salaymeh, Arianne Shahvisi, and Sohail Jannesari examine, in a 2026 paper, the wrecking of Palestinian health systems, with focus on Gaza since October 2023. They use the lens of necropolitics, a way of thinking about power exercised by exposing people to death. Long-term damage before that date and its sharp acceleration afterward are reviewed.

The authors argue that wrecking hospitals and then channeling survival through controlled aid reduces a population to bare survival while deepening dependence and control. Bioethics, they contend, needs biopolitical tools to name such extremes honestly. The piece is an argument aimed at ethics readers and health policy readers rather than a data study.
pmc-13570837:
Yi Piao and colleagues survey, in a 2026 report, electronic health record databases available in Japan as regulators there promote real-world data for drug approval and safety monitoring. Internet searches and interviews with eight database companies charted what each system holds, how records are built, and what limits them.

Strengths include wide patient coverage and ready access to laboratory values. Weaknesses include an inability to follow patients who switch hospitals, information lost during data abstraction, mostly backward-looking collection, and no shared standard between databases. Most studies so far simply observe safety and effectiveness. The report gives researchers a realistic map of Japanese record data before they design a study.
pmc-13571537:
Marisa Avvedimento argues, in a 2026 commentary, that success after transcatheter aortic valve implantation should count nonfatal complications, not only survival and a working valve. As the catheter procedure spreads to younger patients with decades ahead, early setbacks can bend the whole recovery path.

The commentary discusses a post-hoc analysis of the randomized LANDMARK trial covering 742 patients who survived the first month. Nearly a quarter had suffered an early safety event such as stroke, major bleeding, kidney injury, valve leakage, or a new pacemaker. The analysis asked whether those events predicted later death or poorer quality of life. Programs are urged to judge themselves on durable, comfortable recovery.
pmc-13573337:
Kun Wang, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 study of a gel that delivers a gene message to worn spinal discs. Disc wear is a chief cause of lasting low back pain, and no current therapy truly reverses it. A gene scan hunt pointed to a protein called ISOC1 as a strong target.

The team packed modified RNA for ISOC1 into an injectable gel that senses acid, since worn discs turn acidic. Released in that setting, ISOC1 drives the tagging and disposal of MYC, a growth switch. That disposal turns down MYC's target SBSN, which shields disc cells from lactate-linked damage and death. In rats, gel placed in the disc kept it hydrated, slowed tissue loss, and cut scarring of the outer ring. No harm showed elsewhere in the body.
pmc-13574437:
Firat Bedir and Velit Demir published a children's cohort study in two thousand twenty-six on symptoms that linger after common lung viruses. Long COVID is well studied, but lasting symptoms after RSV and flu in children were less clear. The team compared all three infections at one Istanbul hospital system.

They followed over five thousand seven hundred children with lab-confirmed infections. Four to six weeks later, about a quarter of RSV cases still had symptoms. The shares for COVID-19 and flu were similar, around a fifth. The symptom mixes differed sharply by virus. RSV left breathing and feeding trouble in young infants. COVID-19 leaned toward thinking and body-wide complaints in school-age children. The authors say follow-up should fit the virus.
pmc-13574837:
Jeandre Deon Kotze, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 trial of chair tilt and brain oxygen during shoulder surgery. Surgeons often sit patients up like a beach chair, a pose tied to rare but grave brain harm from low blood flow. The team compared the usual surgeon-chosen tilt against a fixed lower tilt of thirty degrees.

Forty-five adults having elective shoulder surgery were split at random between the two tilts. A forehead sensor tracked brain oxygen throughout, and dips of a fifth or more counted as warning events. The usual group averaged near thirty-nine degrees of tilt. Warning dips struck three patients in all, two in the usual group and one in the fixed group, a gap too small to judge. Two thirds of patients needed drugs to prop up blood pressure. No brain harm showed after surgery.
pmc-13574937:
Chenfeng Hua and colleagues published a 2026 study presenting a machine that mimics human breathing. Inhalation studies need realistic airway models. Animal tests and static models fall short. The team printed an airway from a real chest scan. The replica runs from windpipe to small bronchi.

Programmable control reproduces several breathing patterns. Nose, mouth, or combined routes can be selected. Gas exchange is built into the system. Airflow split between lungs matched human values. Particle deposits differed by breathing pattern as expected. Such a platform can test inhaled drugs and pollutants. It reduces reliance on animal experiments.
pmc-13575137:
Zhanar Kaliyeva and four colleagues tune a recipe for ceramic wall products made from power plant ash and other wastes in a 2026 study. Using ash from the Ekibastuz plant in place of clay could cut waste piles and clay use. The team varied ash share, other waste mixes, pressing time, and firing heat.

Blocks were pressed at 15 megapascals, dried, and fired between 900 and 1100 degrees Celsius. The best mix held 20 percent ash, fired at the top temperature with the longest pressing, reaching a strength of 43.5 megapascals with low water uptake. Raising ash to 30 percent weakened blocks through extra pores. Mixed-waste versions were acceptable yet never beat the tuned ash-only mix.
pmc-13575237:
Tahar Kernif leads a 2026 pilot study profiling the microbes inside ticks in northern Algeria using their proteins. Ticks carry bacteria that can affect people, livestock, and wildlife, yet functional data on North African tick microbes are scarce. The team used high-resolution mass spectrometry, a method that identifies proteins from their fragments.

Three tick species were sampled: one Rhipicephalus type and two Hyalomma types. The search found 40 bacterial genera across 32 families and four phyla. Makeup differed by tick genus and by collection site, pointing to both species and geography effects. Common genera included Streptomyces, Bacillus, and Escherichia. Peptides from Coxiella, a known tick partner microbe, appeared often. The authors offer the survey as a first protein-level map for the region.
pmc-13576137:
Shanshan Pan and five colleagues compare two spectacle designs for slowing short-sight in children in a 2026 real-world study. One design uses rings of tiny aspherical lenslets, the other spreads light with diffusion optics. Both aim to ease the eye growth that drives myopia.

The study followed 159 children aged 6 to 13 at a Nanjing hospital for one year, split evenly among the two designs and plain lenses. Both special designs slowed prescription change and eye lengthening far more than plain lenses, with no clear gap between them. In the younger band, the diffusion design's edge over plain lenses missed the strict statistical bar after correction. Older age linked to slower lengthening in both treatment groups. The authors call for bigger trials in the youngest children.
pmc-13576337:
Yuan Zhou and five colleagues test a camera-based method for recording implant positions in full dentures, in a 2026 dental study. For dentures fixed on several implants, the record of implant positions must be highly accurate. Photogrammetry uses a special camera and coded posts to capture positions digitally, promising a faster route than putty impressions.

Twenty toothless arches, ten upper and ten lower, each holding four to eight implants, were recorded both ways. Half the group repeated the camera method a month later to check consistency. Software then compared distances and angles between implants across the two methods. Statistical tests found no significant differences on the measures reported. The authors present photogrammetry as a credible clinical alternative for full-arch implant records, within the limits of this small sample.
pmc-13578237:
Zhikun Zhao and co-authors set out a 2026 framework for rebuilding the chain of events that unfolds after a disaster strikes. In the gap before a formal inquiry starts, how one event set off the next is often murky, and that fog slows the work of investigators.

Their method starts with event patterns drawn from disaster system theory, then mines news reports to pull out chain steps and the links between them. Grouping steps by meaning cleans up names so the same event is not counted twice. A scored review then checks how well the rebuilt chain holds together. The authors present the chain as an early aid for inquiry teams, giving them a first map of what happened while facts are still thin.
pmc-13578437:
Lijun Zhang and colleagues dissected how a phage enzyme kills drug-resistant mycobacteria, the germs behind tuberculosis. LysB enzymes, borrowed from viruses that attack mycobacteria, are promising antibiotic alternatives, and earlier work tied their power to a peptidoglycan-binding domain at one end. Their 2026 study asked what that domain actually does in TM4LysB and related enzymes.

The end domain proved crucial for killing, not by gripping its target better or by boosting chemistry, but likely by ferrying the enzyme to its cell-wall target layer. A conserved folded shape in the catalytic domain also proved essential for both chemistry and delivery, setting LysB apart from related cutinase enzymes. The authors point to both features as design guides for new antimycobacterial enzymes.
pmc-13580537:
Lei Chen and nine colleagues published an engineering study in two thousand twenty-six on a computer chip that works with microwaves. Some neural networks compute with waves passing through layered material instead of transistors. Optical versions are hard to make and scale, and microwave versions were bulky tabletop setups.

The team built the network on a chip using a standard semiconductor process. Linked couplers and phase shifters form the diffracting layers in a millimetre-scale footprint. The chip is over ten thousand times smaller than earlier microwave versions and answers in about two nanoseconds. Tests covered reading handwritten digits, cancelling interference between users, and helping a drone sense obstacles. Accuracy passed eighty-six percent across the demos.
pmc-13581937:
Yang and coauthors map brain shifts in migraine onto large brain networks. Migraine is a common illness that can block work and daily life. Brain scans at rest show patchy shifts in local brain activity. Those shifts vary a lot from study to study.

The team pooled 31 scan studies with more than 1,200 patients. Control groups held just over 1,000 healthy adults. A network method linked each patch to shared brain circuits. Diverse local shifts met on a small set of networks. The team also matched those networks to brain chemical maps. Shared networks may explain why local results seemed at odds.
pmc-13582337:
Alexander Wendt, Kolja Klett, Jan Benda, Benjamin Lindner, and Jan Grewe test whether faster-firing neurons really transmit information over a wider bandwidth, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Intuition says neurons spiking more often should follow faster input changes. The team measured information transmission with the coherence function. Its width defines what they call coding bandwidth.

Experimental data from weakly electric fish were reexamined. Biologically inspired neuron models fitted to real neurons were also simulated. Both showed a significant relation between firing rate and coding bandwidth. For the classic leaky integrate-and-fire model, analysis gives a linear relation at high firing rates. At very low rates, though, bandwidth stops depending on firing rate entirely. There the membrane time constant alone sets it, defying the simple intuition.
pmc-13582937:
Xiangtian Ling and colleagues mapped the eye-surface microbiome of children and teens, sorting it into five community types. The germs living on the eye's surface help guard eye health, but their mix is complex and hard to tailor to one child. Their study took eye swabs from 1,006 young people aged 3 to 18, giving 1,246 samples, and grouped the germ mixes by their lead germs.

Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria led overall, with Staphylococcus, Corynebacterium, and Streptococcus as core germs. The five eye types, each led by a different germ, tracked with age, background, and eye scores, but not sex, while their predicted food-energy pathways matched heavily. The authors offer the types as a frame for studying eye germs and health.
pmc-13583537:
Zhiyao Ma and colleagues listen to engineered cartilage breathe, and read its future in the rhythm, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Pellets of nasal cartilage cells, support stem cells, and mixtures of both were cultured for twenty-seven days while oxygen consumption was recorded non-stop. The question: can metabolism forecast matrix quality without destroying the sample?

Breathing fell into three phases: condensation, matrix synthesis, then maturation. The mix ratio steered everything. Cartilage-rich pellets turned on the hyaline program early and made the most of the slippery matrix molecule, peaking at three-to-one. Stem-cell-rich pellets breathed late and long, built the stiffest tissue at one-to-three, but flirted with hypertrophy markers. A late dip in breathing marked settling in most groups. The authors propose oxygen monitoring as an in-process gauge for tissue factories.
pmc-13585037:
Sona Bhardwaj and colleagues review the eye as a back door into the brain for parasites in this 2026 paper. The brain sits behind strong barriers, yet the eye grows from the same tissue, joins the brain through the optic nerve, and enjoys a sheltered immune status. That mix could let some parasites settle in the eye and later reach the brain.

The review tracks parasites such as Toxoplasma gondii, plus amoebas and worms that infect the eye. Routes include riding inside immune cells, breaking the blood-retina barrier during inflammation, traveling along the optic nerve, and waking up after lying quiet in eye tissue. Toxoplasma gives the firmest case so far. For most other parasites, direct proof of eye-to-brain spread is still thin, and the authors frame the idea as a warning worth testing.
pmc-13585837:
Kosaku Torii, Akimitsu Iizuka, and Mitsuro Kanda reflect on a blood antibody that may forecast immunotherapy results in esophageal cancer. The cancer type, squamous cell carcinoma of the food pipe, is often found late and tends to return. Immune checkpoint drugs are a first-line choice when it cannot be cut out. Still, some patients worsen fast on them, and doctors lack a cheap way to spot those patients ahead of time.

Their linked study measured an antibody called IgA in the blood of 20 patients before treatment. Patients with high IgA responded only rarely, while seven in ten with low IgA responded, and their disease also stayed quiet for less time. The authors note the test is cheap and easy to repeat, but the group was small, so larger studies must confirm the signal.
pmc-13585937:
Valentine Williams and colleagues run a pilot trial of stem cell therapy for arthritis in cats. Osteoarthritis is common in older cats but easy to miss, since cats hide pain and mostly just move less. Thirty-five pet cats with the disease joined across six vet clinics. They were assigned by chance to one of two doses of uterine-derived mesenchymal stromal cells, given by vein twice, or to salt water as a placebo.

Three months on, owners and vets rated treated cats as improved far more often than placebo cats, across pain and daily-life scores at both dose levels. Side effects tied to treatment were mostly brief stomach upset or drooling in the first day, and they appeared in the placebo group as well. The team calls the approach well tolerated and worth a larger trial.
pmc-13586037:
Evangelia Sereti and five colleagues combined a DNA-repair blocker with a vessel-disrupting drug against prostate cancer in mice. Olaparib blocks PARP, an enzyme tumors use to fix DNA damage. The partner compound, NOV202, wrecks tumor blood vessels and destabilizes cell scaffolding. Two prostate cancer cell lines, differing in BRCA2 status, were grown as tumors in mice. Animals received either drug or both for twenty-one days in the twenty twenty-six study.

Each drug alone slowed tumor growth in both models. NOV202 was the stronger single agent, and adding olaparib improved control modestly. Tumor tissue was stained for DNA damage, repair activity, oxygen shortage, growth, vessels, and cell death. Cell experiments checked for synergy. The combination's logic is complementary attack: starve the tumor while blocking its repair crews.
pmc-13587337:
Marco Spada and Francesco Porta argue for treating later-onset urea cycle disorders before crisis hits, in this 2026 clinical perspective. These inherited conditions block the body's way of clearing ammonia, a waste that poisons the brain. Milder forms can stay quiet into adulthood, then flare under illness, fasting, or a heavy protein load, and care today usually starts only after symptoms show.

The authors focus on glycerol phenylbutyrate, a drug already used to hold ammonia down. Quiet blood readings, they warn, can hide slow brain injury building in patients who look stable, since both ammonia and its partner glutamine strain nerve cells. Their proposal is a shift from reacting to pre-empting: start the drug earlier in chosen patients to cut the risk of lasting brain harm. They frame the case from published work and their own practice.
pmc-13587737:
Najia Hamrouni and four co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-six on pulling two dyes from water with crab shell char, aided by ultrasound. The dyes, malachite green and rhodamine B, are common pollutants. Char from blue crab shells beat raw shell bits on heat strength and pore shape. A design search set the best soak time, dye load, and heat.

At those settings the char cleared near all of both dyes. Sound waves then pushed the rates higher still, with a peak at a mid power. Light tests of the sound field backed the peak. The team credits tiny jets and shock waves from bursting bubbles for the boost.
pmc-13588637:
Malik and colleagues emulated a clinical trial in 2026 to test whether semaglutide, a weekly injection for diabetes and weight, prevents first major heart and brain events. Their patients were obese adults with type 2 diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Arthritis limits activity and fuels inflammation, compounding heart risk. Using a large United States database, they matched about a thousand new users with the same number starting other second-line diabetes drugs.

Over two years, semaglutide users had fewer of the combined events, about 13 percent against about 17 percent in controls. The gain was driven mainly by less new heart failure, at about 9 percent against about 13 percent, and users needed less escalation of arthritis drugs. Heart attack, stroke, and death alone did not split as clearly. The authors argue the drug's heart protection extends to this high-risk group, while noting emulation cannot replace a real trial.
pmc-13589137:
Huijuan Xu and eight colleagues hunt chicken genes that slam the door on two leukosis viruses. Avian leukosis viruses cause tumors and immune damage in poultry, with no vaccine available, so breeding resistance is a prime strategy. Entry of the A and K subgroups depends on a cell receptor built by the tva gene, and six resistant versions of that gene were known. The team screened Qingyuan partridge chickens for them in their 2026 study.

Five resistant versions turned up in the breed. In cell tests, one version, tvar2, blocked both viruses completely, while the other four sharply cut the K virus's success. Live bird infections matched the dish results. The resistant versions were widespread in the breed, with some flocks carrying them at high rates. The authors offer these gene versions as ready targets for breeding programs.
pmc-13592137:
Anna Charytonowicz and colleagues ran a randomized eye trial in 2026. Both arms treated glaucoma during cataract surgery. One arm implanted a stent device in the eye's drain. The other arm cut the drain open with a dual blade tool. Patients had open-angle glaucoma or high eye pressure. One surgeon operated on sixty-eight eyes. Success meant a set pressure drop or a low final pressure. Follow-up ran up to a year after surgery.

Both methods lowered eye pressure by a similar share. Pressure fell by about a seventh in each group. Glaucoma drug counts fell to zero on average in both. Full success rates at six months were close. Swelling and blood in the eye occurred more with the blade. All such events cleared without surgery. The authors call both options effective and safe. They warn that long-term proof thins as follow-up shrinks.
pmc-13592237:
Adnan Ishaq, Louise Male, and Neil R Champness tune color changing crystals by mixing two halides in one framework. Their polymers link zinc and a naphthalene based unit that darkens under light when it gains an electron. Chloride and bromide versions share the same structure, so blends across the full range could be grown. The strength of the color change grew steadily with bromide share, they found.

Computer calculations explain the trend: bromide's electron cloud overlaps the acceptor unit better than chloride's, easing electron transfer. Ishaq and the team call the result a clean composition property rule. Such dial a response behavior could serve data storage, sensing, and light driven catalysis where a graded reply beats an on off switch.
pmc-13592637:
Juliana Ofosua Addo leads a team measuring fear of childbirth among pregnant women at a primary care clinic in Kumasi, Ghana. Earlier African studies mostly split results by first time versus experienced mothers without hunting separate causes in each group. Their survey of 282 antenatal patients used a standard fear questionnaire, then ran separate models for the two groups to expose what drives fear in each.

About twenty two percent of women scored in the high to severe fear range, and first time mothers scored clearly higher. For them, family abuse history and late clinic booking raised fear. For experienced mothers, partner violence and unplanned pregnancy raised it, while schooling and strong family support lowered it. Addo and the team call for fear screening tailored to each group.
pmc-13593237:
Akiyoshi Suzuki and sixteen co-authors published an imaging study in twenty twenty-six on artificial intelligence measuring the aorta on plain CT scans. Contrast scans show the aorta crisply but are not always possible; plain scans are murkier, and measuring them by hand is slow. Seventy-nine patients who had both scan types formed the test set.

Diameters at nine standard landmarks were measured three ways and the errors compared against a one and a half millimeter tolerance. AI-assisted readings on plain scans differed from the contrast reference about as much as expert manual readings did, inside the cutoff everywhere. The AI route was also faster. The authors conclude machine help makes plain-scan aorta surveillance clinically trustworthy.
pmc-13594237:
Benilde García-de-Teresa and colleagues report a girl with classic dyskeratosis congenita despite carrying only one mutated DKC1 copy, a puzzle solved by sharply skewed X shut-off. DKC1 variants cause X-linked dyskeratosis congenita, a telomere illness, but one-copy girls rarely show disease because kind shut-off mutes the mutant copy. This 2026 case study tells of a female patient with patchy colour and bone-marrow failure carrying a new de novo DKC1 variant.

Sharply skewed shut-off switched on the mutant allele in skin cells but the healthy allele in bone marrow. The authors guess that bone-marrow pressure backing healthy cells picked a trisomy 9 clone that still could not restore normal blood making. The study confirms the variant as likely disease-causing and highlights the tangle of skewed shut-off in telomere illnesses.
pmc-13595437:
Congcong Li and colleagues surveyed nearly every student at a vocational film and television college in eastern China about e-cigarette use, reasoning that future media professionals may model behavior for young audiences. More than nine thousand students answered in April and May 2025, a response rate above ninety-nine percent.

Current vaping was uncommon, at about two percent, yet the pattern of who vaped was telling. Weak knowledge of tobacco harms multiplied the odds nearly fivefold, and having a mother who smoked raised them roughly ninefold, the strongest single factor. Older year groups, male students, seeing smoking in public, both parents smoking, and smoking roommates all added risk. Nearly half the students had seen e-cigarette advertising. The authors call for longitudinal work and special attention to students raised in smoking-normalized settings.
pmc-13595637:
Jackie Zhanbiao Li and co-authors measured what generative AI did for hospitals, using data from 160 hospitals across thirty-one Chinese provinces between 2021 and 2024. Their 2026 study drew on 1,440 hospital records to test whether the technology improved care, and what conditions shaped the effect.

Generative AI use was linked with sharper diagnosis, smoother daily work, and happier patients. The gains were not evenly spread: hospitals in regions with deeper industrial digitalization captured clearly more benefit, a sign that the technology lifts a digital base already there rather than replacing it. The authors frame the results for policy makers weighing where AI investment will pay off, arguing that pairing rollout with broader digital updates matters. They also cast the study as a window on how new tools spread through a health system.
pmc-13602037:
Elskamp and co-authors study who watches for drug clashes inside clinical trials, and who owns that duty. Trial patients often take other drugs alongside the study drug, and bad pairings can harm them. The team asked whether doctors running trials and pharmacists share a clear view of the task. They interviewed trial investigators and surveyed hospital and community pharmacists. The study also checked how drug details reach outside pharmacies.

Investigators mostly judged current monitoring good enough. Still, they asked for clearer duties and more digital tools. Pharmacies reported gaps in what they learn about study drugs. The authors argue sharper role lines would make trials safer. Better data flow is a second clear need.
pmc-13603337:
Shihao Xuan and ten co-authors study drug-resistant bacteria in farmed mink in China's Shandong Province. The germ Proteus mirabilis can cause illness and can hoard resistance genes on farms. The team sampled 373 mink on six farms and recovered sixty-eight isolates of the germ. Nearly all resisted several drugs, and more than half made an enzyme that defeats key antibiotics.

The team read the full genomes of those enzyme makers. Most carried a known resistance gene family; three carried one of the most feared. The isolates all formed strong biofilms. The paper warns that mink farms can act as stores of resistance that may reach people.
pmc-13604737:
Wei Gu and four co-authors hunt for allergy genes whose effects switch on only in particular states of CD4 T cells. Allergic rhinitis is common but genetically messy. Using expression data across forty-six T cell activation profiles, they ran transcriptome-wide Mendelian randomization against rhinitis genome-wide results.

Over fifty thousand gene-profile pairs were tested after removing the MHC region. One hundred twenty-nine genes passed the first screen; colocalization and further statistical filters narrowed the field, and cross-database comparison left a nine-gene overlap set. Single-cell and receptor analyses in a small patient set added context, though the authors label those findings hypothesis-generating. Metabolite screening rounded out the search for drug targets.
pmc-13605937: Ekkehart Paditz and Silke Anna Theresa Weber edited a volume in 2026 on child sleep medicine. It gathers articles on sleep in infancy, childhood, and adolescence. The editors note that no single shared understanding spans the whole field yet. Contributors bring varied current perspectives and findings. The volume opens a series on advances in the specialty. It serves clinicians and researchers who work with young patients and their sleep problems.
pmc-13607037:
Jae Min Lee and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six retrospective study on removing bile drainage catheters earlier. Patients with acute bile duct inflammation often get a drain through the liver. No guideline says when that catheter should come out.

Records covered hundreds of patients at one center. One group had removal within about a week to ten days, another later. Complication rates after removal were low and nearly equal in both groups. Leaks forming fluid pockets were the most common issue in each. The findings support earlier removal once blockage clears.
pmc-13608337:
Zhongshuai Hu and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six study of water-based epoxy coatings protecting steel reinforcement in harsh construction settings. Salt water, freeze-thaw cycles, and seawater eat unprotected rebar inside concrete. Greener water-based coatings promise a strong defence without solvent pollution.

Four coating recipes added graphene compounds, iron oxide, or zinc-based pigments to ribbed steel bars. Bars endured marine soaking, wet-dry cycling, de-icing salt freezing, baking in saline soil, and seawater-mixed concrete. Electrochemical monitoring tracked corrosion currents, all far below bare steel. A statistical model then predicted service life, supporting coated rebar for durable coastal infrastructure.
pmc-13611637: Piotr Rzymski's notice corrects reference errors in his published review of side benefits of seasonal flu vaccination. The notice is a correction only. It fixes mismatched citations in the sections on trained immunity and on future research directions. The notice supplies the proper numbers and the full details of the studies that should have been cited. Two papers on flu vaccination and responses to COVID-19 vaccination now appear as references 124 and 125. Nothing in the review's arguments or conclusions changes.
pmc-13612137:
Cihan Şin leads a ten-author team testing a scanning trick for bladder cancer in 2026. The tracer used in FDG PET scans drains into the bladder and can hide tumors in its wall. The team gave patients the diuretic furosemide and imaged twice to flush the view. Their question was practical: can the scan tell whether cancer has invaded the bladder muscle, the fact that decides between bladder-sparing treatment and major surgery? The cohort held 105 patients.

Distant spread turned up in 30 patients, changing their management. Among 75 patients who went on to surgical sampling, the scan separated malignant from benign lesions with 78.0 percent sensitivity. In the 59 confirmed cancers, every measured quantity ran higher in muscle-invasive T2 tumors than in shallower ones. Volume and glycolysis measures discriminated best: area-under-curve 0.814 for the first and 0.830 for the second. The authors propose these numbers as stand-in markers for preoperative staging.
pmc-13615737:
Andrew Doerrler and colleagues read uranium in ancient Siberian rocks to test what killed Earth's first big life forms, in this study from twenty twenty-six. The Ediacara biota, soft and strange, vanished as the Cambrian age began, alongside a sharp swing in the carbon record. Two rival stories blame the oceans: a spread of oxygen-free water, or a flood of oxygen.

Uranium isotopes in sea-floor carbonates record how much of the ocean lacked oxygen. The Siberian values stayed low before, during, and after the carbon swing, the signature of widespread oxygen poverty throughout. Neither story fits: oxygen levels did not lurch either way at the boundary. The authors instead blame falling seas and harsh, salty shallows, which would strand and dry the mostly motionless biota. Cambrian animals then radiated in seas that stayed short of oxygen for ages after.
pmc-13616537:
Fulvio Cacciapuoti and six colleagues report a seventy-six-year-old man whose heart scan pointed confidently to the wrong kind of amyloidosis. He had heart failure, kidney disease, and a heart-rhythm disorder, and testing showed a monoclonal protein in his blood. His bone scan showed the strongest grade of tracer uptake, a pattern textbook-linked to transthyretin amyloidosis.

A heart muscle biopsy overturned the picture: the amyloid was the light-chain type, which needs entirely different, urgent treatment. That therapy began, but he died of severe pneumonia. The authors stress that when a monoclonal gammopathy is present, even top-grade scan uptake cannot settle the type, and tissue confirmation remains essential.
pmc-13617237:
Liang Fang and four colleagues present a new way to combine signals from the many receiver coils used in magnetic resonance spectroscopy, a scan type that measures brain chemistry without surgery. The best existing method needs clean noise samples from the tail of each signal, which real scans often lack. Their method, called AOC-JD, instead extracts noise information from the differences between repeated scans and their average.

The technique rests on joint diagonalization, a mathematical step that untangles two correlation patterns at once. Computer simulations and scans of living human brains tested it against older approaches. When noise tails were missing or too short, the new method lifted signal quality well above the standard singular value method and matched the original optimized method where that method could run. The authors offer it as a reliable option for multichannel spectroscopy data that defeat the older routine.
pmc-13619637:
Ezequiel Córdova and colleagues report month eleven and twelve results from the VOLITION study, a 2026 phase 3b trial for people starting HIV treatment. Participants first took a daily two-drug pill combining dolutegravir and lamivudine for up to sixteen weeks. Once the virus was suppressed, each person could choose to switch to long-acting injections of cabotegravir plus rilpivirine every two months, or stay on pills.

Among 171 starters, nearly everyone reached viral suppression, with a median time of about four weeks. Most eligible participants chose the injections, and most of those kept the virus suppressed at month eleven. One person had confirmed treatment failure with drug resistance. Both regimens were well tolerated, and satisfaction rose after the choice point. The authors argue that offering an early switch respects personal needs without losing control of the virus.
pmc-13620337:
Navid Mirmohammadsadegh and Mohsen Amin review a strategy for helping cancer immunotherapy work in solid tumors: sending in enzymes to chew through the tumor's defenses. Solid tumors wrap themselves in a dense matrix plus a sugary cell coating that blocks immune cells and drugs while broadcasting suppressive signals. The review calls barrier-cutting enzymes path cleansers.

Enzyme families are sorted by what they cut, whether matrix fibers or the sugar coat, and some do extra work by tweaking signals or attacking tumors directly. Delivery tricks aim the enzymes at tumors to limit harm elsewhere, and engineering can soften the immune reaction against the enzymes themselves. Risks and weak evidence spots get honest treatment. The authors suggest better patient selection and computer-guided enzyme discovery could move the idea from promising papers toward real clinical use.
pmc-13620837:
Saeid Sedghi, Zahra Keshtmand, and Saba Hosseini tested friendly bacteria and their leftovers as protection against infection damage in male rats. E. coli infections of the urinary and genital tract can injure kidneys, wreck sperm production, and cut fertility. Twenty-eight rats were split into four groups: healthy controls, infected animals, and two infected groups fed a three-strain Lactobacillus mix either alive, as probiotics, or as inactivated postbiotic material.

Infection scarred kidney and testis tissue, raised inflammation and cell-death gene activity, weakened antioxidant defenses, and degraded sperm count and shape. Both supplements blunted each of those harms and partly restored tissue structure. Sperm viability and shape improved alongside. The authors argue such mixtures could become add-on therapy for infection-linked male infertility and kidney damage, though rat results still need a long bridge to patients.
pmc-13621437:
Hao Fan led a large team showing that a natural fat in breast milk trains a newborn's immune system, in a 2026 study. Trans-vaccenic acid is the main natural trans fat in human milk and comes only from the mother's diet, since the body cannot make it. Mouse mothers fed extra amounts of it nursed pups whose immune development the team then tracked.

The pups carried more fresh, untrained CD4 T cells, the helper cells that coordinate immune attacks, and they fought infections better. The fat rewired those cells through a receptor and a DNA-organizing protein, tilting them toward the virus-fighting type with help from a key transcription factor. Pups exposed early through nursing kept stronger antiviral defenses as adults. The authors present one milk molecule as proof that maternal diet can imprint immunity for the long term.
pmc-13623437:
Giovanna Petrucci and colleagues published a 2026 study asking whether melanoma, the most dangerous skin cancer, switches on platelet activity in the body. Activated platelets release thromboxane, a chemical that helps tumours grow in several gut cancers. The team measured a urine breakdown product of thromboxane as a stand-in for platelet activity, and a second marker for another inflammatory chemical.

The study compared thirty patients with stage one to three melanoma, twenty-four with basal cell carcinoma, a milder skin cancer, and thirty-eight healthy volunteers matched by age and sex. The thromboxane marker ran higher in melanoma patients than in either other group, while the basal cell group looked like healthy controls. Six stage four melanoma patients showed the highest levels of all. The second marker did not differ between groups. The authors propose the urine test as a warning sign for melanoma worsening, worth testing further.
pmc-13626837:
Miki Kamiyama leads a large team writing to the editor about a blood vessel receptor that sheds its outer half during inflammation. Tie1 helps govern how vessel lining cells answer both growth signals and inflammatory ones, and its outer domain is clipped off and spilled into the blood when inflammation strikes. The team pinpointed the clipping site and bred mice whose Tie1 cannot be cut, then checked vessel growth and inflammatory responses side by side.

The uncuttable mice were born normal, in expected numbers, and their retinal vessels grew without obvious fault, showing that new vessel growth does not need the clip. Inflammatory stimulation told a different story, with responses governed by whether shedding could occur. One receptor thus runs two programs, and a single cut decides which one answers.
pmc-13628137:
Kasandra Bélanger and nine colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that a llama immunised with an mRNA vaccine package can yield useful nanobodies quickly. Nanobodies are the small single-domain antibody fragments found in camel family animals, valued for their stability and their ability to reach tight spots on target proteins.

The llama received lipid nanoparticle shots carrying mRNA for the coronavirus spike protein. The team then built an immune library from its blood and fished for binders using living cells displaying the spike, which keeps the protein in its natural shape. The search returned several strong spike binders, including two clones that blocked the spike from engaging its human cell receptor, proof that the route can deliver functional candidates fast.
pmc-13628637:
Chris D. Phillips and five colleagues characterised what vagus nerve stimulation does to the heart and breathing of mice. The treatment is approved for epilepsy, depression, and stroke recovery, yet most physiology comes from rats and larger animals, while mice offer unmatched genetic tools for digging into mechanisms.

In anaesthetised mice, stimulation of either the left or right vagus nerve reliably slowed heart rate and breathing rate in most animals, with no sex differences. Cutting the nerve's outgoing fibres erased the heart effect, showing direct downward control, while the breathing effect vanished after cuts on either side, pointing to brain feedback circuits. The authors offer the setup as a simple way to verify that stimulation cuffs work in mouse studies.
pmc-13628837:
Shih-Han Kao and sixteen colleagues explored whether DNA fragments floating in blood can reveal the type and severity of a traumatic brain injury. Published in 2026, their work uses pigs, because brain scans, the current gold standard, often miss subtle injuries. Injured brain cells release cell-free DNA whose chemical methylation marks identify the tissue it came from.

The team produced four injury patterns in swine, mild and moderate, by impact and by rotation, then sequenced the blood DNA. Each pattern carried a distinct brain-linked methylation signature, and brain spectroscopy measurements independently confirmed changes in the matching regions. A targeted test tracked injury progression over time. The authors present the approach as a candidate non-invasive biomarker, pending wider validation.
pmc-13629137:
Joévin Burnel and colleagues report a measurement study, published in 2026, building a clinical test battery for hip function and testing how reliable its scores are. Ninety-four healthy recreational adults completed hip motion, strength, and hopping tests, with a smaller group retested a week later, to produce reference values for judging injured patients against.

Motion and hopping tests proved highly reliable, while strength tests were reliable but noisy at the individual level. The popular Limb Symmetry Index, which compares the two legs as a ratio, was unreliable, needing roughly a quarter change before any difference could be trusted. The authors advise judging absolute values against their own error margins and reference ranges instead.
pmc-13629237:
Harris and colleagues show that gains passed from parent worms to their offspring can become costs two generations later, in 2026 evolutionary biology research using the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. The team starved worm larvae, then tracked fitness in their children and great-grandchildren under both starvation and plentiful food. Theory predicted that intergenerational effects, felt by children, might trade off against transgenerational effects, felt by later descendants, and the experiment tests that prediction directly.

Starved worms themselves lost marked fitness, yet their direct offspring gained fitness in both food settings tested. Great-grand offspring then paid fitness costs, reversing the children's advantage. Computer simulations of competing genotypes showed the short-term strategy still wins: lines exploiting the children's boost outcompete rivals despite the deferred debt. Harris argues adaptive effects across generations cannot be assumed helpful overall, since a gain for children may be intrinsically linked to harm for great-grandchildren.
pmc-13629537:
Robert Englander and thirteen colleagues collect the hard lessons from twenty years of competency-based training. They write for a global team of educators in this field. Such training judges learners by what graduates can clearly do. This paper examines what breaks once the new systems go live.

The problems are sorted around the model's five core parts. They run from setting outcome skills to whole-programme judging. A working fix is offered for each recurring problem. Examples show how programmes adjusted order, pacing, and judging when real cohorts met the theory. The authors distil the experience into lessons learned. The lessons aim at educators designing such systems. They also aim at those rescuing systems in their own schools.
pmc-13630437:
Verónica Sánchez Escudero and five colleagues measured insulin and insulin resistance in fifty prepubertal children with isolated premature pubarche, the early appearance of pubic hair without other puberty signs. Published in 2026, the Spanish study compared the children with age- and sex-matched reference values and probed whether body fat explained any differences.

Normal-weight children with the condition matched the population average on both measures. Children carrying excess fat, by contrast, showed clearly raised insulin and resistance scores. Higher values also appeared in children who had been formula-fed and in those with advanced bone age, although both links ran through adiposity. The authors conclude that fatness, not the early hair itself, drives the metabolic signal.
pmc-13633337:
Koji Furukawa and five colleagues published this 2026 review of a heart valve flaw tied to dangerous rhythms. In mitral annular disjunction, the ring that anchors the mitral valve partly separates from the heart muscle. The flaw often travels with Barlow's disease, a degenerative valve condition. Patients can suffer rhythm disturbances or sudden death even after a repair that fixes the leak. The authors searched twenty-five years of literature and built their synthesis on forty-one chosen papers.

Wide separation, scarring seen on scans, and fainting episodes mark the higher-risk patients in the studies they reviewed. Repair can erase the separation itself, yet scarred tissue beneath may persist and keep firing abnormal rhythms. The authors propose a framework that combines structure, electrical signs, imaging, and symptoms to sort risk before and after surgery. They stress the framework is a hypothesis needing prospective testing, not a proven guide.
pmc-13639537:
Hoang Le Huy Nguyen presents a 2026 analysis comparing simple health indices for predicting death in older adults who already have cardiovascular disease. The indices came from three families: nutrition scores, an inflammation score, and a waist-based body measure.

The analysis used survey data from 1,804 Americans aged sixty and over, collected between 2009 and 2018 and linked to death records. Two nutrition scores tracked cardiovascular death most steadily, while the inflammation signal faded once early deaths were excluded. The waist measure predicted overall death only. The author calls the findings a starting point needing outside confirmation.
pmc-13643137:
Lili M Kim and six colleagues present a genome-wide phenotype screen of Bacillus subtilis, the model bacterium for the firmicute group that includes many pathogens and helpful gut species. More than a quarter of its genes remain uncharacterized despite decades of study.

Their compact CRISPR interference library can dial down every protein-coding gene, and the pooled library was grown in about 150 stress conditions. Mining the results revealed an essential gene working in protein secretion, two unknown genes guarding the cell wall, and rules behind amino acid sharing between cells. The authors release the dataset as a hypothesis engine for firmicute biology.
pmc-13643637:
Yoshitaka Tateishi and three colleagues present a 2026 review of a germ strain that may help labs study a slow lung disease. The strain is a type of Mycobacterium taken from a patient whose lung disease grew worse until surgery was needed.

In mice, this strain causes disease that keeps growing. Germ counts rise, tissue swells, and high doses can kill. That makes it useful for testing new drugs in live animals. The strain also resists a key drug and can be changed in the lab, which is rare in its group. The review weighs this strain against others now used in mouse work.
pmc-13645937:
Naoya Fujita and seven colleagues present a 2026 case of a fifty-five-year-old man whose failing pancreas caused body-wide swelling that first looked like heart or kidney trouble. He had earlier lost part of his stomach to surgery. On arrival he had gained sixteen kilograms, struggled to breathe, and passed frequent pale watery stools. Blood tests showed very low protein and pancreatic enzyme levels, and scans showed a shrunken pancreas with fluid in the chest and abdomen.

Stool and urine tests confirmed the pancreas was not releasing digestive enzymes, a failure called exocrine insufficiency. Raised IgG4 levels and older imaging pointed to an immune-related pancreatic disease as the likely root, with the stomach surgery adding strain. Protein infusions, water pills, and enzyme capsules brought rapid improvement. The authors warn doctors not to miss this treatable cause when swelling and low protein appear together after stomach surgery.
pmc-13646137:
Juliane Wagner and seven colleagues sort 700 patients hospitalized for bleeding in the mouth after dental surgery into hidden groups based on their mix of illnesses. Records came from one center covering 2011 to 2021. Most patients were older, and more than four fifths were taking blood-thinning medicine. A statistical grouping method was applied to patients carrying at least two conditions, using eleven illness markers.

Five groups emerged, from a small group marked by vein clots and heart disease to a large group with broad multi-system illness. Blood thinner type differed by group: older vitamin K blockers clustered in the clot and valve groups, while newer direct drugs peaked in the hypertension and heart disease group. Repeat testing found the grouping moderately stable. The authors say the groups show how varied these bleeding patients are, which may help hospitals plan care for each pattern.
pmc-13647137:
Marko Rajkovic and nine colleagues use brain scanning to compare a core memory skill, telling very similar experiences apart, across sight and hearing. This skill, called pattern separation, is usually tied to a small hippocampal region named the dentate gyrus. Forty-six volunteers aged nineteen to seventy-nine completed alternating visual and sound versions of a similarity task inside the scanner. Meaningless shapes and made-up two-syllable words served as material.

Vision behaved as expected, yet hearing told a different story: no hippocampal activation appeared during the sound task. Instead, language and control areas on the left side of the brain carried the work. Older participants discriminated worse on behavior tests, though brain signals did not mirror the deficit cleanly. The authors read the split as a double dissociation between the senses. They also caution that aging blood vessels and fading senses complicate brain scan reading across the lifespan.
pmc-13648037:
Weiyue Jin and four colleagues investigate how microalgae respond when excess ammonium, a nitrogen source, becomes toxic and limits growth. Comparing gene activity across two algae and rice, they look for response pathways shared between microalgae and higher plants.

The photosynthesis antenna protein pathway appeared in all three species, and major LHCII antenna genes were consistently turned down under ammonium stress. When the team overexpressed one such gene in both algae, growth traits improved, though the gains differed by species, involving cell density, fresh weight, and chlorophyll. The results point to a conserved photosynthetic role in ammonium tolerance, with downstream effects that vary between species.
pmc-13648137:
Hayley Barnes led a 2026 small study testing prednisolone for Australian cases of artificial-stone silicosis with progressive massive fibrosis, a severe lung disease with no drug treatment short of transplant. Silicosis cases have resurged with engineered stone benchtops, and inflammation drives the scarring. The team gave seven adults three months of prednisolone in a pre-post design, measuring PET scan activity, lung function, and symptoms at three and twelve months.

Baseline scans showed high tracer uptake in fibrotic areas in every participant. After three months, peak uptake fell significantly, from an average of 6.7 to 4.2, and the share of lung above a high-uptake threshold also fell significantly. Lung function and symptom scores did not change significantly, and no serious adverse events occurred. Clinicians get early evidence that short-term steroids cool inflammation in this disease, with larger trials needed to find the best immune strategy and long-term effects.
pmc-13649137:
Rosita Asawa and ten colleagues chart which proteins of the malaria parasite Plasmodium vivax the human immune system actually recognises, using a peptide array covering the parasite's entire protein catalogue. Vivax malaria threatens billions, yet few vaccine candidates or field diagnostics exist because its immunogenic proteins were barely mapped.

The array held millions of peptides, probed with blood from infected and never-exposed people. The team found 283 proteins commonly recognised by symptomatic patients, including invasion proteins, pore proteins, and many uncharacterised ones. Asymptomatic people showed a distinctive response pattern against one protein family that might mark protection. The dataset is offered as a resource for detection tools and vaccine design.
pmc-13649437:
Chenrong Cai and Yang Wang asked if a slim body mass score can hide a real risk of type 2 diabetes in Japanese adults. They reused data from a large health check cohort and split 12,940 adults with a score under the obesity line into four groups by belly fat and fatty liver.

Over the follow-up years, 201 people developed diabetes. Rates were by far the highest in those with both belly fat and fatty liver, at more than ten times the rate of those with neither. Fatty liver alone also raised risk a lot, while belly fat alone did not reach a firm link. Adding these traits to a standard risk model did not sharpen its forecasts, though. The authors say body mass alone misses key risk.
pmc-13650137:
Zhe Yu and twelve colleagues, publishing in 2026, work on making a nutrient-rich diploid potato usable as feed in place of wheat. The potato carries generous vitamin C and protective plant compounds, but it also holds anti-nutritional factors, mainly solanine and trypsin inhibitors, that can harm the gut.

In zebrafish, those factors disturbed gut microbes and triggered oxidative stress and inflammation, which quieted a growth-signaling pathway and slowed growth. The team paired genetic selection of the potato line with steam cooking. Heat brought the harmful compounds down to safe levels while the cooked potato kept more of its vitamin C and yellow pigments than ordinary potatoes or wheat diets. Fish on the processed feed showed calmer inflammation, restored growth signaling, and better growth and digestion. The authors frame the pairing of breeding and processing as a template for other high-value crops.
pmc-13650537:
Don R Bergfelt reviews ovarian stimulation strategies that free fertility treatment from the calendar, drawing lessons from cattle and horses. In women, recognizing that egg-bearing follicles emerge in waves across the cycle made it possible to start stimulation at any point. Clinicians can even run two stimulations in one cycle for patients with little time to spare.

Yet response varies even within the same cycle phase, because the starting wave stage, the presence of a dominant follicle, and the maturity of the leftover hormone-producing structure all differ.
